body:
* * *

#### Catching Jev-er: Teaching a multi-agent system to triage messy questions.

The artificial intelligence industry has spent the past few years racing to build increasingly intelligent large language models (LLMs).

LLMs got bigger, got better at reasoning and now accept longer context windows.

Then, on [15 September 2026](https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev), something rather different arrived.

Meet Jev, the world’s first commercially released “System One” model.

And here’s the interesting part: **Jev doesn’t generate text. It makes decisions.**

Unlike a conventional generative LLM, Jev doesn’t produce free-form text. Instead, you give it a set of possible answers, and it evaluates them, returning confidence scores for the available options.

Think multiple-choice questions rather than essay writing.

### Why the hype?

According to benchmarks published by TypeSafe AI, Jev delivers competitive classification accuracy at a fraction of the cost of state-of-the-art LLMs:

In addition, as we’ll soon see, Jev is absurdly fast.

The implication is that you might not always need to use a LLM for classification and tool calling. Jev would be able to do it too.

### End of story?

Not quite. There’s always a caveat.

Though Jev’s model architecture is unknown, it is the first model to be classified as a “Systems One” model. This borrows from the definition of “Systems One” first coined by Daniel Kahneman in his book “[Thinking, Fast and Slow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thinking,_Fast_and_Slow)”, which is now the cornerstone of behavioral economics.

The theory is this: systems one is our fast, automatic, intuitive state of decision-making.

As an example, imagine if your colleague sitting next to you at work got surprised by other colleagues with a “happy birthday” song. You might react by singing along without thinking. That’s a system one response.

System Two, on the other hand, describes slower, more deliberate thinking. It’s what happens when we consciously work through a difficult problem, such as solving a quadratic equation.

Of course, the two systems aren’t completely independent. Our intuition frequently informs our deliberate reasoning, and deliberate reasoning can override our intuition.

But the distinction is useful: **System One reacts. System Two reasons.**

This distinction is important when building AI agents.

Jev might be excellent at deciding which tool should handle a request. But deciding which tool to call is not the same as reasoning through the problem, executing a multistep workflow, and synthesizing the results.

In other words, **Jev might make an excellent bouncer. That doesn’t mean it should run the entire nightclub.**

#### Important Fineprint

Jev 1.13 (the latest model) is said to have a [context window of 64k tokens](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/community/jev) — far less than the 1 million token context window of state-of-the-art LLMs.

[TypeSafe AI is pushing the envelope though](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/community/jev). Jev 1.14 (in preview) is said to have a long-context mode which takes up to 262k tokens. TypeSafe AI caveats that Jev is less accurate and slower in this mode — so don’t go stuffing entire documents or chat histories at it.

Since the launch of Jev, many [open-sourced “System One” models](https://huggingface.co/openjev/openjev) have been released — most involve [finetuning a smaller LLM like Qwen 3.5:9bn](https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev) to do classification. Not all of these models are trained via the [reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions (RLCD)](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.38850v1) regime like Jev though.

Other closed-sourced systems one models like [Liquid AI’s d1 model](https://www.liquid.ai/blog/d1-decision-model) have also since been released.

What we’re witnessing might be the beginning of a second AI race: not to build models that can reason about everything, but to build models that can make narrow, reliable decisions extraordinarily quickly.

### How should you use Jev then?

TypeSafe AI provides many [cookbooks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks#cookbooks) demonstrating how Jev can perform tasks traditionally handled by specialized models. For example, Jev can be used to rerank retrieved text chunks — a task typically assigned to a dedicated reranker.

[LangChain published an integration package with TypeSafe AI](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/integrations/providers/typesafe#model-routing) that ships with two default middlewares — `ModelRoutingMiddleware` and `AutoModeMiddleware` that aim to use Jev in different settings:

The spirit of these recipes is this: Jev can be used at decision-making points that would otherwise require an LLM. But just because Jev can make a decision doesn’t necessarily mean it should. The trick is identifying decisions that don’t require extensive reasoning, and determining whether Jev can make them reliably.

At the time of writing, I haven’t read any of these cookbooks. Instead, I wanted to approach Jev from first principles and figure out where it might fit into my own multi-agent systems.

What follows is my own experiment, rather than an adaptation of an existing recipe. I hope you find it useful!

I’ll walk through the architecture, implementation, and experiments below. You can also find the complete code in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/Jever/tree/main).

### The idea

One of the challenges of building agentic applications is that you never quite know what questions your users will throw at your agents.

User questions might be abstract, multipart, direct, or simply badly written. Depending on the question, an agent might benefit from asking for clarification, decomposing the request into smaller questions, or rewriting it into something more precise.

More commonly, however, we simply rely on the raw intelligence of the LLM to figure everything out, including which tools and skills to invoke.

**Let’s change that.**

In my experiment, I’ll create a hierarchical multi-agent system with a supervisor agent, a forex exchange agent and a web search agent; and use Jev to be the bouncer at the door.

#### The tools

There are two tools.

My forex exchange agent uses a forex tool around Frankfurter’s generous public forex API:

```python
import requests
from langchain.tools import tool

@tool
def get_forex_exchange_rate(base_currency: str, target_currencies: list[str]) -> dict[str, float]:
    """
    Get the current forex exchange rate between two currencies.

    Args:
        base_currency (str): The base currency code (e.g., "USD").
        target_currencies (list[str]): A list of target currency codes (e.g., ["EUR", "GBP"]).

    Returns:
        dict[str, float]: A dictionary mapping each target currency to its exchange rate.
    """
    res = requests.get(
        "https://api.frankfurter.dev/v2/rates",
        params={"base": base_currency, "quotes": ",".join(target_currencies)},
        timeout=10,
    )
    rates = {row["quote"]: row["rate"] for row in res.json()}
    return rates
```

My web search tool leverages [Tavily’s](https://www.tavily.com/pricing) generous free tier:

```python
from langchain_tavily import TavilySearch

tavily_tool = TavilySearch(
    max_results=5,
    topic="general",
    include_answer=False,
    search_depth="basic",
)
```

### Jev as the bouncer

I want Jev to intercept every user query before my supervisor agent sees it, and determine whether the query needs further work. If so, perform the query enrichment so that we can maximize the mileage (and hopefully save tokens) of our multi-agent system.

LangChain’s `before_agent` agent middleware hook is the perfect place to implement this, and can be used either as a function or within a class that subclasses `AgentMiddleware` .

Let’s start by defining the middleware’s constructor and the middleware hook method:

```python
class QueryEnrichmentMiddleware(AgentMiddleware):    
    def __init__(self, llm, classifier = None, threshold: float = 0.80):
        super().__init__()
        self.llm = llm
        self.classifier = classifier or TypeSafeClassifier()
        self.threshold = threshold
        self.handlers = {
            "decomposable": self.decompose_query,
            "enrichable": self.enrich_query,
            "needs_clarification": self.clarify_query,
        }

    def before_agent(self, state: AgentState, runtime: Runtime) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
        messages = state["messages"]
        if not messages or not isinstance(messages[-1], HumanMessage):
            return None
        query = messages[-1].text

        next_action = self.query_classify(query).choices["next_action"]
        handler = self.handlers.get(next_action.choice)
        if next_action.confidence < self.threshold or handler is None:
            return None
        return {
            "messages": [
                HumanMessage(
                    content=handler(query), 
                    id = messages[-1].id
                )
            ]
        }
```

We want to extract the last human message, classify it, handle it, and then send it to the supervisor agent. Importantly, `before_agent`must return either a dictionary object or `None`in or LangChain will return an error.

With that in mind, it’s time to write our handlers:

```python
def enrich_query(self, query: str) -> str:
    """Helper function to enrich user queries"""
    return self.llm.invoke(
       "Rewrite the following user query for clarity. "
       "Preserve the original meaning and all explicit constraints. "
       "Do not invent missing details or answer the question. "
       "Return only the rewritten query.\n\n"
       f"User query: {query}"
    ).content
    
def decompose_query(self, query: str) -> str:
     """Helper function to decompose user queries"""
     sub_queries = self.llm.invoke(
        f"The user's query is: {query}. "
        "Your role is to decompose this query into sub-queries that can be answered separately. "
      )
     return (
         f"Original user query: {query}\n\n"
         f"Suggested sub-questions:\n{sub_queries.content}\n\n"
         "Use these sub-questions to guide your analysis. "
         "Combine related operations where appropriate, "
         "and synthesize the results into a single response."
     )

def clarify_query(self, query: str) -> str:
    """Helper function to inject prompt to clarify user queries"""
    return (
         f"Original user query: {query}\n\n"
         "The request may be ambiguous or missing essential information. "
         "Ask the user one concise clarification question before proceeding. "
         "Do not assume missing details."
    )
```

-   `enrich_query` uses an LLM to replace the original query by rewriting it to be clearer and more specific
-   `decompose_query` uses an LLM to decompose the original query into sub questions, then appends these sub questions on top of the original query
-   `clarifiy_query` nudges the LLM to seek user clarification — wrapping the original user query.

#### Now for the query classification method

This is where Jev comes in.

LangChain’s TypeSafe AI integration docs are extremely instructive. In essence, Jev has 3 primary primitives:

Of these, `Noul` is the only primitive that does not return a confidence score (remember that machine learning class?).

`Choice` is the equivalent of a normal classification task, and `Score` is a subset of `Choice` , used for questions where the answer is a position on a spectrum — for example, on a scale of 1–5, how much does it hurt when your agent hallucinates.

For our bouncer, we’re interested in choosing between several possible actions: rewrite, decompose, clarify, or leave the query alone. That makes `Choice` a natural fit.

The code:

```python
def query_classify(self, query: str) -> ClassifierResponse:
    """Helper function to classify user queries using Jev"""
    return self.classifier.invoke(
        {
            "state": query,
            "questions": {
                "next_action": Choice(
                    instructions = "Should this query be decomposed into multiple sub-queries?",
                    criteria = {
                        "decomposable": "Does the query have multiple distinct sub-queries that can be answered separately?",
                        "direct": "Is the query a single, direct question that can be answered without additional context or information?",
                        "enrichable": "Should the query be re-written to be clearer so that it can be answered more effectively?",
                        "needs_clarification": "Does the query require additional context or clarification before it can be answered?",
                    }
                )
            }
        }
    )
```

#### Taking it out for a spin

Let’s see Jev classify something using our middleware:

```python
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-6-luna")
decomposable_query = (
    "What is the current exchange rate between USD and EUR, "
    "and can you also provide the latest news on the European Central Bank's "
    "monetary policy?"
)

query_middleware = QueryEnrichmentMiddleware(llm=llm)
response = query_middleware.query_classify(query=decomposable_query)
print(
  response.choices["next_action"].choice, 
  response.choices["next_action"].confidence
)

# decomposable 1.0
```

Jev classified the query as `decomposable` with a confidence score of `1.0`. Given that the request contains two distinct questions, that's hardly surprising.

### Assembling the multi-agent system

Let’s first start by wrapping our sub agents and their tools in LangChain’s `SubAgentMiddleware` :

```python
from deepagents.backends import StateBackend
from deepagents.middleware import SubAgentMiddleware

subagent_middleware = SubAgentMiddleware(
    backend=StateBackend(),
    subagents = [
        {
            "name": "Forex_Expert",
            "description": "An expert in forex exchange rates and currency markets.",
            "tools": [get_forex_exchange_rate],
            "model": llm,
        },
        {
            "name": "Web_search",
            "description": "An expert in searching the web for information.",
            "tools": [tavily_tool],
            "model": llm,
        },
    ]
)
```

The `SubAgentMiddleware` class wraps every subagent as a `task` tool for the supervisor agent — so we don’t have to define any further tools.

> Notice the `backend` parameter. It deserves an article of its own, so I'll leave that discussion for another time. For this demonstration, `StateBackend` keeps things simple.

Next, let’s instantiate the checkpointer and create the supervisor agent:

```python
conn = sqlite3.connect("jever.db", check_same_thread=False)
checkpointer = SqliteSaver(conn)

agent = create_agent(
    model = llm,
    tools = [], # LOOK NO TOOLS!
    middleware = [query_middleware, subagent_middleware],
    checkpointer=checkpointer,
)
```

Running the agent against the same query, we get:

```python
response = agent.invoke(
    {"messages": [ HumanMessage(content=decomposable_query),]},
    {"configurable": {"thread_id": "thread-4",}}
)

# Truncated response
### USD to EUR: The latest rate lookup returned US$1 ≈ €0.8920. 
### ...
### ECB monetary policy: As of 15 October 2026, the latest rate decision I 
### could verify was on 10 September. The ECB raised its key rates by 0.25 
### percentage point, ....
```

### It’s what our traces tell us that’s interesting

The first trace shows the expected execution pattern. Jev classified the request as decomposable, our middleware generated the sub-questions, and the supervisor subsequently invoked both specialist agents in parallel before synthesizing their responses.

Importantly, Jev didn’t select the specialist agents. That decision remained with the supervisor.

In one run, my supervisor agent actually got one of its subagents to do a web search to verify the findings of a previous subagent run:

That’s an example of adaptive orchestration.

Rather than executing a predetermined sequence of steps, the supervisor made a subsequent decision based on the information available.

To me this proves that it is quite dangerous to simply replace the supervisor agent with Jev, because:

-   Jev is unable to synthesize a final response from subagent replies,
-   Jev can classify predefined next actions, but it doesn’t offer the same open-ended reasoning and generation capabilities as a conventional LLM supervisor.

Jev did an amazing job as a bouncer though.

#### How did the Jev-ed agents do for other question types?

I then ran the multi-agent system across 3 more query types:

```python
direct_query = "What is the current exchange rate between USD and EUR?"
enrichable_query = "Usain Bolt fast how training he?"
needs_clarification_query = "fasdlkfaleuraoi34"

tests = [direct_query, enrichable_query, needs_clarification_query]
answers = []
for i, test in enumerate(tests):
    response = agent.invoke(
        {"messages": [ HumanMessage(content=test),]},
        {"configurable": {"thread_id": f"thread_{i}",}}
    )
    answers.append(response['messages'][-1].content[-1]['text'])
```

And the Jev-ed agent did well for them:

```python-repl
The latest rate available to me is 1 USD ≈ 0.8916 EUR. 
---
Bolt trained for explosive speed, not long-distance running....
---
What would you like me to do with “fasdlkfaleuraoi34”?
```

An important point is the `enrichable_query` question:

Jev classified the deliberately poorly written question as `enrichable`, as expected. However, its confidence score fell below our threshold of 0.80. Consequently, the middleware left the original query untouched and allowed the supervisor to handle it directly.

#### How did the baseline do?

Here’s the code I used to run the baseline:

```python
baseline_agent = create_agent(
    model = llm,
    tools = [], # LOOK NO TOOLS!
    middleware = [subagent_middleware],
    checkpointer=checkpointer,
)

baseline_tests = [decomposable_query, direct_query, enrichable_query, needs_clarification_query]
baseline_answers = []
for i, test in enumerate(baseline_tests):
    response = baseline_agent.invoke(
        {"messages": [ HumanMessage(content=test),]},
        {"configurable": {"thread_id": f"baseline_thread_{i}",}}
    )
    baseline_answers.append(response['messages'][-1].content[-1]['text'])
```

Their metrics on LangSmith were pretty interesting:

Now here’s where things get interesting.

For our multipart question (rows 4 and 8), the baseline agent took **2 minutes and 21 seconds** to complete its response.

With Jev-powered query enrichment, the same task took just **11.69 seconds**.

That’s approximately a **12× reduction in execution time**, despite the additional classification and query decomposition steps.

I repeated the baseline experiment several times, and the results remained substantially slower. Even my fastest baseline run took approximately 1.5 minutes.

So what happened?

My hypothesis is that the decomposed query helped the supervisor understand how to distribute the work across its specialist agents, avoiding unnecessary deliberation or repeated tool invocations.

However, there’s an important caveat: Jev didn’t perform the decomposition itself. It classified the query as requiring decomposition, after which another LLM generated the sub-questions.

Consequently, this experiment doesn’t isolate how much of the improvement came from Jev versus the decomposition step.

> What it does demonstrate is that **conditionally preprocessing a complex query can substantially change how an agent executes it**.

Interestingly, the differences for the other question types were relatively small.

My suspicion is that GPT-6-Luna was already capable of handling those simpler requests without assistance.

This raises an interesting question: would a more capable supervisor narrow the performance gap, or would a smaller model benefit even more from query enrichment?

That’s an experiment for another day.

### Final thoughts

So, does your AI agent need a bouncer? Perhaps.

Jev is an interesting addition to the AI engineer’s toolbox. Rather than replacing the reasoning capabilities of an LLM, it offers an alternative for making fast, inexpensive decisions at specific points in an agentic workflow.

In my experiment, Jev helped determine whether incoming queries needed clarification, rewriting, decomposition, or no intervention at all. The results were encouraging, particularly for multipart questions, where the Jev-powered system completed one task nearly 12 times faster than the baseline. Of course, this is a small experiment, and more rigorous testing is needed to determine how much of that improvement came from Jev’s classification versus the subsequent LLM-powered query decomposition.

But that’s not really the point. **The interesting opportunity isn’t replacing LLMs with Jev. It’s identifying where we don’t need an LLM in the first place.** Not every decision requires an expensive reasoning model, and not every user query needs additional processing. Sometimes, a lightweight classifier is all we need to decide what happens next.

As agentic systems become increasingly sophisticated, I suspect we’ll see more specialized models working alongside general-purpose LLMs, each doing what they’re best at.

And that’s how you catch Jev-er. 😎

body:
* * *

#### _A dollar you have to take someone’s word for_

Cryptocurrency has a volatility problem.

The entire construct of cryptocurrency is trust-based through the use of blockchain. Unlike fiat currencies like USD, cryptocurrencies are unregulated, but can be exchanged for fiat currencies.

However, a quick google search shows the price fluctuation of bitcoin:

Imagine receiving your salary in cryptocurrency, only to discover that your purchasing power has fallen by 10% before you’ve paid your bills.

One solution is to create a cryptocurrency that doesn’t fluctuate in value. Just create a token and promise everyone that it’s worth one US dollar.

**Welcome to stablecoins, where blockchain technology meets a centuries-old financial concept: someone promising that their money is worth something else.**

In this article, I’ll explain what stablecoins are in great detail. Specifically, how their exchange rates are maintained, and what happens when those mechanisms fail.

As with my previous articles, all my code can be found in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/Blockchain/blob/0cce06e1f6fbe0a8c82e2d3d2da2e7667c2c3c95/notebooks/8.%20stablecoins.ipynb).

### 1\. What is a stablecoin?

Simply put, a stablecoin is a cryptocurrency designed to maintain a stable value relative to another asset, typically a fiat currency like the US dollar.

Say I were to create my own TitusCoin (TTC) and peg it to USD, then my objective would be:

**1 TTC = 1 USD**

Simple enough. Problem solved, right?

Right. And then some.

#### **1a. Banks transfer money between themselves and facilitate payments between individuals and organizations.**

However, some payment and settlement systems operate within specific business hours, particularly when transactions cross national borders. Transactions can also take time to settle, depending on the payment infrastructure and institutions involved. Stablecoins circumvent these issues. **A stablecoin can be transferred between blockchain addresses at any time, even when conventional banking systems are closed.**

The transfer can settle on-chain without waiting for the next banking day, although converting the stablecoin back into fiat currency may still depend on banking infrastructure and the issuer’s redemption arrangements.

That’s potentially useful for cross-border transactions, payments, and financial institutions moving value between counterparties.

#### 1b. Stablecoins can also provide an alternative to holding currencies that experience significant volatility.

For example, someone holding a currency that is rapidly depreciating against USD might choose to convert part of their holdings into a USD-denominated stablecoin.

This reduces their exposure to their domestic currency, although it introduces other risks, including exposure to the US dollar and the stablecoin issuer.

### 2\. So can anyone create a stablecoin?

Stablecoins are still a cryptocurrency and trust is still the key. I could create a million TitusCoins (TTCs) and call myself a millionare, but my declaration does not mean anyone will believe it.

Let me explain using the age old-economics concepts of demand and supply.

#### Remember the Asian Financial Crisis of 1997?

Before the Asian Financial Crisis, Thailand maintained an exchange-rate regime that kept the Thai baht closely tied to the US dollar at 25 Baht to 1 USD.

The Bank of Thailand had to intervene in foreign exchange markets to maintain this rate. If too many people wanted to sell Baht for USD, the central bank would have to defend its currency by using its foreign exchange reserves to purchase Baht.

Here’s the problem: **The Bank of Thailand did not have an unlimited supply of US dollars.**

During the 1990s, speculators began questioning whether Thailand could maintain its exchange-rate regime. Wealthy investors, including funds associated with George Soros, made bets against the Baht by shorting it.

These investors deliberately hoarded USD and aggressively borrowed and sold Baht for even more USD, anticipating that the currency would eventually depreciate. The Bank of Thailand continued defending the exchange rate using its foreign reserves and other market interventions.

But the pressure became increasingly difficult to sustain. And Thailand eventually abandoned its exchange-rate regime and allowed the Baht to float. The currency depreciated sharply, contributing to a financial crisis that spread across much of Asia.

The lesson: **You can promise that your currency is worth a fixed amount of another currency. But maintaining that promise requires resources and market confidence.**

_Reference:_ [_Lessons learnt from the Asian Financial Crisis (Bank of Thailand)_](https://www.bot.or.th/en/our-roles/special-measures/Tom-Yum-Kung-lesson.html)

### 3\. Let’s create TitusCoin

Time to establish a fictional financial institution called Titus Bank and a stablecoin cryptocurrency called TitusCoin (TTC). My promise is straightforward:

> **Anyone holding 1 TTC can redeem it for 1 USD, subject to the bank’s redemption arrangements.**

To back that up, I ensure that Titus Bank must hold at least USD 1 in reserves for every TTC issued.

So, if Alice deposits USD 100 into Titus Bank, I mint 100 TTC and send the tokens to her blockchain address. I’d also have to find some way to put USD 100 in my bank. That way if Alice wants her money back, I destroy or burn those tokens and release USD 100 from my reserves.

This is the basic concept behind a **fiat-backed stablecoin**, such as [USDC, issued by Circle](https://www.circle.com/usdc).

### 4\. But does 1 TTC always equal 1 USD?

Not necessarily. There’s an important distinction between the value promised by Titus Bank and the price at which TTC actually trades on cryptocurrency exchanges.

I can’t stop Alice from selling her TTC to Bob for USD 1.10, or some other amount. The issuer’s promised redemption value and the market price are two different things — the market price depends on what buyers and sellers are willing to pay.

And as we saw in the Asian Financial Crisis, it depends largely on whether people believe the issuer can honor its promise.

#### The USDC depegging incident of March 2023

[In March 2023, Silicon Valley Bank (SVB), a major US financial institution, collapsed](https://www.investopedia.com/what-happened-to-silicon-valley-bank-7368676). [Unfortunately for Circle, approximately USD 3.3 billion of its reserves (roughly 8% of its reserves) were deposited with SVB](https://www.cnbc.com/2023/03/11/stablecoin-usdc-breaks-dollar-peg-after-firm-reveals-it-has-3point3-billion-in-svb-exposure.html).

When SVB failed, uncertainty emerged over whether Circle could recover those funds. And the cryptocurrency market reacted.

[USDC, which was supposed to maintain a value of USD 1, briefly traded around USD 0.87–0.88 on secondary markets](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.07442v1).

No blockchain failures or cyberattacks. The market was simply uncertain whether Circle could access enough reserves to honour redemptions. Nonetheless, Circle maintained its commitment to redeem eligible USDC holdings at USD 1 per token.

Following intervention by US authorities to protect depositors at SVB, confidence recovered, and USDC returned towards its peg.

**A stablecoin’s price doesn’t remain at USD 1 simply because its issuer says it should.** So what actually keeps the market price close to the promised value?

### 5\. Greed is the main market force maintaining the exchange rate

More specifically, arbitrage.

Imagine that 1 TTC = USD 1.20 on a cryptocurrency exchange. That’s interesting, especially when you remember Titus Bank’s promise of issuing 1 TTC for every USD 1 deposited.

Which means, you could:

-   Deposit USD 100 with Titus Bank.
-   Receive 100 newly minted TTC.
-   Sell those 100 TTC on the market for USD 120.
-   Pocket the USD 20 difference.

20% profit!

The problem is every other investor will do the same thing.

As more TTC tokens are minted and sold, supply increases which pushes the market price back to USD 1.

So what happens if say 1 TTC = USD 0.90? Titus Bank still promises 1 TTC for USD 1. So you could:

-   Purchase 100 TTC on the market for USD 90.
-   Redeem those tokens with Titus Bank.
-   Receive USD 100.
-   Pocket the USD 10 difference.

And every other investor will do the same. So demand for TTC increases, and when those tokens are redeemed, they are burned, which reduces the circulating supply. Which pushes the price to return to USD 1.

This is the fundamental arbitrage mechanism behind a redeemable fiat-backed stablecoin.

Isn’t it beautiful that nobody needs to perform these transactions out of kindness? Greed makes things work out.

> But this only works reliably when redemption is accessible, transaction costs are manageable, and investors believe Titus Bank can actually pay them.

### 6\. What about using another cryptocurrency to maintain the peg?

What if, instead of keeping US dollars in a bank, we used another cryptocurrency to maintain the value of TTC?

Let’s introduce TitusFloat (TTF), a cryptocurrency whose price fluctuates freely.

Instead of promising that every TTC is backed by an actual US dollar, our protocol allows users to exchange TTC for **USD 1 worth of TTF**.

Notice the difference? We’re promising that 1 TTC can be exchanged for however many TTF tokens are worth USD 1 at the prevailing market price.

Say 1 TTF = USD 100:

-   If Alice redeems 1 TTC, we burn her TTC and issue her 0.01 TTF. That’s USD 1 worth of TTF.
-   If TTF falls to USD 50, redeeming 1 TTC would instead create 0.02 TTF

#### 6a. The mechanism of maintaining the peg is conceptually similar

If TTC trades below USD 1, arbitrageurs can purchase discounted TTC and exchange it through the protocol for USD 1 worth of newly issued TTF.

For example:

-   If 1 TTC trades at USD 0.90.
-   Investors each purchase 100 TTC for USD 90.
-   They redeem those tokens through the protocol and receive USD 100 worth of TTF.
-   They then sell the TTF on the market.
-   The TTC tokens are burned during redemption, reducing their circulating supply.

Now supposed TTC trades above USD 1:

-   Investors could use USD 1 worth of TTF to mint a new TTC then sell it for more than USD 1.
-   The newly minted TTC increases the supply, pushing its market price down.

#### 6b. But this mechanism doesn’t necessarily work.

Supposed 1 TTF initially trades at USD 100.

When someone redeems 1 TTC, the protocol only needs to mint 0.01 TTF to give them USD 1 worth of tokens. But what happens if TTF’s price falls ?

As TTF becomes cheaper, the protocol has to issue more TTF to honour the same USD 1 redemption.

And what are investors likely to do with the TTF they receive?

Sell it.

After all, they wanted to redeem their TTC for something worth one US dollar. They didn’t necessarily want to hold a volatile cryptocurrency.

But as more TTF is minted and sold, the additional supply and selling pressure can cause TTF’s market price to fall further. Which means the protocol must issue even more TTF to honour subsequent redemptions.

Which creates even more selling pressure.

Which causes the price to fall further.

The vicious part: this is all done **automatically via code**. The protocol automatically increases the quantity of TTF issued per redemption! The mechanism trying to save the peg is the hyperinflation engine. This is the ailment of algorithmic stablecoins.

This isn’t just theoretical by the way.

#### 6c. Terra/LUNA: When the stablecoin collapsed

[In May 2022, the Terra ecosystem suffered one of the most spectacular collapses in cryptocurrency history.](https://mitsloan.mit.edu/cfi/anatomy-a-run-terra-luna-crash)

TerraUSD (UST) was an algorithmic stablecoin designed to maintain a value of USD 1, and its peg mechanism depended on another cryptocurrency, LUNA.

Under the protocol’s original design, users could exchange 1 UST for USD 1 worth of LUNA, and vice versa, through the mint-and-burn mechanism. When UST began losing its peg, investors rushed to exit their positions.

The protocol attempted to restore the peg by allowing UST to be redeemed for newly minted LUNA. But that created enormous quantities of additional LUNA, causing a price collapse — and more tokens minted to maintain redemption value.

The supply of LUNA exploded from hundreds of millions of tokens to trillions in a matter of days. Its market price collapsed from tens of dollars to tiny fractions of a cent.

Ultimately, tens of billions of dollars in market value disappeared from the Terra ecosystem.

And perhaps the most unsettling part is that the collapse didn’t require someone to break the blockchain’s cryptography

Phew. That was a lot of economics theory. And we haven’t written a single line of code yet.

### 7\. First, we need a ledger

We’ll create a toy fiat-backed stablecoin and demonstrate how its transactions can be recorded on a blockchain.

First, we need a ledger to keep track of how many TTC tokens each person owns.

Our `TokenLedger` class will manage token balances, minting, burning, and transfers. Whenever a token operation occurs, we'll broadcast a corresponding transaction and include it on our blockchain, reusing the mempool implementation from my previous articles.

> For simplicity, our token balances are maintained in a Python dictionary, while the blockchain records the associated transaction events. In a production token implementation, balance updates would ordinarily be enforced as part of the blockchain’s smart contract state.

**The important distinction is that our blockchain records token activity, not the actual US dollars held by Titus Bank.**

```python
class TokenLedger:
    """Minimal on-chain token ledger for stablecoin and HTLC lessons."""

    def __init__(
        self, symbol: str, blockchain: Blockchain, network: Network
    ) -> None:
        """Attach this ledger to one chain and one gossip network."""
        self.symbol = symbol
        self.blockchain = blockchain
        self.network = network
        self.balances: dict[str, float] = {}
        self.total_supply: float = 0.0

    def record_payload(self, payload: str, tx_id: str | None = None) -> None:
        """Gossip ``payload`` as a ``Transaction`` and include it from the origin."""
        tx = Transaction(
            tx_id or f"{self.symbol}-{len(self.blockchain.chain)}",
            payload,
        )
        origin = self.network.node_names[0]
        self.network.broadcast(tx, origin)
        self.network.include(origin, tx.tx_id, self.blockchain)

    def _record(self, record: dict[str, str | float]) -> None:
        """Gossip a token event as a ``Transaction``, then include it."""
        event = str(record.get("event", "EVENT"))
        self.record_payload(
            json.dumps(record, sort_keys=True),
            tx_id=f"{self.symbol}-{event}-{len(self.blockchain.chain)}",
        )

    def mint(self, to: str, amount: float) -> None:
        """Create tokens for ``to`` and record a ``MINT`` receipt."""
        self._require_positive(amount)
        self.balances[to] = self.balances.get(to, 0) + amount
        self.total_supply += amount
        self._record({"event": "MINT", "symbol": self.symbol, "to": to, "amount": amount})

    def transfer(self, sender: str, receiver: str, amount: float) -> bool:
        """Move tokens between holders without changing supply"""
        self._require_positive(amount)
        if self.balances.get(sender, 0) < amount:
            return False
        self.balances[sender] -= amount
        self.balances[receiver] = self.balances.get(receiver, 0) + amount
        self._record(
            {
                "event": "TRANSFER",
                "symbol": self.symbol,
                "from": sender,
                "to": receiver,
                "amount": amount,
            }
        )
        return True

    def burn(self, holder: str, amount: float) -> bool:
        """Destroy tokens and shrink supply."""
        self._require_positive(amount)
        if self.balances.get(holder, 0) < amount:
            return False
        self.balances[holder] -= amount
        self.total_supply -= amount
        self._record(
            {"event": "BURN", "symbol": self.symbol, "holder": holder, "amount": amount}
        )
        return True
```

Our ledger can:

-   `mint` / `burn` — create or destroy tokens and change `total_supply`.
-   `transfer` — move tokens; supply stays put. Ownership moved, nothing was created.

### 8\. Next we need a `FiatBackedIssuer`

Now that we can create, destroy, and transfer TTC, we need someone to guarantee that every TTC is backed by one US dollar.

If I haven’t said so already, welcome to Titus Bank 🏦

In code, Titus Bank will be represented by a `FiatBackedIssuer` class that maintains a separate record of its USD reserves.

It needs three important methods.

-   `deposit_and_mint` — When someone deposits USD, Titus Bank records the deposit and asks `TokenLedger` to mint the corresponding amount of TTC.
-   `redeem` — When someone wants their money back, Titus Bank asks `TokenLedger` to burn the TTC and reduces its reserve balance accordingly.
-   `record_reserve_loss` — This is where things get interesting. The bank can record a loss of USD reserves **without modifying the token ledger or creating a blockchain transaction**. This method is particularly important — the blockchain cannot independently determine whether the issuer has sufficient reserves, and USD reserves exist outside our blockchain. Therfore, a change in these reserves would not affect the number of TTC in circulation.

```python
class FiatBackedIssuer:
    def __init__(self, name: str, ledger: TokenLedger) -> None:
        """Bind this issuer to one token ledger."""
        self.name = name
        self.ledger = ledger
        self.reserve_usd: float = 0.0

    def deposit_and_mint(self, to: str, usd_amount: float) -> None:
        """Record fictional USD reserves and mint the matching token amount."""
        TokenLedger._require_positive(usd_amount)
        self.reserve_usd += usd_amount
        self.ledger.mint(to, usd_amount)

    def redeem(self, holder: str, token_amount: float) -> bool:
        """Burn tokens and release the corresponding fictional reserve amount."""
        TokenLedger._require_positive(token_amount)
        if self.reserve_usd < token_amount:
            return False
        if not self.ledger.burn(holder, token_amount):
            return False
        self.reserve_usd -= token_amount
        return True

    def record_reserve_loss(self, usd_amount: float) -> bool:
        """Record an off-chain loss against this fictional issuer's reserves."""
        TokenLedger._require_positive(usd_amount)
        if self.reserve_usd < usd_amount:
            return False
        self.reserve_usd -= usd_amount
        return True

    @property
    def reserve_ratio(self) -> float:
        """Return the fictional reserve amount divided by issued token supply."""
        if self.ledger.total_supply == 0:
            return 1.0
        return self.reserve_usd / self.ledger.total_supply

    @property
    def backing_per_token(self) -> float:
        """Return simplified fictional backing per token, not a market price."""
        return min(1.0, self.reserve_ratio)
```

### 9\. Taking our stablecoin blockchain for a spin

We’ll use the same proof-of-stake blockchain in my [previous article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/proof-of-stake-the-mining-free-blockchain-ddae684ffec5) and extend it a little:

```python
class StableCoinBlockchain(Blockchain):
    """PoS blockchain extended with a readable name and proposer rewards."""

    def __init__(self, name: str, validators: list[Validator]) -> None:
        """Name this chain and reuse the parent PoS genesis."""
        super().__init__(validators)
        self.name = name

    def add_block(self, data: str) -> tuple[Block, Validator]:
        """Append a block through the shared PoS implementation and pay its proposer."""
        block, proposer = super().add_block(data)
        proposer.stake += BLOCK_REWARD + FEE_PER_TX
        return block, proposer

    def accept_candidate(self, block: Block) -> None:
        """Append a mempool-included candidate and pay its named proposer."""
        super().accept_candidate(block)
        proposer = next(v for v in self.validators if v.name == block.proposer)
        proposer.stake += BLOCK_REWARD + FEE_PER_TX
```

Then, reusing the `Network` class from my [previous article on mempools](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/introducing-mempools-the-one-time-gossip-pays-off-9fbc92701f70) and wiring everything togther:

```python
nodes = ["Titus-Node-1", "Titus-Node-2"]
network = Network(nodes, random.Random(7))
chain = StableCoinBlockchain(
    "TitusChain",
    [Validator("Titus-Node-1", 250), Validator("Titus-Node-2", 150)],
)
tituscoin = TokenLedger("TTC", chain, network)
titus_issuer = FiatBackedIssuer("Fictional Titus Bank", tituscoin)
```

Let’s imagine Alice deposits USD 1000 with Titus Bank. Titus Bank would then have to mint 1000 TTC.

```python
titus_issuer.deposit_and_mint("Alice", 1_000)

print(f"Alice: {tituscoin.balances['Alice']:.0f} TTC")
print(f"Supply: {tituscoin.total_supply:.0f} TTC")
print(f"Reserve: ${titus_issuer.reserve_usd:,.0f} fictional USD")
```

Output:

```python-repl
Alice: 1000 TTC
Supply: 1000 TTC
Reserve: $1,000 fictional USD
```

Now suppose Alice decides to pay Bob 250 TTC. Would Titus Bank need to mint another 250 TTC?

Of course not. We’re simply transferring ownership of existing tokens.

```python
supply_before_transfer = tituscoin.total_supply
reserve_before_transfer = titus_issuer.reserve_usd
transfer_succeeded = tituscoin.transfer("Alice", "Bob", 250)

print(tituscoin.balances)
print(f"Supply still: {tituscoin.total_supply:.0f} TTC")

# {'Alice': 750, 'Bob': 250}
# Supply still: 1000 TTC
```

Alice now has 750 TTC while Bob has 250 TTC. Total supply of TTC remains at 1,000 TTC.

Now let’s say Bob redeems 100 TTC:

-   Titus Bank would then have to release 100 USD to Bob, and total supply changes.
-   The `TokenLedger.burn` removes Bob’s 100 TTC on-chain and reduces `reserve_usd` by 100 off-chain. Both of which are coordinated by `FiatBackedIssuer.redeem`

```python

redemption_succeeded = titus_issuer.redeem("Bob", 100)

print(f"Bob: {tituscoin.balances['Bob']:.0f} TTC")
print(f"Supply: {tituscoin.total_supply:.0f} TTC")
print(f"Reserve: ${titus_issuer.reserve_usd:,.0f} fictional USD")

Bob: 150 TTC
Supply: 900 TTC
Reserve: $900 fictional USD
```

#### Notice that a problem off the chain does not rewrite the token ledger

Say Titus Bank records a USD 180 reserve loss. Token balances and total supply should not automatically shrink!

Instead, `FiatBackedIssuer.record_reserve_loss` changes only `reserve_usd` . Alice and Bob’s TTC are in tact and total supply remains at 900.

```python
supply_before_loss = tituscoin.total_supply
balances_before_loss = tituscoin.balances.copy()
blocks_before_loss = len(chain.chain)
loss_recorded = titus_issuer.record_reserve_loss(180)

print(f"Reserve after loss: ${titus_issuer.reserve_usd:,.0f} fictional USD")
print(f"Supply after loss: {tituscoin.total_supply:.0f} TTC")
print(f"Reserve ratio: {titus_issuer.reserve_ratio:.0%}")
print(f"Backing per TTC: ${titus_issuer.backing_per_token:.2f}")
print(f"Blockchain valid: {chain.is_valid()}")

# Reserve after loss: $720 fictional USD
# Supply after loss: 900 TTC
# Reserve ratio: 80%
# Backing per TTC: $0.80
# Blockchain valid: True
```

Importantly, Titus Bank can no longer redeem every TTC for USD 1 because of a lack of reserves. But nobody knows that — shh…

### Moving forward

We’ve established why stablecoins exist, how their exchange rates are maintained, and what happens when the mechanisms supporting those exchange rates fail.

We’ve also created our own fictional stablecoin, TitusCoin, using the same proof-of-stake blockchain and mempool concepts from my previous articles.

But it’s fictional of course. Nothing is technically stopping me from creating my own stablecoin and declaring myself a billionaire — getting everyone else to believe I’m a billionaire is the hard part.

But there are other interesting questions worth exploring as well.

Suppose there are now two independent fictional banks, Titus Bank and Mary Bank that need to settle accounts after hours.

-   Titus Bank issues TitusCoin (TTC), while Mary Bank issues MaryCoin (MTC).
-   Both stablecoins exist on different blockchains.

How would these transactions be coordinated? Well, that’s where things get interesting.

I guess our journey continues.

body:
* * *

#### The heist where you borrow the money first

[Last time](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/introducing-smart-contracts-340c20cbe672), I compared smart contracts to vending machines: put in $2, press B4, get a Snickers. No clerk, no judgment calls. A smart contract is code at an address that gives the same output every time it’s called, and it can call other contracts.

We built three of them.

-   First, an Automated Market Maker (AMM) pool: a contract holding two piles of tokens, Ether (ETH) — a cryptocurrency — and USD, that quotes a price purely from the ratio between them. Its one rule: multiplying the two piles together must always give the same number, so selling ETH in pushes its price down.

> Think of it as a puddle. Toss in a pebble and the water barely moves. Cannonball into it and it splashes everywhere. But a splash tells you about the puddle, not the ocean. In my code, one big sale crashed ETH’s price 69% in this pool while it stayed $2,000 everywhere else.

-   A lending protocol loans USD to borrowers by ascertaining the value of their collateral from their ETH, and liquidates borrowers whose collateral fell below a specific threshold of their debt. This price could come from the AMM pool, or from an external source, such as:
-   A price feed stored reported prices, acting as an oracle.

Our lending protocol took a shortcut: it read its ETH price straight off the AMM pool. One call, and the puddle’s number became its truth. I hinted at a fix, taking the median of several independent price reports, without showing why it works.

This time we break it. I’m a huge fan of the [Ocean’s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean%27s) movies, but they needed eleven specialists. Ours needs one: you, wearing every hat. Then we’ll see why the median stops the whole thing cold.

As before, all the code is in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/Blockchain/blob/0cce06e1f6fbe0a8c82e2d3d2da2e7667c2c3c95/notebooks/7.%20flash_loans.ipynb). We’ll be reusing the classes from my previous article.

### Act One: Alice executes a heist with ETH she owns

Meet Alice, our attacker, with 40 ETH. She participates in a pool that is shallow: 50 ETH and $100,000.

A borrower has posted 10 ETH against a $12,000 loan: at $2,000/ETH (USD100k : 50 ETH) that’s a collateral ratio of 1.67, comfortably above the 1.5 threshold.

> Pause and predict: What happens if Alice sells all 40 ETH into the pool?

```python
nodes = ["Node A", "Alice-Node", "Bob-Node", "Farid-Node"]
validators = [
    Validator("Node A", 100),
    Validator("Alice-Node", 80),
    Validator("Bob-Node", 70),
    Validator("Farid-Node", 50),
]
owned_network = Network(nodes, random.Random(7))
owned_chain = Blockchain(validators)

# Same two contracts, neither buggy. The lending rule still asks the puddle about the ocean.
owned_pool = AMMPool("amm-thin.eth", 50.0, 100_000.0)
owned_lending = LendingProtocol("lending-thin.eth", owned_pool)
owned_lending.call(
    "open_loan", borrower="victim", collateral_eth=10.0, debt_usd=12_000.0
)

# TX1: Alice dumps 40 ETH she already owns. The cheap price is now public. Crime scene, open floor plan.
alice_eth = 40.0
usd_from_dump, dump_tx, dump_block = submit_call(
    owned_network,
    owned_chain,
    "Alice-Node",
    "tx-dump-40eth",
    owned_pool,
    "swap_eth_for_usd",
    eth_in=alice_eth,
)
manipulated_price = owned_pool.spot_price
victim_ratio = owned_lending.collateral_ratio(owned_lending.loans["victim"])

# TX2: liquidate at that public photograph, then buy ETH back at the price she herself created.
seized, liq_tx, liq_block = submit_call(
    owned_network,
    owned_chain,
    "Alice-Node",
    "tx-liquidate-victim",
    owned_lending,
    "liquidate",
    borrower="victim",
)
usd_for_buyback = usd_from_dump - seized.debt_usd
eth_bought_back = owned_pool.call("swap_usd_for_eth", usd_in=usd_for_buyback)
alice_final_eth = eth_bought_back + seized.collateral_eth
profit_eth = alice_final_eth - alice_eth

print(f"{dump_block.proposer} included {dump_tx.tx_id} in Block #{dump_block.index}")
print(
    f"DUMP: Alice sells {alice_eth:.2f} ETH of her own for ${usd_from_dump:,.2f}; "
    f"AMM price becomes ${manipulated_price:,.2f}/ETH."
)
print(
    f"The cheap puddle is now public. Victim ratio at this price: {victim_ratio:.2f}."
)
print(f"{liq_block.proposer} included {liq_tx.tx_id} in Block #{liq_block.index}")
print(
    f"LIQUIDATE: pay ${seized.debt_usd:,.2f} debt and seize "
    f"{seized.collateral_eth:.2f} ETH."
)
print(
    f"BUY BACK: remaining ${usd_for_buyback:,.2f} buys {eth_bought_back:.2f} ETH."
)
print(
    f"Alice started with {alice_eth:.2f} ETH, ends with {alice_final_eth:.2f} ETH, "
    f"profit {profit_eth:.2f} ETH."
)
```

Output:

```python-repl
Alice-Node included tx-dump-40eth in Block #1
DUMP: Alice sells 40.00 ETH of her own for $44,444.44; AMM price becomes $617.28/ETH.
The cheap puddle is now public. Victim ratio at this price: 0.51.
Alice-Node included tx-liquidate-victim in Block #2
LIQUIDATE: pay $12,000.00 debt and seize 10.00 ETH.
BUY BACK: remaining $32,444.44 buys 33.18 ETH.
Alice started with 40.00 ETH, ends with 43.18 ETH, profit 3.18 ETH.
```

**Read the result.** Alice deliberately sells 40 ETH into a pool that only had 50 ETH. Price collapses 69% — not because ETH crashed, but because she displaced most of the puddle.

At $617/ETH, the victim’s 10 ETH is worth $617 against $12,000, i.e. the collateral ratio is 0.51. The protocol, following its rules correctly, marks them liquidatable.

Alice then pays the $32,444 required to buy ETH back — at the depressed price she herself created and reaps **3.18 ETH** of pure profit, extracted from someone who never did anything wrong.

That’s why a lender should never treat a single thin pool’s spot price as the truth.

### Act Two: The same heist with a flash loan

Act One had a barrier: you needed to own enough ETH like Alice to move the pool. A flash loan removes this requirement. The idea sounds insane the first time you hear it: a contract will lend you **unlimited money with zero collateral, no credit check, and no questions asked**.

The catch is brutal— the money must be back by the end of this transaction. If it is not, the entire transaction reverts and it is as though nothing happened.

Think of it like borrowing a suitcase of cash on the condition that you hand the exact suitcase back before you finish walking through the lobby.

You can take the money.

You can use it.

You can even make a profit with it.

But if you reach the exit without returning the suitcase, the entire walk through the lobby is rewound.

That sounds like a very safe loan.

And it is — **for the lender.**

The lender doesn’t need to trust Alice because Alice never gets to keep the borrowed principal. The loan either comes back before the transaction ends, or the transaction doesn’t happen. And this is enforced by the code of the flash loan smart contract.

So why offer this at all?

**Fees.** Real flash-loan providers charge fees for the temporary use of their liquidity. The lender gets paid without taking the usual credit risk of an unsecured loan.

Now change exactly one thing from Act One: Alice owns zero of the 40 ETH. The provider has 1,000 ETH available. Alice borrows 40 ETH.

She now has the same 40 ETH that previously belonged to her — except this time she only has it temporarily.

And because the loan, the manipulation, the liquidation, the buyback, and the repayment can all happen inside one transaction, nobody gets a chance to step between the pieces.

Five operations:

1.  **Borrow** 40 ETH.
2.  **Dump** the 40 ETH into the shallow AMM, crushing its spot price.
3.  **Liquidate** the victim using that manipulated price.
4.  **Buy back** ETH cheaply with the USD recovered from the dump.
5.  **Repay** the original 40 ETH.

If anything fails, the whole thing rewinds. If everything succeeds, whatever ETH remains after repayment belongs to Alice.

And here’s the deliciously uncomfortable part:

**We already know exactly how much should remain.**

We just watched Alice do the same thing in Act One with her own money. Now she does it with **0 ETH.**

And she still walks away with **3.18 ETH**.

### Act Three: The heist fails

**Now let’s change exactly one thing from Act Two:** the victim has 40 ETH instead of 10 against the same $12,000 debt.This means that even after Alice’s attempted attack, the victim should survive.

Like Act Two, Alice still borrows 40 ETH and dumps all 40 ETH into the same shallow AMM.

```python
failed_tx = Transaction(
    "tx-flash-victim2",
    "Flash-loan against Victim2",
)

network.broadcast(
    failed_tx,
    origin="SketchyGuy-Node",
)

included_failed, failed_block = network.include(
    "SketchyGuy-Node",
    failed_tx.tx_id,
    chain,
)

print(
    f"{failed_block.proposer} included {included_failed.tx_id} "
    f"in Block #{failed_block.index} (execution comes next)."
)
```

We create the same shallow AMM, the same $12,000 loan, and the same flash-loan provider. The only difference is the victim’s collateral:

```python
failed_pool = AMMPool(
    "amm-victim2.eth",
    50.0,
    100_000.0,
)

failed_protocol = LendingProtocol(
    "lending-victim2.eth",
    failed_pool,
)

failed_protocol.open_loan(
    "Victim2",
    40.0,
    12_000.0,
)

failed_provider = FlashLoanProvider(1_000.0)
```

Before executing the attack, we record the state of the world:

```python
failed_before = (
    failed_pool.eth_reserve,
    failed_pool.usd_reserve,
    tuple(sorted(failed_protocol.loans)),
    failed_provider.eth_available,
)
```

Now Alice’s attack:

-   She dumps the borrowed ETH.
-   The AMM price collapses.
-   Then she attempts the liquidation. But this time, the protocol checks victim’s collateral ratio and refuses.

```python
def failed_attack_action(
    amount_eth: float,
) -> tuple[float, AttackTrace]:

    failed_pool.swap_eth_for_usd(amount_eth)

    failed_observation["price"] = failed_pool.spot_price

    failed_observation["ratio"] = (
        failed_protocol.collateral_ratio(
            failed_protocol.loans["Victim2"]
        )
    )

    failed_protocol.liquidate("Victim2")
```

The result:

```python-repl
SketchyGuy-Node included tx-flash-victim2 in Block #2
(execution comes next).

Attempted dump moved AMM price to $617.28/ETH.
Victim2 ratio after dump: 2.06;
liquidation is rejected.

Attack transaction: REVERTED
```

The AMM really did hit **$617.28**.

But the victim’s collateral ratio was still **2.06**, comfortably above the **1.50** liquidation threshold. So `liquidate()` rejected the operation. And once that happened, the flash-loan transaction reverted.

-   The AMM reserves were restored.
-   The loan record was restored.
-   The flash-loan provider’s balance was restored.

Everything returned to its pre-transaction state.

### This is the part that is easy to misunderstand.

The price manipulation **did happen during execution**. It just didn’t survive the transaction. If a required step fails, the successful steps that came before it don’t get to stay behind as souvenirs.

But notice what did not happen: nobody looked at Alice’s transaction and said: “Hmm. This appears to be an attack. Let’s stop her.”

Only rules encoded in code within smart contracts are evaluated. In Act Two, every rule check passed, so the attack succeeded. In Act Three, `liquidate()` failed its rule check, so the transaction reverted.

### The defence: stop asking the puddle

Act Three failed because, even at the manipulated price, the victim’s collateral ratio remained above the liquidation threshold.

But what if Alice had a flash loan of 100 ETH? The failure in Act Three wasn’t that flash loans suddenly stopped working. It was that **this particular amount of manipulation wasn’t enough to make the victim liquidatable**. Give Alice enough capital, and she may be able to push the puddle far enough.

So the real defence cannot be “make the puddle deeper.” It has to be **stop asking the puddle for the market price in the first place.**

My previous article already gave the fix: **stop asking the puddle.** Don’t make the lending protocol trust a single price source that an attacker can manipulate with a large enough trade. Point the lending protocol at a `MedianOracle` instead and the attack dies — because the liquidation no longer depends on the AMM puddle.

A median of three sources survives one liar and fails against two. If those “independent” sources are themselves thin AMM pools, a flash loan large enough can move two of them in the same transaction.

```python
# Three reports, one median. No ML. Sort, pick the middle, ignore how loud the liar was.
defense_oracle = MedianOracle(
    [
        PriceReport("exchange-A", 2_005.0),
        PriceReport("exchange-B", 1_995.0),
        PriceReport("reference-feed", 2_000.0),
    ]
)
defense_pool = AMMPool("amm-defense.eth", 50.0, 100_000.0)
# price_source overrides the puddle. 
defense_protocol = LendingProtocol(
    "lending-defense.eth", defense_pool, price_source=defense_oracle
)
defense_victim_loan = defense_protocol.open_loan("defense-victim", 10.0, 12_000.0)
defense_pool.swap_eth_for_usd(40.0)
defense_ratio = defense_protocol.collateral_ratio(defense_victim_loan)

try:
    defense_protocol.liquidate("defense-victim")
except PositionNotLiquidatableError:
    defense_rejected = True
else:
    defense_rejected = False

def defense_verdict(defense_rejected: bool) -> str:
    """Return a short label for whether the median-priced liquidation ran.

    Args:
        defense_rejected: True if ``liquidate`` raised.

    Returns:
        ``liquidation rejected`` or ``liquidation executed``.
    """
    return "liquidation rejected" if defense_rejected else "liquidation executed"

print(f"Manipulated AMM spot price: ${defense_pool.spot_price:,.2f}/ETH")
print(
    f"Median oracle price: ${defense_oracle.price:,.2f}/ETH; "
    f"protocol ratio: {defense_ratio:.2f}"
)
print(f"Defense result: {defense_verdict(defense_rejected)}")
```

The result:

```python-repl
Manipulated AMM spot price: $617.28/ETH
Median oracle price: $2,000.00/ETH; protocol ratio: 1.67
Defense result: liquidation rejected
```

**Read the result.** The AMM really moved to $617.28. The protocol read the median price of $2,000 and rejected the liquidation.

Aggregation did not make the AMM honest — **the AMM was always honest!**

It was honestly reporting the price implied by the liquidity sitting in its pool. The bug was asking that price to answer a question it wasn’t qualified to answer: _“What is ETH really worth?”_

The defence wasn’t to make the puddle honest. **It was to stop asking the puddle.**

### Thinking of what we just did

Here’s a reality bite: Flash loan attacks are not hypothetical.

Flash loan oracle manipulation has drained hundreds of millions of dollars from real protocols, repeatedly, for years, in attacks that were structurally identical to the one above.

And the uncomfortable part is that the failure often wasn’t some exotic bug hiding in a thousand lines of Solidity.

The code could be audited. The contracts could execute exactly as written. The liquidation logic could be perfectly correct.

**There was a contract asking a puddle about the ocean.**

And an attacker realized that if the puddle was shallow enough, they could move it. The vulnerability was trusting a price source that an attacker could manipulate.

Median feeds, TWAPs, deeper liquidity, freshness limits, circuit breakers: these are layers of defence, each addressing different failure modes. None is magic, and all require understanding the assumptions underneath them.

This isn’t to say that smart contracts are safe now. In my view, DeFi remains a bit of a wild west, evolving daily.

Nonetheless, I will tentatively end my exploration of the more volatile side of DeFi here, though I have a feeling this won’t be my last article about it.

In my next article, I’ll explore something intriguing — **stablecoins, a token that claims to be a dollar.**

#### References (honestly too many):

-   Qin, K., Zhou, L., Livshits, B., & Gervais, A. (2021). [Attacking the DeFi Ecosystem with Flash Loans for Fun and Profit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.03810).
-   Aave. [Flash Loans](https://aave.com/docs/developers/flash-loans).
-   Adams, H., Zinsmeister, N., & Robinson, D. (2020). [Uniswap v2 Core](https://uniswap.org/whitepaper.pdf)
-   \[Medium Article\] Traroe, P. [The 5 Biggest Flash Loan Attacks](https://blog.hashex.org/the-5-biggest-flash-loan-attacks-7cd1b872045a) (2022)
