body:
* * *

#### What they are and how they work with Blockchain

My odyssey into blockchain has been getting progressively more interesting.

What started as curiosity to understand how Bitcoin works has turned into a series of articles where I keep opening increasingly suspicious-looking boxes and asking, _“Okay, but what actually happens inside?”_

So far I’ve covered how blocks get proposed ([PoW](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/understanding-blockchains-from-scratch-f14c454af32f), then [PoS](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/proof-of-stake-the-mining-free-blockchain-ddae684ffec5)), how a [Merkle tree](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/inside-opencerts-how-merkle-trees-verify-singapores-digital-diplomas-61f60d13700e) lets you prove one credential belongs to a much bigger set without hauling out the whole set, how [permissioned chains](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/introducing-permissioned-chains-1d8a71f5b09a) handle endorsement and stale-state conflicts, and how transactions live in a messy, half-agreed-upon [mempool](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/introducing-mempools-the-one-time-gossip-pays-off-9fbc92701f70) before they ever make it into a block. If any of those are fuzzy, the earlier articles are still there — this one assumes you’ve got the gist.

With the exception of OpenCerts, the blockchains in my articles so far have mainly been about **ledgers:**

> Alice sends Bob some tokens, a validator checks the transaction, the network agrees on what happened and the blockchain records it.

There is, however, a rather important assumption hiding underneath all of this: **_The blockchain already knows everything it needs to know._**

If Alice sends Bob 10 tokens, the blockchain doesn’t need to phone anyone to ask whether Alice really sent Bob 10 tokens.

The transaction _is_ the information.

The blockchain can compare that transaction against its existing state, apply the relevant rules, and — assuming everything checks out — record the result.

But now imagine that our blockchain needs to know something that **does not** **originate on the blockchain.**

And this is where things get interesting.

Because once we give the blockchain **programs that actually do things**, those programs are going to want information about a world that exists outside the blockchain.

That brings us to **smart contracts,** and eventually, to **oracles**.

As before, all my code can be found in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/Blockchain/blob/main/notebooks/6.%20oracles_and_smart_contracts.ipynb).

### What a smart contract actually is

A smart contract is like a vending machine.

You put in the required amount of money, press B4, and a Snickers falls out (yum). The machine has rules. All you have to do is satisfy them.

In Ethereum, a smart contract is program code deployed to the blockchain. Other participants can send transactions requesting that the contract execute a particular function. The resulting execution can change the blockchain’s state.

And here is the important part:

> The blockchain does **not** understand that you have asked it to “swap some ETH for USD.”

> It understands something much more mechanical — Call the contract at this address, invoke this function, and provide these arguments.

The contract’s code determines what happens next. **Smart contracts are very deterministic programs**.

These programs live in a shared environment where thousands of machines may independently execute the same instructions and must arrive at the same result.

Here’s what a simple smart contract could look like, recycling our PoS blockchain and mempool classes from Articles 2 and 5:

```python
class SmartContract:
    def __init__(self, address: str) -> None:
        """Store the address this contract will be called at."""
        if not address:
            raise ValueError("Contract address must be non-empty.")
        self.address = address

    def call(self, method: str, **kwargs: Any) -> Any:
        """Invoke a public method by name."""
        if method.startswith("_") or method == "call":
            raise AttributeError(
                f"{self.address} has no public method {method!r}."
            )
        func = getattr(self, method, None)
        if not callable(func):
            raise AttributeError( 
                f"{self.address} has no public method {method!r}."
            )
        return func(**kwargs)
```

The important idea here is surprisingly small.

-   A contract has an **address**.
-   It has **code**.
-   And that code exposes methods that can be called.

In our simplified blockchain, a contract call is represented as a transaction, which can enter the mempool, be included in a proposed block, and then be executed.

So the simplified flow is:

> **Contract call → Transaction → Mempool → Block → Execution → State change**

Which means the mempool we built in the previous article still matters.

Our shiny new smart contract has not escaped the machinery we already built. We’ve simply given the machinery something more interesting to execute.

```python
def submit_call(
    network: Network,
    chain: Blockchain,
    origin: str,
    tx_id: str,
    contract: SmartContract,
    method: str,
    **kwargs: Any,
) -> tuple[Any, Transaction, Block]:
    arg_preview = ", ".join(f"{k}={v!r}" for k, v in kwargs.items())
    description = f"{contract.address}.{method}({arg_preview})"
    network.broadcast(Transaction(tx_id, description), origin=origin)
    tx, block = network.include(origin, tx_id, chain)
    result = contract.call(method, **kwargs)
    return result, tx, block
```

**A transaction can ask a contract to run some code, and running that code can change blockchain state.**

### Swap contracts aren’t a major leap from the basics

An **automated market maker (AMM)** allows users to trade against liquidity held inside the pool using a mathematical pricing rule.

One of the simplest and most famous AMM designs is the **constant-product AMM**. Its entire personality can be summarised by one equation:

`**x × y = k**`

Here, `x` is the amount of ETH in the pool and `y` is the amount of USD.

-   The product `k` should remain constant.
-   So if someone adds ETH to the pool, the amount of USD in the pool must decrease accordingly.
-   The pool does not need a human market maker deciding what the trade should cost.

The math decides. And it is just code.

```python
class AMMPool(SmartContract):
    def __init__(
        self, address: str, eth_reserve: float, usd_reserve: float
    ) -> None:
        """Create a pool at ``address`` with the given reserves."""
        super().__init__(address)
        if eth_reserve <= 0 or usd_reserve <= 0:
            raise ValueError("AMM reserves must be positive.")
        self.eth_reserve = eth_reserve
        self.usd_reserve = usd_reserve

    @property
    def spot_price(self) -> float:
        return self.usd_reserve / self.eth_reserve

    @property
    def constant_product(self) -> float:
        return self.eth_reserve * self.usd_reserve

    def swap_eth_for_usd(self, eth_in: float) -> float:
        if eth_in <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Swap input must be positive.")
        k = self.constant_product
        new_eth_reserve = self.eth_reserve + eth_in
        new_usd_reserve = k / new_eth_reserve
        usd_out = self.usd_reserve - new_usd_reserve
        self.eth_reserve, self.usd_reserve = new_eth_reserve, new_usd_reserve
        return usd_out

    def swap_usd_for_eth(self, usd_in: float) -> float:
        if usd_in <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Swap input must be positive.")
        k = self.constant_product
        new_usd_reserve = self.usd_reserve + usd_in
        new_eth_reserve = k / new_usd_reserve
        eth_out = self.eth_reserve - new_eth_reserve
        self.usd_reserve, self.eth_reserve = new_usd_reserve, new_eth_reserve
        return eth_out
```

The pool has two important pieces of state:

-   how much ETH it holds
-   how much USD it holds

And it has rules governing what happens when somebody swaps one asset for the other.

Suppose someone sells ETH to the pool:

-   The pool now has **more ETH**.
-   To maintain `x × y = k`, it must therefore have **less USD**.
-   The difference between the old and new USD reserves is what the trader receives.

### Same price for any size trade?

The intuition is tempting. Sell a little ETH, get about $2,000 worth of USD. Sell a lot of ETH, get… more of the same deal, just scaled up.

Not quite.

We’ll start with a pool containing 50 ETH and $100,000 USD, so the initial spot price is:

`$100,000 ÷ 50 = $2,000 per ETH`

Then we’ll make two identical pools, because I want two experiments that start from exactly the same state.

One is a small trade:

> Sell 1 ETH.

The other is a large trade:

> Sell 40 ETH.

Think of the pool as a puddle. Toss a pebble in and the water barely moves. Cannonball into it and it splashes everywhere. The AMM works the same way — a small trade barely disturbs the reserves, a large one sloshes the price around.

We’re about to prove that with numbers instead of a metaphor, but keep the puddle in your head. It’s the whole intuition for what “price impact” means.

```python
# Three identical puddles. The pebble and boulder must not share state.
initial_pool = AMMPool("amm-initial", 50.0, 100_000.0)
small_trade_pool = AMMPool("amm-pebble", 50.0, 100_000.0)
large_trade_pool = AMMPool("amm-boulder", 50.0, 100_000.0)

# call() is the public surface — same path a later Block will take.
small_usd_out = small_trade_pool.call("swap_eth_for_usd", eth_in=1.0)
large_usd_out = large_trade_pool.call("swap_eth_for_usd", eth_in=40.0)
small_impact = (small_trade_pool.spot_price / initial_pool.spot_price - 1) * 100
large_impact = (large_trade_pool.spot_price / initial_pool.spot_price - 1) * 100
constant_product_preserved = abs(
    large_trade_pool.constant_product - initial_pool.constant_product
) < 1e-6

print(
    f"Initial pool: {initial_pool.eth_reserve:.2f} ETH and "
    f"${initial_pool.usd_reserve:,.2f}; spot price ${initial_pool.spot_price:,.2f}/ETH"
)
print(
    f"Small 1 ETH sale: receives ${small_usd_out:,.2f}; "
    f"price ${small_trade_pool.spot_price:,.2f}/ETH ({small_impact:.2f}%)"
)
print(
    f"Large 40 ETH sale: receives ${large_usd_out:,.2f}; "
    f"price ${large_trade_pool.spot_price:,.2f}/ETH ({large_impact:.2f}%)"
)
print(f"x * y preserved within floating-point tolerance: {constant_product_preserved}")
```

The output:

```python-repl
Initial pool: 50.00 ETH and $100,000.00; spot price $2,000.00/ETH
Small 1 ETH sale: receives $1,960.78; price $1,922.34/ETH (-3.88%)
Large 40 ETH sale: receives $44,444.44; price $617.28/ETH (-69.14%)
x * y preserved within floating-point tolerance: True
```

And there’s our first glimpse of **price impact**.

-   Selling just 1 ETH moves the displayed price from $2,000 to about $1,922 — a roughly **3.9% decrease**.
-   But selling 40 ETH — almost the entire original ETH reserve — moves the displayed price all the way down to about **$617**.

The AMM is doing exactly what we told it to do. The pool is simply responding to a very large trade relative to its available liquidity.

There is no external ETH/USD price feed involved. The AMM doesn’t know what ETH is worth anywhere else. It only knows the ratio of the two assets sitting inside itself.

And because that number exists on-chain, **another smart contract can read it.**

That opens up a much more interesting possibility: What if a lending protocol uses this number to decide whether someone’s loan is safe?

### The lending contract: a loan that asks the puddle

Now let’s give our AMM a customer who cares rather more about its price than a trader does.

We’ll build a tiny lending protocol (another smart contract). It accepts ETH as collateral and allows a borrower to take on USD-denominated debt. If the value of the collateral falls too far relative to the debt, the position can be liquidated.

We’ll set the minimum collateral ratio at **1.5**. Concretely in code:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Loan:
    collateral_eth: float
    debt_usd: float

class LoanNotFoundError(Exception):
    """Raised when a borrower has no open loan."""

class PositionNotLiquidatableError(Exception):
    """Raised when liquidation is attempted on a still-healthy position."""

class LendingProtocol(SmartContract):
    def __init__(
        self,
        address: str,
        pool: AMMPool,
        liquidation_ratio: float = 1.5,
        price_source=None,
    ) -> None:
        """Configure the protocol's price source and liquidation threshold."""
        super().__init__(address)
        if liquidation_ratio <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Liquidation ratio must be positive.")
        self.pool = pool
        self.liquidation_ratio = liquidation_ratio
        self.price_source = price_source
        self.loans: dict[str, Loan] = {}

    def open_loan(
        self, borrower: str, collateral_eth: float, debt_usd: float
    ) -> Loan:
        """Open a loan for ``borrower`` and return it."""
        return self.add_loan(borrower, Loan(collateral_eth, debt_usd))

    def add_loan(self, borrower: str, loan: Loan) -> Loan:
        """Register an open loan for a borrower."""
        if not borrower:
            raise ValueError("Borrower name must be non-empty.")
        self.loans[borrower] = loan
        return loan

    def collateral_ratio(self, loan: Loan) -> float:
        """Return collateral value divided by debt."""
        price = (
            self.price_source.price
            if self.price_source is not None
            else self.pool.spot_price
        )
        return loan.collateral_eth * price / loan.debt_usd

    def liquidate(self, borrower: str) -> Loan:
        """Seize and remove a borrower's loan if it is unhealthy."""
        if borrower not in self.loans:
            raise LoanNotFoundError(f"No loan for {borrower}.")
        loan = self.loans[borrower]
        if self.collateral_ratio(loan) >= self.liquidation_ratio:
            raise PositionNotLiquidatableError("Position is still healthy.")
        return self.loans.pop(borrower)
```

There are a lot of lines here, but most of them are bookkeeping. The interesting part is much smaller:

> When the protocol wants to calculate the collateral ratio, it asks for a price:

```python
price = (
    self.price_source.price
    if self.price_source is not None
    else self.pool.spot_price
)
```

Right now, we haven’t given it another price source, so it falls back to the AMM.

```python
baseline_pool = AMMPool("amm-baseline", 50.0, 100_000.0)
baseline_protocol = LendingProtocol("lending-baseline", baseline_pool)
victim_loan = baseline_protocol.call(
    "open_loan", borrower="victim", collateral_eth=10.0, debt_usd=12_000.0
)
baseline_ratio = baseline_protocol.collateral_ratio(victim_loan)

print(f"At ${baseline_pool.spot_price:,.2f}/ETH, victim collateral ratio: {baseline_ratio:.2f}")
print("Liquidation threshold: 1.50; verdict: HEALTHY")
```

The output:

```python-repl
     
At $2,000.00/ETH, victim collateral ratio: 1.67
Liquidation threshold: 1.50; verdict: HEALTHY
```

The position is healthy. The collateral ratio is 1.67 which is above the target ratio of 1.5.

### Put the contracts on the chain

At this point we have two contracts.

-   `amm.eth` is the puddle. It holds ETH and USD, and its reserve ratio gives us a price.
-   `lending.eth` is the loan desk. It holds loans and decides whether they are healthy.

No new block is required for that inner call. Using the same classes from articles 2 and 5:

```python
# Same validators / Network / Blockchain as articles 2 and 5. 
nodes = ["Node A", "Alice-Node", "Bob-Node", "Farid-Node"]
validators = [
    Validator("Node A", 100),
    Validator("Alice-Node", 80),
    Validator("Bob-Node", 70),
    Validator("Farid-Node", 50),
]
network = Network(nodes, random.Random(7))
chain = Blockchain(validators)

#   amm     = the puddle    (AMMPool, which IS a SmartContract)
#   lending = the loan desk (ALSO a SmartContract). No water of its own.
amm = AMMPool("amm.eth", 50.0, 100_000.0)
lending = LendingProtocol("lending.eth", amm)

# 'Deploy' here is a receipt, not bytecode. The objects already exist in 
# memory. The notary files the form.
network.broadcast(Transaction("tx-deploy-amm", "Deploy AMMPool at amm.eth"), origin="Node A")
network.broadcast(Transaction("tx-deploy-lending", "Deploy LendingProtocol at lending.eth"), origin="Node A")
_, deploy_amm_block = network.include("Node A", "tx-deploy-amm", chain)
_, deploy_lending_block = network.include("Node A", "tx-deploy-lending", chain)

# Bob's loan, then Alice's pebble. Two shouts into the group chat, two stamps.
bob_loan, bob_tx, bob_block = submit_call(
    network,
    chain,
    "Bob-Node",
    "tx-open-loan",
    lending,
    "open_loan",
    borrower="Bob",
    collateral_eth=10.0,
    debt_usd=12_000.0,
)
alice_usd, alice_tx, alice_block = submit_call(
    network,
    chain,
    "Alice-Node",
    "tx-swap-1eth",
    amm,
    "swap_eth_for_usd",
    eth_in=1.0,
)
bob_ratio_after_pebble = lending.collateral_ratio(lending.loans["Bob"])
valid, message = chain.is_valid()
```

Alice’s 1 ETH sale barely registers on her — **but it moves the one number Bob’s entire position depends on**. **His collateral ratio slides from 1.67 to 1.60**. Still healthy, still above the 1.50 line — but Bob never touched his loan. He just happened to be priced against a puddle someone else disturbed.

> That’s the whole danger of an on-chain price feed in one sentence: _your_ safety depends on _everyone else’s_ behavior toward the same pool.

And that is where things get interesting. Because the blockchain has absolutely no idea what ETH is worth outside its own state.

### Introducing Oracles

A smart contract is deterministic. Every node executes the same transaction and must land on the same result — if one node computes `$2,000` and another computes `$1,742.31`, they no longer agree on the state of the blockchain, and the whole system has a rather serious problem.

That determinism comes with an awkward limitation: **a smart contract cannot simply look outside the blockchain for information**. It cannot make an HTTP request to an exchange, read a local file, check the weather, or ask an external database what happened five seconds ago.

> Every node needs to be able to execute the same logic from the same available inputs, so allowing arbitrary external information into that process would destroy the very consistency we rely on.

This is the same trade-off we have been seeing throughout the series. The blockchain is extremely good at agreeing on what happened **inside the system**. It is much less capable of knowing what is happening **outside the system**.

A lending protocol, however, needs information from outside. So somebody has to tell it.

That is the job of an **oracle**: a mechanism for bringing external information into the deterministic world of the blockchain.

For our toy implementation, we will keep this deliberately simple. A price feed is **just another smart contract at another address**, with storage for the reports it receives.

We will create a `PriceReport` to represent an individual oracle, and two small pieces of logic for the lending protocol: one to calculate the collateral ratio at a given price, and one to decide whether that ratio has crossed the liquidation threshold.

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PriceReport:
    source: str
    eth_price_usd: float

def collateral_ratio(
    collateral_eth: float, debt_usd: float, eth_price_usd: float
) -> float:
    if collateral_eth <= 0 or debt_usd <= 0 or eth_price_usd <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Collateral, debt, and price must be positive.")
    return collateral_eth * eth_price_usd / debt_usd

def should_liquidate(ratio: float, threshold: float = 1.5) -> bool:
    return ratio < threshold
```

> In a real oracle system, “source” would need to mean something more substantial than a string supplied by the caller. In our toy implementation, it is deliberately just a label — because I want the reader to see exactly where the trust problem begins.

The interesting question is no longer what the lending contract does once it has a price. We already know that part: multiply the collateral by the price, divide by the debt, and liquidate if the ratio falls below 1.5.

The interesting question is **which price should it use in the first place?**

That question turns out to be much harder.

### Take the median

Let’s start with the simplest possible price feed. It receives reports from different sources and stores them on-chain.

In this toy model, I’m splitting the oracle into two pieces: `PriceFeed` represents the on-chain feed that stores reports, while `MedianOracle` represents the aggregation rule that decides which of those reports the protocol should use.

```python
class PriceFeed(SmartContract):
    def __init__(self, address: str) -> None:
        """Create an empty feed at ``address``."""

        super().__init__(address)
        self.reports: list[PriceReport] = []

    def report(
        self,
        source: str,
        eth_price_usd: float,
    ) -> PriceReport:
        if eth_price_usd <= 0:
            raise ValueError(
                "Reported price must be positive."
            )

        posted = PriceReport(source, eth_price_usd)
        self.reports.append(posted)
        return posted

    @property
    def latest(self) -> PriceReport:
        return self.reports[-1]

    @property
    def price(self) -> float:
        return statistics.median(
            report.eth_price_usd
            for report in self.reports
        )
```

There are two interesting things hiding in this very small class.

-   First, the feed does not know whether a report is true. The `source` field is just a label.
-   Second, the feed now has a choice about what it considers its price. It can use `latest`, meaning whatever the most recent report said, or it can aggregate several reports using some rule.

For our first experiment, let’s give it three reports: two around $2,000 and one deliberately wrong report at $1,200.

```python
# Fourth box, fourth address.
feed = PriceFeed("feed.eth")

network.broadcast(
    Transaction(
        "tx-deploy-feed",
        "Deploy PriceFeed at feed.eth",
    ),
    origin="Node A",
)

_, deploy_feed_block = network.include(
    "Node A",
    "tx-deploy-feed",
    chain,
)

assert isinstance(deploy_feed_block, Block)

collateral_eth = 10
debt_usd = 12_000

incoming_reports = [
    ("tx-report-a", "independent-feed-a", 2_005.0),
    ("tx-report-lie", "malicious-feed", 1_200.0),
    ("tx-report-b", "independent-feed-b", 1_995.0),
]

print(
    f"Same loan: {collateral_eth} ETH / "
    f"${debt_usd:,} debt. Threshold 1.50."
)

print(
    f"Deployed {feed.address} "
    f"in Block #{deploy_feed_block.index}"
)

print()

for tx_id, source, price in incoming_reports:
    _, tx, block = submit_call(
        network,
        chain,
        "Node A",
        tx_id,
        feed,
        "report",
        source=source,
        eth_price_usd=price,
    )

    assert isinstance(block, Block)

    latest_ratio = collateral_ratio(
        collateral_eth,
        debt_usd,
        feed.latest.eth_price_usd,
    )

    latest_verdict = (
        "LIQUIDATE (wrong)"
        if should_liquidate(latest_ratio)
        else "HEALTHY"
    )

    print(block)

    print(
        f"  latest on {feed.address}: "
        f"${feed.latest.eth_price_usd:,.0f}/ETH "
        f"from {feed.latest.source}"
    )

    print(
        f"  if lending trusts only Block #{block.index}: "
        f"ratio {latest_ratio:.2f} -> {latest_verdict}"
    )
```

And this is where the problem becomes visible:

```python-repl
Same loan: 10 ETH / $12,000 debt. Threshold 1.50.
Deployed feed.eth in Block #5

Block #6 proposed by Node A
  data: feed.eth.report(
      source='independent-feed-a',
      eth_price_usd=2005.0
  )

  latest on feed.eth: $2,005/ETH from independent-feed-a
  if lending trusts only Block #6:
      ratio 1.67 -> HEALTHY

Block #7 proposed by Node A
  data: feed.eth.report(
      source='malicious-feed',
      eth_price_usd=1200.0
  )

  latest on feed.eth: $1,200/ETH from malicious-feed
  if lending trusts only Block #7:
      ratio 1.00 -> LIQUIDATE (wrong)

Block #8 proposed by Node A
  data: feed.eth.report(
      source='independent-feed-b',
      eth_price_usd=1995.0
  )

  latest on feed.eth: $1,995/ETH from independent-feed-b
  if lending trusts only Block #8:
      ratio 1.66 -> HEALTHY
```

The loan has not changed at all. Bob still has 10 ETH locked as collateral and still owes $12,000.

What changed was the number that the lending protocol treated as the price of ETH.

When the latest report says $2,005, Bob’s collateral ratio is 1.67 and the position is healthy. When the latest report suddenly says $1,200, the ratio falls to exactly 1.00 and the same liquidation rule says Bob should be liquidated. When another report of $1,995 arrives, the ratio climbs back to 1.66.

Nothing about the blockchain itself has gone wrong here. Every report was a valid transaction, every transaction was included in a valid block, and the `PriceFeed` stored exactly what it was instructed to store.

> The problem is that **a valid piece of blockchain state is not necessarily a true statement about the outside world**.

So instead of trusting whichever report arrived last, one simple approach is the median: sort the values and take the one in the middle — yup, it’s that simple.

```python
class MedianOracle:
    def __init__(
        self,
        reports: list[PriceReport],
    ) -> None:
        if not reports:
            raise ValueError(
                "At least one price report is required."
            )

        self.reports = reports

    @property
    def price(self) -> float:
        return statistics.median(
            report.eth_price_usd
            for report in self.reports
        )
```

Now we can apply that rule to the three reports already stored in `feed.eth`.

```python
median_oracle = MedianOracle(feed.reports)

median_ratio = collateral_ratio(
    collateral_eth,
    debt_usd,
    median_oracle.price,
)

print(
    f"Median of every report stored at {feed.address}: "
    f"${median_oracle.price:,.0f}/ETH"
)

print(
    f"If lending reads the median instead of the latest Block: "
    f"ratio {median_ratio:.2f} -> HEALTHY"
)

print(
    f"Chain length: {len(chain.chain)}. "
    "The three reports are still sitting on their own Blocks."
)
```

The median is $1,995, giving Bob a collateral ratio of 1.66.

Why median rather than average? **Because the median is resistant to a single extreme outlier.** With reports of $2,005, $1,200 and $1,995, the average is pulled down by the malicious report, while the median simply takes the middle value: $1,995.

This is a useful defence, but it is important to understand what it actually defended against.

It did not make the AMM more honest. The AMM was already being completely honest about its own state. If somebody trades a large amount of ETH into the pool, its reserves really do change, and its reserve ratio really does change with them.

The defence is instead about **which information the lending protocol chooses to treat as authoritative**.

### More oracles ≠ more truth

The same problem appears in our toy example in another form. The `source` field looks reassuring because we have names such as `independent-feed-a` and `independent-feed-b`, but the blockchain has no idea whether those sources are actually independent.

The blockchain gives us a remarkably strong guarantee about the information it contains: nodes can agree on what was submitted and what the contracts did with it.

It does not give us a guarantee that somebody submitted the truth.

At this point, our little financial system has all the pieces needed to become dangerous. The AMM provides a price based on its reserves. The lending protocol uses a price to decide whether a loan is safe. The price feed provides another route for information to enter the system. Every individual component can behave exactly according to its rules while the overall system still produces a very bad outcome.

The next question is what happens when someone deliberately takes advantage of that gap.

Which is a story for another time.

body:
* * *

#### The one time gossip pays off

In my [previous article on permissioned chains](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/introducing-permissioned-chains-1d8a71f5b09a), we encountered the problem of race conditions.

In a system where transactions are constantly being proposed against shared state, two perfectly legitimate transactions can race against each other. One may change the state before the other reaches validation, making the second transaction stale. Multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) catches that conflict; the client can then re-execute against the latest state and try again.

That got me wondering: **what happens in public chains, where participants may not even see the same information at the same time?**

Transactions and blocks have to propagate across a distributed network, and that propagation isn’t instantaneous. A transaction might reach one node before another. A block might arrive after a competing block has already been seen elsewhere. At any given moment, different participants can therefore have different views of what is happening.

So what does each participant actually know at any given moment — and how does the network eventually converge on a shared history?

This article explores how this gap is plugged on public blockchains.

As before, all my code can be found in [my GitHub repository.](https://github.com/tituslhy/Blockchain/blob/main/notebooks/5.%20mempools_and_oracles.ipynb)

### The idea of networks

**“The blockchain”** is **not** a single thing sitting somewhere on the internet. A blockchain is a **sequence of blocks**. But that sequence has to be stored, checked, and updated by computers participating in the blockchain network. These computers are called **nodes**.

A node is simply a computer running the blockchain’s software. It maintains its own local view of the blockchain and communicates with other nodes over the network.

The **network** is therefore the collection of nodes and the connections between them. The blockchain is the history those nodes are collectively maintaining.

You can think of it like a shared document, except there is no single document sitting on a central server. Instead, many participants keep their own copy and communicate with one another to keep those copies in agreement.

That distinction becomes important because the copies are not necessarily identical at every instant.

When a new transaction is created, it has to travel through the network before other nodes can learn about it. When a new block is created, it also has to propagate through the network. Network communication takes time, so different nodes can temporarily have different information. Conceptually:

```plaintext
                 NETWORK
        ┌───────────┼───────────┐
        │           │           │
      NODE A      NODE B      NODE C
        │           │           │
     mempool     mempool     mempool
        │           │           │
        ▼           ▼           ▼
   candidate     candidate    candidate
   transactions  transactions transactions
        │           │           │
        └───────────┼───────────┘
                    │
              consensus /
             block creation
                    │
                    ▼
              NEW BLOCK
                    │
                    ▼
              propagated
              through network
                    │
        ┌───────────┼───────────┐
        ▼           ▼           ▼
      NODE A      NODE B      NODE C
        │           │           │
        └── blockchain history ┘
```

### This is where **mempools** come in.

A mempool is a node’s local collection of valid transactions that it has heard about but that have not yet been included in a block.

There is therefore no single, global mempool shared by the entire network.

Think of it like a group chat where everyone is receiving the same messages, but not necessarily at the same time or in the same order. Alice might have already received messages A, B, and C. Bob might have A and C but not B. Carol might have heard about B first.

They’re all participating in the same conversation. They just don’t have exactly the same view of it yet.

Our toy network models this deliberately. Each node gets its own mempool, and transactions propagate between nodes independently.

Assuming we are recording a list of transactions in a public blockchain:

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass 

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Transaction:
    tx_id: str
    description: str
```

A network is then a set of nodes, each with its own mempool:

```python
class Network:
    """A set of nodes, each holding its own local mempool.

    There is no shared, global mempool here on purpose: `broadcast`
    delivers a transaction to each peer independently and probabilistically,
    modelling how gossip reaches honest nodes at different times.
    """

    def __init__(self, node_names: list[str], rng: random.Random) -> None:
        """Create one empty mempool per node.
        """
        if not node_names:
            raise ValueError("A network needs at least one node.")
        self.node_names = list(node_names)
        self.rng = rng
        self.mempools: dict[str, dict[str, Transaction]] = {
            name: {} for name in node_names
        }

    def broadcast(self, transaction: Transaction, origin: str) -> None:
        """Deliver a transaction to its origin, then probabilistically to peers.
        """
        if origin not in self.mempools:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown origin node: {origin}")
        self.mempools[origin][transaction.tx_id] = transaction
        for name in self.node_names:
            if name != origin and self.rng.random() < 0.5:
                self.mempools[name][transaction.tx_id] = transaction

    def mempool_ids(self, node_name: str) -> list[str]:
        """Return a node's currently known transaction IDs, sorted.
        """
        if node_name not in self.mempools:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown node: {node_name}")
        return sorted(self.mempools[node_name])
```

The important ideas here are that:

-   The network does not contain a single blockchain object
-   The network has no global mempool

Instead, each node maintains its own local copy of the chain. The network is the communication layer through which nodes exchange transactions and blocks.

At some point, honest nodes may look like this:

```plaintext
Alice
  blockchain: [B1, B2, B3]
  mempool:    [TX4, TX5]

Bob
  blockchain: [B1, B2, B3]
  mempool:    [TX4]

Carol
  blockchain: [B1, B2, B3]
  mempool:    [TX5, TX6]
```

Their blockchain histories currently agree, but their mempools do not.

### Gossip: Useful precisely because it is imperfect

Gossip is how transactions spread through the network. A node forwards information to its peers, which can then forward it to their peers, and so on.

It improves the chance that other nodes — including a future block proposer — receive a transaction. But it does not guarantee that every node receives it immediately, or even that every node has heard about it at the same moment.

Our code makes this imperfection explicit. We use a seeded random generator so the demonstration is repeatable. The `50%` probability is deliberately artificial; it gives us a simple way to model transactions reaching honest nodes at different times.

Watch for the different transaction lists at each node, rather than treating any one node as having the network’s definitive mempool:

```python
nodes = ["Node A", "SketchyGuy-Node", "Emma-Node", "Farid-Node"]
network = Network(nodes, random.Random(7))
transactions = [
    Transaction("tx1", "Alice pays Bob"),
    Transaction("tx2", "Carol pays Titus"),
    Transaction("tx3", "Titus pays Alice"),
    Transaction("tx4", "Bob pays Carol"),
]
origins = ["Node A", "SketchyGuy-Node", "Emma-Node", "Node A"]

for transaction, origin in zip(transactions, origins):
    network.broadcast(transaction, origin)

print("Each node has its own mempool:")
for node in nodes:
    print(f"  {node}: {network.mempool_ids(node)}")

mempool_sizes = [len(network.mempool_ids(node)) for node in nodes]
print(f"Average local mempool size: {statistics.mean(mempool_sizes):.2f}")
```

> Pause and predict: after four broadcasts, will every node have all four transaction IDs?

Output:

```python-repl
Each node has its own mempool:
  Node A: ['tx1', 'tx2', 'tx3', 'tx4']
  SketchyGuy-Node: ['tx1', 'tx2', 'tx4']
  Emma-Node: ['tx1', 'tx3', 'tx4']
  Farid-Node: ['tx2', 'tx3', 'tx4']
Average local mempool size: 3.25
```

Node A has all four transaction IDs, while every other node is missing one.

Nothing has gone wrong. The nodes simply have **different views because the transactions have not propagated to everyone yet**.

And this distinction matters when we move from transactions to blocks.

A transaction being present in one node’s mempool does not mean that every node knows about it. Likewise, a transaction being known by many nodes does not mean that it has become part of the blockchain.

A transaction can be **submitted** to a node, **propagated** through gossip, **included** in a proposed block, and eventually **confirmed** as that block becomes part of the accepted chain.

Each stage depends on information reaching the relevant participants.

Which brings us to the next question:

**If a block proposer can only see the transactions that have reached its own node, what happens when it has an incomplete view of the network?**

### From transactions to block proposals

Transactions sitting in mempools are not yet part of the blockchain. A node must turn these transactions into a block proposal.

In a [proof-of-stake blockchain](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/proof-of-stake-the-mining-free-blockchain-ddae684ffec5), that job is assigned to a validator selected by the protocol. The proposer looks at the transactions available to it and constructs a candidate block.

And there is an important constraint here: **A proposer can only choose from the information it has received.**

#### Simply sending a transaction directly to the next scheduled proposer is not a great solution.

The scheduled proposer might be delayed. It might be temporarily unavailable. It might refuse to relay the transaction. And even if that proposer receives it, the rest of the network still needs an opportunity to learn about and independently validate the resulting block.

#### **Gossip solves a different problem.**

Rather than trying to predict exactly which validator will propose the next block, a transaction can spread through the network so that many independently validating nodes have an opportunity to receive it.

That means a future proposer is more likely to have the transaction in its local mempool when its slot arrives. The question is:

> **_“Which transactions does the proposer know about when it is time to build a block?”_**

### Introducing the idea of slots

We now need one more piece of the puzzle: **time**.

Proof of stake divides time into discrete **slots**. For each slot, the protocol determines which eligible validator gets the opportunity to propose a block (like my elaboration in my [previous article on PoS blockchains](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/proof-of-stake-the-mining-free-blockchain-ddae684ffec5)).

All validators need to be able to independently determine who that proposer is. Otherwise, different validators could disagree about who was entitled to propose the block.

For this article, I do this deterministically in code. I’m deliberately simplifying the real mechanism here: what matters is that every validator can independently arrive at the same proposer assignment.

```python
def assign_proposer(
    validators: list[Validator], slot: int, epoch_seed: str
) -> Validator:
    """Deterministically pick a slot's proposer from a stake-weighted lottery.

    This hashes a documented ``epoch_seed`` and ``slot`` number so every
    validator can reproduce the same assignment independently -- a real
    protocol needs that reproducibility (a stand-in for VRF/RANDAO-style
    eligibility proofs), whereas per-call proposer selection does not.
    """
    if not validators or sum(v.stake for v in validators) <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Proposer assignment needs positive validator stake.")
    seed = hashlib.sha256(f"{epoch_seed}:{slot}".encode()).digest()
    pick = int.from_bytes(seed, "big") % sum(v.stake for v in validators)
    cumulative = 0
    for validator in validators:
        cumulative += validator.stake
        if pick < cumulative:
            return validator
    raise RuntimeError("Unreachable proposer-selection state.")
```

The epoch seed is shared, and every validator can run the same calculation to arrive at the same result.

> Caveat: Real proof-of-stake protocols use more sophisticated randomness and selection mechanisms. [Ethereum](https://ethereum.org/developers/docs/consensus-mechanisms/pos/block-proposal/), for example, uses RANDAO-based pseudo-random proposer selection, weighted by effective validator balance.

And now we have all the pieces needed for the interesting part.

We have a network where nodes can have different local views, a gossip mechanism that takes time to propagate information, and a protocol that assigns a specific proposer to each slot.

So what happens if **the protocol correctly selects the next proposer, but that proposer has not yet received the previous block?**

### A fork caused by delay, not dishonesty

We will re-use our `Block` and `Blockchain` classes from the PoS article. This time, we’ll schedule different proposers while deliberately giving them **different views of the chain**.

The slot 2 proposer has not received Block #1, so it honestly builds on the latest tip it knows: Genesis. Both candidate blocks therefore point to Genesis.

```python
validators = [
    Validator("Node A", 100),
    Validator("SketchyGuy-Node", 80),
    Validator("Emma-Node", 70),
    Validator("Farid-Node", 50),
]
validators_by_name = {validator.name: validator for validator in validators}
epoch_seed = "notebook-5"

chain = Blockchain(validators)
genesis = chain.chain[0]
slot_1_proposer = assign_proposer(validators, 1, epoch_seed)
slot_2_proposer = assign_proposer(validators, 2, epoch_seed)
assert slot_1_proposer.name != slot_2_proposer.name

block_1 = chain.propose_candidate(
    ", ".join(network.mempool_ids(slot_1_proposer.name)), slot_1_proposer.name
)
proposal_time_views = {
    "Node A": {genesis.hash},
    "SketchyGuy-Node": {genesis.hash, block_1.hash},
    "Emma-Node": {genesis.hash, block_1.hash},
    "Farid-Node": {genesis.hash, block_1.hash},
}
assert block_1.hash not in proposal_time_views[slot_2_proposer.name]
block_2_alt = chain.propose_candidate(
    ", ".join(network.mempool_ids(slot_2_proposer.name)), slot_2_proposer.name
)

print(f"Slot 1 proposer: {slot_1_proposer.name} creates Block #1.")
print(
    f"Slot 2 proposer: {slot_2_proposer.name} has NOT received Block #1; "
    "it builds on Genesis."
)
print("\nPropagation fork (both arrows leave Genesis):")
print("          Genesis")
print("     +----+----+")
print("     |         |")
print("   Block #1    Block #2-alt")
print(f"   {slot_1_proposer.name:<12} {slot_2_proposer.name}")
```

> Pause and predict: if the next proposer has not seen a valid earlier block, can deterministic proposer assignment alone prevent a fork?

The output:

```python-repl
Slot 1 proposer: Farid-Node creates Block #1.
Slot 2 proposer: Node A has NOT received Block #1; it builds on Genesis.

Propagation fork (both arrows leave Genesis):
          Genesis
     +----+----+
     |         |
   Block #1    Block #2-alt
   Farid-Node   Node A
```

Farid-Node proposes Block #1, while Node A honestly proposes Block #2-alt from Genesis because its local view is delayed.

**The fork is caused by information asymmetry, not dishonest behaviour.**

This is an important distinction.

Farid-Node and Node A are two _different_ validators, each honestly proposing for its own correctly assigned slot. Neither validator has signed two conflicting blocks for the same slot.

So, in this scenario, **neither validator gets slashed**. They simply proposed blocks based on different views of the latest chain tip.

The deterministic proposer schedule answered one question:

> **_Who is supposed to propose?_**

It did not answer another:

> **_What block does that proposer believe is the latest valid block?_**

And that second question depends on network propagation.

### Attestations: turning local views into votes

We now have two competing blocks, both produced honestly:

-   **Block #1** was proposed by Farid-Node in slot 1.
-   **Block #2-alt** was proposed by Node A in slot 2, because Node A had not yet received Block #1.

The network now needs to decide which branch to follow.

This is where **attestations** come in.

Validators don’t magically acquire a global view of the network before voting. They attest to the chain they currently see. In our toy model, that means each validator votes for the candidate tip present in its local view.

This gives us an interesting consequence:

> **_Different validators can vote for different blocks without any of them necessarily being dishonest._**

At the moment of attestation, Block #1 has had longer to propagate. Block #2-alt is newer and, in our deliberately simplified scenario, has only reached its own proposer.

We therefore derive each validator’s vote directly from the blocks it has actually received rather than hand-picking the votes to produce a particular outcome.

The code below then assigns each vote the validator’s stake and adds the stake supporting each candidate.

```python
def attestation_weight(
    tip_hash: str,
    votes: dict[str, str],
    validators_by_name: dict[str, Validator],
) -> int:
    """Sum the stake of every validator whose vote names ``tip_hash``."""
    unknown = set(votes) - set(validators_by_name)
    if unknown:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown attesters: {sorted(unknown)}")
    return sum(
        validators_by_name[name].stake
        for name, voted_hash in votes.items()
        if voted_hash == tip_hash
    )
```

Our fork-choice function is intentionally tiny. It simply selects the candidate with the greatest attestation weight.

```python
def fork_choice_two_tips(
    candidate_tips: list[Block],
    votes: dict[str, str],
    validators_by_name: dict[str, Validator],
) -> tuple[Block, dict[str, int]]:
    """Pick the candidate tip with the most attestation-weighted stake."""
    candidate_hashes = {block.hash for block in candidate_tips}
    invalid_votes = set(votes.values()) - candidate_hashes
    if invalid_votes:
        raise ValueError("An attestation names an unknown candidate tip.")
    weights = {
        block.hash: attestation_weight(block.hash, votes, validators_by_name)
        for block in candidate_tips
    }
    if len(set(weights.values())) != len(weights):
        raise ValueError("Teaching model requires an explicit tie-break rule.")
    winner_hash = max(weights, key=weights.get)
    return next(block for block in candidate_tips if block.hash == winner_hash), weights
```

There is one deliberate simplification here.

A real blockchain’s fork-choice mechanism is considerably more sophisticated than “add up the stake and pick the largest number.” It has to account for things such as the protocol’s voting rules, chain structure, and tie-breaking behaviour.

But for this article, we only need one idea:

> **_Fork choice gives weight to the different views held by validators._**

Let’s see what happens with our actual network state.

```python
# By attestation time, Block #1 (slot 1) has had longer to propagate, so every
# node that already had it in `proposal_time_views` still has it. Block #2-alt
# is brand new: only its own proposer has received it so far. No node holds
# both, so each vote below is just "the block this node has actually seen" —
# read out of `proposal_time_views`, not hand-picked to fit a story.
attestation_time_views = dict(proposal_time_views)
attestation_time_views[slot_2_proposer.name] = attestation_time_views[
    slot_2_proposer.name
] | {block_2_alt.hash}

def vote_for_known_tip(known_block_hashes: set[str]) -> str:
    """Return the block hash a validator with this local view would vote for.

    Prefers Block #1 whenever it is known -- in this scenario no validator
    ever holds both candidates at once, so this never needs a real
    tie-break rule between two simultaneously-known tips.
    """
    return block_1.hash if block_1.hash in known_block_hashes else block_2_alt.hash

votes = {
    name: vote_for_known_tip(known_hashes)
    for name, known_hashes in attestation_time_views.items()
}

print("\nView-derived attestations:")
for name, voted_hash in votes.items():
    label = "Block #1" if voted_hash == block_1.hash else "Block #2-alt"
    print(f"  {name} received {label} and votes for {label}.")

winner, weights = fork_choice_two_tips(
    [block_1, block_2_alt], votes, validators_by_name
)
winner_label = "Block #1" if winner.hash == block_1.hash else "Block #2-alt"
print(f"Block #1 stake weight: {weights[block_1.hash]}")
print(f"Block #2-alt stake weight: {weights[block_2_alt.hash]}")
print(f"Canonical tip: {winner_label}")

chain.accept_candidate(winner)
valid, message = chain.is_valid()
print(
    f"Chain length after fork resolution: {len(chain.chain)}; "
    f"valid? {valid} -- {message}"
)
```

The output:

```python-repl
View-derived attestations:
  Node A received Block #2-alt and votes for Block #2-alt.
  SketchyGuy-Node received Block #1 and votes for Block #1.
  Emma-Node received Block #1 and votes for Block #1.
  Farid-Node received Block #1 and votes for Block #1.
Block #1 stake weight: 200
Block #2-alt stake weight: 100
Canonical tip: Block #1
Chain length after fork resolution: 2; valid? True -- Chain is valid.
```

Block #1 wins because SketchyGuy-Node, Emma-Node, and Farid-Node already had it in their local view, contributing 80 + 70 + 50 = 200 stake, versus 100 stake from Node A, which has only its own Block #2-alt proposal.

**Fork choice follows the attestation weight behind each received view, not the block’s slot number.**

### Thinking about what we just learnt

A transaction originates somewhere. Gossip carries it between nodes. Different nodes receive it at different times. A proposer builds a block from its local view. Other validators attest to the blocks they have seen. Fork choice then gives the network a mechanism for converging on one history.

**That is the connection between the network and the blockchain.**

The blockchain is the shared history. The network is the collection of nodes that propagate, validate, propose, and vote on that history.

At any given moment, individual nodes may have incomplete or even conflicting views. But through communication and consensus, those local views can eventually converge on a common chain.

In other words, we have been studying how a blockchain deals with **incomplete and inconsistent information inside its own network**.

But there is a more fundamental problem.

Suppose the transaction says:

```
"Team A won the football match 2–1."
```

Our validators can check whether the transaction is properly formed and whether it was included in a valid block. But they cannot determine from the blockchain itself whether Team A actually won the match.

The network can agree on a fact. **It cannot, by itself, discover whether that fact is true in the outside world.**

So how does information from outside the blockchain get into the network in the first place? And once it arrives, **how can the blockchain trust it?**

That’s a rabbit hole for another time: **oracles.**
