body:
* * *

#### A blockchain where the guest list matters

In my previous articles, I covered blockchains that operate using (i) [proof-of-work (PoW)](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/understanding-blockchains-from-scratch-f14c454af32f), aka mining, and (ii) [proof-of-stake (PoS)](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/proof-of-stake-the-mining-free-blockchain-ddae684ffec5). In the [third article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/inside-opencerts-how-merkle-trees-verify-singapores-digital-diplomas-61f60d13700e), I extended the PoS blockchain with Merkle trees to explore how the same ideas can be used to create tamper-evident educational credentials.

All three articles have something in common: **the blockchain is public and permissionless.**

In the PoW blockchain, miners race to perform computational work for the right to add the next block. In the PoS blockchain, proposers are randomly selected, weighted by the stake they put up. Other participants then independently verify that the proposed block follows the rules.

But nobody ever had to prove who they were. If `"Sketchy-Guy-Node”` played by the rules, his block does get added to the blockchain as well. That makes sense when the whole point is to build a network that anyone can participate in.

But what if that isn’t what we want?

Imagine three banks running a shared settlement ledger. They don’t necessarily want random strangers joining the network. They don’t need a proof-of-work energy bill or a speculative token just so participants can stake it. And they probably don’t want `["51% of the CPU"](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/1/51-attack.asp)` [or](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/1/51-attack.asp) `["51% of the stake"](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/1/51-attack.asp)` deciding the truth when the actual participants are a small, known, named group of institutions — institutions that would very much like a court to be able to determine **who signed what**.

This is where **permissioned blockchains** come in.

Instead of asking:

> **Who has earned the right to write the next block?**

we can ask:

> **Who is allowed to participate, and whose approval is required for this transaction?**

That seemingly small change gives us a very different kind of blockchain. In this article, we’ll build our own permissioned consortium chain, modelled loosely on [**Hyperledger Fabric**](https://hyperledger-fabric.readthedocs.io/en/latest/whatis.html).

> Hyperledger Fabric is an open-source, enterprise-grade permissioned distributed ledger platform designed for situations where the participants in a blockchain network are **known organizations rather than anonymous strangers**. Unlike Bitcoin or Ethereum, participants have cryptographic identities, and policies can specify which organizations are allowed to perform particular actions or must approve particular transactions. Its modular architecture was designed with enterprise use cases such as banking, finance, insurance and supply chains in mind.

And the architecture is quite different from the toy PoW and PoS chains we’ve built so far. Our Fabric-inspired chain will follow:

`**execute → endorse → order → validate**`

Multiple known organizations can independently execute a proposed transaction and cryptographically endorse its result. An ordering service then determines transaction order and packages transactions into blocks. Finally, peers validate that the required endorsements and other rules have been satisfied before committing the transaction to their ledgers.

Same broad goal — multiple parties maintaining a shared, tamper-evident history.

**Very different assumptions about who those parties are.**

As before, all my codes for this article can be found in my [GitHub repository.](https://github.com/tituslhy/Blockchain/blob/main/notebooks/4.%20permissioned_chains.ipynb)

### Writing our Membership Service — gives permission to even show up

`MembershipService` is a deliberately tiny stand-in for one part of what Hyperledger Fabric handles through [**Membership Service Providers (MSPs)**](https://hyperledger-fabric.readthedocs.io/en/latest/msp.html). In a real Fabric network, participants have cryptographic identities — typically X.509 certificates issued by trusted Certificate Authorities (CAs) — while MSP configuration defines which identities an organization recognizes and what roles those identities can play.

We’re going to collapse all of that machinery into a humble Python class 😂

No entry in the registry, no participation: `Peer.endorse()` checks `is_registered()` before doing anything else and throws if you’re not on the list.

This is the permissioned chain’s first and most fundamental departure from the previous articles:

> **Identity is a precondition, not an emergent property of computational effort or economic stake.**

```python
import hashlib

def sha256(data: str) -> str:
    """Return the hex-encoded SHA-256 digest of a UTF-8 encoded string."""
    return hashlib.sha256(data.encode()).hexdigest()

class MembershipService:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        """Initialize an empty registry of member organizations."""
        self.registered_orgs: set[str] = set()

    def register(self, org_name: str) -> None:
        """Add an organization to the registry, granting it participant identity."""
        print(f"  [MembershipService] Registered org: {org_name}")
        self.registered_orgs.add(org_name)

    def is_registered(self, org_name: str) -> bool:
        """Return True if the given organization is a registered participant."""
        return org_name in self.registered_orgs
```

### Writing the ledger’s state: a versioned key-value world, not just a list of blocks

In this blockchain, multiple orgs can _concurrently_ propose transactions against the same shared state, so we need to answer a sharper question than “what’s the current balance?” — we need to ask **“what version of this key was I looking at when I computed my answer?”**

Our `WorldState` therefore tracks two things: the current value associated with each key, and the version of that key.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class WorldState:
    """Versioned key-value ledger state: current balances 
    plus a per-key write version counter."""

    balances: dict[str, float] = field(default_factory=dict)
    versions: dict[str, int] = field(default_factory=dict)

    def version_of(self, key: str) -> int:
        """Return the current version number of a key, or 0 if it 
        has never been written."""
        return self.versions.get(key, 0)

@dataclass
class ExecutionResult:
    """The proposed effect of a chaincode run: what it wants to write, 
    and the versions it read."""

    write_set: dict[str, float]
    read_versions: dict[str, int]
```

Hang onto `version_of()` — it's the hook the whole optimistic-concurrency story further down is built on.

`ExecutionResult` is what a chaincode run produces: a `write_set` (what it wants to change) and `read_versions` (what versions it _assumed_ were current when it computed that write set). Neither is applied to `WorldState` yet — this is a **proposal**, not a commit.

### Chaincode: the business logic, run speculatively

“Chaincode” is Fabric’s term for the business logic encoded in a smart contract. `transfer_chaincode` is about as simple as one gets: check a balance, then compute a new pair of balances.

The important part isn’t the arithmetic — it’s **when this runs**.

Executing this function does not touch the real ledger. It runs speculatively against the current state and produces an `ExecutionResult`: the values it wants to write, plus the versions of the values it read along the way.

An endorsing peer can then sign the result of that simulation.

For our toy implementation, we’ll make this especially visible: multiple peers independently execute the same proposal, hash the resulting `write_set`, and we’ll require those hashes to agree. Real Fabric carries considerably more information in its proposal responses and endorsements, but the intuition we’re trying to capture is the same:

```python
def transfer_chaincode(state: WorldState, frm: str, to: str, amount: float) -> ExecutionResult:
    if state.balances.get(frm, 0) < amount:
        raise ValueError(f"Insufficient funds: {frm} has {state.balances.get(frm, 0)}, needs {amount}")
    return ExecutionResult(
        write_set={frm: state.balances.get(frm, 0) - amount, to: state.balances.get(to, 0) + amount},
        read_versions={frm: state.version_of(frm), to: state.version_of(to)},
    )
```

**Execution produces a proposed state change; it does not commit that change.**

### And now: Execute → Endorse → Order → Validate

Why bother separating execution from ordering?

Public and permissioned blockchains still share one awkward problem: multiple organizations that do not necessarily trust one another are trying to maintain a shared ledger.

Fabric tackles that problem by separating responsibilities.

First, endorsing peers **simulate** a proposed transaction and sign the resulting proposal response. The client collects enough endorsements to satisfy the transaction’s endorsement policy.

Only then does the transaction move to the ordering stage.

The ordering service has a deliberately narrower job: **establish a consistent transaction order and package transactions into blocks.** It does not execute the chaincode to decide what the transaction should do.

Our toy `OrderingService.order()` is therefore almost insultingly simple on purpose:

`proposals in → ordered proposals out`

```python
from collections.abc import Callable

@dataclass
class Endorsement:
    peer_name: str
    result_hash: str

@dataclass
class Peer:
    name: str
    membership: MembershipService

    def endorse(self, chaincode: Callable, state: WorldState, *args) -> tuple[Endorsement, ExecutionResult]:
        if not self.membership.is_registered(self.name):
            raise PermissionError(f"{self.name} is not a registered participant.")
        result = chaincode(state, *args)
        result_hash = sha256(json.dumps(result.write_set, sort_keys=True))
        return Endorsement(peer_name=self.name, result_hash=result_hash), result

@dataclass
class ProposedTransaction:
    description: str
    endorsements: list[Endorsement]
    execution_result: ExecutionResult

class OrderingService:
    def __init__(self, name: str) -> None:
        self.name = name

    def order(self, proposals: list[ProposedTransaction]) -> list[ProposedTransaction]:
        print(f"  [{self.name}] Sequencing {len(proposals)} proposal(s).")
        return list(proposals)
```

Real Fabric ordering services are distributed systems in their own right. Modern Fabric deployments can use a Raft-based ordering service so multiple ordering nodes agree on the sequence of transactions even if individual nodes fail.

And importantly, being ordered does **not** mean a transaction is valid.

That comes next.

### Finally, the ledger itself

This block looks quite different from the PoW and PoS blocks we built earlier.

There’s no `nonce`, because nobody is mining. There’s no `proposer` or `stake`, because nobody is winning a validator lottery either. Instead, there’s an `orderer` field: not the winner of a competition, just a record of which ordering service sequenced these transactions into this block.

There’s another important difference.

In our earlier toy chains, we tended to ask whether an entire block was valid before accepting it.

Fabric separates those ideas more sharply:

> **A transaction can be ordered into a block and still fail validation afterward.**

If that happens, the transaction remains part of the blockchain’s immutable history, but its write set is **not** applied to world state.

That distinction is important enough that we’ll model it explicitly.

```python
class Block:
    """A tamper-evident block carrying a batch of ordered transactions, 
    each pending its own validation code."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        index: int,
        transactions: list[ProposedTransaction],
        previous_hash: str,
        orderer: str,
    ) -> None:
        """Create and hash a new block from an already-ordered batch of 
        transactions.
        """
        self.index = index
        self.timestamp = time.time()
        self.transactions = transactions
        self.previous_hash = previous_hash
        self.orderer = orderer

        # Validation happens after ordering.
        self.validation_codes = ["NOT_VALIDATED"] * len(transactions)

        self.hash = self.compute_hash()

    def compute_hash(self) -> str:
        """Compute this block's SHA-256 hash over its index, timestamp, 
        transactions, previous hash, and orderer."""
        tx_contents = [
            {
                "description": tx.description,
                "write_set": tx.execution_result.write_set,
                "read_versions": tx.execution_result.read_versions,
                "endorsements": [
                    {
                        "peer_name": e.peer_name,
                        "result_hash": e.result_hash,
                    }
                    for e in tx.endorsements
                ],
            }
            for tx in self.transactions
        ]

        block_contents = json.dumps(
            {
                "index": self.index,
                "timestamp": self.timestamp,
                "transactions": tx_contents,
                "previous_hash": self.previous_hash,
                "orderer": self.orderer,
            },
            sort_keys=True,
        )
        return hashlib.sha256(block_contents.encode()).hexdigest()

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        """Return a human-readable summary of the block, including 
        per-transaction validation codes."""
        return (
            f"Block #{self.index}: "
            f"{len(self.transactions)} transaction(s), "
            f"validation={self.validation_codes}\n"
        )
```

#### A very different looking blockchain

Notice that the main event, `validate_and_commit_block()` below, happens **after a block has already been created and appended to the chain**.

That is a very different mental model from the `is_valid()` method in the previous articles. There, validation meant re-walking the blockchain and checking that the chain itself had not been tampered with.

Here, we’re asking a different question:

> **Which transactions inside this already-ordered block are actually allowed to change world state?**

The block stays in the chain either way. Validation determines whether each transaction’s write set gets applied.

```python
class PermissionedBlockchain:
    """A consortium ledger where blocks are cut by ordering, then 
    validated (and applied to state) after the fact."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        required_endorsers: set[str],
        min_endorsements: int,
        orderer_name: str,
    ) -> None:
        """Initialize the chain with an empty genesis block and an empty world 
        state.
        """
        self.required_endorsers = required_endorsers
        self.min_endorsements = min_endorsements
        self.orderer_name = orderer_name

        self.chain: list[Block] = [
            Block(
                index=0,
                transactions=[],
                previous_hash="0" * 64,
                orderer=orderer_name,
            )
        ]

        self.state = WorldState()

    def add_ordered_block(
        self,
        transactions: list[ProposedTransaction],
    ) -> Block:
        """Cut a new block from an already-ordered batch of transactions and 
        append it to the chain.

        This is the ordering-service side of the pipeline: it has no opinion
        on whether any transaction in the batch is actually valid.
        """
        previous_block = self.chain[-1]

        block = Block(
            index=len(self.chain),
            transactions=transactions,
            previous_hash=previous_block.hash,
            orderer=self.orderer_name,
        )

        self.chain.append(block)

        print(
            f"  [{self.orderer_name}] "
            f"Created Block #{block.index} with "
            f"{len(transactions)} transaction(s)."
        )

        return block

    def validate_and_commit_block(self, block: Block) -> list[bool]:
        """Validate every transaction in a block and apply valid ones to world
        state.

        For each transaction, checks (in order): the endorsement policy is
        satisfied, a minimum number of endorsements was collected, all
        endorsers agree on the result, and no read key's version has changed
        since the transaction was endorsed (MVCC). The block's
        `validation_codes` are updated in place; the block itself is never
        removed or re-sequenced, even if every transaction in it turns out
        invalid -- only the *state-changing effect* of invalid transactions
        is withheld.
        """
        results: list[bool] = []

        for i, tx in enumerate(block.transactions):
            print(f"  Validating: {tx.description}")

            endorser_names = {e.peer_name for e in tx.endorsements}

            if not endorser_names.issuperset(self.required_endorsers):
                print("    INVALID: missing required endorsers")
                block.validation_codes[i] = "INVALID_ENDORSEMENT_POLICY"
                results.append(False)
                continue

            if len(tx.endorsements) < self.min_endorsements:
                print("    INVALID: not enough endorsements")
                block.validation_codes[i] = "INVALID_QUORUM"
                results.append(False)
                continue

            if len({e.result_hash for e in tx.endorsements}) > 1:
                print("    INVALID: endorsers disagree")
                block.validation_codes[i] = "INVALID_ENDORSER_MISMATCH"
                results.append(False)
                continue

            mvcc_conflict = False

            for key, read_version in tx.execution_result.read_versions.items():
                current_version = self.state.version_of(key)

                if current_version != read_version:
                    print(
                        f"    INVALID: MVCC CONFLICT on '{key}' -- "
                        f"endorsed against version {read_version}, "
                        f"current is {current_version}"
                    )
                    block.validation_codes[i] = "INVALID_MVCC_CONFLICT"
                    results.append(False)
                    mvcc_conflict = True
                    break

            if mvcc_conflict:
                continue

            for key, new_value in tx.execution_result.write_set.items():
                self.state.balances[key] = new_value
                self.state.versions[key] = self.state.version_of(key) + 1

            block.validation_codes[i] = "VALID"
            results.append(True)

            print("    VALID: write set committed to WorldState")

        return results
```

This is where “permissioned” earns its keep:

-   `**add_ordered_block()**` does the _ordering service's_ job: take whatever batch of transactions arrived, cut a `Block` around them, append it to the chain. It has zero opinion on whether any of those transactions are legitimate.
-   `**validate_and_commit_block()**` does the _committer's_ job: walk every transaction in that already-appended block and, for each one, check:

1.  **Endorsement policy** — did _all_ `required_endorsers` actually sign off? (Here: both banks, always — a strict "everyone must agree" policy. Real Fabric policies can be richer, e.g. "any 2 of 3".)
2.  **Quorum** — at least `min_endorsements` signatures, full stop.
3.  **Agreement** — do all endorsers’ `result_hash`es match? If two honest-looking endorsers computed _different_ write sets, something is wrong (bug, malicious peer, or stale state) — mark it invalid rather than guess who's right.
4.  **MVCC conflict check** — for every key the transaction _read_, is `state.version_of(key)` still what the endorsers assumed? If someone else's transaction already landed and bumped that version, this proposal is stale — mark it invalid, no matter how honest it was.

Only a transaction that passes all four gates gets its write set applied to `WorldState`, with its `validation_codes` entry set to `"VALID"`. Everything else gets a specific `INVALID_*` code — and stays on the chain anyway, permanently, as a record that it was ordered but failed validation.

The block itself is never rolled back or re-cut just because something inside it turned out to be invalid. That’s the whole point of separating **“put these transactions in order”** from **“decide which of them may update world state.”**

Real Fabric follows the same broad principle: transaction validation happens after ordering, and an invalid transaction can remain recorded in the blockchain while its state changes are excluded from world state. A block does not have to disappear merely because transactions inside it fail validation.

### Then: what happens when two transactions collide?

Gate #4 above is where **optimistic concurrency control (OCC)** lives.

“Optimistic” because nobody locks anything up front — every peer just executes hopefully, assuming nothing else will change the state before their transaction lands.

Most of the time that’s true, and we avoid the cost of locking.

When it isn’t, `validate_and_commit_block()` catches the stale read during validation, marks that transaction `INVALID_MVCC_CONFLICT`, and leaves it right where it is in the blockchain.

Nobody cheated. The transaction wasn’t necessarily malformed. **The world simply changed between execution and validation.**

The client can respond with a shrug: re-run EXECUTE against whatever the state looks like now, collect fresh endorsements, get the new transaction ordered into a fresh block, and try again.

That’s what `propose_with_retry()` below demonstrates.

```python
def propose_with_retry(
    description: str,
    peers: list[Peer],
    chaincode: Callable,
    chain: PermissionedBlockchain,
    orderer: OrderingService,
    args: tuple,
    max_attempts: int = 3,
) -> bool:
    """The client-side retry loop -- what a real Fabric SDK does
    automatically. On an MVCC conflict, don't give up: re-run EXECUTE
    against whatever the CURRENT state now is, and try again. This is
    the 'optimistic' half of optimistic concurrency control -- pay the
    retry cost only on an actual collision, not on every transaction.

    Every attempt still gets ordered into its own block and validated,
    even a failing one -- a rejected attempt leaves an INVALID block
    behind on the chain, it just never touches WorldState.
    """
    for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
        print(f"  Attempt {attempt}: {description} (fresh EXECUTE against current state)")
        endorsements: list[Endorsement] = []
        execution_result: ExecutionResult | None = None
        for peer in peers:
            endorsement, result = peer.endorse(chaincode, chain.state, *args)
            endorsements.append(endorsement)
            execution_result = result
        tx = ProposedTransaction(description, endorsements, execution_result)
        ordered = orderer.order([tx])
        block = chain.add_ordered_block(ordered)
        results = chain.validate_and_commit_block(block)
        if results[0]:
            return True
        print("    -> stale, retrying...\n")
    print(f"  Gave up after {max_attempts} attempts.")
    return False
```

Time to give our permissioned chain a spin.

### Demo: The tale of three banks with one shared ledger

The scenario: `Bank-A`, `Bank-B`, and `Bank-C` jointly run a settlement ledger. None of them trusts the other two's arithmetic, so the endorsement policy requires **all three** to independently compute and agree on every transaction before it commits. Nobody is mining. Nobody is staking. Everybody is, presumably, billing hours.

```python
membership = MembershipService()
membership.register("Bank-A")
membership.register("Bank-B")
membership.register("Bank-C")
peer_a = Peer("Bank-A", membership)
peer_b = Peer("Bank-B", membership)
peer_c = Peer("Bank-C", membership)
peers = [peer_a, peer_b, peer_c]

chain = PermissionedBlockchain(
    required_endorsers={"Bank-A", "Bank-B", "Bank-C"},
    min_endorsements=3,
    orderer_name="Shared-Ordering-Service",
)
orderer = OrderingService("Shared-Ordering-Service")
chain.state.balances = {"Alice-Account": 1000.0, 
                        "Bob-Account": 500.0, 
                        "Carol-Account": 0.0}
```

#### Here comes the race condition

Two clients prepare transactions at roughly the same time:

-   Alice pays Bob **$200**
-   Alice pays Carol **$150**

Both transactions are executed and endorsed before either one has changed `WorldState`, so both simulations see `Alice-Account` at **version 0**, with a balance of $1,000.

Let’s create both transactions first without ordering or committing either one:

```python
e_a1, res1 = peer_a.endorse(
    transfer_chaincode, chain.state,
    "Alice-Account", "Bob-Account", 200.0
)
e_b1, _ = peer_b.endorse(
    transfer_chaincode, chain.state,
    "Alice-Account", "Bob-Account", 200.0
)
e_c1, _ = peer_c.endorse(
    transfer_chaincode, chain.state,
    "Alice-Account", "Bob-Account", 200.0
)

tx1 = ProposedTransaction(
    "Alice pays Bob $200",
    [e_a1, e_b1, e_c1],
    res1,
)

e_a2, res2 = peer_a.endorse(
    transfer_chaincode, chain.state,
    "Alice-Account", "Carol-Account", 150.0
)
e_b2, _ = peer_b.endorse(
    transfer_chaincode, chain.state,
    "Alice-Account", "Carol-Account", 150.0
)
e_c2, _ = peer_c.endorse(
    transfer_chaincode, chain.state,
    "Alice-Account", "Carol-Account", 150.0
)

tx2_stale_attempt = ProposedTransaction(
    "Alice pays Carol $150",
    [e_a2, e_b2, e_c2],
    res2,
)
```

At this point, **nothing has been committed**.

Both transactions have all three required endorsements, and because neither transaction has changed `WorldState`yet, both were calculated against `Alice-Account` version 0.

But look at what they independently calculated:

**Transaction 1**

Alice: $1,000 → $800  
Bob: $500 → $700

**Transaction 2**

Alice: $1,000 → $850  
Carol: $0 → $150

Both calculations are perfectly correct **given the state they saw when they executed**.

The problem appears when we try to put them in order.

```makefile
print("=== ORDER + VALIDATE: Tx1 happens to get sequenced first ===\n")
ordered1 = orderer.order([tx1])
block1 = chain.add_ordered_block(ordered1)
chain.validate_and_commit_block(block1)
```

The output:

```python-repl
=== ORDER + VALIDATE: Tx1 happens to get sequenced first ===

  [Shared-Ordering-Service] Sequencing 1 proposal(s).
  [Shared-Ordering-Service] Created Block #1 with 1 transaction(s).
  Validating: Alice pays Bob $200
    VALID: write set committed to WorldState
[True]
```

Now transaction 2 will fail because the `WorldState`has changed:

```python
print("\n=== Tx2's ORIGINAL (now-stale) endorsement finally reaches ORDER + VALIDATE ===\n")
ordered2 = orderer.order([tx2_stale_attempt])
block2 = chain.add_ordered_block(ordered2)
results = chain.validate_and_commit_block(block2)
print(f"  First attempt succeeded? {results[0]}\n")
```

The output:

```python-repl
=== Tx2's ORIGINAL (now-stale) endorsement finally reaches ORDER + VALIDATE ===

  [Shared-Ordering-Service] Sequencing 1 proposal(s).
  [Shared-Ordering-Service] Created Block #2 with 1 transaction(s).
  Validating: Alice pays Carol $150
    INVALID: MVCC CONFLICT on 'Alice-Account' -- endorsed against version 0, current is 1
  First attempt succeeded? False
```

And there it is.

Transaction 2 was perfectly valid when it was executed and endorsed. But by the time it reached validation, Transaction 1 had already changed `Alice-Account` from version 0 to version 1.

Why not just apply Transaction 2 anyway?

Because its write set says Alice’s new balance should be **$850** — a number calculated from the old $1,000 balance.

But Alice is now actually at **$800**. Blindly applying that stale write set would overwrite $800 with $850, effectively making $50 of Alice’s first payment disappear.

So the validator doesn’t try to be clever. It simply asks:

**“You calculated this using version 0. Is version 0 still current?”**

No. Alice is now at version 1.

Transaction 2 is therefore marked `INVALID_MVCC_CONFLICT`. It stays recorded in Block #2, but its write set never touches `WorldState`.

Our client retries:

```swift
print("=== Client retries automatically, re-executing against CURRENT state ===\n")
success = propose_with_retry(
    "Alice pays Carol $150", peers, transfer_chaincode, chain, orderer,
    ("Alice-Account", "Carol-Account", 150.0),
)
print(f"\n  Eventually succeeded? {success}\n")
```

The output:

```python-repl
=== Client retries automatically, re-executing against CURRENT state ===

  Attempt 1: Alice pays Carol $150 (fresh EXECUTE against current state)
  [Shared-Ordering-Service] Sequencing 1 proposal(s).
  [Shared-Ordering-Service] Created Block #3 with 1 transaction(s).
  Validating: Alice pays Carol $150
    VALID: write set committed to WorldState

  Eventually succeeded? True
```

The final state:

```python-repl
=== Final state ===
  Balances: {'Alice-Account': 650.0, 'Bob-Account': 700.0, 'Carol-Account': 150.0}
  Versions: {'Alice-Account': 2, 'Bob-Account': 1, 'Carol-Account': 1}
  Chain length: 4 blocks
```

And now the numbers add up.

Alice started with $1,000, paid Bob $200, then successfully retried her $150 payment to Carol:

**$1,000 − $200 − $150 = $650**

Notice the versions too. `Alice-Account` changed twice, so it has reached version 2. Bob and Carol were each updated once, so both are at version 1.

And the chain contains **four blocks**:

-   Block #0 — genesis
-   Block #1 — Alice → Bob $200: `VALID`
-   Block #2 — original Alice → Carol $150: `INVALID_MVCC_CONFLICT`
-   Block #3 — retried Alice → Carol $150: `VALID`

Block #2 didn’t disappear just because its transaction failed.

**The blockchain remembers what happened. World state remembers what actually took effect.**

### Concluding thoughts

A permissioned chain starts from a fundamentally different assumption than a public chain: **we already know who is allowed to participate.**

That changes the mechanism.

In our toy public chains, PoW and PoS determine who gets to propose the next block — either by winning computational work or by being selected according to stake. In our permissioned chain, there is no mining race and no validator lottery. Known members execute transactions, endorse their results, an ordering service sequences them, and validators check whether those transactions are still valid when they reach the commit stage.

And that’s where things get interesting.

In a system where transactions are constantly being proposed against shared state, two perfectly legitimate transactions can race against each other. One may change the state before the other reaches validation, making the second transaction stale. MVCC catches that conflict; the client can then re-execute against the latest state and try again.

Which led me to another question.

**What happens on a public blockchain when different participants don’t see the same information at the same time?**

Transactions and blocks have to propagate across a distributed network, and that propagation isn’t instantaneous. A transaction might reach one node before another. A block might arrive after a competing block has already been seen elsewhere. So what does each participant actually know at any given moment — and how does the network eventually converge on a shared history?

That sent me down another rabbit hole.

**A story to be shared another time.**

body:
* * *

#### How Ethereum and Merkle trees power Singapore’s tamper-proof diplomas.

If you’ve attended a Singapore university, you may have noticed something unusual about the digital copy of your diploma: instead of receiving a PDF, you might have received a file ending in `.opencert`.

Open it in a text editor and things get even stranger.

Instead of a beautifully formatted diploma, you’re greeted by what looks like a giant JSON object filled with fields, hashes, signatures and other decidedly _non-diploma-looking_ things.

Yet upload that same file to [OpenCerts](https://opencerts.io), and your diploma appears

More importantly, OpenCerts can verify that the credential is authentic and hasn’t been tampered with.

That immediately piqued my interest.

Blockchain is best known for cryptocurrencies, but the underlying technology has applications far beyond moving money around. OpenCerts is a particularly interesting example because the application is tangible: many of us in Singapore may already have one of these cryptographically verifiable documents sitting somewhere on our computers.

And underneath the blockchain component lies an elegant data structure that first got me interested in blockchain technology in the first place: **the Merkle tree**

In this article, we’ll take OpenCerts apart conceptually and explore the cryptography that makes this kind of verification possible. We’ll build a Merkle tree ourselves, generate and verify Merkle proofs, deliberately tamper with documents to see what breaks, and finally connect the whole thing to a blockchain.

The interesting part is that we don’t need to store an entire diploma on-chain.

We only need enough cryptographic evidence to prove that the diploma we hold is the same document that was originally issued.

And that turns out to be a surprisingly fun thing to build from scratch.

All the code used in this article can be found in [my GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/Blockchain/blob/main/notebooks/3.%20merkle_trees.ipynb).

### The problem

I’ve previously written about [proof-of-work (PoW)](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/understanding-blockchains-from-scratch-f14c454af32f) and [proof-of-stake (PoS)](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/proof-of-stake-the-mining-free-blockchain-ddae684ffec5), exploring how blockchains can maintain a shared history that is extremely difficult to rewrite.

-   In PoW, miners expend computational work to add blocks. Rewriting history doesn’t mean changing just one block — an attacker would also have to redo the work required for the blocks that follow it and catch up with the rest of the network.
-   PoS replaces mining with validators who put economic value at risk. Validators participate in proposing and validating blocks, and malicious behaviour can result in their stake being **slashed**.

**Once something has been committed to the blockchain, quietly rewriting that history is extremely difficult.**

That sounds useful for official credentials.

So why bother with the `.opencert` format? Why not simply put everyone’s diploma directly onto the blockchain?

Imagine a university graduates **8,000 students** in one cohort. Putting all 8,000 diploma records directly on-chain would be expensive and inefficient. Even worse, blockchains are deliberately transparent: publishing the actual credentials on-chain could expose graduates’ private academic information.

#### Okay. So don’t publish the diplomas. Hash them instead?

A university could take all 8,000 diplomas, concatenate them together, hash the enormous blob, and publish just that single fingerprint to the blockchain.

Problem solved? Not quite.

Suppose I later want to prove that **my** diploma was one of those 8,000 documents.

To reproduce that same giant hash, a verifier would need the other 7,999 diplomas too (recall that the final hash is different if the content changes by even a little bit). We’d have successfully reduced what gets stored on-chain to one hash, **but made individual verification spectacularly inconvenient — and destroyed everyone else’s privacy in the process**.

What we really want is something rather specific:

> **Commit thousands of documents using one hash, while allowing any individual document to be verified independently without revealing the others.**

### The Merkle tree solution

A **Merkle tree** solves this by hashing documents in pairs, repeatedly, until only one hash is left — the **Merkle root**:

```plaintext
              Root
             /    \
           H01    H23
          /  \    /  \
        H0   H1  H2   H3
        |    |    |    |
        D0   D1   D2   D3
```

`D0` through `D3` represent the individual diplomas at the leaves of the tree. Each diploma is hashed, neighbouring hashes are combined and hashed again, and the process continues upward until the entire collection is represented by a single root hash.

Only that **Merkle root** needs to be published — for example, by anchoring it to a blockchain.

Whether the university issued 8 diplomas, 8,000 diplomas or 800,000 diplomas, the root itself remains a single fixed-size hash.

Here’s the clever part.

Suppose I want to prove that my diploma belongs to a batch of 8,000 credentials.

I don’t need the other **7,999 diplomas**.

I only need a small set of neighbouring hashes **along the path from my diploma to the root**. This is called a **Merkle proof**.

The number of hashes required grows logarithmically with the number of documents. For 8,000 documents, that’s only about **13 hashes** rather than thousands of other diplomas.

Using those hashes, anyone can independently work their way back up the tree:

```plaintext
My diploma
    ↓ hash
My leaf hash + sibling hash
    ↓ hash
Parent hash + sibling hash
    ↓ hash
...
    ↓
Merkle root
```

If the calculated root matches the root that was originally published, the verifier has cryptographic evidence that this diploma belonged to the committed batch.

Change even a single character in the diploma and its hash changes. That change propagates all the way up the tree, producing a different Merkle root.

Verification fails.

And this gives us the property we were looking for:

**A university can commit an entire batch of credentials using a single hash, while allowing each graduate to independently prove that their particular credential belongs to that batch — without needing, revealing, or even seeing anyone else’s diploma.**

And here’s where that strange `.opencert` file from the beginning of the article starts to make sense.

The `.opencert` file doesn’t just contain the information printed on your diploma. It also carries the cryptographic information needed to verify that credential — including the proof that connects your individual document back to the batch that was committed.

In other words, when you upload your `.opencert` file to OpenCerts, the verifier doesn’t need to download thousands of other graduates’ diplomas.

**The evidence needed to verify your particular credential travels with the credential itself.**

Conceptually, you can think of it like this:

```plaintext
.opencert file
│
├── Your credential data
│   ├── Name
│   ├── Degree
│   ├── University
│   └── ...
│
└── Cryptographic proof
    ├── Sibling hash
    ├── Sibling hash
    ├── Sibling hash
    └── ...
              │
              ▼
         Merkle root
              │
              ▼
          Blockchain
```

That weird-looking JSON isn’t an unfortunate alternative to a PDF.

**It’s part of what makes the diploma independently verifiable.**

That is the idea we’re going to build from scratch.

### Building a Merkle tree from scratch

Our Merkle tree only needs to do three things:

1.  Hash every diploma into a leaf.
2.  Repeatedly hash pairs of nodes until only the Merkle root remains.
3.  Generate the sibling hashes needed to prove that one diploma belongs to the tree.

We’ll also write a separate `verify_proof()` function. Importantly, the verifier doesn’t need access to the original tree — only the diploma being checked, its Merkle proof, and the expected root.

```python
import hashlib

def sha256(data: str) -> str:
    """Deterministic hash helper used throughout."""
    return hashlib.sha256(data.encode()).hexdigest()

class MerkleTree:
    """A binary tree of hashes, built bottom-up from a list of documents.

    Each document becomes a "leaf" (individually hashed). Leaves are
    paired up and hashed together to form the next layer up. This
    repeats until exactly one hash remains -- the "Merkle root" -- which
    is the ONLY thing that needs to be published on-chain.
    """

    def __init__(self, documents: list[str]) -> None:
        if not documents:
            raise ValueError("Need at least one document to build a tree.")
        self.leaves: list[str] = [sha256(doc) for doc in documents]
        self.layers: list[list[str]] = [self.leaves]
        self._build()

    def _build(self) -> None:
        """Repeatedly hash pairs of the current layer until one hash remains."""
        current = self.layers[0]
        while len(current) > 1:
            next_layer: list[str] = []
            for i in range(0, len(current), 2):
                left = current[i]
                # odd count -> duplicate the last item so it can pair with itself
                right = current[i + 1] if i + 1 < len(current) else current[i]
                next_layer.append(sha256(left + right))
            self.layers.append(next_layer)
            current = next_layer

    @property
    def root(self) -> str:
        """The single hash summarizing the ENTIRE batch of documents."""
        return self.layers[-1][0]

    def get_proof(self, leaf_index: int) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
        """Build the minimal sibling-hash path proving a document's membership.

        This is the entire point of the structure: instead of needing
        ALL other documents, you need exactly one sibling hash per
        LEVEL of the tree -- log2(N) hashes total, not N-1.
        """
        proof: list[tuple[str, str]] = []
        index = leaf_index
        for layer in self.layers[:-1]:  # every layer except the root itself
            is_right_node = index % 2 == 1
            pair_index = index - 1 if is_right_node else index + 1
            if pair_index < len(layer):
                sibling_hash = layer[pair_index]
            else:
                sibling_hash = layer[index]
            position = "left" if is_right_node else "right"
            proof.append((position, sibling_hash))
            index //= 2
        return proof

def verify_proof(leaf_hash: str, proof: list[tuple[str, str]], root: str) -> bool:
    """Independently recompute the root from a leaf hash + its proof, and
    check it matches the published root -- without ever seeing any other
    document in the batch.
    """
    current_hash = leaf_hash
    for position, sibling_hash in proof:
        if position == "left":
            current_hash = sha256(sibling_hash + current_hash)
        else:
            current_hash = sha256(current_hash + sibling_hash)
    return current_hash == root
```

There are two sides to this implementation.

-   `MerkleTree` belongs to the **issuer**. It has all the diplomas and constructs the tree.
-   `verify_proof()` belongs to the **verifier**. Notice that it doesn’t accept a `MerkleTree` at all: `verify_proof(leaf_hash, proof, root)`

That’s deliberate. An employer verifying my diploma shouldn’t need access to a university’s database — or anyone else’s diploma.

```python
print("=== University A issues 8 diplomas in one graduation batch ===\n")
diplomas = [
    "Diploma: Alice Tan, Computer Science, 2026",
    "Diploma: Bob Lim, Chemical Engineering, 2026",
    "Diploma: Carol Ng, Economics, 2026",
    "Diploma: Titus Lim, MITB AI, 2026",
    "Diploma: Emma Koh, Mathematics, 2026",
    "Diploma: Farid Rahman, Physics, 2026",
    "Diploma: Grace Wong, Biology, 2026",
    "Diploma: Hafiz Ismail, Statistics, 2026",
]
tree = MerkleTree(diplomas)
print(f"Merkle root (the ONLY thing the university publishes on-chain):\n  {tree.root}\n")

print("=== Titus wants to prove HIS diploma is in the batch ===\n")
titus_index = diplomas.index("Diploma: Titus Lim, MITB AI, 2026")
proof = tree.get_proof(titus_index)
print(f"  Titus's diploma is at position {titus_index} of {len(diplomas)}.")
print(f"  His proof needs only {len(proof)} sibling hashes "
        f"(not the other {len(diplomas) - 1} diplomas!):")
for pos, h in proof:
    print(f"    combine on the {pos}: {h[:16]}...")
```

The output:

```python-repl
=== University A issues 8 diplomas in one graduation batch ===

Merkle root (the ONLY thing the university publishes on-chain):
  f97175862043d258e0a467d6e777832d375b30d018ad8b1985e52eb6467c0782

=== Titus wants to prove HIS diploma is in the batch ===

  Titus's diploma is at position 3 of 8.
  His proof needs only 3 sibling hashes (not the other 7 diplomas!):
    combine on the left: 4b2493046335dc12...
    combine on the left: 4374db001d70618f...
    combine on the right: bdda8da6694c5eeb...
```

Now let’s see what happens when an employer verifies my diploma:

```python
print("\n=== Employer verifies, using ONLY Titus's document + his proof + the public root ===\n")
titus_leaf_hash = sha256("Diploma: Titus Lim, MITB AI, 2026")
is_valid = verify_proof(titus_leaf_hash, proof, tree.root)
print(f"  Verified genuine? {is_valid}")

print("\n=== What if Titus tries to upgrade his own grade after the fact? ===\n")
forged_leaf_hash = sha256("Diploma: Titus Lim, MITB AI, 2026, FIRST CLASS HONOURS")
is_valid_forged = verify_proof(forged_leaf_hash, proof, tree.root)
print(f"  Verified genuine? {is_valid_forged}")
The output:
```

```python-repl
=== Employer verifies, using ONLY Titus's document + his proof + the public root ===

  Verified genuine? True

=== What if Titus tries to upgrade his own grade after the fact? ===

  Verified genuine? False
```

### What just happened?

We created a batch of eight diplomas, hashed them into a Merkle tree, and published only one value: the Merkle root.

When Titus later wants to prove that his diploma belongs to that batch, he does not need the other seven diplomas. He only needs:

```
His diploma
+
3 sibling hashes
+
the expected Merkle root
```

If the final result equals the published Merkle root, the diploma was part of the original committed batch. Changing even one character changes the document hash and changes every parent hash above it. Eventually:

```
Calculated root != Published root
```

Verification fails.

### Anchoring the Merkle root

We are assuming that the Merkle root is correct.

Imagine if the university simply hosted the root on a normal web server:

```
university_A.edu.sg/graduation/2026/root.txt
```

A verifier could download the root and check Titus’s diploma against it.

That works — until someone who controls the server changes both the credential and the published root.

The Merkle proof would still be mathematically valid. But it would just be proving membership in a **different tree**.

The solution? Blockchain of course.

```
8,000 diplomas
      ↓
 Merkle tree
      ↓
ONE Merkle root
      ↓
  Blockchain
```

The blockchain is not storing everyone’s academic credentials. It is storing a cryptographic commitment to the batch.

Let’s write some more code to prove the point. To make this resemble the OpenCerts model a little more closely, let’s package each graduate’s credential together with its Merkle proof.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Certificate:
    """What a graduate actually keeps -- self-contained and independently
    verifiable forever, no tree required after issuance."""
    holder: str
    content: str
    proof: list[tuple[str, str]]

def issue_batch(holders: list[str], contents: list[str]) -> tuple[dict[str, Certificate], str]:
    """University A's one-time issuance: build the tree, hand out proofs, let the
    tree die. Returns (certificates, root-to-be-published-on-chain)."""
    tree = MerkleTree(contents)
    root = tree.root
    certificates = {
        holder: Certificate(holder=holder, content=content, proof=tree.get_proof(i))
        for i, (holder, content) in enumerate(zip(holders, contents))
    }
    return certificates, root

def verify_certificate(cert: Certificate, published_root: str) -> bool:
    """Standalone verification: only this certificate + an on-chain root."""
    return verify_proof(sha256(cert.content), cert.proof, published_root)
```

Our `Certificate` class is **not the actual OpenCerts schema** — it’s a deliberately simplified teaching model. But it captures the important idea: the graduate keeps their credential data together with the cryptographic evidence needed to verify it.

Using the blockchain code from [my previous article on PoS](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/understanding-blockchains-from-scratch-f14c454af32f):

```python

print("=== Step 1: University A builds the Merkle tree for a diploma batch ===\n")
holders = ["Alice Tan", "Bob Lim", "Carol Ng", "Titus Lim"]
majors = ["Computer Science", "Chemical Engineering", "Economics", "AI Engineering"]
contents = [f"Diploma: {h}, {m}, 2026" for h, m in zip(holders, majors)]

certificates, merkle_root = issue_batch(holders, contents)
print(f"  Merkle root of this 4-diploma batch: {merkle_root[:24]}...")
print(f"  {len(certificates)} Certificate objects handed out, tree already gone.\n") 

print("=== Step 2: the root gets submitted to a PoS blockchain as a transaction ===\n")
validators = [
    Validator("Acme-Node", stake=500),
    Validator("Guy-A-Node", stake=100),
    Validator("SketchyGuy-Node", stake=50),
]
chain = Blockchain(validators)

# a few unrelated prior blocks, so this isn't suspiciously the first thing ever
chain.add_block("Some unrelated earlier transaction batch", num_transactions=5)
chain.add_block("Another unrelated batch", num_transactions=3)

diploma_block, proposer = chain.add_block(
    data=merkle_root, num_transactions=len(certificates)
)
print(f"  {proposer.name} won the lottery for this slot and included University A's transaction.")
print(f"  {proposer.name} earned {BLOCK_REWARD + len(certificates) * FEE_PER_TX:.2f} coins for it.")
print(f"  {diploma_block}")
```

Notice something subtle: after `issue_batch()` returns, **we throw the Merkle tree away**.

We don’t need it anymore.

Each graduate has their own credential and proof, while the blockchain preserves the root. Years later, those two pieces are enough to perform verification.

The output:

```python-repl

=== Step 1: University A builds the Merkle tree for a diploma batch ===

  Merkle root of this 4-diploma batch: f0c1f18b7c16292e7fda4d25...
  4 Certificate objects handed out, tree already gone.

=== Step 2: the root gets submitted to a PoS blockchain as a transaction ===

  Guy-A-Node won the lottery for this slot and included NUS's transaction.
  Guy-A-Node earned 2.40 coins for it.
  Block #3 proposed by Guy-A-Node (4 txs)
  data (Merkle root): f0c1f18b7c16292e7fda4d25...
```

Now if an employer wanted to verify the credential, the employer wouldn’t need the same Merkle tree or university A’s database. All the employer needs is the credential itself (i.e. the proof that travels with it), and the Merkle root anchored on-chain.

```markdown
Credential
    +
Merkle proof
    +
On-chain root
    ↓
Verification
```

```python
print("=== Step 3: years later, an employer verifies Titus's certificate ===\n")
titus_cert = certificates["Titus Lim"]

published_root = diploma_block.data
is_valid = verify_certificate(titus_cert, published_root)
print(f"  Looked up block #{diploma_block.index} on-chain, read its root.")
print("  Verified using ONLY Titus's own certificate + that root.")
print(f"  Verified genuine? {is_valid}\n")
```

The output:

```python-repl
=== Step 3: years later, an employer verifies Titus's certificate ===

  Looked up block #3 on-chain, read its root.
  Verified using ONLY Titus's own certificate + that root.
  Verified genuine? True
```

And this separates the responsibilities rather neatly:

-   **The Merkle tree makes verification efficient.**
-   **The Merkle proof lets one graduate prove inclusion without revealing everybody else’s credentials.**

**The blockchain provides a difficult-to-rewrite place to anchor the root.**

Put together, we get a credential that can be independently checked without placing the credential itself on-chain.

**Merkle trees solve the scaling and privacy problem. Blockchain solves the trust problem.**

### In conclusion

At the beginning of this article, we started with a strange question: why does a digital diploma come as a weird-looking `.opencert` file instead of just a PDF?

Hopefully, it looks a little less strange now.

A university doesn’t need to put thousands of diplomas onto a blockchain. Instead, cryptographic hashes can represent those documents as leaves of a Merkle tree, reducing an entire graduation batch to a single Merkle root.

Each graduate can then carry the information needed to prove that their particular credential belonged to that batch — without needing access to anyone else’s diploma.

Perhaps the most important thing we discovered is that the blockchain doesn’t actually contain the diploma.

It doesn’t need to. It only needs to preserve enough cryptographic evidence for someone, years later, to ask:

_Is this the same credential that was originally committed?_

Change the credential, and its hash changes. Change the hash, and the reconstructed Merkle root changes. If that root no longer matches the commitment that was originally anchored, verification fails.

That is what I find fascinating about blockchain technology.

Cryptocurrency may be its most famous application, but the underlying ideas — hashing, Merkle trees, distributed consensus and immutable commitments — are much more general.

Sometimes they’re securing billions of dollars in digital assets.

And other times they’re quietly sitting inside a weird JSON file containing your university diploma.
