body:
* * *

#### A brief introduction on agent skills and why they matter

In October 2025, Anthropic taught the world how to build agents properly for the second time. The first lesson was Model Context Protocol. This one is agent skills.

The problem skills solve is context overload.

Want your agent to do 50 things? Great — give it 50 tools. This is where things start to go south.

The [Berkeley tool calling leaderboard](https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/leaderboard.html) shows it plainly: as the number of available tools grows, tool-selection accuracy tends to fall.

One reason is context. Tool definitions aren’t free. Each tool brings its name, description and argument schema into the model’s context. As the toolbox grows, so does the amount of information the model has to reason over – whether most of it is relevant to the task or not.

Take an exaggerated example: 50 custom tools, each with 20 arguments and a chunky description. Now add a 2,500-word system prompt and a lengthy conversation history. Before the agent has done anything useful, we’ve already filled its context with a small technical manual.

Anthropic’s answer is elegantly simple: progressive disclosure.

Don’t give the model every instruction upfront. Give it enough information to know what capabilities exist, then load the detailed instructions only when they’re needed.

Or, in Anthropic’s terminology: skills

[Anthropic’s own article](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/equipping-agents-for-the-real-world-with-agent-skills) on the topic remains the canonical reference for the idea, and I still go back to it regularly.

I’ll use LangChain for the examples below, but the concepts apply across most LLM orchestration frameworks – only the abstractions differ.

All my code used for this article can be found in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/glowing-guide/blob/main/notebooks/4.%20skills.ipynb).

### What is a skill, actually?

#### The analogy

Imagine it’s dinner time and you’re craving ramen.

Before you start cooking, you recall how to make ramen. If you’re like me, that’s probably whatever you remember from the last packet of instant noodles you massacred.

If you’re a ramen chef, it’s different. You recall years of training: how to prepare the broth, cook the noodles, slice the chashu, season the tare, and assemble the bowl.

That’s your skill. It’s knowledge about how to perform the task. And why my ramen capabilities stop at instant noodles instead of a tonkotsu broth.

Then you reach for the pot, knife, ladle, boiler and stove.

Those are your tools.

A chef needs both. But they’re not the same thing.

Owning a very expensive ladle does not make you a ramen chef.

Agents work the same way.

A tool gives an agent the ability to do something: search the web, query a database, execute code or call an API.

A skill gives the agent knowledge about how to approach a task: which tools to use, in what order, what constraints to follow, and what a good result looks like.

Put differently: tools provide capabilities; skills provide know-how.

#### In code

A skill is a folder with a markdown file in it. That’s it. That’s the whole primitive.

```markdown
skills/
└── weather-skill/
    ├── SKILL.md          # frontmatter + instructions
```

Inside, `SKILL.md` contains YAML frontmatter describing the skill, followed by its instructions in plain English:

```markdown
---
name: weather-skill
description: Get current weather for a location. Use when the user
  asks about weather, temperature, or conditions anywhere.
---

# Get weather skill

.... {other instructions here}
```

This convention is increasingly showing up across agent frameworks and coding copilots. The plumbing differs, but the basic idea is remarkably consistent: a skill lives in a folder, with a SKILL.md file describing what it does and how to do it.

**Unlike a tool, only the frontmatter goes into the system prompt**. Two lines. The body — which might be four hundred lines of gnarly domain procedure — loads only when the model decides the skill is relevant and reads the file.

> That’s progressive disclosure, and it’s the whole trick.

Compare that to a tool. A tool is a Python function whose **entire signature** is exported to a JSON schema and bound to the model at construction time. Every tool you bind costs context on every turn, forever, relevant or not.

A skill costs very little context until it’s needed.

### Let us build a light harness

Skills are rapidly becoming a first-class concept across coding copilots and agent frameworks, so there are already plenty of batteries-included options.

[LangChain’s deepagents package](https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents) gives you `create_deep_agent()`, pre-wired with planning middleware, subagent delegation, summarisation, a todo list, a virtual filesystem, and skills.

It works out of the box and it’s genuinely good. I’ll write about it properly next time.

**We’re not going to use it.** Because when everything is pre-wired, it’s easy to miss what each wire does.

Our harness in this article is built from LangChain’s plain `create_agent()` .

Let’s start by creating a simple agent with two tools:

```python
from dotenv import find_dotenv, load_dotenv

from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.tools import tool
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

_ = load_dotenv(find_dotenv())

llm = ChatOpenAI(
    model="gpt-5.6-luna",
    use_responses_api=True, 
    reasoning={"effort": "low"},  #The reasoning is medium by default so set this to l
)

@tool
def get_weather(location: str) -> str:
    """
    Get the weather for a given location
    """
    return f"The weather in {location} is sunny"

@tool
def get_exchange_rate(currency_from: str, currency_to: str) -> str:
    """
    Get the exchange rate between two currencies
    """
    return f"The exchange rate for {currency_from} to {currency_to} is 1.00"
```

Say we want a weather skill and a forex skill, each steering the agent toward the right tool for its domain. Three questions fall out of that:

1.  How do you load a skill for the agent?
2.  How do you get progressive disclosure?
3.  How do we make sure the agent consults the skill before reaching for the tool? Otherwise, we’ve just added more context and called it architecture.

All good questions with simple answers, thankfully.

**Question 1.** You read a skill with a `read_file` tool. That's the whole mechanism. No magic.

**Question 2** is answered by the file format itself. At startup, we read only each skill’s frontmatter – its name and description – and expose that lightweight catalogue to the agent.

When a request arrives, the agent uses the descriptions to decide which skill is relevant. Only then does `read_file` pull the full SKILL.md into context.

**Question 3 is the interesting one.**

Giving an agent access to skills doesn’t mean it’ll actually use them.

If `get_weather` is already sitting in its tool list, what’s stopping the model from calling it immediately and completely ignoring our lovingly handcrafted weather-skill?

So we need to give the agent one simple rule in the system prompt: before using a domain tool, consult the relevant skill.

LangChain wraps questions 2 and 3 up neatly in `SkillsMiddleware`.

### Using skills to guide tool use

For this experiment, I wrote two skills, namely:

```markdown
skills/
└── weather-skill/
    ├── SKILL.md          
└── forex-skill/
    ├── SKILL.md
```

How you write a `SKILL.md` is entirely up to you, but I advice making it as clearly written as possible so there is no ambiguity. Include examples. Here’s what I wrote for `forex-skill/SKILL.md` (truncated):

```markdown
---
name: forex-skill
description: Get live exchange rates between two currencies. Use this whenever the user asks about currency conversion, exchange rates, how much something costs in another currency, or comparisons like "is the dollar strong right now" — even if they don't use the words "forex" or "exchange rate" explicitly (e.g. "how much is 500 SGD in yen", "should I exchange money now or wait"). Always use this instead of guessing from memory, since exchange rates move constantly and Claude's training data has no visibility into current rates.
---

# Forex Skill

Fetches the live exchange rate between two currencies and reports it back in a clear, practical format.

## Instructions

1. **Identify both currencies.** Convert casual references to standard 3-letter ISO codes before calling the tool (e.g. "dollars" → ask which dollar: USD, SGD, AUD, etc.; "yen" → JPY; "pounds" → GBP).
2. **Handle ambiguous currency names.** If the user says something like "dollars" or "pounds" without specifying which country, ask them to clarify before calling the tool — don't assume USD/GBP by default.
3. **Call the `get_exchange_rate` tool**, passing both currency codes:

   ```python
   get_exchange_rate(currency_from="<code>", currency_to="<code>")
   ```

4. **If the tool call fails or returns an error**, tell the user plainly that the rate lookup failed — don't fall back to guessing a rate from memory.
5. **Call once per currency pair.** For multi-currency questions (e.g. "compare SGD to USD, EUR, and JPY"), call the tool separately for each pair.
6. **Do the math for the user.** If they gave an amount ("convert 500 SGD to JPY"), multiply it out yourself using the returned rate — don't just hand back the raw rate and leave them to calculate it.

## Output format

...

## Examples

...
```

Notice that the skill explicitly tells the agent to use `get_exchange_rate` for forex-related questions. Once loaded, the skill gives the model clear procedural guidance about which tool to use and when.

For more specialised workflows, the instructions can go further: call tool A first, inspect its result, then call tool B only if condition C is met.

Now to make them discoverable.

In LangChain:

-   `SkillsMiddleware` discovers your `SKILL.md` files and injects their frontmatter into the system prompt. Discovery and advertising. Nothing else.
-   `FilesystemMiddleware` hands the agent actual tools — `read_file`, `ls`, `glob`, `grep`, `execute` — and lets you allowlist which ones it sees.
-   The **backend** decides where files live, and whether shell execution exists at all.

> In Langchain: Skills advertise. Middleware provides. Backend decides what’s real.

### Experiment 1: Skills in Files

Our first harness reads skills off disk, so we use a filesystem backend:

```python
from deepagents.backends import FilesystemBackend
from deepagents.middleware import FilesystemMiddleware, SkillsMiddleware

backend = FilesystemBackend(root_dir="../", virtual_mode=True)

agent = create_agent(
    model=llm,
    tools=[get_weather, get_exchange_rate],
    middleware=[
        SkillsMiddleware(backend=backend, sources=["./skills/"]),
        FilesystemMiddleware(
            backend=backend,
            tools=["read_file"],   # read_file and nothing else
            system_prompt=None,
        ),
    ],
)
```

When files are involved, use LangChain’s `FilesystemBackend` and `FilesystemMiddleware` abstractions.

The important part is the root directory. `FilesystemBackend` establishes the filesystem boundary, and the paths passed to `SkillsMiddleware` are resolved within it.

Here, `./skills` means the `skills/` directory beneath our configured root.

We then pass the same backend to `FilesystemMiddleware`, exposing only `read_file`. That’s all the agent needs to progressively load a skill.

#### Give it a spin

Ask it about the weather and it does exactly what we designed:

```python
>>> agent.invoke({"messages": [HumanMessage("What is the weather in Singapore?")]})

Singapore is currently **sunny**. It's a good time for outdoor plans.
```

The important part isn’t that it called `get_weather`. It could already do that. The important part is that it consulted the skill first.

**Notice what the skill isn’t doing**. It isn’t providing capability – `get_weather` already exists as a bound tool. The skill is documentation the model reads on demand, explaining when and how to use something it already has.

That’s a legitimate pattern, and for many existing codebases it’s probably the right one. You keep typed signatures and validated arguments, while giving the model far richer guidance than you’d reasonably cram into a tool description. A four-hundred-word skill can carry decision rules, examples, edge cases and multi-step procedures without permanently stuffing all of them into context.

Do also notice what the `SkillsMiddleware` class did — it injected a system prompt into our agent to remind it to access its skills.

### Experiment 2: Remote skills

> **Question 4:** we’ve been reading SKILL.md off the local filesystem. What if the skills live somewhere else – a bucket, a registry, another team’s repo?

Nothing says the source of a skill has to be your local filesystem.

Thankfully, Langchain allows for seeding skills straight into agent’s state during invocation with `StateBackend`:

```python
from urllib.request import urlopen
from deepagents.backends import StateBackend
from deepagents.backends.utils import create_file_data

backend = StateBackend()

skill_url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/.../langgraph-docs/SKILL.md"
with urlopen(skill_url) as response:
    skill_content = response.read().decode('utf-8')

skills_files = {
    "/skills/langgraph-docs/SKILL.md": create_file_data(skill_content),
}

agent = create_agent(
    model= llm
    middleware=[
       SkillsMiddleware(
          backend=backend,
          sources=["./skills/"]
       ),
       FilesystemMiddleware(backend=backend)
    ]
)

result = agent.invoke(
    {
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is langgraph?"}],

        # seeded into the in-state filesystem. needed for the first run
        "files": skills_files, 
    },
)
```

For this experiment, I pulled the skill from a raw GitHub URL. The agent answered from it without the skill ever touching my local disk.

Which points at something bigger than a config option. Skills become a distribution format. Fetch them over HTTP. Load a different set per tenant. Let users bring their own. Version them independently of your deployment. Your agent’s repertoire stops being hard-coded into the application and starts looking more like a manifest.

> Sit with the cost for a second, though: you are downloading markdown from the internet and injecting it into your system prompt. Whatever you’re imagining right now about how that goes wrong – yes.

Production systems need to care about provenance, trust, versioning and what capabilities a remotely supplied skill is allowed to reach. We’ll leave that particular nightmare for another day.

### Experiment 3: Zero tools

> **Question 5:** every skill so far has pointed at a tool we wrote. What if we delete all domain tools and point the skill at a script instead?

This is the one I actually wanted to try. Here’s the whole skill:

```markdown
---
name: weather-skill
description: Get current weather for a location. Use when the user asks
  about weather, temperature, or conditions anywhere.
---

# Get weather skill

To get the weather of a location, run:

```bash
python skills/weather-skill/scripts/get_weather.py "<location>"
```

Returns JSON with weather condition. Parse and present naturally.

Run this script on each location the user asked for, one at a time.
```

And a script that does the obvious thing:

```cpp
#skills/weather-skill/get_weather.py
def main():
    location = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else None
    if not location:
        print(json.dumps({"error": "location argument required"}))
        sys.exit(1)
    print(json.dumps({"location": location, "weather": "sunny"}))

if __name__ == “__main__”:
    main()
```

To run that, the agent needs a shell. That’s a backend decision, which is where backends stop being plumbing and start being the design:

```python
from deepagents.backend import LocalShellBackend

backend = LocalShellBackend(
    root_dir=str(Path.cwd()),
    virtual_mode=False,
    inherit_env=True,
)

middleware = [
    FilesystemMiddleware(
        backend=backend,
        tools=["read_file", "ls", "glob", "execute"],
        system_prompt=None,
    ),
    SkillsMiddleware(backend=backend, sources=["./skills/"]),
]

agent = create_agent(model=llm, middleware=middleware)   # no tools=
```

Not a single `@tool` in the file.

> **ONE GOTCHA WORTH ITS OWN PARAGRAPH**

> The `tools=[…]` allowlist is separate from what the backend can do. `LocalShellBackend` supports execution, but if `execute` isn’t in that list the tool is never created and never mentioned in the system prompt. The model doesn’t know it’s missing. It just quietly produces a plausible answer instead of running anything.

The other tools (`ls` and `glob`) allow for the agent to find the correct file if its initial execution fails due to a non-existent file.

#### Hold on. Did it actually run?

I asked for the weather in Sydney and Melbourne:

```python-repl
Today's weather:
**Sydney:** Sunny
- **Melbourne:** Sunny
```

Lovely. Except — how do I know the python script ran?

#### The fix is logging – but not to stdout.

Stdout is the data channel between script and model; the skill file explicitly tells it to parse that as JSON. Add logging to stdout and you’ve mixed debug noise into the payload — all of which are visible to the LLM.

Log to a file instead:

```python
from pathlib import Path
import logging

LOG = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "skill.log"
logging.basicConfig(
    filename=LOG, level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s [pid=%(process)d] %(message)s",
)
logging.info("invoked argv=%r cwd=%s", sys.argv, os.getcwd())
```

Run it again and look at what lands in `skill.log`:

```python-repl
22:29:55,316 [pid=45724] invoked argv=[...get_weather.py, 'Sydney']    cwd=.../notebooks
22:29:55,316 [pid=45724] resolved location=Sydney
22:29:56,795 [pid=45725] invoked argv=[...get_weather.py, 'Melbourne'] cwd=.../notebooks
22:29:56,795 [pid=45725] resolved location=Melbourne
```

Works.

> Note: Always leave independent evidence that execution happened. Here it’s four lines of logging. In production it might be structured logs, traces, or telemetry.

LangSmith shows that the agent did read the `SKILL.MD` file and executed the .py file twice, once for each city as specified by the skill.

### The bug that explained the whole design

Here’s the LangSmith trace from an earlier run. It worked – but it took the scenic route

Three wasted calls before it found the door.

The model read the skill at `/skills/weather-skill/SKILL.md` and concluded the script must be at `/skills/weather-skill/scripts/get_weather.py`. Structurally correct. Completely wrong root – because those two tools were living in different universes.

The model was handed directions in room numbers, then put in a taxi with a driver who only knows street addresses. Both systems valid. Nobody hired an interpreter. Which leads me to the next point.

### What is virtual\_mode?

It’s a path translation layer that only the filesystem tools speak.

Turn it on and your `root_dir` is presented to the model as though it were `/`. It also blocks `../` traversal, so `read_file` can’t wander into your SSH keys. Turn it off and paths are used as-is: what the model says is what hits the disk.

The problem is that `execute` never got the memo. It hands your command string to a subprocess, and that string doesn’t pass through the translator. It goes straight to bash, which lives on the real filesystem and has never heard of your virtual namespace.

It’s `chroot` for the file tools while the shell runs outside the jail. Which is why the [docs](https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/backends/local_shell/LocalShellBackend) are blunt that virtual mode provides no security once shell execution is enabled. It isn’t a weak jail. It’s a jail with the door propped open and a sign on it.

### The accidental argument for the whole design

Look again at steps 3 and 4. The path was wrong, and the agent ran pwd, ran find, worked out where it actually was, and recovered.

A bound tool cannot do that. When a tool’s signature is wrong it fails, and that’s the end of the story. When a shell command is wrong, the agent can go and look.

That’s the strongest thing I can say for the tool-less design, and I got it entirely by accident, from a bug.

### So which one should you build?

All three harnesses work. They differ in where capability lives, and everything else follows from that.

1.  **Capability in bound tool functions, skill as documentation:** you keep schema validation and loud failures, and you redeploy to add anything. Reach for it when you already have tools and the model keeps picking the wrong one.
2.  **Capability in state, seeded per call:** skills become a manifest you can version, distribute, and scope per tenant. Many failures go quiet – bad markdown doesn’t necessarily throw, it just underperforms. Reach for it when skills are user-supplied or vary per caller.
3.  **Capability in files on disk, with a programming shell (either a sandbox or in my case – a shell on my computer):** you add capability by dropping a folder, and failures become recoverable because the agent can investigate. Reach for it when capability changes faster than you can deploy.

The third one changed how I think, but the tradeoff deserves saying plainly. You swap a typed signature for a string handed to a shell. You lose argument validation. You lose the guarantee that a capability exists before runtime. And you’re one careless `SKILL.md` away from an agent running something you didn’t intend.

### But do you actually need skills?

Be honest about the example you’ve just read. Two tools. One weather script that always says sunny. No agent needs progressive disclosure for that.

So if the criteria isn’t tool count, what is it?

Skills earn their place when capability alone isn’t enough. That tends to happen in three situations.

1.  **Long, deep conversations.** And deep conversations tend to be code conversations – nothing bloats a context window faster than source files. It’s no accident that coding agents keep converging on some version of skills. Without some way to selectively load context, large repositories quickly become a context-allocation problem.
2.  **Too many tools.** The original problem we opened with. Fifty schemas surfaced at instantiation, accuracy in freefall.
3.  **Standards that have to hold.** This is the least discussed of the three and, I’ve come to think, the most important.

Ask Claude to build you a website and watch what happens when its frontend design skill is available: before writing the implementation, it can stop and read the house rules.

Claude can already code. Extraordinarily well. It does not need instructions on how to write React. So why the detour?

Do it a few times and you’ll see. The output is consistently – almost suspiciously – good. Not merely competent. Tasteful, in the same way, every time. That consistency is the skill.

Which brings me to the part worth sitting with. The skill isn’t supplying capability. It’s supplying judgement.

The model knew how to code before it opened that file. What it didn’t know was which of ten thousand defensible choices this particular house considers correct. Which type pairings this house considers intentional rather than templated. When this house uses a numbered list for structure and when it considers one decoration. That isn’t knowledge. That’s taste – and taste is precisely the thing that will not compress into a function signature.

### Concluding Thoughts

Good instructions still matter. What skills change is who has to be good at writing them.

A skill is the best prompt anyone in your organisation ever wrote, applied every single time, by everyone, without them ever needing to know it exists.

That isn’t a context optimisation. That’s how craft gets distributed.

> Tools package capability. Skills package judgement. Progressive disclosure is how you deliver that judgement without carrying all of it all the time.
summary: Explains how to implement agent skills as progressively disclosed instructions in a LangChain agent, comparing file-based, remote, and tool-free setups and debugging execution with logging.

body:
* * *

#### **Five Architectures. Five Different Answers to the Same Question.**

Every team building with LLMs eventually reaches the same moment.

The first agent works.

Then someone asks, _“What if we add another agent?”_

One agent becomes three. Three become eight. Before long, you’re no longer writing prompts — you are designing an organisation of AI workers that need to coordinate, share information, recover from failures and decide who should do what.

Building the individual agents is rarely the difficult part.

**Designing how they work together is.**

This article focuses on five useful ways of organising multi-agent systems. Some, particularly hierarchical systems and explicit workflows, appear frequently in modern agent applications. Others, such as blackboard and adversarial architectures, are less commonly encountered in day-to-day LLM development but offer valuable ways to reason about coordination, control, and iterative improvement.

The examples in this article use LangChain and LangGraph, but the ideas themselves are framework-agnostic. I’ve truncated the code in the article for an easier read. The full source code can be found in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/glowing-guide/blob/main/notebooks/3.%20multi_agent_patterns.ipynb).

In this article, I’ll be using the fundamental and technical analysis tools used in my previous [LangChain 1.0 article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/langchain-a-second-look-6ed720e27fec) and my [LangGraph article on concurrent agent workflows](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-second-look-at-langgraph-when-command-sends-becomes-common-sense-720a851cf8a8).

### 1\. Hierarchical Multi-Agent Systems

Though there are no official statistics on the prevalence of different multi-agent architectures, this is by far the most common pattern I’ve encountered in practice.

The easiest way to understand a hierarchical multi-agent system is to start with a standard agent:

```python
from fundamental_analysis_tools import evaluate_fundamentals
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from technical_analysis_tools import technical_analysis

agent = create_agent(
    model=llm,
    tools=[technical_analysis, evaluate_fundamentals]
)
```

Which looks just like:

This agent has access to two tools. When a user asks a question, the LLM decides which tool to invoke and combines the results into a final answer.

Now comes the key idea.

**A hierarchical multi-agent system is simply an agent whose “tools” happen to be other agents instead of Python functions.**

Rather than calling a function directly, the supervisor delegates work to specialist agents. Those specialists may have their own tools, memory, prompts, or even coordinate additional sub-agents of their own.

In other words, we replace this:

```
Supervisor
├── Technical Analysis Tool
└── Fundamental Analysis Tool
```

With:

```
Supervisor
├── Technical Analyst Agent
│   ├── Tool A
│   ├── Tool B
│   └── ...
└── Fundamental Analyst Agent
    ├── Tool C
    ├── Tool D
    └── ...
```

Because every specialist is itself an agent, the hierarchy can continue for multiple levels. A supervisor may coordinate several teams, each with its own supervisor and collection of domain experts.

The following example illustrates exactly this idea. We first build a specialist analysis team, then expose that entire team as a single “tool” to a higher-level supervisor that also manages a weather expert.

```python
from langchain.tools import tool
from langgraph_supervisor import create_supervisor

@tool
def get_weather(city: str) -> str:
    """Use this tool to get the weather of a city or location"""
    return f"The weather is sunny in {city}"

weather_expert = create_agent(
    model=llm,
    tools=[get_weather],
    name="weather_expert"
)

technical_analyst_agent = create_agent(
    model=llm,
    tools=[technical_analysis],
    name="technical_analyst"
)

fundamental_analyst_agent = create_agent(
    model=llm,
    tools=[evaluate_fundamentals],
    name="fundamental_analyst"
)

analysis_squad = create_supervisor(
    [technical_analyst_agent, fundamental_analyst_agent],
    model=llm,
    supervisor_name="analysis_supervisor",
    prompt=(
        "You are a team supervisor managing a fundamental analyst and a "
        "technical analyst..."
    )
)

analysis_app = analysis_squad.compile(
    name="fundamental_and_technical_analyst"
)

supervisor_graph = create_supervisor(
    [analysis_app, weather_expert],
    model=llm,
    prompt=(
        "You are a team supervisor managing a fundamental analyst, a "
        "technical analyst and a weather expert..."
    )
)

supervisor = supervisor_graph.compile()
```

Notice what happened here: The top-level supervisor does **not** know how to perform technical analysis or fundamental analysis itself.

Instead, it simply knows that the **Analysis Team** can answer investment-related questions, while the **Weather Expert** can answer weather-related questions.

Each team becomes a reusable building block that can be composed into larger systems, much like functions in traditional software engineering.

#### When should you use a hierarchical architecture?

Hierarchical systems work well when responsibilities can be cleanly divided into specialist domains.

The architecture is intuitive, modular and easy to extend. Adding a new capability is often as simple as creating another specialist agent and registering it with the supervisor.

**Its biggest limitation, however, is the supervisor itself.** Every request flows through that central coordinator, making it both a routing bottleneck and a single point of failure. As systems grow larger, the supervisor’s routing decisions also become increasingly important — poor delegation can negate the benefits of specialisation altogether.

> **Implementation note:** I used `langgraph_supervisor` purely to illustrate the architectural pattern because it makes the hierarchy visually obvious.

> [It is **not** the approach currently recommended by the LangGraph team](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langgraph-supervisor). The library is maintained primarily for backwards compatibility, and the recommended pattern today is to expose sub-agents as tools and compose them directly. This integrates more naturally with features such as `AgentMiddleware`, which I covered in my [earlier article on LangChain 1.0](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/langchain-a-second-look-6ed720e27fec).

### 2\. Explicit Multi Agent Workflows

The previous architecture delegates orchestration to a supervisor agent. An alternative is to define the orchestration yourself, constructing the workflow node by node and edge by edge.

This is the lowest-level and most flexible approach. Rather than allowing an LLM to decide freely what may happen next, you explicitly define the system’s control-flow boundaries: which nodes may run, how work can move between them, where branches converge, and when execution must end.

Consider a query that requires both fundamental and technical analysis. A sequential supervisor might delegate to one specialist and then the other. An explicit workflow can instead plan the required tasks and fan them out concurrently:

```python
def execute_plan(
    plan: Plan,
    state: State,
) -> Command[
    Literal[
        "fundamental_analysis_agent",
        "technical_analysis_agent",
        "respond",
    ]
]:
    gotos = [
        Send(
            step.action.agent_to_use,
            {"query": step.action.query_to_send},
        )
        for step in plan.steps
    ]

    if not gotos:
        gotos.append(
            Send("respond", {"messages": state["messages"]})
        )

    return Command(goto=gotos)

def router(state: State) -> Command[
    Literal["fundamental_analysis_agent", "technical_analysis_agent", "respond"]
]:
    # Get plan
    query = state['messages'][-1].content
    response = llm_planner.invoke(query) #invoke planner
    return execute_plan(response, state)
```

The router first produces a plan. Each plan step is then translated into a separate unit of work and dispatched using LangGraph’s `Send` abstraction.

If the plan calls for both fundamental and technical analysis, both specialists can run concurrently. If the user asks about two companies, the workflow can launch separate copies of the same specialist — one for each company — before combining their findings downstream.

The graph still defines the permitted execution boundary:

The important distinction is that the workflow cannot invent new control flow at runtime.

Once the response node has consolidated the specialists’ findings, execution ends. The system cannot spontaneously return to the router, request another analysis round, or refine its answer unless you explicitly define an edge that permits it.

This gives you considerably more control than a supervisor-based architecture.

It also gives you considerably more responsibility.

Supporting concurrent execution requires more than merely connecting a router to several agents. You must define:

-   how the task is decomposed;
-   how each unit of work is represented;
-   how parallel branches update shared state;
-   when all required branches have completed;
-   and how their results are merged safely.

In other words:

> **The framework provides the orchestration primitives, but you must design the orchestration.**

#### When to use explicit multi agent workflows

Explicit workflows are especially useful when: you need auditable control-flow boundaries for compliance or safety, or the required architecture does not fit a standard supervisor pattern.

The principal weakness is that every behaviour must be designed and implemented deliberately.

### 3\. Agent Swarm

A swarm takes a fundamentally different approach from a hierarchical architecture.

In a hierarchical system, there is a single supervisor responsible for deciding which specialist should work on a task next. A swarm removes that supervisor entirely.

One useful way to think about a swarm is as an **agent society**.

Rather than relying on a single “smart” supervisor, intelligence is **distributed across the society of agents**. Each specialist contributes a small part of the reasoning process before handing the conversation to another specialist whenever appropriate. The final answer therefore emerges from the interactions between agents rather than from a centrally orchestrated execution plan.

The implementation in LangGraph reflects this idea quite naturally: Each agent is given one or more **handoff tools** that allow it to transfer control directly to another specialist.

```python
from langgraph_swarm import (  
    create_handoff_tool,
    create_swarm,
)

## We'll have to redefine our all agents to include the handoff tool
weather_expert = create_agent(
    model=llm,
    tools=[
        get_weather,
        create_handoff_tool(
            agent_name="technical_analyst",
            description="Transfer for technical analysis related questions"
        ),
        create_handoff_tool(
            agent_name="fundamental_analyst",
            description="Transfer for fundamental analysis related questions"
        ),
    ],
    name="weather_expert"
)
technical_analyst_agent = ...
fundamental_analyst_agent = ...

swarm_workflow = create_swarm(
    [fundamental_analyst_agent, technical_analyst_agent, weather_expert],
    default_active_agent="weather_expert" #a default agent must be specified.
)

swarm = swarm_workflow.compile()
```

The important part here is to `create_handoff_tool` , or explicitly creating a tool that tells the agent which other agent to handoff to. In a swarm setting, that’s every other agent.

The important concept here isn’t the API itself — it’s the `create_handoff_tool()` abstraction.

Unlike a normal tool, which interacts with an external system, a handoff tool transfers execution to another agent. Every specialist can hand work directly to another specialist, the reasoning path is determined collaboratively rather than by a central planner.

#### When should you use a swarm?

Swarms work well when the execution path is difficult to predict in advance. The trade-off is that decentralisation comes at a cost.

> Since no agent has a complete view of the overall execution, conversations may bounce between specialists **unnecessarily,** increasing latency and token consumption. It also becomes harder to understand why a particular reasoning path was taken, making debugging and observability more challenging than in hierarchical systems.

Whether that trade-off is worthwhile depends entirely on the problem you’re trying to solve.

### 4\. Blackboard Multi Agent Systems

A blackboard architecture takes a very different approach to coordination.

[Instead, they collaborate through a shared, central workspace known as the **blackboard**](https://stacks.stanford.edu/file/druid:nh044zx3884/nh044zx3884.pdf).

Each specialist inspects the current state of the board, determines whether it can contribute, and — if selected — writes a partial result back to it. The board is then inspected again, allowing a different specialist to build on the updated solution.

The defining idea is simple:

> **Agents do not decide whom to talk to. The evolving solution determines which specialist becomes useful next.**

A classical blackboard system has three components.

#### a. The blackboard

The blackboard is a structured, shared solution space.

It is not merely a chat history, message log, or collection of agent responses. Instead, it represents the evolving state of the problem through named panels or levels.

**Each specialist reads from this common workspace and writes only to the panel it owns.**

```python
class Blackboard(TypedDict, total=False):
    query: str
    
    # Problem frame
    problem_framed: bool
    ticker: str | None
    location: str | None
    wants_technical: bool
    wants_fundamental: bool

    # Specialist panels
    technical: dict | None
    fundamental: dict | None
    environmental: dict | None

    # Integrated solution
    synthesis: str | None

    # Control state
    next_knowledge_source: str | None
    cycles: int
```

This structure is what separates a genuine blackboard architecture from a system where several agents merely append messages to shared memory.

#### b. Knowledge sources

The specialists in a blackboard system are traditionally called **knowledge sources**.

Each knowledge source defines two things:

-   a **condition** describing when it is able to contribute;
-   an **action** describing what it writes to the blackboard when activated.

For example, the technical-analysis specialist becomes eligible only when the board contains a ticker symbol, the user has requested technical analysis, and the technical panel is still empty.

```python
def can_analyse_technicals(board: Blackboard) -> bool:
    return (
        board.get("ticker") is not None
        and board.get("wants_technical", False)
        and board.get("technical") is None
    )
```

> **All specialists do not call one another, expose handoff tools, or even need to know which other knowledge sources exist.**

All coordination happens through the blackboard.

#### c. The control component

The control component repeatedly inspects the blackboard, identifies which knowledge sources are currently eligible, and selects one to activate.

```python
def control_component(board: Blackboard) -> dict:
    eligible = [
        source
        for source in KNOWLEDGE_SOURCES #these are subagents
        if source.precondition(board)
    ]
    if not eligible:
        return {"next_knowledge_source": None}
    chosen = max(
        eligible,
        key=lambda source: source.priority,
    )
    return {
        "next_knowledge_source": chosen.name,
        "cycles": board.get("cycles", 0) + 1,
    }
```

> The next action is not determined entirely by the original user request or by a predefined sequence of edges. It is determined by the current state of the partial solution.

After every contribution, the controller evaluates the board again:

```
inspect → identify eligible specialists → activate one
       → contribute → inspect again
```

The LangGraph topology reflects this loop directly:

A typical execution trace might look like this:

Notice how every knowledge source returns control to the controller before another specialist is activated.

The technical analyst does not decide to invoke the weather expert, nor does the weather expert know that the synthesiser exists. Instead, after every contribution the controller re-inspects the blackboard and asks a single question:

> **Given the current state of the solution, which knowledge source is now eligible to contribute?**

Only then is the next specialist activated. This repeated return to the controller is the defining characteristic of a blackboard architecture.

#### Execution is deliberately sequential

Classical blackboard systems generally activate only one knowledge source during each control cycle.

This is not merely an implementation limitation.

> Every contribution changes the state of the board and may enable, disable, or alter the priority of other specialists.

The useful next action only becomes apparent after the previous contribution has changed the solution.

Running every eligible specialist concurrently would assume that all useful work can be identified from the same initial state. A blackboard architecture instead assumes that each contribution may change what becomes relevant next.

#### When should you use a blackboard architecture?

Blackboard systems work well when:

-   a solution must be constructed incrementally;
-   multiple independent specialists can contribute different representations or partial findings;
-   the appropriate next action depends on what has already been discovered;
-   and the workflow cannot be fully determined in advance.

[Blackboard architectures originated in systems such as Hearsay-II for speech understanding and were later applied experimentally to specialised problems including planning, signal interpretation, structural analysis, and monitoring](https://stacks.stanford.edu/file/druid%3Anh044zx3884/nh044zx3884.pdf). They are historically important, although they are far less commonly encountered in modern agent development.

The architecture’s greatest strength is modularity. Sub agents remain independent, and new specialists can be added by defining their preconditions and contributions.

**Their main weakness is complexity.** The blackboard schema, activation rules, priorities, termination conditions, and control policy must all be designed carefully. The architecture also tends to be sequential, which can increase latency.

### 5\. Actor-Critic (Adversarial) Multi Agent Systems

The final architecture for this article takes a different approach from others — instead of dividing work between specialists, it assigns agents **opposing roles**.

One agent produces an answer. Another attacks it. The goal is not collaboration in the usual sense. It is to improve the final output by deliberately exposing it to criticism.

The simplest version looks like this:

The **actor** produces a draft. The **critic** identifies weaknesses. The actor revises the draft, and the cycle continues until the critic is satisfied.

At first glance, this seems reasonable. In practice, it contains a serious flaw.

> A critic prompted to be strict, sceptical, or adversarial will **almost always find something else to criticise**. That is not necessarily a failure of the critic. Harshness is the role it was given.

The problem is that the same agent responsible for finding defects is also effectively being asked to decide when no more defects matter.

Those are two different responsibilities. A more reliable architecture separates them:

```
actor → critic → judge
  ↑                 |
  └──── revise ─────┘
```

-   The critic reports problems.
-   The judge decides whether those problems justify another revision round.

This distinction is the key to making adversarial systems terminate reliably. **The critic finds faults. The judge decides whether the faults matter.**

By separating these roles, the critic can remain uncompromising without being given control over when the system stops.

#### a. The Actor

The actor is responsible for producing the work.

Depending on the task, this may be a report, code implementation, research summary, plan, or recommendation.

On the first round, the actor creates an initial draft. On later rounds, it receives the current draft together with the critic’s findings and the judge’s priorities.

Conceptually:

```python
def actor(state: AdversarialState) -> dict:
    if state.get("latest_critique") is None:
        prompt = f"Produce a first draft.\n\nTASK: {state['task']}"
    else:
        prompt = (
            "Revise the current draft.\n\n"
            f"TASK:\n{state['task']}\n\n"
            f"CURRENT DRAFT:\n{state['draft']}\n\n"
            f"CRITIQUE:\n{state['latest_critique']}\n\n"
            f"JUDGE'S PRIORITY:\n{state['latest_verdict']['focus']}"
        )

    draft = llm.invoke(prompt).content

    return {
        "draft": draft,
        "round": state.get("round", 0) + 1,
    }
```

The actor’s role is not to defend the previous answer. It is to improve it.

#### b. The critic

The critic is deliberately adversarial.

Its job is to search for unsupported claims, logical gaps, missing edge cases, vague reasoning, inconsistencies, and anything else that weakens the artifact.

Free-text criticism creates a practical problem: it is difficult to measure whether the system is improving. For this reason, I suggest using structured outputs for greater flexibility:

```python
class Issue(BaseModel):
    severity: Literal["blocking", "major", "minor"]
    description: str

class Critique(BaseModel):
    issues: list[Issue]
    summary: str
```

For example, you could give the issue a severity and map it to a score:

```python
def weighted_issue_score(issues: list[dict]) -> int:
    weights = {
        "blocking": 5,
        "major": 2,
        "minor": 1,
    }

    return sum(
        weights[issue["severity"]]
        for issue in issues
    )
```

This produces a crude but useful convergence signal. A draft whose score falls from `14` to `6` to `2` is clearly improving, even if the total number of comments remains similar.

#### c. The judge

The judge evaluates the critic’s findings on their merits. The judge is the only LLM role allowed to recommend acceptance:

```python
class Verdict(BaseModel):
    decision: Literal["accept", "revise"]
    reasoning: str
    focus: str

def judge(state: AdversarialState) -> dict:
    verdict = llm.with_structured_output(Verdict).invoke(
        [
            HumanMessage(
                content=(
                    "Evaluate the critic's findings on their merits. "
                    "Accept if only minor issues remain. "
                    "Request revision only for blocking or material problems.\n\n"
                    f"DRAFT:\n{state['draft']}\n\n"
                    f"CRITIQUE:\n{state['latest_critique']}"
                )
            )
        ]
    )

    return {
        "latest_verdict": verdict.model_dump(),
    }
```

This separation allows the critic to remain severe while the judge remains pragmatic.

#### Why a watchdog is still necessary

The actor, critic, and judge are all LLM-driven.

> **That means none of them can be trusted to guarantee termination.**

The critic may keep generating new issues. The actor may fail to fix them. The judge may repeatedly request another revision even when the system has stopped making meaningful progress.

A **deterministic** watchdog therefore sits outside the debate loop. It enforces two conditions that no model gets to negotiate.

**i. A hard round cap**

The system must have an absolute upper limit because even well-designed review loops can behave unpredictably. A hard cap ensures that cost and latency remain bounded

**ii. Stalemate detection**

A round cap eventually stops a bad loop. A stalemate detector stops when it detects that progress has ceased. For example, consider these weighted issue scores:

```
round 1: 12
round 2: 8
round 3: 8
round 4: 9
```

The system is no longer converging. A simple watchdog can detect this:

```python
def watchdog(state: AdversarialState) -> dict:
    round_number = state.get("round", 0)
    scores = state.get("issue_counts", [])

    if round_number >= HARD_ROUND_CAP:
        return {
            "halt_reason": "hard round cap reached",
        }

    if len(scores) >= STALEMATE_WINDOW:
        window = scores[-STALEMATE_WINDOW:]

        if window[-1] >= window[0]:
            return {
                "halt_reason": (
                    f"stalemate detected: {window}"
                ),
            }

    return {}
```

This deterministic layer is important because it prevents the models from governing their own resource consumption.

#### Finalisation must distinguish success from exhaustion

A review loop that stops because the judge accepted the draft is not equivalent to one that stopped because it hit the round limit.

-   A clean acceptance can return the response directly.
-   A capped or stalled run should return the best available draft response together with unresolved material issues. This prevents the system from presenting an exhausted loop as a successful review.

The resulting architecture looks like this:

#### When should you use an adversarial architecture?

Adversarial systems work well when the quality of an artifact can be improved through repeated review.

The architecture is especially useful when a single generation pass is likely to produce a plausible but incomplete answer.

Its main weakness is cost.

Every revision round introduces additional model calls, latency, and tokens. The actor may also overcorrect, fixing one issue while introducing another. Critics can become repetitive, and judges can be inconsistent.

The system therefore needs explicit convergence signals, bounded iteration, and honest reporting when review does not complete successfully.

* * *

### Choosing an architecture

After exploring these five architectures, one thing becomes apparent.

They are not fundamentally distinguished by the number of agents involved, the framework used, or whether they call tools.

They differ in **who is responsible for deciding what happens next.**

-   In a **hierarchical architecture**, the **supervisor** decides which specialist should act next.
-   In an **explicit workflow**, **the developer** decides by defining the control flow explicitly.
-   In a **swarm**, **the currently active agent** decides whether to continue working or hand the task to another specialist.
-   In a **blackboard architecture**, **the evolving state of the shared solution** determines which knowledge source becomes useful next.
-   In an **adversarial architecture**, **the critic and judge** collectively decide whether another revision round is worthwhile, while deterministic control ensures the process eventually terminates.

Every framework — LangGraph, CrewAI, Google ADK, AutoGen, or one that hasn’t been released yet — is ultimately choosing one or more answers to the same question:

> **Who decides what happens next?**

### Final Thoughts

Perhaps the most surprising lesson is that these ideas aren’t new.

Blackboard systems date back to the 1970s. Hierarchical planning, opportunistic control, distributed problem solving and adversarial review all existed decades before large language models.

What LLMs changed wasn’t the architectures themselves. They changed what could occupy the nodes.

Where we once connected handwritten algorithms, we now connect reasoning agents.

**We now have different ways of organising intelligence.**

body:
Authors’ Note: This article is **jointly written** by [James Koh, PhD](https://medium.com/u/780706b02d58) and [Tituslhy](https://medium.com/u/c50ac8f269da) (“Titus”). Since Titus’ [previous Medium article on Claude Code](/mitb-for-all/how-i-use-claude-code-3b1fd852305b), Titus and James have been comparing notes from their individual use of Claude Code. There were simply too many lessons , so here we are. We’ve done our best to blend our writing styles: James writes the way he teaches, and Titus writes more tongue-in-cheek (his MITB groupmates will know exactly what that means).

As in Titus’ MITB days, James has the final say. (Removed by James, and then reinstated subsequently)

We want to start with a confession.

There is no specific GitHub repository for this article. Instead, what follows is a collection of lessons harvested from multiple projects we scaffolded purely to learn Claude Code.

[Titus’ previous article](/mitb-for-all/how-i-use-claude-code-3b1fd852305b) covered: (i) designing CLAUDE.md files, (ii) sub-agent architectures, (iii) custom commands, and (iv) the Ralph Wiggum loop — a technique for terraforming an entire code repository into existence after `uv init`.

This article extends some of those lessons, quietly buries others, and introduces a few you haven’t seen before. _Section 0 is only for those who have never used Claude CLI before. If you are already using the CLI, go straight to Section 1._

## 0\. Starting set-up

To start off, I first want to go back to the very basics, of how to get Claude Code on your CLI to begin with. Creating a guide with screenshots isn’t easy when everything is already up and running… Good thing I have another (Windows) laptop and can start everything from scratch.

First, open Powershell and type the following. Note that the command is different if you use CMD.

```
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex
```

You will see the nice-looking ‘successfully installed!’ text in green. However, if you rush on attempting to launch `claude`now, there will be an error. You need to set up the `PATH`, which can be done by pasting the command line below in your Powershell. There is no hardcoding, and hence you can use it directly as is without worrying that our usernames differ.

```
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("PATH", "$env:USERPROFILE\.local\bin;$([Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('PATH', 'User'))", "User")
```

(back to my main laptop now..)

Launch ClaudeCode on the terminal. Note that you must see the claude picture to know that you are in. Perform `/login` (Claude suggests auto-complete for you).

If you authenticate via the first option, you will be given a link to paste into the browser.

You should see a green `Login Successful`.

Suppose you exit (with `Ctrl+C`) and re-enter (with `claude`), you will see a welcome back message, without needing to log in again.

Now, install the Langsmith plugin in Claude Code. Note that your Git ssh keys should already be set up when running the following, because the process involves cloning from [https://github.com/langchain-ai/langsmith-claude-code-plugins.git](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langsmith-claude-code-plugins.git).

```
/plugin marketplace add langchain-ai/langsmith-claude-code-plugins
/plugin install langsmith-tracing@langsmith-claude-code-plugins
/reload-plugins
```

This will be helpful for section 4 later.

## 1\. Extending CLAUDE.MD files in Claude Code

In his previous Medium article, Titus made the case for keeping `CLAUDE.md` lean and focused. That advice holds, but as projects get larger, we may need to include architectural guidelines, domain knowledge, testing requirements, or other specialized guidelines. If everything is inside a single markdown file, we may end up with a wall-of-text which no one wants to touch, as well as take up a chunk of the context window even though not everything is required.

Claude Code addresses this problem through ‘rules’. That is, individual Markdown files stored under `.claude/rules/`. Instead of one large instruction file, you split project knowledge into smaller focused files like `database.md`, `error-handling.md`, `coding-standards.md`, `testing.md`. Every file in the directory is discovered recursively, so you can organize them into subfolders just like how you actually think about the project. For example the following.

```
yourprojectname/
└── .claude/
    ├── CLAUDE.md 
    └── rules/
        ├── architecture/
        │   ├── database.md
        │   └── integrations.md
        ├── development/ 
        │   ├── error-handling.md
        │   └── coding-standards.md
        ├── frontend/
        │   ├── react.md 
        │   └── styles.md 
        └── quality/
            ├── acceptance-criteria.md
            └── testing.md
```

An obvious benefit is maintainability. We can keep the data engineering stuff separate from the frontend stuff. The more interesting thing is on how each rule is loaded.

### Always-on rules

A rule with no frontmatter is loaded at launch, with the same priority as `.claude/CLAUDE.md`. For example, within `.claude/rules/architecture/database.md` (see above structure) we can have:

```
# Database Rule
Always use parameterized queries. Never interpolate user input directly
into SQL strings.
Do not expose raw database errors to users.
```

We should be clear about the benefit. An always-on rule enters the context window every single session, just like `CLAUDE.md` does. Splitting your instructions across numerous always-on rule files instead of one `CLAUDE.md` saves nothing in tokens. We still benefit from neater organization, but there’s no difference in terms of context.

### Path-scoped rules

A rule becomes path-scoped by adding a `paths:` field to the rule’s frontmatter. Claude loads that rule only after it first reads a file whose path matches one of the specified glob patterns. If your session never touches those files, the rule never enters the context window. This is where context savings come in.

For example, `.claude/rules/architecture/database.md` could contain:

```
---
paths:
  - "data/**"
  - "src/services/**"
---

# Database Rules
Always use parameterized queries. Never interpolate user input directly
into SQL strings.
Do not expose raw database errors to users.
```

The folders under `.claude/rules/` do not need to mirror the project directories exactly. Their purpose is to organise the instructions. The `paths:` field inside each rule determines which source files the rule applies to.

The full project directory could be something like

```
yourprojectname/
└── .claude/
│   ├── CLAUDE.md 
│   └── rules/
│       ├── architecture/
│       │   ├── database.md
│       │   └── integrations.md
│       ├── development/ 
│       │   ├── error-handling.md
│       │   └── coding-standards.md
│       ├── frontend/
│       │   ├── react.md 
│       │   └── styles.md 
│       └── quality/
│           ├── acceptance-criteria.md
│           └── testing.md
├── src/ 
│   │   ├── services/ 
│   │   ├── models/ 
│   │   └── util/
├── frontend/
├── data/ 
└── scripts/
```

In this example, the database rule above (in `.claude/rules/architecture/database.md`) applies only to files under `data/` and `src/services/`.

If you start a new session to work exclusively on `frontend/`, the database rule never enters the context window. That’s the real token saving right there.

### Things to note about rules

Path-scoped rules are triggered on read, not on write. If Claude creates a new file matching the rule’s path without first reading another matching file, the rule does not kick in. For important conventions that must be applied whenever Claude creates a new file, keep the rule always on or enforce it with a hook.

A word of caution that you should not treat rules like things Claude ‘remembers’, because that is not the case. Rules are context that gets discovered and loaded (or missed if not set up properly). We want to put domain-specific guidance into path-scoped rules so it appears only when relevant, and use always-on rules if you want it to hold everywhere, keeping `CLAUDE.md`as a short list of facts.

Rules are delivered as context after the system prompt, which is why they act as guidance but not guarantees. If you need something to always happen at a specific moment , such as blocking potentially destructive command, the a \`PreToolUse\` or \`PostToolUse\` hook is the right way to go. Rules shape behavior, while hooks enforce it (which brings us to the next section).

## 2\. Run custom logic with Hooks

### What are Hooks?

Hooks are user-defined actions (shell commands, scripts, LLM prompts) that fire automatically at specified points in Claude Code’s lifecycle. The ‘points’ could be before Claude runs a shell command, or after it edits a file, or even when Claude thinks it’s done. We don’t need to simply hope that Claude behaves as instructed, we want it to 100% happen.

Once defined, Claude Code monitors the event listeners in your hook scripts, mapping an event (like `PreToolUse`) and an optional matcher (like `Bash`) to a handler. When a matching event occurs, Claude passes JSON context to the hook handler, which can inspect the input, take action, and return a decision.

Hooks are configured in `.claude/settings.json`, and can be inspected using the `/hooks` command inside Claude Code as well. You may also use `.claude/settings.local.json` for project-specific settings that should apply only to you. It takes precedence, and you should add to `.gitignore`.

### Example use-case for hooks

An example that provides practical value-add even for personal projects is to log all changes made with a time-stamp, and a one-sentence summary. First, we create the following in `.claude/settings.json`.

```
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write|NotebookEdit",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "python \"${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/log_edit_summary.py\"", "timeout": 30 }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Notice the nested key `PostToolUse`within the json. It is a type of event.

### What are Events?

Events are specific ‘points’ (or moments) that happen in the lifecycle of a session. Hooks can listen for these.

In Claude’s official documentations, ~30 different events are defined, along with a description of when it fires (ie. gets triggered). The screenshots below shows some example to illustate.

In our example `settings.json`, we included a`PostToolUse` which fires after a tool call finishes.

What then are the tools? Basically anything below. Claude also explicitly stated in its [documentations](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#posttooluse) that `PostToolUse` “matches on tool name, same values as PreToolUse”.

Note that things like `Edit` and `Write` are not commands. Instead, they are built-in Claude Code tools.

### Hook Execution

Back to our same example, we have `"matcher": "Edit|Write|NotebookEdit"`. Since it is under `PostToolUse`, what happens will be that after Claude calls `Edit` or `Write` or `NotebookEdit`, it executes the command `python log_edit_summary.py` (where I truncated the file path for readability).

The python script (disclaimer: I generated it with Claude), would look something like the following:

```
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""PostToolUse hook: summarize an Edit/Write/NotebookEdit in one sentence via `claude -p`
and append it to logs/edit-log.md. Must never crash or block the user's session."""

import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from datetime import datetime, timezone

MAX_SNIPPET = 2000
MAX_SUMMARY = 200

def truncate(text, limit):
    if text is None:
        return ""
    text = str(text)
    return text if len(text) <= limit else text[:limit] + "...(truncated)"

def build_blob(tool_name, tool_input):
    if tool_name == "Edit":
        old = truncate(tool_input.get("old_string"), MAX_SNIPPET)
        new = truncate(tool_input.get("new_string"), MAX_SNIPPET)
        return f"--- before ---\n{old}\n--- after ---\n{new}"
    if tool_name == "Write":
        content = truncate(tool_input.get("content"), MAX_SNIPPET)
        return f"--- new file content ---\n{content}"
    if tool_name == "NotebookEdit":
        source = truncate(
            tool_input.get("new_source") or tool_input.get("content"), MAX_SNIPPET
        )
        cell_id = tool_input.get("cell_id", "unknown")
        edit_mode = tool_input.get("edit_mode", "unknown")
        return f"--- notebook cell {cell_id} ({edit_mode}) ---\n{source}"
    return truncate(json.dumps(tool_input), MAX_SNIPPET)

def get_summary(file_path, blob):
    prompt = (
        "In one short sentence, describe what this code edit changed. "
        "Respond with only the sentence, no preamble.\n\n"
        f"File: {file_path}\n\n{blob}"
    )
    try:
        result = subprocess.run(
            ["claude", "-p", "--disallowedTools", "Edit,Write,NotebookEdit,Bash"],
            input=prompt,
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            timeout=25,
            cwd=tempfile.gettempdir(),
        )
        first_line = result.stdout.strip().splitlines()[0] if result.stdout.strip() else ""
        return truncate(first_line, MAX_SUMMARY) or "(summary unavailable)"
    except Exception:
        return "(summary unavailable)"

def main():
    try:
        payload = json.load(sys.stdin)
    except Exception:
        return 0

    tool_name = payload.get("tool_name", "unknown")
    tool_input = payload.get("tool_input", {}) or {}
    file_path = (
        tool_input.get("file_path")
        or tool_input.get("notebook_path")
        or "(unknown file)"
    )

    blob = build_blob(tool_name, tool_input)
    summary = get_summary(file_path, blob)

    project_dir = os.environ.get("CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR", os.getcwd())
    log_path = os.path.join(project_dir, "logs", "edit-log.md")
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(log_path), exist_ok=True)

    timestamp = datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")
    line = f"- **{timestamp}** — `{file_path}` ({tool_name}): {summary}\n"

    try:
        with open(log_path, "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            f.write(line)
    except Exception:
        pass

    return 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main() or 0)
```

It resides within `.claude/hooks/` and, when invoked, executes `claude -p --disallowedTools "Edit,Write,NotebookEdit,Bash"` amongst other things. The list of tools explicitly disallowed is there to ensure we won’t end up in any recursive loop (ie. avoid the scenario where invoking the hook invokes yet another hook etc.). The ‘one-sentence summary’ is obtained via a prompt, within the `get_summary` function.

The end result is that when Claude makes changes to your repo, you get a time-stamped line added to your logs, something like the following:

Having covered rules and hooks, let us move on.

## 3\. Working entirely offline?

All Titus’ nephew wanted was to add the [No Batidao](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ovj8Gb_cVgY) song to a piano app. There was one problem. Titus was showing off the app on an iPad. No laptop. No Claude Code CLI.

Context: Titus was testing out Cursor at the time, and promptly burned through his entire monthly free-tier token limit in three hours. The casualty of that experiment: a piano web app for his children, vibe-coded into existence. The logic: expose them to music without buying an actual instrument, which would cost significantly more than a Claude/Cursor Pro subscription and take up space in a Singaporean apartment that has no room for a piano.

Titus’ children loved it. The nephew was less impressed. He had no interest in “Twinkle Twinkle Little Star”; he had more acquired taste. Specifically, energetic Brazilian funk music.

In the previous article, Titus covered running Claude Code in remote control mode, but that requires the CLI running on an actual machine. It turns out, Claude Code also has cloud sandboxing. Navigate to the Claude app, select “Code”, create a new session, and point it at your GitHub repository:

Claude spins up a cloud container, clones the repo, and you’re off.

From there, you simply chat with Claude to ship code. When it’s done, it seeks your approval before committing to a new feature branch. Features, shipped from a phone, while babysitting a nephew with niche music taste.

One important caveat: this only works if your latest code is already pushed to GitHub. If it’s sitting uncommitted on your local machine, Claude can’t see it — it clones from source.

Claude created and published a new feature branch with its code while Titus was entertaining his nephew.

## 4\. Add Observability to Claude Code

Data scientists decide on data, not vibes.

Adding observability confers insight into Claude Code’s trajectory (how it got to its final answer step by step), and the individual inputs and outputs of each step it took.

Adding observability gives you insight into Claude Code’s full trajectory — how it reached its answer, what steps it took, and what each step cost. Without it, you’re essentially reviewing the final painting without ever seeing the brushstrokes.

Practical applications:

-   **Comparing tools:** Give Claude Code and Codex the same task, trace both, and compare token spend, reasoning quality, and raw output — before committing to an annual subscription.
-   **Choosing your model:** Should you run Opus or Sonnet? That’s a data question. Analyze a corpus of traces before deciding.

Though Titus uses LangSmith here, most major LLM observability platforms work with Claude Code.

**Setup:** Sign up for LangSmith, grab an API key, create .claude/settings.local.json, and add:

```
{
  "env": {
    "TRACE_TO_LANGSMITH": "true",
    "CC_LANGSMITH_API_KEY": "<LangSmith API key>",
    "CC_LANGSMITH_PROJECT": "my-project"
  }
}
```

That’s the entire setup. LangSmith will automatically pick up Claude Code traces.

For context on value: Titus deliberately burned through his full session token limit on the piano project. LangSmith reported this would have cost USD $10 on a raw API key. The Claude Pro subscription at USD $20/month is great value for money.

An advantage of LangSmith is its copilot function. Chat with the platform, offload trace analysis to an LLM, and get actionable recommendations without having to read hundreds of spans yourself.

## 5\. Tap into Claude Code’s Rich Plugin Ecosystem

One underrated advantage of Claude Code’s CLI over other AI coding tools is its plugin marketplace — and it moves fast. New plugins land here first, before trickling out to other copilots like Codex.

To explore, type:

```
/plugins
```

You’ll see the full marketplace, sorted by installs. Here are some of our favorites.

### **a. Superpowers**

Titus’ previous article covered setting up multi-agent systems manually — planning requirements, defining roles, spawning subagents. The [“Superpowers” plugin](https://claude.com/plugins/superpowers) teaches Claude’s main agent to do all of that on its own, without being explicitly asked.

Titus wanted to add a “play along” feature to his piano app but forgot to configure subagents. Claude did it anyway: delivered a comprehensive task list, spawned subagents, and even assigned a Claude Opus subagent specifically for the final code review. Titus was initially worried about the token cost of Opus doing sub agent work. He needn’t have been — Sonnet handled orchestration, Opus only stepped in for the review pass.

### Tempted to not write your own sub agents?

Defining subagents forces you to decompose the problem, which means Claude inherits your decomposition instead of having to derive it. That’s always **cheaper** than letting the main agent figure out its own task structure mid-flight. Superpowers is doing that decomposition work for you, which is convenient but costs tokens to reason through it.

For complex projects where you actually understand the architecture, your decomposition will almost certainly be tighter than what Superpowers derives autonomously.

For [Ralph-loop](https://ai.sulat.com/ralph-wiggum-explained-the-claude-code-loop-that-keeps-going-3250dcc30809) style greenfield scaffolding, where you’re running for a long time and the task structure is knowable upfront, pre-defined subagents are the right call. Each subagent handles its slice, returns a tight summary, and the main agent’s context stays relatively clean _because it never had to do the work itself_. The key is that the summaries are bounded. A subagent that builds the database layer returns “done, here’s what I built” — not the entire build log.

The two approaches (defining custom sub agents or leaving it to superpowers) are not competing — they’re situational. Define your own subagents when you understand the architecture upfront. Let Superpowers handle decomposition when you’re exploring, debugging, or the task structure isn’t yet clear. The plugin earns its keep precisely in the moments where you haven’t thought it through yet.

### b. Playwright

Before signalling completion, Claude ran a battery of automated tests — including launching Titus’ piano app in Chrome, interacting with it like a real user, and taking screenshots for analysis. All this made possible by the [Playwright plugin](https://claude.com/plugins/playwright).

Titus was looking at his phone when his laptop started playing the piano by itself.

Claude had found a bug in its own code, fixed it, and shipped.

### c. Frontend Design

Titus builds almost exclusively in Chainlit and Streamlit — not exactly known as the glamorous end of the UI spectrum. And yet his vibe-coded apps look genuinely better than his coded apps. The [Frontend Design plugin](https://claude.com/plugins/frontend-design) is a big reason why: tell Claude what you want to build, and it applies design best practices automatically — typography, spacing, color, layout — without you having to ask. For developers who know what good UI looks like but couldn’t describe why, this plugin quietly does the heavy lifting.

### d. Context7

[Context7](https://claude.com/plugins/context7) gives Claude the ability to pull live, version-specific documentation and code examples from source repositories directly into its context window. The practical effect: fewer hallucinated APIs, fewer deprecated method calls, fewer “why is this not working” moments that turn out to be a version mismatch from 2022.

One honest caveat: the quality of this plugin is only as good as the docs it pulls from. Well-maintained libraries shine here; poorly documented ones less so. Browsing the codebase directly is often more reliable — but it burns tokens fast (PS we both recommend looking through the code base yourself). Context7 is a reasonable middle ground, and worth having in your toolkit.

### e. Ralph Loop

Covered in part (d) of [Titus’ previous article](/mitb-for-all/how-i-use-claude-code-3b1fd852305b). If you’re starting a greenfield project and want to go from empty repo to production-ready scaffold without writing boilerplate by hand, [this is the one to reach for first](https://claude.com/plugins/ralph-loop).

—

There are far too many excellent Claude Code plugins to cover here, and we barely scratched the surface. Suggestion: before starting any new project, browse [Claude’s official plugin page](https://claude.com/plugins). You’ll find integrations you didn’t know you needed — for example, Claude Code can even invoke Postman directly, which means API testing without leaving your terminal.

## Conclusion

When we started experimenting with Claude Code, we thought we were learning a new coding tool.

We were wrong. We were really learning a different way to build software.

### Good prompts matter, good engineering matters more

Good engineering means decomposing problems, creating reusable rules, instrumenting your workflows, choosing the right tools, and building feedback loops that make every future project easier than the last. Claude Code just happens to be an excellent environment for putting those ideas into practice.

Whether you’re building an enterprise platform, a weekend side project, or games for children (as Titus frequently does), the lesson is the same:

Don’t think of AI as something that writes code for you. Think of AI as a team you’re leading. Like every good engineering team, the better the architecture, tooling, documentation, and processes, the better the outcomes become.

We’re still in the early days. The plugin ecosystem is growing weekly. Models are improving monthly. Entire workflows that felt impossible a year ago now feel routine.

Perhaps the biggest shift isn’t technological at all. It’s that software engineering is quietly becoming less about typing code and more about designing systems that continuously amplify human capability.

Right now, the only real bottleneck isn’t what AI can build — it’s how ambitious we’re willing to be. And we’re incredibly excited to be a part of this future.
