body:
* * *

#### **An honest evaluation of using Antigravity for coding**

In my previous article on Claude Code, I shared how I optimize my workflow to get the most out of its context window and token budget. Those techniques work well, but you might still run into usage limits.

During the period when Anthropic was more [aggressively throttling usage](https://www.infoworld.com/article/4151196/anthropic-throttles-claude-subscriptions-to-meet-capacity.html), the restrictions frequently coincided with my peak coding hours — 1pm–7pm GMT (9pm onwards in Singapore). Unfortunately, that’s also when I spend most evenings working on personal projects.

[Anthropic has since increased available compute capacity](https://www.anthropic.com/news/higher-limits-spacex), but the experience raised an interesting question:

#### **What do you do when you run out of Claude tokens?**

One option is [Claude Max at USD100/month — roughly five times the cost of Claude Pro (USD20/month)](https://claude.com/pricing). Personally, it made more sense to look for a similar plan with a different provider than to quintuple my monthly subscription cost.

Since I already had a Google One storage subscription, Antigravity was the obvious place to start. My goal was simple: determine whether it was compelling enough to justify upgrading my aging 200GB storage plan to Google AI Plus/Pro. With Google now bundling AI features into its subscription tiers, upgrading storage increasingly means upgrading your AI capabilities as well.

This article explores how my attempt at using Antigravity for coding, where it fits into my workflow, and whether I think it’s a worthwhile alternative when Claude Code isn’t available.

* * *

### There isn’t one Antigravity, but three

The first thing that tripped me up: Antigravity isn’t a single product. It’s really three different interfaces built on the same underlying system. They all do broadly the same thing, but the experience changes depending on how you access it.

#### a. Antigravity CLI

This is the most familiar interface if you’ve used Claude Code before and replaces the [discontinued Gemini CLI](https://developers.googleblog.com/an-important-update-transitioning-gemini-cli-to-antigravity-cli/).

Installation is straightforward:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://antigravity.google/cli/install.sh | bash
```

Then you spin it up with:

```bash
agy
```

This launches the Antigravity CLI in your terminal. Like Claude Code, it’s IDE-agnostic — you could be writing code in VS Code, Neovim, or even Notepad, and the workflow still works the same way.

One useful detail: the CLI is currently the only place where you can see your Antigravity token usage in real time. You can check it with:

```bash
/usage
```

That’s also where things get a little sobering — I definitely managed to burn through my allocation faster than expected 😅

You’ll notice two usage bars. At the moment, Antigravity allows access to the Gemini and Claude model families (including OpenAI’s GPT-OSS). Each comes with its own usage limits, and once you hit one cap in one bucket you can switch to the other.

If you’ve used Claude Code, this CLI will feel very familiar. A lot of the interaction patterns map **almost** 1:1.

#### b. Antigravity IDE

The IDE version feels closer to tools like Cursor.

It’s essentially a VS Code–based environment where AI isn’t bolted on as an extension, but the foundation of the entire editor experience.

Installation is straightforward from the [official Google Antigravity IDE download page](https://antigravity.google/product/antigravity-ide).

If you’ve used Cursor or GitHub Copilot inside VS Code, Antigravity will feel immediately familiar. You get a chat interface alongside your main editor window, with tight integration into your workspace.

One interesting detail: you can highlight terminal output and immediately chat with the agent about it. The same applies to code, comments, or any selected text — the agent can act directly on whatever you’re focusing on.

In practice, the IDE becomes the agent’s full workspace. Compared to the CLI, where interaction is more constrained, the IDE version gives the agent much deeper access to your project context. Every terminal run, text selection and comment is visible by the agent.

If you’re actively building an application, this is likely where you’ll spend most of your time.

#### c. Antigravity 2.0

At this point, you might think Antigravity is just CLI + IDE. But there’s also a higher-level view layer that acts like a command center for multiple sessions and environments.

The idea is simple: once you have multiple Antigravity instances running, you need a way to monitor or kick off all of them from one place. This layer provides that overview, letting you see and manage active agents across different contexts.

It’s less about writing code directly, and more about orchestration — keeping track of what each agent is doing across your workflow.

In Claude Code, Codex, or any other CLI copilot, you would have to run `claude --resume <session-id>` . In Antigravity you never have to.

### Coding experiment: building a Jigsaw Puzzle app

To test this properly, I decided to build something non-trivial: a [Jigsaw Puzzle app](https://image-jigsaw-app.vercel.app/) for my kids (mostly to keep them entertained and reduce household chaos). The requirements were straightforward:

-   Upload any image or choose from 3 defaults
-   Select difficulty (Easy / Medium / Hard)
-   Slice image into draggable puzzle pieces
-   Snap pieces into place on a board
-   Show a win screen when completed
-   Fully responsive on desktop and mobile (including orientation changes)

In case you’re interested in my antigravity setup, my GitHub repo can be found [here](https://github.com/tituslhy/ImageJigsawApp).

#### Unlike Claude Code

1.  Antigravity is organized around a `.agents` folder.
2.  Antigravity **does not allow** writing any custom sub agents. Instead, Antigravity asks that you trust it with the goal, and it’ll spawn sub agents as needed. At a [demo during Google’s I/O 2026 keynote](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T_fnhr5lVBw), Antigravity spawned 93 sub agents in parallel and ran them for over 12 hours. The final product was able to autonomously launch a version of the game _Doom._
3.  Antigravity does not have a `/commands` . Custom `/` actions are stored in `.agents/workflows` .

Conceptually, everything else is familiar:

-   It supports AGENTS.md-style instructions
-   It reads GEMINI.md, which takes priority over AGENTS.md.
-   Rules exist, similar to other agentic coding tools
-   Skills are available for extending behavior

One interesting detail is the “Activation Mode” dropdown for rules. It makes rule injection much more intentional — you can selectively activate context instead of loading everything globally. This helps keep instruction files lightweight while still allowing targeted control when needed.

#### The setup experiment

To get a feel for the system, I wrote a `/setup` Antigravity workflow to bootstrap the repository from scratch and executed it directly from the Antigravity IDE chat interface.

That alone consumed a surprising amount of resources — about 38% of my Gemini model quota in a single run.

That was my first real signal that the system behaves very differently from Claude Code in terms of token economics.

#### The jigsaw build

In Antigravity 2.0, I ran:

```plaintext
Build the JigsawIt puzzle app as described in GEMINI.md.

The app is complete when:
- A user can upload any image OR pick from 3 defaults
- They can choose Easy / Medium / Hard difficulty
- The image is sliced into puzzle pieces on a board
- Pieces can be dragged and snapped into place
- A win screen appears when all pieces are correctly placed
- The app is responsive on desktop and mobile including screen tilt

Run npm run dev when done and confirm it loads without errors.
```

#### First run: speed vs correctness

The most immediate impression was speed.

Antigravity moved fast — noticeably faster than Claude Code in my setup. Within a short time, it had scaffolding, UI components, and a running dev server.

I briefly wondered if I was about to see the “93 sub-agent swarm” behavior from demos — dozens of sub-agents working in parallel. In practice, I didn’t observe anything close to that level of orchestration during my run.

What I got instead was simpler: fast generation, followed by a working-but-not-correct implementation.

#### Debug loop and model switching

The initial build **did not** work correctly. The fix iteration was quick, but also incomplete.

At that point, I hit my Gemini usage limit.

So I switched to Sonnet.

Sonnet was able to fix the issue, but I also ran into its token limits and could not fix the rest of the gaps I found later on with Antigravity.

### Takeaways

If there’s one consistent observation, it’s this:

> Antigravity is extremely fast

But that speed comes with trade-offs in correctness and token consumption. In my case, I ended up bouncing between models just to stabilize a single working version of the app.

It also highlighted a practical difference in how models behave under an agentic system. [Gemini 3.5 Flash was co-optimized for use with antigravity](https://antigravity.google/blog/gemini-3-5-flash-in-google-antigravity). In my experience however, Claude Sonnet felt more consistent and frictionless for iterative debugging with Antigravity.

#### Token economics matter more than expected

Antigravity’s free usage is structured around weekly limits. That means you can hit caps quickly during intense building sessions, especially when working in longer agent loops.

This is different from tools with free tier tokens that reset monthly. You will be able to get more work done within a single coding session if you use these tools, but have to wait longer for the token limits to refresh after.

The practical implication is simple: for Antigravity users, you need to build in smaller, more intentional increments if you want to avoid breaking flow mid-session.

#### Still, more tokens are needed

In my experience, Antigravity’s token limits feel tight enough that longer sessions can run out sooner than expected — especially when using heavier planning models in agent mode. [And I’m not the only one](https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/google-ai-pro-quota-on-antigravity-is-far-too-restrictive/144912).

This suggests Antigravity may not be designed for the same usage pattern as Claude Code, where long-running, deeply iterative sessions are more common.

The result is a trade-off between staying within the intended “fast loop” design, or prioritizing reasoning quality at the cost of quickly exhausting quotas.

Either way, the takeaway is that Antigravity probably benefits from clearer guidance on how it is meant to be used within its own ecosystem, especially around model selection and expected usage patterns.

### The rest of the payload

Antigravity’s token limits are real. But they’re not the whole story. The Google AI Pro isn’t just a juiced up Antigravity subscription — it’s an entire ecosystem upgrade with many other interesting pieces.

#### Introducing Jules: Dispatch and Walk Away

Google’s free tier allows you to use the [Jules coding agent](https://jules.google.com/) — an autonomous coding agent where you can dispatch tasks (PRs, etc.) to and walk away. Simply connect it to GitHub, and tell it what you want to do. Then shut your laptop and do something else.

**A quick technical note:** [The default LLM for Jules on the free tier is Gemini 2.5 Pro](https://jules.google/docs/usage-limits/), which isn’t Google’s latest model. However, the architectural choice here is fascinating: the backbone for the autonomous Jules agent relies on a heavy-lifting reasoning model, whereas the preferred engine for the Antigravity IDE is the faster, lower-latency Gemini 3.5 Flash.

Furthermore, you can’t currently select which LLM to use inside Jules — Google handles the model routing entirely behind the scenes. To unlock their next-generation reasoning engine (Gemini 3 Pro), you’ll need that Google AI Pro subscription.

Nonetheless, it’s not lost on me that I still had to use Claude Code with Sonnet to rescue the app after Jules pushed a few strange commits.

#### Control your Google apps with Gemini

Similarly, the Gemini app operates independently of Antigravity quotas and can even extend into system-level integrations like Google Home control, depending on setup. I was able to make Gemini control my Google Home devices:

I was also able to ask Gemini for photos of my children at different age groups — it shows remarkable understanding of photographs stored in Google Photos.

#### Other goodies

The list of benefits of the free tier is already remarkable. Aside from the above, there is also:

-   NotebookLM as personalized RAG over your documents. I’ve not tested this fully, but I know that you can even [create a podcast over your documents](https://notebooklm.google/)!
-   Gemini is still the only LLM that can natively answer questions over a video file input, and
-   Gemini has the ability to generate images, songs and video.

[The goodies list from Google AI pro is even longer](https://one.google.com/about/google-ai-plans/?utm_source=g1&utm_medium=paid_media&utm_campaign=sem_aimarketingpage&gclsrc=aw.ds&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23825868886&gbraid=0AAAAAC_C9PToviMuyNt491GTrqvgExRtN&gclid=CjwKCAjw3ejRBhAdEiwADkqPnwkRrz0TdH8KlUjuR0G8eDsn-0ujYP-CcclEc81AdyyDj5v8AeEZKRoCvkUQAvD_BwE). Free USD 10 Google Cloud Platform credits monthly, free YouTube premium lite and Google Home premium subscriptions for starters. SGD30 for all of that is genuinely hard to argue with.

Presently, these do feel like adjacent pieces of the same ecosystem rather than tightly coupled components. But Google is the only company that is able to compete on every single technological frontier. I think it’s only a matter of time before these pieces begin to feel like extensions of each other.

### Final thoughts

Despite similarities in setup with tools like VS Code, Cursor, and Claude Code, Antigravity feels less like a replacement — or even a backup — and more like a different operating mode entirely.

_Antigravity is fast, ambitious, and genuinely impressive in bursts. Upgrading to a Google AI Pro plan confers_ **_plenty_** _of side benefits as well. But in my view, it is evident that Google’s state of AI for coding is an order of magnitude away from the likes of Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor, at least._

_Maybe that view changes as the limits expand. Until then, Claude Code stays on. Antigravity stays interesting._

body:
* * *

#### Here’s an alternative to the lobster — and it might be better

Everyone wants a personal AI assistant these days.

If you’ve been anywhere near the AI space recently, you’ve heard of OpenClaw. Its logo is a lobster claw. The internet ran with it. In China, there are mass [“lobster gatherings”](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/east-asia/china-tech-giants-alibaba-baidu-openclaw-craze-ai-5999441) where people learn to install and use it. And honestly, the hype is deserved — OpenClaw can hook up to almost any messaging platform, email client, or calendar, and it’s open-sourced. People use it to automate their lives. Some take it further and run entire [one-person companies (OPCs)](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cy41n17e23go) on it.

But here’s the catch.

-   You still need to hook up an LLM — either an API key or an LLM subscription.
-   OpenClaw’s lack of sandboxing has spawned a fragmented ecosystem of forks: [nanoclaw](https://github.com/nanocoai/nanoclaw), [ironclaw](https://www.ironclaw.com/), [zeroclaw](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw) — different versions of the same thing with slightly different feelings about Docker.
-   If you’re a developer, you also end up juggling multiple tools — OpenClaw for general tasks, Claude Code for coding, something else for your desktop and/or mobile experience.

If your goal is zero spend and one assistant that does everything including writing code, OpenClaw isn’t quite the answer.

This is what I use instead.

**Imagine having all of this — for free:**

1.  General purpose assistant capabilities — hook up to WhatsApp, email, messaging platforms, and chat naturally
2.  Claude Code-style agentic coding capabilities that work directly in your repositories
3.  Freedom to use any LLM — including free cloud models or personal models, so your token spend is literally $0
4.  A desktop app experience when you want it
5.  An assistant that grows with you — remembering your preferences, context, and working style over time

### Meet Hermes

Pronounced “Her-meez”, Hermes Agent is an open-source, self-improving AI agent framework created by [Nous Research](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/) that runs continuously as a background service on your own self-hosted infrastructure.

The feature that immediately caught my attention wasn’t the messaging integrations or the coding capabilities.

It was this:

> Hermes can write its own skills.

Most AI assistants forget everything the moment you close the tab. Hermes actually learns. It watches itself work, figures out what it did well, and writes itself a little cheat sheet for next time.

#### Core Features

-   **Self-Improving Learning Loop (repeated. Can’t emphasize enough how amazing this is)**: It analyzes its own performance after completing tasks to write, refine, and saves custom `.md` skill files.
-   **Three-Layer Memory:** Retains context across separate chat sessions using full-text search databases alongside distinct user and agent identity snapshots.
-   **Multi-Platform Gateway:** Connects with over 20 messaging services including Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, and Matrix.
-   **Scheduled Automations:** Supports natural language cron scheduling for running background reports, system audits, and nightly backups unattended.
-   **Isolated Subagents:** Spawns temporary, sandboxed worker agents via RPC to handle parallel workstreams at a reduced token cost.
-   **Sandboxing (what OpenClaw couldn’t do):** Offers terminal execution across six distinct backends, including local terminal, Docker containers, and remote SSH servers.

Hermes is only as good as the model driving it.

> Always pair Hermes with a strong LLM.

Weak models driving Hermes produce what I can only describe as “creatively unhinged” behavior — the kind where your agent confidently reorganizes your entire file system based on vibes.

### Installing Hermes

To install Hermes, just visit [NousResearch’s main Hermes website](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/) and download the desktop application — it comes shipped with everything else.

#### The normal way to set up Hermes

In your command line, type:

```bash
hermes setup
```

The setup installer will walk you through each step of the installation process. The only setup that is strictly compulsory is the LLM service.

#### The better way to set up Hermes

[Download and install Ollama](https://ollama.com/download) to your local laptop. Ollama comes with pre-defined launch commands for different services.

Once you have Ollama installed, pull any Ollama model you want and run:

```bash
ollama launch hermes --model <your_ollama_model>
```

Ollama handles **everything** for you.

All models that you install on your local laptop using `ollama pull` belong to you. Hermes is also hosted on your own computer. The entire stack runs under your control. No vendor lock-in, no subscription requirements. Just your computer.

But if something is too good to be true, it often is.

LLMs require huge storage overhead and memory requirements. Unless you have a personal NVIDIA GPU server hooked to your laptop, or a high spec MacBook pro, you’re going to notice problems:

1.  You can only download very small LLMs on a normal laptop —not only do these run extremely slowly on your computer but the LLM’s answers leave a lot to be desired.
2.  Your computer will start “freezing” more — because LLMs require a lot of RAM overhead. Despite having a MacBook Pro that felt powerful in 2021, Hermes took more than 2 minutes to reply to “hi” when I used Gemma4:31b on Ollama. Also, my MacBook pro started sounding like a jet taking off despite me closing almost every other running process like Chrome.
3.  Your computer will heat up — this impacts battery life. My Macbook’s battery life dips very quickly whenever Hermes was running.

Where possible, use the best mixture of experts model that your computer can store and run. I use Qwen3.6:35b, a powerful mixture of experts LLM by Alibaba with [only 3 billion active parameters at any time](https://qwen.ai/blog?id=qwen3.6-35b-a3b). Gemma4:31b is a dense model with all 31b parameters active every time, which was why it was slower and drained battery life faster.

The other solution? Simple — don’t run the LLM on your laptop at all.

Hermes also works with any paid LLM subscription — t[hough Anthropic restricts Claude Pro tokens to their own apps](https://bitcoinfoundation.org/news/crypto-companies-news/anthropic-claude-restrictions/).

Also, Ollama provides hosted cloud models that can be used without running large models locally (these include state-of-the-art LLMs such as [MiniMax-m3](https://ollama.com/library/minimax-m3)). Most LLMs are accessible through their [generous free tier](https://ollama.com/pricing).

> Ollama Cloud is incredible value — I’ve never hit my free tier limits despite using MiniMax-m3 (a model with [capabilities comparable to Claude Opus 4.7 with a cost comparable to Claude Haiku](https://www.minimax.io/models/text/m3)) unless I use Hermes for coding in CLI mode. More on that later.

So, if you’re using minimax-m3, run:

```bash
ollama launch hermes --model minimax-m3:cloud
```

This launches Hermes and will still prompt you to set up other services such as your messaging platform if you haven’t done so. When the setup is complete, you’ll be able to see your messenger app as its own key-value pair in your `~/.hermes/config.yaml` :

```yaml
whatsapp:
    allowed_users:
        - "your_handphone_number"
    enabled: true
    mode: bot
```

All of Hermes’ setup files can be found in `~/.hermes` — and it’s a lot! Hermes comes with many bundled skills and tools just like OpenClaw!

An important tip I’d leave is to set up a fallback model pointing to your local LLM if you have one. That way there will never be service interruptions after you max out your use of the best model.

### Installing MCP Tools

You can extend Hermes’ capabilities by giving it even more tools!

In my opinion, an LLM without the ability to search the web will always have stale context — it’s relying on its own training data. So my first priority was to give it a web search tool. You could self-host your own (for example DuckDuckGo is free, FireCrawl can be self-hosted via Docker), or use a managed service like me. I use [Tavily AI which has 1000 free searches per month on the free tier](https://www.tavily.com/pricing?utm_term=tavily&utm_campaign=Tavily+Brand+-+General+-+global&utm_source=adwords&utm_medium=ppc&matchtype=p&device=c&utm_content=795629308483_350829835669&utm_position=&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23289739393&gbraid=0AAAABB_ZBWqd07VPqiUbhnB6UUeLPYmqh&gclid=Cj0KCQjwi8nRBhDhARIsAHZf_paCX6h5RF17OA1NhlITfu5WPToY3jDkBB3ZDi6f9SsLro_1z0t2OrYaAh55EALw_wcB) — very generous.

I then wanted to give Hermes control of my browsers so it could use Chrome to search for stuff in case the web search tool reaches its rate limit. Hermes would then be able to open Chrome and “google” for information as though I was searching for it myself.

In the spirit of general purpose assistance, I also gave Hermes access to GitHub MCP so that it can search and respond to issues for me.

The way to do it is to edit your config.yaml file by including a `mcp_servers` block:

```yaml
mcp_servers:
    chrome-devtools:
        args:
            - -y
            - chrome-devtools-mcp@latest
        command: npx
    github: #to review GitHub Issues
        command: npx
        args:
            - -y
            - "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"
        env:
            GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN: "your_github_PAT" #Set this up first
    tavily:
        type: url
        url: https://mcp.tavily.com/mcp/?tavilyApiKey=your_tavily_api_key
```

> Important! Whenever you update the config.yaml file, remember to run \``` hermes gateway restart` `` in your terminal for these to take effect

Do note that Hermes will always have the exact same skills and MCP tools – because Hermes definitions are global and all read from `~/hermes`.

### 1\. Hermes as a personal assistant

Time to take Hermes out for a spin. I primarily use Hermes on WhatsApp. To ping Hermes, simply message yourself:

I created a dummy GitHub issue in one of my repositories that just said ‘Hermes can you read this?’, and asked Hermes to reply it.

Hermes read it, replied professionally, and offered to open a PR. Absolute overachiever:

Obviously I made it do other things like search the Internet specifically using Chrome instead of Tavily — to see if it could open my Windows and control them. It could use Chrome for general purpose tasks but not for social media platforms like LinkedIn because it did not have my credentials (this was also an intentional test). Importantly, Chrome knows it’s being controlled by “automated test software” (see screenshot below) which was why Hermes’ couldn’t simply log in.

If you’re like me you’re probably wondering what if the conversation gets too long? How do you reset it?

Just type `/new` into WhatsApp and you get a new chat session 😁

I suggest refreshing conversation sessions frequently – especially when you change topics. This just keeps the context fresh for optimal agent performance.

Hermes is also able to do work on your computer for you – like organize contents or write new files. I got Hermes to write an agents.md file for an idea of an app I had.

Occasionally, Hermes might ask you for approval. Just reply `/approve` on WhatsApp to approve its request.

#### Bonus: Evidence that Hermes learns from context

Hermes was initially running into issues with Chrome due to browser built security – CAPTCHA/CloudFlare for example. Hermes made a note to adapt its usage of the Chrome MCP tool. It’s better – but I’d still have to manually click pictures that have bicycles to clear the CAPTCHA stage.

> Remember to leave your laptop running – it can sleep but don’t close it or Hermes would be unreachable

### 2\. Hermes as a CLI Copilot

Hermes can be used in CLI Copilot mode as well. Create a new terminal window in your code repository and type:

```bash
hermes
```

This opens a beautiful interactive command line interface like Claude Code:

You can then start asking it to do stuff just like you would Claude Code.

#### Unlike Claude Code…

You don’t create a `.hermes` folder in your code repository, or write sub agents in markdown files, or skills. You could write custom skills and hooks in your global Hermes folder (`~/.hermes`) if you wish, but NOT sub agents.

Instead, Hermes’ main agent will decide on its own when it wants to spawn sub agents to tackle tasks in parallel. Really cool!

I use Ollama Cloud which only allows for ONE cloud model to be used at any point in time. So I had to configure the LLM to be used as sub agents. To do this, edit your `~/.hermes/config.yaml file`. I used my local Ollama LLM:

```yaml
delegation:
    api_key: ollama
    api_mode: ""
    base_url: http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1
    child_timeout_seconds: 600
    default_toolsets:
        - terminal
        - file
        - web
    inherit_mcp_toolsets: true
    max_concurrent_children: 3
    max_iterations: 50
    max_spawn_depth: 1
    model: qwen3.6:35b-mlx
    orchestrator_enabled: true
    provider: custom
    reasoning_effort: ""
    subagent_auto_approve: false
```

> Remember to run “hermes gateway restart” after you make changes to config.yaml

🚨**: Hermes decides on its own when to spawn sub-agents** — but like any good delegator, it works better when the work is already broken down.

My preference:

-   Ask Hermes to write a `tasks.md` first. In that prompt, tell it to flag which tasks can run in parallel.
-   Then kick it off: _"Run tasks 2A, B, and C simultaneously once task 1 is done."_ Hermes dispatches, coordinates, and reports back. You just sit there looking like a genius engineering manager.

#### Want to keep working with Hermes CLI away from your desk?

Hermes CLI requires you to “handoff” the current state to your messaging service. In your Hermes CLI, simply type `/handoff` and select your messaging service.

Wait until you see your messaging service register the handoff:

Now you can continue working on your code with Hermes away from your desk. I was reviewing task outputs on WhatsApp while pushing a trolley in the supermarket.

This is what peak developer productivity looks like, apparently.

### 3\. Hermes as a Desktop App

Hermes comes with a Desktop App too. The best part? You’re able to see **all** your chat sessions with Hermes across every medium.

Each Hermes agent has the exact same skills and MCP tools as configured in the global `~/.hermes/config.yaml` file. So the experience you get is very consistent.

You can use Hermes Desktop like you would use ChatGPT/Claude.

#### 4\. Hermes as a Python Library

If you’ve made it this far and you’re thinking “Awesome I want this but in code” – good news. Hermes is also a pip-installable Python library, and yes, it’s a proper LangChain alternative.

Since this article is about Hermes as a personal assistant, I’ll leave the framework deep-dive for another day. But if you want to start building, feel free to consult the [official docs](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/guides/python-library).

### Want to see Hermes logs?

You can now see Hermes agent logs as it runs tasks. In your terminal, run:

```bash
hermes dashboard
```

This spins up a web UI on [http://localhost:9119](http://localhost:9119). This dashboard is the central command center for all of Hermes’ activities. You can also edit models, MCP, etc., via this dashboard instead of `~/.hermes/config.yaml`. Changes made here will propagate over. I still prefer the yaml approach though.

To see the logs, click “logs” on the left hand side panel of the dashboard:

Note: I’ve noticed that the logs don’t always stream in real time. So do expect some latency.

### It’s not all sunshines and rainbows though

Like all open-source products, the learning curve for Hermes is harder, and the experience differs across users.

#### There will be integration friction

I’ve deliberately not onboarded my Google services on Hermes. Because it’s not straightforward — you’d have to setup OAuth2 in Google Cloud Platform (GCP) by yourself first, and then hook it up to Hermes. I can’t imagine people outside the software space setting up their own GCP accounts and projects just for Hermes.

In Claude and ChatGPT, all this is done in **one click**. In Gemini, it’s zero clicks. You’re already logged in to your Google account. I’ve OAuth2 set up in GCP for a different project but did not use it to avoid debugging potential integration issues with Hermes. Especially when there are frictionless alternatives.

#### Any subscription service can do it better

Unfortunately, whatever you think that Hermes can do, it’s almost certain that any subscribed service (Claude, ChatGPT, etc.) does it better.

Hermes is deliberately modular — which is both its superpower and its curse. Modular means flexible. It also means there are seventeen different places things can break, and when they do, you’re your own IT department. There’s no support ticket. There’s no customer success manager.

Subscription services win on this front — not because they’re smarter, but because someone actually thought about how all the pieces connect before shipping it to you. The integration interfaces are part of the product. With Hermes, the integration interfaces are part of your weekend.

#### The biggest motivation for Hermes is personal AI

There’s one more thing subscription services can never give you though: your data stays yours. If you’re running a local LLM, nothing leaves your machine. Your conversations, your tasks, your agents — all of it, entirely under your control. The question is what would you do with Hermes that you’d never with Claude because you wouldn’t want it on Anthropic’s servers?

### **So who is Hermes actually for?**

Not anyone who flinches at the words “OAuth2” or “config.yaml.”

Hermes is for the developer who looked at every subscription AI assistant and thought: _I could build something better than this_. And then actually did.

The tradeoff is real: subscription services win on polish, integration, and not making you feel like your own IT helpdesk at 11pm — but so is the cost, the vendor lock-in, and the quiet discomfort of knowing your most personal conversations are training someone else’s model.

There’s so much more ground I’ve yet to explore with Hermes. But the fact remains: Personal AI assistants aren’t a pipe dream anymore. They’re already here. They’re free. They run on your machine, remember your preferences, write their own skills, and will absolutely keep working while you push a trolley through the supermarket.

Feel free to not pick up the lobster claw.

body:
* * *

#### Notes from an early experiment – by no means the final word

I want to start with a confession.

The only terminal commands I personally typed to build a full-stack stock analysis service were `uv init` and `uv add <package>`

Everything else — the architecture, the backend, the UI, the MCP tools, the debugging, the iteration — was Claude. I described what I wanted. Claude built it in one shot.

The experience was equal parts impressive and terrifying. GenAI has come so far.

This is what I learned.

* * *

### First, let’s get the obvious question out of the way

It is June 2026. The question is no longer “do you use AI for coding?” The question is “how do you use it without your codebase turning into an archaeological dig site of half-implemented features and quietly broken modules?”

Most engineers I know have settled into one of three categories of tools:

#### Chat applications

ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, etc. The copy-paste era. You describe the problem, you get code back, you paste it in, you hope for the best. These have gotten dramatically better at integrating directly with IDEs — but the fundamental interaction model is still conversational. You’re talking _about_ the code more than working _in_ it.

#### IDE copilots

Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, etc. These live inside your editor. They suggest, they autocomplete, they can apply changes directly. Most require explicit approval before touching anything — which is simultaneously a very good thing and a very annoying thing, often in the same five-minute window.

#### CLI agents

Claude Code, Codex CLI, Hermes, etc. This is the different category. These don’t suggest — they _do_. They inspect entire codebases, modify multiple files, run tests, debug failures, refactor, and iterate. They feel less like assistants and more like junior engineers who have been given terminal access and a task description and told to figure it out.

The junior engineer analogy is important. Because like actual junior engineers, the quality of their output depends enormously on how well you’ve set them up to succeed.

> “The real mistake isn’t choosing the wrong model. It’s thinking the model is the point.”

Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity CLI — these are not LLMs. They are orchestration layers _built around_ LLMs. They manage context selection, tool usage, file access, planning, and execution loops. The harness often matters as much as the model inside it.

Which means benchmarks comparing raw model outputs are largely irrelevant to real-world agentic performance. You are not comparing models. You are comparing systems.

* * *

### What I actually built (vibed)

To test these ideas properly, I decided to do something concrete: build an entire full-stack stock MCP service using Claude Code, touching as little code myself as possible.

The stack: [FastMCP](https://gofastmcp.com/getting-started/welcome), yfinance, pandas, numpy, ta, and a [Prefab UI](https://prefab.prefect.io/docs/welcome) library for the dashboard rendering. The goal: a service where you could ask for a technical analysis snapshot of any stock and get back a fully rendered interactive dashboard — Bollinger Bands, RSI, MACD, the works — not just a wall of JSON.

The result — it works. Here’s MSFT being analysed in real time:

#### **What the MCP produces**

Ask “Give me a technical analysis snapshot for MSFT” in the Claude Desktop App and you get back a **full interactive dashboard** with Bollinger Bands, RSI chart, and MACD histogram. Real data. Real render. Zero hardcoded anything.

Claude calling the MCP tool and rendering the UI from a single natural language prompt.

> If you’re wondering whether MCPs can return fully interactive applications rather than simple tool responses, the answer is yes. That’s a fascinating topic in its own right, and one I’ll cover in a future article.

The project lives at my [GitHub](https://github.com/tituslhy/StockMCPService/tree/main) if you want to clone and run it yourself. But the more interesting story is how it got built — because the architecture decisions I made before writing a single line shaped everything.

Here are some lessons I learnt from my vibe coding experience.

* * *

### Five tips for Vibe Coding

#### Tip #1: Keep the main agent’s context clean

The fastest way to degrade agentic performance is to let a single agent do everything. The main agent accumulates codebase context, tool outputs, planning history, and partial decisions. Even with compaction, performance degrades as context grows.

When this happens, the instinct is to switch to a stronger model. Opus instead of Sonnet. This helps temporarily (Opus is known to be much better at reasoning with long contexts) and costs you significantly more, but it doesn’t fix the underlying problem. You’re giving a better brain to a system that is structurally broken.

The fix is architectural: split work into specialised sub-agents with narrow responsibilities. Each agent runs in isolation, does its job, and exits. The main agent becomes a pure orchestrator — it assigns work, evaluates outputs, and decides next steps. Nothing pollutes the central context.

This single change has an outsized impact on cost, stability, and output quality. It’s the most important thing I did.

#### Tip #2: Treat skills as deferred context, not static instructions

Skills are usually misunderstood as prompt libraries — a place to dump instructions you want Claude to remember. That framing leads to bloated skill files that load everything upfront and conflict with each other in subtle ways.

Better framing: skills are _deferred context modules_ that load only when needed. Instead of injecting all instructions at session start, the agent pulls in relevant behavior definitions based on what it’s actually doing.

This prevents context bloat, improves precision, avoids conflicting instructions, and keeps large instruction sets manageable. The goal is progressive disclosure — the agent knows everything is available, but only loads what’s relevant right now.

#### Tip #3: CLAUDE.md is a control surface, not documentation

This one took me a while to internalise. CLAUDE.md is **not** a place to describe your project. It is a mechanism to control agent behavior.

A good CLAUDE.md contains three things: minimal project context, architectural conventions, and behavioural rules for situations where Claude might otherwise improvise badly. Everything else is noise. Verbosity hurts more than it helps — agents don’t need encyclopaedic documentation, they need constraints.

The most important thing in my CLAUDE.md wasn’t the stack description or the file structure. It was this line:

```
Always use subagents. Never implement in this context.
```

Eight words of constraint outperformed six paragraphs of guidance.

#### Tip #4: Use permissions as intentional friction

Permissions influence agent behavior more than prompts do. A well-designed `.claude/settings.json` defines how freely the agent can operate — and the goal is not maximum autonomy or maximum restriction. It's calibrated friction.

Too much restriction and you slow iteration to a crawl. Too little control and you get chaotic or unsafe behavior — the kind where Claude helpfully refactors three files you weren’t asking it to touch and breaks something subtle in the process.

Most real-world failures in agent systems are not model failures. They are governance failures. The model did exactly what it was allowed to do.

#### Tip #5: Don’t rebuild what already exists

Claude Code is part of a broader ecosystem — MCP servers, plugins, external tools — that often provides more leverage than prompt engineering alone. A useful heuristic: if it feels like it should already exist, it probably does.

The Ralph Wiggum loop, which I’ll explain below, is a perfect example. I didn’t build a custom orchestration layer. I installed a plugin in one command and had a working agentic loop.

* * *

### The actual build: how it came together

If you’re still around, thank you for not simply going to my repo to copy all my Claude markdown files. The thinking is important because it influenced the decision on what markdown files to write (generate).

I’ll go through each step one at a time.

#### a. Designing the CLAUDE.md contract

Before touching Claude Code, I spent time in the Claude Desktop App designing the system architecture. The CLAUDE.md I ended up with was less a document and more a control contract — a precise specification of how Claude should behave inside this repository.

The most critical part wasn’t the stack description. It was the execution loop:

```markdown
## How to work

Always use subagents. Never implement in this context.

For every task in prd.md:
1. Spawn planner → returns spec + file manifest
2. Spawn code-developer → returns implemented files
3. Spawn code-reviewer → returns findings
4. If findings non-trivial → spawn code-developer again
5. Spawn unit-tester → returns test results
6. Mark task complete only when reviewer approves + tests pass
7. Log completion in activity.md

Do not paste implementation, specs, or test output into this context.
Return one-line summaries only.
```

That last instruction — _return one-line summaries only_ — is doing more work than it looks like. It’s what keeps the main context clean across the entire build.

#### b. The multi-agent setup

I used four sub-agents, each defined as a markdown file. If you’ve spent time with LangChain, this will be a surprise: there’s no Python, no LangGraph node definitions, no dependency injection. Just markdown.

My code-reviewer sub agent reads like this:

```markdown
---
name: code-reviewer
description: |
  Specialist for ALL code review work. Delegate here when:
  - New code was just written and needs a review pass
  - User asks to "review", "check", or "audit" code
  - A bug was fixed and the fix needs scrutiny
  - Security or performance concerns are raised
  Do NOT review code in the main thread. Always delegate here.
model: sonnet
tools:
  - Read
  - Glob
  - Grep
  - Bash
---

# Code Reviewer Agent

You are a specialist code reviewer. You read code and return actionable findings.
You do not implement fixes — you identify issues and explain them clearly.

## Workflow

1. **Read the target file(s)** — understand what the code is trying to do
2. **Review for:**
   - Correctness — does it do what the spec/comment says?
   - Input validation — are parameters checked before use?
   - Error handling — are exceptions caught where they should be?
   - Type hints — are they present and accurate?
   - Security — any injection risk, hardcoded secrets, unsafe defaults?
   - Readability — would a teammate understand this in 6 months?
3. **Run static checks** if available (`ruff check`, `mypy`, or equivalent)

## Output contract

Return to the main agent:

- A severity-tagged list of findings: `[critical]`, `[warning]`, `[suggestion]`
- For each finding: file, line number, what the issue is, and a concrete fix
- An overall verdict: `approved`, `approved with suggestions`, or `needs changes`

Keep it tight. No preamble, no metrics, no summaries of what the code does well
unless it's directly relevant to a finding.
```

Each sub agent’s markdown file is saved under `.claude/agents/`in the repo’s root folder:

```
.
|- .claude
   |- agents
      |- code-developer.md
      |- code-reviewer.md
      |- planner.md
      |- unit-tester.md
|- CLAUDE.MD
```

The main agent (Opus) acts purely as an orchestrator. It assigns tasks, evaluates results, and advances workflow state. It never writes code. It never reviews code. It only manages the pipeline.

This effectively turns the system into a lightweight agent-driven CI pipeline — except the entire pipeline was designed in a Claude desktop conversation and lives in four markdown files.

#### c. Generating the prd.md

At the start of the project, the repository was empty. No requirements, no spec, no feature list.

Instead of writing these manually, I had Claude interview me. It asked questions, I answered, and at the end it generated a `prd.md` with every task defined in JSON format — structured enough for the agents to parse, specific enough to be actionable.

I triggered this through a custom Claude command: `/create-prd`. The command lives in `.claude/commands/create-prd.md` and produces three files:

`prd.md` — all tasks in JSON format, with a `"passes": false` flag on each that only flips to `true` when reviewer approves and tests pass.

`activity.md` — current task state so the main agent always knows what's pending, in progress, or done.

`prompt.md` — the definition of done, derived from the interview, read at the start of every task execution.

Claude has a [specific skill](https://github.com/jamesrochabrun/skills/blob/main/skills/prd-generator/SKILL.md) to generate prds, but I wanted to trigger it via a custom command instead of a prompt in Claude Code.

To do this, create a new custom Claude Command in the commands subfolder (ps it’s yet another markdown file):

```
.
|- .claude
   |- agents
      |- code-developer.md
      |- code-reviewer.md
      |- planner.md
      |- unit-tester.md
   |- commands
      |- create-prd.md
|- CLAUDE.MD
```

The `create-prd.md` file I used looked something like this:

Now when you run `/create-prd` (our custom command) in the Claude Code terminal, the main agent will start to consult you on your requirements!

#### d. The Ralph Wiggum Agent Loop

Hilariously named after a character from The Simpsons, the Ralph Wiggum loop is, at its core, a while loop:

```python
while tasks_remaining and num_iterations < max_iterations:
    pick next task
    spawn fresh agent session
    execute
    validate
    repeat
```

The key idea is **isolation**. Every task runs in a clean context. Nothing accumulates. Nothing leaks between tasks. The agent that builds the RSI tool has no memory of building the Bollinger Bands tool. It just gets its spec and does its job.

In theory, this sounds straightforward. In practice, getting another system to reliably orchestrate Claude Code sessions is non-trivial. **But there is a Claude Code plugin for it!** In Claude Code run:

```bash
/plugin install ralph-wiggum@claude-plugins-official
```

Then restart Claude Code and you’re good to go!

> **One important caveat:** the loop still operates within the same overall Claude Code environment! This is exactly why sub-agents matter — and why the planner is itself delegated rather than the main agent.

* * *

### Firing the starting gun 💥

To start, I ran `/create-prd` to generate the requirements document.

Then I invoked Claude Code’s Ralph Loop Plugin:

```bash
/ralph-loop:ralph-loop "Read PROMPT.md and follow it. Each iteration: 
find the first task in prd.md with \"passes\": false, execute it via 
the CLAUDE.md subagent workflow (planner -> code-developer -> code-reviewer 
-> unit-tester), mark it \"passes\": true only when the reviewer approves 
and tests pass, then append a dated line to activity.md. When EVERY task in 
prd.md is \"passes\": true, output <promise>ALL TASKS COMPLETE</promise>." 
--completion-promise "ALL TASKS COMPLETE" --max-iterations 15
```

To ensure that Claude Code knows that the Ralph loop has completed, always include a prompt to output: `<promise> your_promise_sentence </promise>` in the prompt.

> Definitely ensure it matches the completion promise argument — or it’ll loop until max iterations.

#### Bonus: Here’s how to work with Claude Code on your Phone

Right after you run the Ralph Loop Plugin, run this command in your Claude Code CLI:

```bash
/rc
```

This allows the Claude Code to be remotely controlled — **from your mobile phone!** That way you can approve Claude’s requests on your phone, and even add follow-up questions to it.

And that is how work gets done while you’re away from your desk. Or in my case, at the supermarket.

> **Important!** Do not close your computer. It can go to sleep, but the moment you shut the screen everything ceases to run.

### Testing it

The application was developed at a scarily fast pace — genAI is that capable. Test coverage was 98%. But the best “test” was to run the application.

Since this was an MCP on my local computer, I chose to run it in stdio mode (do feel free to refer to a [previous article I wrote on MCPs](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/model-context-protocol-hype-or-necessity-998874d95bc6) if you’d like more info!).

Go to your main Claude config file (`~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json` for Mac users) and add:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "stock-mcp": {
      "command": "uv",
      "args": [
        "--directory",
        "your/folder/path/StockMCPService",
        "run",
        "python",
        "main.py"
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

Then restart the Claude desktop application and chat with Claude like nothing happened.

Claude is intelligent enough to use the MCP tools when needed. That bring us back full circle to my first image of the article — Claude rendering a beautiful plot with technical analysis of Microsoft:

### Feels like magic doesn’t it? 🪄

And there’s still so much I haven’t learnt yet – writing custom hooks in Claude code for example.

Did this project take me zero effort?

Far less than you’d expect. Most of my time wasn’t spent coding at all.

Most of my time was spent chatting — with the Claude Desktop app. This time was spent discussing about the approach as well as to write the markdown files — yup all my skills, subagent markdown files, etc., were all written by Claude too!

My other role was to review Claude’s outputs. And this is by far the most challenging role — even though I have a code reviewer sub agent. GenAI agents develop good code at such high volumes it was impossible for me to review everything. I sampled files and read some code — it was very well written.

Which meant that I was mostly restricted to being an app tester, with nitpick comments like “make the color palette more contrasting”.

To get a second opinion on the code, I brought in another GenAI reviewer: [CodeRabbit](https://www.coderabbit.ai/), a code-review agent that is free for open-source GitHub repositories.

Out of the box, CodeRabbit is extremely thorough. Depending on your perspective, that’s either reassuring or exhausting. Left at its default settings, it will happily generate a long list of findings ranging from genuine bugs to stylistic preferences. On its first run it nitpicked so many things — mostly markdown files in the .claude folder.

I wanted it focused on correctness rather than nitpicks, so I created a `.coderabbit.yaml` file to define how reviews should be conducted:

```yaml
language: "en-US"

reviews:
  profile: "chill" #this is the most important setting here
  request_changes_workflow: false
  high_level_summary: true
  poem: false
  review_status: true
  collapse_walkthrough: false
  sequence_diagrams: false
  assess_linked_issues: false
  related_issues: false
  related_prs: false
  suggested_labels: false
  suggested_reviewers: false
  auto_review:
    enabled: true
    drafts: false

  tone_instructions: >
    Be relaxed and pragmatic. Only flag real bugs, security issues, and
    logic correctness problems. Do not comment on style, formatting, naming, or
    other minor preferences -- ruff, mypy, and isort already enforce those.
    Skip "nitpick" comments entirely. Keep remaining comments short.

  finishing_touches:
    docstrings:
      enabled: false
    unit_tests:
      enabled: false

  path_filters:
    # Only review the core service code.
    - "main.py"
    - "tools/**"
    - "ui/**"
    # Never review docs, agent/skill config, or non-code files.
    - "!**/*.md"
    - "!.claude/**"
    - "!**/__pycache__/**"
    - "!**/*.pyc"

chat:
  auto_reply: true
```

With this, CodeRabbit approved the entire codebase… and then flagged the only file I wrote myself: `.coderabbit.yaml`.

Make of that what you will 😂

### In closing

When people ask whether AI will replace software engineers, I think they’re asking the wrong question.

The more interesting question is what happens when software engineers stop spending most of their time writing software.

Building this project didn’t feel like programming in the traditional sense. It felt like architecture, review, orchestration, and quality control.

I wasn’t typing code.

I was designing systems that produced code.

That’s a subtle distinction, but an important one.

The surprising part is that the bottleneck wasn’t generation. Claude could generate code all day.

The bottleneck was judgment.

What should be built?  
Is it correct?  
Is it maintainable?  
Does it actually solve the problem?

Those questions never went away.

The keyboard just became a much smaller part of answering them.

body:
* * *

#### The answer is not vibe coding

In 2012, Harvard Business Review wrote an article acclaiming the data scientist as the [sexiest job in the 21st century](https://hbr.org/2012/10/data-scientist-the-sexiest-job-of-the-21st-century). Since then many have aspired to break into the field, but the nature of a data scientist has changed.

Look into job descriptions across the board and you’ll realize a few things:

1.  Most require generative AI expertise. Specifically, how to build agentic applications.
2.  Some (actually many) jobs require languages and tools that traditionally had nothing to do with data science — like Kubernetes and full stack development skills — React.js, TypeScript for frontend web development. Something I never thought would be asked of a data scientist.

The lines between frontend, backend, data, software, and DevOps engineers and roles like data scientists, AI engineers, and MLOps engineers are becoming increasingly blurred.

So what exactly is happening?

### The emergence of generative AI is the reason

When ChatGPT came out in end 2022, the trajectory of AI accelerated dramatically, changing the way we work and live.

In my opinion (feel free to disagree):

-   **2023 is the year of retrieval augmented generation (RAG) chatbots.**

People quickly discovered that chatbots hallucinated easily, so grounding them with retrieved knowledge became essential. This also gave birth to an entire ecosystem of **vector databases**.

-   **2024 is the year of agents and multi-agent systems and how to orchestrate them.**

It was no longer just LangChain and LangGraph. Developers started running into real pain points, and new frameworks such as LlamaIndex, Autogen, CrewAI, and Agno emerged with their own approaches to agent orchestration. I’ve written about most of these frameworks myself.

Prompt engineering slowly fell out of fashion as developers discovered it was easier to orchestrate LLMs using workflows.

-   **2025 is the year of protocols — model context protocol, agent-to-agent protocols (A2A), etc., and DeepSeek.**

Model Context Protocol, agent-to-agent communication, and other interoperability standards began appearing. The key idea was simple: agents built using different frameworks should still be able to communicate with each other. And agents should be able to connect and use any tool.

Existing frameworks adapted, and new ones emerged — ADK, Pydantic AI, and many others.

Around the same time, DeepSeek released its GRPO training recipe, which effectively democratized the training of reasoning models for anyone with access to a GPU.

Wall Street reacted with a [frenzy](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-02-02/deepseek-nvidia-financial-markets-frenzy-ai-race/104866302) of short selling.

-   **2026 is starting to look like the year of copilots.**

Tools like [Claude Code](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code), [OpenAI’s Codex](https://github.com/openai/codex), [Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli), [OpenCode](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode), and [OpenClaw](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw) have made enormous waves. Several companies — including [Anthropic](https://fortune.com/2026/01/29/100-percent-of-code-at-anthropic-and-openai-is-now-ai-written-boris-cherny-roon/) and [OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/) now claim that generative AI writes and ships most of their code.

### The uncomfortable reality

Has generative AI improved the lives of the masses?

Not everyone would agree.

[Fears of being replaced by AI remain widespread](https://www.bbc.com/worklife/article/20230418-ai-anxiety-artificial-intelligence-replace-jobs). Ironically, the first people to feel that pressure were data scientists and software engineers themselves. Since 2024, mass layoffs have affected many talented engineers. You probably know someone who was impacted. I certainly do.

> Companies increasingly believe they don’t need more engineers — they just need more LLM tokens. And tokens are much cheaper than salaries.

At the same time, universities are producing more AI graduates than ever before. Enrolment into AI-centric courses is rising rapidly, [while other fields see declining interest](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/today/big-read/university-enrolment-trends-changes-accountancy-humanities-computing-5973121).

The result is a strange market dynamic: a growing supply of technical talent competing for roles that are simultaneously evolving and shrinking.

There is another interesting side effect.

Generative AI has been so successful as a narrative that it has buoyed the stock market. Companies announcing “AI initiatives” can [attract significant investor capital](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/singapore/southeast-asia-digital-economy-artificial-intelligence-investment-5459761) almost instantly

This trend has become so visible that the Monetary Authority of Singapore [recently warned that AI and technology companies may be trading at inflated valuations](http://medium.com/r?url=https%3A%2F%2Ffinance.yahoo.com%2Fnews%2Fsingapore-financial-regulator-warns-ai-181931647.html). Some analysts are beginning to whisper about a [potential AI bubble](http://medium.com/r?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.channelnewsasia.com%2Fsingapore%2Fai-bubble-tech-stocks-economy-semiconductors-manufacturing-5462361), reminiscent of the dot-com era.

### Oh — you’re still here?

If you’re waiting for the positive spin on the above, I’m unfortunately unable to provide it.

However, I can share how I’ve personally adapted.

I graduated with a master’s degree in AI in 2023 — right in the middle of the generative AI renaissance. Fortunately, I’m still in a role where I build and ship real systems for a living.

So instead of offering optimism, I’ll offer something hopefully more useful: **practical adaptation**.

Here’s the first one.

### 1\. Update your personal skills.md diligently

Since the rise of agent-driven development, many GitHub repositories have started filling up with markdown files like these:

```
.gemini/
.claude/
agents.md
skills.md
.cursor/rules
```

These files provide context that tells different agents how to behave in different environments when contributing to a repository.

And increasingly, something surprising is happening.

Many of these markdown files are now **written by agents themselves**.

As agents become capable of writing anything from Python, C++ to Terraform, the burden on humans has shifted.

We are no longer just writing code.

We are **auditing it**.

The ability to review and challenge agent-generated code is becoming one of the most important skills for modern engineers and data scientists.

Ironically, this means the solution is **not** to blindly chain more generative AI systems together.

> For example:

> You might use Claude Code to generate code and open a pull request (PR).

> Another AI system, say CodeRabbit reviews the PR, rejects it, and opens a Jira ticket.

> That Jira ticket then triggers Claude Code to generate a new patch.

> Congratulations — you’ve now built a workflow where two autonomous agent systems argue with each other across GitHub and Jira while quietly burning LLM tokens. And you are paying for the privilege.

A better approach is: If you expect an agent to write Terraform code, then **learn Terraform yourself**.

Your goal is not to replace your knowledge with AI. Your goal is to **raise the quality bar** for the AI.

> When an agent produces mediocre code, you should be able to tell it:

> _“This design is wrong.”_

> Or better yet:

> _“Here’s how to make it sharper.”_

Your personal **skills.md** should evolve alongside the agents you use.

> **Important: focus on skills, not certifications.** Certifications of today might be irrelevant tomorrow.

I’ve personally picked up — and written about — tools like Liquibase ([article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/introducing-liquibase-how-to-version-control-your-db-d5a08f764c09)), Nginx ([article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/nginx-the-single-server-swiss-army-knife-3445197f8f86)) and Helm ([article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/helm-charts-the-multi-server-orchestra-conductor-18dc88665fc1)), and I’m currently learning Terraform.

Terraform is especially important to audit. Infrastructure mistakes are expensive — a single incorrect change can inflate your cloud bill while your agents happily burn LLM tokens.

I’ve also never accepted agent contributions to my code without auditing them myself.

In the age of AI-assisted development, the most valuable engineers are not the ones who rely on agents blindly.

They are the ones who can **challenge them**.

Besides, can you imagine how bad it looks when you’re questioned on your code contributions and all you can manage is “um…the AI did it”?

Not to mention, a wide, sharpened, evolving set of technical skills is the best career insurance.

### 2\. Sharpen systems thinking

Many users approach AI coding agents with two implicit expectations:

-   AI will handle everything required to build my application.
-   AI will get everything right on the first attempt.

Both expectations are unrealistic.

Because AI can _appear_ capable of doing everything, some people simply paste their product requirements into a prompt, ask the model to build the entire application, and walk away.

They return later only to discover that the AI built the wrong thing entirely.

The problem is not just capability — it is **context**.

Large language models (LLMs) operate within a finite context window. As more information is added, [research shows that model performance tends to degrade](https://redis.io/blog/context-rot/). Important instructions compete with less relevant information, and the model may focus on the wrong parts of the prompt.

In other words, the model may technically have the information it needs — but still make the wrong decision. So don’t just throw your entire requirements document at it.

A better approach is to break the application into **smaller, well-defined tasks**, and feed them to the agent system step by step.

But that raises an important question.

How do you decide what those tasks should be?

The answer is **systems thinking**.

Instead of asking an AI to build an entire application at once, design the architecture first. Define the components, the responsibilities of each piece, and how they interact.

Then build the system feature by feature.

AI can write code remarkably well.

But **humans still need to design the system.**

#### **For example, imagine you are asked to design a generative-AI-driven investment system for quantitative traders.**

The requirements sound simple:

-   The system must ingest new market information in real time.
-   It must generate portfolio recommendations based on existing holdings.
-   And it must respond within **three seconds**.

Go.

Before you even start drawing the architecture, a few uncomfortable questions appear.

Market updates arrive every second. If the agent takes three seconds to respond, the recommendation may already be outdated by the time it is generated.

The system also needs to run continuously for **every ticker**, which means the computational requirements — and LLM costs — could explode very quickly.

So perhaps running a full analysis on real-time data isn’t the right approach. But we may still want to ingest that data for later analysis.

Another question appears.

> Are you really expecting the LLM to analyze the raw market data by itself?

Almost certainly not.

In practice, you would give the model tools to perform the heavy lifting. If those tools can already generate buy or sell signals, then the obvious question becomes:

> Why do we need the LLM in the critical path at all?

**A more realistic design might look like this:**

Run batch analysis on historical data — daily, weekly, or monthly — to determine trading ranges.

For example:

• If price > $X → sell

• If price < $Y → buy

Now when real-time prices arrive, the system only needs to evaluate a simple boundary condition.

That decision can easily be made in under three seconds.

And suddenly the architecture becomes dramatically simpler.

You can offload the coding to the agent, but certainly not the thinking.

### 3\. Ship code

Coding is like a muscle — stop using it and it atrophies.

Rely too heavily on code agents and it’s like paying someone else to go to the gym for you, while still expecting Thor-level biceps in your own arms.

It doesn’t work that way.

At the same time, it would also be strange to ignore copilots entirely. They are genuinely useful tools. So strike a balance.

At work, if time allows, write the code yourself first and let the copilot sharpen or optimize it.

At home, build personal projects for fun and learning — and for those projects, insist on writing most of the code yourself. I spend time on personal projects regularly and find it one of the best ways to keep up with the rapidly evolving generative AI landscape.

These projects don’t have to be large. Sometimes it’s just 30 minutes every few days working on something small, but meaningful to you.

As long as you learn something, it’s time well spent.

Because the fastest way to lose your engineering intuition is to stop building things.

### 4\. Always be ready to explain ideas

Despite everything AI can do, the hype is still far ahead of reality.

AI tools are now widely accessible, which means your colleagues from non-technical backgrounds are experimenting with agents too. That’s not a bad thing — but it does change the role of the data scientist.

Increasingly, we become the people who need to explain things:

-   Why your friend’s agent failed.
-   Why a system needs more development time instead of being “copiloted into existence” .

> In other words, stakeholder management is becoming a core skill for data scientists.

To do that well, you need to genuinely understand how these systems work — how agents differ, where they fail, and what their real limitations are.

You’ll also find yourself pulled into more conversations about technology stacks and infrastructure.

> For example, someone might say:

> “Let’s self-host Phoenix — it’s open source, so it’s free, right?”

> Not exactly.

Open source software still requires infrastructure, compute, storage, and operational overhead. Someone needs to explain that, size that and design that.

How are you supposed to know all of this you ask?

I chat with LLM applications like ChatGPT/Gemini/Claude frequently about these matters. It usually starts as a general wondering (“why does every genAI framework have first class integrations only with Postgres and not any other DB?”) that gets more interesting as the chat evolves — and I end up learning something new each time.

As AI tools multiply, these conversations will only become more common.

> Consider just a few examples of developer copilots:

> • GitHub Copilot

> • Cursor

> • Claude Code

> • OpenAI Codex

> • Gemini CLI

> Do you know how they differ?

Because sooner or later, someone will ask you.

### 5\. Learn TypeScript

Yeah you read that right.

Python still dominates the model layer: training, experimentation, and fine-tuning. But in practice, most teams rarely fine-tune models anymore — unless you’re in a research team. It is often easier to prompt the LLM differently.

TypeScript, however, is fantastic for building things that humans actually interact with (the applications and now even the agents) in real time.

The irony is profound.

The frontend language — JavaScript’s stricter cousin — the one data scientists once believed they didn’t need, is quietly becoming the lingua franca of the agent tooling layer.

Look around the modern AI developer ecosystem:

-   [Claude Code](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code) — Python, AND TypeScript
-   [Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli) — TypeScript
-   [OpenCode](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode) — TypeScript
-   [OpenClaw](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw) (and all other lobster claw descendants)— TypeScript

• Many popular model context protocols (MCPs) are heavily TypeScript. For example [Postman’s MCP](https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-mcp-server), [Google Chrome DevTools MCP](https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp), [Playwright’s MCP](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright-mcp), etc.

And something interesting happened.

Nobody formally announced this shift. It just… happened.

One day you looked up and realized the coolest AI tools were installed with:

```bash
npm install
```

Not:

```bash
pip install
```

Frameworks like [LangChain](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchainjs) even have a JavaScript SDK that keeps pace with their Python versions.

But here’s the surprising part.

Many of the newest agentic coding tools — Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenClaw— aren’t even built on frameworks like LangChain. They talk directly to model APIs using SDKs from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI.

TypeScript itself is simply a type-safe version of JavaScript — the language that powers nearly every website on the internet.

Because of that, it has an enormous advantage: developers can use a single language across the entire stack: frontend, backend, APIs, and increasingly, AI tooling.

It may not match the raw speed of compiled languages like Java or Rust, but its dominance comes from something simpler:

> One language to build everything.

The future data scientist looks a lot more like a software engineer than many of us expected.

I didn’t expect to say this as a data scientist, but TypeScript is currently at the top of my learning list — which incidentally closes the loop on the first point I made: picking up new skills.

### Concluding Thoughts

Beyond the practical tips I’ve shared, perhaps the more important question is this: _why did you become a data scientist in the first place?_

In a [previous article about my personal journey](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/how-i-became-a-data-scientist-2d8831531a4c), I wrote:

> The most compelling thing about artificial intelligence isn’t the hype or the job title. It’s the beauty of modeling data to create something that resembles actual intelligence — through the lens of mathematics, expressed in code.

That still rings true today, although perhaps the context has shifted slightly.

Generative AI applications are incredibly fun to build, and they carry the potential to meaningfully improve our quality of life.

Imagine an AI agent handling travel bookings, acting as your personal tour guide overseas, or helping optimize your financial portfolio, personalizing your children’s education curriculum to optimize their learning (not their grades). What if your AI agent serves as your confidante to scream at when days are hard?

What would you do with the time freed up from worrying?

Personally, I’d spend more time with my children — nurturing their curiosity for learning, guiding them in the Christian faith, and helping them grow into people who carry genuine empathy and concern for their fellow human beings.

What I won’t do is ask AI agents to do my work or my thinking for me.

AI can help us build remarkable things. But curiosity is still human.
