body:
* * *

#### A Deep Dive into Load Balancing and Reverse Proxying with Docker Compose

The considerations for developing and deploying an application are vastly different.

During **development**, the main goal is simple: make the code work. As long as it runs on your favorite localhost, life is good.

But during **deployment**, a new set of questions arise:

-   **Traffic:** Can your app handle hundreds of requests hitting it at once?
-   **Security:** Your application should run on an HTTPS URL — but does that mean you need _one signed certificate per endpoint_ if you have 100 APIs?
-   **Speed:** Users are _allergic_ to latency.
-   **Fault tolerance:** Does your app die when there’s a bug?

It’s a whole new world.

When I looked through my own developer toolkit, I realized there was one tool I’d always taken for granted. I’d copy–paste config files or vibe-code them, never really understanding _why_ they worked.

Today, I decided to finally cross it off my “to learn properly” list.

Ladies and gentlemen, allow me to introduce [**Nginx**](https://nginx.org/) — the unsung hero of modern web deployment.

Most software engineers already know and love it.

Unfortunately, I was _not_ one of those.

I’d always deployed my apps directly via Docker or [IIS Manager](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/iis/get-started/getting-started-with-iis/getting-started-with-the-iis-manager-in-iis-7-and-iis-8)… until I discovered what Nginx actually _does_.

### The problem that Nginx solves

Nginx (pronounced “Engine-X”) acts as a **reverse proxy**.

That means all your backend services (APIs) and frontend services (websites) can run on _any_ private port — while only **Nginx** listens on the public-facing one.

When a user clicks a button that calls an endpoint, Nginx routes that request behind the scenes to the correct service, shielding your internal structure and improving both performance and security.

The magic happens in **one file: nginx.conf**.

Unlike Dockerfiles, docker-compose.yml, or GitHub Action YAML files, there is only ever one canonical `nginx.conf`. This single file controls traffic routing, load balancing, WebSocket support, and much more — it truly holds immense power.

I’ll explain more via code. As always, my code can be found in my [GitHub repository.](https://github.com/tituslhy/nginx-playground/tree/main)

### Developing our app

We’ll build a simple LLM-driven search app — our main focus will be understanding **how Nginx handles all the traffic for it** .

```python
# src/on_chat_start.py

import chainlit as cl

import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv, find_dotenv

from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import AgentWorkflow
from llama_index.core.memory import ChatMemoryBuffer
from llama_index.core.workflow import Context
from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI
from llama_index.tools.tavily_research import TavilyToolSpec

from openinference.instrumentation.llama_index import LlamaIndexInstrumentor
from phoenix.otel import register

_ = load_dotenv(find_dotenv())

def setup_agent():
    llm = OpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini")
    tavily_tool = TavilyToolSpec(api_key=os.getenv("TAVILY_API_KEY"))
    agent = AgentWorkflow.from_tools_or_functions(
        tavily_tool.to_tool_list(),
        llm=llm,
        system_prompt="You're a helpful assistant that can search the web for information."
    )
    memory = ChatMemoryBuffer.from_defaults()

    ## Setup session variables
    cl.user_session.set("agent", agent)
    cl.user_session.set("context", Context(agent))
    cl.user_session.set("memory", memory)
    
    ## Setup tracing
    tracer_provider = register(
        endpoint="http://phoenix:4317"
    )
    LlamaIndexInstrumentor().instrument(tracer_provider=tracer_provider)
```

This file contains a function to set up Chainlit’s session variables once the web application is up and running.

-   We instantiate the OpenAI model, the Tavily web search tool, and wrap them together into a LlamaIndex agent.
-   We then set up our `ChatMemoryBuffer` to confer our agent chat history capabilities, and
-   Set up our Arize Phoenix LLM observability tool.

> We set the endpoint to “phoenix:4317” instead of the default localhost because we will be spinning up our Phoenix instance and Chainlit application using Docker compose.

> Applications spun up using a single compose file can call each other **by name** by virtue of a shared network.

```python
# src/on_message.py
import chainlit as cl

from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import (
    AgentStream, 
    ToolCallResult
)
from llama_index.core.base.llms.types import (
    ChatMessage, 
    MessageRole
)
    
async def invoke_agent(message: cl.Message) -> str:
    agent = cl.user_session.get("agent")
    memory = cl.user_session.get("memory")
    context = cl.user_session.get("context")
    
    chat_history = memory.get() 
    msg = cl.Message(content="")
    
    handler = agent.run(
        user_msg=message.content,
        chat_history=chat_history,
        ctx=context
    )
    
    async for event in handler.stream_events():
        if isinstance(event, AgentStream):
            await msg.stream_token(event.delta)
        elif isinstance(event, ToolCallResult):
            with cl.Step(name=f"{event.tool_name} tool with arguments: {event.tool_kwargs}", type="tool"):
                continue       

    response = str(await handler)
    await msg.update()
    memory.put(
        ChatMessage(
            role = MessageRole.USER,
            content= message.content
        )
    )
    memory.put(
        ChatMessage(
            role = MessageRole.ASSISTANT,
            content = str(response)
        )
    )
    cl.user_session.set("memory", memory)
    return response
```

When we receive a message, we load the session variables and invoke the agent. We then update the session’s memory so that our agent has the latest messages for its context.

We are going to spin up the app using Docker, [**which does not recommend using a**](https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/use-secrets/) `[**.env**](https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/use-secrets/)` [**file**](https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/use-secrets/) (though this still works) to pass secrets. This is because .env secrets can end up baked into the image — and therefore inspectable at runtime. Instead, Docker expects secrets to be provided via a `<secret_name>.txt` file. I’ve stored my `OPENAI_API_KEY` and `TAVILY_API_KEY` in their respective secret files inside a secrets folder.

We need a small utility function to load these secrets at runtime:

```python
# utils/utils.py

import os
from Pathlib import Path

def get_secret(name: str):
    if name in os.environ:
        return os.environ[name]
    secret_path = Path(f"/run/secrets/{name}")
    if secret_path.exists():
        return secret_path.read_text().strip()
    return None

def get_secrets():
    secrets = ["OPENAI_API_KEY", "TAVILY_API_KEY"]
    for secret in secrets:
        if os.getenv(secret) is None:
            value = get_secret(secret)
            if value:
                os.environ[secret] = value
                logging.info(f"Loaded secret {secret} from file.")
            else:
                logging.warning(f"Secret {secret} not found in environment or file.")
```

Finally, here’s the app.py that calls our defined functions with some logging:

```python
#app.py 
import chainlit as cl
import logging

from src.on_chat_start import setup_agent
from src.on_message import invoke_agent
from utils.utils import get_secrets

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="[%(asctime)s] [%(levelname)s] [%(name)s] - %(message)s"
)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

get_secrets()

@cl.on_chat_start
async def on_chat_start():
    setup_agent()
    logger.info("Agent setup complete")

@cl.on_message
async def on_message(message: cl.Message):
    
    # Invoke agent
    response = await invoke_agent(message=message)
    logger.info(f"Agent Response: {response}")
```

This app.py is deliberately kept very thin — so feel free to use it as a template and just edit the `invoke_agent` and `setup_agent` functions to your use case.

We can spin up a Chainlit server using `chainlit run app.py` , but we will be doing this using Docker to simulate deployment.

### Deploying our app phase 1 (Docker)

Docker is simply amazing.

Docker solves the problem of “it works on my computer but not yours”. Imagine you’re moving desks: Docker is the box that lets you pack up your app and move it to a different server. If Docker can spin up your app on your laptop, it will work on any deployment server too.

We’ll first start by building a Docker image of our application. This is done using a Dockerfile:

```bash
# docker/Dockerfile

FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm

# Set work directory in the container
WORKDIR /app

# Install curl and uv
RUN pip install uv

# Copy requirements files
COPY ../pyproject.toml ../uv.lock ./

# Install dependencies using uv
RUN uv sync

# Copy the rest of the application
COPY .. .

# Add virtual environment bin to path
ENV PATH="/app/.venv/bin:$PATH"

CMD ["chainlit", "run", "app.py", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
```

Here’s what’s happening step by step:

1.  **Base image** — We start from a slim Python 3.13 image. This gives us a consistent environment across all machines.
2.  **Working directory** — All code will live in /app inside the container.
3.  **Install uv** — We install the uv package first because we’ll use it to manage project dependencies.
4.  **Install dependencies** — We copy pyproject.toml and uv.lock into the container and run uv sync.
5.  **Copy the rest of the code** — The .. copies everything from the parent folder (remember, this Dockerfile lives in ./docker).
6.  **Set virtual environment path** — Ensures any Python executables installed in the venv are on $PATH.
7.  **Run the app** — CMD launches Chainlit on host 0.0.0.0 and port 8000.

> `host 0.0.0.0` tells the app to listen on **all available network interfaces** inside the container, not just the localhost interface. This is required for external connections (like Nginx) to reach it.

Think of the Docker image as a packed box from your old desk — it contains everything your app needs to run anywhere.

#### Running the App with Docker Compose

We can build and run the image simultaneously using docker-compose.yml:

```yaml
services:

  chainlit:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: docker/Dockerfile
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    secrets:
      - OPENAI_API_KEY
      - TAVILY_API_KEY
    networks:
      - chainlit-net

  phoenix:
    image: arizephoenix/phoenix:latest
    ports:
      - "6006:6006"
      - "4317:4317"
    networks:
      - chainlit-net

secrets:
  OPENAI_API_KEY:
    file: ./secrets/openai_api_key.txt
  TAVILY_API_KEY:
    file: ./secrets/tavily_api_key.txt
   
networks:
  chainlit-net:
    driver: bridge
```

Key points:

-   The build key under chainlit tells Docker how to build the image for this service.
-   Secrets are mounted at runtime via files in the secrets folder, which is safer than baking them into the image.
-   Both services are connected to the same Docker network (chainlit-net), allowing them to communicate by name.

**Note:** Ensure that your `.dockerignore` file looks like this:

```bash
.env
images/
.python-version
chainlit.md
.chainlit/
.venv/
secrets/
```

This prevents secrets, virtual environments, and other unnecessary files from being sent to Docker during the build process.

Once done, run:

```bash
docker-compose -d --build
```

This builds your Chainlit image, pulls the Phoenix image from Docker Hub, and spins them up in their respective containers. 🎉

Congratulations! You now have a working app running in Docker.

### Deploying our app phase 2 (Scaling)

But it’s not over yet. Imagine you have **50 users** using your application and it suddenly crashes. Now nothing works — the entire app is down.

A first improvement is to add `restart: unless-stopped` to each service in your docker-compose.yml. This ensures the app automatically restarts if it crashes.

✅ Better resilience — but it introduces a new problem:

-   If **user 27** triggers a crash, all 49 other users experience an app restart in the middle of their session.
-   Frustrated, user 27 tries the same action again — and the cycle repeats.

You now have 50 unhappy users. 😬

#### Scaling with multiple containers

A natural next idea is to run multiple instances of the Chainlit service. You can do this with:

```bash
docker-compose down
docker-compose up -d --scale chainlit=3
```

Now you have three containers: `chainlit_1`, `chainlit_2`, and `chainlit_3`.

But here’s the problem:

```bash
Error response from daemon: failed to set up container networking: driver 
failed programming external connectivity on endpoint chainlit-3: Bind for 
0.0.0.0:8000 failed: port is already allocated
make: *** [build_scale] Error 1
```

❌ Only **one container per host port** is allowed. Since all three containers try to bind to host port 8000, the second and third fail.

You could map each container to a different host port (e.g., 8000, 8001, 8002), but that creates a new challenge:

> _How do you route your users to the correct container?_

This is where Nginx comes in — it acts as a reverse proxy **and** load balancer, routing all user requests to the available Chainlit containers behind the scenes.

With Nginx handling traffic, you can safely scale multiple backend containers **without exposing multiple host ports**, while also adding features like load balancing, sticky sessions, and WebSocket support.

### Deploying our app phase 3 (Nginx)

Now that we’ve handled scaling our Chainlit containers, it’s time to **introduce Nginx** as a reverse proxy.

In your docker-compose.yml file, add an Nginx service:

```yaml
nginx:
    image: nginx:latest
    container_name: nginx_proxy
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
    networks:
      - chainlit-net
    restart:
      unless-stopped
```

-   Docker will pull the Nginx image from Docker Hub.
-   It spins up a container on **host port 8080**.
-   The container uses the nginx.conf file located in the ./nginx folder in our repository.

#### Adjusting the Chainlit service

Next, remove the ports mapping from the Chainlit service:

```yaml
  chainlit:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: docker/Dockerfile
    env_file:
      - .env
    networks:
      - chainlit-net
    restart:
      unless-stopped
```

-   This avoids the **port conflict problem** we saw earlier.
-   Nginx will handle all routing, so there’s no need to expose individual container ports.

#### The magical nginx.conf file

Like Docker Compose, Nginx configuration files are structured as **key-value pairs**, but the values are **code blocks** wrapped in curly braces {}.

All nginx.conf files start with an events block, which sets the maximum number of connections a worker can handle:

```
events {
    worker_connections 1024;
}
```

-   This means each worker process can handle up to 1024 simultaneous connections.
-   For our 3 replicas, we’ll never need anywhere near that.

```
http{
    upstream chainlit_app {
        server chainlit:8000;
        least_conn;
    }
}
```

-   The http block specifies what we are serving — our Chainlit app (or static files).
-   `upstream chainlit_app` names the pool of backend servers serving the Chainlit application.
-   `server chainlit:8000` points to the Chainlit service; Nginx can reach it by its **service name** (‘chainlit’) because all services in the **docker-compose.yml** share the same Docker network. This is a fundamental Docker Compose feature.
-   `least_conn` ensures that **new connections** are routed to the replica with fewest active connections. Once a WebSocket handshake completes, the connection stays pinned to that replica.

> 💡 **Tip:** Removing `least_conn` defaults to **round-robin** mode, which cycles requests across replicas. That works for standard HTTP APIs, but **not for Chainlit**.

> Chainlit uses **WebSockets**, which are long-lived connections that never close.

> If Nginx routes a user mid-connection to a different replica, the WebSocket breaks — potentially crashing the container and Nginx itself.

> Using `least_conn` keeps WebSocket connections stable while distributing load intelligently.

#### Adding the Nginx Server Block

Finally, let’s complete our Nginx setup by adding the following block inside the http section:

```
server {
        listen 8080;

        location / {
            proxy_pass http://chainlit_app;

            # Set headers to pass necessary information to the Chainlit app
            proxy_set_header Host $host;
            proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

            # WebSocket support for Chainlit's interactive features
            proxy_http_version 1.1;
            proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
            proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
        }
    }
```

Let’s unpack what’s happening here.

-   **listen 8080:** This tells Nginx to listen for incoming HTTP requests on port 8080 — the same port we exposed in our docker-compose.yml.

> 💡 _Tip:_ If you are deploying nginx with a secure certificate. You must include the path to the signed secure certificate. Here’s a link to a [good example](https://medium.com/@palash-fin/deploying-chainlit-application-using-nginx-c95069360983).

-   **location / { … }:** Defines what to do when someone visits / (i.e., the root of our site). In this case, Nginx forwards the request to the upstream group chainlit\_app that we defined earlier.

So, if you hit [http://localhost:8080](http://localhost:8080,) (the root) Nginx will immediately route the request to one of your Chainlit containers — whichever has the least number of active connections.

#### What about all the `proxy_set_header lines` ?

These lines often get copy-pasted from Stack Overflow or GitHub gists without much context — but they’re actually crucial. Let’s break them down:

**proxy\_set\_header Host $host;**

-   Sends the original Host header (the hostname the client requested) to your app.

> 💡 _Tip:_ `$host` usually resolves from the server\_name directive. You could also use `$http_host`, which includes the port if specified — both work for most setups.

**proxy\_set\_header X-Real-IP $remote\_addr;**

-   Adds the client’s actual IP address — as seen by Nginx — to the request header. This is useful for logging or rate-limiting at the application level.

**proxy\_set\_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy\_add\_x\_forwarded\_for;**

-   Appends the client IP to the chain of proxies the request has passed through.
-   For example, if multiple Nginx or load balancers are chained together, you get the _full path_ of IPs that forwarded the request.
-   Internally, `$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for` automatically includes `$remote_addr` for you, so it’s safe to use.

**proxy\_set\_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;**

-   Tells the backend whether the original connection was http or https.
-   This helps the app generate the right absolute URLs — for instance, ensuring redirects go to https:// instead of [http://.](http://.)

#### Suporting WebSockets (and why it matters for Chainlit)

At the end of our server block, you’ll see three important lines:

```bash
# Enable WebSocket connections for Chainlit
proxy_http_version 1.1;
proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
```

Let’s break down what’s really happening here — and why each line matters.

**proxy\_http\_version 1.1:**

-   By default, Nginx proxies requests using HTTP/1.0, which doesn’t support persistent connections — meaning every request opens and closes its own socket.
-   WebSockets (which Chainlit uses), on the other hand, **_require_ a continuous, two-way connection** between the client and the server.
-   Setting proxy\_http\_version 1.1 upgrades the proxying behavior to HTTP/1.1, enabling features like Connection: keep-alive and — most importantly — **protocol upgrades**, which are essential for WebSockets.

**proxy\_set\_header Upgrade $http\_upgrade;**

-   The Upgrade header is part of the WebSocket handshake.
-   When a browser or Chainlit client wants to establish a WebSocket connection, it sends an HTTP request like this:

```
GET /socket HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
```

That Upgrade: websocket line tells Nginx:

_“Hey, this isn’t just a normal HTTP request — I want to upgrade to the WebSocket protocol.”_

The `$http_upgrade` variable simply captures that value (websocket) from the incoming request and forwards it along to the backend service.

**proxy\_set\_header Connection “upgrade”;**

-   This works together with the previous line. It ensures Nginx forwards the Connection: upgrade header to your backend so the protocol upgrade can complete successfully.
-   Without this line, Nginx might treat it like a normal HTTP request — and your WebSocket handshake would fail silently. You’d see Chainlit freeze or throw Error: WebSocket connection closed unexpectedly.

### Spin everything up🚀

To make things more fun, I’ve added a little utility function so we can see which container is actually serving our request.

Using Python’s built-in socket library, we can grab the hostname and IP address of the running container.

```python
#% utils/utils.py
import os
import socket

def get_container_info() -> str:
    """Gets unique information about the container."""
    hostname = socket.gethostname()
    try:
        ip_address = socket.gethostbyname(hostname)
    except socket.gaierror:
        ip_address = "N/A"
    container_id = os.uname().nodename
    return (
      "Served by Container:\n"
      f"- **Hostname:** `{hostname}`\n"
      f"- **Internal IP:** `{ip_address}`\n"
      f"- **Container ID:** `{container_id}`"
    )
```

Next, let’s adapt our app.py to display this info whenever a new message is received:

```python
import chainlit as cl
import logging

from src.on_chat_start import setup_agent
from src.on_message import invoke_agent
from utils.utils import get_secrets, get_container_info

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="[%(asctime)s] [%(levelname)s] [%(name)s] - %(message)s"
)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

get_secrets()

@cl.on_chat_start
async def on_chat_start():
    setup_agent()
    logger.info("Agent setup complete")

@cl.on_message
async def on_message(message: cl.Message):
    
    # Added this block
    container_info = get_container_info()
    logger.info(f"Container Info: {container_info}")
    await cl.Message(content=f"📦 {container_info}").send()
    
    response = await invoke_agent(message=message)
    logger.info(f"Agent Response: {response}")
```

Now, rebuild and scale up your containers:

```bash
docker compose down 
docker-compose up -d --build --scale chainlit=3
```

🎉 **And there you have it!**

A fault-resilient, load-balanced Chainlit deployment with three replicas behind Nginx.

Head over to [**http://localhost:8080**](http://localhost:8080) (the Nginx URL), and you’ll see your app running beautifully.

Now send a message:

### 🧭 Why Your Conversation Stays on One Container (TCP Persistence ≠ Sticky Sessions)

You’ll notice something interesting — it’s _always the same chainlit container_ serving your requests!

Wait, didn’t we specify `least_conn` in our Nginx config?

Great question.

Chainlit uses WebSockets, which are **stateful** (long-lived) connections. Traditional HTTP requests are **stateless.** Once a client connects to a container, the connection remains “sticky” — it doesn’t hop between replicas.

This stickiness ensures stability (no dropped sessions), but it also means that traditional round-robin or least-connection load balancing won’t rebalance existing clients automatically.

Nginx only routes you to the container with the _least number of connections_ **at the very start** of your chat session — and then it sticks.

That’s because WebSocket connections are long-lived and stateful. Once your browser opens a WebSocket to a particular Chainlit replica, Nginx won’t keep rebalancing you — it’ll just keep that tunnel open.

If you want to see load-balancing in action, ask a friend (from a different device or location) to connect to your app at: http://<your\_ip\_address>:8000

They’ll likely be serviced by a different Chainlit container!

#### ⚠️ Note on IP Addresses

Your **IP address** (public or local host) is _not_ the same as your Docker container’s internal IP. Docker uses an isolated internal network for containers — this is by design.

To programmatically fetch a container’s own hostname and IP, you can use Python’s built-in socket library:

```python
import socket
hostname = socket.gethostname()
ip_address = socket.gethostbyname(hostname)
print(f"Hostname: {hostname}, IP: {ip_address}")
```

### 🔍 Proof that Nginx sees 3 Chainlit replicas

Run the following command to confirm all containers are up:

```bash
docker ps
```

You should see **three Chainlit** containers, one **Nginx**, and one **Phoenix** (if you’re using it).

Copy the container ID of your nginx container, and run:

```bash
docker exec -it <nginx_container_id> /bin/bash
```

This opens up an interactive terminal with the Nginx container.

Now run this command to install namespace lookup utilities:

```bash
apt-get update && apt-get install -y dnsutils
```

Then run a namespace lookup for chainlit:

```bash
nslookup chainlit
```

🎉 **Tada!** You’ll see that Nginx resolves the chainlit hostname to **three different IPs** — one for each container replica.

That’s how Nginx knows about all your running services, even though it sticks you to one of them for WebSocket stability.

### 🧠 Thinking of what we just did

We just spun up **three replicas** of our chatbot application using Docker and managed traffic to them with **Nginx** — all while maintaining the **statefulness** required by WebSockets.

Let’s revisit the **deployment concerns** we talked about earlier and see how this setup stacks up:

1.  🚦**Traffic:** Nginx routes traffic to the app with the _least number of active connections_ — at least at the start of a conversation
2.  🧱 **Fault tolerance:** Now for something fun — let’s break things a little.

Run this command to stop one of your Chainlit containers (make sure it’s _not_ the one currently serving your conversation):

```bash
docker stop <one-chainlit-container-not-serving-your-conversation>
```

Then… just keep chatting.

You’ll notice your conversation **still works!** 🎉

> Of course, users who were connected to the container you killed will lose their session — but that’s expected in a stateful WebSocket setup.

Fault tolerance: _unlocked._

3\. 🔒 **Security:** Securing your deployment is simple — just make Nginx **listen on port 443** and attach a **single valid SSL certificate**.

You don’t need a separate certificate for each replica — Nginx handles it at the gateway level.

4\. ⚡ **Speed:** Nginx is capable of running multiple worker processes and handling thousands of concurrent connections. That said, performance ultimately depends more on your **network bandwidth** and **application logic** than Nginx itself.

### Summary

In my view, Nginx elegantly addresses **Traffic**, **Fault Tolerance**, and **Security** — and can even front **multiple services** if needed.

All you need to do is add more upstream and corresponding location blocks to your `nginx.conf`.

### 🎭 Plot Twist

And yet… here’s the twist.

Despite how cool this setup looks, **Nginx is rarely used for load balancing in production with Docker**.

Why? Because in our setup, _everything runs on one machine._

That machine — your laptop, your EC2 instance, whatever — is a **single point of failure**.

If someone trips over the power cable or your system runs out of memory, every container dies together. 💀

That’s why production-grade deployments usually happen across **multiple servers** (a.k.a. a _cluster_), with load balancing happening at the **server level**, not just the container level.

Docker alone can’t do that natively.

To scale properly, you’d use a container orchestration platform like:

-   **AWS Elastic Container Service (ECS)** — for managed container clusters.
-   **Kubernetes** — to orchestrate and scale containers across nodes.
-   **Helm** — as a package manager for Kubernetes (it handles rollbacks, upgrades, and repeatable deployments).

In these instances, the Nginx service manages the cluster’s ingress — so it still serves its purpose as a reverse proxy.

**Still!** Nginx _shines_ in single-server setups.

It’s elegant, fast, and rock-solid — the kind of tool that makes you look like you’ve tamed chaos itself.

That said, like most YAML-driven tools, debugging it can be maddening. It’s hard to tell _what_ broke — and even harder to understand _why_ — unless you know how the underlying applications actually work (not just the code).

I’ll be honest: this is where I still have lots to learn. I got into data science and AI because I was enamoured with the math behind the magic — coding was just a way to make it real. Writing those 30 lines in my `nginx.conf` took me half a day, a few sighs, and more coffee than I’d like to admit. ☕️

But yes, you can now proudly stroll into your next stand-up and declare:

> _“I’ve added scalability and robustness to our deployment.”_

_(No one needs to know it’s all on one machine… yet.)_ 😎

title: A very simple introduction to gRPC
outline: PS: I’m still learning as I go too
⚖️ If gRPC Is So Fast… Why Isn’t Everyone Using It?
intro: FastAPI has become a staple in Python backends — and for good reason: it’s just awesome. I build all my API backends with it. body:
* * *

#### PS: I’m still learning as I go too

FastAPI has become a staple in Python backends — and for good reason: it’s just awesome. I build all my API backends with it.

In my [previous article on concurrency and parallelism](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-crash-course-in-asynchronous-python-12e0cc523033), I showed how to use asyncio, threading, and multiprocessing to handle tasks, threads, and processes asynchronously. I recommended using asyncio instead of threading because Python’s Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) means only one thread can execute Python bytecode at a time — so multiple tasks in multiple threads are essentially the same as multiple async tasks in a single thread. Using these techniques, I demonstrated speedups of up to 5×.

But what if I told you Python could run your deployments even faster? [Up to 10x](https://medium.com/@EmperorRXF/evaluating-performance-of-rest-vs-grpc-1b8bdf0b22da).

Here’s the catch: the approach is a bit… unpythonic.

All my code is available in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/grpc_playground).

#### **🚀 What Is gRPC?**

gRPC (Google Remote Procedure Call) is a high-performance framework for building distributed systems and microservices. Unlike traditional REST APIs (where FastAPI usually lives) that rely on HTTP/1.1 and JSON, [gRPC uses HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers (Protobuf) for fast, compact, and efficient communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GRPC). It supports all types of streaming (unary, server, client, bidirectional) and is perfect for architectures built using different programming languages.

> The gRPC speedup comes from: HTTP/2’s multiplexing (reducing latency) and Protobuf’s binary serialization (reducing payload size), compared to HTTP/1.1 and JSON.

Here’s why it’s unpythonic: gRPC enforces a contract-first approach via .proto files, meaning types must be declared upfront — no relying on Python’s forgiving dynamic typing. Strictly speaking, gRPC is not a language, but has native support for multiple languages (Python being one of them). And honestly, that’s about all I know so far — I’m not a trained software engineer, just a curious data scientist .

Ready to see it in action? Let’s build a simple to-do app. We’ll have a gRPC backend talking to an SQL database, and a FastAPI backend pinging the gRPC service while handling concurrency. Here’s the project structure:

```
.
|- todoService
   |- models #models used for gRPC and FastAPI
      |- request_models.py # for FastAPI
      |- todo_models.py # for gRPC
   |- protos #files used for gRPC
      |- todo_messages.proto
      |- todo_services.proto
   |- server.py
|- Makefile
|-app.py #the FastAPI app
```

### Starting out in gRPC

We first define our `todo_messages.proto` file, which declares schemas for our gRPC system — similar to how we use Pydantic models in FastAPI:

```go
syntax = "proto3";

package todos;

message Todo {
  int32 id = 1;
  string task = 2;
}

message AddTodoRequest {
  string task = 1;
}

message EditTodoRequest {
  int32 id = 1;
  string task = 2;
}

message TodoId {
  int32 id = 1;
}

message RemoveTodoRequest {
  int32 id = 1;
}

message Empty {}
```

Jaw dropped yet? Where’s the Python? **NOWHERE.**

gRPC is statically typed, unlike Python. You can’t just do:

```python
def add(a, b): 
    return a + b
```

What’s the problem you ask? Well you could easily throw in a float, an integer, a string, a list, a tuple, etc., into the function. Only Python is this forgiving. Static-typed languages require explicit input and output types for every method.

So, as an example:

```go
message Todo {
  int32 id = 1;
  string task = 2;
}
```

Here, Todo is a message passed into or out of gRPC. The `id` is an integer, `task` is a string, and each field has a **tag number** (the 1 and 2) — hence `string task = 2;`. Oh, and don’t forget the semicolons at the end of each line!

Notice that our file has an additional line: `package todos;`

This is recommended but not strictly needed. It defines a namespace for protobuf messages and services and helps avoid name collisions if there are multiple `.proto` files or large objects.

Another good thing about proto files is that you can import from other proto files so proto files don’t have to be super lengthy!

Here’s the services proto file encapsulating the logic using the models defined before:

```go
syntax = "proto3";

package todos;

import "todoService/protos/todo_messages.proto";

service TodoService {
    rpc AddTodo (AddTodoRequest) returns (Todo);
    rpc EditTodo (EditTodoRequest) returns (Todo);
    rpc GetTodo (TodoId) returns (Todo);  
    rpc ListTodos (Empty) returns (ListTodosResponse);
    rpc RemoveTodo (RemoveTodoRequest) returns (RemoveTodoResponse);
}

message ListTodosResponse {
  repeated Todo todos = 1;
}

message RemoveTodoResponse {
  bool success = 1;
}
```

The main thing you need to know here is the `service` definition. Here is the part where we specify the input and output schemas to the service.

The `repeated` keyword under `ListTodosResponse` simply means that we can have more than one `Todo` returned.

All in all, the `todo_service.proto` file specifies that we have a total of five backend services that allow us to add/edit/get/list and remove todos.

### Where’s the Python Part?

Now we get to it. In your command line, run the following command:

```bash
python -m grpc_tools.protoc \
 -I. \
 --python_out=. \
 --grpc_python_out=. \
 todoService/protos/todo_messages.proto \
 todoService/protos/todo_service.proto
```

This uses the **Python grpc\_tools SDK** to consume your .proto files and generate the necessary .py files for your gRPC service.

For each .proto file, you’ll get **two Python files**:

-   \_pb2.py: contains Python classes that map directly to your Protobuf message definitions.
-   \_pb2\_grpc.py: defines the gRPC service stubs (for clients) and servicers (for servers).

### ⚙️ That Command Looks… Long 😅

It is. Which is why I automate it with a **Makefile**:

```makefile
.PHONY: generate_todo_service clean_todo_service

# Generates the todo service GRPC files
generate_todo_service:
   python -m grpc_tools.protoc \
   -I. \
   --python_out=. \
   --grpc_python_out=. \
   todoService/protos/todo_messages.proto \
   todoService/protos/todo_service.proto
  
# removes the todo_service files except for the proto files
clean_todo_service:
   rm -f todoService/protos/todo_messages_pb2.py \
   todoService/protos/todo_service_pb2.py \
   todoService/protos/todo_service_pb2_grpc.py \
   todoService/protos/todo_messages_pb2_grpc.py
```

The .PHONY line tells make that these aren’t files, just _commands_.

With this, you can easily generate or clean your gRPC files:

```bash
make generate_todo_service
make clean_todo_service
```

🧹 `make clean_todo_service` wipes everything generated by grpc\_tools, giving you a clean slate to rebuild.

> PS: Use Makefiles, .sh files or .bat files (for Windows) to automate tasks like unit testing, clean-ups and long command executions. Your brain will thank you later.

### 🚫 Hands Off the Generated Files

One golden rule: **don’t manually edit the generated files.**

They’re auto-generated directly from your .proto contracts — which means any manual change will be overwritten the next time you regenerate them.

Next up, we’ll inherit from the generated servicer classes to actually implement our business logic — starting with our database setup.

Then, we’ll build on top of these servicer classes to connect our service to a database.

### 🧱 Defining Our SQL Schema

Let’s start by setting up our database.

In /todoService/models/todo\_models.py, we’ll define a simple SQL schema using **SQLModel** — a lightweight ORM **built by the same creator of FastAPI**, combining the best of **SQLAlchemy** and **Pydantic**.

```python
from sqlmodel import SQLModel, Field, create_engine, Session

class Todo(SQLModel, table=True):
    id: int | None = Field(default=None, primary_key=True)
    task: str
    
engine = create_engine("sqlite:///todos.db", echo=True)

def init_db():
    SQLModel.metadata.create_all(engine)

def get_session():
    return Session(engine)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    init_db()
```

This creates a simple Todo table in SQLite.

Feels a lot like FastAPI? That’s because [**SQLModel** was written by the same author — Sebastián Ramírez](https://sqlmodel.tiangolo.com/).

To initialize your database, run:

```bash
python todoService/models/models.py
```

You’ll see a new `todos.db` file pop up — that’s your SQLite database ready to roll.

### Defining our gRPC server

We’ve defined our .proto contracts and database — now it’s time to actually **deploy the gRPC service**.

If you peek into the `todo_service_pb2_grpc.py` file (the main entry point), you’ll notice something that looks… alarming:

**Why is everything raising a** `**NotImplementedError**` **?!**

That’s because gRPC expects _you_ to implement the methods defined in your .proto file. It only provides the interface — you bring the logic through inheriting the `TodoServiceServicer`class.

Here’s what that looks like in `/todoService/server.py`:

```python
import grpc
from concurrent import futures
from sqlmodel import select
import logging

from todoService.protos import (
    todo_messages_pb2,
    todo_service_pb2,
    todo_service_pb2_grpc
)
from todoService.models.todo_models import Todo, get_session

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

class TodoServiceServicer(todo_service_pb2_grpc.TodoServiceServicer):
    def AddTodo(self, request, context):
        with get_session() as session:
            new_todo = Todo(task=request.task)
            session.add(new_todo)
            session.commit()
            session.refresh(new_todo)
            
            # Returns the gRPC message
            return todo_messages_pb2.Todo(
                id=new_todo.id,
                task=new_todo.task
            )
    
    def EditTodo(self, request, context):
        with get_session() as session:
            todo = session.get(Todo, request.id)
            if not todo:
                context.set_code(grpc.StatusCode.NOT_FOUND)
                context.set_details('Todo not found')
                return todo_messages_pb2.Todo()
            
            # Update the task
            todo.task = request.task
            session.commit()
            session.refresh(todo)
            return todo_messages_pb2.Todo(
                id=todo.id,
                task=todo.task
            )
    
    def GetTodo(self, request, context):
        with get_session() as session:
            todo = session.get(Todo, request.id)
            if not todo:
                context.set_code(grpc.StatusCode.NOT_FOUND)
                context.set_details('Todo not found')
                return todo_messages_pb2.Todo()
            return todo_messages_pb2.Todo(
                id=todo.id,
                task=todo.task
            )
    
    def ListTodos(self, request, context):
        with get_session() as session:
            todos = session.exec(select(Todo)).all()
            return todo_service_pb2.ListTodosResponse(
                todos = [
                    todo_messages_pb2.Todo(id=t.id, task=t.task)
                    for t in todos
                ]
            )
    
    def RemoveTodo(self, request, context):
        with get_session() as session:
            todo = session.get(Todo, request.id)
            if not todo:
                return todo_service_pb2.RemoveTodoResponse(success=False)
            session.delete(todo)
            session.commit()
            return todo_service_pb2.RemoveTodoResponse(success=True)
```

Each method starts a new SQL session, performs the operation, and returns a response model based on the Protobuf definitions we wrote earlier.

> 💡 **Pro tip:** Always use a `with` statement when working with SQL databases in Python. It ensures the session is automatically closed when the block exits — no dangling connections, no leaks.

To serve:

```python
#server.py

def serve():
    server = grpc.server(futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10))
    todo_service_pb2_grpc.add_TodoServiceServicer_to_server(TodoServiceServicer(), server)
    server.add_insecure_port('[::]:50051')
    server.start()
    logger.info("Server started on port 50051")
    try:
        server.wait_for_termination()
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        server.stop(0)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    serve()
```

We’re spinning up a `**ThreadPoolExecutor**` with up to 10 workers — this allows the gRPC service to handle multiple requests concurrently.

Why threads and not asyncio? Because I’m deliberately using the **synchronous gRPC SDK** for simplicity and easier debugging.

> Just in case: If you switch to the async version (grpc.aio), remember: you’ll also need to convert your SQL operations into async equivalents.

Let’s break it down:

-   🧵 **max\_workers=10** — allows up to 10 threads to handle requests.
-   🔧 **add\_TodoServiceServicer\_to\_server(…)** — registers our Todo service implementation.
-   🌐 **\[::\]:50051** — listens on all interfaces, port 50051.
-   ⏳ **wait\_for\_termination()** — keeps the service running until you manually stop it.

To start your server, run:

```bash
python -m todoService.server.py
```

And our gRPC server is up!

### ⚖️ If gRPC Is So Fast… Why Isn’t Everyone Using It?

Good question.

While gRPC is blazing fast, it’s not always the right tool for every job.

-   **Complexity:** As your codebase grows, .proto files (and the subsequently generated .py files) can multiply quickly. Managing them across multiple microservices is quite time-consuming.
-   **Pythonic Comfort:** Frameworks like **FastAPI** are friendlier, easier to debug, and come with built-in niceties — automatic docs, validation, and type safety.
-   **Practical Speed:** For most backend APIs, FastAPI is _already fast enough_. The difference only matters when ultra-low latency or polyglot microservices are involved.

In short:

> **Use gRPC** for backend-to-backend, high-performance communication.

> **Use REST/FastAPI** for public APIs and frontend integrations.

### 🌉 Our FastAPI Layer

Now for the fun part — let’s wrap our gRPC service inside a **FastAPI layer**.

This gives us the best of both worlds: human-friendly REST endpoints backed by gRPC performance.

Here’s the top of our app.py:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Path, Body
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

import asyncio
import grpc
from todoService.protos import (
    todo_messages_pb2,
    todo_service_pb2,
    todo_service_pb2_grpc,
)
from todoService.models.request_models import (
    TodoCreate,
    TodoUpdate,
    TodoResponse,
    TodoListResponse,
    DeleteResponse,
    TodoCreateBatch,
    TodoDeleteBatch,
    BatchResponse
)

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
logging_lock = asyncio.Lock()

tags_metadata = [
    {
        "name": "Todos",
        "description": "Operations for managing individual todos",
    },
    {
        "name": "Batch Operations",
        "description": "Bulk operations for creating or deleting multiple todos at once",
    },
    {
        "name": "System",
        "description": "Health checks and system information",
    },
]

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    # Setup: Create gRPC channel and stub
    channel = grpc.aio.insecure_channel('localhost:50051')
    stub = todo_service_pb2_grpc.TodoServiceStub(channel)
    app.state.grpc_channel = channel
    app.state.grpc_stub = stub
    logger.info("gRPC channel and stub created")
    
    yield 
    
    # Teardown: Close gRPC channel
    await channel.close()
    logger.info("gRPC channel closed")

app = FastAPI(
    title="Todo API",
    description="REST API wrapping gRPC Todo Service",
    version="1.0.0",
    lifespan=lifespan,
    openapi_tags=tags_metadata,
)

app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["*"], #specify this to be your frontend in production
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
)
```

A few things are happening here:

-   🔒 Defining a logging\_lock using an `asyncio.Lock` object: so that there won’t be any race conditions when logging concurrent tasks.
-   🧩 We’re defining **metadata** to organize endpoints in Swagger UI.
-   🔄 We use **lifespan** to manage our gRPC channel’s lifecycle. Specifically, we set the gRPC channel and stub within the lifespan object — we’ll be using the stub to invoke the gRPC backend.
-   🌍 We add **CORS middleware** so frontend clients can talk to our API. This isn’t necessary but a good to have. At production, change the `allow_origins` argument to be just the frontend URL.

> Note: Logging is thread safe (unlike print) by nature so a `logging_lock` is strictly not needed. But I wanted to practice using it.

### ✨ Defining Our Endpoints

Let’s start with the single operation endpoints. Each endpoint simply invokes a gRPC method using our stub:

```python
@app.post("/todos", response_model=TodoResponse, status_code=201, tags=["Todos"])
async def create_todo(todo: TodoCreate = Body(..., example={"task": "Buy groceries"})):
    """Creates a new todo item"""
    
    try:
        request = todo_messages_pb2.AddTodoRequest(task=todo.task)
        response = await app.state.grpc_stub.AddTodo(request)
        
        return TodoResponse(
            id=response.id,
            task=response.task
        )
    except grpc.RpcError as e:
        logger.error(f"gRPC error: {e.code()} - {e.details()}")
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=f"gRPC error: {e.details()}")

@app.get("/todos", response_model=TodoListResponse, tags=["Todos"])
async def list_todos():
    """Gets all todo items"""
    
    try:
        request = todo_messages_pb2.Empty()  
        response = await app.state.grpc_stub.ListTodos(request)
        todos = [
            TodoResponse(id=todo.id, task=todo.task)
            for todo in response.todos
        ]
        return TodoListResponse(todos=todos)
    
    except grpc.RpcError as e:
        logger.error(f"gRPC error: {e.code()} - {e.details()}")
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=f"gRPC error: {e.details()}")

@app.get("/todos/{todo_id}", response_model=TodoResponse, tags=["Todos"])
async def get_todo(todo_id: int = Path(..., description="The ID of the todo to retrieve")):
    """Get a specific todo by ID"""
    
    try:
        request = todo_messages_pb2.TodoId(id=todo_id)  
        response = await app.state.grpc_stub.GetTodo(request)
        
        # Check if todo was found (empty response means not found)
        if response.id == 0 and response.task == "":
            raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Todo not found")
        
        return TodoResponse(id=response.id, task=response.task)
    
    except grpc.RpcError as e:
        if e.code() == grpc.StatusCode.NOT_FOUND:
            raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Todo not found")
        logger.error(f"gRPC error: {e.code()} - {e.details()}")
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=f"gRPC error: {e.details()}")

@app.put("/todos/{todo_id}", response_model=TodoResponse, tags=["Todos"])
async def update_todo(todo: TodoUpdate, todo_id: int = Path(..., description="The ID of the todo to update")):
    """Update an existing todo"""
    try:
        request = todo_messages_pb2.EditTodoRequest(
            id=todo_id,
            task=todo.task
        )
        response = await app.state.grpc_stub.EditTodo(request)
        
        # Check if todo was found
        if response.id == 0 and response.task == "":
            raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Todo not found")
        
        return TodoResponse(
            id=response.id,
            task=response.task
        )
    except grpc.RpcError as e:
        if e.code() == grpc.StatusCode.NOT_FOUND:
            raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Todo not found")
        logger.error(f"gRPC error: {e.code()} - {e.details()}")
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=f"gRPC error: {e.details()}")
       
@app.delete("/todos/{todo_id}", response_model=DeleteResponse, tags=["Todos"])
async def delete_todo(todo_id: int = Path(..., description="The ID of the todo to delete")):
    """Delete a todo"""
    try:
        request = todo_messages_pb2.RemoveTodoRequest(id=todo_id)
        response = await app.state.grpc_stub.RemoveTodo(request)
        
        if not response.success:
            raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Todo not found")
        
        return DeleteResponse(
            success=True,
            message=f"Todo {todo_id} deleted successfully"
        )
    except grpc.RpcError as e:
        logger.error(f"gRPC error: {e.code()} - {e.details()}")
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=f"gRPC error: {e.details()}")
```

Simple, right?

Each route converts incoming REST requests into a gRPC message, sends it to the backend, and converts the result back into JSON for the client.

### ⚡ Batch Operations with AsyncIO

Here’s where FastAPI and asyncio shine.

Instead of handling batch operations sequentially, we can run them **in parallel**:

```python
@app.post("/todos/batch", response_model=BatchResponse, status_code=201, tags=["Batch Operations"])
async def create_todos_batch(batch: TodoCreateBatch = Body(..., example={"tasks": ["Task 1", "Task 2"]})):
    """Creates multiple todo items in a batch"""
    
    try:
        # Create all todos in parallel using asyncio.gather
        tasks = [
            app.state.grpc_stub.AddTodo(todo_messages_pb2.AddTodoRequest(task=task))
            for task in batch.tasks
        ]
        
        responses = await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)
        
        results = []
        success_count = 0
        failed_count = 0
        
        async with logging_lock:
            for response in responses:
                if isinstance(response, Exception):
                    logger.error(f"Error creating todo: {response}")
                    results.append({"success": False, "error": str(response)})
                    failed_count += 1
                else:
                    results.append({"success": True, "id": response.id, "task": response.task})
                    success_count += 1
        
        return BatchResponse(
            success_count=success_count,
            failure_count=failed_count,
            results=results
        )
        
    except Exception as e:
        logger.error(f"Batch creation error: {e}")
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=str(e))

@app.delete("/todos/batch", response_model=BatchResponse, tags=["Batch Operations"])
async def delete_todos_batch(batch: TodoDeleteBatch = Body(..., example={"ids": [1, 2, 3]})):
    """Deletes multiple todo items in a batch"""
    
    try:
        
        #Delete all todos in parallel
        tasks = [
            app.state.grpc_stub.RemoveTodo(todo_messages_pb2.RemoveTodoRequest(id=todo_id))
            for todo_id in batch.ids
        ]
        
        responses = await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)
        
        # Process results
        success_count = 0
        failed_count = 0
        
        async with logging_lock:
            for response in responses:
                if isinstance(response, Exception) or not response.success:
                    logger.info(f"Error deleting todo: {response}")
                    failed_count += 1
                else:
                    success_count += 1
        
        return BatchResponse(
            success_count=success_count,
            failure_count=failed_count,
            results=[]  # No results needed for delete
        )
        
    except Exception as e:
        logger.error(f"Batch deletion error: {e}")
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=str(e))
```

This spins up all the gRPC calls at once — drastically cutting down latency for large batches.

We also use an `asyncio.Lock` for safe logging and consistent console output across tasks.

> **Best practice:**

> \- Use asyncio.gather() for parallel tasks of the same type.

> \- If you’re managing multiple task types, consider asyncio.Queue — each with its own lock and worker coroutine.

Finally:

```python
#app.py
if __name__ == "__main__":
    import uvicorn
    uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)
```

✅ And that’s it — you now have:

-   A **gRPC backend** (fast, type-safe, and efficient),
-   A **FastAPI wrapper** (developer-friendly and debuggable),
-   And **async-powered batch endpoints** that scale beautifully.

body:
* * *

#### How (and when) to undertake task parallelism in Python

Ever looked at your seniors’ Python code and seen `async` and `await` everywhere? Seems simple enough — just add async to a function and await to its call, right? Not quite.

Google why, and you’ll often get something like “it doesn’t block the thread so things can run concurrently”. But can I tell you the truth? Most people are using this wrongly or are mostly just copying from cookbook examples (especially in generative AI).

This article stems from a “eureka” moment when everything clicked for me.

All codes are available in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/parallelism).

### 1\. The difference between a “normal” and async function

Simply put, synchronous functions are “thread-blocking”. This means that no other tasks can commence unless this task is completed!

#### **Think of it like being at a restaurant.**

With a “synchronous” approach, you couldn’t place your order until the person in front of you gets their meal — how annoying would that be? Luckily, most restaurants don’t work this way: you place your order and wait, while the kitchen prepares multiple meals at the same time. That’s more like what asynchronous code allows.

#### Back to code

Likewise, asynchronous functions don’t block the thread — they allow other tasks to run while waiting for I/O or long-running operations to complete.

Let’s mock up a list of documents to show the point:

```python
import nest_asyncio
nest_asyncio.apply() # nest asynchronous processes within Jupyter Notebook

docs = [f"doc {i}" for i in range(5)]
```

Here’s the way we learnt in any Python class to process documents — just process a document one by one in a loop:

```python
import time
from tqdm.notebook import tqdm

start_time = time.time()

def process_document(document_name: str) -> str:
    time.sleep(5) # simulating a blocking task    
    return f"{document_name} processed."

for doc in tqdm(docs):
    print(process_document(doc))

end_time = time.time()
print(f"Total time taken: {end_time - start_time} seconds")

# Total time taken: 25 seconds
```

So how do we make this asynchronous? First, let’s turn the function into an async one:

```python
import asyncio

async def aprocess_document(document_name: str) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(5) # simulating a blocking task    
    return f"{document_name} processed."
```

You might try using it like this:

```python
start_time = time.time()

for doc in tqdm(docs):
    result = await aprocess_document(doc)

end_time = time.time()
print(f"Total time taken: {end_time - start_time} seconds")
```

> And then be shocked when you notice it still takes **25 seconds — zero improvement!**

Why? Because this code **isn’t concurrent** — tasks are still running sequentially, one at a time.

Instead, you can run all tasks concurrently using asyncio.gather:

```python
start_time = time.time()
results = await asyncio.gather(
    *[aprocess_document(doc) for doc in docs]
)
end_time = time.time()
print(f"Total time taken: {end_time - start_time} seconds")
# Total time taken: 5 seconds
```

Wow — that’s a huge speed-up!

Python’s asyncio library starts all tasks at the same time and gathers the results once they complete. Since tasks run concurrently, the total runtime drops dramatically.

### 2\. So why don’t we make every function async?

“Why not just make every function asynchronous and never block the thread?” — a reasonable question. Let’s use some code to see why this isn’t always a good idea.

#### Synchronous functions have tracebacks that are easier to debug

Consider the function below. We expect the function to always blow up when `n=2` come rain or shine.

```python
def fetch_doc(n):
    time.sleep(0.1 * n) # simulate I/O
    if n == 2:
        raise ValueError(f"Bad doc {n}")
    return f"doc {n}"

for i in range (5):
    print(fetch_doc(i))
```

```python-repl
ValueError: Bad doc 2
```

Straightforward, right? The traceback is simple and points directly to the line that caused the error.

Async tracebacks get messy:

```python
async def afetch_doc(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1 * n) # simulate I/O
    if n == 2:
        raise ValueError(f"Bad doc {n}")
    return f"doc {n}"

tasks = [asyncio.create_task(afetch_doc(i)) for i in range(5)]
results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
```

The traceback now stretches across multiple internal asyncio frames. Imagine this if your function has many await calls — the error path can get very long and confusing.

**Why do async functions have such complex tracebacks?** Because tasks are resumed at different points in time. Concurrency introduces complexity into debugging.

#### Async functions have coding overhead

You really need to have a clear mental model of what is happening (which tasks run concurrently at any given time) because things get messy really quickly. Consider the following code block:

```python
async def acheck_if_doc_exists(doc_name: str) -> bool:
    await asyncio.sleep(5) # simulating a DB call
    return doc_name in docs

async def aread_document(doc_name: str) -> str:
    if await acheck_if_doc_exists(doc_name): # notice the await here
        await asyncio.sleep(5)
        return f"{doc_name} exists. Content: Lorem ipsum..."

print(await aread_document("doc 1"))
```

And here’s a common beginner mistake:

```python
# Forgot to await!
print(aread_document("doc 1"))
```

Output:

```python-repl
<coroutine object aread_document at 0x...>
RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'aread_document' was never awaited
```

**What’s happening?** The result of an async function is a **coroutine**, not the actual value. The task only executes when you await it. Otherwise, Python just tells you, “I’m working on it,” but nothing actually happens.

### 3\. By the way, concurrency does not mean parallelism

So far, we’ve been running tasks concurrently using asyncio. But here’s the catch: **all of that was happening in a single thread!**

Think of a thread like a social media thread:

-   On Twitter, one thread talks about subject A, another about B.
-   In computer science, a thread works on a task (subject A), while another thread can work on the same or a different task. Multiple threads let you work on multiple things “at the same time,” potentially in true parallel.

And Python has a library to do this!

```python
import threading
```

And now we can create different threads to do different tasks:

```python
def process_info_in_threads(document_name: str, thread_name: str):
    thread_id = threading.current_thread().ident
    print(f"\n{thread_name} running on thread ID: {thread_id}")

    ## Process document with our function from before##
    result = process_document(document_name)

    print(f"\n{thread_name} finished on thread ID: {thread_id}")
    return result
    
start_time = time.time()

threads = []
for i, doc in tqdm(enumerate(docs)):
    working_thread = threading.Thread(target=process_info_in_threads, args=(doc,f"Worker {i}",))
    threads.append(working_thread)
    working_thread.start()

# Wait for all threads
for t in threads:
    t.join()

end_time = time.time()
print(f"Total time taken: {end_time - start_time} seconds")
```

```python-repl
Worker 0 running on thread ID: 6262042624
Worker 1 running on thread ID: 6278868992
Worker 2 running on thread ID: 6295695360
Worker 3 running on thread ID: 13035925504
Worker 4 running on thread ID: 13052751872

Worker 0 finished on thread ID: 6262042624
Worker 2 finished on thread ID: 6295695360
Worker 1 finished on thread ID: 6278868992
Worker 3 finished on thread ID: 13035925504
Worker 4 finished on thread ID: 13052751872

Total time taken: 5 seconds
```

Wow! 5 seconds — instead of the 25 seconds using the “normal” synchronous approach. But you might notice something: this is **the same total time as our asyncio approach**.

And if you rerun the code, the output order can change:

```python-repl
Worker 0 running on thread ID: 6262042624
Worker 0 finished on thread ID: 6262042624
Total time taken: 5 seconds
```

Are your other workers asleep you wonder?

Let me address the “sleeping worker problem” first.

#### Introducing race conditions

This is a classic race condition. Imagine you and a friend editing a Google Doc: whoever hits Save last “wins,” and the document could end up looking very different depending on the order of edits.

`print()` is not “thread-safe” in Python. This means that multiple threads “race” to print at the same time and so the output gets lost!

Let’s fix it — with a lock

```python
print_lock = threading.Lock()

def fix_process_info_in_threads(document_name: str, thread_name: str):
    thread_id = threading.current_thread().ident
    
    # Thread-safe printing
    with print_lock:
        print(f"{thread_name} running on thread ID: {thread_id}")
    
    # Process document
    result = process_document(document_name)
    
    # Thread-safe printing
    with print_lock:
        print(f"{thread_name} finished on thread ID: {thread_id}")
    
    return result

start_time = time.time()

threads = []
for i, doc in enumerate(docs):  # Fixed: was tqdm(enumerate(doc))
    working_thread = threading.Thread(
        target=fix_process_info_in_threads, 
        args=(doc, f"Worker {i}")
    )
    threads.append(working_thread)
    working_thread.start()

# Wait for all threads
for t in threads:
    t.join()

end_time = time.time()
print(f"Total time taken: {end_time - start_time:.2f} seconds")
```

And now we see the output we expect.

Race conditions happen in `asyncio` too! Tasks “race” each other to the finish line. So the asyncio package has its own \`lock\` capability as well — this means that **you have to be extremely careful when coding concurrent tasks!**

> In general, **race conditions** occur when two or more tasks or threads access the same piece of information at the same time.

#### Why does threading take the same time as asyncio?

Because Python’s threads are not truly parallel. Yes, you read that right. In Python, multiple threads can run _concurrently_, but not _in parallel_.

Here’s the difference:

-   **Concurrency** = making progress on multiple tasks within the same span of time. For example, in one day you might work on a report, a presentation, and some code.
-   **Parallelism** = tasks running literally at the same time. Think of typing an email with one hand while stirring coffee with the other — both start, run, and end simultaneously.

#### Why no true parallelism in Python threads?

This limitation comes from Python’s design. Python uses the **Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)** — a mutex that prevents multiple native threads from executing Python bytecode at the same time.

That means:

-   Only one thread can execute Python code at a time.
-   Threads take turns accessing the interpreter.

For CPU-intensive tasks, this often means **no speedup at all** — and sometimes even worse performance because of the extra overhead of switching between threads.

Many popular Python frameworks (like **NumPy** and **pandas**) are fully synchronous — and that’s fine. They don’t benefit from async because their heavy lifting happens in optimized C code under the hood, outside of Python’s GIL.

> In general, use Python’s asyncio as much as you can instead of Python’s threading because Python’s GIL means that they work the same. Use Python’s Threading if the framework does not have an async/await methods.

It’s much easier to manage context sharing within the same thread (async) than between threads (threading).

### 4\. But Python is still able to achieve true parallelism

Python can achieve _true parallelism_ — but only with processes, not threads.

That’s why you need to match your approach to the type of task:

-   Concurrency works best for I/O bound tasks — these are tasks that require a lot of waiting with no actual compute work. For example, boiling water. You can do other work as the water is boiling.
-   Parallelism works best for CPU bound tasks — these are tasks that require active work. For example, chop 50 onions. In this case you don’t have any free hands to do anything else.

In fact, there is no benefit to making CPU bound tasks asynchronous. Let me show you what I mean:

```python
# worker_functions.py
import time

def cpu_intensive_work(n):
    """Heavy computation"""
    total = 0
    for i in range(n * 1_000_000):
        total += i ** 2
    return total

def io_intensive_work(delay):
    """I/O simulation"""
    time.sleep(delay)
    return f"Slept for {delay} seconds"
```

Here we have two fully synchronous functions to simulate CPU work and IO work.

> **Note:** Parallelism in Python requires pickling/serializing the function to send it to other processes — and that’s why these functions have to be in a .py file because Python thinks that the task is in a function called “main” by default. This function does not exist in our Jupyter Notebook.

Now let’s call it in our notebook in three different ways:

```python
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor
from worker_functions import cpu_intensive_work, io_intensive_work

# --------------------------
# CPU-bound benchmarks
# --------------------------

def test_threadpool_cpu():
    cpu_tasks = [100, 200, 300, 400]
    start = time.time()
    with ThreadPoolExecutor() as executor:
        results = list(executor.map(cpu_intensive_work, cpu_tasks))
    print(f"ThreadPoolExecutor (CPU): {time.time() - start:.2f}s")

def test_processpool_cpu():
    cpu_tasks = [100, 200, 300, 400]
    start = time.time()
    with ProcessPoolExecutor() as executor:
        results = list(executor.map(cpu_intensive_work, cpu_tasks))
    print(f"ProcessPoolExecutor (CPU): {time.time() - start:.2f}s")

async def async_cpu_test():
    cpu_tasks = [100, 200, 300, 400]
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    start = time.time()
    with ProcessPoolExecutor() as executor:
        results = await asyncio.gather(*[
            loop.run_in_executor(executor, cpu_intensive_work, task)
            for task in cpu_tasks
        ])
    print(f"Asyncio + ProcessPool (CPU): {time.time() - start:.2f}s")
```

**The** `**test_threadpool_cpu**`**method:** We use a `ThreadPoolExecutor` which executes the `cpu_intensive_work`asynchronously within the same thread. This is the pure concurrency approach — you could also use `asyncio.gather()` as before, but a `ThreadPoolExecutor` also supports executing in multi-threaded environments.

A quick note on threads: you can specify the maximum number of threads in a `ThreadPoolExecutor` or leave it to the default like we did (this spins up a minimal of 5 workers). This default aims to balance performance, especially for I/O-bound tasks, without overwhelming the system’s resources:

**🧠 Why Does the Default number of threads Use CPU Count?**

The default value of max\_workers is influenced by the number of CPUs to accommodate I/O-bound tasks, which spend significant time waiting for external resources (like network responses). Having more threads than CPUs allows the system to continue processing other tasks while some threads are waiting, improving overall throughput.

#### 🔹results = list(executor.map(cpu\_intensive\_work, cpu\_tasks))

This line of code to invoke the ThreadPoolExecutor doesn’t read naturally at first glance. So let me break this down a little:

**executor.map:**

-   Think of it like Python’s built-in map(), but it runs in **parallel** using the thread pool.
-   It takes a **function** (cpu\_intensive\_work) and an **iterable** (cpu\_tasks) and applies the function to each element of the iterable.

**executor.map returns a generator-like object**

-   executor.map doesn’t immediately return a list; it returns an **iterator** that will produce results as tasks finish.
-   That’s why we wrap it in list(): to **collect all the results into a list** so you can use them immediately.

* * *

**The** `**test_processpool_cpu**`**method:** A`ProcessPoolExecutor` is where parallelism occurs. We literally use a different CPU core to execute the exact same task. Each CPU core would then have its own Python GIL and therefore true parallelism occurs! As before, we get to specify the number of “workers” (only that these are upper-bounded by `os.process_cpu_count` ).

> In Python’s concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor, the max\_workers parameter specifies the **maximum number of worker processes** that can run concurrently to execute submitted tasks. These processes are managed by the executor to handle tasks asynchronously.

> **Default Behavior**: If you don’t specify the max\_workers parameter when creating a ProcessPoolExecutor, Python sets it to the number of **logical CPU cores** available on your system. This is determined using os.cpu\_count(), which returns the number of CPUs in the system, including logical cores if hyperthreading is enabled. For instance, on a system with 4 physical cores and hyperthreading enabled, os.cpu\_count() might return 8, indicating 8 logical cores.

**The** `**async_cpu_test**` **method:** We first get the current running loop (asyncio’s concurrent event manager), and tell the loop to run tasks asynchronously in parallel within the `ProcessPoolExecutor` . This aims to explore the “ultimate” combination of concurrent parallelism — concurrent tasks running at the same unit of time. After all, if either is good on its own, combining them should be better. Right?

The results:

```python-repl
=== CPU-bound ===
ThreadPoolExecutor (CPU): 45.47s
ProcessPoolExecutor (CPU): 19.42s
Asyncio + ProcessPool (CPU): 20.32s
```

Look at how big the difference is the moment we parallelize the tasks with `ProcessPoolExecutor` . Like getting your right hand and your left hand to dice garlic cloves is way faster than using just one hand.

But there really isn’t a difference whether you make the parallel tasks run asynchronously or not. Because we’re not really waiting for anything.

In I/O bound tasks however, parallelism makes no difference:

```python
# --------------------------
# I/O-bound benchmarks
# --------------------------

def test_threadpool_io(n_tasks=10, delay=1, max_workers=10):
    start = time.time()
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=max_workers) as executor:
        results = list(executor.map(io_intensive_work, [delay] * n_tasks))
    print(f"ThreadPool (I/O, {n_tasks} tasks, {max_workers} workers): {time.time() - start:.2f}s")

async def test_asyncio_io(n_tasks=10, delay=1):
    start = time.time()
    results = await asyncio.gather(*[asyncio.sleep(delay) for _ in range(n_tasks)])
    print(f"Asyncio (I/O, {n_tasks} tasks): {time.time() - start:.2f}s")

def test_processpool_io(n_tasks=10, delay=1, max_workers=10):
    start = time.time()
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=max_workers) as executor:
        results = list(executor.map(io_intensive_work, [delay] * n_tasks))
    print(f"ProcessPool (I/O, {n_tasks} tasks, {max_workers} workers): {time.time() - start:.2f}s")
```

In the code block above, I use threading, asyncio and then asyncio + multiprocessing to simulate an I/O bound task (just sleeping to simulate waiting). The results:

```python-repl
=== I/O-bound ===
ThreadPool (I/O, 10 tasks, 5 workers): 2.01s
ThreadPool (I/O, 10 tasks, 20 workers): 1.01s
Asyncio (I/O, 10 tasks): 1.00s
ProcessPool (I/O, 10 tasks, 20 workers): 1.10s
```

Here’s the breakdown of what the experiment shows:

#### a. ThreadPoolExecutor with limited workers

-   With **5 workers**, you only have 5 “slots” to run tasks at once.
-   I scheduled **10 tasks**, each takes 1 second.
-   So the first 5 start, take ~1s, finish → then the next 5 start, another ~1s.
-   Total ≈ **2s**.

This is like having **5 waiters serving 10 tables**: half the tables get served, then the other half.

#### b. ThreadPoolExecutor with more workers

-   With **20 workers**, you have way more than enough slots for your 10 tasks.
-   All 10 can run at once, each waits 1s → total ≈ **1s**.

This is like hiring **20 waiters for 10 tables**: everyone’s order is taken at the same time.

#### c. Asyncio

-   Async doesn’t rely on a pool of OS threads. Instead, the **event loop** just keeps track of when each task is ready to resume.
-   All 10 tasks call asyncio.sleep(1) → the loop suspends them, sets timers, and resumes them all after 1s.
-   Again, total ≈ **1s**.

This is like having **one very efficient waiter with a perfect memory**, who tells everyone “I’ll come back in 1 minute,” then circles back exactly on time.

#### d. Process Pool (separate kitchens, separate chefs)

-   Instead of more waiters in the same kitchen, you hire **entirely new chefs in new kitchens** 🧑‍🍳🔥.
-   Each has their _own stove and fridge_ (own Python interpreter, no GIL).
-   They can all cook at the same time, without blocking each other.
-   But you have to **transport the raw ingredients to each kitchen** and later **bring back the finished dishes** (serializing data between processes). That’s the overhead.
-   For _complicated cooking (CPU-bound)_ this pays off big. For _just waiting for the oven to ding (I/O)_, it’s overkill.

Again it takes just 1 second. Why? The difference is in the waiting time for the result (like calling somebody else’s API). No actual CPU computing is done on our end.

### Wrapping up

Here’s a quick summary of our article:

**I/O-bound tasks**

-   It doesn’t matter whether you use **threads, processes, or asyncio** — performance is basically the same.
-   The real “win” comes from **concurrency**: letting the program do something else while waiting on I/O.
-   That’s why ThreadPool, asyncio, and asyncio+ThreadPool all landed around ~1 second.

**CPU-bound tasks**

-   **Threads don’t help** because of Python’s Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) — they still run one at a time (~45s).
-   **Processes do help** (via ProcessPoolExecutor or asyncio + ProcessPool). Each process runs in a separate Python interpreter, so you get true parallelism across CPU cores (~19–20s).
-   **Asyncio alone doesn’t speed up CPU work** — it just makes orchestration around processes easier.

### Learning by analogies

-   **Asynchronous** → Ordering food at a restaurant without waiting for the guy before you.
-   **Concurrency** → Breathing, blinking, thinking, and coding — all interleaved by one person.
-   **Parallelism** → My teammates and I coding different features at the same time.

Next time you’re deciding between **threads, processes, or asyncio**, remember:

-   I/O = **concurrency**
-   CPU = **parallelism**
-   Use the right tool for the job.
