body:
* * *

#### Part three of the “Building a Hypermodern GenAI App” series

In [Act One](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/would-you-like-an-llm-with-that-a-bento-cloud-drive-thru-7e70f77277d2) of this series, we served a Qwen3 8Bn reasoning LLM with vLLM and scaled it using Bento Cloud — all in Python.

In [Act Two](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/would-you-like-context-with-that-a-rag-as-a-service-drive-thru-2e5a2867102a), we turned that LLM into a full retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) service with Qdrant Cloud and Llama Cloud. Thanks to Llama Parse, even diagrams, charts, and tables became instantly RAG-ready.

Act Three is where things get exciting: we’ll take everything we’ve built so far and wrap it into an agent.

### The Hypermodern Agent

Agents are everywhere. Almost every new generative AI app today calls itself “agentic.”

I’ve previously written about frameworks like [LlamaIndex](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multi-agent-multiverse-part-3a-llamaindex-workflows-c0f614c15b88), [LangGraph](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multi-agents-multiverse-part-1-langgraph-2ac56f1b5b3c), [CrewAI](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multi-agent-multiverse-part-4-crewai-147ada6db54c), and [Autogen](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multi-agent-multiverse-part-2-autogen-5401a0075d75). They still dominate, but new players are rising: [IBM’s BeeAI](https://github.com/i-am-bee/beeai-framework) (built around their ACP protocol), [Google’s Agent Development Kit (ADK)](https://github.com/google/adk-python), [Pydantic AI (“FastAPI for agents”)](https://ai.pydantic.dev/), and [Agno](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno) — which has already hit 32.6k GitHub stars, almost matching CrewAI.

Multi-agent frameworks promise a lot, and splitting work across agents often ensures robustness. But orchestration comes at a cost: it can be buggy. Why did the manager agent pick agent B instead of A for the task? Nobody knows.

That’s why apps like ChatGPT, Gemini, or Qwen’s “Think Longer” mode often stick to a single-agent setup powered by reasoning LLMs. Chat applications need to be fast. Users (myself included) expect instant replies. Waiting feels like being stuck on a customer support hotline.

Yet when you try apps like Manus AI, Claude Code, or GitHub Copilot, it’s clear they’re multi-agent systems. How are they so fast and yet so good?

That’s what we’ll explore in Act Three. We start with a brief discussion of agents before diving into the code.

All codes are available in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/deep-agents-bento-llama-stack).

### The idea of a deep agent

At the heart of every agent framework isn’t the LLM — it’s the agent.

Early agents were built on the [**ReAct** framework (“Reasoning and Acting”)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629), which structured decision-making into explicit **Thought → Action → Observation** loops.

ReAct acted as a compatibility layer. It allowed any text-generation model — even those without native function calling — use tools by wrapping them in natural language prompts. The tradeoff was higher verbosity and token usage, but the upside was huge: transparent reasoning, universal applicability, and easier debugging across legacy or specialized models. My friend [Jinkett](https://medium.com/u/4298d8c06a21) covers this in greater detail in [his article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/part-iv-llamaindex-react-workflows-are-we-thinking-enough-232cd44a6677).

Today, most agents rely on the function calling capabilities baked directly into LLMs during model training. [Tools are defined with JSON schemas, and the model outputs structured calls rather than free-form text](http://medium.com/r?url=https%3A%2F%2Fplatform.openai.com%2Fdocs%2Fguides%2Ffunction-calling%2Ffunction-calling). This makes agents faster, cheaper, and more reliable — eliminating parsing errors and reducing token usage.

In practice, nearly every modern agent is now a function-calling agent.

#### LangChain writes the next page of the playbook

LangChain studied apps like Manus AI and developed a new framework: the **deep agent**.

In their view, the base function-calling agent is “shallow.” It works fine for simple tasks but struggles with complex workflows that require planning and extended execution.

Take Manus AI. Ask it how to switch from data scientist to quantum computer scientist, and you’ll see it:

1.  Plans a step-by-step roadmap
2.  Asks for feedback or more input
3.  Executes each step one at a time — showing results instantly, and letting you interrupt or adjust at any stage

The breakdowns are remarkably detailed, even down to tool execution. Some tools run directly in computer terminals, with real-time stdio streams. All of it executes at impressive speed, wrapped in a sleek user interface.

So what is a deep agent? According to LangChain, it’s essentially a **collection of shallow agents with detailed prompts and tools**.

At first glance, the code in the [Deep Agents repo](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/tree/master) looks just like a shallow agent (see red mark 1 in the screenshot).

But a closer look at the docs reveals how the depth is created:

### The default planning and file system tools

Each deep agent comes equipped with default tools:

1.  write\_todos: Breaks down the user’s query into a list of todos, written to the scratchpad
2.  write\_file: Write a new file
3.  read\_file: Read a file from a filepath
4.  ls: List all the files within the agent’s state
5.  edit\_file: Edit a file given a filepath

Each tool comes with [detailed tool descriptions](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/blob/master/src/deepagents/prompts.py) and few-shot examples, including when _not_ to use it. Developers can also add their own tools, but importantly, these never replace the default ones.

### Sub Agents

Here’s where it gets weird. In the docs, a sub-agent in Deep Agents is defined as a `TypedDict`.

It gets weirder. Each sub-agent can have its own tools — but those tools are just a list of strings?!

Digging deeper into the soure code (see red marks):

Red mark 1: Each deep agent will always have 1 default sub-agent (“general-purpose”) with access to the same tools as the top level agent.

Red mark 2a and 2b: Each `TypedDict` sub-agent will be used to create more shallow agents.

> In other words: **a deep agent is really just a shallow agent that uses other shallow agents as tools.**

### The system prompt

Developers can override the system prompt, but by default, it enforces that the agent always uses the built-in tools provided.

### So…how do we build this?

Be prepared: you’ll run into syntax errors, especially when wiring up sub-agents

Since deep agents can consume a lot of tokens, I used **LangSmith** for observability. You can get started by creating a free account on [LangSmith](https://smith.langsmith.com/) and get your API key — the [free tier of LangSmith](https://www.langchain.com/pricing) allows for 5,000 traces per month. Add the following to your `.env` file

```bash
LANGSMITH_API_KEY=your_api_key
LANGSMITH_TRACING=true
```

Now we’re ready to write some code.

#### Step 1: Spin up the MCP Services

In [Act One](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/would-you-like-an-llm-with-that-a-bento-cloud-drive-thru-7e70f77277d2), we deployed our RAG engines on **Llama Cloud** (backed by vLLM on Bento Cloud). In [Act Two](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/would-you-like-context-with-that-a-rag-as-a-service-drive-thru-2e5a2867102a), we exposed them as **MCP services**. We’ll now use those MCP endpoints as tools for our deep agents. Turn on your Bento Cloud deployment and run:

```undefined
python index_mcp.py
```

Then connect with LangChain:

```python
from langchain_mcp_adapters.client import MultiServerMCPClient
from dotenv import load_dotenv, find_dotenv

_ = load_dotenv(find_dotenv())

client = MultiServerMCPClient(
    {
        "mcp_zero_and_alita_rag": {
            "url": "http://localhost:8000/mcp",
            "transport": "streamable_http"
        }
    }
)
tools = await client.get_tools()
```

LangSmith automatically traces calls when using LangChain/LangGraph once the environment variables are loaded. For other SDKs, you’d need to manually import and instrument the LangSmith library.

#### Step 2: Setup the model

For this article, I used **OpenAI’s gpt-oss:20b on Ollama** as the “deep agent” model. (I didn’t deploy it on Bento Cloud because of size.)

```python
from langchain_ollama import ChatOllama

model = ChatOllama(
    model="gpt-oss:20b",
    temperature=0,
)
```

#### Step 3: Define the query and baseline instructions

```python
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage, SystemMessage
from prompts.single_agent_prompt import baseline_instructions

query = """How does Alita enable agents to create and deploy MCP tools if 
the agent deems that the tool does not exist? Can Alita be used with MCP 
Zero?"""
```

#### Step 4: Establish a baseline with a “shallow” agent

Always benchmark first — it gives you something to compare deep agent performance against.

```python
from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent

response = ""

react_agent = create_react_agent(
    model=model,
    tools=tools,
)

messages = [
    SystemMessage(content=baseline_instructions),
    HumanMessage(content=query)
]

async for chunk in react_agent.astream(
    {"messages": messages},
    stream_mode="values"
):
    if "messages" in chunk:
        chunk['messages'][-1].pretty_print()

response += chunk['messages'][-1].content
splits = response.split("\n")

with open("../reports/react_report.txt", "w") as f:
    for split in splits:
        f.write(split + "\n")
```

#### Step 5: Create a “solo mode” deep agent

A deep agent without extra sub-agents:

```python
from deepagents import create_deep_agent

base_deep_agent = create_deep_agent(
    model=model,
    tools=tools,
    instructions=baseline_instructions
)

response = ""

async for chunk in base_deep_agent.astream(
    {
        "messages": [
            {"role": "user", "content": "How does Alita enable agents to create and deploy MCP tools if the agent deems that the tool does not exist?"}
        ]
    },
    stream_mode="values"
):
    if "messages" in chunk:
        chunk['messages'][-1].pretty_print()
        
response += chunk['messages'][-1].content
splits = response.split("\n")

with open("../reports/single_deep_agent_report.txt", "w") as f:
    for split in splits:
        f.write(split + "\n")
```

I had to explicitly write my own report-saving code here because the built-in file tools caused **Pydantic validation errors**. I raised a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/issues/83); Harrison Chase (the founder of LangChain) quickly responded that my model wasn’t strong enough for the default tools (Deep Agents assume Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 4). It was surprising, since OpenAI’s gpt-oss:20b performs at the o3-mini level and the gpt-oss:20b model was used their repo in an example

#### Step 6: Deep agent with sub agents

Here’s where it gets messy. Sub-agents are defined as `TypedDict` objects with a list of strings for tools. I created two sub-agents:

1.  **Alita MCP Zero Agent** — specialized in answering MCP Zero + Alita queries
2.  **Report Enhancement Agent** — improves and saves the final report

```python
from prompts.multi_agent_prompt import (
    crew_instructions,         #top level agent prompt
    alita_mcp_zero_prompt,     #sub agent with the mcp zero tool
    report_improvement_prompt   #sub agent to edit the report
)
from langchain_core.tools import tool

@tool
def write_report_to_file(report: str):
    """Use this tool to write the final report to a file!"""
    
    splits = report.split("\n")
    with open("../reports/multi_agent_report.txt", "w") as f:
        for split in splits:
            f.write(split + "\n")
    return "Report written!"

@tool
def enhance_report(report: str):
    """Use this tool to enhance writing of the final report"""
    
    messages = [
        SystemMessage(content=report_improvement_prompt),
        HumanMessage(content=f"Report: {report}")
    ]
    response = model.invoke(messages)
    
    return response.content
```

I chose to write some of my own tools that did the exact same functions as LangChain’s default tools for Deep Agents because of the Pydantic validation errors mentioned before.

The Deep Agents framework requires tool names to be consistent, so I had to map them back into the top-level tool list:

```python
## This was from our MCP tool list
tools_by_name = {}
for tool_ in tools:
    tools_by_name[tool_.name] = tool_

alita_mcp_zero_sub_agent = {
    "name": "alita-mcp-zero-agent",
    "description": "Used to answer questions about MCP Zero and Alita.",
    "prompt": alita_mcp_zero_prompt,
    "tools": tools_by_name,
}
```

```python
report_enhancement_sub_agent = {
    "name": "report-enhancement-agent",
    "description": "Used to enhance the writing of the final report and write report to a file.",
    "prompt": report_improvement_prompt,
    "tools": {
        "write_report_to_file": write_report_to_file,
        "enhance_report": enhance_report},
}

## This is the final tool list to be passed to the top level agent
tools_final = tools + [enhance_report, write_report_to_file]
```

> Interestingly, the tools for sub agents are not a list of strings! I passed it as a key-value-pair object. I’m just as confused as you are but this came after quite some debugging on my end.

Note that all sub agents use the same LLM as the top agent (a gpt-oss:20b served on Ollama).

Finally, wire it all together:

```python
agent = create_deep_agent(
    model = model,
    tools = tools_final,
    instructions = crew_instructions,
    subagents = [alita_mcp_zero_sub_agent, report_enhancement_sub_agent],
).with_config({"recursion_limit": 1000})

response = ""

async for chunk in agent.astream(
    {
        "messages": [
            {"role": "user", "content": "How does Alita enable agents to create and deploy MCP tools if the agent deems that the tool does not exist?"}
        ]
    },
    stream_mode="values"
):
    if "messages" in chunk:
        chunk['messages'][-1].pretty_print()
        
response += chunk['messages'][-1].content
```

> Importantly, every tool used by every agent must also be made visible to the top level agent. Frankly, I still don’t understand the reason for this but I complied so that there won’t be any errors.

### Observing our agents 🔎

#### Here was how our react agent (baseline) performed:

Notice that it only took 1.1k tokens and 180s despite only one tool call. Bear in mind that our LLM deployed on vLLM (Qwen3:8b) is also a reasoning LLM, so is our top level LLM (GPT-OSS:20b) for our react agent. Both LLMs reasoned through the question and tool call results before nailing the final answer.

#### Here was how our “solo mode” deep agent performed:

The “deep agent” took 10 seconds more and 4.8k tokens (more than 4 times more)! Notably, the deep agent only made just one tool call — the same tool call as the baseline setup.

#### Here was how our deep agent with sub agent crew performed:

This setup took almost 40k tokens and more than 400 seconds (6 minutes and 40 seconds) for just one question! It started out by calling the alita documentation — twice with the exact same query!

Then it decided to get started on its report writing tasks and called the report writing sub agent, which then called the enhance report “tool” and the “write\_report\_to\_file” tool to write the final report to a txt file.

### How good are the reports?

The reports were so extensive — I didn’t read them 🤣

Instead, I built an **LLM-as-a-judge** using the same gpt-oss:20b model to evaluate them automatically.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from tqdm.notebook import tqdm
from collections import defaultdict

class ResultCard(BaseModel):
    score: float = Field(..., description="Score from 1-10 where 10 is the highest possible score.")
    reason_for_score: str = Field(..., description="The reason that this score was given. Share why the result didn't score 10, or what went well and didn't.")
    
reports = os.listdir("../reports")

# we're still using gpt-oss on Ollama
model_with_tools = model.bind_tools([ResultCard])
requirements = baseline_instructions
res = defaultdict(dict)
query = "How does Alita enable agents to create and deploy MCP tools if the agent deems that the tool does not exist?"

for report in tqdm(reports):
    report_name=report.split(".txt")[0]
    with open(os.path.join("../reports", report), "r") as file:
        text = file.read()
        result = model_with_tools.invoke(
            f"""
            You are a teacher grading 3 reports.
            
            This is the report's focus: {query}
            
            These are the requirements for the report: {requirements}
            
            This is the final report: {text}
            
            Grade the final report on a score of 1-10 and give reasons for your score. Your score should
            include the report's structure, the report's depth and how well the report is written.
            Be critical but fair. Share why the result didn't score 10, or what went well and didn't.
            
            Use the tool to return the final result.
            """
        )
        # res[report_name] = result
        res['score'][report_name] = result.tool_calls[-1]['args']['score']
        res['reason'][report_name] = result.tool_calls[-1]['args']['reason_for_score']
```

This setup uses Pydantic’s BaseModel abstractions to inform the LLM of the expected response schema. Let’s see how the reports measure up:

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(res)
df.head()
```

👉 And the verdict? The reports were **comparable across all setups**. Surprisingly, the **solo deep agent** edged out with a 9/10, while the others scored solid 8/10s.

### Thinking of what we just did

Despite the big differences in tokens and runtime, the report quality didn’t improve proportionally. Sometimes, “more depth” just means more overhead.

The deep agent setup shows that multi-agent systems still matter, since complex tasks often require them. But latency will always be a trade-off.

So why not just use a single reasoning LLM instead?

Here’s my take:

-   **Separation of concerns** → Multi-agent systems naturally break tasks into smaller, specialized roles.
-   **Cost efficiency** → Reasoning LLMs use “reasoning tokens” on top of normal tokens, which drives costs up. In many cases, it’s cheaper to run multiple non-reasoning LLMs than one large reasoning model.

In our case, we used a mid-size reasoning LLM (gpt-oss:20b) as both the top-level agent and its sub-agents, while delegating RAG to a smaller reasoning LLM (qwen3:8b on Bento Cloud). That mix worked reasonably well…if speed of replies were not an issue.

But it’s worth noting: the “deep agent” isn’t a typical multi-agent system. It shines best when powered by strong reasoning LLMs — like [Anthropic’s Claude 4 Sonnet](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-4).

### **Closing Thoughts**

Classical defaults exist for a reason: they work. But hypermodern thinking isn’t about safety — it’s about the user on the other side of your app.

**Meet Sarah.** She asks a question about your company’s services and waits. Your Deep Agent, powered by Claude Sonnet 4, deliberates for 30 seconds before delivering a perfect answer. Sarah’s impressed — once. By her third query, she’s checking her phone. By her tenth, she’s switching tabs. _Intelligence that makes users wait isn’t intelligence at all. Users don’t want PhD-level reasoning — they want fast, reliable answers._

**Meet David.** He’s a financial analyst using your RAG chatbot to pull insights from regulatory documents. Your setup uses a typical PDF parser and everything is parsed as plain text. Flowcharts become gibberish, table headers are confused with body text, and nested structures vanish. After ten nonsensical responses, David abandons the system and reads the PDFs manually.

**Meet Alex.** He’s building an internal GenAI service. His tech stack demands a local LLM for data security, plus Kubernetes, Ansible and Terraform to serve a reasoning LLM and vector databases. Days turn into weeks wrestling with infrastructure. By the time the service is barely usable, the team has moved on. The “best practice” buried him in complexity.

Our hypermodern journey proved something essential: the best tools are the ones that actually work for everyone. If Alex struggles to build it, the architecture fails the developer. If David can’t get meaningful answers, the system fails the user. If Sarah abandons your app because it’s slow, sophistication fails the user.

_Hypermodern GenAI isn’t about rejecting proven patterns. It’s about finding the sweet spot: users get answers fast and reliably; developers ship without drowning in complexity; businesses don’t blow budgets on compute._

**Cook for everyone at the table, not just the cookbook. The best architecture is the one where all worlds win.**

body:
* * *

#### Part two of the “Building a Hypermodern GenAI App” series

In [Act One](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/would-you-like-an-llm-with-that-a-bento-cloud-drive-thru-7e70f77277d2) of this series, we served a Qwen3 8Bn reasoning LLM using the vLLM framework. We then extended its capabilities by spinning up and orchestrating replicas with Bento Cloud — all using just Python.

In a [previous article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/service-please-3-ways-to-serve-an-llm-ca5ead2547e6), I shared that vLLM is by far the most performant way to serve an LLM, thanks to its KV-caching capabilities. This allows for faster inferencing and higher concurrent request handling. However, all that speed would be wasted if the application gets inundated with high user traffic.

I only know some Kubernetes and have never coded Terraform or Ansible, so debugging across three different frameworks would take forever. Bento Cloud solved that problem by letting us code services in pure Python and easily serve them using a command-line interface.

With our LLM ready, we can now move on to building a generative AI application. Act Two begins here.

### The Hypermodern Twist on Retrieval Augmented Generation

Ask any data scientist what they’re building in 2023, and they’ll say “RAG.” Say you’re building a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) application today, and you might get a quizzical look. “Isn’t that a 10-minute thing?” they’ll ask.

Well, yes and no.

#### “Easy”?

Building a basic RAG application is indeed easy. But making it adequate for real-world use takes careful tuning. There are many hyperparameters to adjust — like how many chunks to retrieve from a vector database — and several methods to improve performance.

My friend [Jinkett A. Yee](https://medium.com/u/4298d8c06a21) explored this in his series ([article #1](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/building-evaluating-rag-has-never-been-easier-with-llama-index-45db211c3921), [article #2](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/part-ii-llama-index-rag-improvements-chainlit-workflows-d20205091d4f), [article #3](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/part-iii-lets-explore-llamaindex-events-workflows-and-agents-490584516c2d)) of RAG articles using LlamaIndex, while building a RAG service over the Harry Potter series. Some innovative approaches he shared include:

-   **Pre-retrieval processing methods**: Hypothetical Document Embeddings, Sub Question Query Decomposition, and condensing the question before retrieval.
-   **Enhanced retrieval methods**: Hybrid search using sparse and dense embeddings. Sparse embeddings ensure that retrieval also accounts for keywords in the query.
-   **Agentic methods:** Adding a reflection loop so that the agent reflects on the result of the RAG tool — and invoke it again if necessary.

> PS: I highly recommend reading Jinkett’s articles. They’re very thoughtfully crafted and entertaining to read. Of course, it also helps that I’m a huge fan of both LlamaIndex and Harry Potter.

Other methods exist as well — reranking, GraphRAG (which I covered in a [previous article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/graphrag-for-the-win-c19d580debd7)), etc. The effectiveness of each method depends on the documents and the types of questions users ask. In Jinkett’s case (and for any Harry Potter fan), it was crucial to retrieve and reason across multiple books and link episodes together.

Here’s the catch though: optimize your RAG “too much” and latency gets impacted. A slow chatbot application won’t be used by anyone.

A good RAG application is anything but easy.

#### “Quick”?

Yes, anyone can build a basic RAG application quickly. Building an advanced one, however, is a time-consuming process. At minimum, you’d need a vector database and an embedding model — plus additional neural models for things like sparse-dense hybrid search or reranking.

Many cookbooks abstract this away by spinning up every service with Docker and relying on API-based models from providers such as OpenAI’s text-embedding model. But in Act Two, we’re going to build an advanced RAG application even faster than “10 minutes” — and we’re going to do it with **no code**. Just like in Act One, we’re breaking away from these cookbook approaches.

…And then we’re going to interact with the application using code 😂— this is Act Two after all, and we still have one more Act to go.

All code is available in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/deep-agents-bento-llama-stack).

### Introducing Qdrant Cloud

Vector databases became hugely popular with generative AI in 2023, but Qdrant had already been around since 2021, leveraging vector similarity for unstructured objects. Despite the “similarity” across offerings from other vector database companies, Qdrant remains hugely popular and continues to lead with many firsts.

Qdrant was among the first to:

1.  Support [multimodal RAG](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/multimodal-search/),
2.  Support [gRPC connections](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/interfaces/) (even to local Docker instances),
3.  Improve sparse embeddings with their own [BM42 model](https://qdrant.tech/articles/bm42/), and
4.  Incorporate [maximum marginal relevance (MMR) capabilities](https://qdrant.tech/blog/qdrant-1.15.x/).

[A typical release note](https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/releases/tag/v1.15.0) looks chock full of features — and [CEO Andre Zayarni’s](https://www.linkedin.com/in/zayarni/) announcements on LinkedIn are often as entertaining as they are informative.

[Built on Rust](https://qdrant.tech/), Qdrant is also blazing fast.

And Qdrant is generous too. Beyond giving away free T-shirt swag on LinkedIn (I’m lucky to own two!), Qdrant also offers a generous free tier on Qdrant Cloud. Every user can spin up a cluster and get a dedicated vector database, backed by a 99.5% SLA — reliable enough to power real portfolio projects without constantly spinning Docker up and down.

And that’s exactly what we’ll do here. Head over to [Qdrant Cloud](https://cloud.qdrant.io/) and sign up for a free account. Then create your first cluster with the defaults — you should have a screenshot that looks like this:

> Note: Select the “API Keys” tab to get your personal Qdrant Cloud API key

Now we’re ready to upsert documents into the vector database and build our RAG application.

### Introducing Llama Cloud

LlamaIndex has been at the forefront of the LLM orchestration framework space for awhile and I’ve written a couple of articles about them.

In my [first article on LlamaIndex](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multiverse-part-3-llamaindex-798344050c49), I shared how LlamaIndex began as a supporting framework to LangChain, focused on retrieval and data indexing for RAG applications. Since then, it has evolved into a general-purpose LLM framework with strong agentic capabilities — and I think we’re much better off because of it. I’ve also [written about LlamaIndex Workflows](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multi-agent-multiverse-part-3a-llamaindex-workflows-c0f614c15b88) as a compelling alternative to LangGraph for orchestrating multi-agent systems, and about [deploying these workflows with **Llama Deploy**](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multi-agent-multiverse-part-3b-deploying-llamaindex-workflows-df18381d36b9), its open-source workflow deployment framework.

#### So how good is LlamaIndex at RAG?

[An experiment by tonicAI](https://www.tonic.ai/blog/rag-evaluation-series-validating-rag-performance-openai-vs-llamaindex) revealed that a basic RAG application using LlamaIndex alone (built using 5 lines of code) significantly outperformed a RAG application using the OpenAI Assistant, even though both were working with the same data sources. The key difference often lies in the quality of data indexing and retrieval: if retrieval is wrong, the LLM’s answer will be wrong too.

Although many advanced RAG techniques exist (and LlamaIndex is at the forefront of this), LlamaIndex has placed more focus on the quality of the **data parsed from documents**. If your documents are full of charts, diagrams, or tables, a typical parser will flatten everything into a single string. The LLM then loses the meaning encoded in positions and relationships — which are crucial in things like flowcharts and tables.

Can multimodal LLMs solve this? Not really. Without extra processing, they still treat everything as one long string.

Not so with LlamaIndex. Its **Llama Parse** is remarkably accurate — good enough to [“RAG” on a train schedule (which is only tables), flowcharts, or even mathematical equations](https://www.llamaindex.ai/blog/introducing-llamaparse-premium). And it’s not just a feature — Llama Parse comes with its own dedicated SDK as part of **Llama Cloud**.

#### A generous free tier

While Llama Parse isn’t open-sourced, it is available through an exceedingly generous free tier. Depending on your document, you can also choose the level of agentic intervention in Llama Parse for information extraction. The basic level (already better than OCR) consumes 3 Llama Cloud credits per page, while the most advanced level costs 90 credits per page.

Yet, every user gets **10k free credits every month**.

#### The Llama Runs: Other Llama Cloud Capabilities

Aside from Llama Parse, Llama Cloud also offers:

-   **Llama Extract** — a vast improvement over structured output parsing,
-   **Llama Cloud Index** — parses documents with Llama Parse, creates an advanced vector index for RAG, and stores it in the cloud,
-   **Llama Report** (coming soon) — generate detailed, insightful reports from multiple data sources. The Python SDK is already available, and once again, it’s a big leap beyond the current state of the art.

I’ve played with all of them, and I’m a huge fan

#### Creating our first Llama Cloud Index

Create your free account with [Llama Cloud](https://cloud.llamaindex.ai/) to get started!

At the home page, click the “create” button under “Index”:

Give your index a unique name (“qualified-stingray” doesn’t really mean anything) and upload your documents by drag and drop.

Next we’ll configure our data sink — which is our vector database. The default is “Managed” which means that Llama Cloud will spin up a vector database in the backend and manage it for us. I’m not sure what vector database LlamaIndex spins in the background, but I only want to use my favorite vector database — Qdrant 😂

So click “Configure Data Sink” and create your collection and key in your Qdrant Cloud API key and URL to your running Qdrant Cloud Cluster.

Once you’ve done this, select your configured data sink.

Next, you can simply leave the Embedding Model as is. You could also configure your own API key so that LlamaIndex will use your vendor to generate embeddings. Otherwise, LlamaIndex will use their OpenAI API key to get OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small model to generate the embeddings for us with no additional cost, and upsert them into Qdrant Cloud for us.

For the remaining options, I only selected “use-case oriented settings” to be “Scientific papers”, because I wanted to RAG a couple of interesting papers in the generative AI space. Under the hood this invokes Llama Parse’s most advanced settings — 90 credits per page.

Ready? Hit “Deploy Index”!

Tada done! For anyone keeping score, we’ve only taken up to two minutes at this point (including with Qdrant Cloud).

Select “Playground” in Llama Cloud and you have a RAG application!

#### Want to see your documents?

Click on “Cluster UI” on the Qdrant Cloud home page, and you’ll see that we have a collection ready of our documents upserted:

### But is our RAG advanced?

Yes it is. Under playground settings you can select the number of chunks to retrieve, number of results post re-ranking, and even add metadata filters to help your LLM more.

I’ve kept to the default — 30 chunks retrieved with 6 chunks reranked. The chatbot is blazing fast with references hyperlinked in the text. Click on any of those references like “1” and you’ll see the node referenced.

### Playing with Llama Cloud Index in code

Calling the index in code is just as simple — there are only a handful of lines.

```python
from llama_index.indices.managed.llama_cloud import LlamaCloudIndex
from dotenv import load_dotenv, find_dotenv
import os

_ = load_dotenv(find_dotenv())  # read local .env file

alita_index = LlamaCloudIndex(
  name="alita-index",
  project_name="Default",
  organization_id="bf9b425c-54cb-4182-a93f-8ac6aed04348",
  api_key=os.environ.get("LLAMA_CLOUD_API_KEY"),
)

# For retriever mode
# nodes = alita_index.as_retriever().retrieve(query)
```

Since we’re now outside the Llama Cloud environment, we’ll need to bring our own LLM. Let’s reuse our **Qwen3–8B vLLM model deployed on Bento Cloud from Act One**:

```python
from llama_index.llms.openai_like import OpenAILike
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

llm = OpenAILike(
    model="Qwen/Qwen3-8B",
    api_key=os.getenv("BENTO_CLOUD_API_KEY"),
    api_base=f'{os.getenv("qwen3_endpoint_url")}/v1',
    is_chat_model=True,
    is_function_calling_model=True,
    temperature=0,
    timeout=600,
)
alita_query_engine = alita_index.as_query_engine(llm=llm)
response = alita_query_engine.query(query)

display(Markdown(f"**Response:** {response}"))
```

> 👉 **Note:** LlamaIndex provides a lightweight OpenAILike wrapper for OpenAI-compatible LLMs that aren’t from OpenAI. They do this because OpenAI’s SDK changes frequently, and the official LlamaIndex OpenAI integration updates just as quickly — so separating them avoids breaking code.

We then wrap the LLM into a query engine and pass in our query. Done!

**Total time elapsed: ~2 minutes 30 seconds.**

> Make sure your Bento Cloud vLLM service is running before trying this.

### Composite Retrieval

What if you want to query across **multiple Llama Cloud indexes at once**?

The Python SDK supports this too. I created another index on Llama Cloud and tested composite retrieval.

```python
from llama_cloud import CompositeRetrievalMode
from llama_index.indices.managed.llama_cloud import (
    LlamaCloudCompositeRetriever,
)

retriever = LlamaCloudCompositeRetriever(
    name="Alita and MCP Zero Retriever",
    api_key=os.environ.get("LLAMA_CLOUD_API_KEY"),
    create_if_not_exists=True,
    mode=CompositeRetrievalMode.FULL,
    rerank_top_n=6,
)
retriever.add_index(
    alita_index, description="Knowledge base for the Alita paradigm for agents"
)
retriever.add_index(
    mcp_zero_index, description="Knowledge base of the (model context protocol) MCP zero paradigm"
)
```

This mounts multiple sub-indexes into a **single composite retriever**, allowing queries across them simultaneously.

⚡ Tip: write **meaningful descriptions** for each index — the retriever actually uses them to improve accuracy.

### Building a RAG Query Engine

With our retriever ready, we can assemble a **query engine** over it using LlamaIndex’s `RetrieverQueryEngine` abstraction:

```python
from llama_index.core import get_response_synthesizer
from llama_index.core.query_engine import RetrieverQueryEngine

response_synthesizer = get_response_synthesizer(llm=llm)

query_engine = RetrieverQueryEngine(
    retriever=retriever,
    response_synthesizer=response_synthesizer,
)

response = query_engine.query(
    "What is Alita and what is MCP Zero? Can Alita and MCP zero work together?"
)
```

Here, we also set up a `response_synthesizer`, which [controls how the LLM generates an answer from retrieved chunks](https://docs.llamaindex.ai/en/stable/module_guides/querying/response_synthesizers/). By default, LlamaIndex uses its standard synthesizer, but you can switch to more advanced modes:

-   **“refine”** → sequentially processes each retrieved chunk, refining the answer step by step.
-   **“tree summarize”** → recursively summarizes groups of chunks into a single final answer.
-   Or, define your **own custom synthesizer**.

### Deployment

One limitation of query engines: **they always perform retrieval** — even for trivial queries like “Hello.” That’s why RAG query engines aren’t usually deployed directly as standalone apps.

Instead, LlamaIndex allows query engines to be wrapped as QueryEngineTools, which can then be attached to agents. But in our case, we’ll avoid that path, because of what’s coming in **Act Three**.

We’ll instead deploy our indexes as **Model Context Protocol (MCP) services**. (I’ve covered MCPs in detail in a [previous article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/model-context-protocol-hype-or-necessity-998874d95bc6), so I won’t repeat that here.)

Here’s the setup:

```python
#index_mcp.py

import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv, find_dotenv

from fastmcp import FastMCP
from llama_index.indices.managed.llama_cloud import LlamaCloudIndex
from llama_index.llms.openai_like import OpenAILike

from typing import Annotated

_ = load_dotenv(find_dotenv())
LLAMA_CLOUD_API_KEY = os.environ['LLAMA_CLOUD_API_KEY']
kwargs = {
    'dense_similarity_top_k': 10,
    'sparse_similarity_top_k': 20,
    'enable_reranking': True,
    'alpha': 0.5,
    'rerank_top_n': 8
}
llm = OpenAILike(
    model="Qwen/Qwen3-8B",
    api_key=os.getenv("BENTO_CLOUD_API_KEY"),
    api_base=f'{os.getenv("qwen3_endpoint_url")}/v1',
    is_chat_model=True,
    is_function_calling_model=True,
    temperature=0,
    timeout=600,
)
mcp = FastMCP(
    name='Alita and MCP Zero Knowledge Base',
    port=8000,
    host="0.0.0.0",
)

@mcp.tool()
async def alita_documentation(
    query: Annotated[str, "The question to ask about the Alita framework in complete sentences."]
) -> str:
    """Use this tool to answer questions about the Alita framework"""
    alita_index = LlamaCloudIndex(
        name="alita-index",
        project_name="Default",
        organization_id="bf9b425c-54cb-4182-a93f-8ac6aed04348",
        api_key=LLAMA_CLOUD_API_KEY,
    )
    alita_engine = alita_index.as_query_engine(llm=llm, **kwargs)
    response = alita_engine.query(query + " Be verbose and exhaustive in your reply.")
    return str(response)

@mcp.tool()
async def mcp_zero_documentation(
    query: Annotated[str, "The question to ask about the MCP zero framework in complete sentences."]
) -> str:
    """Use this tool to answer questions about the MCP Zero framework"""
    mcp_zero_index = LlamaCloudIndex(
        name="mcp-zero-index",
        project_name="Default",
        organization_id="bf9b425c-54cb-4182-a93f-8ac6aed04348",
        api_key=LLAMA_CLOUD_API_KEY,
    )
    mcp_zero_engine = mcp_zero_index.as_query_engine(llm=llm, **kwargs)
    response = mcp_zero_engine.query(query + " Be verbose and exhaustive in your reply.")
    return str(response)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="streamable-http")
```

Notice we’ve deliberately kept the indexes separate instead of using composite retrieval. This way, the final agent decides which tool to use, rather than relying on a single router. That router would otherwise pick based on vector similarity between your question and each index description.

We’ve also introduced **extra keyword arguments** (kwargs) at the top to fine-tune query behavior, giving us tighter control over retrieval and reranking.

To spin up the service, just run `python index_mcp.py` and our MCP will be accessible on `http:localhost:8000/mcp`.

### Thinking about what we just did

Building an advanced RAG isn’t usually easy — but with Llama Cloud and Qdrant Cloud, it felt almost effortless. Through a few clicks, we created a baseline advanced RAG application, which we can further fine-tune by adjusting playground parameters in Llama Cloud. And this all leveraged Llama Cloud’s advanced agentic-level document parsing.

We deployed our RAG services as an MCP to add an extra layer of abstraction, preventing unnecessary retrieval tasks for questions like “Where is the nearest McDonald’s?” It also converts our RAG tools into reusable services for any agent written in any framework.

### Looking forward to Act Three

As Act Two concludes, it might feel like our “hypermodern” approach leans heavily on the cloud — almost like we’ve “cheated” in application development. Yet these cloud-powered applications are far more reliable than if we were building everything from scratch without ample time or resources.

More importantly, Act Two demonstrates the **power of orchestration and proper indexing**: by combining Llama Cloud’s parsing, Qdrant Cloud’s vector search, and MCP services, we can turn even complex knowledge bases into a queryable, responsive system in minutes rather than days.

The “clouding” across generative AI companies (as much as I love open-source non-commercial tools, I get that everyone needs to earn a living) makes this possible — and sometimes ridiculously easy.

In Act Three, we’ll take a different path. We’ll pursue an “unclouded” approach, developing and deploying an agentic service capable of answering questions from these knowledge bases — showing how much of this orchestration we can **bring in-house** while still keeping it fast and robust.

body:
* * *

#### Part one of the “Building a Hypermodern GenAI App” series

The generative AI space sometimes feels like a buffet – dozens of dishes that all taste suspiciously similar. By day, I’m using LangChain and my team’s go-to stack for LLMs, vector databases, and observability. By night, I use LlamaIndex and tinker with whatever shiny new toy catches my eye.

But here’s the thing: the deeper you go into these stacks, the more everything blends together. Read enough cookbooks and you’ll swear they were written by the same chef. _In the end, it’s the same sunny side egg plated differently — the logo on the apron doesn’t change the taste_

### Introducing Hypermodernity

Add “hyper” to a word and it usually sounds negative – like hyperactive (too active). But in chess, hypermodernism has a more subtle meaning.

Classical chess training teaches you to control the center squares early with pawn moves. The hypermodern school flips this on its head: you let your opponent occupy the center, then apply pressure on the center squares, turning these squares into attack targets.

That’s exactly the flavor of this article series: a hypermodern approach to building GenAI apps. We’ll cook with modern tools, but instead of following the usual recipes, we’ll season them differently – rethinking the playbook, and serving up something a little unexpected.

We’ll phase our development across three “acts.” This article focuses on **Act One**: deploying an open-sourced LLM on a close-sourced platform without spending a dime.

All codes are available in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/deep-agents-bento-llama-stack).

### Introducing Bento Cloud

In my [previous article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/service-please-3-ways-to-serve-an-llm-ca5ead2547e6), I introduced vLLM’s novel KV caching approach that sets it apart from other methods to serve an LLM — enabling it to perform up to 3x faster than Ollama while handling more concurrent requests. vLLM’s performance is out of this world. It’s likely adopted in the technology stack of many LLM vendors, even those serving open-sourced LLMs.

In that article, I demonstrated how to deploy a Llama 3.2 3Bn LLM with vLLM using a NVIDIA T4 GPU on a free-tier Google Colab runtime. Although successful, the approach of using one server wouldn’t work in production settings for apps with high user traffic. The sheer number of requests will cause performance issues, leaving many users waiting for the LLM’s response.

That’s why deploying a vLLM model is no mean feat. To handle high user traffic, deploying vLLM in production usually requires:

-   [Kubernetes](https://kubernetes.io/) for orchestration and load balancing across replicas.
-   [Terraform](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform) to spin up and tear down servers (to be used as replicas) by code
-   [Ansible](https://docs.ansible.com/) for configuration management of the servers spun up by Terraform

That’s where Bento Cloud comes in.

[Launched by BentoML in 2024](https://www.bentoml.com/blog/introducing-bentocloud), Bento Cloud extends the BentoML SDK with all the bells and whistles needed to get into production faster. With BentoML, you can wrap your application as a RESTful API, and it handles the hard parts like provisioning and autoscaling across replicas. It’s flexible too: deploy locally, on your own cloud, or straight to Bento Cloud — which is what we’ll do in this article.

For vLLM deployments, BentoML drastically lowers the production barrier. That’s why we’re exploring it here.

### Getting Started

Create a [free Bento Cloud account](https://cloud.bentoml.com/signup?_gl=1*1odthsa*_gcl_au*Mzc3NTUzNTYzLjE3NTUxMjUxMTE.) — new users get **$10 in free credits** for GPU servers.

Just remember: check the **$/hr rate** of each GPU type, and shut down deployments when not in use to stretch your credits.

The BentoML team have also kindly provided an [example repository](https://github.com/bentoml/BentoVLLM) with many different LLMs served on Bento Cloud using vLLM. We will be adapting the codes here to deploy a Qwen3:8bn reasoning LLM.

### What is a Bento? 🥡

A bento is the atomic unit of “stuff” in BentoML — like pods to Kubernetes and containers to Docker. Minimally, a bento comprises of a service, and a requirements.txt. Ours has a bit more:

### 🛎️ The Service

The service (or the “app”) contains the source code to be hosted on Bento cloud.

#### The Input ➡️

We’ll start by defining an input schema with **Pydantic’s** `**BaseModel**` to enforce strict type checking.

This schema will pass configuration options into BentoML, and most importantly, it’s what we’ll use to serve our vLLM model via `vllm serve`.

```python
# service.py

from __future__ import annotations

import logging, json, os, typing, collections.abc, contextlib, httpx
import pydantic, bentoml, fastapi
from starlette.responses import RedirectResponse

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

class BentoArgs(pydantic.BaseModel):
    tp: int = 1
    attn_backend: str = ‘FLASHINFER’
    skip_flashinfer: bool = False
    piecewise_cudagraph: bool = True
    reasoning_parser: str | None = None
    tool_parser: str | None = None
    max_model_len: int | None = None
    autotune: list[int] | None = None
    hf_system_prompt: str | None = None
    include_system_prompt: bool = True
    sharded: bool = False

    ##### Most Important Arguments ####
    name: str = ‘qwen3-8b’
    gpu_type: str = ‘nvidia-h100-80gb’
    model_id: str = ‘Qwen/Qwen3-8B’
    v1: bool = True
    hf_generation_config: dict[str, float | int] = pydantic.Field(
        default_factory=lambda: {‘repetition_penalty’: 1.0, ‘temperature’: 0.6, ‘top_p’: 0.9}
    )
    ####################################

    post: list[str] = pydantic.Field(default_factory=list)
    cli_args: list[str] = pydantic.Field(default_factory=list)
    envs: list[dict[str, str]] = pydantic.Field(default_factory=list)
    exclude: list[str] = pydantic.Field(default_factory=lambda: ['*.pth', '*.pt', 'original/**/*'])
    metadata: dict[str, typing.Any] = pydantic.Field(
        default_factory=lambda: {
          'description': 'Qwen3-8B',
          'provider': 'Qwen',
          'gpu_recommendation': 'an Nvidia GPU with at least 80GB VRAM (e.g about 1 H100 GPU).',
        }
    )
```

A few important points:

-   **v1=True** tells Bento to use vLLM v1 — which only runs on GPUs with compute capability ≥ 8.0 (e.g., NVIDIA H100). Note: Tesla T4s have a compute capability of 7.5.
-   **gpu\_type** (e.g., “nvidia-h100–80gb”) tells Bento Cloud which GPU to spin up.
-   **model\_id** points to the Hugging Face model you want to serve (e.g., “Qwen/Qwen3–8B”).

The other arguments have safe defaults — you only need to touch them if you want deeper customization.

#### The App ✨

```python
# service.py

bento_args = bentoml.use_arguments(BentoArgs)

image = (
    bentoml.images.Image(python_version='3.12')\
    .system_packages('curl', 'git')\
    .requirements_file('requirements.txt')
)
if POST := bento_args.post:
    for cmd in POST:
        image = image.run(cmd)
if not bento_args.skip_flashinfer:
    image = image.run(
        'uv pip install --no-progress https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128/flashinfer/flashinfer_python-0.2.6.post1%2Bcu128torch2.7-cp39-abi3-linux_x86_64.whl'
    )
hf = bentoml.models.HuggingFaceModel(bento_args.runtime_model_id, exclude=bento_args.exclude)
openai_api_app = fastapi.FastAPI()
```

We pass in the `BentoArgs` into the `bentoml` package and specify the base Python image (3.12) to use for this “bento”. We further tag the requirements.txt file from our folder so that BentoML can `pip install` from it in Bento Cloud at deployment.

Finally, we specify our `HuggingFaceModel` by parsing out the parameters in `BentoArgs` and specify our app — surprise! It’s a `FastAPI` app!

To mount it:

```python
# service.py

@bentoml.asgi_app(openai_api_app, path=’/v1')
@bentoml.service(
    name=bento_args.name,
    envs=[
        {‘name’: ‘UV_NO_PROGRESS’, ‘value’: ‘1'},
        {‘name’: ‘VLLM_SKIP_P2P_CHECK’, ‘value’: ‘1'},
        {‘name’: ‘VLLM_USE_V1', ‘value’: ‘1' if bento_args.v1 else ‘0'}, #delete this is compute capability of GPU <8.0
        {‘name’: ‘VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND’, ‘value’: bento_args.attn_backend},
        *bento_args.runtime_envs,
    ],
    image=image,
    labels={
        ‘owner’: ‘titus-lim',
        'type': 'prebuilt',
        'project': 'bentovllm',
        'openai_endpoint': '/v1',
        **bento_args.additional_labels,
    },
    traffic={'timeout': 300},
    endpoints={'livez': '/health', 'readyz': '/ping'},
    resources={'gpu': bento_args.tp, 'gpu_type': bento_args.gpu_type},
)
class LLM:
    hf = hf

    def __init__(self):
        self.stack = contextlib.AsyncExitStack()
        self.client = httpx.AsyncClient(base_url='http://0.0.0.0:3000/v1')
```

_In theory a_ **_Bento_** _is_ essentially a container (like Docker), but in Python it’s represented as a double decorated class:

-   `@bentoml.asgi_app` wires up the FastAPI app.
-   `@bentoml.service` defines deployment metadata (resources, envs, labels, etc.).
-   This is where we plug in our BentoArgs object to configure the service.

> Importantly, you must specify `/v1` in:

> 1\. The path of your `@bentoml.asgi_app` handler,

> 2\. As a value tagged to `openai_endpoint` under the labels parameter of your `@bentoml.service` handler,

> 3\. In the `base_url` parameter of `self.client` on initialization.

> This ensures compatibility out of the box with OpenAI, because OpenAI’s `base_url` (the URL we ping to interact with OpenAI LLMs) always has a path of `v1` . The typical vLLM app also serves it on v1.

#### Start up 🚀

Each class converted into a Bento must further define a few more methods including two decorated methods — `@bentoml.on_startup` and `@bentoml.on_shutdown` .

```python
# service.py

    @bentoml.on_startup
    async def init_engine(self):
        import vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server as vllm_api_server

        from vllm.utils import FlexibleArgumentParser
        from vllm.entrypoints.openai.cli_args import make_arg_parser

        args = make_arg_parser(FlexibleArgumentParser()).parse_args([
            '--no-use-tqdm-on-load',
            '--disable-uvicorn-access-log',
            '--disable-fastapi-docs',
            *bento_args.additional_cli_args,
        ])
        args.model = self.hf
        args.served_model_name = [bento_args.model_id]

        router = fastapi.APIRouter(lifespan=vllm_api_server.lifespan)
        OPENAI_ENDPOINTS = [
            ['/chat/completions', vllm_api_server.create_chat_completion, ['POST']],
            ["/responses", vllm_api_server.create_responses, ["POST"]],
            ['/models', vllm_api_server.show_available_models, ['GET']],
            ['/health', vllm_api_server.health, ['GET']],
            ['/ping', vllm_api_server.ping, ['GET']],
        ]

        for route, endpoint, methods in OPENAI_ENDPOINTS:
            router.add_api_route(path=route, endpoint=endpoint, methods=methods, include_in_schema=True)
        openai_api_app.include_router(router)

        self.engine = await self.stack.enter_async_context(vllm_api_server.build_async_engine_client(args))
        self.tokenizer = await self.engine.get_tokenizer()
        self.vllm_config = await self.engine.get_vllm_config()
        await vllm_api_server.init_app_state(self.engine, self.vllm_config, openai_api_app.state, args)
```

The `@bentoml.on_startup` hook spins up vLLM inside Bento’s lifecycle: it creates the engine, mounts the router, and injects state into the root app.

#### **A vLLM router? 📡**

This is where Bento’s philosophy matters: **BentoML requires a single root FastAPI/ASGI app to orchestrate lifecycle hooks, health probes, scaling rules, and logging**. That way, Bento can inject lifecycle hooks, health probes, traffic rules, and logging consistently across _all_ services.

But the `vLLM serve` command already spins up a full OpenAI API compatible FastAPI app on its own.

If we ran vLLM’s app directly inside Bento, we’d end up with _two root apps_ fighting for control — Bento’s and vLLM’s. That doesn’t work, because Bento needs to orchestrate _its_ app as the single entry point for deployment.

👉 The solution is to treat vLLM not as a full app, but as a **router**. We import its OpenAI-compatible endpoints and mount them onto Bento’s root app (`openai_api_app`). That way:

-   Bento still “owns” the top-level FastAPI app, satisfying its lifecycle contract.
-   vLLM still exposes its familiar /v1 OpenAI-compatible routes.
-   You get the best of both worlds: Bento handles deployment/lifecycle, while vLLM handles inference logic.

This is why you see `openai_api_app.include_router(router)` — we’re embedding vLLM into Bento’s app instead of letting it run separately.

The router defines a handful of **OpenAI-compatible endpoints** (completions, responses, models, health, ping).

Finally, we initialize the vLLM engine, tokenizer, and config, and bind them into the app’s state via `.init_app_state()`.

#### ⏻ Shut down

```python
# service.py

    @bentoml.on_shutdown
    async def teardown_engine(self):
        await self.stack.aclose()
```

Bento automatically calls this when scaling down or restarting replicas, ensuring vLLM shuts down cleanly.

#### Heartbeat ـــــــــــــــﮩ٨ـ❤️ﮩ٨ـﮩﮩ٨ـ

```python
# service.py

    async def __is_ready__(self) -> bool:
        resp = await self.client.get('/ping')
        return resp.status_code == 200

    async def __is_alive__(self) -> bool:
        resp = await self.client.get('/health')
        return resp.status_code == 200
```

Finally, we include heartbeat handlers to handle pings for healthchecks.

-   `__is_ready__` → readiness probe (can I serve traffic now?)
-   `__is_alive__` → liveness probe (is the process still healthy at all?)

### 📂️ The TOML and requirements file

The service does not need an `if__name__=="__main__":` block to spin up the application. BentoML services are launched via the bentoml command-line interface (CLI), rather than a traditional Python entrypoint.

-   The requirements.txt file specifies the packages needed for the service. BentoML will pip install from this file.
-   The pyproject.toml file can be a little confusing because pyproject.toml files are also used for pip installing packages. In BentoML’s case, the file specifies the input arguments to be injected into the `BentoArgs` class — which is then passed to the `@bentoml.service` decorated class.

The most important section in the pyproject.toml file is `[tool.bentoml.build.args]` where you define core runtime parameters:

```ini
[tool.bentoml.build.args]
name = "qwen3-8b"
gpu_type = "nvidia-h100-80gb"
tp = 1
autotune = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40]
max_model_len = 16548
model_id = "Qwen/Qwen3-8B"
reasoning_parser = "qwen3"
tool_parser = "hermes"
```

-   Be sure to specify the `model_id` parameter to match the model’s listing on HuggingFace exactly.
-   Since we’re serving Qwen3–8B, we also need to find the corresponding [tool parser](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/features/tool_calling.html) and [reasoning parser](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/v0.9.0/api/vllm/reasoning/qwen3_reasoning_parser.html) suggested (and written) by vLLM, or write them ourselves. These parsers define how the LLM interprets reasoning steps and tool calls — so picking the right one is crucial for correct behavior.
-   Use the `[max_model_len](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/6641)` parameter if you’re running into out of memory errors on your GPU — because some GPUs cannot fit an input context that is too long especially when running concurrent requests.
-   Finally, the `gpu_type` parameter is the default GPU that you want Bento Cloud to use for your service. Here we’ve gone big and requested an H100 GPU 😅

Another key section is `[tool.bentoml.build.args.hf_generation_config]` :

```ini
[tool.bentoml.build.args.hf_generation_config]
temperature = 0.6
top_k = 20
top_p = 0.95
presence_penalty = 1.5
```

Here, we specify the default arguments for our `LLM` class. This is to avoid any initialization errors right off the bat.

### The ".`bentoignore"` file 👻

This works just like .`dockerignore` or `.gitignore`: list the files you don’t want bundled when building your bento. (BentoML borrows many concepts from Docker, which makes it easy to pick up if you’ve used Docker before.)

* * *

### Spinning up our service 💫

In your command line, run:

```bash
 bentoml cloud login
```

BentoML will prompt you for your API key or to create one:

Once logged in, go to the folder and run:

```bash
bentoml deploy service:LLM
```

💥 Got an error? Yup, that’s because I asked for an NVIDIA H100 GPU… on the free tier. Classic champagne taste on a beer budget moment 😅

To see the list of GPU instances available, run:

Since I had only $10 credits, I went with an NVIDIA L4 GPU. Just for fun, I spun up three replicas instead of one:

```python
bentoml deploy service:LLM --instance-type "gpu.l4.1" --scaling-min 1 --scaling-max 3
```

> Why not deploy an even larger model? I tried to deploy the GPT-OSS 20B but received an error message stating that the model’s size (in GB) exceeded free-tier limits.

Note: Qwen3 is **not** a gated model on HuggingFace. If you are using a gated LLM, do create a HuggingFace API key secret first and pass it into your deploy service command:

```python
bentoml secret create huggingface HF_TOKEN=$HF_TOKEN
bentoml deploy service:LLM --instance-type "gpu.l4.1" --secret huggingface --scaling-min 1 --scaling-max 3
```

### Chatting with our LLM

Ready to take our LLM for a spin? Since our deployment is OpenAI API compatible, we can just use the OpenAI SDK directly!

```python
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv, find_dotenv
from openai import OpenAI

_ = load_dotenv(find_dotenv())

client = OpenAI(
    base_url=f'{os.getenv("qwen3_endpoint_url")}/v1', #add "/v1"
    api_key=os.getenv("BENTO_CLOUD_API_KEY"),
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="Qwen/Qwen3-8B",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
        {"role":"user", "content":"Explan what quantum computers are and how they work like I'm a 16-year-old."},
    ],
)
```

### Did we melt our GPUs?

Thankfully, BentoML has a collection of many useful dashboards to answer this question:

Can it go faster? Yes. With stronger GPUs that we don’t have access to. But this is already not bad at all.

### Thinking of what we just did

#### The speed to deployment perspective

We just deployed an open-sourced model on a closed-sourced platform in pure Python (yes, just one .py file) — and skipped the pain of resource prep, orchestration, and picking up new ops toys like Kubernetes, Terraform, or Ansible.

All that in under half a day’s work.

#### The performance perspective

vLLM is already very fast. Add robustness to your vLLM deployment and it’s chef’s kiss.

#### The cost perspective

Though we’re on the free tier, let’s stay real: GPUs aren’t cheap. The screenshot below shows BentoML’s hourly GPU rates.

Imagine using several NVIDIA B200s to host a Kimi K2 model (only 1 trillion parameters), and then spinning more NVIDIA B200s to serve as replicas. Poof — budget gone faster than free snacks at the office pantry.

In contrast, API calls to closed-sourced LLMs, and even open-sourced ones on vendors like AWS Bedrock are often cheaper under low traffic. I spent $1.75 total in Bento Cloud (yes, I deployed other models “for fun”), and it would’ve been even less if I’d just used OpenAI GPT models. Tokens are free in our case, but hardware isn’t — and your wallet will feel the pinch.

So under low traffic, paid APIs win on cost. But the value of the open-source path isn’t thriftiness — it’s control, customization, and data privacy. Think of it as the difference between renting a hotel room (convenient) and owning your house (painful, but it’s yours).

#### The monitoring perspective

BentoML gives slick dashboards, but they’re fully aggregated — so you can’t really tell who’s the office “GPU hog.” The fix? Add a [LiteLLM Proxy Server layer](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/simple_proxy) over BentoML and issue API keys per project or per team. Instant visibility, instant accountability. Plus you can add different rate limits per API key to be kind to your wallet.

🤩 Bonus: the same trick works on closed-sourced LLM deployments too.

> Do feel free to check out [my article on LiteLLM](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-litellm-649d48a0c2c7) for more details on how to setup the proxy server layer!

### In closing

We pulled off a solid vLLM deployment — all open source, all robust, and all without ever betraying Python. The secret sauce? A cheeky little hack, plus BentoML’s generosity with free credits. Honestly, the SDK makes Python feel like it comes with superpowers.

And this is just Act One. In Act Two of our hypermodern adventure, we’ll try the same stunt on a retrieval-augmented generation setup.

**_Spoiler Alert_**_: still Python, still fun, and still without spending a dime._

body:
* * *

#### Can we really do without prompts?

Ask anyone who’s used a generative AI app, and they’ll tell you: large language models (LLMs) can be inconsistent — sometimes returning wildly different answers to the exact same question. Ask anyone who builds these apps or trains the LLMs, and… you’ll hear the same story.

Prompt engineering emerged as a way to tame this unpredictability. The idea is simple: write instructions (prompts) that shape an LLM’s behavior toward a desired outcome before the LLM interacts with any user. In practice, though, getting this right can be a Herculean task. For example, Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.1 ships with a [**system prompt longer than 2,500 words**](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/release-notes/system-prompts#august-5-2025).

Worse still, a prompt that works beautifully for one LLM may fail spectacularly on another. This means prompt engineering will remain a moving target for as long as generative AI exists.

### Introducing DSPy

Enter **DSPy** — an ambitious open-source framework designed to shift the paradigm. Instead of painstakingly crafting prompts yourself, DSPy generates and tunes them for the LLM you’re using. Your role? Declare the desired outcome and code the workflow — DSPy takes care of the rest.

[First released in 2023, DSPy began as a research project in Databricks co-founder Matei Zaharia’s Stanford lab](https://www.databricks.com/blog/optimizing-databricks-llm-pipelines-dspy). It quickly gained traction and [found its way into Databricks’ production environment](https://www.databricks.com/blog/dspy-databricks), where it now powers modular LLM pipelines, automated prompt optimization, and seamless deployment via Databricks Model Serving and Vector Search.

I’ve used DSPy in several of my own project ideas, and in a [previous article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/hyde-and-seek-when-hallucination-leads-the-way-17a9800734fe) I showed how to integrate it with **LlamaIndex**’s vector retrieval strategies to boost the performance of Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) applications. This piece builds on that work — offering a more rounded introduction to DSPy and where it can fit into your GenAI stack, and ultimately my candid take on whether it’s something I reach for often.

All the example code in this article is available in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/dspy-playground/tree/main).

### Importing an LLM in DSPy

Like many modern LLM frameworks, DSPy uses **LiteLLM** under the hood to instantiate its LLM class. If you hit issues when calling a model, the [LiteLLM Python SDK documentation](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/#basic-usage) should be your first stop.

> For a deeper dive, I’ve also written a [separate article about LiteLLM’s framework and proxy server](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-litellm-649d48a0c2c7) — recommended if you want to understand how LiteLLM works behind the scenes.

```python
import dspy

lm = dspy.LM(
   "ollama_chat/gpt-oss:20b", 
   api_base="http://localhost:11434", 
   api_key="fake"
)
dspy.configure(lm=lm)
```

In this article, we’ll be using [**OpenAI’s new gpt-oss**](https://huggingface.co/blog/welcome-openai-gpt-oss) — generously open-sourced — and running it via **Ollama**. Much like many HuggingFace models, Ollama makes it easy to call this LLM locally.

By setting the `dspy.configure` argument, we tell DSPy to use our defined language model for all operations unless specified otherwise. That means you only define it once for your entire workflow.

To invoke the LLM directly, just pass a list of messages in **OpenAI-compatible** format — a list of dictionaries, each with a role and content key:

```python
lm(
 messages=[
  {"role": "user", 
   "content": "Hi! How many 'r's are there in strawberry?"}
 ]
)
```

### Can I get your signature please?

Signatures are at the heart of DSPy’s design. They’re your **declaration of how you want the LLM to behave**, and they’re one of the most distinctive features I’ve seen in any LLM framework.

Let’s start by loading a document:

```python
from llama_index.core import SimpleDirectoryReader
# import os

# if not os.path.exists("../docs"):
#    os.makedirs("../docs")

# !wget https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.20286 -O "../docs/alita_paper.pdf"

docs = SimpleDirectoryReader("../docs").load_data()
doc_text = "\n\n".join([d.get_content() for d in docs])
```

Now let’s tell the LLM to summarize the entire document:

```python
summarize = dspy.ChainOfThought("full_document -> summary")
response = summarize(full_document=doc_text)
```

Here:

-   The **signature** is `ChainOfThought` — one of DSPy’s built-in signatures that prompts the LLM to **think sequentially** when generating its answer.
-   The string `“full_document -> summary”` declares what input to expect and what output to produce.
-   This “arrow” syntax is incredibly convenient — you describe your I/O in one line, and DSPy handles the rest.

#### Utilizing GPT-OSS’ context window without a vector DB

Since **gpt-oss** has a 128k token context window, we can read in an entire document without chunking it into a vector database — and still ask questions about it:

```python
zero_vector_db = dspy.Predict(
    dspy.Signature(
        'document: str, question: str -> answer: str',
        instructions='Only use the document to answer the question and nothing else.'
    )
)

question = 'How does ALITA help LLMs to achieve autonomous reasoning?'
response = zero_vector_db(question=question, document=doc_text)
```

> **Tip:** If you have multiple inputs or outputs, separate them with a comma. DSPy also supports **type annotations** inside the signature.

In this example, I’ve added an extra instructions line (optional) because gpt-oss is a strong model — I didn’t want it to answer without actually using the document.

So…what prompt is our LLM using? Just run:

```python
dspy.inspect_history()
```

The system message will show the **auto-generated prompt** DSPy built from our signature. Scroll further and you’ll see the user message, which includes both the question and the full document. (My screenshot is truncated for brevity.)

### Coding Custom Signatures for a DSPy Workflow

DSPy doesn’t limit you to strings with arrows — you can fully code out signatures. Let’s build an **advanced RAG pipeline** with **question rewriting** and **decomposition**. We’ll use LlamaIndex’s vector retrieval capabilities and DSPy for the rest.

First, create our vector index in **LlamaIndex**:

```python
from llama_index.core import VectorStoreIndex, Settings
from llama_index.embeddings.ollama import OllamaEmbedding

Settings.embed_model = OllamaEmbedding(model_name="nomic-embed-text")

index = VectorStoreIndex(docs, embed_model=Settings.embed_model)

base_retriever = index.as_retriever(similarity_top_k=6)
```

Now define our DSPy signatures:

```python
from tqdm.notebook import tqdm

class GenerateAnswer(dspy.Signature):
    """Answer questions with short factoid answers."""
    context = dspy.InputField(desc="May contain relevant facts")
    question = dspy.InputField()
    answer = dspy.OutputField(desc="Often between 1-10 sentences.")

class RewriteQuestion(dspy.Signature):
    question = dspy.InputField()
    rewritten_questions: list[str] = dspy.OutputField(
        desc="Decompose this question into sub questions or rewrite the original user question if necessary to improve retrieval from a vector database. Otherwise return the original question."
    )
```

Any custom signature must:

-   Inherit from `dspy.Signature`
-   Use `dspy.InputField` for inputs
-   Use `dspy.OutputField` for outputs

Here, `GenerateAnswer` is the signature for the **intermediate step**, while `RewriteQuestion` is the **first step** for decomposing or rewriting the query. DSPy won’t automatically know the sequence — so we instrument that in a **workflow module**.

#### Creating our DSPy workflow (PyTorch Style):

All DSPy workflows must:

-   Inherits from `dspy.Module`
-   Define a `forward` method (just like PyTorch). This is required by DSPy.

```python
class RAG(dspy.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.retriever = base_retriever
        self.rewriter = dspy.Predict(RewriteQuestion)
        self.generate_answer = dspy.ChainOfThought(GenerateAnswer)
        self.consolidate_answer = dspy.Predict(
            dspy.Signature(
                'original_question: str, sub_answers: list[str] -> consolidated_answer:str',
                instructions="Consolidate the sub answers into a coherent answer within a few paragraphs that answers the original question."
            )
        )
        
    def query_rewrite(self, question: str):
        return self.rewriter(question=question)
    
    def forward(self, question: str):
        question_rewrite = self.query_rewrite(question)
        sub_answers = []
        for q in tqdm(question_rewrite.rewritten_questions):
            print(f"\n----\nProcessing question: {q}")            
            context = self.retriever.retrieve(q) #the LlamaIndex component
            sub_answer = self.generate_answer(context=context, question=q)
            print(f"\nAnswer to {q}: {sub_answer}")
            print(f"\nSub question answer reasoning: {sub_answer.reasoning}\n----\n")
            sub_answers.append(sub_answer)
        prediction = self.consolidate_answer(original_question=question, sub_answers=sub_answers)
        return prediction
```

The constructor defines:

-   **Retriever**: LlamaIndex retriever
-   **Rewriter**: `RewriteQuestion` signature
-   **Answer generator**: `GenerateAnswer` signature
-   **Answer consolidator**: String-based signature for merging sub-answers

In our forward method:

-   The workflow starts by breaking the original query into a list of sub-queries.
-   Each sub-query is sent to the vector database for retrieval, and the results are passed to the LLM to generate an answer for that sub-query.
-   These answers are collected in a sub\_answers list, and finally, the LLM consolidates them into a single, coherent answer to the original question.

One of the neat features DSPy offers is the `.reasoning` attribute, which exposes the LLM’s internal thought process for any tool call. I took advantage of this to print out exactly how OpenAI’s shiny new open-source LLM was reasoning through each step in the forward method.

To stress-test the setup, I fed it a deliberately messy, multi-question prompt in broken English (Singlish):

```python
engine = RAG()
pred = engine(
    """How Agent become autonomous with Atila? 
    Alita use Model context protocol? 
    It write own tools? Tools deploy where?"""
)
```
