body:
* * *

The generative AI space has mushroomed by leaps and bounds since [ChatGPT’s launch on 30 Nov 2022](https://www.forbes.com/sites/bernardmarr/2023/05/19/a-short-history-of-chatgpt-how-we-got-to-where-we-are-today/). Today, there are not only more LLM service providers — but also an exciting number of open-source models that match or even outperform their closed-source counterparts.

Using a closed-source LLM has clear benefits: you get a state-of-the-art model **and** outsource the heavy lifting of serving it to the provider. For example, using a massive model like DeepSeek’s 671B is far simpler via API — because realistically, one GPU just won’t cut it.

But what if you want to serve your own LLM —that is, host it and expose it as a REST API endpoint?

First, you need to **download** the model — which can be tedious or even unmanageable depending on your storage and bandwidth. Then, you’ll need to provision enough **compute and memory** to handle multiple concurrent requests smoothly. Finally, you have to ensure that your serving of the model is OpenAI API–compatible, or you’ll have to adapt or rewrite parts of LLM frameworks to orchestrate your generative AI application.

So… why would anyone _want_ to go through all that?

A fair question. Here are some good reasons:

#### 1\. Reliability

LLM providers like OpenAI and Anthropic impose rate limits per API key (e.g., requests per minute) to maintain fairness and stability. If your app serves many users via a single key, some requests may be delayed — not due to bugs, but because you’ve hit your quota. Running your own LLM removes this bottleneck.

#### 2\. Security

Industries like healthcare and finance operate under strict data protection regulations. Sending sensitive data to a third-party LLM provider may be unacceptable or even illegal. In such cases, serving your own LLM — within your network — is the only viable way to leverage generative AI while staying compliant.

#### 3\. Finetuning

An extension of the points above: sometimes, you need to finetune an LLM on highly sensitive data — like proprietary knowledge that forms the “secret sauce” of your business. In such cases, keeping the entire workflow local is not just ideal — it’s essential.

### LLMs served — 3 ways

There are many ways to serve an LLM — just like there are countless ways to cook eggs 🍳. In this article, I’ll walk through **three ways I’ve personally tried** to serve an LLM — using my trusty personal MacBook. Each one offers a different balance of **simplicity**, **flexibility**, and **performance**, all with OpenAI API compatible services.

All codes can be found in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/OysterShell).

### 1\. My personal favorite — Ollama 🦙

Ollama was founded in [the winter 2021 batch](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/ollama) of the illustrious [Y Combinator program](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/ollama). Its aim was to allow all users to serve open-sourced LLMs on their local machines easily.

And the community clearly loves it — [Ollama’s GitHub repo](https://github.com/ollama/ollama) has a jaw-dropping **147k stars**. For comparison:

-   Hugging Face Transformers: also 147k
-   LangChain: 112k
-   PyTorch: 91.6k
-   FastAPI: 87.5k

It’s my personal favorite because it’s **fast, local, and dead simple** to use.

To get started:

1.  Install Ollama following their [instructions](https://ollama.com/download).
2.  Open your terminal and run:

```bash
ollama pull qwen3
```

This will download a Qwen 3 8Bn model — a reasoning LLM! You can browse the official [Ollama model library](https://ollama.com/search) for available choices.

Now, you might notice Ollama’s model selection feels limited compared to Hugging Face. But here’s a cool surprise: **you can also run Hugging Face models in Ollama**, as long as they support the gguf format.

On Hugging Face, click **“Use this model”** on the right panel — if the model is Ollama-compatible, you’ll see an Ollama icon and instructions to pull it directly.

In fact, here’s an example using my own fine-tuned LLM from a past article — pulled straight from Hugging Face and served via Ollama!

Even better: you **don’t need to run** `**ollama serve**` **manually**. Once pulled, any model is automatically available as a REST API at `http://localhost:11434` as long as Ollama is running in the background!

#### Invoking Ollama

In my opinion, the coolest way to invoke the Ollama service is this:

```python
from openai import OpenAI

ollama_url = "http://localhost:11434/v1/"
ollama_llm = "qwen3"

ollama_client = OpenAI(base_url=ollama_url, api_key="fake")

response = ollama_client.chat.completions.create(
    model=ollama_llm, 
    messages = [
        {"role": "user", "content": prompt}
    ]
)

display(Markdown(response.choices[0].message.content))
```

Yes! Our Ollama LLM is suddenly looks like an OpenAI model. 🎉

Thanks to Ollama’s API compatibility with OpenAI, it’s super easy to drop it into existing OpenAI-based workflows.

That said, given how quickly the official OpenAI Python SDK evolves — such as introducing the new`[responses](https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/responses)` [endpoint](https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/responses) and [deprecating support for the](https://community.openai.com/t/completion-models-are-now-considered-legacy/656302) `[completion](https://community.openai.com/t/completion-models-are-now-considered-legacy/656302)` [endpoint](https://community.openai.com/t/completion-models-are-now-considered-legacy/656302) — this approach might eventually break. Fortunately, Ollama provides its own dedicated Python SDK:

```python
from ollama import chat, ChatResponse

response: ChatResponse = chat(
    model=ollama_llm, 
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": prompt}
    ]
  )

print(response['message']['content'])
```

Given Ollama’s massive popularity, there are many dedicated integrations with many LLM orchestration frameworks. In LangChain, use the`ChatOllama` abstraction from the `langchain_ollama` package. For LlamaIndex, use the`Ollama` abstraction from the `llama-index-llms-ollama` extension. Both work smoothly out of the box.

#### Something Strange (and Cool)

If you poke around Ollama’s GitHub repo, you might notice something unexpected:

**The majority of the Ollama framework is written in Go!** 🧠

That’s pretty cool — especially since Go is often cited as being up [to 100 times faster than Python](https://medium.com/@dmytro.misik/go-vs-python-web-service-performance-1e5c16dbde76)! Ollama’s inferencing is also built on top of llama.cpp (“C Plus Plus”), which is yet another programming language that runs faster than Python.

### 2\. The new, cool way — Docker 🐳

Ollama’s clean syntax instantly reminded me of Docker — and to my pleasant surprise, I discovered that Ollama was founded by two ex-Docker engineers! Even more unexpectedly, not long after I connected the dots, Docker itself [announced native support for model serving via the Docker engine](https://www.docker.com/blog/introducing-docker-model-runner/). Coincidence? Maybe. Cool? Definitely.

**Docker’s model engine is gaining traction quickly**, extending from Mac to now supporting Windows and Linux. The best part? You don’t need to install anything extra — just update Docker Desktop and it’s ready to go.

To enable the model engine via CLI:

```bash
docker desktop enable model-runner --tcp=12434
```

#### Eerily similar to Ollama

The command above enables the model-runner feature and exposes pulled models at [http://localhost:12434](http://localhost:12434,) — very similar to how Ollama works.

The rest of Docker’s syntax also feels suspiciously Ollama-like. To pull a model:

```bash
docker model pull ai/qwen3:8B-Q4_0
```

To invoke it with the OpenAI Python SDK:

```python
docker_url = "http://localhost:12434/engines/v1"
docker_llm = "ai/qwen3:8B-Q4_0"
docker_client = OpenAI(base_url=docker_url, api_key="fake")

prompt = "Why is the sky blue?"
response = docker_client.chat.completions.create(
    model=docker_llm,
    messages = [
        {"role": "user", "content": prompt}
    ]
)
```

And yes — if you peek into [Docker Model Runner’s GitHub repo](https://github.com/docker/model-runner) (which only has 38 stars), you’ll see the bulk of it is also written in Go, just like Ollama.

Like Ollama, Docker’s Model Engine includes an inferencing component built on top of llama.cpp! Both Docker and Ollama support CUDA, CPU, and MPS for LLM serving — though I’d strongly advise against trying this on CPU… unless you’re working on becoming a more patient human being.

#### Differences with Ollama

Docker doesn’t yet have a dedicated Python SDK. That means you’ll need to rely on OpenAI-compatible clients like LangChain’s `ChatOpenAI`. But this comes with a catch — if OpenAI ever changes its SDK, Docker integrations could break.

**LlamaIndex has an existing solution.**

You can use the `OpenAILike` wrapper, a drop-in replacement for OpenAI-style-like models that aren’t by OpenAI:

```python
from llama_index.llms.openai_like import OpenAILike

llm = OpenAILike(
    model = docker_llm,
    api_base = docker_url,
    api_key = "fake",
    is_chat_model = True,
    is_function_calling_model = True,
    temperature = 0
)

response = llm.complete("Hi!")

display(Markdown(str(response)))
```

There’s one more caveat — Docker Model Runner only supports models from Docker Model Hub for now, not HuggingFace. And yes, the selection is still quite limited.

#### So… Why even use Docker model runner?

Here’s the key idea: use Docker to serve LLMs _without_ needing to embed Ollama inside your container. With Docker Model Runner, you can define LLM services directly inside docker-compose.yml, no extra setup needed.

Here’s a sample Docker compose file from [Docker’s documentation](https://docs.docker.com/ai/compose/models-and-compose/) (PS: use docker-compose 2.38 and above).

```yaml
services:
  chat-app:
    image: my-chat-app
    models:
      - llm

models:
  llm:
    model: ai/smollm2
```

### 3\. The “enterprise” way — vLLM ️🖖

You might think the story ends here — what more could there be to say?

But despite the ease of use and slick performance of tools like Ollama and Docker Model Runner, I can say with confidence: **almost no enterprise serves their LLMs using either tool 🤣.**

**vLLM is just that good.**

[Launched on 20 June 2023](https://blog.vllm.ai/2023/06/20/vllm.html), vLLM entered the scene with a key innovation: **PagedAttention.** It solves a big problem: GPUs often waste a lot of memory trying to save everything in one go.

#### 🚧 How Traditional Memory Storage Works:

-   When a model processes input, it generates “key” and “value” data for each token.
-   These are stored continuously in GPU memory (right next to each other), which is inefficient — imagine reserving a full bookshelf when you only need one shelf.
-   This causes gaps (wasted space) and limits how many things the model can handle at once. Traditional systems waste up to 60%–80% of the memory just storing these key-value pairs.

#### ⚙️ How PagedAttention Fixes It:

-   Instead of a big contiguous memory block, PagedAttention splits the memory into **fixed-size chunks**, or “pages” (like pages in a book).
-   These pages can be stored anywhere in memory — not in one big contiguous block.
-   When the model needs to retrieve data to generate text, it only loads the **necessary pages —** the PagedAttention kernel efficiently identifies and fetches the required blocks.
-   This saves memory and lets GPU space be used more efficiently. In fact, vLLM reports that typical memory waste drops to **below 4%**!

The result? Better batching, higher GPU utilization, and dramatically improved **throughput**.

And I’m not exaggerating — when serving the same LLM, [**vLLM has been benchmarked to be up to 3× faster than Ollama**, while being able to handle more concurrent requests](https://robert-mcdermott.medium.com/performance-vs-practicality-a-comparison-of-vllm-and-ollama-104acad250fd). Even more impressive: **the majority of vLLM’s codebase is written in Python (not Go)**!

Born out of UC Berkeley’s Sky Computing Lab, vLLM is now maintained by the open-source community and has earned over **52k GitHub stars**.

🚨 One downside: **vLLM is CUDA-first**. It doesn’t support MPS (so no MacBooks), and CPU performance is minimal. You’ll need access to a GPU (like Colab’s free ones) to make it shine — and that’s what we’re going to do in our code!

#### Using vLLM on Colab to serve our own LLM

_I found this_ [_really great cookbook_](https://medium.com/@hakimnaufal/trying-out-vllm-deepseek-r1-in-google-colab-a-quick-guide-a4fe682b8665) _and adapted it in the following code segments._

🔧 **Setup tip**: When starting your Google Colab session, make sure to select a **T4 GPU** from the runtime settings.

Let’s begin by installing the required libraries:

```python
!pip install -qU pyngrok vllm huggingface-hub
```

You can check your GPU usage with:

You should see something like 0MiB / 15360MiB if nothing has been loaded into the GPU yet.

#### Step 1: Choose and Authenticate for the LLM

We’ll serve **Llama 3.2–3B Instruct**, a gated model by Meta – it’s the largest model I could serve on a free tier Colab instance. Since it’s gated, you’ll need to [request access](https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) and authenticate with Hugging Face:

```python
from huggingface-hub import login
login()
```

#### Step 2: Serve the LLM with vllm

According to vLLM’s docs, you can serve any LLM on HuggingFace Hub using a simple CLI:

```bash
vllm serve <model_name>
```

This runs a REST API on port 8000.

💥 **But here’s the catch**: That gives you basic chat capabilities — but no tool use yet!

**To run everything from Colab (instead of your local CLI), we’ll use Python’s subprocess module to invoke the server with the correct flags:**

```python
!wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vllm-project/vllm/refs/heads/main/examples/tool_chat_template_llama3.1_json.jinja

import subprocess
model = 'meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct'

# Start vllm server in the background. The default hosting url is http://localhost:8000
vllm_process = subprocess.Popen([
    'vllm',
    'serve',  # Subcommand must follow vllm
    model,
    '--enable-auto-tool-choice',
    '--port', '8000',
    '--tool-call-parser', 'llama3_json',
    '--api-key', 'token-abc123',
    '--chat-template', 'tool_chat_template_llama3.1_json.jinja',
    '--trust-remote-code',
    '--max-model-len', '16548', #reducing the max model length because it exceeded the KV cache limit
], stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE, start_new_session=True)
```

**Why so many flags? 🤔**

To enable **tool calling**, just setting — enable-auto-tool-choice isn’t enough. You also need to specify:

-   The **chat template** (`--chat-template`)
-   The **tool call parser** (`--tool-call-parser`)

That’s why we used `wget` to grab the correct Jinja template from GitHub.

You might wonder: _Why does vLLM require you to set these explicitly? Shouldn’t it know which template to use based on the model?_

Well, vLLM was designed to be flexible. It lets developers experiment with custom chat templates and parsers to optimize how tool calling works — especially since different models behave differently with the same tools.

We also:

-   Set our own `api-key`
-   Used `trust-remote-code`, which is needed for some HuggingFace-hosted models
-   Tuned `max-model-len` to avoid out-of-memory crashes caused by exceeding the KV cache

These are all part of getting the server to run smoothly.

**What’s** `**start_new_session=True**` **for?**

By default, subprocesses in Python inherit the same process group as the parent (your Colab notebook, in this case). Setting `start_new_session=True` ensures the server process runs in a _new_ session, which makes it easier to manage independently — like stopping it later without affecting the notebook. Think of it like launching a new terminal tab that doesn’t share context with the old one.

We then define some utility functions to monitor the subprocess. This lets us view the stdout and stderr logs in real time — which is how I figured out the exact flags needed earlier!

```python
import requests
import time
from typing import Tuple
import sys

def check_vllm_status(url: str = "http://localhost:8000/health") -> bool:
    """Check if VLLM server is running and healthy."""
    try:
        response = requests.get(url)
        return response.status_code == 200
    except requests.exceptions.ConnectionError:
        return False

def monitor_vllm_process(vllm_process: subprocess.Popen, check_interval: int = 5) -> Tuple[bool, str, str]:
    """
    Monitor VLLM process and return status, stdout, and stderr.
    Returns: (success, stdout, stderr)
    """
    print("Starting VLLM server monitoring...")

    while vllm_process.poll() is None:  # While process is still running
        if check_vllm_status():
            print("✓ VLLM server is up and running!")
            return True, "", ""

        print("Waiting for VLLM server to start...")
        time.sleep(check_interval)

        # Check if there's any output to display
        if vllm_process.stdout.readable():
            stdout = vllm_process.stdout.read1().decode('utf-8')
            if stdout:
                print("STDOUT:", stdout)

        if vllm_process.stderr.readable():
            stderr = vllm_process.stderr.read1().decode('utf-8')
            if stderr:
                print("STDERR:", stderr)

    # If we get here, the process has ended
    stdout, stderr = vllm_process.communicate()
    return False, stdout.decode('utf-8'), stderr.decode('utf-8')
```

Finally, we invoke the monitor and gracefully handle failure or user interruption:

```python
try:
    success, stdout, stderr = monitor_vllm_process(vllm_process)

    if not success:
        print("\n❌ VLLM server failed to start!")
        print("\nFull STDOUT:", stdout)
        print("\nFull STDERR:", stderr)
        sys.exit(1)

except KeyboardInterrupt:
    print("\n⚠️ Monitoring interrupted by user")
    # # This should just exited the process of probing, not the vllm, if you want it then you coul uncomment this.
    # vllm_process.terminate()
    # try:
    #     vllm_process.wait(timeout=5)
    # except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
    #     vllm_process.kill()

    stdout, stderr = vllm_process.communicate()
    if stdout: print("\nFinal STDOUT:", stdout.decode('utf-8'))
    if stderr: print("\nFinal STDERR:", stderr.decode('utf-8'))
    sys.exit(0)
```

Give it some time, and you should see something like this:

But here’s a shocking twist:

Even _before_ running the LLM, vLLM has already consumed over **12GB** of our **15GB** GPU memory! 😱

That’s because **vLLM reserves 90% of GPU memory by default** — you’ll need to control this using the`--gpu-memory-utilization` flag when serving your LLM.

> ⚠️ Be careful: allocating too little GPU memory can cause **out-of-memory errors** during inference.

#### Step 3: Accessing our LLM from a public URL

Now, I wanted to call my vLLM service from my **local Jupyter Notebook**, rather than from the default localhost:8000 port on my running Colab instance.

> If you try opening localhost:8000 in your Chrome browser while using Colab, you’ll see… nothing. That’s because Colab’s localhost isn’t your machine’s localhost.

#### **Step 3a: Authorize ngrok**

So, I signed up for a **free** [**ngrok**](https://ngrok.com/) **account**, grabbed my `ngrok_auth_token`, and used it to create a **public proxy URL** that forwards traffic to Colab’s localhost:8000.

```python
!ngrok config add-authtoken {ngrok_auth_token}
```

#### Step 3b: Expose your local vLLM server

```python
from pyngrok import ngrok

port = 8000
# Open a ngrok tunnel to the HTTP server
public_url = ngrok.connect(port).public_url
print(f" * ngrok tunnel \"{public_url}\" -> \"http://127.0.0.1:{port}\"")
```

```python-repl
* ngrok tunnel "https://9398efd88ee3.ngrok-free.app" -> "http://127.0.0.1:8000"
```

🎉 You now have a **free public URL** to access your Colab-based vLLM server from **anywhere**!

To test that your vLLM deployment is working, visit your public ngrok URL and append /docs to it — this brings up Swagger UI for vLLM’s OpenAI-compatible API.

#### Step 4: Use our vLLM deployment!

Like Ollama and Docker, we can use the OpenAI Python SDK to invoke our LLM deployment.

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://9398efd88ee3.ngrok-free.app/v1",
    api_key="token-abc123",
)

completion = client.chat.completions.create(
  model="meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct",
  messages=[
    {"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}
  ]
)

print(completion.choices[0].message)
```

When using LangChain, we can simply use LangChain’s `ChatOpenAI`

```python
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

def add(a: int | float, b: int | float) -> str:
    """Use this tool to add two integers or floats."""
    return a+b

llm_openai = ChatOpenAI(
    model="meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct",
    temperature=0,
    api_key="token-abc123",
    base_url="https://9398efd88ee3.ngrok-free.app/v1",
)
openai_agent = create_react_agent(llm_openai, tools=[add])
async for chunk in openai_agent.astream(
    {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "what is 7+21?"}]},
    stream_mode="updates"
):
    print(chunk)
```

> ⚠️ **Heads-up:** You might see VLLMOpenAI class in LangChain and think it’s tailor-made for this setup — but it doesn’t support tool binding. Stick with ChatOpenAI if you’re planning to use tools.

If you’re using LlamaIndex, go with the `OpenAILike` abstraction.

Also worth noting: vLLM exposes a native Python SDK (from vllm import LLM), but that’s meant for direct development or offline batch inference — not for serving behind an API. Similarly, both the`llama-index-llms-vllm` and `langchain-community-llms-vllm` are designed for that offline mode.

#### Step 5: Clean up

Don’t just close your Colab notebook! To stop your vLLM process, run:

```python
vllm_process.terminate()
vllm_process.wait()
```

Now you can disconnect your GPU runtime and close your notebook.

### Concluding thoughts

We explored three ways to serve your own LLM — Ollama, Docker, and vLLM. All three are popular in the open-source community, and while Docker Model Runner is relatively new, its adoption is likely to grow rapidly given Docker’s central role in DevOps.

**vLLM stands out for its exceptional performance** — it’s incredibly fast and handles concurrent requests efficiently. I believe many hosted LLM providers like [Fireworks AI](https://fireworks.ai/), [Together AI](https://www.together.ai/), and others use vLLM as part of their tech stack to serve open-source models. Even some proprietary LLM providers may be leveraging vLLM internally, especially when paired with specialized hardware like [Groq](https://groq.com/) or [SambaNova](https://sambanova.ai/).

At this point, I’m not aware of any other open-source framework that matches **vLLM’s performance at scale**. Its ability to optimize memory and throughput is genuinely impressive.

But vLLM isn’t perfect. You’ll often find yourself wrestling with complex CLI flags, tweaking chat templates and tool parsers to get things working just right — only to encounter brittle bugs, especially when swapping in newer, better models as they’re released.

That’s where Ollama and Docker shine. They offer a developer-friendly, fuss-free setup that’s _ridiculously_ easy to use. Docker still lacks tight integration with open-source LLM tooling, but Ollama makes up for it by supporting any LLM in .gguf format. They outperform vLLM in every area _except_ raw performance — but in production, that one factor often trumps everything else.

A key caveat: **none of these services include throttling or usage tracking out of the box**. I highly recommend adding a [LiteLLM proxy server](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-litellm-649d48a0c2c7) (covered in my previous article) to your stack, so you can monitor usage, apply rate limits, and route traffic intelligently across your apps.

Finally, Ollama’s seamless support for any HuggingFace-hosted .gguf model makes it the best place to start. You can even pull my fine-tuned model from the Hub. If you’re just beginning to explore local LLMs, try spinning one up with Ollama today — it’s the easiest on-ramp you’ll find.

body:
* * *

#### A useful addition to any LLM technology stack

Imagine this scenario:

> You’re part of a generative AI team at a company with access to every major LLM on the market. You’ve even fine-tuned and deployed a few models locally for proprietary use cases.

> But every month, your team’s cloud budget is getting wrecked.

> Despite having access to multiple LLM vendors — and your own self-hosted models — it’s a nightmare to track usage, monitor cost spikes, or standardize deployments.

> Worse, you discover that every team is building their own wrappers for each LLM API. Swapping one model for another (say, Fireworks AI → DeepSeek) isn’t as easy as flipping a switch — it means rewriting code, debugging new interfaces, and adjusting prompts.

“I can’t be the only person facing this,” you think — and you’re absolutely right.

### About LiteLLM

Born out of the illustrious [Y Combinator program](https://www.ycombinator.com/), **LiteLLM** is a lightweight, powerful abstraction layer that **unifies LLM API calls** across providers — whether you’re calling OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, Ollama, or your own local GGUF models.

It also supports **cost tracking, admin dashboards**, model fallback, caching, and more — making it easy to run GenAI systems at scale.

Even better? It’s open-source, comes with a Python SDK, and has a great self-hosted proxy server solution to fit enterprise or hybrid-cloud deployments.

### Introducing LiteLLM’s Python SDK

Why “lite”? Because **LiteLLM** is a _lightweight_ wrapper that makes working with multiple LLM providers feel as simple as working with OpenAI.

It standardizes different LLM APIs into a **single, OpenAI-compatible interface** — so you can treat any model (even local ones like Ollama) as if it were an OpenAI ChatCompletion object.

That means no new method names to learn. No specialized wrappers to write. Just plug-and-play.

```python
from litellm import completion

tools = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "get_current_weather",
            "description": "Get the current weather in a given location.",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "location": {
                        "type": "string",
                        "description": "The city and state, e.g. San Francisco, CA",
                    },
                    "unit": {
                        "type": "string",
                        "enum": ["celsius", "fahrenheit"],
                        "description": "The unit of temperature.",
                    },
                },
                "required": ["location"],
            }
        }
    }
]

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather like in Boston today?"}]

response = completion(
  model="ollama/llama3.1",
  messages=messages,
  tools=tools
)
print(response.choices[0].message.tool_calls[0].function)
```

```python-repl
Function(arguments='{"location": "Boston, MA", "unit": "fahrenheit"}', name='get_current_weather')
```

**In this example**, we used a **Llama 3.1** model deployed locally via **Ollama** — but [LiteLLM supports **100+ models**](https://docs.litellm.ai/#call-100-llms-using-the-openai-inputoutput-format) across cloud providers, open-source ecosystems, and self-hosted deployments.

It’s become such a foundational piece of the ecosystem that frameworks like **CrewAI** and **Giskard** rely on LiteLLM as their **default LLM abstraction**. When you define an LLM in CrewAI, you’re actually instantiating a LiteLLM class under the hood — powering all the agentic behavior.

Let’s walk through how to create an agent using LiteLLM in LlamaIndex — my favorite orchestration framework.

```python
import nest_asyncio
from llama_index.llms.litellm import LiteLLM
from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import ReActAgent, AgentStream
from llama_index.core.tools import FunctionTool

nest_asyncio.apply()

def add(a:int|float, b:int|float) -> int|float:
    """Adds 2 integers or floats"""
    return a+b

llm = LiteLLM("ollama/deepseek-r1:latest")

agent = ReActAgent(
    tools=[FunctionTool.from_defaults(add)],
    llm=llm
)
handler = agent.run("What is 21.921 + 23.21?")
async for event in handler.stream_events():
    if isinstance(event, AgentStream):
        print(event.delta, end="", flush=True)
```

The best part? You can switch models on the fly by just changing the string inside the `LiteLLM` object (or the `completion`method in the first example) — everything else stays exactly the same.

Okay, so this solves the second problem: developers reinventing the wheel by writing their own wrappers.

Truth be told, more LLM service providers (except _ahem_ AWS Bedrock 😤) are gradually adopting OpenAI-compatible APIs. So over time, this deviation from OpenAI API issue will improve — but until then, **LiteLLM offers a clean, unified interface that works today.**

### Introducing LiteLLM Proxy Server

The LiteLLM Proxy Server tackles the biggest problem head-on: managing multiple LLMs, embeddings, and guardrails across different use cases — all in one place.

The idea is simple: spin up a central proxy server to expose every model you use. Want to keep costs under control?

✅ Set request-per-minute limits per model (especially for pricier ones)

✅ Generate API keys per model, team, or user — so you know who’s using what

✅ Built-in monitoring helps you trace failed requests and debug quickly

And the best part? **Setting up your own LiteLLM proxy server is easier than you think.** It supports multiple deployment options out of the box:

🐳 **Docker** — use LiteLLM’s pre-built image or build from the pip package

☁️ **Terraform** — provision infrastructure as code

☸️ **Kubernetes** — run the server at scale

🔧 **Helm Charts** — deploy Kubernetes services using a streamlined interface

Of these, I only use Docker regularly. My Kubernetes experience is limited to what I’ve picked up from online courses — and I’ve never touched Helm Charts or Terraform.

Which is why I decided to challenge myself and spin up my own LiteLLM proxy server using **Helm Charts**.

### What are Helm Charts?

**Helm Charts** are essentially **package managers for Kubernetes,** an open-sourced container orchestration platform that handles load balancing, deployment, and scaling of containers across a cluster of machines. Instead of writing raw YAML files from scratch every time, Helm allows you to:

-   📦 Define **reusable templates** and configuration values
-   🚀 **Install, upgrade, and version-control** Kubernetes applications
-   💡 Deploy complex systems like LiteLLM Proxy with just **one command**

This makes Helm especially useful in production setups, where **consistency**, **reusability**, and **versioning** are critical.

### 🛠️ Installing Helm and Kubernetes

To use Helm Charts locally, you’ll first need a working Kubernetes setup. Here’s a quick checklist:

1.  To install Helm Charts on your computer, follow the instructions [here](https://helm.sh/).

-   Mac users rejoice! The command is just:

```bash
brew install helm
```

2\. Kubectl — Install Kubectl using the guide [here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/setup/).

-   This is the CLI used to control and interact with your cluster.

3\. A tool to spin up Kubernetes clusters:

-   [Minikube](https://minikube.sigs.k8s.io/docs/start/?arch=%2Fmacos%2Farm64%2Fstable%2Fbinary+download) (my personal pick), or
-   [Kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/docs/user/quick-start/) (kubernetes-in-docker).

I personally use Minkube because I was following Maximillian Schwarzmuller’s [Kubernetes course on Udemy](https://www.udemy.com/course/docker-kubernetes-the-practical-guide/) — highly recommended.

To keep things tidy, I also set Minikube to always run using Docker containers (so I can prune and restart easily if something breaks):

```bash
minikube config set driver docker
```

### 🚀 Now to spin everything up

#### Start by **pulling the Helm charts** for LiteLLM into your project folder:

```bash
helm pull oci://ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-helm
```

#### Unzip the helm package:

```bash
tar -zxvf litellm-helm-0.1.2.tgz
```

#### 🛠️ Configure your values.yaml

Before we do anything we should inspect the helm charts folder. In your folder you should see something similar to this:

What we need to do is edit the `values.yaml` file to include the LLMs that we want to host. To do this, locate the `proxy_config` section and specify the models you want to host, as well as their provider-specific connection details (for e.g. API keys) under `model_list`:

```yaml
proxy_config:
  model_list:
    # At least one model must exist for the proxy to start.
    - model_name: llama3.1-8b
      litellm_params:
        model: ollama/llama3.1
        api_base: http://host.docker.internal:11434
    - model_name: qwen2.5-7b
      litellm_params:
        model: ollama/qwen2.5
        api_base: http://host.docker.internal:11434
```

> 💡 **Tip**: You can also use [http://localhost:11434](http://localhost:11434) as your api\_base — that’s the default Ollama endpoint.

Notice how the model references use the `{provider}/{model_name}` format — just like the LiteLLM Python SDK.

#### 🔐 Add Admin Credentials

To access the LiteLLM Proxy UI and administer your proxy server, add the following environment variables under the envVars section:

```yaml
envVars: 
  PROXY_MASTER_KEY: sk-1234
  UI_USERNAME:  admin
  UI_PASSWORD:  admin
```

-   `PROXY_MASTER_KEY`: This is your admin key — it gives you full control over virtual keys, users, budgets, and usage tracking. Store this securely; if lost, you’ll be locked out of the admin routes.
-   `UI_USERNAME` and `UI_PASSWORD`: These are the credentials you’ll use to log into the proxy dashboard.

#### 🗄️ About the Database

If you scroll further in values.yaml, you’ll also see a **PostgreSQL configuration** block.

The Helm chart automatically spins up a database using the credentials defined here — no need to set up your own backend separately. ✅

#### ⚙️ Start the Kubernetes Cluster

Fire up Minikube:

```bash
minikube start
```

If your terminal explodes into a sea of emojis, congratulations 🎉 — your cluster is live!

PS: The command to spin down your minikube cluster is

```bash
minikube stop
```

#### 📦 Install the Helm Chart

Now install the chart into your Kubernetes cluster:

```bash
helm install lite-helm ./litellm-helm
```

#### 🌐 Access the Proxy Server

To forward traffic from your local machine to the LiteLLM service inside Kubernetes, run:

```bash
export POD_NAME=$(kubectl get pods --namespace default -l "app.kubernetes.io/name=litellm,app.kubernetes.io/instance=lite-helm" -o jsonpath="{.items[0].metadata.name}")
export CONTAINER_PORT=$(kubectl get pod --namespace default $POD_NAME -o jsonpath="{.spec.containers[0].ports[0].containerPort}")
kubectl --namespace default port-forward $POD_NAME 8080:$CONTAINER_PORT
```

Your LiteLLM proxy should now be accessible at: `[http://localhost:8080](http://localhost:8080)` 🎉

By default, you’ll land on the **Swagger UI** — a REST API interface showing available endpoints. To access the **admin dashboard**, click the **“LiteLLM Admin Panel on /ui”** link.

Tada! Our Ollama models are right there!

#### 🗝️ Time to gatekeep our models

On the left hand side of your LiteLLM Proxy Server UI, click on “**Virutal Keys**”, and click “**Create new key**”.

Now it gets fun — you’re about to issue your own API key!

1.  Give the key a name.
2.  Select which models it applies to.
3.  Configure additional constraints:

-   **Max budget** (in USD)
-   **Tokens per minute**
-   **Requests per minute**
-   **Expiry duration**
-   **Guardrail deployments**

> 💡 Note: Vector store access is only available on **LiteLLM Enterprise**, but everything else is available in the open-source tier.

For my key, I set a **requests per minute limit of 5** — which means if the key hits that quota, subsequent requests will queue until the next minute.

> ⚠️ **Important**: Be sure to copy and save the generated API key now. You **won’t** be able to view it again after this step.

#### 🧪 Test It in the Playground

LiteLLM’s admin UI also includes a built-in playground! Just click **“Test Key”**.

-   Paste in your newly created API key
-   Select the LLM you want to use
-   Start chatting via the web UI

That’s it — you’ve now deployed your own fully managed, multi-LLM gateway using Helm, Kubernetes, and LiteLLM. 🔥

#### In the event of guardrails and MCP servers

You can configure guardrails and when to invoke them — pre, post or during model call, or even during logging!

There are however, some limitations on guardrail integration. Most of the provided options appear to be integrated on a cloud service provider — except for Presidio which is a PII Python framework.

LiteLLM also recently released a new feature on their proxy server to also allow for [MCP server integration](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/mcp)! This allows us to add MCP server deployments onto LiteLLM (allowing these servers to be accessed via a fixed endpoint), and allows us to restrict or allow access to these servers by API key and team. Like our LLMs, we can also track costs of our MCP as well as the usage. This feature is currently in beta mode.

We will be skipping both these steps in our exploration.

### 👨🏻‍💻 Time to call it in code

Now for the fun part: using your deployed LiteLLM Proxy in actual code.

But first — save your virtual API key to a .env file to keep things clean and secure.

#### Using LangChain 🦜

Just treat your LiteLLM model like an OpenAI one. Seriously 😄

```python
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langchain.schema import HumanMessage, SystemMessage
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv, find_dotenv
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

_ = load_dotenv(find_dotenv())

os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"] = os.getenv("QWEN_API_KEY")

langchain_llm = ChatOpenAI(
    openai_api_base="http://localhost:8080",
    model = "qwen2.5-7b",
    temperature=0.1,
    extra_body={
        "metadata": {
            "generation_name": "titus-generation-langchain-client",
            "generation_id": "langchain-client-gen-id1",
            "trace_id": "langchain-client-trace-id1",
            "trace_user_id": "langchain-client-user-id1"
        }
    }
)

messages = [
    SystemMessage(
        content="You are a helpful assistant."
    ),
    HumanMessage(
        content="Why is the sky blue?"
    ),
]
response = langchain_llm.invoke(messages)
display(Markdown(response.content))
```

> _✅_ **_It works!_** _You’re calling a model through LiteLLM using LangChain like it’s native OpenAI._

#### Using LlamaIndex 🦙

Same deal here — use the `AzureOpenAI` interface to wrap your LiteLLM endpoint:

```python
from llama_index.llms.azure_openai import AzureOpenAI

llamaindex_llm = AzureOpenAI(
    engine="qwen2.5-7b",               # model_name on litellm proxy
    temperature=0.0,
    azure_endpoint="http://localhost:8080", # litellm proxy endpoint
    api_key="sk-1234",                    # litellm proxy API Key
    api_version="2025-04-01-preview",
)
response = llamaindex_llm.complete("Hi!")
display(Markdown(str(response)))
```

```python-repl
Hello! How can I assist you today? Feel free to ask me any questions or let me
know if you need help with anything specific.
```

> _✅_ **_You now have LlamaIndex fully wired up through LiteLLM._**

#### Using the OpenAI SDK — with tools! ֎

LiteLLM also works seamlessly with the OpenAI Python SDK.

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="http://localhost:8080",
    api_key=os.getenv("LLAMA_API_KEY")
)

tools = [{
    "type": "function",
    "name": "get_weather",
    "description": "Get current temperature for a given location.",
    "parameters": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "location": {
                "type": "string",
                "description": "City and country e.g. Bogotá, Colombia"
            }
        },
        "required": [
            "location"
        ],
        "additionalProperties": False
    }
}]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama3.1-8b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the weather like in Paris today?"}],
    tools=tools,
    extra_body={ # pass in any provider-specific param, if not supported by openai, https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/completion/input#provider-specific-params
        "metadata": {
            "generation_name": "titus-generation-langchain-client",
            "generation_id": "langchain-client-gen-id1",
            "trace_id": "langchain-client-trace-id1",
            "trace_user_id": "langchain-client-user-id1"
        }
    }
)

print(response.choices[-1].message.tool_calls)
```

> _🔍 You’ll see the expected tool call response, just like you would with native OpenAI._

#### 🆕 Bonus: OpenAI’s responses.create API

This new endpoint allows for **text+image input** and **structured output —** and our deployment on LiteLLM’s proxy deployment works here too!

```python
response = client.responses.create(
    model="llama3.1-8b",
    input=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the weather like in Paris today?"}],
    tools=tools,
    extra_body={ # pass in any provider-specific param, if not supported by openai, https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/completion/input#provider-specific-params
        "metadata": {
            "generation_name": "titus-generation-langchain-client",
            "generation_id": "langchain-client-gen-id1",
            "trace_id": "langchain-client-trace-id1",
            "trace_user_id": "langchain-client-user-id1"
        }
    }
)
print(response.output)
```

```python-repl
[ResponseOutputMessage(...)]
```

> _✅_ **_Boom!_** _You’ve now got LangChain, LlamaIndex, and OpenAI SDK all routed through your own proxy._

### 🧐 Inspecting our LLM usage

To see the utilization of our LLMs, simply click “usage” on the left side panel of the LiteLLM proxy server UI.

This opens up a sleek, built-in dashboard that gives you insights into usage patterns across:

-   🔢 Individual **models**
-   👥 Different **teams**
-   🔐 Specific **API keys**

These insights are critical for **fine-tuning your LLM strategy at the use-case level**. You can throttle expensive models, optimize access policies, and avoid unexpected billing spikes — all while keeping local compute (for self-hosted models like Ollama) from being overloaded.

> _💡_ **_Note:_** _You’ll see $0 as total spend here — because we’re using_ **_Ollama_**_, a locally hosted LLM platform._

### ⚠️ It’s Not All Smooth Sailing

While LiteLLM Proxy works beautifully in most use cases, I did run into some hiccups when integrating with **LangGraph** and **LlamaIndex** agents.

#### 🌀 LangGraph: The Tool Loop Spiral

When I created an agent with LangGraph, the tool was called endlessly — clogging up my stdout.

Okay, not _endlessly_ — the proxy’s request-per-minute limit (5 RPM in my case) throttled it. So every minute, it would just try again another 5 times. 😅

Here’s a simplified version of my LangGraph code:

```python
from langchain_core.tools import tool
from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent

@tool
def get_weather(city: str) -> str:  
    """Get weather for a given city."""
    return f"It's always sunny in {city}!"

agent = create_react_agent(
    model = langchain_llm,
    tools=[get_weather],
    prompt="""You are a helpful assistant. When you need to use a tool:

1. First, call the appropriate tool
2. Wait for the tool result
3. Then provide a complete response using the tool result

Always provide a text response after using any tool. Never return empty content.

Example:
User: "What's the weather in Singapore?"
Assistant: I'll check the weather in Singapore for you.
[calls get_weather tool]
Tool result: "It's always sunny in Singapore!"
Assistant: Based on the weather information, it's always sunny in Singapore!
"""
)
response = agent.invoke(
    {
        "messages": [
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": "What is the weather in Singapore?"
            }
        ]
    },
    debug=True
)
```

The agent calls the tool to eternity (capped at 5 requests per minute )— and beyond.

#### 🤖 LlamaIndex: Returns Tool Call as Raw JSON

With **LlamaIndex**, the agent didn’t invoke the tool at all. It returned the intended tool call as a plain string — no actual execution.

-   With LlamaIndex, the agent simply returns the tool call as a string without actually calling the tool:

```python
from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import FunctionAgent
from llama_index.core.tools import FunctionTool

def add(a: int | float, b: int | float) -> int|float:
    """Use this tool to add 2 integers or floats"""
    return a + b

agent = FunctionAgent(
    llm=llamaindex_llm,
    tools=[FunctionTool.from_defaults(add)]
)
response = await agent.run("What is 76+12?")
print(str(response))
# Output:
# '{"name": "add", "arguments":{"a": 76, "b": 12}}'
```

So the agent _knew_ it needed the tool… but stopped short of actually calling it.

### 🚨 Why This Happens

To be fair, all three of these libraries — **LangGraph**, **LlamaIndex**, and **LiteLLM** — are in hyper-growth mode. Each pushes 2–3 releases **per week** on GitHub. That pace makes integration bugs inevitable.

I’ve raised these issues with the LiteLLM core team, and I’m hopeful for better interop down the line.

* * *

### 🤔 Thinking About What We Just Did

With just one solution — **LiteLLM Proxy** — we tackled two major pain points in enterprise GenAI:

-   ✅ **Budget overruns**
-   ✅ **Tech debt** from writing too many custom wrappers

And that’s no small feat.

#### 🧩 The OpenAI API Compatibility Problem

OpenAI API compatibility might seem like a solved problem, but in reality, **it’s far from trivial**.

Even though many vendors have made their APIs _OpenAI-like_, frameworks like **LangChain** and **LlamaIndex** still write **custom wrappers** for each provider. Why?

Because OpenAI’s API evolves rapidly — often in ways that break assumptions or behaviors.

To address this, LlamaIndex even introduced a special LLM class called `OpenAILike —` a [thin wrapper](https://docs.llamaindex.ai/en/stable/api_reference/llms/openai_like/) designed to work with any model that exposes OpenAI-style APIs. It’s a clever abstraction, but it still requires effort to implement and maintain.

#### 🔁 Continuous Change = Continuous Breakage

Here’s just one example:

The [completions API is now deprecated](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/completions) in favor of `chat.completions.create()` — a subtle shift that broke compatibility for libraries relying on the old style.

Even the responses API is new — and isn’t supported by most wrappers yet.

It is also not uncommon to code out your own LLM deployment on FastAPI — now you’re the one [coding out OpenAI endpoints](https://medium.com/data-science/how-to-build-an-openai-compatible-api-87c8edea2f06) to make the deployment OpenAI API compatible.

#### 🧘 LiteLLM: Calm in the API Chaos

LiteLLM sits in the middle of all this chaos and just says:

> _“Use the OpenAI SDK. I’ll handle the differences.”_

It acts as a normalization layer so that no matter which LLM or provider you choose — Anthropic, Groq, Ollama, Fireworks, Together, DeepSeek — you write once, and route as needed. LiteLLM’s continued success in handling these changes have seen it adopted by popular frameworks like CrewAI and Giskard.

#### 🛠️ The Centralized Admin Problem

Before LiteLLM, building a proper admin layer meant rolling your own:

-   Proxy servers
-   Virtual key systems
-   Rate limiting logic
-   Budget monitoring dashboards

Now? LiteLLM Proxy gives you all of that — **open-source** and ready to deploy. And thanks to its OpenAI-compatible endpoints, it even works seamlessly with your favorite SDKs (yes, **AzureOpenAI** is just a subclass of OpenAI’s SDK).

### ⏱️ A Final Thought

It didn’t even take us that long to set all of this up.

If you already have Helm and Kubernetes installed, spinning up your own LiteLLM Proxy is a **1-minute effort**.

body:
* * *

#### Why coding on the job feels nothing like class

Like most of my classmates, I’m a proud graduate of the [Master of IT in Business](https://masters.smu.edu.sg/programme/master-of-it-in-business) (MITB) AI track program at the Singapore Management University. One of my favorite electives was a breadth module outside my AI focus — Agile and DevSecOps, from the Digital Transformation track. Unlike the AI classes packed with dense math and algorithms, this one was all about the practical side of software engineering.

Specifically, it introduced me to the process side of software: sprint planning, retrospectives, pair programming, test-driven development — and the automation and security side through CI/CD pipelines under DevSecOps. These were the “best practices,” and we even simulated them as part of a group project that accounted for most of our grade.

During one of my periodic catch-ups with MITB friends, I chatted with [Kelvin](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kelvinleezm/) — the practicum manager of the MITB Digital Transformation track and our instructor for the course, whom I’m lucky enough to call a friend. I told him I still look back fondly on that class, mostly because real-world work feels so far from the textbook ideals we practiced.

We laughed, and he encouraged me to write about this — so here it is.

In this article, I’ll highlight some of the differences between what we learned in the classroom and what I’ve experienced in the workplace. I’ll also do my best to explain why these differences exist.

### Agile Project Management

In an agile software development environment, you’d typically translate a user requirement into the following structure:

-   **Project:** A page where all work for the project is tracked and organized.
-   **Epics:** Broad, overarching goals — for example, “This chatbot can analyze structured data.” Every project contains at least one epic.
-   **Stories:** Smaller units of work stemming from an epic — for example, “This chatbot can compute correlations across stock prices of different tickers from Yahoo Finance.” Epics usually consist of multiple stories. Each story includes a [story point score](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/estimation) (the higher the number the more complex and time-consuming the story) for effort estimation (some stories span multiple sprints) as well as a clear “[Definition of Done](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/definition-of-done)” so there’s no ambiguity about completion.
-   **Tasks:** These are smaller, actionable units of work tied to a story. Tasks can be further broken down into sub-tasks if needed, allowing for finer granularity in managing work. Both tasks and stories together make up the [product’s backlog](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/scrum/backlogs), helping teams prioritize and track progress effectively.
-   **Comments:** Clarifications, attachments, or other supplementary information on any of the above.

All of this is then scheduled into [sprints](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/scrum/sprints) — typically one or two-week cycles where the team aims to deliver a minimum viable product (MVP), followed by a [sprint retrospective](https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook/plays/retrospective) to demo the work, discuss what went well, and plan the next sprint. Daily [stand-ups](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/scrum/standups) help everyone stay in sync.

Pretty intense, right? That’s why tools like [Jira](https://www.atlassian.com/software/jira) and [Confluence](https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence) exist — Jira organizes all these items into cards on a [Kanban board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanban_board) as they move across states like “In Progress,” “Blocked,” or “Done,” while Confluence stores sprint retrospectives and team knowledge.

#### **And then there’s reality.**

In a less-than-ideal world — especially in a lean team — developers often wear all these hats at once: builder, product owner, and project manager.

It’s not necessarily a bad thing — there’s zero chance of miscommunication (you’re literally talking to yourself) and zero technical knowledge gaps. But it also means you’ll probably be fronting meetings with end-users and juggling administrative tasks — requirements gathering, scope negotiations, and status updates — that feel much less fun than writing code.

Plus, your end-users often aren’t [certified scrum product owners](https://www.scrumalliance.org/get-certified/product-owner-track/certified-scrum-product-owner), so forget about polished user stories or a proper definition of done — most of the time, we work straight off a Microsoft Word doc or email thread.

And because there’s hardly time to do a textbook-style breakdown, we often just create one “project” as a task and skip epics and stories entirely.

Do we plan sprints? Not really. When you’re a one-person army, every day is its own sprint. The real goal of using Jira is to document our projects for accountability to our bosses — all while keeping administrative overhead to a minimum.

### GitHub for version control

Every developer knows this — when working on GitHub, it’s best to fork the main repository to your own account, then spin up a new branch for each feature or bug fix. This keeps the main branch of the working repository (which is often used for code deployment) clean.

That way when you commit your code, you only touch your personal fork and relevant branch. To integrate everything, you would raise a pull request (PR), which then gets reviewed before merging. Before you commit your code, it’s also good practice to add [pre-commit hooks](https://pre-commit.com/) to ensure that you identify any simple issues before it reaches GitHub, and ensure that you’re only committing high-quality code (for example using [mypy](https://github.com/python/mypy) for static type checking just in case you’re passing a float to a function that expects a string). Pre-commit hooks can also be used for linting your code to ensure that the format is standardized (no ugly wide spaces) so it’s easier on the eyes.

Ideally, you’d also keep frontend and backend code in separate GitHub repositories for a better separation of concerns.

#### In reality, everyone commits to the main branch — without forking

Yeah, you read that right.

In lean teams, developers are superhuman. Not only are they a one-person army (frontend, backend, scrum master, product owner), they’re usually juggling multiple projects at once — so imagine repeating this ideal process across four or five repos.

What this means is that your one GitHub repo is the repository. No forks, no feature branches — just the main branch.

If you’re lucky enough to work on a bigger project, you might have a small team. One person will set up the repo and then everyone just commits straight to `main`. There’s simply no time for anything else.

I’ve only recently started using pre-commit hooks myself, and honestly, they’re one of the most annoying parts of my workflow. My code usually runs perfectly fine — but some checker like mypy will nitpick tiny things that in my opinion have zero real-world impact.

I dutifully refactor my code for the comments by all other pre-commit hooks…and remove mypy entirely because it is too fussy. 😅

Not only do my colleagues not use pre-commit hooks, they wait until after deployment to push their code — some even forget to push their code. Pretty dangerous — because you lose any version history and can’t easily roll back if something breaks.

Wait until you hear the next part.

### “Test-driven development (TDD)”

[TDD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test-driven_development) is one of those best practices we learned in class. The idea is that you write test cases first — to clarify requirements and make sure the code you eventually write solves the right problem. Plus, high test coverage means you know exactly what’s working and what isn’t.

#### But in reality, we write test cases after coding — if we write them at all.

In most lean teams I’ve seen, the focus is on shipping features as fast as possible to satisfy end-users. Tests are usually an afterthought — written only if there’s a formal requirement or if someone feels guilty. Since you’re writing the test cases out of formality you tend to ensure the tests pass, which defeats the purpose.

Personally, I imposed this discipline on myself only recently — when I was working solo on a large-scale enterprise project and wanted to dot every i and cross every t. That’s how I discovered the power of mocking (which I wrote about in my [last article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-guide-to-code-testing-rag-agents-without-real-llms-or-vector-dbs-51154ad920be)). Tests were still an afterthought though — I did not write the test cases first.

But honestly? I was still the exception, not the norm.

### “Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment (CI/CD)”

You’ve probably guessed where this is going.

At the end of each sprint, you have an MVP ready for some user acceptance testing (UAT). But what happens when you complete new features and push them to main after your pull request clears a code review?

Ideally, you’d go through a whole pipeline:

-   Run [integration tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integration_testing) and [end-to-end tests](https://circleci.com/blog/what-is-end-to-end-testing/) (beyond the [unit tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_testing) from earlier),
-   Run code analysis with tools like [SonarQube](https://www.sonarsource.com/products/sonarqube/),
-   Scan for vulnerabilities using something like [CodeQL](https://codeql.github.com/),
-   Build a new Docker image to containerize your app — ensuring it runs anywhere without dependency issues,
-   Push the Docker image to a repository,
-   Deploy your app — either on a single server with [Docker](https://www.docker.com/) or at scale with [Kubernetes](https://kubernetes.io/)/[Helm Charts](https://helm.sh/), using [Terraform](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform) to provision servers, balance traffic, and tear down resources when no longer needed, and [Ansible](https://docs.ansible.com/) to maintain consistent server configuration.

Sounds like a lot, right?

That’s why [DevOps engineers](https://www.atlassian.com/devops/what-is-devops/devops-engineer) exist — and I have immense respect for them.

#### **In reality, none of the above is done**

You just`streamlit run` / `uvicorn app.py`or deploy your app straight to [Internet Information Services (IIS) manager](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/iis/get-started/getting-started-with-iis/getting-started-with-the-iis-manager-in-iis-7-and-iis-8) — because you simply have too much on your plate

Again, I’ve only started implementing proper CI/CD this year on a large-scale enterprise project — that I was building myself. Taking some great [Docker](https://www.udemy.com/course-dashboard-redirect/?course_id=3490000) and [GitHub Actions courses](https://www.udemy.com/course-dashboard-redirect/?course_id=4900166) really helped me get there. But it can be incredibly frustrating — especially when you hit new errors you’ve never seen before, all while knowing your code itself is fine. Also, the number of people I’ve met across my career who know how to code in Terraform is countable on one hand — and I’ve not met anyone who knows how to code in Ansible.

The temptation to just deploy and move on is very real.

### What about code review and pair programming?

You’ve probably guessed — these are not done either. Code reviews take too long, and pair programming means two developers are writing code for one app instead of two apps.

### Which parts of the Agile and DevSecOps class made it to the workplace?

Great question! One of the most memorable lessons from class that actually made it into the workplace is this: **the code is the documentation**.

Now, that might sound appalling — like a lesson that _shouldn’t_ have made it out of the classroom. But the motivation behind it is practical: developers often don’t have the time to write and maintain separate documentation, especially when it gets outdated the moment the code is refactored.

How will new developers catch up you ask? By reading the code.

That said, the adoption of this “best practice” is mostly unintentional — it happens simply because no one has the time to write proper documentation. Personally, I try to impose some discipline: I write docstrings and annotations in my code and always include a README.md on GitHub that outlines the app’s architecture, setup and file structure (for more complex code bases). I know I’m the exception — in fact, the most common feedback I get from my seniors is that I’m too verbose. But I don’t plan to change. **I believe it’s important to be as helpful as possible to the next developer reading your code — even if that developer is future me**.

One of my seniors at work once said he’d rather rewrite the entire application than read someone else’s code — it’s just faster for him. I couldn’t believe it (still can’t). After all, when you inherit a codebase and something breaks, your first instinct is usually to debug — not rebuild. Thankfully, he’s the outlier. Ironically, he’s also one of the best data scientists I’ve worked with — so perhaps for him, rewriting _is_ more efficient.

I, on the other hand, force myself to read through everyone’s code — even his — because rewriting from scratch risks introducing bugs, missing user requirements, taking longer, and losing valuable learning opportunities to improve your own coding skills. Reading code is painful, but almost always worth it.

### Re-examining the motivation for this article

If you’re a student in the MITB Digital Transformation track, there’s probably an earthquake where you are — because your jaw just hit the ground so hard it sent tremors. The gap between school and the workplace is that wide. But I strongly recommend the Agile and DevSecOps class — it’s a very important class that is taught extremely well.

If you’re a faculty member of the DT track, I’m profusely apologetic for being guilty of not fully implementing all the best practices I learned in class — I hope you haven’t fainted and are still reading this apology.

If you’re a developer in a similar situation as I am, you’re probably chuckling hard to yourself because you can identify with everything I’m saying. And if you’re a developer _not_ in that situation, there’s a chance what I’ve written still struck a chord — are all these practices strictly necessary?

The answer is yes and no.

Clearly, agile, scrum, and DevSecOps exist for a reason. Before they came along, things were even worse! Imagine dealing with endless Gantt charts, day-long project meetings, migration conflicts, new bugs from lack of testing, and no version control.

These innovations have massively improved software reliability and made the project experience better for both users and developers — both groups who are clearly way too busy.

But they also bring new learning curves, challenges, and new roles: DevOps engineers, project managers, scrum masters, scrum product owners — you are truly needed and appreciated.

Like any project with many members, miscommunications and friction are inevitable. But all fires start with sparks. Nobody can do it all alone.

### Closing thoughts

The divide between what we learn in school and what we actually do at work can feel vast — sometimes frustratingly so. But it’s important to remember that the classroom teaches ideals, frameworks, and best practices designed to build solid foundations. The real world, especially in lean and fast-moving teams, demands flexibility, pragmatism, and juggling multiple roles.

Both worlds have value. The classroom challenges us to think systematically and aspire to excellence; the workplace pushes us to be creative problem solvers under real constraints. As professionals, our growth lies in navigating between these two realities — adapting best practices to fit context without losing sight of quality. In the end, perfection can’t be the enemy of good — we take what works, and discard what hinders.

For developers, understanding this gap can temper expectations and spark valuable conversations about how to prepare for industry realities. For practitioners, it’s a reminder that even imperfect processes move us forward, and collaboration across roles is vital.

I want to emphasize that these are reflections from my _past experiences_. I’ve worked as a data scientist across startups, the public service, and multinational corporations — always in ambitious, lean teams focused on improving data-driven decision-making, though with different goals and constraints. Some of the teams I’ve been part of had minimal project management practices — sometimes just a weekly check-in — and didn’t even use Git. So what I’ve shared above reflects the _best_ I’ve encountered so far in software product development. I’m currently in the midst of a job transition, and I’m curious (and hopeful) to see how things will evolve from here.

I hope this article resonates with your experiences, and I’d love to hear how you navigate the theory-versus-practice challenge in your own work.
summary: Compares classroom Agile and DevSecOps practices with workplace software development, explaining how lean teams handle project planning, Git workflows, testing, CI/CD, and code review differently.
