body:
* * *

#### You don’t have to know everything to move forward

Have you ever felt like a fraud at your own job? That sinking feeling that everyone around you is going to discover you have no idea what you’re doing?

That’s imposter syndrome — and it’s something I wrestle with often.

It’s worst when you have past failures to back it up.

Back in my undergraduate days, I scored a C+ in my coding class and carried that scar for years. Even in my AI masters and my career as a data scientist, I felt like I was coasting on luck .

Even right now those feelings still sneak up on me.

But I’ve also proven them wrong time and again.

### **Imposter syndrome is normal**

And it’s not a psychological condition of any sort. [Research suggests that 70% of us](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/commentary/imposter-syndrome-paranoia-inadequate-performance-workers-anxiety-2724791) will feel a dose of imposter syndrome at some point. That means you’re in good company — and it doesn’t make you any less capable.

Just because nobody talks about it doesn’t mean it isn’t real.

This article is for anyone facing imposter syndrome in any field. My hope is that by sharing my story, you’ll feel less alone — and more worthy than you believe.

### Postgrad AI class

That day was especially dense — AI classes at the postgraduate level often feel like trying to take a sip of water from a fire hose. Self-directed learning is expected. Assignments? Brutal. They’re not like the regular homework in my undergraduate days — they’re challenging questions that test every concept, sometimes with a leaderboard to see who did best. Projects feel like mini Y Combinators.

By the time class ended at 10 PM, I was exhausted.

Unlike a typical class day, I stood up, turned around, and wondered aloud, “what just happened?”

That triggered wry smiles and shrugs from everyone around me. It hit me — it wasn’t just me!

On the train home, I asked my friend — one of the top students in our class — if he ever felt like we were in over our heads.

“All the time,” he replied. “**Just fake it till you make it**.”

That remark changed my whole mindset since.

### What “Fake It Till You Make It” really means

> **Fake it till you make it** doesn’t mean pretending you understand everything.

_It means_ trusting that you don’t have to know everything to move forward — and telling yourself you’ll succeed regardless.

_Because nobody has infinite knowledge, and nobody expects you to._

And this is true! We must first recognize that we have all that we need to succeed – professors, peers, open-source knowledge bases, and even generative AI applications.

So where’s the “fake” part?

**It’s in telling yourself that you will succeed — before you fully believe it.**

But nobody succeeds by telling ourselves that they will and then do nothing. That’s where personal strategies come in.

### My Go-To Strategies when Imposter Syndrome Hits

#### 1\. Be biased to action

> “Worrying is like a rocking chair — it gives you something to do, but it gets you nowhere” (Glenn Turner).

Break big tasks into tiny pieces and just do _something_, anything to move the needle.

#### Case study 1: Writing my first API endpoint at work

My master’s was full of cutting-edge AI research, but I had no idea what an “endpoint” was. Writing and deploying code to one was my first task at my new workplace after graduation.

“Oh no,” I thought. “I’m about to be outed as an imposter.”

That’s where imposter syndrome can paralyze you — you feel like you can’t even begin.

So I made my code work in a Jupyter Notebook first. Then I took a walk. And then I told myself “just do it”.

I skimmed the FastAPI documentation, copied a [simple hello world example](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/first-steps/) and launched my first Swagger page.

That was the light bulb moment — I simply replaced the `return {"message":"hello world"}` part with my working notebook code. Ugly? Sure. Needed refactoring? Definitely. But it worked!

**By pushing forward, you prove your fears wrong — one small action at a time.**

#### 2\. Ask everyone for feedback but don’t take all of it

I read [“Coders” by Clive Thompson](https://www.amazon.sg/Coders-They-Think-Changing-World/dp/1529019001/ref=pd_sbs_d_sccl_1_1/356-3954218-4511868?pd_rd_w=7H2Rt&content-id=amzn1.sym.fa1e205d-c8c3-4dce-9cda-722dde89cff3&pf_rd_p=fa1e205d-c8c3-4dce-9cda-722dde89cff3&pf_rd_r=J0PKT080YB0WCCNE8Q3Z&pd_rd_wg=t6Fyj&pd_rd_r=19555ee9-9bfe-4bac-94de-39f46568a4ab&pd_rd_i=1529019001&psc=1) and it’s one of my favorite books of all time. One of the most memorable ideas was that there are no niceties in coding — when your code breaks, you don’t get a polite note from Python; you get a full-blown TRACEBACK error stack.

Thompson explains that the daily job of a coder is to grind through endless failures and frustrations— often because the intended fix breaks something else. Coding can be personality-altering work.

That’s why feedback from coders can feel especially sharp — they spend their days staring down raw errors. Compliments are also rare — when our code runs without an error, Python doesn’t say, “good job, bro!”

This is partly why coders can be so defensive about their work — and also why nobody loves asking for feedback.

But you should always ask for it. Assume anyone who gives you feedback wants you to improve — **but don’t take _every_ comment**.

#### Case Study 2: Deploying a generative AI chatbot over dashboards

My task was to build a chatbot that could reason over 800 metrics displayed across hundreds of dashboards — all of them built by a team of software engineers and powered by their respective APIs, and hosted on an internal company website.

I mounted my chatbot as [a “copilot” chat bubble](https://docs.chainlit.io/deploy/copilot) on top of the existing web application, using a state-of-the-art multi-agent architecture. I was so proud of it. ✨

I added icing-on-the-cake features like text-to-speech, translation, and voice input so people could talk to the bot in their preferred language and get the answer spoken back to them.

And then the feedback started rolling in — some of the harshest I’d ever received:

-   “It’s too slow!” ⏱️_️️_
-   “It crashed when the big boss demo-ed it to a visitor! _”_💥
-   “The bot’s replies are too long!” 📝
-   “The bot’s replies are too brief!” 🤐
-   “The bot is inaccurate!” 🎯❌

I took all this on the chin — and had a pretty bad day.

⏱ A quick look at the logs revealed what was going on. My bot had to ping every single API endpoint asynchronously whenever someone asked, “Give me an overview of the company’s performance.” That takes time — especially if nobody’s willing to say which metrics matter most (you guessed it: “They’re all important”).

In other words, instead of reading or zooming in on the dashboards they actually cared about, users just took the easy way out and asked the bot to summarize everything in the universe for them.

💥 And the demo crash? That was a classic API failure. One of the developers changed the API’s endpoint address without telling me. Of course there was an error – and it was a graceful message because I caught the exception. It didn’t really “crash” as reported, but nobody likes seeing that a query failed — especially in a setting where the big boss was showing off the app to a distinguished guest. The user could have asked any other question (hitting a different API endpoint) and it would have worked fine.

📝 And the issue with reply lengths? Easy to solve too — I cached the bot’s most detailed response and displayed a short 200-word summary by default, with a “see full answer” option.

🎯❌ And then there was the “issue” with inaccuracy. Sometimes the bot would return what looked like a confident, reasonable answer — one that even I thought was correct — but the user would still insist it was off-target. The real problem was that their question was often so vague or broad that even I couldn’t tell what they were actually asking _🤷_‍_._ Though the bot repeatedly followed up for clarification, they rarely gave enough detail. So my bot would hazard its most sensible guess once it deemed it has enough information, and respond… only for the user to say it was wrong.

Once, a user asked the bot about correlations between metrics and then complained that my bot used Pearson’s correlation — even though it gave a solid, accurate answer, filtered to only the top 5 most correlated metrics. The user insisted that it was inaccurate: “it shouldn’t be mathematical.” 🤯 Honestly, I wasn’t sure what they expected. To this day, I still don’t know how to compute correlation without math! Maybe just eyeball charts that move in the same direction?

**But here’s the bigger point:**

When you pour your heart into your code, it feels impossible not to take every bit of feedback personally. That’s okay.

Just remember that not every comment is equally actionable — and often what people _really_ want is for your app to succeed, though their tone may not suggest so. Defend your work when you know it’s good, but listen carefully enough to spot the underlying issue.

That’s how you grow — and that’s what will make your next version better.

#### 3\. Remember that your best is all you can give

In Coders, Clive Thompson introduces [Dennis Crowley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Crowley), the programmer behind [_Dodgeball_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dodgeball_%28service%29), an early social-networking app for mobile devices.

Crowley famously described himself as “the worst programmer in the world,” yet still built an app that became popular enough for Google to take notice.

His account of Google’s acquisition process is absolutely hilarious.

First came a technical interview — which went terribly. One of the questions Crowley recalled was:

> “You lose your keys in the Lower East Side. What algorithm would you write to navigate the streets so that you can find your keys without ever going over the same street twice?”

Crowley, who’d never taken a formal programming class, was lost.

Then came the code review — and wow, was it brutal.

Here’s the exact quote from the book:

> “They were, as Crowley recalls, generally appalled. ‘They’d look at the PHP code like, “This is crazy.” And it was not Beautiful Mind crazy! It was like, “You’re an idiot” crazy.”

And yet Crowley had built something that people loved — using the best knowledge and tools he had at the time.

#### Case Study 3: Optimizing matches between resumes and job descriptions

> PS I also wrote about this experience in my [article recounting my journey as a data scientist](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/how-i-became-a-data-scientist-2d8831531a4c).

My first ever natural language processing project at work was to build a skills bank for resumes and job descriptions to help optimize job-candidate matches.

Any experienced data scientist will tell you this is trivial with modern large language models (LLMs). Even before LLMs, someone with a strong text-analytics background could build up a solid algorithm quickly.

That someone was not me.

I was still relatively new to coding. Plus, I was working at a startup and didn’t have the luxury of time.

So I did it the only way I knew — with regular expressions.

I manually read every document, wrote down every skill, and painstakingly constructed one _insanely_ long regex to capture all of them. It was messy and needed updates every time new skills cropped up — but it worked.

I’m sure my bosses and colleagues thought it was crazy too, but nobody had a better solution under such tight constraints.

That code probably doesn’t exist anymore — if I were still there, I’d have thrown it into the fire myself — but at the time, it was my absolute best.

* * *

If you only have $5, you can’t buy something that’s worth $10. Likewise, you can only give your best — and that’s enough.

When you give your best, people can see it, whether or not you hit the perfect outcome. The results may take their own path. Maybe someone will come along to improve your work, or maybe you’ll be the one to revisit it. Either way, your best is all you can offer — and often, that’s exactly what’s needed.

And despite Crowley’s disastrous interview, Google bought _Dodgeball_ anyway.

#### 4\. Celebrate small wins

This is one of the best ways to be kind to yourself — and to those around you.

Finished coding a tricky module? Go grab a coffee.

Completed training your model? Even if it wasn’t perfect, take a short walk.

Pat yourself on the back often, and treat yourself to something special when you hit a bigger milestone.

#### Case Study 4: Writing Medium Articles

I started writing Medium articles last August, encouraged by [Dr. James Koh](https://medium.com/@byjameskoh/about) — one of the best instructors in my master’s program and someone I’m lucky to call a friend.

When I published my first article, I smiled and went to grab an ice-cold drink to reward myself. Achievement unlocked.

That night, I was amazed to see people had left claps on my article. I thought what I’d written wasn’t even that good — but it made my night and encouraged me to keep writing, logging my wacky experiment ideas, even if they never took off or burst into flames.

Fast forward to today, and this is article number 30. The most surprised person in all of this? Definitely me.

When I look back, I realize that many of my articles started as rough drafts built on other people’s original cookbooks — some so well-written they needed only minor tweaks. What was my real contribution? My own spin: applying the code to my use cases, evaluating the results, re-engineering code, sharing improvements — and sometimes even submitting those improvements as pull requests. To my amazement, they were accepted into the frameworks’ official GitHub repos.

That’s what keeps me going — my articles weren’t just one-way broadcasts; they were conversations. Positive comments, claps, and even encouragement from the original founders of some of the frameworks I wrote about humbled me deeply.

And did I celebrate? Absolutely. Every saved draft. Every article published.

When article number 15 went live, I rewarded myself with a new keyboard for work. After article 25, I ate chocolate ice cream for three days straight (oops!). If you have any ideas on how to celebrate article 30 I’m all ears.

And I also learned the power of paying it forward — making a habit of lifting up others just as they had lifted me. Even in my feedback and advice, I look for genuine positives to highlight before suggesting areas for improvement.

**Because celebrating small wins is contagious — and the joy you give to yourself and to others grows even faster than you’d expect.** 🎉

### Putting it all together

Overcoming imposter syndrome isn’t about convincing yourself you’re perfect or waiting until you feel “qualified enough.” It’s about moving forward anyway — one small step at a time — and celebrating those steps as real wins.

Whether it’s pushing yourself to tackle a daunting task, choosing which feedback to act on, or appreciating your own progress, the secret is recognizing that your best _is_ enough.

That mindset doesn’t just help you survive — it gives you permission to grow. Every bug you fix, every line of code you push, every skill you add to your toolkit is proof you belong exactly where you are.

And when you celebrate those small wins? You make sure you’ll have the energy, optimism, and resilience to keep going.

That’s what will carry you past the self-doubt — not perfection, not someone else’s validation — but your own commitment to learning, creating, and showing up every day. 💪

body:
* * *

#### Introducing an old friend: LangServe

Since its launch into the burgeoning generative AI space in October 2022, LangChain has achieved a cult following. At that time, it was the only framework that could reliably orchestrate LLM application components.

It is now 2025 and the framework has a staggering 110k GitHub stars, making it one of the most popular frameworks to ever exist on GitHub. To give you a sense of its reach: LangChain now has more GitHub stars than

1.  Pandas (45.7k),
2.  PyTorch (90.9k),
3.  FastAPI (86.4k) and
4.  Scikit-Learn (62.4k)

These are quintessential frameworks used by almost every data scientist. Unsurprisingly, LangChain is a requested skill for almost any job focused on generative AI.

As the first mover with dominant market adoption, LangChain gained a unique advantage: the ability to spot gaps in the space and build for them quickly. This has led to the launch of many accompanying and (mostly) familiar frameworks that greatly shaped the generative AI landscape:

1.  [LangServe](https://python.langchain.com/docs/langserve/) (July 2023) — LangChain’s deployment framework
2.  [LangSmith](https://docs.smith.langchain.com/) (October 2023) — LangChain’s observability framework
3.  [LangGraph](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/concepts/why-langgraph/) (January 2024) — LangChain’s multi-agent system orchestration framework
4.  [LangMem](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langmem/) (February 2025) — LangChain’s framework for long-term memory management

Strictly speaking, these frameworks are modular and can exist without each other (but work best together). Nonetheless, these frameworks represent LangChain’s unique vision of the space, and their launch has led to a dramatic evolution in LangChain’s original framework.

LangChain’s quick evolution will undoubtedly result in deprecation of some code modules — kept alive only for backward compatibility. The LangServe framework is one such example: no new features are being added, and even community feature contributions are no longer accepted.

### Introducing LangServe

Originally, LangChain featured many “chain” abstractions — like `QAChain`, `ConversationalChain`, and others. Over time, these were refactored into a more flexible system: **runnables** — composable units that can be linked using the pipe (`|`) operator. When invoked, the query flows through the runnable in the sequence defined by the pipe.

**LangServe** was developed to align with this evolution. It allows you to **deploy runnables as RESTful API endpoints** — in just one line.

> **But isn’t it easy to just use FastAPI to deploy any runnable?**  
> Absolutely. In fact, **LangServe uses FastAPI under the hood**. So you still get Swagger documentation and OpenAPI compliance — for free.

But **LangServe goes further** as we will see later in the article.

All codes can be found in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/urban-enigma).

### Writing our LangChain Runnable

In this article, I’ll be building a gatekeeping runnable to screen away harmful queries and texts. This is part of the layering strategy I was writing about in my [previous article on redteaming LLM applications](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/think-your-rag-app-is-safe-giskard-might-prove-you-wrong-6c88b08c5f7a).

For this task, I’ll be using [**Meta’s Llama Guard 3**](https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-Guard-3-8B) — a Llama 3.1 8B model instruction-tuned to detect harmful text across 14 categories (yup an LLM trained for multi-class classification). Thanks to its extensive fine-tuning, it’s surprisingly resistant to prompt trickery (trust me, I’ve tried).

For any given input, Llama Guard 3 returns either:

-   `"safe"`, or
-   `"unsafe"` along with the detected harmful category or categories.

Llama Guard 3 [performs well on public benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.06674) like the **OpenAI Moderation Evaluation** dataset and **ToxicChat**. It’s open-source, so it’s not invincible — but realistically, it’s hard to beat for most practical use cases (or for most humans).

Llama Guard 3 is available on Ollama. To pull the model locally, just run:

```bash
ollama pull llama-guard3
```

Now let’s build our runnable:

```python
from langchain_ollama import OllamaLLM
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

## Defining runnable components
llm = OllamaLLM(model="llama-guard3", temperature=0)
parser = StrOutputParser()
prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages(
    # Now we instantiate our list of messages
    [
        (
            "system",
            "You are a helpful assistant."
        ),
        ("human", "{input}") #input is a placeholder
    ]
)

## Defining the runnable by piping the components together
chain = prompt | llm | parser

## Test our runnable with a query
response = chain.invoke(
    {"input": "Why is the sky blue?"} 
)
display(Markdown(f"**Response:** {response}"))
```

```python-repl
Response: safe
```

I’ve already walked through the fundamentals of using LangChain in a [previous article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multiverse-part-1-langchain-023a899d294e), so I won’t go into further detail here.

**Next up — let’s deploy this runnable.**

### Serve the app

```python
# app.py

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware

from langchain_ollama import OllamaLLM
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser
from langserve import add_routes

app = FastAPI(
    title="LangChain Llama Guard Server",
    version="1.0",
    description="A Llama Guard Runnable built using Langchain's Runnable interfaces served on LangSmith",
)

# Set all CORS enabled origins
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["*"],
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
    expose_headers=["*"],
)

# Define runnable
llm = OllamaLLM(model="llama-guard3", temperature=0)
parser = StrOutputParser()
prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages(
    [
        (
            "system",
            "You are a helpful assistant."
        ),
        ("human", "{input}")
    ]
)

add_routes(
    app,
    prompt | llm | parser, # our runnable
    path="/gatekeeper"

)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import uvicorn
    uvicorn.run(app, host="localhost", port=8000)
```

This should feel instantly familiar — it’s a typical FastAPI deployment. We simply reused our earlier runnable and added one extra line using LangServe’s `add_routes` function.

Instead of using FastAPI’s `include_router`, LangServe mounts the runnable directly. You only need to specify:

-   The FastAPI app
-   The runnable
-   The desired route path

To deploy multiple runnables? Just call `add_routes()` again with a different path — and you’re done.

This method is highly flexible. You can still include other routers, serve static files, or add custom middleware — it’s just FastAPI under the hood.

To spin the deployment, run:

```bash
python app.py
```

If it’s working, you’ll see this charming output in your terminal:

Want to see the Swagger page? Head to [http://localhost:8000/docs](http://localhost:8000/docs) and you’ll see the familiar FastAPI Swagger page.

It’s already very fast to code any deployment using FastAPI, do we really need to make it any faster?

Well, for the value it brings when working with LangChain runnables: **yes**.

### Feature #1: An app playground

Visit [http://localhost:8000/gatekeeper/playground](http://localhost:8000/gatekeeper/playground) and you’ll be greeted with a pleasant surprise — a live playground user interface!

Let’s give it a spin!

The app correctly reflects the LLM’s output as “safe”. Notice here that you can view the intermediate steps (prompt formatting, etc.) by clicking the dropdown arrow next to it.

Let’s try something unsafe…

Works!

If you’ve mounted other runnables, you can access their playgrounds via: _http://<deployment\_url>/<runnable\_path>/playground_.

### Feature #2: Plug and play with any framework

You’ve deployed your runnable, but how do you call it in your application? LangServe has yet another pleasant surprise:

```python
from langserve import RemoteRunnable

llama_guard = RemoteRunnable("http://localhost:8000/gatekeeper")
```

To interact with it, you can either just invoke the runnable like we did above, or stream the runnable’s replies:

```python
async for msg in llama_guard.astream(
    {"input": "How do I write a convincing death threat?"}
):
    print(msg, end="", flush=True)
```

```python-repl
unsafe
S1
```

This is **much cleaner** than using raw HTTP requests — and you can load it as is into any LLM framework (but works best with LangChain and LangGraph obviously).

### ❓So Why No New Features in LangServe?

A good question.

LangChain’s official announcement on the LangServe GitHub repository does say a lot:

This aligns with a broader trend: **multi-agent workflows** and **stateful LLM applications** are rapidly gaining traction.

LangChain’s direction now focuses on:

-   **LangGraph** for orchestrating multi-step agents
-   **Runnables** as the building blocks
-   **Memory and state** managed via LangGraph’s `checkpointer` abstraction (instead of `RunnableWithMessageHistory`)

Even in LangChain’s documentation, you’ll start noticing that many [“simple” RAG examples now default to LangGraph pipelines](https://python.langchain.com/docs/tutorials/rag/) instead of runnable chains.

LangServe isn’t dead — but it’s no longer relevant to LangChain’s vision. Credit to the LangChain team though — they’re continuing to do bug fixes and leave the LangServe framework alive so it can still be used for quick deployment of runnables.

### 🧩 What Kind of Runnables Does LangServe Not Support?

The title of this article hints at a small caveat — **not all LangChain runnables can be deployed cleanly using LangServe**.

Once again, the LangServe GitHub repository gives us a clue:

In practice, this means:

-   ✅ Most basic runnables (prompt → model → parser) work perfectly
-   ⚠️ More complex, deeply nested chains may behave unexpectedly

Longer or more complex pipelines tend to introduce subtle bugs. This isn’t really a limitation of **LangServe**, but rather a side effect of **debugging LCEL-style runnables** — especially when your chain includes branching logic, retrievers, memory modules, or custom callables.

#### 🤖 What About Chat History?

Another limitation I noticed while using the LangServe playground: **you can’t easily configure chat history.**

Even though the playground shows intermediate steps, there’s no built-in support for multi-turn context. Using a`RunnableWithMessageHistory` also means you need to spin up a database to persist threads so that you can pass in the correct chat history. I know how to do this in LangGraph, but I really don’t know how to do this with LangChain and LangServe. You would have to process chat history upstream before stuffing everything into the input prompt for the LLM.

LangChain’s newer guidance is to use **LangGraph’s checkpointer abstraction** for managing conversation history — and for good reason. It’s more robust, scalable, and flexible across multi-agent workflows.

### 📢 **Good news**: Simple runnables still carry real value!

Take our Llama Guard deployment for instance. In your application logic, you could:

-   ✅ Route all _incoming_ user queries through Llama Guard first, and only allow “safe” queries to proceed.
-   ✅ Route all _outgoing_ LLM replies through Llama Guard again before displaying them to the user.

This simple check prevents harmful content from ever reaching the user, while still logging flagged inputs/outputs for further investigation.

You can deploy your **own finetuned model** using LangServe as well:

```python
 add_routes(
    app,
    ChatHuggingFace(...),
    path="/proprietary_llm",
)
```

You can even deploy custom **business logic** using LangChain’s`RunnableLambda`:

```python
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableLambda

def is_superuser(
    credentials: Dict[Literal["username", "password"], str]
) -> bool:
    return credentials == {"username": "admin", "password": "admin"}

runnable = RunnableLambda(is_superuser)

print(runnable.invoke({"username": "admin", "password": "admin"}))
```

```python-repl
True
```

Now let’s get fancy — what if you want both your LLM guard and custom logic to run in parallel?

```python
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableParallel

# Final runnable
map_chain = RunnableParallel(
    guard_chain = guard_chain,
    superuser_chain = runnable,
)

add_routes(
    app,
    map_chain,
    path="/gatekeeper"
)
```

Now our playground will look a little different:

This works, but with a small catch:

The **LangServe playground** becomes harder to use — now users must input fields for both chains. It’s still functional, but the UX suffers. In most cases, it’s better to mount each runnable on its own endpoint for clarity and usability.

PS, to invoke a parallel chain:

```python
from langserve import RemoteRunnable

parallel_runnable = RemoteRunnable("http://localhost:8000/gatekeeper")
response = parallel_runnable.invoke(
    {
        "input": "Why is the sky blue?", 
        "root": { # follow the name that you see in the LangServe playground
            "username": "admin",
            "password": "admin"
        }
    }
)

print(response)
```

This returns:

```python-repl
{'guard_chain': 'safe', 'superuser_chain': False}
```

### 🏁Conclusion

**LangServe is a great tool for deploying simple LangChain runnables as RESTful API endpoints.**

-   It gives you a working deployment in _just a few lines of code_
-   It comes with a live Swagger playground (perfect for demos!)
-   It integrates cleanly with FastAPI, LangChain, and any downstream orchestrator

It’s also a great way to immediately **impress your bosses and colleagues** (_I did this at work too!_). Just spin up a LangServe endpoint, share the playground URL, and let them interact with your LLM tool directly — no extra frontend work needed. And it took me just 3 minutes to code everything out.

If your architecture leans toward **microservices**, LangServe shines — mount multiple endpoints, one runnable per path, and stitch them together in your application logic.

But remember:

> **LangServe is best for lightweight runnables.** Complex logic? Consider other options like the LangGraph platform.

The LangChain team has made it clear: **LangServe will remain stable, but won’t receive new features**. It’s still a reliable tool in your LLM toolbox — just know its limits.

body:
* * *

#### ⚠️ Health warning: Sleepless nights ahead.

Data scientists build machine learning models that power many of the apps we use today. But any data scientist will very quickly tell you that the most important thing isn’t the model, it’s the data.

> As the age-old saying goes: **Garbage in garbage out.**

This goes for any generative AI application as well. It doesn’t matter how fantastic your large language model (LLM) is — if your underlying knowledge base is outdated, your chatbot will be too.

But building data pipelines to keep data fresh is easier said than done. You have to think about **latency**, **volume**, **refresh rates**, and **integration points**. As someone from a data science background with minimal data engineering experience (seriously — I just write SQL scripts to dump data out), I used to feel totally lost… and sometimes still do.

That changed when I built my first **Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)** app at work. Suddenly, keeping the knowledge base fresh became a top priority.

My favorite solution? **Change Data Capture (CDC).** In this article, I’ll walk you through how to build a simple CDC pipeline using **Apache Airflow**.

All code can be found in [my GitHub repo](https://github.com/tituslhy/sturdy-telegram/tree/main).

### Introducing change data capture

Every RAG application starts with a set of documents — your initial knowledge base. But what happens when those documents get updated? Or when new ones are added?

Should we re-ingest everything into the vector database from scratch each time? **Definitely not.**

It’s much more efficient to ingest only what has changed — the **incremental updates**. But how do we detect those changes?

This quickly becomes a **Python problem**, not a generative AI one. The core idea is simple: keep a log of the **last modified date** for each document, and periodically check for any updates or new additions. When a change is detected, trigger an ingestion run for updated or new documents.

This concept is called [**Change Data Capture (CDC)**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Change_data_capture) — a common technique in data engineering to track and process incremental updates in databases or document stores.

Though I code almost exclusively in Python, there are several orchestration frameworks that make it easier to build pipelines like this — [**Apache Airflow**](https://airflow.apache.org/), [**Prefect**](https://www.prefect.io/), and more recently, [**CocoIndex**](https://cocoindex.io/) (which is specifically optimized for RAG workflows).

All of these are well-loved in the data community.

I’ll be honest: I started with **Apache Airflow** simply because I saw my colleagues using it — I was thinking that made it easier to ask for help when I got stuck. Feel free to use any of the other frameworks if you find them easier!

### Cold start: Ingesting documents into a vector database the first time

Before we can track document changes, we need to set up the initial knowledge base. Let’s start by writing a static ingestion pipeline — just enough for our chatbot to have some context to work with.

First, spin up a local **Qdrant** vector database using Docker:

```bash
docker run -p 6333:6333 -p 6334:6334 \
    -v "$(pwd)/qdrant_storage:/qdrant/storage:z" \
    qdrant/qdrant
```

With Qdrant running, we can move on to document ingestion. I’ll be using **LlamaIndex** for orchestration — but feel free to swap in any framework you prefer.

```python
from llama_index.core import (
    Settings, 
    SimpleDirectoryReader,
    StorageContext,
    VectorStoreIndex, 
)
from llama_index.embeddings.ollama import OllamaEmbedding
from llama_index.vector_stores.qdrant import QdrantVectorStore
from qdrant_client import QdrantClient, AsyncQdrantClient

# Define embedding model
Settings.embed_model = OllamaEmbedding(model_name="nomic-embed-text")

# Define vector database
client = QdrantClient(url="http://localhost:6333",)
aclient= AsyncQdrantClient(url="http://localhost:6333")
vector_store = QdrantVectorStore(
    client=client,
    collection_name="Airflow_Experiment",
)
storage_context = StorageContext.from_defaults(vector_store=vector_store)

# Load documents
documents = SimpleDirectoryReader("../../docs").load_data(show_progress=True)

# Convert documents into chunks, convert chunks into vector embeddings, and
# store vector embeddings into the vector database
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(
    documents=documents,
    storage_context=storage_context,
    embed_model=Settings.embed_model,
)
```

### From Notebook to Pipeline: Coding with Apache Airflow

What I love about **Apache Airflow** is that it lets me take code I’ve written in a Jupyter Notebook and turn it into a production-ready data pipeline — without needing to rewrite everything.

Airflow visualizes your pipeline as a **DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph)**. And you don’t even have to construct the graph manually — Airflow infers it from how your tasks are defined and sequenced.

Here’s one best practice: **make each task atomic**. That means breaking your logic into clear, testable steps. This makes it easier to debug and rerun only the parts that fail.

Let’s refactor the code above into two Airflow tasks.

#### 🧩 Step 1: Serialize Documents

```php
from airflow.decorators import dag, task
from airflow.providers.standard.sensors.filesystem import FileSensor
from airflow.providers.standard.operators.empty import EmptyOperator
from airflow.models.baseoperator import chain

import os
from datetime import datetime
from typing import List, Literal, Dict, Any

import pandas as pd

# Define global variables
COLLECTION_NAME = "Airflow_Experiment"
EMBEDDING_MODEL_NAME = "nomic-embed-text"
EMBEDDING_DIMENSION = 768
QDRANT_URL = "http://localhost:6333"

# ─── TASKS ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
@task
def serialize_documents(paths: List[str]) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
    from llama_index.core import SimpleDirectoryReader
    from llama_index.core.schema import Document
    if not paths:
        return []
    docs = SimpleDirectoryReader(input_files=paths).load_data()
    serialized = []
    for doc in docs:
        serialized.append(doc.model_dump())
    return serialized
```

This task reads documents from the given file paths and serializes them into JSON-compatible objects.

> Note: We import libraries **inside the task.** Strictly speaking this isn’t necessary, but preferred. When Airflow parses your DAG files (e.g. every scheduler heartbeat), it executes the top‑level code so if you have a big library (think `torch`, `tensorflow`, or custom modules that do complex initialization), importing it globally can slow down DAG parsing and eat up memory in the scheduler or workers. By moving that import into the task body, you only pay the cost when the task actually runs.

#### 🧩 Step 2: Ingest into Vector DB

```python
@task
def ingest_serialized_documents(serialized_docs: List[Dict[str, Any]]) -> None:
    from llama_index.core.schema import Document
    from llama_index.core import StorageContext, VectorStoreIndex
    from llama_index.embeddings.ollama import OllamaEmbedding
    from llama_index.vector_stores.qdrant import QdrantVectorStore
    from qdrant_client import QdrantClient, AsyncQdrantClient

    if not serialized_docs:
        return
    # reconstruct Document objects
    documents = [Document(**d) for d in serialized_docs]
    # setup Qdrant vector store
    client = QdrantClient(url=QDRANT_URL)
    aclient = AsyncQdrantClient(url=QDRANT_URL)
    embed_model = OllamaEmbedding(
        model_name=EMBEDDING_MODEL_NAME,
        # base_url="http://ollama:11434",  # Default is localhost:11434
    )
    vs = QdrantVectorStore(
        client=client,
        aclient=aclient,
        collection_name=COLLECTION_NAME,
    )
    storage_ctx = StorageContext.from_defaults(vector_store=vs)
    VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(
        documents, 
        storage_context=storage_ctx,
        embed_model = embed_model,
    )
```

These tasks form the core of our initial ingestion pipeline — but the full DAG still needs:

-   A check for whether the Qdrant collection already exists — or we’ll face ingestion errors
-   Conditional creation of the collection if it doesn’t
-   A way to track document updates (so we don’t reprocess everything each time)

#### 🧩 Step 3: Qdrant collection tasks

These steps are the easiest so let’s tackle them first:

```python
@task.branch
def check_or_create_collection(name: str) -> Literal["create_collection", "skip_create_collection"]:
    from qdrant_client import QdrantClient

    client = QdrantClient(url=QDRANT_URL)
    cols = client.get_collections().collections
    return "skip_create_collection" if any(c.name == name for c in cols) else "create_collection"

@task
def create_collection(name: str) -> None:
    from qdrant_client import QdrantClient
    from qdrant_client.http.models import VectorParams

    client = QdrantClient(url=QDRANT_URL)
    client.create_collection(collection_name=name, vectors_config=VectorParams(size=EMBEDDING_DIMENSION, distance="Cosine"))
```

To check for collection, we just need to see if the global collection name specified is within Qdrant’s list of collections. We then specify another step that runs only if the collection name does not exist. Notice here we haven’t yet orchestrated the code logic (if-else), just the functions, but you’ll immediately notice that the `check_or_create_collection` function is decorated with `task.branch`, indicating that this is a branch in the final DAG.

#### 🧩 Step 4: Tracking documents

The best way to do this is using a database of some sort. Since I’m working with a single static folder on my local machine, I opted for a lightweight approach: tracking document updates using a local CSV file. The function below looks for the csv file and loads it into a pandas DataFrame:

```python
@task
def load_last_read(csv_path: str) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
    if os.path.exists(csv_path):
        df = pd.read_csv(csv_path, parse_dates=["last_read_date"])
        return df.to_dict(orient="records")
    return []
```

The pandas DataFrame is then converted into a list of dictionaries, which is passed into the next task to determine which documents need updating — i.e., those with a newer modified timestamp than what’s recorded.

```python
@task()
def find_new_files(folder: str, last_read_records: List[Dict[str, Any]]) -> List[str]:
    from datetime import datetime as _dt
    last_read = pd.DataFrame(last_read_records) if last_read_records else pd.DataFrame(columns=["file_path", "last_read_date"])
    all_pdfs = [os.path.join(folder, f) for f in os.listdir(folder) if f.lower().endswith(".pdf")]
    new_files = []
    for path in all_pdfs:
        mtime = _dt.fromtimestamp(os.path.getmtime(path))
        prev = last_read.loc[last_read.file_path == path, "last_read_date"]
        if prev.empty or mtime > prev.iloc[0]:
            new_files.append(path)
    return sorted(new_files)
```

Finally, we need a step to **update the CSV log after ingestion completes**. This function updates the pandas DataFrame and writes it back to the CSV file:

```python
@task
def update_last_read(paths: List[str], csv_path: str) -> None:
    df = pd.read_csv(csv_path, parse_dates=["last_read_date"]) if os.path.exists(csv_path) else pd.DataFrame(columns=["file_path", "last_read_date"])
    from datetime import datetime as _dt
    for path in paths:
        mtime = _dt.fromtimestamp(os.path.getmtime(path))
        if path in df.file_path.values:
            df.loc[df.file_path == path, "last_read_date"] = mtime
        else:
            df = pd.concat([df, pd.DataFrame([{"file_path": path, "last_read_date": mtime}])])
    df.to_csv(csv_path, index=False)
```

The logic is straightforward:

-   If the file path already exists in the DataFrame, we update its timestamp.
-   If it’s new, we add a fresh row.
-   Finally, we overwrite the CSV with the updated info.

The last piece of the puzzle is sensing when new files are added to the folder. Thankfully, Airflow provides a handy `FileSensor` abstraction for this, so we don’t have to write a custom polling function.

With all the steps complete, we’re now ready to **assemble the final DAG**.

### 🛠️ Assembling our DAG

Every Airflow pipeline starts with a `@dag` decorator.Here, we define the DAG’s ID, schedule, and some sensible defaults:

```python
# ─── DAG DEFINITION ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
@dag(
    dag_id="qdrant_document_ingestion",
    start_date=datetime(2025, 1, 1),
    schedule="@hourly",
    catchup=False,
    default_args={"owner": "airflow", "retries": 2},
    tags=["qdrant", "vector_db", "doc_ingest"],
)
def qdrant_document_ingestion():
    ...
```

**Why these settings matter:**

-   `**@hourly**` keeps your knowledge base fresh every 60 minutes.
-   `**catchup=False**` ensures you don’t accidentally backfill old runs.
-   **Retries** give you resilience in case of transient failures.

### 📁 Step 1: Wait for the Documents Folder

We don’t want the DAG to fail just because the folder isn’t ready yet. Airflow’s `FileSensor` handles this elegantly:

```python
# ─── DAG DEFINITION ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
@dag(
    dag_id="qdrant_document_ingestion",
    start_date=datetime(2025, 1, 1),
    schedule="@hourly",
    catchup=False,
    default_args={"owner": "airflow", "retries": 2},
    tags=["qdrant", "vector_db", "doc_ingest"],
)
def qdrant_document_ingestion():
    wait_dir = FileSensor(
      task_id="wait_for_docs_folder",
      fs_conn_id="fs_default",
      filepath=DOCS_FOLDER,
      poke_interval=15,
      timeout=600,
      mode="poke",
  )
```

> **Key point:** This task “pokes” the filesystem every 15 seconds (for up to 10 minutes) until the folder is available. It’s a great way to gate your pipeline on external readiness.

### 🧭 Step 2: Ensure the Qdrant Collection Exists

Before we ingest anything, we need to make sure the Qdrant collection exists. We use a branching task to check and create if needed:

```python
# ─── DAG DEFINITION ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
@dag(
    dag_id="qdrant_document_ingestion",
    start_date=datetime(2025, 1, 1),
    schedule="@hourly",
    catchup=False,
    default_args={"owner": "airflow", "retries": 2},
    tags=["qdrant", "vector_db", "doc_ingest"],
)
def qdrant_document_ingestion():
    ... #all codes above
    branch = check_or_create_collection(COLLECTION_NAME)
    skip   = EmptyOperator(task_id="skip_create_collection")
    create = create_collection(COLLECTION_NAME)
```

The `check_or_create_collection` task returns either `"create_collection"` or `"skip_create_collection"`, directing the DAG to run one of the next steps accordingly.

> ✅ This ensures **idempotent behavior** — the collection is only created if it doesn’t already exist.

### 📄 Step 3: Load Logs and Detect Updates

Next, we load our CSV log of past ingestions and compare it to what’s currently on disk. If we detect fresh or modified files, we serialize them, ingest them into Qdrant, and update the tracking log:

```python
# ─── DAG DEFINITION ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
@dag(
    dag_id="qdrant_document_ingestion",
    start_date=datetime(2025, 1, 1),
    schedule="@hourly",
    catchup=False,
    default_args={"owner": "airflow", "retries": 2},
    tags=["qdrant", "vector_db", "doc_ingest"],
)
def qdrant_document_ingestion():
    ... #all codes above
    last_read  = load_last_read(DATA_PATH)
    new_paths  = find_new_files(DOCS_FOLDER, last_read)
    serialized = serialize_documents(new_paths)
    ingest     = ingest_serialized_documents(serialized)
    update = update_last_read(new_paths, DATA_PATH)
    chain(
        wait_dir,
        branch,
        [create, skip],
        new_paths,
        serialized,
        ingest,
        update,
    )

# Remember to run the function or Airflow won't detect the DAG!
qdrant_document_ingestion()
```

Finally, we use Airflow’s `chain` helper to make the dependencies clear to Airflow. This ensures that tasks execute **in the correct order**, respecting all branching logic and upstream dependencies.

Save the final script into a folder named “DAG” — by default Airflow will look for updates to this folder and load your written DAGs for monitoring and execution.

> ✅ **Pro tip:** Just defining the function isn’t enough — you must _call_ it in the script so that Airflow registers the DAG at parse time.

### 🖥️ Interacting with Airflow

Airflow has a very nice user interface (built on Flask) that lets you visualize your DAGs and monitor their runs. To spin it up locally, just run:

```bash
airflow standalone
```

**But this is where the nightmare begins.**

Chances are… you still won’t see your DAG. Why?

### 📁 Your DAG Isn’t Being Watched

By default, Airflow watches the `~/airflow/dags` folder. If your project’s DAG file is located elsewhere (e.g., `my_project/dags/`), it won’t be detected. To fix this, open your `airflow.cfg` file — usually found in `~/airflow/airflow.cfg` — and update the following line:

```ini
dags_folder = /your/actual/project/folder/dags
```

Still no DAG?

### 🔄 “Not time to refresh bundle dags-folder”

Even after fixing the folder, Airflow might still not show your DAG. You’ll see log messages like this:

> dag-processor | \[2025–06–16T16:07:43.217+0800\] {manager.py:528} INFO — Not time to refresh bundle dags-folder

This means it’s waiting to refresh the folder (typically every 30 seconds). But even after waiting, it might not show up.

💡 **Fix**: Force Airflow to reparse your DAG with:

```python
airflow dags reserialize
```

Boom — your DAG appears! 🎉

### 🔌 Now… Execution Fails?!

You run the DAG… and it immediately fails. Airflow can’t find Qdrant. What gives?

That’s because Airflow doesn’t know how to connect to Qdrant yet. Head to the UI:

-   Click **Admin** → **Connections**
-   Click **\+ Add**
-   Create a new connection with your Qdrant details

Still no luck?

### 🧩 Install Missing Qdrant Provider

You likely need to install the Qdrant provider package for Airflow to use that connection:

```python
pip install apache-airflow-providers-qdrant
```

Whew. You’re almost there.

### 💥 One More Failure…

Now the DAG fails again — right at the first step: the FileSensor. This time, it’s because you haven’t configured a default filesystem connection.

Create another connection under **Admin → Connections**, this time with:

-   Conn ID: `fs_default`
-   Conn Type: `File (path)`
-   Extra: `{ "path": "/" }` (or whatever root your files are under)

And yes, this also requires another provider package:

```bash
pip install apache-airflow-providers-standard
```

### ⁉️ Our DAG runs… but so many tasks are skipped?

This puzzled me. I saw the DAG execute — but several steps, especially downstream ones, were silently skipped.

Turns out, Airflow **intelligently skips** downstream tasks based on upstream results.

I didn’t quite understand why, so I updated the `@task` decorator of `find_new_files`:

```python
@task(
    trigger_rule="none_failed_min_one_success"
)
def find_new_files(folder: str, last_read_records: List[Dict[str, Any]]) -> List[str]:
    ... #code unchanged
```

This trigger rule tells Airflow:

> “Run this task if at least one upstream task succeeded, regardless of skipped statuses.”

### ✅ What success looks like

Here’s a screenshot from the very first step — our `FileSensor` watching the docs folder. You can see that it’s up and running, **poking the folder every 15 seconds** for any changes.

At this point, I dragged a PDF into the folder, and it was **immediately detected**:

That detection triggered the rest of the pipeline automatically.

Take a look at the DAG run:

-   ✅ All steps executed in sequence.
-   ⏭️ Only `**check_or_create_collection**` was skipped — because Airflow saw the Qdrant collection already exists.
-   📥 The document was ingested successfully.

And yes — we can now **see the chunks and their embeddings inside Qdrant**! Just head over to `http://localhost:6333/dashboard` and check your collection.

### ☕ Ah… The Sweet Taste of Success

After only 8 hours of knocking into walls…

### 💻→🤯→😤→🥹→😎

This was one of those moments that reminded me _why_ I have a love–hate–love-again relationship with coding.

Airflow is powerful — but you have to master its power.

Your RAG application will now be able to call on new / updated documents that exist within the Qdrant collection!

This was my first foray into Airflow, inspired by the [DeepLearning.ai Airflow course](https://www.deeplearning.ai/short-courses/orchestrating-workflows-for-genai-applications/) and my colleagues.

I’ve always had deep respect for the data engineering profession — but now, I’m honestly _awestruck_. I came _this close_ to throwing my laptop across the room from all the debugging and failed runs.

And yet, data engineers show up _every day_, calmly managing the pipelines that power data-driven decisions across entire organizations. They are steady. Even-tempered. And essential.

### 🚨 **Important: This Is _Not_ Production Ready**

Running `airflow standalone` is [great for development](https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/stable/administration-and-deployment/production-deployment.html) — but it comes with serious limitations:

-   It uses **SQLite**, which [doesn’t support concurrent writes](https://narendrapalach1.medium.com/why-sqlite-is-not-for-production-ba72777e3367). This means no multi-user access, no scaling, and very fragile behavior.
-   There is **no resilient worker system** — no Celery executor, no distributed task queue. If the scheduler or worker crashes, your pipeline dies (I experienced this firsthand).
-   **No centralized log storage**, which makes debugging in distributed environments much harder.

In production, **resilience is non-negotiable**. You should be:

-   Using **PostgreSQL** or **MySQL** for the metadata database.
-   Running **CeleryExecutor** (or KubernetesExecutor) for proper task distribution.
-   Deploying Airflow across **multiple nodes** with health checks, retries, and monitoring.

🐳 **What About Docker?**

Funny you should ask.

Airflow _does_ provide a [comprehensive Docker Compose setup](https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/stable/howto/docker-compose/index.html) to spin up the full stack locally — webserver, scheduler, Redis, PostgreSQL, and more. But even that setup is **not production-grade**. And they say so clearly in their docs.

**Why?**

Because while Docker Compose is great for development, production needs **horizontal scaling** and **node-level fault tolerance** — the kind of orchestration Kubernetes (or Helm charts) is built for. Also, [Airflow candidly shares](https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/stable/howto/docker-compose/index.html) that the “best way to recover from any problem in Docker deployment is to clean up and restart from scratch”.

Basically: Docker is your training wheels. Production is a high-speed bike race — and you’re going to need better gear.

### Conclusion

✅ Made it this far? You’re now dangerous enough to build real-time RAG pipelines with Airflow and Qdrant.

Just don’t ship it to prod without proper infra support 😅

Increasingly, data scientists are expected to know _everything else_ — not just modeling or prompting. I’ll admit I’m still learning and honestly behind on many of the “non data analytics/ML/AI/genAI” parts of the stack. No, I’m not applying for any data engineering roles soon. 😅

But building these end-to-end generative AI apps (data pipeline, vector database, agent backend service, frontend) has given me real exposure to adjacent domains — and a whole new level of respect for the data engineering profession. It’s been a trial by fire, but one that’s strengthened my patience (I think) and broadened my view.

After all, even the best generative AI application is still **garbage in, garbage out**. And that means data remains the most important piece of the puzzle.

body:
* * *

#### Spoiler alert: memory is yet another application of RAG

It’s 2025, and “agentic applications” have taken center stage in the generative AI landscape. These autonomous agents can now plan, reason, and act — using tools, APIs, and knowledge bases to complete complex tasks. We’ve seen a surge of innovation: tool and agent interoperability protocols, orchestration frameworks, etc. — all pushing agent capabilities forward.

But there’s one simple upgrade that instantly makes **any agen**t better:

**Agent memory.**

In this article, I’ll walk through code examples that demonstrate how long-term memory can immediately upgrade your agent’s performance. You can find the full code in my [GitHub repository.](https://github.com/tituslhy/glowing-enigma)

### A very brief history of memory

Before we dive into code, it’s worth understanding the thinking behind memory implementations in modern LLM applications.

First and foremost:

> _🫠_ Memory isn’t just chat history. But it’s easy to confuse the two.

Most developers (OK, me) start by naively treating memory as nothing more than a running transcript — appending chat history into the LLM’s context window, along with the user’s current query and any RAG-retrieved chunks.

This works — until it doesn’t.

LLM context windows are finite. As chat history grows, you eventually can’t fit the relevant retrieved chunks from your knowledge base. And when that happens, the agent fails to ground its answers.

#### Smarter memory strategies emerged:

-   Summarizing prior messages into a compressed context within token limits. This does lose granularity — kind of like saying “I had a good day” instead of going through the elements of the day that made it good.
-   Buffering only the most recent “n” tokens from the conversation. This loses global context. If you spoke about what you had for dinner, the LLM might forget what you did before dinner.

Chat histories and their management strategies are still widely used today — and they help. But they don’t solve a fundamental problem:

**👉 Chat history is session-bound.**

Tell ChatGPT something important in one thread, and it’s gone in the next. You’ll have to copy-paste context manually — and even then, the response might differ depending on what history is missing.

### Introducing Long-term Memory

While users rarely complain about memory issues explicitly, the UX uplift from persistent memory is immediate and impactful.

**LlamaIndex** was one of the first to introduce a “vector memory” abstraction. In their [launch](https://docs.llamaindex.ai/en/stable/examples/agent/memory/vector_memory/), they emphasized that vector memory is distinct from chat history — it acts as _long-term memory_ for any agent.

It was basically RAG 🤣: vector memory required a vector store, and agents could then retrieve from it when responding.

So now, any agent could reason using:

-   **Short-term memory** (chat history),
-   **Tools** (APIs, calculators, search, etc.), and
-   **Long-term memory** (vector-retrieved chunks)

It was a paradigm shift — but important questions remained:

-   How should short-term memory be _flushed_ into long-term memory?
-   How does an LLM _know_ when to look at long-term memory? Should it always check?

Before LlamaIndex could standardize answers to these questions, **LangChain** released their own memory abstraction: [**LangMem**](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langmem/), with a completely different take.

#### 🔁 LangMem’s Take

LangChain’s **LangGraph** already had support for session persistence via a [_checkpointer_](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/concepts/persistence/) abstraction. Over time, they realized long-term memory could offer much more value — leading to LangMem.

LangMem introduces **three types of long-term memories:**

If you’re confused, you’re not alone — I followed [LangMem’s DeepLearning.AI course](https://www.deeplearning.ai/short-courses/long-term-agentic-memory-with-langgraph/) which walks through how LangMem can be implemented with LangGraph, but it’s still very _low-level_ and takes time to digest (I’m still wrapping my head around it!).

One key idea I picked up: LangMem provides a few additional tools to the agent — one to decide **when to update** memory, and another to decide **when to retrieve** it. This is powerful, but… what if the agent decides **not** to do either?

#### 🦙 Meanwhile, LlamaIndex Evolved Too

[LlamaIndex recently updated their memory system](https://docs.llamaindex.ai/en/stable/examples/memory/memory/) with:

-   StaticMemoryBlock
-   FactExtractionMemoryBlock
-   VectorMemoryBlock (same as RAG)

LlamaIndex also allows developers to:

-   Assign **priority levels** to memory blocks
-   Define a **token ratio** between short-term and long-term memory in each chat
-   Configure how many short-term memory tokens are flushed into long-term memory each time the token ratio condition is met.

I haven’t fully implemented this myself yet — like with LangMem, I’m still exploring how these abstractions work and how to apply them meaningfully.

#### 🧬 Not Just LangChain and LlamaIndex

It’s not just a two-horse race. One emerging framework that caught my attention with its focused approach to memory is [**Mem0AI**](https://mem0.ai/).

In a sea of tooling — vector databases, LLM orchestration platforms, observability dashboards, embedding models, rerankers — **Mem0AI stands out by specializing exclusively in long-term memory**. That alone is rare. Most frameworks treat memory as a bolt-on feature, a checkbox somewhere between prompt engineering and database lookups.

But Mem0AI treats memory as a **first-class citizen**.

That instantly piqued my interest — because while everyone talks about context management, **true persistent memory remains one of the most overlooked (and underbuilt) components in the GenAI ecosystem.**

And sure, you could say: _“Isn’t this just another form of RAG?”_

Well… yes. But also no. Mem0AI is rethinking _how_ memory is updated, retrieved, prioritized, and scoped across sessions — not just _that_ memory exists.

### Introducing Mem0AI

The [Mem0AI technical paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.19413) is an eye-opener.

The paper starts by emphasizing the power of long-term memory — showing how simply integrating Mem0 can lead to **a 26% performance improvement** in LLM applications. That’s not just theoretical; it comes from aligning memory design with _how humans actually converse_.

Here’s their insight:

1.  In human conversations, **relationships evolve over time** — across days, weeks, or even months. These interactions easily outgrow any LLM’s context window. And yet, we expect our AI agents to keep up.
2.  Even more challenging: **real conversations don’t follow a single topic**. You might start by talking to a colleague about work, switch to lunch plans, jump to how your kids are doing — then return to the original topic a week later. Most AI agents today can’t follow that arc. Stuffing everything into the context window? That’s not memory — it’s a **waste of tokens and money**. Agents are forced to reason through heaps of irrelevant information just to guess what matters.

Mem0 tackles this by treating memory not as a blob of transcript, but as a **dynamic, structured representation of long-term knowledge**, designed to support discontinuous, human-like conversations.

#### Mem0 AI’s take on memory

Based on Mem0 AI’s technical paper, their memory system revolves around two key phases: **extraction** and **update**.

**1\. Extraction Phase**

After each interaction (typically a user and assistant message), Mem0 kicks off an extraction step. It produces:

-   A **global summary** of the full conversation history
-   The **last m messages** for recent context
-   The **latest message pair** (user + assistant)

This combination gives the agent both a high-level overview and a short-term temporal view — enabling it to reason across time.

**2\. Update Phase**

Next, Mem0 compares these extracted insights against existing long-term memories. This is where RAG comes in — the system retrieves the top _s_ semantically similar memory entries.

These, plus the candidate new memory (fact), are passed to the LLM through a **tool call interface**. The LLM then chooses one of four actions:

-   ADD → Create a new memory if none exists
-   UPDATE → Augment an existing memory with new info
-   DELETE → Remove outdated or contradicted memories
-   NOOP → Leave everything unchanged

Importantly, Mem0 doesn’t rely on external classifiers. Instead, the LLM itself selects the appropriate memory operation — ADD, UPDATE, DELETE, or NOOP — using its own reasoning capabilities. This ensures memory updates are both semantically accurate and temporally coherent. Impressively, Mem0 even supports **multimodal memory types** — yes, images are supported too.

Since memory operations depend heavily on the LLM’s reasoning ability, using a strong model is recommended. Also, choose a capable vector database that supports multimodal search, like [**Qdrant**](https://qdrant.tech/).

While Mem0’s initial architecture was vector-based, it now supports **graph databases** as well (so the retrieval is richer because you recurse through the relationships as well). Their latest technical paper reports a ~2% performance gain when using graphDBs over vectorDBs — a modest but meaningful improvement, especially at scale.

And yes — Mem0 offers both an enterprise and an open-source version. The enterprise tier includes a generous free allowance, but the open-source package is equally powerful. Just plug in your vector or graph database, and you’re good to go.

That’s exactly what we’ll be doing in this article.

### Coding our app

I was pleasantly surprised to discover that Mem0 already offers [built-in integrations](https://docs.mem0.ai/integrations) with several popular LLM frameworks — including [**LlamaIndex**](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multiverse-part-3-llamaindex-798344050c49), [**LangChain**](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multiverse-part-1-langchain-023a899d294e), [**LangGraph**](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multi-agents-multiverse-part-1-langgraph-2ac56f1b5b3c), [**Autogen**](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multi-agent-multiverse-part-2-autogen-5401a0075d75), and [**CrewAI**](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multi-agent-multiverse-part-4-crewai-147ada6db54c) (and yes, I’ve written articles on all of them!).

As a huge LlamaIndex fan, I jumped straight into testing the integration. And let me tell you — it’s a humdinger. You literally need just **one extra argument** when running our agent. Elevating your agent’s capabilities like this almost feels like cheating.

For this walkthrough, we’ll define an agent with an **internet search tool**. I highly recommend [**Tavily**](https://www.tavily.com/) for this purpose — it’s fast, highly relevant, built for agents, and best of all it comes with a [generous free tier](https://www.tavily.com/#pricing) of **1,000 free API calls per month**.

```python
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv, find_dotenv
from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import FunctionAgent, AgentStream
from llama_index.llms.ollama import Ollama
from llama_index.tools.tavily_research.base import TavilyToolSpec

_ = load_dotenv(find_dotenv())
tavily_tool = TavilyToolSpec(api_key=os.environ.get("TAVILY_API_KEY"))
tools = tavily_tool.to_tool_list()
search_agent = FunctionAgent(
    tools=tools,
    llm=Ollama("qwen3"),
)
```

That’s the agent — just **4 lines of setup** (excluding imports) using LlamaIndex. Now let’s wire up the memory.

We’re going to test **Mem0’s graphRAG** capabilities, so we’ll spin up a **Neo4j instance with Docker**:

```bash
docker run \
    -p 7474:7474 -p 7687:7687 \
    -v $PWD/data:/data -v $PWD/plugins:/plugins \
    --name neo4j-apoc \
    -e NEO4J_apoc_export_file_enabled=true \
    -e NEO4J_apoc_import_file_enabled=true \
    -e NEO4J_apoc_import_file_use__neo4j__config=true \
    -e NEO4JLABS_PLUGINS=\[\"apoc\"\] \
    neo4j:latest
```

Mem0 expects a dictionary-style configuration. Here’s what that looks like:

```python
URL = os.environ["URL"]
USERNAME = os.environ["username"]
PASSWORD = os.environ["password"]

context = {"user_id": "titus"}
config = {
    "llm": {
        "provider": "openai",
        "config": {
            "model": "gpt-4o-mini",
            "temperature": 0.2,
            "max_tokens": 2000,
        }
    },
    "embedder": {
        "provider": "ollama",
        "config": {
            "model": "nomic-embed-text",
            "embedding_dims": 768
        }
    },
    "graph_store": {
        "provider": "neo4j",
        "config": {
            "url": URL,
            "username": USERNAME,
            "password": PASSWORD,
        }
    }
}
```

> **Note:** Pay special attention to the context variable — in a real-world app, you’d pass the user\_id of the active user (not a static string) to scope memory correctly.

Also, you’ll notice I’m using gpt-4o-mini as the LLM for memory, even though the agent runs on qwen3:7B. That’s deliberate. From personal experience, **OpenAI models tend to be more reliable for structured outputs** — I ran into Pydantic validation issues with Ollama-based models during memory updates.

Now, let’s set up our mem0 memory!

```python
from llama_index.memory.mem0 import Mem0Memory

memory = Mem0Memory.from_config(
    context = context,
    config = config,
)
```

That’s it!

Mem0 has also generously provided a utility function to display the graph in their [cookbook](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1PfIGVHnliIlG2v8cx0g45TF0US-jRPZ1?usp=sharing) — so we can use this for debugging. I’ve spruced up the code annotations and [included this function in my GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/glowing-enigma/blob/main/src/graph_utils.py) as well.

### Time to have some fun!

I’ve defined a quick function to invoke our agent:

```python
async def invoke_agent(query: str, return_response: bool = False) -> str | None:
    """Main runner function to invoke our search agent"""
    
    handler = search_agent.run(query, memory=memory)
    async for ev in handler.stream_events():
        if isinstance(ev, AgentStream):
            print(ev.delta, end="", flush=True)
    
    # This function came from Mem0's cookbook
    display_graph(uri=URL, username=USERNAME, password=PASSWORD)
    
    if return_response:
        response = await handler
        return response
```

Now let’s have a chat.

```python
await invoke_agent(
    "I'm a senior data scientist and I enjoy experimenting and
     writing about generative AI projects!"
)
```

```python-repl
That’s awesome to hear, Titus! 
As a senior data scientist passionate about generative AI, I’d love to hear 
about your projects or explore ideas together. Whether you’re experimenting 
with diffusion models, LLMs, or novel applications in Singapore’s tech 
ecosystem, feel free to share! What’s your current focus or a project you’re 
excited about? 😊
```

Our graph looks quite nice actually!

```python
await invoke_agent(
    """
    Let's talk about that later. I'm thinking of diversifying my skillsets 
    beyond machine learning and data science into adjacent fields.
    I keep hearing plenty of buzz in the quantum computing space. 
    
    How do I get started with quantum computing?
    """
)
```

I’ll skip the agent’s actual reply to this question (but it’s available in my notebook on GitHub). Here’s what our graph looks like:

Whoa! Help! Our graph looks so dense after just 1 question! Notice that we can do a lot with these graphs — like tailor the conversation towards the user’s preference.

### Taking a closer look at the integration

Here’s the base code as extracted from [LlamaIndex’s mem0 code](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/main/llama-index-integrations/memory/llama-index-memory-mem0/llama_index/memory/mem0/base.py):

```python
class Mem0Memory(BaseMem0):
    ... #other code omitted for brevity

    @classmethod
    def from_config(
        cls,
        context: Dict[str, Any],
        config: Dict[str, Any],
        search_msg_limit: int = 5,
        **kwargs: Any,
    ):
        primary_memory = ChatMemoryBuffer.from_defaults()

        try:
            context = Mem0Context(**context)
        except Exception as e:
            raise ValidationError(f"Context validation error: {e}")

        client = Memory.from_config(config_dict=config)
        return cls(
            primary_memory=primary_memory,
            context=context,
            client=client,
            search_msg_limit=search_msg_limit,
        )
    
     def get(self, input: Optional[str] = None, **kwargs: Any) -> List[ChatMessage]:
        """Get chat history. With memory system message."""
        messages = self.primary_memory.get(input=input, **kwargs)
        input = convert_messages_to_string(messages, input, limit=self.search_msg_limit)

        search_results = self.search(query=input, **self.context.get_context())

        if isinstance(self._client, Memory) and self._client.api_version == "v1.1":
            search_results = search_results["results"]

        system_message = convert_memory_to_system_message(search_results)

        # If system message is present
        if len(messages) > 0 and messages[0].role == MessageRole.SYSTEM:
            assert messages[0].content is not None
            system_message = convert_memory_to_system_message(
                response=search_results, existing_system_message=messages[0]
            )
        messages.insert(0, system_message)
        return messages
```

From the `.from_config()` method, we notice that there’s an attribute called `primary_memory` . That’s a `ChatMemoryBuffer` class, which means it’s actually the short-term, chat-specific memory!

The `get` method illuminates the interplay between short and long-term memories well. Notice that when the mem0 memory is invoked:

1.  We first get all the short-term messages, buffered to the default token limit.
2.  We then use the formatted messages to search our mem0 tool to get the relevant search results.
3.  Finally, we format the search results and pass along the formatted results along with the chat history back to the agent — so we get an enriched context.

It also gives us another avenue of testing. Let’s test how strong the long-term memory really is.

We’ll wipe the short-term buffer and see what Mem0 can still recall.

```python
memory.reset() #poof! wipe out the short-term memory
handler = search_agent.run(
    "Do you still remember what I do for a living?", 
    memory=memory
)

async for ev in handler.stream_events():
    if isinstance(ev, AgentStream):
        print(ev.delta, end="", flush=True)
```

```python-repl
... # omit the text under <think></think>. Qwen 3 is a reasoning model
I remember you're a senior data scientist based in Singapore with a strong 
interest in generative AI, quantum computing, and diversifying your skillset 
into adjacent fields. You're also keeping an eye on the data science job market 
in Singapore for 2025. How can I assist you further with your goals? 🌟
```

Awesome!

### What just happened?

Even after a memory wipe, Mem0 remembered who I was and what I cared about. This proves that Mem0 isn’t just reactive — it builds persistent, context-rich memories over time.

This lets our agent tailor every response based on past interactions — and it does so while updating the graph database live with each chat. Mem0 has also generously open-sourced their entire codebase. You can explore all the [rich prompts](https://github.com/mem0ai/mem0/blob/main/mem0/graphs/utils.py), [tools](https://github.com/mem0ai/mem0/blob/main/mem0/graphs/tools.py), and [graph integrations](https://github.com/mem0ai/mem0/blob/main/mem0/graphs/configs.py) on their GitHub — it’s incredibly instructive. Mem0 essentially orchestrates all memory behavior through **function calling**!

#### Are there tradeoffs?

Of course.

One of the most immediate is that long-term memories consume part of your LLM’s context window. That means fewer tokens for RAG chunks, tool calls, or short-term history. Some ways to mitigate this include:

-   [**Anthropic’s prompt caching**](https://www.anthropic.com/news/prompt-caching)
-   [**Microsoft’s prompt compression strategy**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12968) (PS: I enhanced [LlamaIndex’s prompt compression module](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/main/llama-index-integrations/postprocessor/llama-index-postprocessor-longllmlingua/llama_index/postprocessor/longllmlingua/base.py) to do just that!)
-   **Using models with ultra-long context windows**, like Google’s **Gemini**. For reference: [Gemini supports up to **1 million tokens**](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/long-context), while [GPT-4o handles **128k**](https://platform.openai.com/docs/models/gpt-4o).

> But before you upload your entire 800 page PDF into Gemini’s system prompt — take note: [a study showed that **performance** **degrades** in long-context generation scenarios](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.04199). That said, Gemini’s degradation isn’t terrible and still outperforms many competitors.

Another tradeoff? Mem0 **invokes memory tools on every turn** — so expect slightly higher LLM usage costs.

But if you’re chasing a more **cohesive, memory-aware user experience**? Totally worth it.

In fact, ChatGPT also uses memories for personalization of its user experience:

I’ve expressed [mixed feelings about GraphRAG before](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/graphrag-for-the-win-c19d580debd7), but this is a **great example of knowledge graphs done right**. I really enjoyed working with Mem0 — especially because it takes such a different (and in my opinion less confusing) approach compared to LlamaIndex and LangMem. It also orchestrates memory more cleanly, which suggests that Mem0’s vision for agentic memory is more fully realized.

It’s also kind of funny: Mem0 has integrations with both LangChain and LlamaIndex yet each continues building its own version of agentic memory. That’s the nature of the space — there’s no single winner. With the sheer momentum and breakneck speed of developments, I expect competition to drive even more innovation.

Strictly speaking, memory isn’t compulsory. But in my view, long-term memory is a “no-regrets” upgrade that improves almost any agentic application.

**Go ahead and give it a shot.**
