body:
* * *

#### ⚠️ Health warning: Sleepless nights ahead

Large language models (LLMs) are amazing.

Trained on vast corpora, they can converse fluently on many topics. But ask them about your internal knowledge base and things will quickly go off the rails — not only might the answer be wrong, it will likely be delivered with alarming confidence.

Retrieval augmented generation (“RAG”) emerged as the solution. By adding a dense embedding model to compute similarity scores between a user’s question and document chunks, we can retrieve the top k most relevant (highest scoring) chunks and plug them into the LLM’s context window. This grounds the LLM’s response, helping it to synthesize a more accurate answer.

While RAG is no longer the buzziest word in generative AI (it’s agentic applications now), it remains a foundational technique in many real-world use cases. For example, Text-to-SQL accuracies were reported to improve by as much 40 percentage points once with a RAG element — something I explored in a [previous article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/text-to-sql-just-got-easier-meet-vanna-ai-your-rag-powered-sql-sidekick-e781c3ffb2c5).

All this makes evaluating RAG systems crucial. But evaluation here is tricky.

-   Unlike conventional machine learning models, we don’t get a clean loss function, and
-   Unlike regular software, we cannot easily write CI-friendly unit tests — RAG systems often depend on vector stores or even GPUs which are not available in testing environments. That’s why I [previously wrote about mock-based testing for RAG](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-guide-to-code-testing-rag-agents-without-real-llms-or-vector-dbs-51154ad920be) — how to unit test logic and structure without needing real LLM calls or infrastructure.

In this article, we’ll go a step further: exploring how to evaluate your RAG application across **three different dimensions**, uncovering its blind spots before your users do.

Unlike mock-based testing, however, **we _do_ need to use an actual LLM, embedding model, and the full set of dependencies used in your real application**. All three evaluation dimensions use an LLM to test an LLM application.

All codes are available in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/bug-free-octo-pancake), specifically the `notebooks/rag.ipynb` Jupyter Notebook.

### **Let’s first start by defining our RAG application**

LlamaIndex allows for RAG applications to be defined in just 5 lines! We’re going to take a few more lines than that because we’re using IBM’s new [Docling](https://github.com/docling-project/docling) reader — a document parsing breakthrough generously open-sourced!

```python
from llama_index.core import Settings, VectorStoreIndex 
from llama_index.core.node_parser import MarkdownNodeParser
from llama_index.readers.docling import DoclingReader
from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI
from llama_index.embeddings.openai import OpenAIEmbedding

Settings.llm = OpenAI(
    model="gpt-4o",
    temperature = 0,
)
Settings.embed_model = OpenAIEmbedding()

reader = DoclingReader()
node_parser = MarkdownNodeParser()

documents = reader.load_data(
    "../data/hbs_oss_study.pdf"
)
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(
    documents = documents,
    transformations = [node_parser],
)
query_engine = index.as_query_engine()
```

And that’s it — a functioning RAG application! We use Harvard Business School’s latest [study](https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/24-038_51f8444f-502c-4139-8bf2-56eb4b65c58a.pdf) on the value of open sourced software (OSS) as our RAG knowledge base. It’s a very interesting article and I encourage everyone to read it!

### **Level 1: Correctness, Relevancy, Faithfulness and Similarity**

The “traditional” way of evaluating RAG is to score the application’s response, query and retrieval across four key categories:

-   **Faithfulness:** Does the answer stay true to the retrieved context? (i.e. no hallucinations)
-   **Relevancy:** Are the retrieved chunks and final answer actually relevant to the user’s query?
-   **Correctness:** Does the answer align with a ground-truth answer, as judged by an LLM?
-   **Similarity:** How close is the generated answer to the reference answer, based on vector similarity?

Fortunately, LlamaIndex already includes evaluations for all of these. Let’s first start by generating an evaluation set (or you could use your own dataset):

```python
from llama_index.core.llama_dataset.generator import RagDatasetGenerator

data_gen = RagDatasetGenerator.from_documents(
    documents,
    llm= Settings.llm,
    question_gen_query="You are a teacher/professor. Using the provided context, formulate a single question and its answer",
    num_questions_per_chunk=10
)
```

Now let’s use LlamaIndex’s `RagEvaluatorPack` to evaluate our RAG application:

```python
query_engine = index.as_query_engine()

rag_evaluator = RagEvaluatorPack(
    query_engine=query_engine, 
    rag_dataset=qa_dataset,
    judge_llm=Settings.llm, #use the same llm that we use to create the dataset to judge
    embed_model=Settings.embed_model
)
benchmark_df = rag_evaluator.run()
```

Presto! Here’s how our application performed:

-   ✅ **Correctness**: 3.88 / 5 (**A-**)
-   ✅ **Relevancy**: 0.89 / 1 (**A**)
-   ✅ **Faithfulness**: 0.97 / 1 (**A+**)
-   ✅ **Similarity**: 0.91 / 1 (**A+**)

These are the kinds of scores we love to see — they show that the **baseline system is solid**. Our RAG pipeline clearly answers questions well.

In fact, you’d be justified in publishing this application right away.

#### But hold on a second…

These scores tell us how **accurate** our RAG system is — but they don’t tell us how **robust** it is.

In AI, _robustness_ refers to how well a system performs under **input variation or attack** — think jailbreaking, prompt injection, etc.

High accuracy on a test set doesn’t guarantee reliability when things go sideways.

And that’s what we’ll explore next.

### Level 2: Redteaming with Giskard’s Scan

Of course, I have another framework to introduce — [Giskard](https://www.giskard.ai/)!

Giskard is a framework that comprehensively scans LLM applications to identify vulnerabilities. [Giskard’s course on DeepLearning.ai](https://www.deeplearning.ai/short-courses/red-teaming-llm-applications/) is also one of the most fun I’ve taken —it’s genuinely fascinating to see how they tease out weaknesses in even the best models.

Giskard’s scan runs the LLM application through a battery of tests across the following domains:

-   Hallucination and misinformation
-   Harmful content generation
-   Prompt injection
-   Robustness
-   Information Disclosure
-   Stereotypes and Discrimination

That is **_a lot of ground to cover_**, but the code to do this is surprisingly simple:

```python
import giskard
import pandas as pd

giskard.llm.set_llm_model("openai/gpt-4o")
giskard.llm.set_embedding_model("openai/text-embedding-ada-002")

def model_predict(df: pd.DataFrame):
    """Wraps the LLM call in a simple Python function.

    The function takes a pandas.DataFrame containing the input variables needed
    by your model, and must return a list of the outputs (one for each row).
    """
    return [str(query_engine.query(question)) for question in df['question']]

giskard_model = giskard.Model(
    model = model_predict,
    model_type = "text_generation",
    name = "Chatbot on Harvard Business School's study on Open Sourced Software (OSS)",
    description = "This model answers questions relating to HBS' study on the value of OSS",
    feature_names = ["question"],
)
examples = [
    "Why is there a difference between the supply side value of OSS and the demand side value of OSS?",
    "Why is OSS important even in enterprise software applications?",
    "How do the authors compute the value of OSS?"
]
giskard_dataset = giskard.Dataset(pd.DataFrame({"question": examples}), target = None)
full_report = giskard.scan(giskard_model,giskard_dataset)
```

We begin by setting the global LLM and embedding model for Giskard.

> **Under the hood, Giskard uses** [**LiteLLM**](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm) **to manage your LLM configurations**, so if you encounter issues here it’s worth checking [LiteLLM’s documentation](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/#basic-usage). LiteLLM acts as a compatibility layer, standardizing API calls across providers to match OpenAI’s format.

Next, we **wrap the application’s prediction logic** in a simple function, then encapsulate that function in a `Giskard.Model` object. This is what Giskard will invoke during the scan.

We then provide a few **seed questions** — Giskard will use these to generate variations and adversarial probes. Importantly, **we don’t need to supply reference answers** — this isn’t about accuracy, but vulnerability.

The dataset is just a list of example questions in a pandas DataFrame, wrapped with `Giskard.Dataset`.

Finally, we kick off the scan. Want to focus on just one area, like hallucination? Just add:

```python
giskard.scan(..., only=["hallucination"])
```

The scan can take a while — mine took about **10 minutes** — and Giskard is transparent about usage. For instance, it warned me upfront that it would make **~365 LLM calls**.

Once done, you can visualize the report directly:

```python
from IPython.display import display
display(full_report)
```

And then… 💥 Oh no! Giskard detected **6 issues**, 5 of which were marked as **major (in red)**.

Under the hallucination and misinformation category, Giskard successfully tricked our LLM by tweaking the question — it picked up on inconsistent outputs!

Under the harmfulness category there were 3 failing samples. One particularly direct test asked how OSS could be exploited for illegal hacking, and our RAG application gave a coherent answer 😬.

Some issues were **false alarms** — for instance, in the bias detection category, Giskard injected a demographic slant. While our LLM didn’t take the bait, it still got penalized for not explicitly debunking the bias.

👉 So take note: **not every red or amber flag signals a real flaw** — it’s important to read each alert carefully and in context.

Getting nightmares yet? 😅 We’re still not done.

Given how crucial RAG is for grounding LLM responses, Giskard has gone one step further: it developed a specialized evaluation suite just for RAG systems — the **RAG Evaluation Toolkit**, or **“RAGET”**.

### Level 3: Redteaming with Giskard’s RAGET

[Giskard’s **RAGET**](https://docs.giskard.ai/en/stable/reference/notebooks/RAGET_IPCC.html) takes stress testing to the next level.

Unlike LlamaIndex’s evaluation (which sticks mostly to direct, clean QA), RAGET deliberately creates challenging question types to probe the limits of your RAG pipeline.

Here’s how those questions are categorized:

-   **Simple**: Questions directly generated from a document excerpt.  
     _E.g.:_ “What is the value of open source software?”
-   **Complex**: Questions made harder via paraphrasing or multi-part structure.  
    _E.g.:_ “What are the demand-side and supply-side values of OSS, and why do they differ?”
-   **Distracting**: Questions with context designed to throw off retrieval.  
    _E.g.:_ “Open-source software is free of charge — so what is its value?”
-   **Situational**: Questions grounded in a user’s context or background.  
     _E.g.:_ “I use a lot of open source frameworks at work — what’s the value of OSS?”
-   **Double**: Two distinct questions packed into one.  
     _E.g.:_ “What is OSS and how is its value measured?”
-   **Conversational**: Follow-up questions within a simulated multi-turn chat. Chat histories are needed here.  
     _E.g.:_ “That makes sense. But how do they actually calculate OSS value?”

And here’s the kicker — **our Level 1 evaluation only covered the “simple” category**!

All the rest? Still lurking as potential blind spots unless we test for them.

#### 💻 The Code (Surprisingly Simple Again)

```python
from giskard.rag import (
    AgentAnswer,
    KnowledgeBase,
    QATestset,
    RAGReport,
    evaluate,
    generate_testset
)

text_nodes = node_parser(documents)
knowledge_base_df = pd.DataFrame(
    [node.text for node in text_nodes], columns=["text"]
)
knowledge_base = KnowledgeBase(knowledge_base_df)
testset = generate_testset(
    knowledge_base, 
    num_questions=120, 
    agent_description="A chatbot answering questions about the Harvard Business School's OSS report"
)
```

This generates a full test suite across all question types using your configured LLM. We also wrap our source documents into a Giskard `KnowledgeBase` object — and then define a callback function to run our RAG pipeline:

```python
from llama_index.core.base.llms.types import ChatMessage
from giskard.rag.metrics.ragas_metrics import (
    ragas_context_precision,
    ragas_context_recall
)

chat_engine = index.as_chat_engine()

def answer_fn(
    question: str,
    history: list[dict] = None,
) -> AgentAnswer:
    if history:
        answer = chat_engine.chat(
            question,
            chat_history=[
                ChatMessage(**chat_history_dict) for chat_history_dict in history
            ],
        )
    else:
        answer = chat_engine.chat(question, chat_history=[])
    return AgentAnswer(
        message = str(answer),
        documents=[source.content for source in answer.sources]
    )
```

Notice we’re using **LlamaIndex’s chat engine abstraction** — because we need chat history. Isn’t LlamaIndex excellent for developer experience? Just change “index.as\_query\_engine” to “index.as\_chat\_engine” and it immediately handles chat history.

The reason: its query engine doesn’t support `chat_history` as input, which we _do_ need when testing **conversational** capabilities.

Finally, we run the evaluation:

```python
report = evaluate(
    answer_fn, testset=testset, 
    knowledge_base=knowledge_base,
    metrics=[ragas_context_recall, ragas_context_precision],
)
```

> If you ran into issues with Giskard’s `RagasEmbeddingsWrapper`, you’re not alone — I did too. It’s due to a bug that I’ve fixed and submitted as a [pull request to Giskard](https://github.com/Giskard-AI/giskard/issues/2177). Feel free to refer to my fix if needed

We specify our metrics to be **recall and precision** as here, as defined by the [Ragas framework](https://github.com/explodinggradients/ragas) — a specialized RAG evaluation toolkit with the [same evaluation metrics that we used back in Level 1](https://docs.ragas.io/en/v0.1.21/howtos/integrations/llamaindex.html). The evaluation might take awhile — it took me 16 minutes.

```python
display(report.to_html(embed=True))
```

**💥Oh no! Our overall correctness score is only 58%!**

At least Giskard graciously suggests where to improve — namely to “focus on improving the generator” (i.e. the LLM’s actual outputs), and to include “questions paraphrasing” capabilities. In other words, Giskard successfully fooled our LLM to answer incorrectly with all the rephrasing and inclusion of distracting contexts.

The final report is impressively detailed (only showing the top level results here), with a full breakdown of how our RAG application performed across different question types and topics.

As you might guess, we did well on **simple questions**, but got absolutely wrecked by **distracting** and **complex** ones. Surprisingly, we held up decently against **double** and **situational** questions — which gives me some hope.

Still, overall… we’re looking at a **sub-50% score** across the board. Ouch.

### Can we actually get a 100% score on all 3 levels?

Giskard’s reports are the stuff of nightmares when I run them on production projects at work — unless I’m running them on someone else’s project, haha.

I’m always amazed at how easily it manages to trick my LLM — often in ways I _can’t_, and believe me, I try hard.

That said, I often wonder: _would real users even ask these kinds of tricky questions?_

But here’s the thing — you can’t control end-user behavior. So I always assume the worst and do my best to harden the system.

So… is it possible to score 100% across all three levels?

👉 **Level 1?** Honestly, it’s **mathematically impossible**. You’re relying on vector similarity and LLM-based judgments — both inherently fuzzy and probabilistic. Nobody would (or should) trust a 100% score on “semantic similarity” for example. Plus we’re already doing very well!

👉 **Level 2?** Yes — this one is achievable. In fact, I’ve consistently hit 100% at work, and I did it in a [previous article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/hyde-and-seek-when-hallucination-leads-the-way-17a9800734fe) (spoiler: I used **HyDE + DSPy** for my article). Even though we didn’t score 100% in this article, do note that of the 365 LLM calls there were only 6 failed cases — so that percentage isn’t too bad.

👉 **Level 3?** I’ve never cracked this one fully — the test set is intentionally challenging and probes complex behaviors across multiple dimensions. We should however be able to score much better than 58%!

#### Is there a tradeoff to scoring A+ on all 3 tests?

Yes, absolutely. Achieving top scores often means adding more components to your RAG system — for example, a **reranker**, **hybrid retrieval** (to include keyword search alongside dense retrieval), or **query rewriting**.

The tradeoff is complexity: more moving parts, more maintenance, and potentially slower inference.

Our current setup is intentionally minimal — just a dense embedding search with no extra layers.

And here’s another reality:  
You might build an app that scores perfectly on all redteaming tests… but still fails user acceptance testing. That’s why it’s often better to **prioritize Level 1 (accuracy)** and **UAT** first, before going all-in on robustness layers.

### The hard truth about LLMs

Let’s talk about something uncomfortable.

In this entire process, we’ve been using the same LLM — GPT-4o — as our RAG engine, our judge LLM, our test LLM… everything.

So the questions arise:

-   Should we be using a “stronger” LLM as judge?
-   Why not just use the **strongest model** everywhere?
-   Could we “game the system” by testing with a weaker LLM that our RAG LLM can easily outperform?

All fair questions.

But here’s what Giskard’s own research shows: **no LLM is perfect**. In their [_Phare_ benchmark](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.11365v2) (which evaluates LLMs across redteaming metrics), every single model — even the top ones — gets tripped up.

Some older LLMs even outperform newer ones in certain areas!

What _is_ consistent, though, is that most models show decent “harm resistance” — likely due to built-in guardrails during training.

But overall? **LLMs remain susceptible**. And crucially:

> 🔒 Never use a weaker LLM as your judge. That defeats the purpose of redteaming.

#### A smarter defense: Layered LLM Systems

One powerful strategy is to **layer your application with different LLMs**. For example:

-   Your **question rewriter** could use a different model from GPT-4o.
-   You could integrate [**Llama Guard**](https://ai.meta.com/research/publications/llama-guard-llm-based-input-output-safeguard-for-human-ai-conversations/) — a fine-tuned 8B model from Meta’s _Purple Llama_ project — to scan for malicious prompts _before_ they reach the core LLM, and to screen generated outputs from your LLM _before_ they’re shown to users.
-   You could add non-generative AI based guardrails – specially finetuned BERT based classifiers to detect certain metrics or even good old regex. These are available in a few frameworks — [guardrails AI](https://www.guardrailsai.com) is one of the most popular and they have a [course on deeplearning.AI](https://www.deeplearning.ai/short-courses/safe-and-reliable-ai-via-guardrails/) too!

This approach makes it significantly harder — for both malicious users and redteaming tools like Giskard — to break your system.

But let’s be honest, **no setup is bulletproof**. There’s still a risk due to:

-   **Training data overlap** across LLMs,
-   Open-source models being **distilled or reverse-engineered** from closed-source ones,
-   And [chilling research](https://llm-attacks.org/) showing that it’s _technically feasible_ to train neural networks that learn shared “backdoors” across LLM families.

### Concluding thoughts

#### 🛡️ **It’s easier to attack than defend.**

Attacks can emerge from unexpected angles — and defenses are often reactive. Sometimes you only discover a weakness after it’s been exploited.

While aiming for A+ scores across the board is admirable, it’s not always necessary. **What matters most is knowing your system’s limits.**

You also shouldn’t wait for perfection before launching — unless your use case is mission-critical. Getting early value from your GenAI app (e.g., saving hours of manual search with RAG) often outweighs chasing perfect test scores.

We should instead take a cue from OpenAI:

Transparency about limitations builds trust. So be upfront with users — **and keep improving**.

body:
* * *

#### Spoiler alert: Text-to-SQL is powered by retrieval augmented generation (RAG)

### The Generative AI Revolution

When [ChatGPT launched in late 2022](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt/), it felt like generative AI had appeared out of nowhere. Suddenly, we had human-like conversations with a machine — and surprisingly accurate answers across a wide range of topics.

One of the earliest practical use cases that emerged was **retrieval augmented generation** (RAG). In a nutshell, RAG:

1.  Uses dense embeddings to perform vector similarity search on a knowledge base, and
2.  Injects the most relevant chunks of data into the LLM’s context window so it can generate a grounded, relevant response.

RAG became synonymous with unstructured data: PDFs, webpages, knowledge bases, allowing LLMs to answer questions on domains not in its training dataset. But the buzz has since shifted — RAG feels less shiny compared to LLM agents and function-calling workflows.

Still, don’t count RAG out.

### RAG Is Quietly Powering Structured Data Too

In fact, RAG is the secret behind many **Text-to-SQL** systems today. This article aims to challenge the myth that RAG is only for free-form text — and show you how it’s being used (effectively!) to query structured datasets.

Let’s start with a simple question:

### Are LLMs good at SQL?

LLMs have been trained on massive amounts of code, including SQL. So, it’s no surprise that developers using ChatGPT or GitHub Copilot can often get decent SQL queries from natural language prompts.

But “decent” isn’t always enough.

In practice, many developers report inconsistent accuracy — particularly for complex queries or unusual schemas. Even powerful models like GPT-4 can struggle to generate correct SQL on the first try.

Snowflake, in fact, ran internal benchmarks that revealed sobering evidence of LLMs in Text-to-SQL performance. That led them to launch **Cortex Analyst**, their own service with a more deliberate approach, yielding promising results as displayed in the following chart.

> **Yes. GPT-4o was tested to only have an accuracy of 51%!**

While Cortex Analyst has shown very promising results (I’ve tested it and it performs well), it’s not open source.

The key takeaway? **We need to rethink how we approach Text-to-SQL.**

### Reintroducing RAG: your old friend in a new role

Recent [research surveys](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.01066) show that more and more Text-to-SQL systems are grounded in RAG-based designs. Some even propose _graphRAG_, which combines graph-based knowledge representation with retrieval and generation (I’ve previously expressed [mixed views on graphRAG](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/graphrag-for-the-win-c19d580debd7)).

In this article, we’ll take a hands-on look at how **traditional vector-based RAG** can be used for structured data — using [**Vanna AI**](https://vanna.ai/), a high-level framework purpose-built for Text-to-SQL.

#### Why Vanna AI?

Vanna abstracts away the orchestration layer of building a Text-to-SQL application powered by RAG. Instead of wrestling with embeddings, prompt templates, and database schema alignment, you can focus on business logic and query accuracy.

We’ll build a complete Text-to-SQL app over **Yahoo Finance stock data**, using Vanna’s Python SDK.

All codes can be found in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/glowing-engine/tree/main).

### 1\. Setup — Ingesting data from Yahoo Finance

First let’s ingest historical stock data from Yahoo Finance into an SQLite database using the `yfinance` Python package.

📁 **Notebook**: notebooks/setup\_db.ipynb

```python
import yfinance as yf
from sqlalchemy import (
    create_engine,
    MetaData,
    Table,
    Column,
    Float,
    DateTime,
    Integer
)
import sqlite3
from datetime import datetime
from tqdm.notebook import tqdm

today = datetime.today().strftime("%Y-%m-%d")

def insert_data(
    db_path: str,
    ticker: str,
    date_start: str,
    date_end: str,
) -> None:
    """Function to insert data into a SQLite  database."""
    
    try:
        data = yf.download(ticker, start=date_start, end=date_end, group_by="ticker")
    except Exception as e:
        raise e
    data = data.xs(ticker, axis=1, level="Ticker")
    data = data.reset_index()
    engine = create_engine(f"sqlite:///{db_path}")
    metadata_obj = MetaData()
    table = Table(
        ticker.lower(),
        metadata_obj,
        Column("id", Integer, primary_key=True),
        Column("date", DateTime),
        Column("open", Float),
        Column("high", Float),
        Column("low", Float),
        Column("close", Float),
        Column("volume", Integer),
    )
    metadata_obj.create_all(engine)
    conn = sqlite3.connect(db_path)
    data.to_sql(
        ticker.lower(),
        conn,
        if_exists='append',
        index=False
    )
    print(f"Ticker {ticker} added to database")

for ticker in tqdm(["ILMN", "AAPL", "NVDA"]):
    insert_data(
        db_path = "../database/stocks.db",
        ticker=ticker,
        date_start="2020-01-01",
        date_end=today
    )
```

At this point, we have a local database containing multiple years of historical data for three major tech stocks. This will serve as the structured dataset that we’ll query using natural language.

### 2\. Now let’s set up Vanna!

Next, let’s configure Vanna — a framework that abstracts much of the boilerplate needed for RAG-powered Text-to-SQL systems.

To get started, we’ll create a `MyVanna`class that inherits from two core Vanna components:

-   `ChromaDB_VectorStore`: Handles vector storage and retrieval.
-   `OpenAI_Chat`: Wraps the LLM (in our case, OpenAI GPT models).

These two parent classes implement all the abstract methods required by Vanna’s `VannaBase`, so our subclass only needs to handle initialization logic.

📁 **Script**: vn.py

```python
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv, find_dotenv
import warnings
from typing import Dict, Optional, Annotated, Tuple, List
import yaml

from vanna.openai.openai_chat import OpenAI_Chat
from vanna.chromadb.chromadb_vector import ChromaDB_VectorStore
from openai import OpenAI
from tqdm import tqdm

_ = load_dotenv(find_dotenv())
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

__curdir__ = os.getcwd()
if "notebooks" in __curdir__:
    chroma_path = "../chroma"
    yaml_file_path = "../config/training.yaml"
else:
    chroma_path = "./chroma"
    yaml_file_path = "./config/training.yaml"

class MyVanna(ChromaDB_VectorStore, OpenAI_Chat):
    """Our main Vanna handler. Inherits from Vanna's ChromaDB_VectorStore
    and OpenAI_Chat which implement many of the abstract methods in Vanna's
    Base class. The only thing we need to do is define the constructor where
    we initialize the different objects."""
    
    def __init__(
        self, 
        config: Optional[Annotated[
            Dict[str, str], 
            """The configuration for the vector store path or the LLM you want to use. 
            For e.g. {'model':'gpt-4o'}"""
        ]]
    ) -> None:
        ChromaDB_VectorStore.__init__(self, config=config)
        OpenAI_Chat.__init__(
            self,
            client = OpenAI(),
            config = config
        )
```

### But what exactly are we storing and querying from the vector store?

This is where the magic begins. We’re going to store **question–SQL pairs** in the vector store — this collection effectively becomes our **training data**. Vanna then builds a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) application on top of this, enabling natural language to SQL translation with high accuracy.

Here’s a simplified look at what Vanna does under the hood:

1.  **User submits a question** (e.g., “What’s the average closing price of NVDA in 2023?”).
2.  Vanna **searches the vector store** — this includes:

-   Data definition language (DDL)/schema information
-   Documentation
-   Stored question–SQL pairs (training data)

3\. The search results are **injected into an LLM prompt**.

4\. The LLM **generates a SQL query**, considering all retrieved context.

> _✅ The more relevant question–SQL pairs we store, the higher the SQL generation accuracy._

> _⚠️ If the LLM can’t find a close match, it falls back to reasoning based on schema/docs alone — which Snowflake estimates to be ~50% accurate. So be prepared for imperfect queries in that case!_

5\. The generated SQL is **executed against the database**, returning a data table.

6\. The table, SQL query, and original question are **fed back into the LLM**, which now generates **Plotly chart code**.

7\. The code is executed, and finally the **figure**, **SQL query**, and **data table** are displayed at the front end.

And the beauty is — all of this is orchestrated by our `MyVanna` class, and we only defined the constructor!

> ✨ Talk about code mileage — never have so few lines of code done so much!

### 3\. 🛠️ Loading Your Training Data & Setting Up Vanna

You could store your training question-SQL pairs in many ways, such as a list of dictionaries. I chose to use a YAML file for readability.

I only wrote a few training queries in my YAML file. For brevity, I’m showing just the first question–answer pair below. The rest are replaced with “…”, but you can refer to the full SQL queries in config/training.yaml.

📁 **Script**: config/training.yaml

```yaml
---
- question: >
    What is the highest historical closing stock price of illumina from 2020-2024, and when did it occur?
  answer: |
    SELECT date, close
    FROM ilmn
    WHERE date BETWEEN '2020-01-01' AND '2024-12-31'
    ORDER BY close DESC
    LIMIT 1;

- question: >
    What is the 7-day (1 week) rolling average of Apple shares from 2020-2024?  
  answer : ...

- question: >
    What is the longest running uptrend in prices of NVIDIA shares?  
  answer: ...

- question: >
    Is there any correlation between Apple and NVIDIA share prices?  
  answer: ...
```

Here’s the function I wrote to load the YAML into a list of (question, answer) tuples:

🔁 Continued from vn.py

```python
def load_query_data(yaml_file_path: str) -> List[Tuple[str, str]]:
    """Returns a list of training queries for LLM training.
    
    This is a mission critical function.
    """
    try:
        with open(yaml_file_path, 'r') as file:
            try:
                documents = yaml.safe_load(file)
                if not isinstance(documents, list):
                    raise ValueError("YAML content is not a list of documents.")
            except yaml.YAMLError as yaml_error:
                raise ValueError(f"Error parsing YAML file: {yaml_error}") from yaml_error
    except FileNotFoundError as fnf_error:
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Error: The file at {yaml_file_path} was not found.") from fnf_error
    except Exception as e:
        raise Exception(f"An unexpected error occurred: {e}") from e

    return [(doc.get('question'), doc.get('answer')) for doc in documents]
    
print("Instantiating Vanna...")
vn = MyVanna(config={
    "model": "gpt-4o",
    "path": chroma_path, #this is the specific key that Vanna looks for (reference: Vanna's ChromaDB_VectorStore source code)
})
```

Next, let’s instantiate our `MyVanna` class and train it. We’ll configure it to use gpt-4o, and point it to our Chroma vector store.

🔁 Continued from vn.py

```python
print("Instantiating Vanna...")
vn = MyVanna(config={
    "model": "gpt-4o",
    "path": chroma_path, #this is the specific key that Vanna looks for (reference: Vanna's ChromaDB_VectorStore source code)
})

print("Connecting Vanna to SQL database...")
vn.connect_to_sqlite("./database/stocks.db")

print("Training Vanna...")
df_ddl = vn.run_sql("SELECT type, sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE sql is not null")
for ddl in df_ddl['sql'].to_list():
    vn.train(ddl=ddl)
vn.train(documentation="Illumina is defined as ilmn")
vn.train(documentation="Apple is defined as aapl")
vn.train(documentation="NVIDIA is defined as nvda")

queries = load_query_data(yaml_file_path=yaml_file_path)
for question, sql in tqdm(queries):
    vn.train(question=question, sql=sql)
```

And finally, Vanna provides a super handy Flask utility to spin up a working web app:

🔁 Continued from vn.py

```python
if __name__ == "__main__":
    from vanna.flask import VannaFlaskApp
    
    app = VannaFlaskApp(vn)
    app.run()
```

#### 🧩 Recap

-   We **instantiated** a MyVanna object with our preferred LLM and ChromaDB location.
-   We **connected** to our SQLite database and extracted its schema.
-   We added **inline documentation** to help the LLM interpret our tables.
-   We **loaded and trained** Vanna with custom question–SQL pairs from a YAML file.
-   And we **launched a full Flask app** with just a few lines of code.

> 🍝 Once again, a chef’s kiss for code mileage. You set up a fully functional RAG pipeline over a SQL database — and it took like 2 minutes (excluding training data prep).

### 4\. 🧑‍💻 Interacting with our Flask App

Once you’ve run the script, Vanna spins up a Flask app at [http://localhost:8084](http://localhost:8084) by default.

And just look at how **clean** the interface is:

You can:

✅ **Browse and edit your training data**

✅ **Ask questions in natural language**

✅ **See the generated SQL query, output dataframe, and Plotly chart**

✅ **Add new question–SQL pairs directly into your training set**

One especially clever feature: if Vanna generates a good SQL query in response to your question, you can save it — with a single click — into your training set. This creates a **self-reinforcing feedback loop**: the more you use it, the better your system gets.

### 🧱 But it’s not perfect…

There are a couple of limitations worth noting:

-   ❌ **Does not directly answer the question**: Vanna gives you a chart and table, but you’re left to decide if it answers your original question. Personally, I found this to be the most annoying part.
-   ❌ **Risk of bad training data:** Since users can add new question–SQL pairs directly into the training data, there’s a risk of injecting inaccurate or misleading queries — especially in multi-user environments.
-   ❌ **Limited UX customization**: Because the framework is high-level, making deep UX changes is hard unless you inherit from `VannaFlaskApp` and customize it. [The script](https://github.com/vanna-ai/vanna/blob/main/src/vanna/flask/__init__.py) spans over 1,200 lines — so expect a learning curve.
-   ❌ **Frontend tweaking needs HTML/JS/CSS**: If you want to refine the frontend UI (e.g., layout, interactivity), you’ll need to supply your own .html, .js and .css files and pass them into the `VannaFlaskApp` constructor. I haven’t done this — mostly because I don’t code in JavaScript.

### 5.💡Bringing Chainlit into the picture

But I do code in (and love) Chainlit! I rewrote the frontend in just 150 lines of pure Python — exactly how I wanted it. The base source code is [generously contributed by Vanna AI](https://github.com/vanna-ai/vanna-chainlit). I simply extended its capabilities and fixed dependency issues from using the latest versions of both frameworks.

While exploring Vanna’s internals, I realized it cleanly separates SQL generation, execution, and plotting so I’ve spaced these out as “steps” in Chainlit.

Even better, it can suggest follow-up questions — so I added that as a new step in Chainlit.

📁 **Script**: app.py

```python
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv, find_dotenv
from typing import List, Dict

import chainlit as cl
from vn import vn
from llama_index.core.base.llms.types import ChatMessage
from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI

_ = load_dotenv(find_dotenv())

@cl.step(type="tool", language="sql", name="write_sql")
async def gen_query(human_query: str):
    sql = vn.generate_sql(human_query)
    return sql

@cl.step(type="tool", name="execute_sql")
async def execute_query(query):
    current_step = cl.context.current_step
    df = vn.run_sql(query)
    current_step.output = df.to_markdown(index=False)
    return df

@cl.step(type="tool", name="plot", language="python")
async def plot(human_query, sql, df):
    current_step = cl.context.current_step
    plotly_code = vn.generate_plotly_code(
        question=human_query,
        sql=sql,
        df=df
    )
    current_step.output = plotly_code
    fig = vn.get_plotly_figure(plotly_code=plotly_code, df=df, dark_mode=True)
    return fig

@cl.step(type="llm", name="follow_up")
async def generate_follow_up(human_query, sql, df):
    current_step = cl.context.current_step
    questions = vn.generate_followup_questions(
        question=human_query,
        sql=sql,
        df=df,
    )
    questions = questions[:3] #we're only taking 3 follow-ups
    current_step.output = ", ".join(questions)
    return questions
```

Next, I chained the steps together and piped the resulting DataFrame into the LLM’s context window using LlamaIndex.

_🔁_ Continued from app.py

```python
@cl.step(type="run", name="run_text_to_sql_engine")
async def chain(human_query: str):
    ## Generate SQL query
    sql_query = await gen_query(human_query)
    
    ## Get dataframe from executing SQL query
    df = await execute_query(sql_query)
    
    ## Get plotly object from plot
    fig = await plot(
        human_query = human_query,
        sql = sql_query,
        df = df
    )
    
    ## Generate follow-up questions
    follow_ups = await generate_follow_up(
        human_query = human_query,
        sql = sql_query,
        df = df
    )
    
    ## Wrap the follow-up questions into a Chainlit button (Action)
    actions = [
        cl.Action(
            name="question",
            payload = {"value": question},
            label = question
        ) for question in follow_ups
    ]

    ## Wrap the chart and dataframe elements into a list for rendering
    ## inline with the final message
    
    elements = [
        cl.Plotly(name="chart", figure=fig, display="inline"),
        cl.Dataframe(data=df, display="inline", name="Dataframe")
    ]
    
    ## Generate insights    
    history = cl.user_session.get("history")
    history.append(
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": human_query + f"Data:\n\n{df}",
        }
    )
    chat_history = prepare_chat_history(history)
    llm = cl.user_session.get("llm")
    
    msg = cl.Message("", type="assistant_message")
    response = llm.stream_chat(chat_history)
    final_response = ""
    
    ### Stream response
    for chunk in response:
        await msg.stream_token(chunk.delta)
        final_response += chunk.delta
    
    ## Update session chat history
    history.append(
        {
            "role": "assistant",
            "content": final_response
        }
    )
    cl.user_session.set("history", history)
    
    msg.elements = elements
    msg.actions = actions
    await msg.send()
```

Finally, we define the Chainlit chat lifecycle: how the app initializes, handles user messages, reacts to follow-up clicks, and offers starter prompts to guide users into the flow.

_🔁_ Continued from app.py

```python
@cl.on_chat_start
async def on_chat_start():
    history = []
    llm = OpenAI(
        model="gpt-4o",
        temperature=0
    )
    cl.user_session.set("llm", llm)
    cl.user_session.set("history", history)

@cl.on_message
async def on_message(message: cl.Message):
    await chain(human_query = message.content)

@cl.action_callback(name="question")
async def action_callback(action):
    message = action.payload['value']
    await chain(message)

@cl.set_starters
async def set_starters():
    return [
        cl.Starter(
            label="What is the highest stock price for Illumina?",
            message="What is the highest ever stock price for Illumina?",
            icon="public/max_price.png",
        ),
        cl.Starter(
            label="NVIDIA overview",
            message="Give me an overview of NVIDIA's share price from 2020-2024",
            icon="public/chart.png",
        ),
        cl.Starter(
            label="Longest bull run",
            message="What is the longest running uptrend for Apple share prices?",
            icon="public/bullrun.png",
        )
    ]
```

Just for fun, we named our app “Bull Run”. Here’s a video of what our app looks like:

With just ~150 lines of Python, we’ve wired up a full-text-to-chart experience using Vanna, Chainlit, and LlamaIndex — with follow-up prompts and inline visualizations.

Best of all, it’s modular and hackable. You can now swap in your own SQL sources, tweak plot logic, or experiment with different LLMs.

### 📌 Text-to-SQL Hits Different with RAG

RAG changes the game. By incorporating documentation, database schema, and example queries, it guides the LLM toward more accurate SQL generation. While it’s not yet at the level of Snowflake’s Cortex Analyst, a **20+ percentage point accuracy boost** is a big win!

### 🦙 Vanna is Surprisingly Powerful

Vanna orchestrates the entire pipeline — perhaps **too** seamlessly!

In this article, we built a full-fledged text-to-SQL application with plotting and basic data analysis, all in under 200 lines of code with the help of Chainlit.

Vanna isn’t obscure either — it’s **well-loved by the open source community** and was [recently awarded the **Google Cloud Ready — BigQuery** designation](https://vanna.ai/blog/vanna-google-cloud-ready-bigquery.html). That badge of confidence comes after three rounds of technical validation by Google Cloud’s engineering team. As Vanna and Google deepen their collaboration, we can expect even more capabilities.

### 🧩 Vanna Isn’t the Only Solution

Snowflake’s Cortex, for instance, also takes a RAG-style approach. Their “semantic view” acts as an enriched representation of the database schema, and training queries provide helpful priors. They even suggest a multi-agent architecture with built-in error correction. (Confession: I think about how to implement that every day.)

Other frameworks also explore this space. **LlamaIndex** also adopts a [RAG-centric approach to text-to-SQL](https://docs.llamaindex.ai/en/stable/examples/index_structs/struct_indices/SQLIndexDemo/), while **LangChain** relies [more on the LLM’s native reasoning capabilities](https://python.langchain.com/docs/tutorials/sql_qa/#convert-question-to-sql-query), which may limit performance on complex queries as we saw in Snowflake’s study.

It’s almost poetic — **a technique born from unstructured data becomes the secret ingredient for querying structured databases.**

### 🔁 Why RAG Matters

RAG is more than a clever trick — **it’s foundational.**

Report generation by agents? That’s just a chain of RAG-powered queries shaped into narrative form. In many modern generative AI apps, **RAG isn’t optional — it’s essential.**

But how do we ensure RAG quality?

By **red-teaming your RAG application** — which we’ll explore in the next article!

body:
* * *

#### IBM’s Bold Move in Agent Interoperability

If you’ve been exploring the generative AI space, you’ve probably come across two foundational ideas: the [**Model Context Protocol (MCP)**](https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol) and the [**Agent-to-Agent (A2A)**](https://developers.googleblog.com/en/a2a-a-new-era-of-agent-interoperability/) protocol

The MCP — proposed by Anthropic — is like a **universal USB port for agent tools**, allowing standardized tool usage across different agent frameworks. When it launched, the ecosystem took notice — companies raced to publish MCP specs for their own platforms.

In my earlier write-ups on the MCP, I:

-   [Built and deployed tools via FastMCP](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/model-context-protocol-hype-or-necessity-998874d95bc6) from scratch (while discussing the broader implications of MCPs), and
-   [Used Atlassian’s official MCP](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/its-2025-take-your-llm-apps-to-the-next-level-with-chainlit-00036c8db1ba) to manage my Jira board as part of my introduction to the Chainlit framework.

In both cases, the MCP added real value — especially on the front end — by simplifying tool integration — users simply add tools by clicks.

I also [explored Google’s A2A protocol](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/agent-to-agent-protocols-a-story-still-being-written-e7e1ffbf3e80), inspired by the MCP but aimed at enabling **agent-to-agent interoperability**. I built a basic A2A demo and found a familiar limitation: **agent discoverability is still clunky** — you need to know where an agent is deployed to interact with it, much like early MCP implementations. Unlike MCP, however, A2A is still evolving and hasn’t reached the same adoption velocity.

### Introducing ACP

Enter [**IBM’s Agent Communication Protocol (ACP)**](https://research.ibm.com/blog/agent-communication-protocol-ai), launched in May 2025 — a month after Google unveiled A2A. Not only did IBM throw its hat into the ring of agentic protocols, IBM has since rearchitected its multi-agent [**BeeAI framework**](https://beeai.dev/) around ACP, making it the backbone of their agent-based approach.

These are major bets from a company known for technological foresight, squaring off against another (Google) with a similar pedigree. The key question: **did IBM get it right?**

More curiously, IBM’s ACP documentation includes a segment highlighting its compatibility with Google’s A2A framework— [which is simply to make ACP agents discoverable on A2A as well](https://framework.beeai.dev/integrations/a2a). In IBM’s [official announcement](https://research.ibm.com/blog/agent-communication-protocol-ai), they added that they will be creating an ACP short course in partnership with DeepLearning.ai — so we have that to look forward to.

In this article, we build our own ACP example and interact with it. This [code is submitted as a pull request (PR) to the official ACP repository](https://github.com/i-am-bee/acp/pull/176).

> **Post-publication note**: This PR has been accepted by the ACP development team! 🎉 The code is now live in the official ACP GitHub repository ([link to codebase](https://github.com/i-am-bee/acp/tree/main/examples/python/llama-index-rag)) — and incidentally, it’s their first example of a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) agent.

### A quick note on the broader ecosystem

Little did I know that there are now at least [12 agent related protocols](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16736) in the ecosystem!

Imagine my surprise when I came across a [video by Laurie Voss](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kqB_xML1SfA) (VP, Developer Relations, LlamaIndex), surveying the **ever-expanding protocol zoo** at the MCP Developers conference. The video is “just” 18 minutes — but it barely scratches the surface. There are just **too many protocols**. Yet it echoed a lot of my own thoughts about the space. Let’s see how ACP performs in practice — and whether it offers something new beyond just buzzwords.

### Building our own ACP

Unlike Google’s A2A, IBM’s ACP framework is a high-level framework requiring us to write fewer lines of code. All we need to do is define the agent, register it with an ACP server, and spin up the service.

The ACP framework takes care of the rest.

Let’s define our agent:

```python
## Reference: https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-guide-to-code-testing-rag-agents-without-real-llms-or-vector-dbs-51154ad920be
from collections.abc import AsyncGenerator

from acp_sdk import Message, MessagePart
from acp_sdk.server import RunYield, RunYieldResume, Server

from llama_index.core import Settings, VectorStoreIndex
from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import FunctionAgent, AgentStream
from llama_index.core.tools import QueryEngineTool, ToolMetadata
from llama_index.core.node_parser import MarkdownNodeParser
from llama_index.readers.docling import DoclingReader
from llama_index.llms.ollama import Ollama
from llama_index.embeddings.ollama import OllamaEmbedding

## Load document
reader = DoclingReader()
node_parser = MarkdownNodeParser()
documents = reader.load_data("https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.09869")

## Create RAG query engine
Settings.llm = Ollama("qwen2.5", temperature=0)
Settings.embed_model = OllamaEmbedding(model_name="nomic-embed-text")

index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(
    documents=documents,
    transformations=[node_parser]
)
query_engine = index.as_query_engine()

## Create the agent
tools = [
    QueryEngineTool(
        query_engine = query_engine,
        metadata = ToolMetadata(
            name="Docling_Knowledge_Base",
            description="Use this tool to answer any questions related to the Docling framework"
        )
    )
]
agent = FunctionAgent(tools=tools, llm=Settings.llm)
```

If you’ve built a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) application with LlamaIndex (or any framework really), these lines of codes should look very familiar: we’re using IBM’s Docling document parser to parse the Docling technical paper into LlamaIndex documents, and building a RAG query engine on top of it.

We then wrap the query engine as a tool and tag it to an agent, all while using Ollama to host a local LLM and a local embedding model. Wrapping it in an agent prevents the RAG query engine from being pinged for irrelevant questions (for example “Where is the nearest MacDonald’s”).

The “agent” is LlamaIndex’s `FunctionAgent` abstraction which is built on top of LlamaIndex’s cutting edge `Workflow` abstraction, an asynchronous object with streaming capabilities.

Now we define how we want the agent to interact with the ACP. In the same script beneath the agent definitions, type:

```python
server = Server()

@server.agent()
async def llamaindex_rag_agent(input: list[Message]) -> AsyncGenerator:
    """LlamaIndex agent that answers questions using the  Docling
    knowledge base. The agent answers questions in streaming mode."""

    query = str(input[-1])
    handler = agent.run(query)
    async for ev in handler.stream_events():
        if isinstance(ev, AgentStream):
            yield ev.delta
    response = await handler
    yield str(response)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    server.run()
```

That’s pretty much it! We define a server object and a callback function to define how our agent runs. Since LlamaIndex’s FunctionAgent streams events, we have the option of implementing streaming on our ACP. Simply use the `.stream_events`method of the `FunctionAgent`, use `yield` instead of `print` , and that’s it — streaming with ACP is done!

That’s it — no complex orchestration, no custom task registries. ACP lets you plug in powerful local agents with minimal friction. Compared to [Google’s A2A](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/agent-to-agent-protocols-a-story-still-being-written-e7e1ffbf3e80) `[TaskManager](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/agent-to-agent-protocols-a-story-still-being-written-e7e1ffbf3e80)`[setup](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/agent-to-agent-protocols-a-story-still-being-written-e7e1ffbf3e80), this feels refreshingly simple.

To spin up the ACP server, simple run:

```bash
uv run agent.py
```

This spins up an ACP server on localhost:8000. If you visit it `localhost:8000/docs` you get the familiar FastAPI Swagger documentation page

> 💡 **Note**: Using the uv package manager is the preferred way. This setup requires a pyproject.toml file that lists your project dependencies. The uv package manager will then create a virtual environment, install the necessary packages, and start the service — all in one go. Plus it’s very fast — [uv is written in Rust](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/).

### Invoke the ACP

To test our agent, create a separate Python file:

```python
# client_stream.py

import asyncio

from acp_sdk.client import Client
from acp_sdk.models import Message, MessagePart, MessageCompletedEvent, GenericEvent

async def client() -> None:
    async with Client(base_url="http://localhost:8000") as client:
        async for event in client.run_stream(
            agent="llamaindex_rag_agent", input="What is Docling?"
        ):
            match event:
                case MessageCompletedEvent():
                    print("\nFinal response:", event.message)
                case GenericEvent():
                    print(event.generic.update)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(client())
```

Even in this part, the ACP abstractions keep things simple. When interacting with the agent in streaming mode, just use `client.run_stream()` . Importantly, you have to specify which agent you’re interacting with because there might be different agents deployed on the same ACP server!

Once done, simply use `match` and `case` to specify what the client should do when encountering a specific event type. In this case, we specify that we want to continue streaming the events if it’s a `GenericEvent` and to print the final message only if it’s a final event.

```bash
uv run client_stream.py
```

### IBM’s take on discoverability — BeeAI

First, start the BeeAI platform with:

```bash
beeai platform start
```

> PS this step can take awhile — it’s applying BeeAI’s helm charts. Impressively, it also starts an Arize Phoenix service for agent observability!

> Note: To stop your beeai platform just type: `_beeai platform stop_`

Next start by spinning up the agent’s server with:

```bash
uv run server
```

You’ll notice something different in your stdout:

```plaintext
(beeai-agents) tituslim@Mac special-parakeet % uv run server
INFO:     Started server process [71722]
INFO:     Waiting for application startup.
INFO:     Application startup complete.
INFO:     Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:8000 (Press CTRL+C to quit)
INFO:     127.0.0.1:53950 - "GET /agents HTTP/1.1" 200 OK
INFO:     HTTP Request: POST http://127.0.0.1:8333/api/v1/providers/register/unmanaged "HTTP/1.1 200 OK"
INFO:     Agent registered to the beeai server.
INFO:     HTTP Request: GET http://127.0.0.1:8333/api/v1/variables "HTTP/1.1 200 OK"
```

Your agent is registered on localhost:8000 **AND** localhost:8333 where a beeai server is running!

At this point, your agent works — but you’re still accessing it by manually specifying its host and port (localhost:8000) like an MCP.

Enter [**BeeAI**](https://github.com/i-am-bee/beeai-framework), the broader multi-agent platform by IBM’s team behind ACP. BeeAI includes a **discovery layer**, letting you locate deployed agents more easily.

The ACP framework is developed by IBM’s BeeAI team, and unsurpisingly, BeeAI has an implementation of how to do this on their framework!

You can install the BeeAI framework from PyPI or directly on the operating system of your computer following their [installation instructions](https://docs.beeai.dev/introduction/installation#homebrew-mac-os-linux).

Once you’ve installed the BeeAI framework and deployed your ACP server, simply type

```bash
beeai list
```

There you have it, our `llamaindex_rag_agent` shows up as the first discoverable agent.

### Calling our discoverable agent on the BeeAI UI

Beeai allows for agents to be interacted with on the beeai user interface, simply run:

```python
beeai ui
```

This spins up a gorgeous chat interface on localhost:8333. Clicking on the left side panel shows the list of discoverable agents, and our agent will be there! You can also select from BeeAI’s other template agents and chat with those.

Let’s ask a question:

Works!

If you’re just starting out, BeeAI even has a [starter template repository](https://github.com/i-am-bee/beeai-platform-agent-starter) for you — simply click “use this template” and select “Create a new repository” and you’ll have your ACP boilerplate code complete with CI/CD action courtesy of BeeAI’s `.github` scripts.

### 💭 Reflecting on what we just did

#### 🐝 Using BeeAI

The BeeAI framework has a strong emphasis on developer experience — far more so than Google’s A2A framework. With BeeAI, many lower-level configurations are abstracted away, which not only speeds up development but also reduces the chance of introducing bugs.

That said, higher-level abstractions can make **debugging harder**. Despite following the [documentation](https://docs.beeai.dev/how-to/build-agents#option-2%3A-production-deployment-sharing-%26-ci%2Fcd) closely, I encountered a persistent Docker issue when using the BeeAI UI. Ironically, the CLI setup was just a few lines of code, but this failed and I wasn’t able to fix it on my own. To their credit, the BeeAI team has been very responsive. I’m confident these early kinks will be resolved soon.

#### 🧠 Using the ACP framework

ACP, the framework underpinning BeeAI, was surprisingly **lightweight and intuitive**. In fact, almost all of our code came from LlamaIndex — ACP simply provided a neat way to wrap and expose it. It only took about 10 minutes to write and submit a working PR to the official ACP repo. To me, that’s the very definition of great developer experience: a framework that lets you elevate your existing code with minimal effort. I genuinely enjoyed using it.

One especially commendable design choice: **ACP is not strictly coupled to BeeAI**. Although it was developed by the BeeAI team and is core to its platform and framework, ACP agents can be made discoverable and callable by **other frameworks** too — provided those frameworks integrate with ACP. That’s a refreshing level of openness in a space where vendor lock-in is common.

> I also strongly recommend the [ACP class on DeepLearning.ai](https://www.deeplearning.ai/short-courses/acp-agent-communication-protocol/) — has really cool examples and is a gentle introduction to the framework!

#### 🔍 What About Discoverability?

So far, agent discoverability in ACP feels quite similar to how tools are discovered by agents in MCP — though BeeAI has made this better.

In BeeAI, _you_ choose which agent to interact with. In contrast, MCP is designed so that _your agent_ chooses which tools (discovered by you) to use. These are fundamentally different interaction models.

That said, we can often simulate a similar experience by keeping a single agent and dynamically swapping its MCP tools.

> Importantly: There’s still no actual agent-to-agent interaction!

ACP hasn’t yet achieved agent-to-agent collaboration — but it _has_ changed how users interact with agents. With the BeeAI platform, you can now deploy a single web app that exposes multiple agents to the user, instead of spinning up one app per agent. Each agent can even have its own set of MCP tools.

This shift introduces new UX opportunities — and possibly new risks (e.g., users accessing agents they shouldn’t). It’s a promising model, but the framework still feels like a **work-in-progress** like the A2A framework**.**

And here’s a fun twist: [**ACP actually began as a fork of MCP**](https://github.com/i-am-bee/acp/discussions/122), but has since veered confidently into A2A territory — closing the loop between tools, agents, and interaction models in IBM’s own style and vision.

#### Thinking about what interoperability looks like

One of Laurie Voss’ comments in his video struck home — something I’d been mulling over since my exploration of the A2A framework:

> _“What’s the difference between calling a tool and invoking an agent?”_

When an agent invokes another agent, it’s essentially treating that agent _as_ a tool. So… why not just stick with tools?

The grand vision behind agent-to-agent communication is coalition-building — agents that can form groups, collaborate, maybe even debate, and collectively solve problems. Imagine asking an agent a question, and then it _adds another agent into a group chat_ with you — the two agents talk it through while you watch (and chime in if needed). That would fundamentally change how we live, work, and interact with digital systems. This collaboration paradigm between agents extends far beyond agents using each other as tools.

But let’s compare that vision to our current state. Strip away the hype, the branding, the launch demos — and we realize we’re still _far_ from that future. That said, at least the journey has begun.

In fact, there are already a dozen competing protocols in the wild — each with its own take (I probably will not be writing about all/more of them). Google search “ACP” and you’ll find _Agent Communication Protocol_ by IBM (this one), and also [_Agent Connect Protocol_ by Cisco](https://outshift.cisco.com/blog/mcp-acp-decoding-language-of-models-and-agents) — another tech heavyweight, throwing its hat into the ring.

So yes, we might chuckle, facepalm, or sigh as the acronyms pile up — but at the heart of it, this flurry of protocols is a signal: **the world is taking agent interoperability seriously and open-sourcing it** (thus far)**.** And that’s something worth celebrating 🥂.

Even if we do it with a wry smile and a good laugh.

body:
