#### Test everything, call nothing

Testing is essential in software development — it helps catch bugs early and ensures reliability before code reaches production. Traditional software testing focuses on “units” of code, hence the term _unit testing_. These tests are often deterministic: `assert func(a, b) == c`.

In generative AI, however, _testing_ usually means something else. It often refers to _red-teaming_ an LLM application, or using another LLM as a judge to detect hallucinations, biases, or confidential data leaks. These evaluation strategies are important — but they’re not the same as testing whether your **code** behaves correctly.

What makes testing GenAI apps difficult is that LLMs are **stochastic** — they generate text token by token, with slight variations even on the same input. As a result, traditional test practices (like asserting exact outputs) often break down.

To make matters worse, calling real LLMs and vector databases isn’t free. If your tests are part of a CI/CD pipeline, they might fail — not because your logic is broken, but because the remote LLM or vector DB wasn’t reachable.

This was a real problem I faced at work: we had a production-ready, agentic microservice built on a GPU server, orchestrated via Docker. It had too many dependencies to spin up cleanly in a GitHub Actions runner — and spinning up a GPU server just to run tests wasn’t cost-effective.

But we still needed test coverage — just _without_ calling real services.

In this article, I’ll walk you through a minimal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) application, and show you how to **unit test it without any real LLM or vector DB**.

All code is in my [GitHub repo](https://github.com/tituslhy/vigilant-sniffle/tree/main), and you can follow along step by step.

### First, the RAG application — to prove it works

```python
from llama_index.llms.ollama import Ollama
from llama_index.embeddings.ollama import OllamaEmbedding
from llama_index.core import VectorStoreIndex
from llama_index.core.node_parser import MarkdownNodeParser
from llama_index.readers.docling import DoclingReader

embed_model = OllamaEmbedding(model_name="mxbai-embed-large")
llm = Ollama("qwen2.5:14b", request_timeout=3600)

## Load document
reader = DoclingReader()
node_parser = MarkdownNodeParser()
documents = reader.load_data("https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.09869")
```

We begin by defining a **local LLM** and **embedding model**, along with the document reader and parser components. Instead of the usual `SimpleDirectoryReader`, we use IBM’s excellent open-source `DoclingReader`.

[Docling](https://docling-project.github.io/docling/#ibm-open-source-ai) is a **document understanding** Python framework that combines multiple open-source AI models and frameworks (like [EasyOCR](https://github.com/JaidedAI/EasyOCR)) to intelligently parse content buried in **tables, images, and complex layouts** — a game-changer for RAG pipelines working with scientific or scanned documents.

Which makes this demo poetic: we’re using **Docling to read the** [**Docling paper**](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.09869) from ArXiv 😄

Now let’s start our local Qdrant server:

```bash
docker run -p 6333:6333 qdrant/qdrant
```

Then configure the Qdrant vector store and ingest the documents:

```python
from llama_index.core import StorageContext
from llama_index.vector_stores.qdrant import QdrantVectorStore
from qdrant_client import QdrantClient, AsyncQdrantClient

client = QdrantClient(host="localhost", port=6333)
aclient = AsyncQdrantClient(host="localhost", port=6333)
vector_store = QdrantVectorStore(
    "docling", 
    client=client,
    aclient=aclient,
    enable_hybrid=True, # dense and keyword embedding hybrid search
    fastembed_sparse_model="Qdrant/bm42-all-minilm-l6-v2-attentions"
)
storage_context = StorageContext.from_defaults(vector_store=vector_store)
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(
    documents = documents,
    storage_context = storage_context,
    transformations = [node_parser],
    embed_model = embed_model
)
```

This parses and vectorizes your document, storing the results in Qdrant for future retrieval.

#### Build the RAG query engine

```python
index2 = VectorStoreIndex.from_vector_store(
    vector_store,
    embed_model=embed_model
)
query_engine = index2.as_query_engine(
    sparse_top_k=10,
    similarity_top_k=6,
    llm=llm
)
response = query_engine.query("Which are the main AI models in Docling?")
```

The query engine is now ready to answer questions from the vector store. But rather than hitting it with arbitrary queries like “Why is the sky blue?”, we can _wrap it as a tool_ and let an agent decide when to use it.

#### Using an agent

```python
from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import FunctionAgent
from llama_index.core.tools import QueryEngineTool, ToolMetadata

tools = [
    QueryEngineTool(
        query_engine = query_engine,
        metadata = ToolMetadata(
            name="Docling_Knowledge_Base",
            description="Use this tool to answer any questions related to the Docling framework"
        )
    )
]

agent = FunctionAgent(tools=tools, llm=llm)
response = await agent.run("What is docling?")
```

This sets up a simple **agentic workflow** using `FunctionAgent`. You now have an agent that selects tools intelligently to answer user questions.

To avoid waiting for the full response and improve interactivity, we can stream the response instead:

```python
from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import AgentStream

handler = agent.run("How is docling an improvement over existing document readers?")

async for ev in handler.stream_events():
    if isinstance(ev, AgentStream):
        print(ev.delta, end="", flush=True)
```

Isn’t it amazing how **LlamaIndex** lets you build full-blown **agentic RAG pipelines** in just a few dozen lines?

Now that we’ve verified our app works, the next step is to **test every unit of code —** without making a single real ping to any service provider.

### Testing our agent

The only way I know to _test your code without calling real services_ is to use **mocking** and **patching**. These techniques let you create “fake” or “substitute” objects that behave like the real thing — but in a **controlled, isolated environment**.

If you’re new to PyTest, the first thing to do is:

1.  Create a tests/ folder
2.  Add a test file like test\_docling\_agent.py _(PyTest identifies any file prefixed with test\_ as a test script)_

Let’s import the frameworks we need:

```python
import pytest
from unittest.mock import patch, MagicMock, AsyncMock
from typing import Any
```

Python has many amazing libraries for testing that cohere seamlessly —we’ll be using just two:

-   unittest: great for structured, class-based **unit testing**
-   PyTest: lightweight and flexible, supports **all types** of tests (unit, integration, smoke, parameterized, etc. — my apologies to my Agile and DevSecOps professor for forgetting all the different types of tests)

#### Our first unit test: Mocking the Docling Reader

```python
class TestDoclingAgentNotebook:
    """
    Unit tests for the docling agent notebook logic, with all external dependencies mocked.
    Synchronous tests are kept in this class for organization and compatibility with pytest.
    """
    
    @patch('llama_index.readers.docling.DoclingReader')
    def test_reader_load_data(self, mock_docling_reader: MagicMock) -> None:
        """
        Test that DoclingReader.load_data returns a document with the expected text.
        All external dependencies are mocked.
        """
        mock_reader = mock_docling_reader.return_value
        mock_doc = MagicMock()
        mock_doc.text_resource.text = 'Sample text.'
        mock_reader.load_data.return_value = [mock_doc]
        docs = mock_reader.load_data('dummy_url')
        assert docs[0].text_resource.text == 'Sample text.'
```

**What’s happening here?**

-   We’re **not actually using Docling**, which saves GPU cycles and avoids real ingestion logic.
-   The @patch(…) decorator replaces DoclingReader with a mock object.
-   Inside the method, mock\_docling\_reader becomes that mock class, and mock\_reader is the mock instance you’d get when calling it.
-   We then define a **mock document**, give it a nested attribute (text\_resource.text), and make mock\_reader.load\_data() return this mock doc.
-   When we call load\_data(“dummy\_url”), it returns our controlled mock document, and we assert its .text matches the expected value.

**Quick notes on mocking and patching:**

-   You can patch inline using `with patch(...)`, but decorating is often cleaner for tests with many patching dependencies.
-   Every patched object must be an input argument to the method.
-   `MagicMock`is a super flexible class that can imitate _any_ method, property, or behavior.
-   Naming your test methods with `test_` ensures PyTest knows they’re test cases.
-   Any method in the class that doesn’t start with test\_ will _not_ be run as a test — useful for setup/teardown helpers or custom utilities.

> This might feel like a play within a play — mocks within mocks — **but that’s the point**. We verified that our logic correctly calls into the document reader and expects the output structure we defined. The real Docling library (and its underlying models) never needed to run.

#### Our next unit tests: Mocking the entire RAG code

```python
class TestDoclingAgentNotebook:
    """
    Unit tests for the docling agent notebook logic, with all external dependencies mocked.
    Synchronous tests are kept in this class for organization and compatibility with pytest.
    """
    
    @patch('llama_index.readers.docling.DoclingReader')
    def test_reader_load_data(self, mock_docling_reader: MagicMock) -> None:
        ... # same code as above

    @patch('qdrant_client.AsyncQdrantClient')
    @patch('qdrant_client.QdrantClient')
    @patch('llama_index.vector_stores.qdrant.QdrantVectorStore')
    def test_vector_store_index_setup_with_qdrant(
        self,
        mock_qdrant_vector_store: MagicMock,
        mock_qdrant_client: MagicMock,
        mock_async_qdrant_client: MagicMock
    ) -> None:
        """
        Test that QdrantVectorStore is initialized with the correct arguments and returns the mock instance.
        All Qdrant-related dependencies are mocked.
        """
        client = mock_qdrant_client.return_value
        aclient = mock_async_qdrant_client.return_value
        vector_store = mock_qdrant_vector_store('docling', client=client, aclient=aclient, enable_hybrid=True, fastembed_sparse_model='Qdrant/bm42-all-minilm-l6-v2-attentions')
        assert vector_store == mock_qdrant_vector_store.return_value

    @patch('llama_index.core.VectorStoreIndex')
    @patch('llama_index.vector_stores.qdrant.QdrantVectorStore')
    def test_load_vector_store_from_qdrant(
        self,
        mock_qdrant_vector_store: MagicMock,
        mock_vector_store_index: MagicMock
    ) -> None:
        """
        Test that VectorStoreIndex.from_vector_store returns the mock index when called with a mocked QdrantVectorStore.
        """
        vector_store = mock_qdrant_vector_store.return_value
        embed_model: Any = MagicMock()
        mock_index = mock_vector_store_index.from_vector_store.return_value
        index = mock_vector_store_index.from_vector_store(vector_store, embed_model=embed_model)
        assert index == mock_index

    @patch('llama_index.core.VectorStoreIndex')
    def test_query_engine(self, mock_vector_store_index: MagicMock) -> None:
        """
        Test that the query engine returns the expected mocked response string.
        """
        index = mock_vector_store_index.return_value
        index.as_query_engine.return_value = MagicMock()
        query_engine = index.as_query_engine(sparse_top_k=10, similarity_top_k=6, llm=MagicMock())
        query_engine.query.return_value = MagicMock(source_nodes=[], __str__=lambda self: 'Query response')
        response = query_engine.query('Test query')
        assert str(response) == 'Query response'
```

At this point this code should read quite easily!

📌 **What we’re testing:**

-   That our Qdrant store initializes correctly — with the right parameters — and returns our mocked object.
-   That calling from\_vector\_store(…) correctly returns a usable `VectorStoreIndex` — again, without needing a live DB.
-   That our LlamaIndex-based query engine works and returns something usable, even when everything is mocked out.

### Testing the Agent Setup and Execution

Let’s move on to testing our **FunctionAgent** and how it responds to queries.

```python
@pytest.mark.asyncio
@patch('llama_index.core.tools.QueryEngineTool')
@patch('llama_index.core.agent.workflow.FunctionAgent')
async def test_agent_with_query_engine_tool_async(mock_function_agent: MagicMock, mock_query_engine_tool: MagicMock) -> None:
    """
    Async test for FunctionAgent.run with a mocked QueryEngineTool.
    Ensures the agent returns the expected response when awaited.
    """
    query_engine_tool = mock_query_engine_tool.return_value
    agent = mock_function_agent(tools=[query_engine_tool], llm=MagicMock())
    mock_function_agent.return_value.run = AsyncMock(return_value='Agent response')
    agent_response = await agent.run('What is docling?')
    assert agent_response == 'Agent response'
```

**🤔 Wait a minute — why is this test outside the class?**

Because Python’s built-in unittest framework doesn’t natively support async def test functions. But **Pytest does**, with the help of the pytest-asyncio plugin.

That’s why any test marked with @pytest.mark.asyncio must live **outside the test class**, unless you’re fully switching to an async-compatible test framework or using third-party workarounds.

**🧪 Recap: What this test is doing**

-   ✅ We’re mocking both the `QueryEngineTool` and the `FunctionAgent` .
-   ✅ We initialize the FunctionAgent using a mocked tool and a mocked LLM.
-   ✅ Then, we override .run() to return “Agent response” asynchronously via `AsyncMock` , the mocking class for everything asynchronous.
-   ✅ Finally, we await the agent and check that it returns the expected string.

It’s pretty much the same flavor of test as the earlier ones — **just async, and outside the test class**.

### 🌀Testing the Agent’s streaming response

This is by far the most complex part — but trust me, we’ll get through it. This portion requires combing through code on LlamaIndex’s GitHub to understand how streaming works with Workflows so that you know what you need to mock and patch.

```python
@pytest.mark.asyncio
@patch("llama_index.core.tools.QueryEngineTool")
@patch("llama_index.core.agent.workflow.AgentStream")
@patch("llama_index.core.agent.workflow.FunctionAgent")
async def test_agent_streaming_mocked_everything(
    mock_function_agent: MagicMock,
    mock_agent_stream_cls: MagicMock,
    mock_query_engine_tool_cls: MagicMock,
) -> None:

    # Step A: Create two **distinct mock events**, each with a unique delta
    ev1 = MagicMock()
    ev1.delta = "Delta1"
    ev2 = MagicMock()
    ev2.delta = "Delta2"
```

We start by patching the FunctionAgent, AgentStream and QueryEngineTool class, then mock two events (ev1 and ev2) and their deltas.

Since LlamaIndex’s FunctionAgent is actually a Workflow, streaming is typically invoked by `handler = agent.run(...)` . Step 2 is to create a fake handler class:

```python
@pytest.mark.asyncio
@patch("llama_index.core.tools.QueryEngineTool")
@patch("llama_index.core.agent.workflow.AgentStream")
@patch("llama_index.core.agent.workflow.FunctionAgent")
async def test_agent_streaming_mocked_everything(
    mock_function_agent: MagicMock,
    mock_agent_stream_cls: MagicMock,
    mock_query_engine_tool_cls: MagicMock,
) -> None:

    # Step A code 
    # Step B: Minimal replacement for the handler returned by agent.run()
    class FakeHandler:
        def __init__(self, events, final_value: str):
            self._events = events
            self._final_value = final_value

        async def stream_events(self):
            """
            Simulates streaming a sequence of intermediate agent events.

            This mimics LlamaIndex's behavior where `agent.run(...)` returns a handler
            that can be iterated over using `async for`, emitting `AgentStream` deltas.

            In our test, each event in `self._events` is expected to be a mock object
            with a `.delta` field (e.g., "Delta1", "Delta2").

            Yielding them one by one simulates how a real LLM might stream out token deltas.
            """            
            for e in self._events:
                yield e

        def __await__(self):
            """
            Allows `await handler` to work.

            Real LlamaIndex handlers (like `StreamingAgentHandler`) support both:
            - `async for` for intermediate events
            - `await` for the final result

            This method defines how `await handler` behaves — it returns the final output
            string (e.g., "FINAL_RESULT") to simulate the conclusion of the agent run.

            Technically, this wraps an async coroutine in `__await__()` so that Python's
            await machinery treats this object like a coroutine.
            """            
            async def _coro():
                """This function implements awaitability for the handler - this FakeHandler is not
                asynchronous, but we need to make it awaitable to mimic the real handler's behavior.
                
                This method simply returns a stored value (self._final_value) when awaited.
                Why define it inside? Because it’s used only here, and it keeps things encapsulated.
                """
                return self._final_value
            return _coro().__await__()

    fake_handler = FakeHandler([ev1, ev2], final_value="FINAL_RESULT")
```

Yup your eyes aren’t fooling you — we defined a `FakeHandler` class inside the function instead of mocking anything, because we need to manually override Python’s default `__await__` function to support our `stream_events`method in our `FakeHandler`.

We’re even going to implement awaitability within our `FakeHandler` class via a nested asynchronous `_coro` function within the `__await__` method, and all it does is return the string that its given within its constructor.

Pretty hilarious and epic at the same time I know. We instantiate our fake handler with both our mocked events and a final value of “FINAL\_RESULT”.

```python
@pytest.mark.asyncio
@patch("llama_index.core.tools.QueryEngineTool")
@patch("llama_index.core.agent.workflow.AgentStream")
@patch("llama_index.core.agent.workflow.FunctionAgent")
async def test_agent_streaming_mocked_everything(
    mock_function_agent: MagicMock,
    mock_agent_stream_cls: MagicMock,
    mock_query_engine_tool_cls: MagicMock,
) -> None:

    # Step A code for mock ev1 and ev2
    # Step B code for FakeHandler
    # Step C: Patch FunctionAgent(...) to return a dummy object whose .run(...) returns the handler
    
    dummy_agent_instance = MagicMock(name="DummyAgent")
    dummy_agent_instance.run.return_value = fake_handler
    mock_function_agent.return_value = dummy_agent_instance

    # Patch QueryEngineTool as well, though we never call its logic in this test
    mock_query_engine_tool_cls.return_value = MagicMock(name="DummyTool")

    # Step D: Import symbols after patching (to pick up the mocks!)
    from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import FunctionAgent
    from llama_index.core.tools import QueryEngineTool, ToolMetadata

    dummy_tool = QueryEngineTool(
        query_engine=MagicMock(),  # unused
        metadata=ToolMetadata(
            name="Docling_Knowledge_Base",
            description="Use this tool to answer questions about Docling",
        ),
    )

    # Step E: Create the agent (returns our patched dummy agent instance)
    agent = FunctionAgent(tools=[dummy_tool], llm=MagicMock())

    # Step F: Run the agent with a dummy prompt string
    handler = agent.run(
      "How is docling an improvement over existing document readers?"
    )
```

Now these parts are more readable — we’re just mocking everything again! Importantly in step C, we set the `dummy_agent_instance` ‘s `run.return_value` to be the `fake_handler` object we defined in step B.

**Steps D-F** are a bit magical: we import _real_ LlamaIndex abstractions _after_ patching, so they pick up the mocks! What we’ve created is a real `FunctionAgent`:

-   With an LLM that’s a `MagicMock`
-   And a `QueryEngineTool` that’s real in type but wraps a mocked query engine.

The lines between real and fake are now beautifully blurred — which is exactly what makes this test both flexible and powerful. We then run this real/fake/who knows agent over an actual query.

```python
@pytest.mark.asyncio
@patch("llama_index.core.tools.QueryEngineTool")
@patch("llama_index.core.agent.workflow.AgentStream")
@patch("llama_index.core.agent.workflow.FunctionAgent")
async def test_agent_streaming_mocked_everything(
    mock_function_agent: MagicMock,
    mock_agent_stream_cls: MagicMock,
    mock_query_engine_tool_cls: MagicMock,
) -> None:

    # Step A code for mock ev1 and ev2
    # Step B code for FakeHandler
    # Step C-F code to patch and run FunctionAgent(...) 

    # Step G: Collect all streamed deltas from the handler
    collected = []
    async for event in handler.stream_events():
        collected.append(event.delta)

    # Step H: Await the handler itself for the final result
    final = await handler

    # Step I: Assertions – critical contract checks
    assert collected == ["Delta1", "Delta2"]
    assert final == "FINAL_RESULT"

    # Step J: Sanity – ensure mocks were called as expected
    mock_function_agent.assert_called_once()
    dummy_agent_instance.run.assert_called_once_with(
      "How is docling an improvement over existing document readers?"
    )
```

Now we invoke the same streaming like you would in a LlamaIndex Workflow and define our tests with `async for even in handler.stream_events()`which collects our two mock events in step A (“Delta1” and “Delta2”). When we `await handler` we get the `final_result` in our `FakeHandler`.

Finally, we asserted that our important instances were called once.

### Running the test in command line

Now it’s time to unleash PyTest on all our test cases. Simply type the following command in your terminal:

```bash
pytest
```

And… it works!

### 💭 Thinking About What We Just Did

Let’s be candid for a moment.

Strictly speaking, none of these tests are _necessary_ in the traditional sense. The LlamaIndex team already tests their abstractions before every release — quite rigorously in fact.

Also, if we’re being purists, some of our tests might not be considered “good unit tests” — because, well, we mocked **everything**. From the vector store to the LLM to the handler logic… it’s like writing a play where all the actors are puppets and the stage is imaginary.

But here’s the thing: In a **DevOps context**, we had no choice.

-   LLM outputs are stochastic — traditional test assertions break easily.
-   Calling real LLMs incurs cost.
-   Our CI runners may not have GPUs, vector DBs, or network access to call Qdrant.

### 🧠 So What Did We Accomplish?

-   **We didn’t spend a cent** — no real LLM calls, no embedding lookups, no GPU compute.
-   **We validated integration logic** — end-to-end wiring between agent, tool, and event handler.
-   **We simulated runtime behavior** — even in streaming workflows.
-   **We learnt two new frameworks** — unittest and PyTest!
-   **We made our code testable** — which is critical for safe refactoring and CI reliability.

Sure, everything was mocked. But these tests helped us reason about the **contracts** between components — what gets called, when, and how. That’s often more valuable in GenAI systems than testing exact outputs

### 🧪 The Invisible Value: DevOps Compliance

If you work in a test-driven development (TDD) environment, or use static code quality tools like **SonarQube**, you’ll know that “test coverage” is a hard requirement.

This was a real issue for me at work — I had started using SonarQube for the first time but [SonarQube’s **Quality Gate** GitHub](https://github.com/SonarSource/sonarqube-quality-gate-action) Action blocked my PR because I had _zero_ test coverage. I literally had to Google “what is coverage?” because I’d never written a proper test case (again sorry professor 😅).

> PS: The passing mark for test coverage is 80%, i.e. your tests must cover 80% of all the code you write

So yes — part of the reason I started testing with mocks and patches was just to stop the DevOps alarms.

> By the way, SonarQube has other more alarmist warnings, like: “Refactor this method to reduce its Cognitive Complexity from 26 to the 15 allowed.” I mean, what does that even mean? It’s like being told your code is too thought provoking.

### 💡 Just a Final Note

Testing isn’t about proving your code is perfect — it’s about making sure it _fails loudly_ when it isn’t. So in my view, it’s always better if someone else writes the tests for your code.

Otherwise, let’s face it — you’ll be tempted to write tests that pass, not tests that break things.

body:
* * *

#### How to train your LLM simultaneously with 10 different “teachers”

Yup, you read that right.

Following our previous articles on [supervised finetuning (SFT)](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/how-to-train-your-llm-teaching-toothless-to-bite-8d9f56fe4b2a), [retrieval-augmented finetuning (RAFT)](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/how-to-raft-your-llm-retrieval-augmented-finetuning-using-unsloth-4c3844a9a6e3), and [group relative policy optimization (GRPO)](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/how-to-train-your-llm-to-reason-grpo-reinforcement-learning-using-unsloth-64af5e82ac3c) of a large language model (“LLM”) we’re taking things even further.

**Imagine this:** you work at a multinational healthcare corporation with hospitals across several jurisdictions. Due to strict data privacy laws, patient data can’t leave the local servers. Yet this data is immensely valuable — rich in triage notes, symptom tracking, and treatment workflows. It would be a huge missed opportunity not to leverage that knowledge, especially when hospitals in other regions could benefit.

Enter _federated supervised finetuning_ — a way to train models collaboratively across silos without moving the data. And with [Flower AI](https://flower.ai/), it’s simpler than you might think.

### Introducing Federated Learning

Federated learning isn’t limited to LLMs — it can also be used to finetune computer vision models, tabular machine learning models, and more.

In the context of LLMs, however, federated learning typically refers to supervised finetuning using [parameter efficient finetuning methods (PEFT)](https://huggingface.co/blog/peft)— but done in a decentralized way. Instead of pooling all the training data into a central location, each data source (or “client”) keeps its data local.

The model travels to the data, learns from it, and only the updated model weights are sent back — not the sensitive data itself.

This setup is especially powerful in regulated industries like healthcare and finance, where data privacy is non-negotiable but shared learning remains incredibly valuable.

Here’s how a typical federated learning loop works, beautifully explained by Flower AI in their [quickstart tutorial](https://flower.ai/docs/framework/tutorial-series-what-is-federated-learning.html#):

1.  **Distribute**: Download a copy of the base LLM to all connected servers (“clients”) that hold local data.
2.  **Train locally**: Each client finetunes the LLM on its own dataset for a fixed number of steps or epochs.
3.  **Send updates**: Clients send back only the updated model weights to a central coordinating server (“server”).
4.  **Aggregate**: The server combines these updates into a single global model. The simplest method is a straight average of the weights (known as [_Federated Averaging_, or _FedAvg_](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.05629)).
5.  **Repeat**: This process is repeated across multiple communication rounds as specified by the user or until convergence

> **So really, the finetuning _method_ remains the same between centralized supervised finetuning (SFT) and federated learning. The key difference lies in the _mechanism_ — centralized SFT brings the data to the LLM, while federated learning brings the LLM to the data.**

Because federated learning is often used in sensitive, distributed settings, additional safeguards are commonly applied to prevent the model from [inadvertently memorizing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06714) private data during training.

One such technique is [**differential privacy (DP)**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.15042) — a technique that adds calibrated statistical noise to model updates. This makes it mathematically improbable for any individual’s data to be isolated or reverse-engineered from the final model, offering a guarantee of privacy.

We’ll implement all of this using the **Flower AI** framework in this article.

All codes can be found in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/fantastic-enigma).

### One more note before we begin coding

Before we dive into code, I highly recommend checking out Flower AI’s federated learning courses on DeepLearning.AI — especially the [_Introduction to Federated Learning_](https://learn.deeplearning.ai/courses/intro-to-federated-learning/lesson/uhuz2/introduction) and [_Federated Finetuning of LLMs with Private Data_](https://learn.deeplearning.ai/courses/intro-to-federated-learning-c2/lesson/gj3qi/introduction). These courses had a huge impact on me, and I still rewatch them from time to time.

For this article, we’ll be adapting from **Lesson 3** of the _Federated Finetuning of LLMs_ course. The accompanying cookbook is excellent — clear, well-structured, and beginner-friendly. If Hugging Face and Flower hadn’t updated their codebases so significantly (the notebook uses much older versions), I probably wouldn’t have needed to change anything! I’ve spruced up the original notebook with extra annotations and explanations in my GitHub repo, and also tweaked the code to prevent issues arising from Python SDK changes.

Do note that the cookbook runs in a _Jupyter Notebook_ and simulates federated learning using **20 clients and 1 server**. That’s far from production-grade — notebooks are great for prototyping, but deployments typically run as .py scripts.

And no, I don’t have 20 GPU servers lying around (just a free Colab T4 instance 😄), so we’ll stick with simulation mode for now. I’ll also include notes later on how to deploy with Flower AI.

### Step 1: Load your training configuration **🧑‍🍳**

Every great dish starts with a recipe — and in this notebook, that recipe is your config file. Here’s our training configuration:

```python
from omegaconf import OmegaConf, DictConfig

cfg_dict = {
    'dataset': {
        'name': 'medalpaca/medical_meadow_medical_flashcards'
    },
    'model': {
        'name': "meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct",
        'quantization': 4,
        'gradient_checkpointing': True,
        'use_fast_tokenizer': True,
        'lora': {
            'peft_lora_r': 16,
            'peft_lora_alpha': 64,
            'target_modules': None}},
    'train': {
        'num_rounds': '${flower.num_rounds}',
        'save_every_round': 5,
        'learning_rate_max': 5e-05,
        'learning_rate_min': 1e-06,
        'seq_length': 1024,
        'padding_side': 'left',
        'evaluate_split': True,
        'training_arguments': {
            'output_dir': None,
            'learning_rate': None,
            'per_device_train_batch_size': 2,
            'gradient_accumulation_steps': 1,
            'logging_steps': 5,
            'max_steps': 250,
            # 'num_train_epochs': 1,
            'report_to': 'wandb',
            'run_name': "llama32_1b_fed_sft_take2",
            'save_steps': 1000,
            'save_total_limit': 10,
            'gradient_checkpointing': '${model.gradient_checkpointing}',
            'lr_scheduler_type': 'constant'}},
    'flower': {
        'num_clients': 20,
        'num_rounds': 2,
        'fraction_fit': 0.2,
        'client_resources': {
            'num_cpus': 2,
            'num_gpus': 1.0
        },
        'dp': {
            'noise_mult': 0.02,
            'clip_norm': 0.5
        }
    }
}

cfg = OmegaConf.create(cfg_dict)
```

If you’ve read my previous articles on SFT, RAFT, or GRPO, the dataset and model sections will look familiar — we’re training a 1B-parameter Llama 3.2 model on a medical dataset using LoRA fine-tuning.

The **new elements** here are under the flower section — this is where federated learning kicks in:

-   **num\_clients**: Sets up 20 clients for the central server to coordinate with.
-   **num\_rounds**: Specifies 2 rounds of federated fine-tuning.
-   **fraction\_fit**: Each round, only 20% of clients (i.e., 4 out of 20) are sampled to participate. You _can_ sample 100%, but this can quickly become a bandwidth bottleneck since **all** clients need to transmit their PEFT model weights back to the server.
-   **dp**: We apply differential privacy with a small noise multiplier (noise\_mult) and a clipping norm (clip\_norm) to cap extreme gradients. This helps reduce the chance of individual data points being leaked from client updates.

This config gives us a good balance of experimentation, resource efficiency, and privacy — all while keeping things runnable on a single Colab T4!

### **👨‍🍳 Step 2: Load the Model — Then Estimate Your Grocery Bill**

Now that we’ve got our ingredients sorted and divided, it’s time to prep the kitchen. Here, we load our model, apply the right quantization, and plug in LoRA adapters to make training lighter. Then we run a quick cost check — like scanning your grocery basket before checkout.

> **📈 Why this matters:**

> Federated fine-tuning isn’t just about accuracy — it’s also about efficiency. Uploading 7B parameters to 20 clients for 3 rounds? The number of parameters sent by the clients to the server alone can overwhelm it. LoRA keeps training light by freezing most weights and only fine-tuning small adapter modules — reducing bandwidth costs by 20x–100x.

```python
import torch
from transformers import (
    AutoModelForCausalLM,
    AutoTokenizer,
    BitsAndBytesConfig
)
from peft import (
    LoraConfig,
    get_peft_model,
    get_peft_model_state_dict,
    set_peft_model_state_dict,
)
from peft.utils import prepare_model_for_kbit_training
from trl import DataCollatorForCompletionOnlyLM, SFTTrainer

def get_model(model_cfg: DictConfig):
    """Load model with appropiate quantization config and
    other optimizations. Notice here that we are returning the
    LoRA model, not the full model."""

    use_cuda = torch.cuda.is_available()
    quantization_config = None
    model_name = model_cfg.name
    if use_cuda:
        if model_cfg.quantization == 4:
            quantization_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True)
        elif model_cfg.quantization == 8:
            quantization_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_8bit=True)
        else:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Use 4-bit or 8-bit quantization. You passed: {model_cfg.quantization}/"
            )

        model_name = model_cfg.name

    model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
        model_name,
        quantization_config=quantization_config,
        torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
        low_cpu_mem_usage=True,
    )

    if use_cuda:
        model = prepare_model_for_kbit_training(
            model, use_gradient_checkpointing=model_cfg.gradient_checkpointing
        )

    target_modules = model_cfg.lora.target_modules
    if target_modules:
        target_modules = list(target_modules)

    peft_config = LoraConfig(
        r=model_cfg.lora.peft_lora_r,
        lora_alpha=model_cfg.lora.peft_lora_alpha,
        lora_dropout=0.075,
        task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
        target_modules=target_modules,
    )

    peft_model = get_peft_model(model, peft_config)
    if not (use_cuda):
        peft_model.enable_input_require_grads()

    if model_cfg.gradient_checkpointing:
        model.config.use_cache = False

    return peft_model

def compute_communication_costs(config, comm_bw_mbps: float = 20):
      """
      We use Flower's helper function to compute communication costs of federated finetuning.
      Get ready to see the savings!
      """
      model = get_model(config.model)

      trainable, all_parameters = model.get_nb_trainable_parameters()

      total_size = 4*all_parameters/(1024**2)
      trainable_size = 4*trainable/(1024**2)

      upload_time_total = total_size/(comm_bw_mbps/8) # Convert Mbps to MBps by dividing by 8
      upload_time_finetune = trainable_size/(comm_bw_mbps/8)

      print(f"Full model:\n\t{all_parameters/1e6:.3f} M parameters\n\t{total_size:.2f} MB --> upload in {upload_time_total:.2f}s @ {comm_bw_mbps}Mbps")
      print(f"Finetuned model:\n\t{trainable/1e6:.3f} M parameters\n\t{trainable_size:.2f} MB --> upload in {upload_time_finetune:.2f}s @ {comm_bw_mbps}Mbps")
      # print(f"In a {comm_bw_mbps} Mbps channel --> {}")

      num_rounds = config.flower.num_rounds
      num_clients_per_round = int(config.flower.num_clients * config.flower.fraction_fit)
      print(f"Federated Learning setting: "
            f"\n\tNumber of rounds: {num_rounds}"
            f"\n\tNumber of clients per round: {num_clients_per_round}")

      print(f"-----------------------------------------------")
      print(f"Total Communication costs (Full model): {2*num_rounds*num_clients_per_round*total_size/1024:.1f} GB")
      print(f"Total Communication costs (Finetuning): {2*num_rounds*num_clients_per_round*trainable_size} MB")
      print(f"Communication savings: {all_parameters/trainable:.1f}x")

compute_communication_costs(cfg, comm_bw_mbps=20)
```

**We save 726.3x communication costs just by PEFT-ing!**

#### **Where’s Unsloth?** 🦥

If you’ve read my previous articles, you’re probably expecting an Unsloth `FastLanguageModel` here. [Unsloth reduces training memory by around 70%!](https://docs.unsloth.ai/) Unfortunately, Unsloth and FlowerAI have several dependency conflicts. At time of writing, using the latest version of FlowerAI would force us to fall back to an outdated version of Unsloth — about 8 to 9 versions behind the current framework.

It is therefore with much sadness that I omit Unsloth from this experiment 😭

### **👨‍🍳 Step 3: Prompt Prep — Set the Table for Fine-Tuning**

Before we can start cooking (i.e., training), we need to set the table properly. That means formatting the prompts, choosing the right tokenizer, and preparing a smart data collator that knows where the “response” part starts.

```python
def formatting_prompts_func(example):
    # Constructing a standard Alpaca prompt 
    # (https://github.com/tatsu-lab/stanford_alpaca#data-release)

    output_texts = []
    mssg = "Below is an instruction that describes a task. Write a response that appropriately completes the request."
    for i in range(len(example["instruction"])):
        text = f"{mssg}\n### Instruction:\n{example['instruction'][i]}\n### Response: {example['response'][i]}"
        output_texts.append(text)
    return output_texts

def get_tokenizer_and_data_collator_and_prompt_formatting(
    model_name: str, use_fast: bool, padding_side: str
):
    # From: https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/en/sft_trainer
    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(
        model_name, use_fast=use_fast, padding_side=padding_side
    )

    tokenizer.pad_token = (
        tokenizer.bos_token if padding_side == "left" else tokenizer.eos_token
    )
    response_template_with_context = "\n### Response:"  # alpaca response tag
    response_template_ids = tokenizer.encode(
        response_template_with_context, add_special_tokens=False
    )[2:]
    data_collator = DataCollatorForCompletionOnlyLM(
        response_template_ids, tokenizer=tokenizer
    )

    return tokenizer, data_collator, formatting_prompts_func

tokenizer, data_collator, formatting_prompts_func = get_tokenizer_and_data_collator_and_prompt_formatting(
    cfg.model.name,
    cfg.model.use_fast_tokenizer,
    cfg.train.padding_side,
)
```

### **🍳 Step 4: Crafting the Flower Client — The Heartbeat of Federated Learning**

In federated learning, the client isn’t just a passive participant. It’s more like a sous-chef in a distributed kitchen — each working on their own station with local ingredients (data), but following the same recipe (model architecture).

#### 🧠 Understanding the Client’s Role

In federated learning, each client is responsible for:

**1\. Receiving the Global Model:** The server sends the current global model parameters to the client.

**2\. Local Training:** The client trains the model on its local dataset, ensuring data privacy and compliance with data governance policies.

**3\. Sending Updates:** After training, the client sends the updated model parameters back to the server for aggregation.

This process allows for collaborative model training without the need to centralize sensitive data.

First, we code out a utility function to adjust the learning rate (optional).

```python
import math

def cosine_annealing(
    current_round: int,
    total_round: int,
    lrate_max: float = 0.001,
    lrate_min: float = 0.0,
) -> float:
    """Implement cosine annealing learning rate schedule. Strictly speaking this
    is not necessary."""

    cos_inner = math.pi * current_round / total_round
    return lrate_min + 0.5 * (lrate_max - lrate_min) * (1 + math.cos(cos_inner))
```

Cosine annealing gradually reduces the learning rate following a smooth cosine curve for each federated learning round. This helps stabilize training by enabling larger updates early on and finer adjustments later, often leading to better convergence and generalization.

And now let’s build out the Flower Client:

```python
from flwr.common import Context
from flwr.common.typing import NDArrays, Scalar
from flwr.client import NumPyClient

from typing import Dict, Tuple, Callable
from collections import OrderedDict
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer

def set_parameters(model, parameters: NDArrays) -> None:
    """Change the parameters of the model using the given ones."""

    peft_state_dict_keys = get_peft_model_state_dict(model).keys()
    params_dict = zip(peft_state_dict_keys, parameters)
    state_dict = OrderedDict({k: torch.Tensor(v) for k, v in params_dict})
    set_peft_model_state_dict(model, state_dict)

class FlowerClient(NumPyClient):
    def __init__(
        self,
        model_cfg: DictConfig,
        train_cfg: DictConfig,
        trainset,
        tokenizer,
        formatting_prompts_func,
        data_collator,
        save_path,
    ):
        self.device = torch.device("cuda:0" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
        self.train_cfg = train_cfg
        self.training_arguments = SFTConfig(**train_cfg.training_arguments)
        self.tokenizer = tokenizer
        self.formatting_prompts_func = formatting_prompts_func
        self.data_collator = data_collator
        self.save_path = save_path

        # instantiate model
        self.model = get_model(model_cfg)

        self.trainset = trainset

    def get_parameters(self, config: Dict[str, Scalar]) -> NDArrays:
        """Return the parameters of the current net."""

        state_dict = get_peft_model_state_dict(self.model)
        return [val.cpu().numpy() for _, val in state_dict.items()]

    def fit(
        self, parameters: NDArrays, config: Dict[str, Scalar]
    ) -> Tuple[NDArrays, int, Dict]:
        """Implement distributed fit function for a given client."""
        set_parameters(self.model, parameters)

        new_lr = cosine_annealing(
            int(config["current_round"]),
            self.train_cfg.num_rounds,
            self.train_cfg.learning_rate_max,
            self.train_cfg.learning_rate_min,
        )

        self.training_arguments.learning_rate = new_lr
        self.training_arguments.output_dir = self.save_path

        evalset = None
        if self.train_cfg.evaluate_split:
            train_test = self.trainset.train_test_split(test_size=0.1, seed=1234)
            trainset = train_test['train']
            evalset = train_test['test']
        else:
            trainset = self.trainset

        trainer = SFTTrainer(
            model=self.model,
            processing_class=self.tokenizer,
            args=self.training_arguments,
            train_dataset=trainset,
            eval_dataset=evalset,
            formatting_func=self.formatting_prompts_func,
            data_collator=self.data_collator,
        )

        metrics = {}
        if self.train_cfg.evaluate_split:
            eval_res = trainer.evaluate()
            metrics['eval_loss'] = eval_res['eval_loss']
            print(eval_res)

        # Do local training
        results = trainer.train()

        metrics = {**metrics, "train_loss": results.training_loss}

        return (
            self.get_parameters({}),
            len(self.trainset),
            metrics,
        )

def gen_client_fn(
    fds,
    tokenizer,
    formatting_prompts_func,
    data_collator,
    model_cfg: DictConfig,
    train_cfg: DictConfig,
    save_path: str,
) -> Callable[[str], FlowerClient]:
    """Generate the client function that creates the Flower Clients."""

    def client_fn(context: Context) -> FlowerClient:
        """Create a Flower client representing a single organization."""

        # Let's get the partition corresponding to the i-th client
        partition_id = int(context.node_config["partition-id"])
        client_trainset = fds.load_partition(partition_id, "train")
        client_trainset = client_trainset.remove_columns(["instruction"])
        client_trainset = client_trainset.rename_column("input", "instruction")
        client_trainset = client_trainset.rename_column("output", "response")
        return FlowerClient(
            model_cfg,
            train_cfg,
            client_trainset,
            tokenizer,
            formatting_prompts_func,
            data_collator,
            save_path,
        ).to_client()

    return client_fn
```

_💡_ A lot of this code should feel familiar if you’ve used PyTorch. We structure the class, define the `fit` method (leveraging Hugging Face’s `SFTTrainer`).

Now let’s initialize the client:

```python
from flwr.client.mod import fixedclipping_mod

save_path = "./my_fl_llama_model"
client = fl.client.ClientApp(
    client_fn=gen_client_fn(
        fds,
        tokenizer,
        formatting_prompts_func,
        data_collator,
        cfg.model,
        cfg.train,
        save_path,
    ),
    mods=[fixedclipping_mod]
)
```

Awesome! Notice that we add a `fixedclipping_mod` to “clip” model updates during finetuning — preventing changes that are too drastic.

### **🧠 Step 5: Configuring the Federated Server — Directing the Symphony 🎻**

While each client trains locally, the server acts as the conductor of the federated learning orchestra. It defines how rounds are configured and how model updates are aggregated.

This cell introduces three essential server-side functions:

```python
from flwr.common import Context

# All docstrings are written by me

def get_on_fit_config():
    """
     • Purpose: This function provides the configuration dictionary sent to each
      client before training begins in a given round.
     • Use Case: Clients can adapt behaviors (e.g., learning rate schedules) based
        on the current round number.
     • Design Pattern: Returns a function (fit_config_fn) that Flower calls at each
      round.

    🧠 Analogy: This is like giving each chef a new cooking instruction every day
    based on how many days the kitchen has been operating.

    """
    def fit_config_fn(server_round: int):
        fit_config = {"current_round": server_round}
        return fit_config

    return fit_config_fn

def fit_weighted_average(metrics):
    """
    • Purpose: Calculates a weighted average of training loss across all clients.
    • Mechanism:
        • Each client’s training loss is scaled by the number of examples it used.
        • This ensures larger datasets have more influence on the final average.
    • Why It Matters: Without weighting, small datasets could skew the overall metric.

    Example:
    # Client 1: 100 examples, loss = 0.5 → 100 * 0.5 = 50
    # Client 2: 200 examples, loss = 0.25 → 200 * 0.25 = 50
    # Weighted average = (50 + 50) / (100 + 200) = 0.333
    """
    # Multiply accuracy of each client by number of examples used
    losses = [num_examples * m["train_loss"] for num_examples, m in metrics]
    examples = [num_examples for num_examples, _ in metrics]

    # Aggregate and return custom metric (weighted average)
    return {"train_loss": sum(losses) / sum(examples)}

def get_evaluate_fn(model_cfg, save_every_round, total_round, save_path):
    """
     • Purpose: Save the global model periodically during training.
     • Conditions:
       • Skip round 0.
       • Save if it’s the final round or every n rounds (save_every_round).
       • How:
         • Reconstruct the model from the config.
         • Load the current global parameters.
         • Save using the HuggingFace save_pretrained method.

    🧠 Why This Matters: In federated learning, there’s no single centralized
    training process. If something goes wrong, saved checkpoints are your recovery
    point.

    🔁 Return Format: Always returns 0.0, {} because evaluation is optional here
    — the function is used mainly for checkpointing.
    """

    def evaluate(server_round: int, parameters, config):
        # Save model
        if server_round != 0 and (
            server_round == total_round or server_round % save_every_round == 0
        ):
            # Init model
            model = get_model(model_cfg)
            set_parameters(model, parameters)

            model.save_pretrained(f"{save_path}/peft_{server_round}")

        return 0.0, {}

    return evaluate
```

#### 🧩 How It All Fits Together

These functions collectively help manage the federated learning lifecycle:

-   Configure each round (get\_on\_fit\_config)
-   Aggregate client metrics meaningfully (fit\_weighted\_average)
-   Persist model state safely (get\_evaluate\_fn)

#### 🛠️ Next Step: Define the server

```python
from flwr.server.strategy import (
    DifferentialPrivacyClientSideFixedClipping
)

def server_fn(context: Context):
    """
    This function returns a configured Flower server app, which will be passed to
    start_simulation() later. It defines:
     • The strategy for aggregation (FedAvg)
     • How rounds behave (e.g., which clients to sample)
     • Optional advanced features like Differential Privacy
    """
    strategy = fl.server.strategy.FedAvg(
        min_available_clients=cfg.flower.num_clients, # total clients
        fraction_fit=cfg.flower.fraction_fit, # ratio of clients to sample
        fraction_evaluate=0.0, # No federated evaluation
        # A (optional) function used to configure a "fit()" round
        on_fit_config_fn=get_on_fit_config(),
        # A (optional) function to aggregate metrics sent by clients
        fit_metrics_aggregation_fn=fit_weighted_average,
        # A (optional) function to execute on the server after each round.
        # In this example the function only saves the global model.
        evaluate_fn=get_evaluate_fn(
            cfg.model,
            cfg.train.save_every_round,
            cfg.flower.num_rounds,
            save_path
        ),
    )

    # Add Differential Privacy to FedAvg strategy
    sampled_clients = cfg.flower.num_clients*strategy.fraction_fit
    strategy = DifferentialPrivacyClientSideFixedClipping(
        strategy,
        noise_multiplier=cfg.flower.dp.noise_mult,
        clipping_norm=cfg.flower.dp.clip_norm,
        num_sampled_clients=sampled_clients
    )

    # Number of rounds to run the simulation
    num_rounds = cfg.flower.num_rounds
    config = fl.server.ServerConfig(num_rounds=num_rounds)

    return fl.server.ServerAppComponents(strategy=strategy, config=config)

server = fl.server.ServerApp(server_fn=server_fn)
```

Now all that we need to do is kickstart the run:

```python
from logging import ERROR

client_resources = dict(cfg.flower.client_resources)
backend_setup = {"logging_level": ERROR, "log_to_driver": False}

fl.simulation.run_simulation(
    server_app=server,
    client_app=client,
    num_supernodes=cfg.flower.num_clients,
    backend_config={
        "client_resources": client_resources,
        "init_args": backend_setup
    }
)
```

### 📤 Upload to HuggingFace Hub

This part is a little tricky. We need to re-import the **base model**, wrap it with our **fine-tuned PEFT adapter**, merge them, and finally push the **merged model** to the Hugging Face Hub:

```python
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig
from peft import PeftModel
import torch

# a. Load the base 4-bit LLM
base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct",
    quantization_config=BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True),
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)

# b. Wrap it with your federated fine-tuned adapter
peft_model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(
    base,
    os.path.join(save_path, "peft_2"),    # path to your adapter folder
)

# c. Merge the base model with the adapter
merged_model = peft_model.merge_and_unload()

# d. Push the merged model to HuggingFace Hub
merged_model.push_to_hub("tituslhy/llama32_1b_federated_finetuned_250steps")
```

### And finally, let’s test it!

```python
from llama_index.llms.huggingface import HuggingFaceLLM
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

# Initialize HuggingFaceLLM
llm = HuggingFaceLLM(
    model_name="tituslhy/llama32_1b_federated_finetuned_250steps",
    tokenizer_name="meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct" #Use meta-llama's default tokenizer
)

prompt = "What are the management strategies for antiphospholipid syndrome?"
response = llm.complete(prompt)

display(Markdown(str(response)))
```

```python-repl

Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is a rare autoimmune disorder characterized by the presence of antibodies against phospholipids, which can lead to blood clots, stroke, and other serious conditions. Management of APS typically involves a multidisciplinary approach, including:

Anti-platelet therapy: Regularly administering medications such as aspirin, clopidogrel, or other anti-platelet agents to prevent blood clots.
Anticoagulant therapy: Using medications like heparin, warfarin, or direct thrombin inhibitors to prevent blood clots.
Surgical interventions: In some cases, surgical procedures like angioplasty or surgery may be necessary to treat complications such as stroke or acute limb ischemia.
Dietary changes: Some studies suggest that a specific diet, such as a low-mercury diet or a Mediterranean-style diet, may help reduce the risk of APS.
Lifestyle modifications: Maintaining a healthy lifestyle, including regular exercise
```

Awesome it works!

### 🚀 Deployment

In a production setting, you’d typically separate your code into client.py and server.py — one for the client-side logic, and one for the server that handles aggregation. You’ll also need to install the `flwr` command-line tool on **all participating machines** (both clients and the server).

Once everything is set up:

-   Spin Flower’s server on server.py on the central server to coordinate updates.
-   Spin Flower’s client services on client.py on each client machine.

⚠️ **Make sure all clients can communicate with the server** — network firewalls and IP misconfigurations are common blockers.

Flower really makes things this simple! Here’s the official [Flower deployment guide](https://flower.ai/docs/framework/how-to-run-flower-with-deployment-engine.html) for reference.

### 🤔 A brief retrospective

OK — we didn’t _actually_ train Toothless with 10 different teachers, but we could have! The code ran smoothly this time, but smooth execution does not always mean success.

For example, not shown here: I also tried using a **much smaller LLM** (EleutherAI/pythia-70m) over a full epoch per client over 2 rounds. The code ran fine — but when I queried the model, it just responded with blank lines (“\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n”) regardless of the question. So, yes, **federated learning doesn’t always go smoothly!**

The real question is — _why?_

A few possible reasons:

-   **Model size matters**: Pythia-70M is much smaller than Llama 3.2 1B, and likely lacked the capacity to learn meaningful patterns — especially with limited data and noisy updates across clients.
-   We used a publicly available, highly curated dataset, which helped. This is unlike our SFT and RAFT articles, where we relied on LLM-generated data of varying quality.
-   **Federated averaging might be a poor strategy** when some clients don’t learn anything meaningful. This highlights the need for **exploratory data analysis (EDA)** to ensure all clients are trained on quality data.
-   The **differential privacy noise level** could be too high, effectively drowning out useful signals— we may need to **tune it down**.
-   We could also try **increasing the fraction of clients sampled** in each round. That way, even if one client performs poorly, the average can still move in the right direction — assuming most clients contribute useful updates.

### Concluding thoughts

The open-source community keeps delivering one incredible framework after another — making it easier than ever to build and ship high-quality AI systems. **Flower AI** is one such gem.

All we really have to do is tune the hyperparameters (and yes, wrangle a few dependency conflicts — but that’s standard fare for developers), and more importantly, **ensure dataset quality across clients**.

This is my **fourth article on LLM finetuning**, and it’s clear that the space remains both vibrant and frustrating — especially when LLMs are involved. **Federated finetuning**, in particular, opens up access to otherwise inaccessible datasets — without compromising data privacy.

That said, **federated finetuning isn’t a silver bullet**. In addition to having **more hyperparameters to tune** (as discussed above), it also requires that **all client servers have an NVIDIA GPU** — or it’ll take forever.

After finishing the Flower AI DeepLearning classes, I couldn’t wait to try this out myself and was thrilled to see it work. Now… if only I had 20 more GPU servers to do this at scale. 😄
