body: * * * The use of knowledge graphs to augment traditional vector-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) isn’t new — but it remains far less mainstream than purely vector-based approaches. This raises a natural question: **does GraphRAG meet a real need, or is it still just a hidden gem waiting to be polished — if ever?** ### What is GraphRAG? GraphRAG blends the structure of a knowledge graph with the flexibility of retrieval-augmented generation. A knowledge graph consists of nodes (entities) and edges (relationships), forming a semantically rich representation of information. In a typical GraphRAG pipeline: - The full text is chunked into documents. - These chunks are vectorized. - An LLM analyzes the chunks to extract entities and relationships, dynamically constructing a knowledge graph. - The graph itself can store metadata — such as chunk vectors as properties of document nodes. Different frameworks approach GraphRAG in unique ways. For instance, [Microsoft’s GraphRAG](https://microsoft.github.io/graphrag/index/default_dataflow/) includes summarization steps, and [LlamaIndex’s Property Graph Index](https://www.llamaindex.ai/blog/introducing-the-property-graph-index-a-powerful-new-way-to-build-knowledge-graphs-with-llms) vectorizes the nodes of the knowledge graph only, not the document chunks! So it’s important to always consult the respective documentation before getting started. ### What We’ll Explore In this article, we’ll walk through a traditional GraphRAG pipeline using LangChain and Neo4j. But more importantly, we’ll dig into the **under-discussed pitfalls** — the _gotchas_ — that may explain why GraphRAG hasn’t yet seen broad adoption. Because sometimes, a “hidden gem” remains hidden for a reason. My code is available at [this GitHub Repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/shiny-engine/tree/main), and is entirely run in Jupyter Notebooks. ### 2\. Crawling Articles with Crawl4AI To retrieve our documents, we’ll use **Crawl4AI**, an open-source, high-performance web scraping framework. It handles even complex layouts (tables, images) with surprising ease — and best of all, it works asynchronously. Crawl4AI is also **100% open source**, with an active GitHub and a helpful [YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCpnV0jtSvh4uifO7C6fSnVg) to complement the [official documentation](https://docs.crawl4ai.com/). If you’re new to it, you’ll find it easy to get up and running. Jupyter notebooks run an event loop by default. That conflicts with `asyncio.run()` or `await`, leading to the infamous error: ``` RuntimeError: This event loop is already running ``` To fix this, we patch the event loop using `nest_asyncio` so we can safely use `await`, `async def`, and `asyncio.gather()` within notebook cells. #### 🧪 Notebook Setup: ```python # main_notebook.ipynb import nest_asyncio from crawl4ai import AsyncWebCrawler, CrawlerRunConfig nest_asyncio.apply() # I've always been interested in pursuing an MBA, so in this notebook, we'll crawl a few recent articles to explore whether it's still a worthwhile investment in 2025. urls = [ "https://www.forbes.com/councils/forbesbusinesscouncil/2025/03/19/reconsidering-the-mba-is-it-still-worth-it/", "https://online.hbs.edu/blog/post/roi-of-an-mba", "https://plannerbee.co/learn-personal-finance/mba-singapore-worth/", "https://www.coursera.org/articles/is-an-mba-worth-it", "https://www.singsaver.com.sg/blog/is-an-mba-worth-it" ] ``` #### 🔍 Asynchronous Web Crawling Code ```python import json import asyncio import time from crawl4ai.extraction_strategy import JsonXPathExtractionStrategy from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter from langchain_core.documents.base import Document text_splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter() async def extract_forbes_hbs_blog(url: str) -> list[str]: """ Crawls a single article and extracts clean text from , <h2>, <h3>, and <p> tags. """ schema = { "name": "Title_H2_P_Sequence", "baseSelector": "//title | //h2 | //h3| //p", "fields": [ {"name": "text", "selector": ".", "type": "text"} ] } strategy = JsonXPathExtractionStrategy(schema, verbose=True) config = CrawlerRunConfig(extraction_strategy=strategy) async with AsyncWebCrawler() as crawler: result = await crawler.arun(url, config=config) if not result.success: raise RuntimeError(f"Crawl failed: {result.error_message}") items = json.loads(result.extracted_content) return [item["text"] for item in items] async def crawl_websites(urls: list[str]) -> list[Document]: """ Crawls multiple URLs and converts each article into LangChain Document chunks. """ all_docs = [] tasks = [extract_forbes_hbs_blog(url) for url in urls] results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True) for content, url in zip(results, urls): if isinstance(content, Exception): print(f"Failed to extract {url}: {content}") continue full_text = "\n\n".join(content) docs = text_splitter.create_documents([full_text], metadatas=[{"source": url}]) all_docs.extend(docs) return all_docs # Run the pipeline start = time.time() results = await crawl_websites(urls) print(f"✅ Crawl completed in {time.time() - start:.2f}s") ``` #### 📘 What This Code Does `**extract_forbes_hbs_blog(url)**` - Uses `JsonXPathExtractionStrategy` to pull structured content from article tags: `<title>`, `<h2>`, `<h3>`, `<p>` - Crawls asynchronously using `AsyncWebCrawler` - Returns a list of clean text segments from the article `**crawl_websites(urls)**` - Calls `extract_forbes_hbs_blog()` for each URL in parallel using `asyncio.gather` - Joins the text, then chunks it into `Document` objects with metadata using LangChain's `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter` **Execution** - The crawl and chunking happen asynchronously - It only took **~3.6s total** for all five articles! #### ⚙️ Why Use `asyncio` Here? `asyncio` is Python’s native async I/O framework. It’s useful when: - Making concurrent web/API requests - Avoiding thread overhead for I/O-bound tasks - Scaling to many URLs without blocking By using `await` and `async def`, and combining tasks with `asyncio.gather`, we gain **massive speedups** over sequential crawls. #### Ingest into Neo4j Make sure you get your Neo4j instance started — either by using [Neo4j Aura](https://neo4j.com/product/auradb/?utm_source=GSearch&utm_medium=PaidSearch&utm_campaign=Evergreen&utm_content=APAC-Search-SEMBrand-Evergreen-None-SEM-SEM-NonABM&utm_term=aura%20db&utm_adgroup=auradb&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=20769286994&gbraid=0AAAAADk9OYoc73_kSpFzBvnJAAtAVmC9K&gclid=Cj0KCQjwoZbBBhDCARIsAOqMEZVGzyGvRc2Z797APAl1DOx6Sti38GPsssbvSCQ8BF1mx0ByMxzJ_fAaAtfhEALw_wcB) or Docker like me. ```bash docker run \ -p 7474:7474 -p 7687:7687 \ -v $PWD/data:/data -v $PWD/plugins:/plugins \ --name neo4j-apoc \ -e NEO4J_apoc_export_file_enabled=true \ -e NEO4J_apoc_import_file_enabled=true \ -e NEO4J_apoc_import_file_use__neo4j__config=true \ -e NEO4JLABS_PLUGINS=\[\"apoc\"\] \ neo4j:latest ``` We’ll be using Groq’s Llama 3.3 70Bn parameter model to build the knowledge graph. Groq’s LLMs run on LPUs (Language Processing Units), which offer significant speed advantages over traditional GPU-hosted models like those on CUDA. This makes real-time graph construction much smoother. ```python import os from dotenv import load_dotenv, find_dotenv from langchain_groq import ChatGroq from langchain_neo4j import Neo4jGraph from langchain_experimental.graph_transformers import LLMGraphTransformer _ = load_dotenv(find_dotenv()) os.environ["NEO4J_URI"] = "bolt://localhost:7687" os.environ["NEO4J_USERNAME"] = "neo4j" os.environ["NEO4J_PASSWORD"] = "langchain" llm = ChatGroq( model="llama-3.3-70b-versatile", temperature=0 ) llm_transformer = LLMGraphTransformer(llm=llm) graph_documents = llm_transformer.convert_to_graph_documents(docs) graph = Neo4jGraph(refresh_schema=False) # Upsert documents to graph graph.add_graph_documents( graph_documents, baseEntityLabel=True, include_source=True ) ``` And that’s all it takes! Thanks to LangChain’s integration with Neo4j, building and ingesting a knowledge graph becomes remarkably seamless — just a few lines of code for some pretty powerful results. Now that the ingestion is complete, we can inspect the resulting knowledge graph structure inside Neo4j Browser. Here’s a snapshot of how the documents have been transformed into interconnected entities and relationships: The yellow nodes represent the text chunks from our crawled articles. Just look at how beautiful this knowledge graph is — so many nodes and edges, all interlinked! #### So what’s next? Naturally, we want to query it and see what insights it can uncover. ```python from langchain_neo4j import GraphCypherQAChain chain = GraphCypherQAChain.from_llm( llm, graph=graph, verbose=True, return_intermediate_steps=True, allow_dangerous_requests=True ) response = chain.invoke( {"query": "What are the considerations when taking an MBA?"} ) print(response) ``` ```python-repl > Entering new GraphCypherQAChain chain... Generated Cypher: MATCH (n:MBA)-[:REQUIRES]->(r:Consideration) RETURN r.name Received notification from DBMS server: {severity: WARNING} {code: Neo.ClientNotification.Statement.UnknownRelationshipTypeWarning} {category: UNRECOGNIZED} {title: The provided relationship type is not in the database.} {description: One of the relationship types in your query is not available in the database, make sure you didn't misspell it or that the label is available when you run this statement in your application (the missing relationship type is: REQUIRES)} {position: line: 1, column: 17, offset: 16} for query: 'MATCH (n:MBA)-[:REQUIRES]->(r:Consideration) RETURN r.name' Received notification from DBMS server: {severity: WARNING} {code: Neo.ClientNotification.Statement.UnknownLabelWarning} {category: UNRECOGNIZED} {title: The provided label is not in the database.} {description: One of the labels in your query is not available in the database, make sure you didn't misspell it or that the label is available when you run this statement in your application (the missing label name is: MBA)} {position: line: 1, column: 10, offset: 9} for query: 'MATCH (n:MBA)-[:REQUIRES]->(r:Consideration) RETURN r.name' Received notification from DBMS server: {severity: WARNING} {code: Neo.ClientNotification.Statement.UnknownLabelWarning} {category: UNRECOGNIZED} {title: The provided label is not in the database.} {description: One of the labels in your query is not available in the database, make sure you didn't misspell it or that the label is available when you run this statement in your application (the missing label name is: Consideration)} {position: line: 1, column: 31, offset: 30} for query: 'MATCH (n:MBA)-[:REQUIRES]->(r:Consideration) RETURN r.name' Received notification from DBMS server: {severity: WARNING} {code: Neo.ClientNotification.Statement.UnknownPropertyKeyWarning} {category: UNRECOGNIZED} {title: The provided property key is not in the database} {description: One of the property names in your query is not available in the database, make sure you didn't misspell it or that the label is available when you run this statement in your application (the missing property name is: name)} {position: line: 1, column: 55, offset: 54} for query: 'MATCH (n:MBA)-[:REQUIRES]->(r:Consideration) RETURN r.name' Full Context: [] > Finished chain. I don't know the answer. ``` **Wait — what?!** This is **gotcha #1**, and it’s an easy one to trip over (and avoid): > **_The starting point of GraphRAG is not Cypher queries_** Even though the LLM tries to infer the correct Cypher query, it often guesses the wrong labels, relationship types, or property keys. 👉 The better approach for GraphRAG? **Start with a vector similarity search**, not Cypher-based querying. The following codes are adapted from this [brilliant LangChain Neo4j article](https://blog.langchain.dev/enhancing-rag-based-applications-accuracy-by-constructing-and-leveraging-knowledge-graphs/). #### **Step 1: Add vector search to our graph** We have to store the vector embeddings of the documents into a vector database. Neo4j has one too! ```python from langchain_neo4j import Neo4jVector from langchain_ollama import OllamaEmbeddings embeddings = OllamaEmbeddings(model="nomic-embed-text") vector_index = Neo4jVector.from_existing_graph( embeddings, search_type="hybrid", node_label="Document", text_node_properties=["text"], embedding_node_property="embedding" ) ``` Here we state that we only want to store the vectors for our Document labelled nodes (i.e. the yellow nodes of our text chunks in our knowledge graph). #### **Step 2: Add fuzzy search over detected entities** To improve recall in our graph queries, we’ll combine vector search with **fuzzy full-text search**. This ensures we still get results even when entity names are slightly misspelled — a common failure point with strict Cypher queries. We’ll be using a Lucene-based fuzzy search of our knowledge graph based on the entities that the LLM detected in our question — this is especially useful if there are typos in the user’s texts. Let’s first write a LangChain runnable to extract entities from texts. ```python from pydantic import BaseModel, Field from typing import List from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate class Entities(BaseModel): """Identifying information about entities.""" names: List[str] = Field( ..., description="All the person/s, organization/s, or business entities that appear in the text", ) prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages( [ ( "system", "You are extracting organization and person entities from the text.", ), ( "human", "Use the given format to extract information from the following" "input: {question}", ), ] ) entity_chain = prompt | llm.with_structured_output(Entities) ``` ✅ Example: ```python entity_chain.invoke({"question": "Who founded OpenAI and where is it based?"}) # → Entities(names=["OpenAI"]) ``` And now: ```python from langchain_neo4j.vectorstores.neo4j_vector import remove_lucene_chars graph.query("CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX entity IF NOT EXISTS FOR (e:__Entity__) ON EACH [e.id]") def generate_full_text_query(input: str) -> str: """ Generates a fuzzy full-text search query from an input string. Each word in the input string is appended with a fuzzy match operator (`~2`) to tolerate up to two character differences (e.g., typos), and combined with logical AND operators for a strict conjunctive search. This is especially useful for querying search indexes or graph databases when matching user-provided input against stored entities with possible misspellings or slight variations. Args: input (str): The input string to be transformed into a full-text query. Returns: str: A constructed full-text search query with fuzzy match operators. """ full_text_query = "" words = [el for el in remove_lucene_chars(input).split() if el] print(words) for word in words[:-1]: print(full_text_query) full_text_query += f" {word}~2 AND" full_text_query += f" {words[-1]}~2" print(f"Full text query generated: {full_text_query.strip()}") return full_text_query.strip() ``` This cell prepares Neo4j for fuzzy entity lookups and defines a helper function to construct robust full-text search queries that tolerate typos and slight variations. For Example - `generate_full_text_query("Gooogle DeepMind")` - `Output: "Gooogle~2 AND DeepMind~2"` - This query can now be passed to Neo4j for fault-tolerant graph retrieval. #### Step 3: Hybrid Retrieval ```python def structured_retriever(question: str) -> str: """ Retrieves the structured neighborhood of entities mentioned in a question. This function performs the following steps: - Extracts named entities from the user's question using an entity extraction chain. - For each entity, performs a fuzzy full-text search against a graph database. - Collects and formats the relationships (incoming and outgoing) around each matched node. Args: question (str): The user's question from which to extract and retrieve related entity data. Returns: str: A formatted string of the graph relationships around the matched entities. """ result = "" entities = entity_chain.invoke({"question": question}) for entity in entities.names: # print("Querying graph...") response = graph.query( """CALL db.index.fulltext.queryNodes('entity', $query, {limit:2}) YIELD node,score CALL { MATCH (node)-[r:!MENTIONS]->(neighbor) RETURN node.id + ' - ' + type(r) + ' -> ' + neighbor.id AS output UNION MATCH (node)<-[r:!MENTIONS]-(neighbor) RETURN neighbor.id + ' - ' + type(r) + ' -> ' + node.id AS output } RETURN output LIMIT 50 """, {"query": generate_full_text_query(entity)}, ) result += "\n".join([el['output'] for el in response]) # print(f"\n\nresult: {result}") return result def retriever(question: str): """ Retrieves both structured and unstructured data relevant to a given question. Combines: - Structured graph-based data from entity neighborhood lookups via `structured_retriever`. - Unstructured semantic matches from a vector index using similarity search. The combined result is a contextual block of structured relationships and relevant textual snippets for further processing or reasoning. Args: question (str): The user's query or natural language question. Returns: str: A combined context string including both structured and unstructured data. """ structured_data = structured_retriever(question) unstructured_data = [el.page_content for el in vector_index.similarity_search(question, similarity_score_threshold=0.5)] final_data = f"""Structured data: {structured_data} Unstructured data: {"#Document ". join(unstructured_data)} """ print(f"\n\n Final data in context: {final_data}") return final_data ``` This cell defines two key functions that combine symbolic (graph-based) and vector-based retrieval to enrich context for downstream tasks like answering questions or generating insights. > _🧠_ **_structured\_retriever(question: str)_**_ > Looks up the symbolic “neighborhood” around named entities by:_ - Extracting key names with a structured `entity_chain`. - Generating fuzzy full-text search queries (using `~2` tolerance) to match similar/misspelled names. - Querying both incoming and outgoing relationships (excluding `:MENTIONS`). - Formatting them as readable relationship strings for easy ingestion. > _🔍_ **_retriever(question: str)_** _Combines:_ - **Structured**: Symbolic graph lookups (relationships and nodes). - **Unstructured**: Vector similarity from embedded text chunks. This hybrid context pipes to downstream LLM tasks. #### Step 4: Constructing our final runnable ```python from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser from langchain_core.runnables import RunnablePassthrough, RunnableParallel template = """Answer the question based only on the following context: {context} Question: {question} """ prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_template(template) chain = ( RunnableParallel( { "context": retriever, "question": RunnablePassthrough(), } ) | prompt | llm | StrOutputParser() ) ``` The RunnableParallel runs two tasks in parallel: - “context” → Pulls from the retriever(question) function (which combines graph-based and vector-based data). - “question” → Passes through the original question unchanged via RunnablePassthrough(). So we first retrieve the context from the question, pass both the context and the question as a prompt to our LLM for an answer, and return only the string output from the LLM. ### Let’s chat with our bot! ```python response = chain.invoke( "What are the benefits of an MBA?") ``` ```python-repl Search query: What are the benefits of an MBA? Querying graph... ['MBA'] Full text query generated: MBA~2 Final data in context: Structured data: Chris Haroun - MEMBER -> Forbes Councils Chris Haroun - FOUNDER -> Haroun Education Ventures, Inc. ... Mba - LEADS_TO -> Emerging Industries Scholarships - FUNDS -> Mba Unstructured data: text: The ROI of an MBA: Is the Degree Worth It? | HBS Online ... ``` Here we see the combined output from our **hybrid retriever** — structured symbolic data from the graph, and unstructured semantic content from traditional RAG. > 🧠 **LLM’s final answer**: > _The benefits of an MBA include:_ > **Career Acceleration**: An MBA teaches decision-making, leadership, and problem-solving. > **Earning Potential**: MBA graduates typically command higher salaries. > **Connections**: Programs connect you with global peers, faculty, and alumni. > **Leadership Skills**: You’ll gain expertise in managing people and organizations. > **Networking**: Executive coaching, career services, and alumni networks help unlock new opportunities. > **Job Prospects**: Employers value the comprehensive skill set of MBA graduates. > **Personal Growth**: Many find the journey transformative and eye-opening. > _Overall, an MBA can accelerate careers, improve income, and foster personal development._ ### ❓ Reflection > _🤔_ **_Question_**_: Based on the LLM’s response, do you think the LLM relied more on the_ **_graph-based symbolic facts_**_, or on the_ **_semantic vector content_**_?_ This is a good moment to pause and think: how did each modality contribute to the final answer? Could the symbolic graph data have helped with surfacing connections like _MBA → Emerging Industries_, or was the output mostly driven by the HBS article in vector search? I tried a few more queries in my notebook, and my **sense** is that the LLM is mostly relying on the unstructured text chunks from the vector search when generating its replies. It’s hard to **prove this definitively**, but the signs are there: the structured graph output — being in the form of raw node → edge → node triples — tends to be less expressive than full-text chunks that explain relationships in natural language. This is more pronounced if the nodes and edges don’t necessarily make sense (to me at least — the “Chris Haroun” node was extracted because it was linked to the document chunk extracted from the vector-based search, but so is every other node linked to “Chris Haroun”!). > This brings up an important **gotcha**: we may be **filling up the LLM’s context window** with symbolic graph data that doesn’t significantly enhance the response. And that’s a key reason why graphRAG, while intellectually appealing, isn’t always practical. **Vanilla vector-based RAG is already very strong**, and unless your graph brings in _truly unique_ structure or provenance, it might not justify the added complexity — or the cost in context tokens. ### Which brings me to my next gotcha: Cost To construct a high-quality knowledge graph, we had to use a fairly powerful LLM. Why not just use a smaller model to save money? Because the **effectiveness of GraphRAG is tightly coupled with the quality of the graph** — and that quality depends heavily on the model’s ability to understand and connect concepts. Here’s a knowledge graph I constructed for an article using Qwen 2.5 7bn: Notice the many **disconnected islands** in the graph. This suggests the model has yet to understand how different parts of the article relate to one another. Here’s my knowledge graph for the same article using Llama 3.3–70bn: This time, the model was able to **“connect the dots”** much more effectively, resulting in a richer and more coherent graph. And that makes a real difference. When we perform a graph traversal for context enrichment, a well-connected graph offers far more **meaningful paths** and **semantic depth** than a sparse one. So while small LLMs are cheaper, the trade-off in graph quality can severely limit the downstream value of GraphRAG. #### A (painful) personal experience Not only does GraphRAG cost more because it requires a more powerful LLM, it **also becomes significantly more expensive** in **domains with densely interconnected content**. A [talented colleague](https://www.linkedin.com/in/stephen1horn/) and I were experimenting with building our own **Apache Spark LLM copilot** using a knowledge graph backbone. We scraped the entire Apache Spark documentation and used a **state-of-the-art LLM from Anthropic on AWS Bedrock** to generate our graph. Fifteen minutes in — and not even 1% through the docs — we were horrified to see a **$50 bill** already. We **canned the GraphRAG approach immediately**. > **My intuition is that GraphRAG might work better in domains that are more abstract or conceptual**, like _responsible AI_ or _ethics policies_. In these kinds of domains, the relationships between ideas — rather than exact text overlaps — carry a lot of meaning. So when a user asks something like _“How do I make my computer vision application align with responsible AI practices?”_, a graph-based approach might help uncover **connections to fairness, transparency, or governance topics** — giving a more holistic answer that a pure vector search might not surface as naturally. ### **The last gotcha: domain experience** GraphRAG’s performance really improves with **more domain-specific engineering**. Not every entity or relationship in a knowledge base is useful — you don’t need to know, for instance, that a document is a PDF. You get better results when you’re deliberate about **what’s important** — and that’s where **Cypher Query Language (CQL)** comes in. The challenge? **Cypher isn’t exactly mainstream** (I only have a rudimentary grasp of it myself), and to really make it work, you’ll need a **graph expert** and **domain experts** who understand the knowledge base deeply — ideally in the same room, tuning queries together. We implemented a **Lucene fuzzy search** for flexibility, but there are much more advanced graph query techniques out there — again, requiring deeper Cypher chops and domain knowledge. This is a stark contrast to **vector-based RAG**, where setup is fast and predictable. Even when doing **metadata engineering** or **contextual retrieval**, vector-based RAG scales across unfamiliar documents — you can “RAG it instead of reading it.” GraphRAG, on the other hand, has these hidden gotchas that make it less plug-and-play and more like a domain-specific engineering project. ### **To GraphRAG or not** To be clear, **GraphRAG has real merits**. The extraction of relationship-based context can **enrich vector-based retrieval** and, in the right setting, **improve answer quality** beyond what pure vector search can do. That said, I’d recommend **exhausting all possible vector-based approaches first** — especially the more advanced techniques like metadata filtering, reranking, and hybrid search — before reaching for GraphRAG. It’s powerful, but it comes with non-trivial costs and complexity. _Disclaimer: All opinions and interpretations are that of the writer, and not of MITB. body:
* * *

#### Part 2

In my [previous article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/its-2025-start-using-chainlit-for-your-llm-apps-558db1a46315), I wrote about how to build a generative AI assistant with Google Map capabilities from the ground up. We did some amazing things:

-   Built an app to support the entire chat lifecycle: login, start chat, handle incoming messages, stop tasks, resume chats, and logout
-   Added **chat starters** to help users kick off conversations
-   Created **chat profiles** to inject different system prompts for our LLM agent
-   Implemented **chat settings** to allow advanced configuration (e.g. choosing different LLMs or tweaking temperature)
-   Built a custom **Canvas** using Google Maps, wrapped into a LlamaIndex Function Agent

We wrapped up steps 1–6 above on our home page. In this article, we’re taking things to the next level (actually, several levels): adding **image generation**, **AutoRAG**, **audio support**, and **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** capabilities.

As before, all my codes can be found in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/sturdy-octo-fortnight).

### 1\. Adding image generation capabilities via Chainlit Commands 🖼️

The ChatGPT interface is able to generate images if you specify for it to do so. We can configure this in Chainlit too. Let’s add the following into app.py:

```python
# <earlier imports>

commands = [
    {"id": "Picture", "icon": "image", "description": "Use DALL-E"},
]

@cl.on_chat_start
async def start():
    """Handler for chat start events. Sets session variables."""
    
    await cl.context.emitter.set_commands(commands)
    ... # <rest of your on_chat_start logic>
```

In Chainlit, commands are defined as a list of dictionaries. Each dictionary must include:

-   `id`: the name of the command (e.g. `"Picture"`)
-   `icon`: a [Lucide icon](https://lucide.dev/icons/) name
-   `description`: a short label for what the command does

These commands are set at the beginning of each chat using `set_commands()`. Once your app is restarted, a **Commands** button will appear in the message bar, letting users choose from your list — as shown below:

Not so fast — clicking the command won’t do anything _yet_. We haven’t wired up the image generation logic. Since Chainlit sends commands via the message bar, we’ll need to modify our `@cl.on_message` handler. Add this code snippet to your app.py:

```python
# <earlier imports and on_chat_start code>
from openai import AsyncOpenAI

openai_client = AsyncOpenAI(api_key="...")

@cl.on_message
async def on_message(message: cl.Message):
    if message.command == "Picture":
        response = await openai_client.images.generate(
            model="dall-e-3",
            prompt = message.content,
            size = "1024x1024"
        )
        logger.info(f"Image generated. Reponse: {response}")
        image_url = response.data[0].url
        elements = [cl.Image(url=image_url)]
        await cl.Message(f"Here's what I generated for **{message.content}**", elements=elements).send()
    else:
        # your on_message logic here.
```

Chainlit automatically detects commands attached to a message, so you can easily branch your logic based on `message.command`.

In this case, when we detect the `"Picture"` command, we treat the user’s message as the prompt and send it to OpenAI’s DALL·E 3 model. Once the image is generated, we extract the URL and use Chainlit’s `cl.Image()` to render it directly in the chat interface.

✨ **Voila!** You now have image generation working inside your chat app — and it looks fantastic.

### 2\. Audio capabilities 🎙️

This next section takes everything we’ve built so far (already “MasterChef” level) and elevates it to “Michelin Star Chef” territory.

At its core, enabling audio capabilities means supporting both **speech-to-text** and **text-to-speech**:

-   For **speech-to-text**, we’ll use OpenAI’s Whisper (yes, we’re already using GPT-4o-mini and DALL·E 3 — OpenAI really is a full-stack LLM shop).
-   For **text-to-speech**, we’ll use my favorite service: [**ElevenLabs**](https://elevenlabs.io/app/speech-synthesis/text-to-speech). It offers high-quality voices (even Singaporean English!) and a generous free tier. Grab an API key to get started.

#### 📦 Setup Code

Here’s our initial setup for handling audio input:

```python
## Setup
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv, find_dotenv
import chainlit as cl
import numpy as np

_ = load_dotenv(find_dotenv())

SILENCE_THRESHOLD = 3500  # Adjust based on your audio level (e.g., lower for quieter audio)
SILENCE_TIMEOUT = 1300.0  # Seconds of silence to consider the turn finished
ELEVENLABS_API_KEY = os.getenv("ELEVENLABS_API_KEY")
ELEVENLABS_VOICE_ID = os.getenv("ELEVENLABS_VOICE_ID")

@cl.on_audio_start
async def on_audio_start():
    """Handler to manage mic button click event"""
    
    cl.user_session.set("silent_duration_ms", 0)
    cl.user_session.set("is_speaking", False)
    cl.user_session.set("audio_chunks", [])
    
    user = cl.user_session.get("user")
    logger.info(f"{user} is starting an audio stream...")
    return True
```

The `on_audio_start` handler instantiates the audio-specific session variables when audio recording starts. Now let’s handle the actual audio stream:

```python
@cl.on_audio_chunk
async def on_audio_chunk(chunk: cl.InputAudioChunk):
    """Handler function to manage audio chunks
    Source: Chainlit Cookbook
    """
    
    audio_chunks = cl.user_session.get("audio_chunks")

    if audio_chunks is not None:
        audio_chunk = np.frombuffer(chunk.data, dtype=np.int16)
        audio_chunks.append(audio_chunk)

    # If this is the first chunk, initialize timers and state
    if chunk.isStart:
        cl.user_session.set("last_elapsed_time", chunk.elapsedTime)
        cl.user_session.set("is_speaking", True)
        return

    last_elapsed_time = cl.user_session.get("last_elapsed_time")
    silent_duration_ms = cl.user_session.get("silent_duration_ms")
    is_speaking = cl.user_session.get("is_speaking")

    # Calculate the time difference between this chunk and the previous one
    time_diff_ms = chunk.elapsedTime - last_elapsed_time
    cl.user_session.set("last_elapsed_time", chunk.elapsedTime)

    # Compute the RMS (root mean square) energy of the audio chunk
    audio_energy = audioop.rms(
        chunk.data, 2
    )  # Assumes 16-bit audio (2 bytes per sample)

    if audio_energy < SILENCE_THRESHOLD:
        # Audio is considered silent
        silent_duration_ms += time_diff_ms
        cl.user_session.set("silent_duration_ms", silent_duration_ms)
        if silent_duration_ms >= SILENCE_TIMEOUT and is_speaking:
            cl.user_session.set("is_speaking", False)
            await process_audio()
    else:
        # Audio is not silent, reset silence timer and mark as speaking
        cl.user_session.set("silent_duration_ms", 0)
        if not is_speaking:
            cl.user_session.set("is_speaking", True)
```

#### 🧠 How This Works

As audio chunks are streamed, we use `numpy` to convert the byte buffer into a numeric array. We also use Python’s `audioop.rms()` to calculate the **energy level** of each chunk. If the energy falls below a threshold for a long enough time (`SILENCE_TIMEOUT`), we assume the user has stopped speaking — and trigger audio processing.

Before we dive into Whisper and ElevenLabs integration, let’s abstract the message generation logic from [earlier](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/its-2025-start-using-chainlit-for-your-llm-apps-558db1a46315) into a reusable function:

```python
async def generate_answer(query: str):
    agent = cl.user_session.get("agent")
    memory = cl.user_session.get("memory")
    chat_history = memory.get()
    msg = cl.Message("", type="assistant_message")
    
    context = cl.user_session.get("context")
    handler = agent.run(
        query, 
        chat_history = chat_history,
        ctx = context
    )
    async for event in handler.stream_events():
        if isinstance(event, AgentStream):
            await msg.stream_token(event.delta)
        elif isinstance(event, ToolCall):
            with cl.Step(name=f"{event.tool_name} tool", type="tool"):
                continue
    
    response = await handler
    await msg.send()
    memory.put(
        ChatMessage(
            role = MessageRole.USER,
            content= query
        )
    )
    memory.put(
        ChatMessage(
            role = MessageRole.ASSISTANT,
            content = str(response)
        )
    )
    cl.user_session.set("memory", memory)
    return msg
```

This lets us reuse the same flow for both text and audio inputs. Now let’s write our function to transform text to speech:

```python
import io
import httpx

@cl.step(type="tool")
async def text_to_speech(text: str, mime_type: str):
    """Our main text to speech function
    Source: Chainlit Cookbook, ElevenLabs Documentation
    """

    CHUNK_SIZE = 1024

    url = f"https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/text-to-speech/{ELEVENLABS_VOICE_ID}"

    headers = {
        "Accept": mime_type,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "xi-api-key": ELEVENLABS_API_KEY,
    }

    data = {
        "text": text,
        "model_id": "eleven_multilingual_v2",
        "voice_settings": {"stability": 0.5, "similarity_boost": 0.5},
    }

    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=25.0) as client:
        response = await client.post(url, json=data, headers=headers)
        response.raise_for_status()  # Ensure we notice bad responses

        buffer = io.BytesIO()
        buffer.name = f"output_audio.{mime_type.split('/')[1]}"

        async for chunk in response.aiter_bytes(chunk_size=CHUNK_SIZE):
            if chunk:
                buffer.write(chunk)

        buffer.seek(0)
        return buffer.name, buffer.read()
```

We are essentially posting a request to our ElevenLabs client to get the audio as a stream of bytes which we return to render as a downloadable element along with our message. The speech-to-text is even easier because it’s just posting the entire speech to OpenAI:

```python
from openai import AsyncOpenAI

openai_client = AsyncOpenAI(api_key="...")

@cl.step(type="tool")
async def speech_to_text(audio_file):
    response = await openai_client.audio.transcriptions.create(
        model="whisper-1", file=audio_file, language="en",
    )
    return response.text
```

The only thing that we need to take note of is the OpenAI invocation of Whisper requires an audio\_file that we must first construct.

📌 **Tip**: Specify a language to improve accuracy. Whisper thinks I speak Malay at times.

And now to finally process the audio stream head on using all our previous functions:

```python
async def process_audio():
    """ Processes the audio buffer from the session
    Source: Chainlit Cookbook
    """
    
    if audio_chunks := cl.user_session.get("audio_chunks"):
        # Concatenate all chunks
        concatenated = np.concatenate(list(audio_chunks))

        # Create an in-memory binary stream
        wav_buffer = io.BytesIO()

        # Create WAV file with proper parameters
        with wave.open(wav_buffer, "wb") as wav_file:
            wav_file.setnchannels(1)  # mono
            wav_file.setsampwidth(2)  # 2 bytes per sample (16-bit)
            wav_file.setframerate(24000)  # sample rate (24kHz PCM)
            wav_file.writeframes(concatenated.tobytes())

        # Reset buffer position
        wav_buffer.seek(0)
        cl.user_session.set("audio_chunks", [])

    frames = wav_file.getnframes()
    rate = wav_file.getframerate()

    duration = frames / float(rate)
    if duration <= 1.71:
        print("The audio is too short, please try again.")
        return

    audio_buffer = wav_buffer.getvalue()
    input_audio_el = cl.Audio(content=audio_buffer, mime="audio/wav")
    whisper_input = ("audio.wav", audio_buffer, "audio/wav")
    transcription = await speech_to_text(whisper_input) #send to Whisper
    
    user = cl.user_session.get("user")
    logger.info(f"Received message: '{transcription}' from {user}")

    await cl.Message(
        author="You",
        type="user_message",
        content=transcription,
        elements=[input_audio_el],
    ).send()

    ## Now to answer the question
    msg = await generate_answer(transcription) #send to gpt-4o-mini
      
    # Send to ElevenLabs
    _, output_audio = await text_to_speech(msg.content, "audio/wav")

    output_audio_el = cl.Audio(
        auto_play=True,
        mime="audio/wav",
        content=output_audio,
    )
    msg.elements=[output_audio_el]
    await msg.update()
```

Here’s what’s happening

-   We first take all the audio chunks and write a .wav file as an element to be appended to a Chainlit message.
-   Since we’ve read the audio buffer in generating this wav file we need to reset the buffer to zero, and wrap the file format and the buffer into a tuple for the OpenAI Whisper Client. We then send everything to OpenAI to get the `transcription` .
-   We send the transcription along with the .wav file as a message **from the user** ( `author=”You”`makes the message pop up on the user’s side of the chat). This .wav file is downloadable and this step is purely for user experience — so the user knows you get the question asked.
-   We then send the raw transcription to the LLM agent to generate an answer, and send the answer to ElevenLabs to generate the audio file, which we then wrap as a Chainlit `Audio` element and append it to the LLM agent’s reply. We send the reply and the audio element as a message.

Wow, that was a lot of code! I wish I could say I wrote it all from scratch, but full credit goes to the Chainlit team — this was adapted from their excellent [audio cookbook](https://github.com/Chainlit/cookbook/blob/main/openai-whisper/app.py).

I spent quite a bit of time studying how it worked and then tailoring it to use [Azure’s Text-To-Speech service](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/speech-service/text-to-speech) at work. It was a great way to learn the internals of audio management while bending it to fit real-world needs (and impress your bosses). Once you’ve added all the code above into app.py, restart the app and watch the magic happen:

Was that magic or what!

### 3\. 🔗 Auto RAG capabilities — upload any file and chat with it!

This is the bread and butter of any LLM application — the ability to RAG files on demand (instead of reading them). Clicking on the file attach icon pins the file as a Chainlit `element` with the message you send. We just need to edit our `on_message` code to cater for this

```python
from llama_index.core import SimpleDirectoryReader
from llama_index.embeddings.ollama import OllamaEmbedding
from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI
from llama_index.core.tools import QueryEngineTool

@cl.on_message
async def on_message(message: cl.Message):
    ... # pre-processing code
    if message.command == "Picture":
        ... # image generation code
    else:
        if len(message.elements) > 0:
           await cl.Message("Processing files").send()
           filepaths = [file.path for file in message.elements]
           filenames = [file.name for file in message.elements]
           documents = SimpleDirectoryReader(input_files=filepaths).load_data()
            
           ## Ingest documents into in-memory Vector Database.
           index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(documents, embed_model=embed_model)
           await cl.Message("Processed uploaded files").send()
            
           openai_llm = cl.user_session.get("llm")
           name = openai_llm.complete(f"Based on these filenames, come up with a short, concise name that describes these documents. For example 'MBA Value Analysis'. Do not return any '.pdf' or file extensions, just the name. Filenames: {', '.join(filenames)}")
           description = openai_llm.complete(f"Based on these filenames, come up with a consolidated description that describes these documents. For example 'Answers questions about animals'. Filenames: {', '.join(filenames)}")
           await cl.Message(f"Uploaded document/s follow the theme: {name}. Here's the general description of the document/s uploaded: {description}").send()

           tool = QueryEngineTool.from_defaults(
                query_engine=index.as_query_engine(similarity_top_k=8, llm=openai_llm),
                name = "_".join(str(name).split(" ")),
                description=str(description)
            )
            agent_tools = cl.user_session.get("agent_tools", [])
            agent_tools.append(tool)
            
            agent = FunctionAgent(tools=agent_tools, llm=openai_llm)
            cl.user_session.set("agent", agent)
            cl.user_session.set("agent_tools", agent_tools)
        
     await generate_answer(message.content) #use our new generate_answer function from before
```

When Chainlit detects uploaded files, it temporarily stores them in a `.files` directory and exposes the paths via `message.elements`. We then:

-   Use `SimpleDirectoryReader` to load the files (works with PDFs, PPTs, Word, Excel, even audio/video if Whisper is available).
-   Create a temporary index for similarity search.
-   Dynamically generate metadata (name and description) for the tool using the OpenAI LLM.
-   Convert the index to a query engine (with just one line of code — thank you LlamaIndex!) and register a `QueryEngineTool` as a tool in this user session for the agent to use.

📌 **Tip**: Swap `SimpleDirectoryReader` with `LlamaParse` for smarter document chunking and cleaner structure.

Note that the uploaded files are tied to the _current user session_. Once the chat ends, those files (and their corresponding tools) are lost unless you implement persistence.

```python
@cl.on_chat_resume
async def on_chat_resume(thread: ThreadDict):
    ... #your on chat resume logic
    await cl.Message("Chat resumed. Do note that previously uploaded documents will not be available in this chat and must be uploaded again").send()
```

### 4\. 🔌 Model Context Protocol: Chat with all tools!

So far, we’ve learned how to:

-   Define tools statically in code (google maps).
-   Dynamically register tools to an agent during a session (auto RAG).

Now it’s time to level up: let’s give our LLM agent the ability to access _any available tools on demand_ based on user needs — using the **Model Context Protocol** (MCP)! I’ve previously written an [article about MCPs](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/model-context-protocol-hype-or-necessity-998874d95bc6) — feel free to check it out, but here’s the gist:

The value of an MCP lies in enabling **dynamic tool availability** at runtime. Your LLM can connect to or disconnect from external services like Jira or Confluence directly in chat — enhancing user flexibility and keeping the frontend experience fluid.

Official vendors often provide Docker-based MCP servers — or you can build your own. For this demo, let’s integrate Jira and allow our LLM to manage tickets in real time.

#### 🛠 Step 1: Handle MCP Connections

When a user connects to an MCP server, we’ll fetch the available tools, unpack them using LlamaIndex’s `to_tool_list_async()`, and update the agent accordingly:

```python
@cl.on_mcp_connect
async def on_mcp_connect(connection):
    """Handler to connect to an MCP server. 
    Lists tools available on the server and connects these tools to
    the LLM agent."""
    
    openai_llm = cl.user_session.get("llm")
    mcp_cache = cl.user_session.get("mcp_tool_cache", {})
    mcp_tools = cl.user_session.get("mcp_tools", {})
    agent_tools = cl.user_session.get("agent_tools", [])
    try:
        logger.info("Connecting to MCP")
        mcp_client = BasicMCPClient(connection.url)
        logger.info("Connected to MCP")
        mcp_tool_spec = McpToolSpec(client=mcp_client)
        logger.info("Unpacking tools")
        new_tools = await mcp_tool_spec.to_tool_list_async()
        for tool in new_tools:
            if tool.metadata.name not in mcp_tools:
                mcp_tools[tool.metadata.name] = tool
                mcp_cache[connection.name].append(tool.metadata.name)
        agent = FunctionAgent(
            tools=agent_tools + list(mcp_tools.values()),
            llm=openai_llm,
        )
        cl.user_session.set("agent", agent)
        cl.user_session.set("context", Context(agent))
        cl.user_session.set("mcp_tools", mcp_tools)
        cl.user_session.set("mcp_tool_cache", mcp_cache)
        await cl.Message(f"Connected to MCP server: {connection.name} on {connection.url}", type="assistant_message").send()

        await cl.Message(
            f"Found {len(new_tools)} tools from {connection.name} MCP server.", type="assistant_message"
        ).send()
    except Exception as e:
        await cl.Message(f"Error conecting to tools from MCP server: {str(e)}", type="assistant_message").send()
```

This ensures any newly discovered tools are merged into the session’s toolset.

#### 🔌 Step 2: Handle Disconnections

When a user disconnects from an MCP server, we’ll cleanly remove its tools:

```python
@cl.on_mcp_disconnect
async def on_mcp_disconnect(name: str):
    """Handler to handle disconnects from an MCP server.
    Updates tool list available for the LLM agent.
    """
    openai_llm = cl.user_session.get("llm")
    agent_tools = cl.user_session.get("agent_tools", [])
    mcp_tools = cl.user_session.get("mcp_tools", {})
    mcp_cache = cl.user_session.get("mcp_tool_cache", {})
    
    if name in mcp_cache:
        for tool_name in mcp_cache[name]:
            del mcp_tools[tool_name]
        del mcp_cache[name]

    # Update tools list in agent
    if len(mcp_tools)>0:
        agent = FunctionAgent(
            tools=agent_tools + list(mcp_tools.values()), #agent still has tools not removed
            llm=openai_llm,
        )
    else:
        agent = FunctionAgent(
            tools=agent_tools,
            llm=openai_llm,
        )
    cl.user_session.set("context", Context(agent))
    cl.user_session.set("mcp_tools", mcp_tools)
    cl.user_session.set("mcp_tool_cache", mcp_cache)
    cl.user_session.set("agent", agent)
    
    await cl.Message(f"Disconnected from MCP server: {name}", type="assistant_message").send()
```

#### 🐳 Step 3: Run Jira MCP via Docker

Jira’s MCP is available on [Docker](https://github.com/sooperset/mcp-atlassian) (do check with the official MCP tool page of the service you’re looking for), so all we need to do is [get a Jira API token](https://support.atlassian.com/atlassian-account/docs/manage-api-tokens-for-your-atlassian-account/), pull the image and run it:

```bash
docker run --rm -p 9000:9000 \
  --env-file ./.env \
  ghcr.io/sooperset/mcp-atlassian:latest \
  --transport sse --port 9000 -vv
```

Once running, click the plug icon in our Chainlit home page to connect.

Yup there are 26 tools!

Now let’s have some fun! Let’s get GPT-4o-mini to check for active issues in our current sprint (note that you’ll need to know at least the project key of your Jira project — in my case it’s “JIRACHAT”)

Since we’ve already written all the features above, let’s resolve these issues!

You can also tell the LLM to complete the sprint! What you get is a nice Jira home page that is clean indicating that the issues have been completed.

_PS: This MCP image also works for Confluence! So you can get your LLM to write sprint retrospectives on Confluence, or use this MCP to RAG Confluence pages._

### It gets better — deployment

Chainlit apps don’t just have to be deployed as standalone web applications. Chainlit apps can also be [mounted as a copilot onto a website](https://docs.chainlit.io/deploy/copilot) as a chat bubble, deployed on [Teams](https://docs.chainlit.io/deploy/teams), [Slack](https://docs.chainlit.io/deploy/slack) or even [Discord](https://docs.chainlit.io/deploy/discord) as a chatbot. The same `app.py` we built has incredible mileage — you barely need to change a thing.

It must be said however, that you tend to lose control over the user experience when deploying Chainlit chatbots via the aforementioned alternatives — because Chainlit must comply to the service requirements of these services. You do need administrative access to deploy on Teams, Slack and Discord which I don’t have so I’ll just briefly demonstrate copilot deployment.

You’re going to have to know quite a bit of JavaScript and use the Chainlit `CopilotFunction` abstraction to shuttle arguments between the frontend and your Chainlit bot — I’ve done this at work with some struggle. The challenge comes from needing to authenticate the user at the main website first, which means that your app.py’s `password_auth_callback` will throw an error.

Instead of adding to our almost 600 line app.py, I’ve elected to code a simple chatbot to quickly help illustrate the core concepts needed:

```python
#simple_app.py

import chainlit as cl
from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI

llm = OpenAI('gpt-4o-mini', temperature=0)

@cl.on_message
async def on_message(message: cl.Message):
    reply = await llm.acomplete(message.content)
    response = await cl.Message(content=str(reply)).send()
    
    if cl.context.session.client_type == "copilot":
        fn = cl.CopilotFunction(
            name="test",
            args={"message": message.content, "response": response.content}
        )
        await fn.acall()
```

Yup it’s just a chatbot that answers questions — we didn’t even implement memory and it doesn’t even have an `on_chat_start`!

If Chainlit detects that the context of the client’s session is copilot mode, the `cl.CopilotFunction` class creates a function call event that is sent from the Chainlit backend to the embedded Copilot widget on your website or application.

When you instantiate it with a `name` and `args`, and then invoke `.acall()`, Chainlit emits a `chainlit-call-fn` event to the front end, carrying those parameters. A corresponding JavaScript event listener on the host page picks up that event, executes the requested action (e.g., updating UI or fetching data), and returns a result via a callback — which is then propagated back into your Chainlit app for further processing

In our index.html, be sure to add the codes in the script tags. This mounts the Chainlit widget as a little chat bubble and instantiates an event listener to pass the message to our Chainlit application.

```xml
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=<device-width>, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Document</title>
</head>
<body>
    <!-- ... -->
  <script src="http://localhost:8001/copilot/index.js"></script>
  <script>
    window.mountChainlitWidget({
        chainlitServer: "http://localhost:8001",
      });
    window.addEventListener("chainlit-call-fn", (e) => {
      const { name, args, callback } = e.detail;
      if (name=="test"){
        callback(args.response); //send the results in this callback function
      }
    });
  </script>
  <!-- ... -->
</body>
</html>
```

Also, be sure to edit your `.chainlit/config.toml` file to allow the origin that your website is deployed on. This is annoying because “\*” typically results in a failure to fetch error so you have to be explicit.

```ini
allow_origins = ["http://127.0.0.1:5500"]
```

The result looks really good!

You can even click the top right hand corner of the chat bubble to expand the chat window. Copilot mode supports all the advanced features we built earlier!

Just be mindful to handle the authentication process in your Chainlit application on your website. The sticking point is passing authenticated user context from the host site into the Chainlit app — especially since `password_auth_callback` doesn’t play nicely with copilot embeds.

If you manage to get auth working cleanly, do drop me a note — I’d love to learn from your setup too!

### **Concluding thoughts**

We’ve covered a lot of ground! Developing LLM applications with Chainlit is genuinely enjoyable — it offers a level of simplicity and flexibility that’s hard to beat. The mileage you can get out of a single `app.py` file is impressive. I hope this series has served as both a practical starting point and a useful cookbook for anyone looking to build with Chainlit.

body:
* * *

_Part 1: I love Streamlit but I use Chainlit exclusively for LLM apps (and you should too)_

If you’ve read my previous articles, you’ll know I often explore agentic applications — and you’ve probably noticed one tool keeps surfacing: Chainlit. That’s no accident. What began as a minimal MVP has matured into one of the most reliable tools in my LLM stack — a true trump card.

This piece is equal parts tribute and hands-on guide, and the first in a two-part series teaching you how to incrementally build a Chainlit-powered application.

Whether you’re just getting started or looking to deepen your Chainlit skills, we’ll walk through every key stage — from managing the chat lifecycle (login, start, stop, resume, logout) to integrating audio, working with model context protocols, and even building your own custom canvas.

Below, you’ll find the final home page — each numbered section visually maps to a key feature we’ll cover throughout the article.

As always, all my code can be found in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/sturdy-octo-fortnight).

_This article walks through features 1 to 6 in the image above — but the GitHub repo contains the complete implementation (1 through 10). Feel free to explore ahead!_

#### 1\. The chat message box

This is the part that will make you want to start using Chainlit immediately. We’ll define a chat engine and get a fully functional UI with just two event-decorated functions.

```python
# app.py
import chainlit as cl

from llama_index.core.chat_engine import SimpleChatEngine
from llama_index.core.base.llms.types import ChatMessage, MessageRole
from llama_index.core.memory import ChatMemoryBuffer
from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI

import logging

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

openai_llm = OpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0)

@cl.on_chat_start
async def start():
    """Handler for chat start events. Sets session variables."""
    cl.user_session.set(
        "agent",
        SimpleChatEngine.from_defaults(
            llm=openai_llm,
        )
    )
    memory = ChatMemoryBuffer.from_defaults()
    cl.user_session.set("memory", memory)

@cl.on_message
async def on_message(message: cl.Message):
    """On message handler to handle message received events"""

    agent = cl.user_session.get("agent")
    memory = cl.user_session.get("memory")
    chat_history = memory.get()
    msg = cl.Message("")
    
    # Get the LLM to stream replies back!
    response = agent.stream_chat(message.content, chat_history=chat_history)
    for token in response.response_gen:
        await msg.stream_token(token)

    # Update chat history
    memory.put(
        ChatMessage(
            role = MessageRole.USER,
            content= message.content
        )
    )
    memory.put(
        ChatMessage(
            role = MessageRole.ASSISTANT,
            content = str(response)
        )
    )
    cl.user_session.set("memory", memory)
    
    await msg.send()
```

Wait a minute — where’s your `def main()` function? And what happened to the usual`if __name__=="__main__"` boilerplate? With Chainlit, you don’t need them. Each function is decorated with an event trigger ( `cl.on_chat_start`, `cl.on_message`), just like JavaScript’s event listeners (onclick, onscroll, etc.). It’s intuitive, elegant, and gets you up and running fast.

You’ll also notice the use of session variables ( `cl.user_session`) to store key-value pairs. This allows for persistence of session variables across different Chainlit functions! Here we implement a simple LlamaIndex Chat Engine powered by OpenAI. By default, Chainlit loads your entire `.env` file when run so you don’t have to explicitly load it using the `load_dotenv()` here.

In your terminal, run the following command:

```bash
chainlit run app.py
```

Chainlit is async-first which is a very important concept of software engineering. The easiest way to understand async? Food.

Imagine going to lunch at a steakhouse with your friends. But instead of being allowed to order right away, you’re forced to wait until everyone in the queue ahead of you has been served. Brutal, right? That’s the **synchronous model** — and how fast food outlets work — though they’re really fast, so the wait isn’t brutal.

In a normal restaurant, you place your order, return to your seat, and wait. Drinks might come first, followed by side dishes and then steaks later. That’s **asynchronous logic**: the waiter doesn’t block the kitchen for you, but everyone still gets their meal when it’s ready. You don’t have to die of thirst just because your steak’s not ready yet.

In Python, you just need to add `async`in front of a function to make it asynchronous — really dead easy. But when calling an async function, remember to add `await`, or it’ll be invoked in synchronous mode, returning a coroutine (a “pending” object) instead of the result you want — which often leads to errors. Chainlit’s cl.Message is always sent or streamed asynchronously, so don’t forget to add `await` — like this: `await cl.Message(“…").send()`or `await msg.stream_token(token)` like our code above.

#### ⏹️ Bonus 1: The Stop Button

Eagle-eyed users might notice something cool — when Chainlit streams the reply, the arrow in the red circle at the bottom of the message box becomes a **“Stop”** button (like ChatGPT). Click it to stop the task mid-execution.

Chainlit provides a handler for that too:

```python
# <earlier code>

@cl.on_stop
async def on_stop():
    await cl.Message("You have stopped the task!").send()
```

This is a good point to [“fork” the conversation](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/concepts/time-travel/#forking) (to borrow LangGraph’s terminology). The user may have sent a message by mistake and might want to edit and resend it, so it’s a good idea to undo the appending of a chat message to the session’s chat history. For now, we’ll simply notify the user that the task was stopped.

#### 2\. User login

Great it works! But what if we want to **restrict access** to our application? Chainlit makes this easy with a built-in authentication handler. In app.py, add the following code:

```python
# <earlier imports>
from typing import Optional

@cl.password_auth_callback
def auth_callback(username: str, password: str) -> Optional[cl.User]:
    """Password auth handler for login"""
    
    if (username, password) == ("admin", "admin"): #For development
        return cl.User(identifier="admin", metadata={"role": "ADMIN"})
    else: 
        return None

@cl.on_chat_start
async def on_chat_start():
  # Now we can see who's starting the conversation!
  user = cl.user_session.get("user")
  logger.info(f"{user.identifier} has started the conversation")
  # <earlier code>

# <earlier code>
```

This sets up a basic login gate. During development, you can use a hardcoded credential like “admin” to access the app. In production you’d replace this with SSO, [OAuth](https://docs.chainlit.io/authentication/oauth) (supported by Chainlit), or even a database-backed check (e.g. [LDAP](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/desktop/ldap/lightweight-directory-access-protocol-ldap-api)). If `None` is returned, Chainlit blocks the user at the login screen — keeping your app secure by default.

Before you restart the app be sure to run:

```bash
chainlit create-secret
```

This creates a `CHAINLIT_AUTH_SECRET` environment variable which you **must copy into your .env file.** This secret is required for Chainlit to validate logins securely.

#### Bonus 2: Logout Handling

But we should also cleanly handle user logouts, especially by clearing cookies to prevent session leaks. Add the following into app.py

```python
# <earlier imports>
from fastapi import Request, Response

# <earlier code>

@cl.on_logout
def on_logout(request: Request, response: Response):
    ### Handler to tidy up resources
    for cookie_name in request.cookies.keys():
        response.delete_cookie(cookie_name)
```

#### 3\. Resuming chats

Just like ChatGPT lets you time-travel through previous conversations, Chainlit can do the same! ✨

To enable this, you’ll need to persist chat histories in a database. Fortunately, the creators of Chainlit — **LiteralAI** — have also built a companion LLM observability tool (also called **LiteralAI**) that makes this easy.

LiteralAI provides a generous free tier and automatically tracks each LLM call within a conversation, storing the full chat thread for you. If you’ve used other observability tools like LangSmith or Arize Phoenix, this will feel familiar — it offers the same kind of logging, tracking, and visual debugging interface. Simply create a free account at [LiteralAI’s web page](https://www.literalai.com/), grab your API key, and paste it into your `.env` file. **No code changes needed!**

Start your app again and ask the same question — you’ll see it show up in your LiteralAI dashboard.

You’ll also notice that previous chats appear in the left panel once you create a new chat — just like ChatGPT! But clicking on them won’t magically resume the session until you implement a **chat resume handler**. Let’s fix that.

Add the following to your app.py file!

```python
# <earlier imports>
from chainlit.types import ThreadDict

# <earlier code>

@cl.on_chat_resume
async def on_chat_resume(thread: ThreadDict):
    """Handler function to resume a chat"""
    
    ## Restore memory buffer
    memory = ChatMemoryBuffer.from_defaults()
    root_messages = [m for m in thread["steps"]]
    for message in root_messages:
        if message["type"] == "user_message":
            memory.put(
                ChatMessage(
                    role=MessageRole.USER,
                    content=message['output']
                )
            )
        else:
            memory.put(
                ChatMessage(
                    role=MessageRole.ASSISTANT,
                    content=message['output']
                )
            )
    cl.user_session.set("memory", memory)
    
    ## Restore agent
    cl.user_session.set(
        "agent",
        SimpleChatEngine.from_defaults(
            llm=openai_llm,
        )
    )
    
    user = cl.user_session.get("user")
    logger.info(f"{user} has resumed chat")
```

All messages persisted in Chainlit are stored as a ThreadDict, which we unpack to reconstruct the conversation. **This is critical: you must restore both the memory and the LLM agent, or your @cl.on\_message handler will fail on resumed chats.**

A bonus of the integration with LiteralAI is the ability to dynamically capture feedback! Simply click the thumbs up/down button and give your feedback and this will also appear in your LiteralAI dashboard.

> Sadly, LiteralAI (the creators of Chainlit) have announced on Discord that they’re discontinuing their business due to fierce competition in the GenAI tooling space (there’s a snippet on the Readme.MD of the [Chainlit GitHub repository](https://github.com/Chainlit/chainlit) as well). As a developer, I’ve benefitted immensely from this ecosystem of innovation, but it’s still a loss — especially when it’s one of your favorite frameworks.

> That said, the team at LiteralAI has gone above and beyond: they’ve open-sourced a [Chainlit data layer repo](https://github.com/Chainlit/chainlit-datalayer) with a [video walkthrough](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a867d470-ccf8-4a6b-8a7d-2b217382a3ed) showing how to set it up locally. I tried it — it works beautifully. I deeply appreciate their generosity in ensuring users aren’t orphaned by their exit.

> The team is now working on a new startup, [**Summon**](https://www.trysummon.com/), which aims to transform any API into an MCP or A2A agent. They’ve even applied to Y Combinator. Needless to say — I’ll be experimenting with it as soon as I can.

#### **Bonus 3: Chat ending handlers**

Just like users can stop tasks, they can also end chats (by starting a new one). Chainlit provides a handler for that too!

This is a great place to implement cleanup logic, save session summaries, or even update an agent’s episodic memory (borrowing a LangGraph term again). For instance, you might summarize the chat history and store it in a vector database to personalize future interactions.

In our case, we’ll just log the event:

```python
# <earlier code>
@cl.on_chat_end
def on_chat_end():
    user = cl.user_session.get("user")
    logger.info(f"{user.identifier} has ended the chat")
```

#### 4\. Chat Starters: To help users start chats

Sometimes, the blinking cursor in an empty chat box can feel intimidating — what do I even ask? That’s where **chat starters** come in: friendly buttons that inject predefined prompts directly into the conversation, giving users a gentle nudge to get going.

Add this snippet to your app.py:

```python
# <earlier code>

@cl.set_starters
async def set_starters():
    """Chat starter suggestions!"""
    return [
        cl.Starter(
            label="Show me Paris",
            message="Show me Paris.",
            icon="/public/paris.png"
        ),
        cl.Starter(
            label="Show me NYC",
            message="Show me NYC.",
            icon="/public/nyc.png"
        ),
        cl.Starter(
            label="Show me Singapore",
            message="Show me Singapore.",
            icon="/public/singapore.png"
        ),
    ]
```

Here, “label” defines the button text the user sees, while “message” is the input sent to your @cl.on\_message function when clicked. The optional “icon” adds a visual flair, making the UI more inviting and user-friendly.

#### 5\. Chat Settings

We’ve done so much already. But we can do more! What if we want to allow the user to choose between different LLMs (or LLM providers) and adjust the temperature of the LLM to allow it to be creative! Chainlit supports this via a built-in settings handler.

We have to adjust our `on_chat_start` function to “send” these settings at the very beginning

```python
from chainlit.input_widget import Select, Switch, Slider
# <earlier imports>
# <tooling code>

@cl.on_chat_start
async def on_chat_start():
    # <earlier code>
    settings = await cl.ChatSettings(
        [            
            Select(
                id="LLM",
                label="OpenAI model to use",
                values=["gpt-4o-mini", "gpt-4o"],
                initial_index=0,
            ),
            Switch(
                id="Greet_on_message",
                label="Greet user when message is received",
                initial=False,
            ),
            Slider(
                id="Temperature",
                label="Temperature of the LLM",
                initial=0,
                min=0,
                max=1,
                step=0.1
            )
        ]
    ).send()

# <earlier code>
```

Chainlit has 3 types of input widgets that we can use for our settings class, a selector, a switch and a slider. In this case we’ve used the selector as an LLM selector, the switch to include an optional greeting to the user whenever a message is received (i.e. before the LLM actually replies), and a slider to allow the user to adjust LLM temperature — in case they want it to be more creative.

We then have to define a Chainlit handler to manage these settings updates. Add the following snippet to the bottom of your app.py

```python
# <earlier code>
@cl.on_settings_update
async def setup_agent(settings):
    """Handler to manage settings updates"""
    
    openai_llm = OpenAI(
        model=settings["LLM"], 
        temperature=settings["Temperature"]
    )
    logger.info(f"New settings received. LLM: {settings['LLM']} | Temperature: {settings['Temperature']}")
    cl.user_session.set("llm", openai_llm)
    
    agent_tools = cl.user_session.get("agent_tools")
    mcp_tools = cl.user_session.get("mcp_tools", {})
    if len(mcp_tools) > 0:
        agent = FunctionAgent(tools=agent_tools + list(mcp_tools.values()),llm=openai_llm)
    else:
        agent = FunctionAgent(tools=agent_tools, llm=openai_llm)
    logger.info("Agent instantiated")
    cl.user_session.set("agent", agent)
    
    cl.user_session.set("greet", settings["Greet_on_message"])

@cl.on_message
async def on_message(message: cl.Message):
    user = cl.user_session.get("user")
    logger.info(f"Received message: '{message.content}' from {user.identifier}")
    
    greet = cl.user_session.get("greet") # check if the user wants to be greeted
    if greet is True:
        await cl.Message(f"Hello there {user.identifier}!").send()

    # earlier on_message code
```

Every time the user changes a setting, the `cl.on_settings_update` handler is triggered, allowing us to automatically rebuild the agent. Neat!

**Bonus 4: Adding an app Logo**

Tired of Chainlit’s default branding? You can easily add your own logo! Just place two image files named logo\_light.png and logo\_dark.png into your ./public folder. Chainlit automatically picks it up when you re-run it and you’ll see it as your app’s logo (_if you can’t, try clearing your browser’s cookies!_).

Want more customization? You can:  
 • Edit color themes via ./public/theme.json  
 • Change logo styles via .chainlit/config.toml (Tailwind CSS syntax)  
 • Add your own CSS with ./public/test.css  
 • Inject JavaScript via ./public/test.js

Chainlit gives you everything you need to make the app truly your own.

#### **_6\. Chat Profiles (Multi-Personality Agents!)_**

Chat profiles can be used to separate your app into multiple different apps — for example, you could restrict the use of tools by chat profiles. We’re not going to restrict tools here. Instead, let’s have fun with it — we’ll use profiles to give our LLM agents some personality style points.

```python
# <all earlier code>

@cl.set_chat_profiles
async def chat_profile():
    """Chat profile setter."""
    
    return [
        cl.ChatProfile(
            name="The Assistant",
            markdown_description="This LLM is your personal assistant",
            icon = "public/assistant.png"
        ),
        cl.ChatProfile(
            name="The Cowboy",
            markdown_description="This LLM is a personal assistant who is also a cowboy",
            icon = "public/cowboy.png"
        )
    ]
```

Let’s edit our `on_chat_start` to dynamically load different system prompts depending on the chat profiles selected.

```python
# <earlier imports>

SYSTEM_PROMPTS = {
    "The Assistant": "You are a helpful AI assistant. You can access tools using MCP servers if available.",
    "The Cowboy": "You are a helpful AI assistant who is also a cowboy! You can access tools using MCP servers if available but answer like a cowboy!",
}

@cl.on_chat_start
async def start():
    """Handler for chat start events. Sets session variables."""
    
    ## New code ##
    system_prompt = SYSTEM_PROMPTS[chat_profile]
    memory = ChatMemoryBuffer.from_defaults()
    memory.put(
        ChatMessage(
            role=MessageRole.SYSTEM, 
            content=system_prompt
        )
    )
    ## New code ##
    # <all other earlier code>

# <all other earlier code>
```

We now get this nice dropdown of different chat profiles at the top and we can see their description when we hover over each profile. The user session’s chat profile gets set whenever the user clicks on a different profile. Let’s give the cowboy profile a shot — yeehaw! 🤠 You’ll see the assistant start talking like it just rode in from Texas.

### The main app: Chainlit Canvas

_Ladies and gents this is the moment you’ve waited for!_

So far we’ve only defined a simple LLM chat engine with **no tools**. How do we get the engine to open up Canvas like ChatGPT and do cool things on it?

In Chainlit, a **Canvas** is simply a custom Element class rendered directly on the webpage. These elements are written as .jsx files and follow Chainlit’s [rules](https://docs.chainlit.io/api-reference/elements/custom) for custom UI rendering. The best part? Even though the code is written in React.js, **you don’t need to install React or manage any npm packages yourself** — Chainlit handles all of that for you automatically. Talk about service excellence.

As a self-professed JavaScript novice (and totally unfamiliar with React), I adapted the [Chainlit Cookbook example for Canvas,](https://github.com/Chainlit/cookbook/tree/main/map-canvas) tweaking the tooling logic to suit our needs _(Heads-up: if you’re using something like Google Maps, you’ll need a valid Google API key)._ I’ve also placed my `Map.jsx` file in my GitHub repository under `./public/elements` .

#### 🛠 Agent + Canvas Integration

We now define a move\_map\_to function that interacts with the Canvas via Chainlit’s `CustomElement`and `CopilotFunction`classes. Here’s the relevant code to define the tool that our agent is going to use:

```python
# app.py

async def open_map(latitude: float = 1.290270, longitude: float = 103.851959):
    """Render a map centered on given coordinates."""
    map_props = {"latitude": latitude, "longitude": longitude, "zoom": 12}
    custom_element = cl.CustomElement(name="Map", props=map_props, display="inline")
    await cl.ElementSidebar.set_title("canvas")
    await cl.ElementSidebar.set_elements([custom_element], key="map-canvas")

@cl.step(type="tool")
async def move_map_to(latitude: float, longitude: float):
    """Move the map to the given coordinates."""
    await open_map(latitude, longitude)
    fn = cl.CopilotFunction(name="move-map", args={"latitude": latitude, "longitude": longitude})
    await fn.acall()
    return "Map moved!"

# <earlier code>
```

#### What’s happening here:

-   `open_map` creates a `CustomElement` with a name that **must match** **your .jsx file under ./public/elements/.** In this case: Map.jsx.
-   We use `ElementSidebar` to display the canvas beside the chat.
-   `move_map_to` is wrapped in `cl.step` so users can trace it in the reasoning chain.
-   `CopilotFunction` Python ↔ JavaScript — passing lat/lng to Map.jsx for rendering.

#### 🤖 Integrating the Tool with the Agent

Let’s initialize our agent with tool support:

```python
from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import FunctionAgent, AgentStream, ToolCall
from llama_index.core.workflow import Context
# <earlier imports>
# <tooling code>

@cl.on_chat_start
async def on_chat_start():
    openai_llm = OpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0)
    agent_tool = FunctionTool.from_defaults(async_fn=move_map_to)
    agent = FunctionAgent(tools=[agent_tool], llm=openai_llm)
    cl.user_session.set("agent", agent)
    cl.user_session.set("context", Context(agent))
    cl.user_session.set("agent_tools", [agent_tool])
    cl.user_session.set("llm", openai_llm)
    cl.user_session.set("memory", ChatMemoryBuffer.from_defaults())

    # <all earlier on_chat_start codes>
```

Finally here’s how we handle tool invocations and stream output:

```python
# <earlier imports>
# <tooling code>
# <on_chat_start code>

@cl.on_message
async def on_message(message: cl.Message):
    user = cl.user_session.get("user")
    logger.info(f"Received message: '{message.content}' from {user.identifier}")
    
    greet = cl.user_session.get("greet")
    if greet is True:
        await cl.Message(f"Hello there {user.identifier}!").send()
    
    agent = cl.user_session.get("agent")
    memory = cl.user_session.get("memory")
    context = cl.user_session.get("context")
    chat_history = memory.get()
    msg = cl.Message("", type="assistant_message")
    handler = agent.run(message.content, chat_history=chat_history, ctx=context)
    async for event in handler.stream_events():
        if isinstance(event, AgentStream):
            await msg.stream_token(event.delta)
        elif isinstance(event, ToolCall):
            with cl.Step(name=f"{event.tool_name} tool", type="tool"):
                continue
    response = await handler
    await msg.send()
    memory.put(ChatMessage(role=MessageRole.USER, content=message.content))
    memory.put(ChatMessage(role=MessageRole.ASSISTANT, content=str(response)))

# <earlier code>
```

### Coming up next: Audio, AutoRAG, MCP, Command

And just like that, we’ve built a history-aware, Google Maps–powered LLM assistant — all within a single Python file. Pretty slick, right?

But we’re far from done.

We’ve yet to implement:

-   ✅ AutoRAG — in-memory, file-based retrieval and chat
-   ✅ Command parsing —structured input for precise, controllable action
-   ✅ Audio support — let your app listen and speak
-   ✅ MCP connection — to trigger other apps within your assistant like Claude Desktop

This article stops at _section 6_, but the [GitHub repo](https://github.com/tituslhy/sturdy-octo-fortnight/tree/main) includes **all features including the above**. Part 2 of this series will walk you through them — or feel free to dive into the code now if you’re eager.

Never has building a powerful LLM assistant been this accessible. If you haven’t tried Chainlit yet, now’s the time — your team will be impressed.
