body:
* * *

_Author’s note: This article was written with some of my friends in mind. The turbulent economy has been tough on them, and I want to remind them to “hang in there” — what’s gold will always shine. I hope this piece inspires you to explore how generative AI can enhance your job search and rekindle the joy of building and discovering._

This article concludes our gentle introduction to the multi-agent multiverse series. So far, the series has explored orchestrating multi-agent systems using the [Autogen](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multi-agent-multiverse-part-2-autogen-5401a0075d75), [LangGraph](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multi-agents-multiverse-part-1-langgraph-2ac56f1b5b3c), and [LlamaIndex](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multi-agent-multiverse-part-3a-llamaindex-workflows-c0f614c15b88) frameworks (including [deployment](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multi-agent-multiverse-part-3b-deploying-llamaindex-workflows-df18381d36b9)).

-   **Autogen** offers high-level abstractions designed around the philosophy of autonomous cooperation among agents.
-   **LangGraph**, in contrast, operates at the other extreme with low-level abstractions that require developers to extensively code multi-agent systems as directed graphs. While this provides maximum control and reliability, it also comes with a higher risk of bugs.
-   **LlamaIndex** strikes a balance by improving upon the directed graph approach, enabling developers to build multi-agent systems declaratively through workflows.

LlamaIndex’s workflow-driven approach has gained considerable traction, influencing other frameworks like Autogen and CrewAI. [Autogen has since incorporated a declarative, workflow-based methodology](https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/0.2/), while CrewAI adopted a flow-based approach after an extensive rewrite.

They say imitation is the sincerest form of flattery. But this raises an intriguing question: did LlamaIndex perfect the workflow approach, or did CrewAI elevate it to the next level?

This article will explore these questions and more, culminating in a new project: developing a job search and preparation multi-agent system. As before, all codes can be found in my [GitHub repo](https://github.com/tituslhy/literate-octo-tribble/).

### Introducing CrewAI

CrewAI emerged in late 2023 and quickly garnered a substantial following with more than 25k GitHub stars today. In my view, CrewAI serves as the “antithesis” of the DSPy framework.

[DSPy’s](https://dspy.ai/) philosophy emphasizes having developers focus on programming core code blocks, while the framework itself manages prompt optimization for large language models (LLMs). This approach arose from the belief that prompts are brittle — you can spend hours adjusting prompts only to get mixed results. It’s frustrating, time-consuming, and often requires plenty of trial and error to achieve optimal results.

CrewAI, in contrast, operates on the premise that [LLMs excel at role-playing,](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.12474#:~:text=Nevertheless%2C%20we%20posit%20that%20LLMs,in%20their%20vast%20training%20corpora.) making prompts a powerful and central component of its design. The library is heavily prompt-driven, which not only differentiates it but also makes it incredibly fun and engaging to use. Naturally, CrewAI’s approach contrasts sharply with LangGraph, offering high-level abstractions that enable fuss-free, bug-minimizing coding.

Consequently, CrewAI’s introduction of workflows strikes a balance between control and abstraction. It offers slightly lower-level control than Autogen while significantly enhancing the capabilities of its abstractions, achieving a middle ground between LlamaIndex and Autogen. Impressively, CrewAI’s workflow abstraction retains all the ‘fun’ of its core design. In fact, I believe it has made the library even more enjoyable to use.

### Using an LLM in CrewAI

Earlier iterations of the CrewAI framework were built on top of LangChain, allowing seamless integration of any LangChain-supported LLM abstraction in CrewAI applications. However, LangChain’s rapid feature development introduced frequent breaking changes between versions. This led to a period of incompatibility, as CrewAI relied on a much earlier version of LangChain.

To address this, CrewAI migrated to LiteLLM — a move I consider a masterstroke. LiteLLM is an exceptional library that standardizes LLM formatting across different service providers while ensuring remarkable stability. The engineering team’s ability to execute this migration with such speed and precision showcases their deep expertise and capability.

To set up an LLM in CrewAI, I recommend reviewing the [CrewAI LLM documentation page](https://docs.crewai.com/concepts/llms) and the [LiteLLM documentation page](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/). Like all orchestration frameworks, the default LLM is OpenAI so if you have your OpenAI API key you’re all set!

### Building our Employment Hero Crew

A “Crew” is CrewAI’s core multi-agent system abstraction. Each crew consists of agents, tools (if needed), and tasks that the agents will complete. As I mentioned earlier, CrewAI encourages creative prompt writing — you need to craft prompts for each agent and their associated tasks. The recommended method for doing this is through YAML files. Here’s an example of our job search agents YAML file:

```yaml
profiler:
  role: >
    Lead Human Resource Manager
  goal: >
    Identify the candidate's main strengths based on their resume.
  backstory: >
    As a veteran human resources manager, you are adroit at distilling the
    main strengths of a candidate from their resume including their technical
    and non-technical abilities. Your insights help guide candidates to the
    best job role for them. 
  allow_delegation: false
  verbose: true

recruiter:
  role: >
    Job Openings Researcher
  goal: >
    Find potential job listings fulfilling the candidate's job requirements.
  backstory: >
    As a veteran recruiter of a recruitment agency, you are adept at finding the 
    right job listings for your candidates. Your skill in identifying suitable 
    openings ensures the best match for job candidates. 
  allow_delegation: false
  verbose: true

matcher:
  role: >
    Job Listings matcher and scorer
  goal: >
    Match the jobs to the candidate and score them, ensuring that the top job 
    listing is the best fit for the candidate.
  backstory: >
    You have a knack for matching the right job positions to the candidate
    using advanced algorithms and scoring techniques. Your scores help
    prioritize the best job listings for candidate preparation. 
  allow_delegation: false
  verbose: true

reporter:
  role: >
    Cover Letter Writing Specialist
  goal: >
    Help the candidate write a cover letter for the top job listing. 
  backstory: >
    You are proficient at writing compelling cover letters for job listings.
    Your cover letters are crisp and elegantly written, giving the employers 
    good reasons for hiring this candidate. 
  allow_delegation: false
  verbose: true
```

Notice that it’s not just about writing the agent’s role, but also their goal and backstory. Under the _role_ section, it’s recommended to write a more grandiose role — e.g., “Principal AI Engineer” instead of just “AI Engineer.” The difference in rank can influence the LLM’s roleplaying. This is further reinforced by the _backstory_, where using rich, imaginative nuances helps shape how the LLM role-plays your ideal profiler, matcher, or whatever role your agent holds. Be as verbose as possible!

Notice that we did not specify our LLM in the `agents.yml` file — that’s because we’re using GPT 4o-mini which is CrewAI’s default model.

Now, let’s take a look at an example of our `tasks.yml` file:

```yaml
candidate_profiling_task:
  description: >
    Analyze the candidate's resume to identify their main strengths and qualifications.
    Highlight the candidate's technical and non-technical abilities to determine their suitability 
    for specific job roles.

research_job_listings_task:
  description: >
    Conduct thorough research to find potential job listings for the candidate.
    Utilize various online resources and databases to gather a comprehensive list of potential listings.
    Ensure that you meet the candidate's preferred job requirements.

    Job Requirements:
    {job_requirements}

  expected_output: >
    A list of 10 potential job listings with brief job listing profiles highlighting their suitability.

match_and_score_listings_task:
  description: >
    Evaluate and match the job listings to the candidate based on their qualifications and suitability.
    Score each job listing to reflect their alignment with the candidate's profile, ensuring a fair 
    and transparent assessment process. 
  expected_output: >
    A ranked list of top 3 listings with detailed scores and justifications for each job position.

cover_letter_task:
  description: >
    Write a compelling cover letter for the candidate for the top job description.
    The cover letter must be crisp and elegantly written, giving the employers good reasons
    on the candidate's fit to the role. It should be at least 300 words long
    including salutations and signing off. Cover the candidate's 2 of the candidate's
    most impressive work experience and highlight the technical depth and rigor
    of these projects as well as their fit to the job listing.
  expected_output: >
    A compelling cover letter expressing the candidate's fit to the top 3 job listings.
```

Notice that we need to write rich and imaginative task descriptions too! Words like _compelling_, _crystallized_, and similar descriptors make a huge difference in the task’s output. Crafting these descriptions with care is key to generating the most effective results.

Also, notice that there are placeholders in the `tasks.yml` file—CrewAI supports this feature. Just remember to pass these as inputs to your Crew later.

Our crew consists of 4 agents and 4 tasks, so each agent performs one task. However, this is not always the case. CrewAI gives developers the flexibility to define crews however they can imagine.

#### Resume Parser Tool

Next, we need to define the tools. For an employment hero crew, the ability to distill insights from a candidate’s resume is essential. Here’s how we can define the _ResumeParser_ tool:

```python
from crewai.tools import BaseTool
from llama_parse import LlamaParse
from typing import Any
import nest_asyncio
nest_asyncio.apply()

class ResumeParser(BaseTool):
    """This tool parses a resume using Llama Parse and returns them into
    string form."""
    
    name: str = "Resume reader"
    description: str = "Parses a pdf resume file neatly for LLM processing"
    parser: LlamaParse = LlamaParse(
        api_key = os.environ["LLAMA_CLOUD_API_KEY"],
        # use_vendor_multimodal_model=True,
        # vendor_multimodal_name="anthropic-sonnet-3.5",
        result_type="markdown"
    )
    
    def find_resume(self) -> str:
        """Method to search 2 levels up for a folder named 'Resume'
        and reads the resume file (a pdf) within this Folder"""
        
        __curdir__ = os.getcwd()
        depth = 0
        resume_dir_path = ""
        
        while (depth<3):    
            if "Resume" not in os.listdir(__curdir__):
                __curdir__ = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(__curdir__, os.path.pardir))
                depth += 1
            else:
                resume_dir_path = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(__curdir__, "Resume"))
                break
        
        return resume_dir_path
    
    def _run(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """Returns the entire resume in string format."""
        
        file_path = self.find_resume()
        resume = os.path.join(
            file_path,
            os.listdir(file_path)[0]
        )
        docs = self.parser.load_data(file_path=resume)
        return {
            "resume": "\n\n".join([doc.text for doc in docs])
        }
```

We’re using LlamaIndex’s best-in-class [LlamaParse](https://www.llamaindex.ai/blog/launching-the-first-genai-native-document-parsing-platform) tool to extract the rich nuances of resume documents, which are often heavily bullet-pointed and organized in tables. We then parse the final result as a string and send it to the LLM for further organization.

Aside from being the best parser in the business (in my opinion), LlamaParse offers an exceedingly generous free tier of 7,000 credits per week. If you don’t activate multimodal LLM support, it’s 1 credit per page — meaning 7,000 pages of parsing for free! It can accurately parse tables into markdown, flowcharts into mermaid diagrams, mathematical expressions into LaTeX, and is completely agnostic — it even works for comics. Here’s an example of my parsed resume. The table format and bullet pointing looks almost entirely intact!

#### Internet Search Tool

Here, we use another tool with an exceedingly generous free tier — Tavily AI, an agent-native internet search tool. Tavily AI’s free tier allows for 1,000 API calls per month! While CrewAI does not have native support for Tavily AI out of the box (they do support the Serper API tool), any LangChain or LlamaIndex tool can be converted into a CrewAI tool. In this case, we instantiate our LlamaIndex Tavily tool and wrap it in CrewAI’s `LlamaIndexTool` abstraction:

```python
from crewai_tools import LlamaIndexTool
from llama_index.tools.tavily_research import TavilyToolSpec

tavily_spec = TavilyToolSpec(api_key=os.environ["TAVILY_API_KEY"])
tavily_tool_list = tavily_spec.to_tool_list()
tavily_tools = [LlamaIndexTool.from_tool(tool) for tool in tavily_tool_list]
```

#### Structuring our output

Like LangChain and LlamaIndex, CrewAI supports structured output out of the box. Instead of having the LLM return long, unorganized chunks of text, you can define a specific structure for the response — a key-value pair where you define the key, and the LLM fills in the corresponding values based on the definition of that key. All you need to do is define the structure of the output you expect and assign it to the respective agents.

In this case, we want our `profiler_agent` to use our resume to develop a comprehensive `CandidateProfile` with our core skillsets, qualifications and experience. The next agent (`recruiter`) will then use this profile to find the best `JobListing` for us, along with a justification of fit. The `matcher_agent` will further filter the curated listings to the top 3 by scoring them, and the `reporter_agent` will then take the `JobListing` and our `CandidateProfile` to craft a cover letter for each top listing. This cover letter will be used to apply for the job!

Here’s an example of how we can define these structures:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Literal, List

## For the profiler agent
class WorkExperience(BaseModel):
    """An intermediate output class"""
    project_title: str = Field(..., description="Name of project")
    summary_of_experience: str = Field(..., description="Short summary of experience")
    skills_exhibited: List[str] = Field(..., description="Skills exhibited during this project")

class CandidateProfile(BaseModel):
    """The final output class for the profiler agent"""
    name: str = Field(..., description="Candidate's name")
    highest_qualification: Literal["Bachelor's Degree", "Masters Degree", "PhD"] = Field(..., description="Candidate's highest qualification")
    field_of_study: str = Field(..., description="Candidate's field of study for highest qualification")
    institution_of_study: str = Field(..., description="Candidate's institution of study for highest qualification")
    technical_skills: List[str] = Field(..., description="List of candidate's technical skills. For example 'machine learning'.")
    non_technical_skills: List[str] = Field(..., description="List of candidate's non-technical skills. For example 'strategic planning'.")
    years_of_experience: int = Field(..., description="Candidate's years of experience")
    current_job_title: str = Field(..., description="Candidate's current job title")
    work_experiences: List[WorkExperience] = Field(..., description="Candidate's job experience")

## For the job search agent
class JobListing(BaseModel):
    """An intermediate output class"""
    company_name: str = Field(..., description="Company name")
    job_title: str = Field(..., description="Job title")
    job_description: str = Field(..., description="Job description")
    required_technical_skills: List[str] = Field(..., description="List of required technical skills. For example 'machine learning'.")
    required_non_technical_skills: List[str] = Field(..., description="List of required non-technical skills. For example 'strategic planning'.")
    years_of_experience_required: int = Field(..., description="Years of experience required")
    reason_for_candidate_fit: str = Field(..., description="Reason for candidate fit to job.")

class JobListings(BaseModel):
    """The final output class for the job search agent"""
    job_listings: List[JobListing] = Field(..., description="List of job listings")

## For the matcher agent
class ScoredListing(BaseModel):
    """An intermediate output class"""
    job_listing: JobListing = Field(..., description="Job listing of interest")
    score: float = Field(..., description="Score of job listing fit to candidate profile on a scale of 1-10.")
    justfication: str = Field(..., description="Justification for score")

class ScoredListings(BaseModel):
    """The final output class for the matcher agent"""
    scored_listings: List[ScoredListing] = Field(..., description="List of scored job listings")

## For the reporter agent
class CoverLetter(BaseModel):
    """An intermediate output class"""
    scored_listing: ScoredListing = Field(..., description="Scored job listing of interest")
    cover_letter: str = Field(..., description="Cover letter for scored listing")

class CoverLetters(BaseModel):
    """The final output class for the matcher agent"""
    cover_letters: List[CoverLetter] = Field(..., description="List of cover letters")
    candidate_profile: CandidateProfile
```

#### Assembling the crew!

We start by parsing the YAML files, tagging each configuration, tool and structured output (if applicable) to its respective agent, and assigning each agent to a specific task.

```python
from crewai import Crew, Agent, Task
from typing import Dict, Tuple

def load_configs(files: Dict[str, str]) -> Tuple[dict, dict]:
    configs = {}
    for config_type, file_path in files.items():
        with open(file_path, 'r') as file:
            configs[config_type] = yaml.safe_load(file)
    return configs['agents'], configs['tasks']

## Load yml files
job_search_agents_config, job_search_tasks_config = load_configs(
    {
        'agents': '../config/job_search_agents.yml',
        'tasks': '../config/job_search_tasks.yml',
    }
)

## Agents
profiler_agent = Agent(
    config = job_search_agents_config['profiler'],
    tools = [ResumeParser()]
)
recruiter = Agent(
    config=job_search_agents_config['recruiter'],
    tools = [*tavily_tools] 
)
matcher = Agent(
    config = job_search_agents_config['matcher'],
)
reporter = Agent(
    config=job_search_agents_config['reporter'],
)

## Tasks
profiling_task = Task(
    config = job_search_tasks_config['candidate_profiling_task'],
    agent = profiler_agent,
    output_pydantic = CandidateProfile,
    expected_output = "A clear candidate profile"
)
research_task = Task(
    config = job_search_tasks_config['research_job_listings_task'],
    agent = recruiter,
    context = [profiling_task],
    output_pydantic = JobListings,
    expected_output = "A list of job listings that fit the candidate profile"
)
scoring_task = Task(
    config = job_search_tasks_config['match_and_score_listings_task'],
    agent = matcher,
    context = [research_task, profiling_task],
    output_pydantic=ScoredListings,
    expected_output = "A list of top 3 job listings ranked with justification"
)
cover_letter_task = Task(
    config = job_search_tasks_config['cover_letter_task'],
    agent = reporter,
    context = [scoring_task, profiling_task],
    output_pydantic=CoverLetters,
    expected_output="A list of cover letters for the top 3 job listings"
)

## Putting it together
job_crew = Crew(
    agents = [
        profiler_agent,
        recruiter,
        matcher,
        reporter
    ],
    tasks = [
        profiling_task,
        research_task,
        scoring_task,
        cover_letter_task
    ],
    verbose = True,
)
```

This is an example of a sequential crew, where each task depends on the output of the previous agent as defined by the `context` parameter. CrewAI also supports hierarchical crews, where a manager agent allocates tasks to member agents, evaluates their results, and decides when the job is complete — very similar to the approach used in Autogen.

In CrewAI the only LLM type call you need to remember is `kickoff()` . Remember to define all placeholders in your YAML file as inputs to the `kickoff` argument!

```python
results = job_crew.kickoff(
    inputs = {
        'job_requirements': 'Generative AI related data scientist jobs or management positions.'
    }
)
```

#### Training the crew

Of course, we could stop right there, but we’re not done yet! CrewAI pushes the boundaries further by being the only multi-agent system framework that supports training!

Here, “training” doesn’t refer to updating the LLM’s weights, but rather conditioning the LLM to generate output more closely aligned with our expectations. This is where DSPy shines, but CrewAI takes a different approach. Instead of relying on a predefined training set of questions and answers, CrewAI allows you to provide feedback after each step completes — remember, the key is to use exciting, descriptive language to guide the process!

To start the training, simply run `job_crew.train()` with the same inputs, specify the number of iterations for the training job, and provide a filename (it must be a `.pkl` file) to store the training results:

```python
job_crew.train(
    inputs = {
         'job_requirements': 'Generative AI related data scientist jobs or management positions.'
    },
    n_iterations = 1,
    filename="titus_training.pkl"
)
```

Here are some screenshots of me providing inputs!

Once done, we can test the crew!

```python
job_crew.test(
    inputs = {
         'job_requirements': 'Generative AI related data scientist jobs or management positions.'
    },
    n_iterations = 1,
)
```

This is similar to running the `kickoff()` method for a single iteration, but with one key difference: at the end of the process, an LLM-as-a-judge (again, GPT-4 mini) will evaluate the quality of the output.

### Assembling the job interview preparation crew

You might be wondering, ‘Where’s the declarative, workflow-LlamaIndex-esque approach?’ So far, we’ve been writing grandiose prompts for each agent and task in our crew, and yet, we’re already seeing some magic unfold. But before we dive into that, let’s define another crew. We’ll then orchestrate both crews using CrewAI’s `flow` abstraction.

In our first crew, we’ve already generated cover letters for each suitable job application. Now, let’s define a second crew that takes the scored listings from the first crew and prepares a list of interview questions based on the job descriptions, along with sample answers drawn from our candidate profile. We’ll even get this crew to prepare an `ElevatorPitch` for us to answer that perennial question: “Tell me about yourself.” I’ll keep the definitions here brief — the steps are similar to what we’ve done before.

```python
job_interview_agents_config, job_interview_tasks_config = load_configs(
    {
        'agents': '../config/job_interview_agents.yml',
        'tasks': '../config/job_interview_tasks.yml',
    }
)

## The structure of the outputs we want
class InterviewQuestion(BaseModel):
    """An intermediate output class"""
    company: str = Field(..., description="Hiring company name")
    job_title: str = Field(..., description="Job title")
    question: str = Field(..., description="Interview question to ask candidate")
    skill_required: str = Field(..., description="What the interviewer is looking out for")
    sample_answer: str = Field(..., description="Sample answer to question based on candidate's profile")

class InterviewPrep(BaseModel):
    """Final output class of the interview prep agent"""
    interview_questions: List[InterviewQuestion] = Field(..., description="List of interview questions")

class ElevatorPitch(BaseModel):
    """Final output class of the elevator pitch agent"""
    interview_prep: InterviewPrep = Field(..., description="Interview Q&A doocument")
    elevator_pitch: str = Field(..., description="Customized elevator pitch for the job description to answer the question 'tell me more about yourself'.")

## Agents
interviewer = Agent(
    config=job_interview_agents_config['interviewer'],
)
pitcher = Agent(
    config=job_interview_agents_config['pitcher'],
)

## Tasks
interview_prep_task = Task(
    config = job_interview_tasks_config['interview_prep_task'],
    agent = interviewer,
    output_pydantic = InterviewPrep,
    expected_output = "A compiled list of interview questions and answers for each job listing"
)
elevator_pitch_task = Task(
    config = job_interview_tasks_config['conversation_starter_task'],
    agent = pitcher,
    output_pydantic = ElevatorPitch,
    context = [interview_prep_task],
    expected_output = "A customized elevator pitch for the job listing."
)

## Crew
interview_crew = Crew(
    agents = [
        interviewer,
        pitcher
    ],
    tasks = [
        interview_prep_task,
        elevator_pitch_task,
    ],
    verbose = True,
)
```

### Go with the Flow

Now it’s time to orchestrate both crews using CrewAI’s declarative Flow abstraction. Each step of the Flow is a function decorated with the event it listens for — the materialization of this event triggers the corresponding function. Here’s an example of how we can define and orchestrate our job search pipeline:

```python
from crewai import Flow
from crewai.flow.flow import listen, start

from typing import Optional
import json

class JobSearchPipeline(Flow):
    @start()
    def job_crew_kickoff(self, inputs: Optional[Dict[str, Any]]= None):
        print("Job crew tasks kickoff...")
        job_crew_results = job_crew.kickoff(inputs=inputs)
        results= job_crew_results.pydantic.model_dump()
        return results
    
    @listen(job_crew_kickoff)
    def log_job_results(self, results: Dict[str, Any]):
        with open("job_crew_results.json", "w") as file:
            json.dump(results, file, indent=4)
        print("Results saved to './job_crew_results.json'")
    
    @listen(job_crew_kickoff)
    def postprocess_job_crew_results(self, results: Dict[str, Any]):
        print("Preparing interview crew inputs...")
        candidate_profile = results['candidate_profile']
        scored_listings =  [
            result['scored_listing']['job_listing'] for result in results['cover_letters']
        ]
        interview_crew_inputs = [
            {
                "candidate_profile": candidate_profile,
                "job_listing": listing
            } for listing in scored_listings
        ]
        return interview_crew_inputs
    
    @listen(postprocess_job_crew_results)
    def log_interview_crew_inputs(self, interview_crew_inputs: List[Dict[str, Any]]):
        with open("interview_crew_inputs.json", "w") as file:
            json.dump(interview_crew_inputs, file, indent=4)
        print("interview crew input saved!")
    
    @listen(postprocess_job_crew_results)
    def interview_crew_kickoff(self, interview_crew_inputs: List[Dict[str, Any]]):
        print("Interview crew tasks kickoff...")
        interview_crew_results = interview_crew.kickoff_for_each(inputs=interview_crew_inputs)
        return interview_crew_results

flow = JobSearchPipeline()
flow.plot()
```

Here, we define an entire pipeline that **starts** with the `job_crew_kickoff` method. This method returns the dictionary representation of the CoverLetters' structured output.  
_Pro Tip:_ It's better to return results in either JSON format or a key-value pair format because **LLMs excel at understanding these formats**.

Next, the `log_job_results` and `postprocess_job_crew_results` steps run because they are **listening** for the output of `job_crew_kickoff`. The results of that step are automatically passed to them.

-   `**log_job_results**`**:** Logs and saves the JSON representation of the job crew's results.
-   `**postprocess_job_crew_results**`**:** Processes the results of the first crew to prepare inputs for the second crew.

Finally, the `log_interview_crew_inputs` and `interview_crew_kickoff` steps handle the interview crew's tasks. While the first crew creates cover letters for the top three job listings, the interview crew needs to ‘kick off’ for each listing. How perfect is it that CrewAI provides a `kickoff_for_each()` function to handle this seamlessly! With the pipeline in place, orchestrating both crews becomes effortless, allowing us to efficiently manage the entire job search workflow. Running `flow.plot()` even saves an interactive HTML file of our flow, showcasing a beautifully rendered digraph that we built with ease—far simpler than using LangGraph!

How do we get the flow to do something? With `kickoff` of course!

```python
results = flow.kickoff(
    inputs = {
        'job_requirements': 'Generative AI related data scientist jobs or management positions.'
    }
)
for result in results:
    display(Markdown(result.pydantic.elevator_pitch))
```

**Savor our success!**  
The best part? This entire project cost me less than USD $0.01 in total.

### Comparing CrewAI, LlamaIndex, Autogen, and LangGraph

Wasn’t that fun? CrewAI makes orchestrating complex multi-agent setups a breeze. It required far fewer lines of code than LlamaIndex and LangGraph while offering more fine-grained control than Autogen.

But is it perfect? Not quite.

You might have noticed that I deliberately skipped over the progress thread of the crew. While fascinating to read, it only becomes easily readable _after_ the crew has executed — during execution it comes at you “fast and furious.” The downside? It’s lengthy, and debugging errors might take some time. To make things trickier, you’d need to write custom code (quite un-CrewAI-like) to parse the `sys.stdout` variable post-mortem to visualize conversation patterns between agents.

This is where Autogen shines — it lets you visualize conversation patterns straight out of the box, saving time and effort during debugging or analysis.

Unlike LlamaIndex and LangGraph, CrewAI’s **Crew** is its atomic unit (i.e., the smallest building block). LlamaIndex and LangGraph, on the other hand, allow multi-agent systems to be defined at the LLM level. This provides a higher degree of customization and control, rather than leaving the Crew to handle everything autonomously.

Where CrewAI truly excels is in its unrivaled ease of use, freeing up time that developers would otherwise spend debugging to focus on writing compelling prompts. CrewAI also offers a training toolkit that helps the Crew provide answers better aligned with user preferences — an incredible and unmatched feature.

Like LlamaIndex and LangGraph, CrewAI Flows can also invoke multi-agent systems from other vendors. This means you can use CrewAI to trigger your colleague’s deployed LangGraph app!

### What about deployment?

Flows and Crews are deployed as RESTful APIs using CrewAI+. The free tier of CrewAI+ even includes 1,000 requests per month. However, I wasn’t entirely comfortable uploading my resume to CrewAI+, so I didn’t deploy this project on the platform. If I were to deploy this, I will write my own FastAPI code.

### Final Thoughts

I genuinely love CrewAI, but I’d rank it as a close second to LlamaIndex. LlamaIndex shines with its ability to create amazing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) applications right out of the box, while also offering more fine-grained control. That said, I find CrewAI’s Flow abstraction to be neater, with its use of decorated event listeners, compared to LlamaIndex’s Workflow abstraction, where events have to be defined as objects — though that approach has its own charm too.

If you’re just starting with multi-agent systems, however, CrewAI is an excellent choice that I wholeheartedly recommend.

With this article, I’ll conclude my gentle introduction to the multi-agent systems multiverse. Throughout this series, I’ve explored the top four most widely used frameworks. It’s worth noting that these frameworks are evolving rapidly, with some releasing more than two updates per week!

While I was experimenting with [CamelAI](https://www.camel-ai.org/) (spoiler alert: it takes a similar “society of LLM agents” approach as Autogen), yet another contender joined the fray — [PydanticAI](https://ai.pydantic.dev/) (FastAPI lovers rejoice!).

To keep this series from growing too long, I’ll place a temporary full stop here, with a promise to return and share more insights into multi-agent systems once I’ve learned and experimented with their latest features myself. Until next time!

body:
* * *

This article continues our exploration of **LlamaIndex workflows**, an integral part of the _Gentle Introduction to the Multi-Agent Multiverse_ series. The multiverse of multi-agent systems is brimming with exciting frameworks — at least six prominent ones, including LangGraph, Autogen, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, CAMEL, and OpenAI Swarm. In this series, we aim to gently introduce readers to four of the most popular frameworks, which I use regularly.

So far, we’ve covered [LangGraph](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multi-agent-multiverse-part-2-autogen-5401a0075d75), [Autogen,](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multi-agent-multiverse-part-2-autogen-5401a0075d75) and [LlamaIndex workflows](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multi-agent-multiverse-part-3a-llamaindex-workflows-c0f614c15b88), albeit without delving into their _human-in-the-loop_ and _deployment_ capabilities. In this article, we’ll address those gaps, with a particular focus on LlamaIndex’s `llama-deploy` library, **the only open-source option for deploying multi-agent workflows**. This “batteries-included” library provides essential tools for building scalable multi-agent backend systems.

Looking ahead, I’ll cover **CrewAI** in a separate article, and perhaps explore the remaining frameworks as I master them. For now, this article is pivotal: not only will we discuss llama-deploy, but we’ll also continue where we left off, introducing LlamaIndex’s _human-in-the-loop_ capabilities.

As always, you can find all the code featured in the multi-agent multiverse series in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/literate-octo-tribble/tree/main).

### Human-in-the-loop: Easier done than said

Let’s dive into the concept of _human-in-the-loop_ by creating a simple workflow. This workflow demonstrates how LlamaIndex can seamlessly integrate human feedback using specialized events.

We’ll begin by importing the necessary libraries:

```python
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv, find_dotenv
import warnings
import nest_asyncio
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
nest_asyncio.apply()
_ = load_dotenv(find_dotenv())

llm = OpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0)
```

#### Defining the Workflow

Next, we’ll define a workflow using LlamaIndex’s core modules:

```python
from llama_index.core.workflow import (
    Workflow,
    step,
    Event,
    Context,
    StartEvent,
    StopEvent
)
from llama_index.core.workflow.events import InputRequiredEvent, HumanResponseEvent
from llama_index.core.chat_engine import SimpleChatEngine

class AnswerEvent(Event):
    query: str

class AskLLM(Workflow):
    def __init__(self, llm = llm,  *args, **kwargs):
        self.user = None
        self.approved_users = ["Titus"]
        self.engine = SimpleChatEngine.from_defaults(llm=llm)
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
```

This workflow centers around a single event: **AnswerEvent**, and is powered by a `SimpleChatEngine` from LlamaIndex, which conveniently manages chat history for us.

Notice that only one user (“Titus”) is authorized to invoke the workflow. Since no user is initially registered, the workflow first prompts the user to identify themselves.

#### Prompting User Identification

```python
@step(pass_context=True)
async def start(self, ctx: Context, ev: StartEvent) -> InputRequiredEvent | AnswerEvent:
    if self.user is None:
        print("Unidentified user. Verifying credentials...\n\n")
        await ctx.set("query", ev.query)
        return InputRequiredEvent(prefix="Please identify yourself: ")
    return AnswerEvent(query=ev.query)
```

The `InputRequiredEvent` pauses the workflow to seek user feedback, acting as a “breakpoint” in execution. This feedback is processed through another special event: `HumanResponseEvent`.

#### Authenticating the User

```python
@step(pass_context=True)
async def authenticate(self, ctx: Context, ev: HumanResponseEvent) -> AnswerEvent | StopEvent:
    user = ev.response
    if user in self.approved_users:
        self.user = user
        query = await ctx.get("query")
        return AnswerEvent(query=str(query))
    return StopEvent(result="Unauthorized user. Please acquire authorization credentials from administrators.")
```

Here, the `HumanResponseEvent` verifies the user. If authentication succeeds, it triggers an `AnswerEvent`; otherwise, it stops the workflow with a rejection message.

#### Generating a Response

Finally, we define the step to process the `AnswerEvent`:

```python
@step
async def answer(self, ev: AnswerEvent) -> StopEvent:
    response = self.engine.chat(ev.query)
    return StopEvent(result=str(response))
```

#### Running the Workflow

To invoke a workflow involving `InputRequiredEvent` and `HumanResponseEvent`, we use a loop to handle events dynamically. Here’s how it works in a Jupyter Notebook:

```python
app1 = AskLLM()
handler1 = app1.run(query="What is OpenAI?")
## Use a for-loop to handle the `HumanResponseEvent`
async for event in handler1.stream_events():
    if isinstance(event, InputRequiredEvent):
        response = input(event.prefix)
        handler1.ctx.send_event(HumanResponseEvent(response=response))
final_result = await handler1
display(Markdown(final_result))
```

**Sample Interaction:**

```python-repl
Unidentified user. Verifying credentials...

Please identify yourself: Titus
OpenAI is an artificial intelligence research organization that aims to develop 
and promote friendly AI for the benefit of humanity...
```

#### Key Takeaways

Wasn’t that surprisingly simple? Using LlamaIndex’s built-in event types, we’ve created a robust _human-in-the-loop_ workflow that:

1.  Authenticates users dynamically.
2.  Pauses for feedback when necessary.
3.  Resumes with contextual continuity.

This example underscores the elegance and power of LlamaIndex for building interactive, human-aware workflows.

However, this approach has its limitations. Imagine your app has a hundred concurrent users, requiring deployment to a RESTful API with a message queuing system. If one user decides to grab a cup of coffee before providing their “feedback,” the entire workflow halts, leaving the other 99 users stuck, and unable to interact with the system. This creates a bottleneck where one user monopolizes valuable time.

Fortunately, LlamaIndex offers an alternative approach to human-in-the-loop workflows that avoids this issue. By using the `StopEvent` class, you can stop the workflow and then restart it using a `StartEvent`. This method requires handling chat history outside of the workflow. For example, if you initially run the app with `app.run(query="...", chat_history=[])`, you can continue the workflow by calling `app.run(query="response to LLM question", chat_history=["original query", "LLM seeks human input"])`.

### Human-in-the-loop (Part 2): Still easier done than said

We’re going to build _human-in-the-loop_ capabilities over [LlamaIndex ‘s self-discovery workflow cookbook recipe](http://self-discovery%20workflow) — and deploy it! The self-discovery approach is a paradigm shift in LLM prompting, in summary, there are 2 stages to solving any given problem:

STAGE-1:

a. SELECT: Selects subset of reasoning Modules.

b. ADAPT: Adapts selected reasoning modules to the task.

c. IMPLEMENT: It gives reasoning structure for the task.

STAGE-2: Uses the generated reasoning structure for the task to generate an answer.

We start by constructing the reasoning modules, and the SELECT, ADAPT and IMPLEMENT prompt templates.

```python
from llama_index.core.prompts import PromptTemplate

_REASONING_MODULES = [
   ... #commented out for brevity. Full code available in GitHub
]

_REASONING_MODULES = "\n".join(_REASONING_MODULES)

SELECT_PRMOPT_TEMPLATE = PromptTemplate(
    "Given the task: {task}, which of the following reasoning modules are relevant? Do not elaborate on why.\n\n {reasoning_modules}"
)

ADAPT_PROMPT_TEMPLATE = PromptTemplate(
    "Without working out the full solution, adapt the following reasoning modules to be specific to our task:\n{selected_modules}\n\nOur task:\n{task}"
)

IMPLEMENT_PROMPT_TEMPLATE = PromptTemplate(
    "Without working out the full solution, create an actionable reasoning structure for the task using these adapted reasoning modules:\n{adapted_modules}\n\nTask Description:\n{task}"
)

REASONING_PROMPT_TEMPLATE = PromptTemplate(
    "Using the following reasoning structure: {reasoning_structure}\n\nSolve this task, providing your final answer: {task}"
)
```

#### The Workflow

The workflow has several events to select, refine and adapt the modules defined above.

```python
from llama_index.core.llms import LLM
from llama_index.core.llms import ChatMessage
from llama_index.core.memory import ChatMemoryBuffer
from typing import List
import json

class SetupEvent(Event):
    task: str

class GetModulesEvent(Event):
    """Event to get modules."""

    task: str
    modules: str

class RefineModulesEvent(Event):
    """Event to refine modules."""

    task: str
    refined_modules: str

class ReasoningStructureEvent(Event):
    """Event to create reasoning structure."""

    task: str
    reasoning_structure: str
```

We start by defining the class constructor and a simple utility method to handle chat history inputs.

```python
class SelfDiscoverWorkflow(Workflow):
    def __init__(
        self,
        llm: LLM = llm,
        chat_history: List[ChatMessage] = [],
        *args,
        **kwargs
    ):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.agent = SimpleChatEngine.from_defaults(llm=llm)
        self.chat_history = chat_history
    
    def process_chat_history(self):
        return [message.dict() for message in self.chat_history]
```

Next, we set up our `JudgeQuery` step, where we integrate human-in-the-loop capabilities. This step uses a simple prompt template to have the LLM judge whether a query is well-formed. If the query is deemed “bad,” the workflow seeks user clarification using a `StopEvent`.

```python
    @step
    async def judge_query(self, ctx: Context, ev: StartEvent) -> StopEvent | SetupEvent:
        """Event to judge whether a query is well-written and to seek
        clarification if the query is not well-written"""
        
        self.chat_history.append(ChatMessage(**{"role": "user", "content": ev.task}))
        
        response = await self.agent.achat(
            f"""
            Given a user query, determine if this is likely to yield good results from a RAG system as-is. If it's good, return 'good', if it's bad, return 'bad', if 
            it's not a question (for e.g. "Hi!", "Thanks!"), return "not a question".
            Good queries use a lot of relevant keywords and are detailed. Bad queries are vague or ambiguous.

            Here is the query: {ev.task}
            """
        )
        print("\n\nJudge Query response: "+ str(response) + "\n\n")
        if str(response) == "bad":
            final_response = await self.agent.achat(
                f"""
                The user has given a poor query. Seek for clarification from the user.
                
                Here's the user's query: {ev.task}
                """,
                chat_history = self.chat_history
            )   
            self.chat_history.append(ChatMessage(**{"role": "assistant", "content": str(final_response)}))
            return StopEvent(str(final_response)) 
        
        elif str(response) == "not a question":
            final_response = await self.agent.achat(
                f"""
                Here's the user's remark or greeting: {ev.task}
                
                Respond to the user politely.
                """,
                chat_history = self.chat_history
            )   
            self.chat_history.append(ChatMessage(**{"role": "assistant", "content": str(final_response)}))
            return StopEvent(str(final_response)) 
        
        return SetupEvent(task=ev.task)
```

From here, we proceed with the rest of the LlamaIndex cookbook recipe and define steps to consume the respective events — selecting modules, refining module selection, implementing the plan, and reasoning from the results.

```python
    @step
    async def get_modules(
        self, ctx: Context, ev: SetupEvent
    ) -> GetModulesEvent:
        """Get modules step."""
        task = ev.get("task")
        
        # format prompt and get result from LLM
        prompt = SELECT_PRMOPT_TEMPLATE.format(
            task=task, reasoning_modules=_REASONING_MODULES
        )
        result = await self.agent.achat(prompt, chat_history = self.chat_history)
        print("\n\nModules selected: " + str(result) + "\n\n")
        self.chat_history.append(ChatMessage(**{"role": "assistant", "content": str(result)}))
        return GetModulesEvent(task=str(task), modules=str(result))

    @step
    async def refine_modules(
        self, ctx: Context, ev: GetModulesEvent
    ) -> RefineModulesEvent:
        """Refine modules step."""
        task = ev.task
        modules = ev.modules
        
        # format prompt and get result
        prompt = ADAPT_PROMPT_TEMPLATE.format(
            task=task, selected_modules=modules
        )
        result = await self.agent.achat(prompt, chat_history = self.chat_history)
        print("\n\nRefined modules: " + str(result) + "\n\n")
        self.chat_history.append(ChatMessage(**{"role": "assistant", "content": str(result)}))
        return RefineModulesEvent(task=task, refined_modules=str(result))

    @step
    async def create_reasoning_structure(
        self, ctx: Context, ev: RefineModulesEvent
    ) -> ReasoningStructureEvent:
        """Create reasoning structures step."""
        task = ev.task
        refined_modules = ev.refined_modules

        # format prompt, get result
        prompt = IMPLEMENT_PROMPT_TEMPLATE.format(
            task=task, adapted_modules=refined_modules
        )
        result = await self.agent.achat(prompt, chat_history = self.chat_history)
        print("\n\nImplementation results: " + str(result) + "\n\n")
        self.chat_history.append(ChatMessage(**{"role": "assistant", "content": str(result)}))

        return ReasoningStructureEvent(
            task=task, reasoning_structure=str(result)
        )

    @step
    async def get_final_result(
        self, ctx: Context, ev: ReasoningStructureEvent
    ) -> StopEvent:
        """Gets final result from reasoning structure event."""
        task = ev.task
        reasoning_structure = ev.reasoning_structure

        # format prompt, get res
        prompt = REASONING_PROMPT_TEMPLATE.format(
            task=task, reasoning_structure=reasoning_structure
        )
        result = await self.agent.achat(prompt, chat_history = self.chat_history)
        print("\n\nReasoning: " + str(result) + "\n\n")
        self.chat_history.append(ChatMessage(**{"role": "assistant", "content": str(result)}))

        return StopEvent(
            result=str(result) + " ||History||: " + json.dumps(self.process_chat_history())
        )
```

Though this might seem complicated at first glance, it was surprisingly quick to implement, thanks to the event-driven, declarative programming paradigm of LlamaIndex Workflow. This is what our final workflow looks like:

Time to take it for a spin:

### Deployment Made Easy: The Llama-Deploy Story

The `llama-deploy` repository provides a simple and effective solution for deploying LlamaIndex Workflows. Each deployment consists of:

-   **Control Plane**: A RESTful API comprising the Orchestrator, ServiceMetadata, and StateStorage. Multiple workflows can be registered to the same Control Plane.
-   **Message Queue**: A RESTful API that handles communication between the Control Plane and all registered workflows. Llama-Deploy supports various production-ready Message Queues such as Redis, Apache Kafka, RabbitMQ, and AWS Message Queues. You can easily set these up in Docker if they’re not already installed on your server.
-   **Workflow Objects**: Deployed as individual RESTful APIs.

**How do we deploy this? With very few lines of code!**

Here’s how we deploy the `Control Plane` :

```python
#core.py
from llama_deploy import (
    deploy_core,
    ControlPlaneConfig,
)
from llama_deploy.message_queues.apache_kafka import KafkaMessageQueueConfig

control_plane_config = ControlPlaneConfig()
message_queue_config = KafkaMessageQueueConfig()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import asyncio

    asyncio.run(
        deploy_core(
            control_plane_config=control_plane_config,
            message_queue_config=message_queue_config,
        )
    )
```

And here’s how we deploy our `SelfDiscovery Workflow`:

```python
#deploy_workflow.py
from llama_deploy import deploy_workflow, WorkflowServiceConfig
from self_discovery_app.deployment.core import control_plane_config
from self_discovery_app.workflows.selfdiscovery import SelfDiscoverWorkflow

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import asyncio
    
    asyncio.run(
        deploy_workflow(
            workflow=SelfDiscoverWorkflow(timeout=3600, verbose = True),
            workflow_config=WorkflowServiceConfig(
                service_name="self_discovery_workflow"
            ),
            control_plane_config=control_plane_config,
        )
    )
```

Notice how minimal the code is — we mainly define the Llama Deploy objects. Keep in mind that you’ll need to specify a port number for each LlamaIndex object if you deviate from the defaults. To execute the deployments, simply run `python -m <script>.py` for each script.

#### Composing your deployment

The order of deployment is crucial. Start by deploying the MessageQueue (e.g., using `docker run ...`), followed by the ControlPlane, and finally, the respective Workflow services. Alternatively, you can streamline the process by composing your deployment using a `docker-compose.yml` file.

The folder structure of my app adhering to the structure from an [example in the llama-deploy GitHub repository.](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_deploy/tree/main/examples/message-queue-integrations)

```
|-.
  |-backend
    |-_app
      |-self_discovery_app
        |-deployment
          |-core.py              <- deploy control plane and message queue
          |-deploy_workflow.py   <- deploy workflows
        |-workflows
          |-self_discovery.py    <- define workflows here
      |-pyproject.toml           <- backend requirements
     |-Kafka
       |-docker
          |-.env.kafka          <- our .env file for kafka message queue
          |-docker-compose.yml  <- our main docker compose file
    |-.env.docker               <- our .env file for the docker image
    |-.env.openai               <- our .env file containing our openai key
    |-Dockerfile                <- Dockerfile to build our workflow app image
    |-logging.ini               <- Logging commands file
  |-frontend
    |-.chainlit                 
    |-app.py                    <- Our frontend code
    |-chainlit.md  
    |-requirements.txt          <- frontend requirements
```

We’ll deploy the backend using Docker Compose. Here’s what the `docker-compose.yml` file looks like:

```yaml
services:
  kafka:
    image: apache/kafka:3.7.1
    hostname: kafka
    container_name: kafka
    ports:
      - "9092:9092"
    env_file:
      - ./kafka/docker/.env.kafka
      - ./.env.docker
    environment:
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 1
      KAFKA_LISTENER_SECURITY_PROTOCOL_MAP: "CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT,PLAINTEXT:PLAINTEXT,PLAINTEXT_HOST:PLAINTEXT"
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: "PLAINTEXT_HOST://localhost:9092,PLAINTEXT://kafka:19092"
      KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: "broker,controller"
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_QUORUM_VOTERS: "1@kafka:29093"
      KAFKA_LISTENERS: "CONTROLLER://:29093,PLAINTEXT_HOST://:9092,PLAINTEXT://:19092"
      KAFKA_INTER_BROKER_LISTENER_NAME: "PLAINTEXT"
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_LISTENER_NAMES: "CONTROLLER"
      KAFKA_OFFSETS_TOPIC_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_GROUP_INITIAL_REBALANCE_DELAY_MS: 0
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_MIN_ISR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_LOG_DIRS: "/tmp/kraft-combined-logs"
    healthcheck:
      test: nc -z localhost 9092 || exit -1
      start_period: 15s
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 5
  control_plane:
    image: self_discovery_app:latest
    command: sh -c "python -m self_discovery_app.deployment.core"
    env_file:
      - ./kafka/docker/.env.kafka
      - ./.env.docker
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    volumes:
      - ./_app/self_discovery_app:/app/self_discovery_app # load local code change to container without the need of rebuild
      - ./logging.ini:/app/logging.ini
    depends_on:
      kafka:
        condition: service_healthy
    platform: linux/amd64
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: ./Dockerfile
    healthcheck:
      test: wget --no-verbose --tries=1 http://0.0.0.0:8000/ || exit 1
      interval: 30s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 20s
      timeout: 10s
  self_discovery_workflow:
    image: self_discovery_app:latest
    command: sh -c "python -m self_discovery_app.deployment.deploy_workflow"
    env_file:
      - ./kafka/docker/.env.kafka
      - ./.env.docker
      - ./.env.openai
    ports:
      - "8001:8001"
    volumes:
      - ./_app/self_discovery_app:/app/self_discovery_app # load local code change to container without the need of rebuild
      - ./logging.ini:/app/logging.ini
    platform: linux/amd64
    depends_on:
      kafka:
        condition: service_healthy
      control_plane:
        condition: service_healthy
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: ./Dockerfile
    healthcheck:
      test: wget --no-verbose --tries=1 http://0.0.0.0:8001/ || exit 1
      interval: 30s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 20s
      timeout: 10s
volumes:
  kafka:
```

#### Explanation

-   The Kafka service is deployed first. Other services depend on it and wait for a successful health check before starting.
-   We use bind mounts to persist container data on the local machine and allow dynamic updates to the app without rebuilding the image.
-   The backend image is built using the `Dockerfile` in the backend folder, which includes Python dependencies.

#### Spinning Up the Backend

Run the following commands to prepare and deploy the backend:

```bash
cd ./backend/_app

## creates the poetry lock file
poetry shell
poetry install
cd ../

docker compose -f ./Kafka/docker/docker-compose.yml --project-directory ./ up --build -d
```

#### Spinning up the frontend

After deploying the workflow, we can interact with it using Llama-Deploy’s `LlamaDeployClient` class. For the frontend, we'll use Chainlit, a framework designed for building conversational interfaces. Here's what the `./frontend/app.py` file looks like:

```python
import json
import chainlit as cl
from llama_deploy import LlamaDeployClient
from llama_deploy.control_plane.server import ControlPlaneConfig

# Configure the Control Plane
control_plane_config = ControlPlaneConfig(host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)

# Initialize the LlamaDeploy client
client = LlamaDeployClient(control_plane_config)

@cl.on_chat_start
async def on_chat_start():
    session = client.create_session()
    cl.user_session.set("session", session)
    cl.user_session.set("history", [])
    await cl.Message("Hi! How can I help you?").send()

@cl.on_message
async def on_chat_message(message: cl.Message):
    session = cl.user_session.get("session")
    history = cl.user_session.get("history")

    if not history:
        result = session.run("self_discovery_workflow", task=message.content)
    else:
        result = session.run("self_discovery_workflow", task=message.content, chat_history=history)

    try:
        # Parse the result and extract response and history
        response, history = result.split(" ||History||: ")[0], json.loads(result.split(" ||History||: ")[1])
        cl.user_session.set("history", history)
        await cl.Message(response).send()
    except Exception:
        cl.user_session.set("history", [{"role": "assistant", "content": result}])
        await cl.Message(result).send()
```

With just a few lines of code, our setup achieves the following:

1.  Establishes a connection to the deployed Control Plane and workflows using `LlamaDeployClient`.
2.  Implements a conversational interface where users can send messages to trigger workflows, with responses tailored to the input.

### Concluding Thoughts

LlamaIndex’s declarative, event-driven approach to multi-agent workflows significantly enhances the developer experience compared to LangGraph. By focusing on defining significant events and the steps consuming these events — rather than every node and edge — it lowers the barriers to entry without compromising reliability.

Human-in-the-loop functionality and workflow deployments are shockingly straightforward, requiring minimal code rewrites. Llama-Deploy, a dedicated and entirely open-source framework, handles deployments seamlessly, with support for a variety of message queue integrations out of the box. This openness and flexibility stand in contrast to proprietary solutions like LangGraph Cloud. LlamaIndex’s thoughtful framework design reflects a strong focus on developer experience, aiming to maximize developer efficiency and code mileage.

Compared to Autogen, LlamaIndex Workflows provide finer control over agent interactions, enabling reliable mapping of conversation flows in multi-agent systems. It’s exciting to see the ongoing rewrite of the Autogen framework, which could potentially adopt similar paradigms to enhance its utility.

The story doesn’t end there. CrewAI has also embraced declarative, event-driven workflows while maintaining its core capabilities of communicative, role-playing agents, serving as a hybrid of Autogen and LlamaIndex Workflows. Its _Crew_ abstraction enables collaborative role-playing among agents, while the _Flow_ abstraction orchestrates multi-crew systems or extends functionalities with pre- and post-processing. These advancements push the boundaries of multi-agent orchestration.

Stay tuned for the next article, where we’ll delve deeper into the CrewAI perspective and its potential impact.
