body:
* * *

In our previous articles, we explored [LangGraph](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multi-agent-multiverse-part-2-autogen-5401a0075d75) and [Autogen](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multi-agent-multiverse-part-2-autogen-5401a0075d75) in a series dedicated to multi-agent LLM systems. We left off with Autogen in the midst of an exciting shift — rewriting its framework to embrace an event-driven workflow architecture. This approach is widely known in contexts like robotic process automation (RPA), where, for example, uploading a document to a folder can trigger a bot to draft an email summarizing the document for user review.

To my knowledge, LlamaIndex is the first framework to bring event-driven workflows into LLM orchestration. In this article, we’ll dive into the flexibility of this paradigm and how it enables multi-agent systems to coordinate seamlessly. As a bonus, we’ll be building a system that brings back some familiar components from past articles: our LangGraph personal assistant, the Autogen stock assistant, and our [HyDE and Seek DSPy-optimized investment definitions agent](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/hyde-and-seek-when-hallucination-leads-the-way-17a9800734fe) are all making a return!

I have introduced the LlamaIndex framework in a [prior article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multiverse-part-3-llamaindex-798344050c49), so I’ll keep it brief: LlamaIndex currently has the highest number of stars among the multi-agent system frameworks we’re exploring, with over 36k on GitHub. As we dive into building workflows, you’ll quickly see why it’s gained such traction!

As before, all codes are available in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/tituslhy/literate-octo-tribble/tree/main).

### Building our Stock Subject Matter Expert

To get started, let’s build a small multi-agent system with three agents. We’ll have our ‘[HyDE-and-seek](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/hyde-and-seek-when-hallucination-leads-the-way-17a9800734fe)’ investment definitions agent, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) agent with specialized knowledge of Apple from a detailed analysis of its SEC report, and a manager agent to coordinate their interactions.

```python
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv, find_dotenv
import warnings
import nest_asyncio
from IPython.display import display, Markdown
from phoenix.otel import register
from openinference.instrumentation.llama_index import LlamaIndexInstrumentor

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
nest_asyncio.apply()
_ = load_dotenv(find_dotenv())

## Log traces using Llama Trace
tracer_provider = register(
  project_name="llama-trace-v1",
  endpoint="https://app.phoenix.arize.com/v1/traces"
)
LlamaIndexInstrumentor().instrument(tracer_provider=tracer_provider)
```

We start by importing our libraries. For LLM tracing, we will be using [Llama Trace](https://phoenix.arize.com/llamatrace/), a hosted LLM tracing tool developed by Arize Phoenix in partnership with LlamaIndex. I’m a big fan of Arize Phoenix — it’s completely free, open-source, and very user-friendly. I’ll cover its use in more detail in future articles.

To build our Apple RAG agent, we first need to ingest Apple’s SEC document. Let’s download the document and start up a Qdrant vector database using Docker:

```bash
wget "https://s2.q4cdn.com/470004039/files/doc_financials/2021/q4/_10-K-2021-(As-Filed).pdf" -O apple_2021_10k.pdf

docker run -p 6333:6333 -p 6334:6334 \
     -v "$(pwd)/qdrant_storage:/qdrant/storage:z" \
     qdrant/qdrant
```

LlamaIndex makes document ingestion and RAG agent setup straightforward. We’re using Qdrant as our vector database to leverage its hybrid vector search capabilities for improved retrieval results.

#### Ingesting documents into a vector database

This portion should be very familiar if you’ve read my [LlamaIndex introduction article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multiverse-part-3-llamaindex-798344050c49) — it’s the same steps!

```python
from llama_index.core import (
    SimpleDirectoryReader,
    VectorStoreIndex,
    StorageContext,
    load_index_from_storage
)
from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI
from llama_index.embeddings.openai import OpenAIEmbedding
from llama_index.vector_stores.qdrant import QdrantVectorStore
from qdrant_client import QdrantClient, AsyncQdrantClient

llm = OpenAI("gpt-4o-mini")
embed_model = OpenAIEmbedding(model="text-embedding-3-small")

## Read document
documents = SimpleDirectoryReader(
    input_files=["./apple_2021_10k.pdf"]
).load_data()

## Instantiate vector store
client = QdrantClient(host="localhost", port=6333)
aclient = AsyncQdrantClient(host="localhost", port=6333)

### delete collection if it exists
if client.collection_exists("Apple_10K"):
    client.delete_collection("Apple_10K")

vector_store = QdrantVectorStore(
    "Apple_10K",
    client = client,
    aclient = aclient,
    enable_hybrid = True,
    fastembed_sparse_model="Qdrant/bm42-all-minilm-l6-v2-attentions",
)

storage_context = StorageContext.from_defaults(vector_store=vector_store)

index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(
    documents,
    storage_context=storage_context,
    embed_model = embed_model
)
```

#### Creating the Apple RAG Agent

```python
from llama_index.core.tools import QueryEngineTool, ToolMetadata
from llama_index.core.agent import FunctionCallingAgent

query_engine = index.as_query_engine(
    similarity_top_k=2, sparse_top_k=12, vector_store_query_mode="hybrid", llm = llm
)

tools = [
    QueryEngineTool(
        query_engine=query_engine,
        metadata=ToolMetadata(
            name="apple_10k",
            description=(
                "Provides information about Apple financials for year 2021. "
                "Use a detailed plain text question as input to the tool."
            )
        )
    )
]

apple_agent = FunctionCallingAgent.from_tools(
    tools=tools,
    llm = llm,
    verbose = True,
)
```

Well… that’s one agent done. Now, let’s integrate it with the code from our [‘HyDE and Seek’](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/hyde-and-seek-when-hallucination-leads-the-way-17a9800734fe) agent and combine them into a LlamaIndex workflow.

```python
## Import dependencies for workflow and setup events
from llama_index.core.workflow import (
    Workflow,
    step,
    Context,
    Event,
    StartEvent,
    StopEvent
)
from llama_index.core.base.llms.types import ChatMessage
from llama_index.core.chat_engine import SimpleChatEngine
from llama_index.core.selectors import LLMSingleSelector
from llama_index.core.prompts import PromptTemplate
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Literal, List, Dict, Optional, Any, Union, Annotated

class AppleEvent(Event):
    query: str

class InvestopediaEvent(Event):
    query: str 

class CompileEvent(Event):
    query: str
    response: str
    source: str

class Reroute(BaseModel):
    reroute: Literal[True, False] = Field(..., description="If the answer is satisfactory, return True. Else return False for rerouting")
    improvements: str = Field(..., description="Suggestions to improve the response.")
```

An event-driven workflow relies on specific ‘events’ to trigger actions. Here, `AppleEvent` activates the Apple RAG agent, `InvestopediaEvent` activates the HyDE and Seek Investopedia agent, and `CompileEvent` consolidates responses.

Since we’re working with multiple agents, we need an effective routing system. We use a Pydantic `BaseModel` for handling routing between agents, as introduced in my [LlamaIndex introduction article.](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multiverse-part-3-llamaindex-798344050c49)

#### Defining our first workflow!

```python
class StockSME(Workflow):
    def __init__(self, manager_llm = llm, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.llm = llm
        
        ## Initialize the "manager"
        self.manager_llm = SimpleChatEngine.from_defaults(llm=manager_llm)
        
        self.choices = [
            ToolMetadata(
                name = "Apple_Agent",
                description = """Choose this option to answer any questions related to Apple's financial performance in 2021
                including risks, opportunities, and financial statements."""
            ),
            ToolMetadata(
                name = "Definitions_Agent",
                description = "Choose this option to answer any questions related to investment definitions such as Ichimoku Cloud"
            )
        ] 
        self.router = LLMSingleSelector.from_defaults(llm=self.llm)
        self.reroute_prompt_template = PromptTemplate(
            """Given the query: {query} and the interim answer: {response}, determine if the interim answer satisfies the question.
            This does not need to be very strict. As long as the interim answer is able to address the question partially, return True."""
        )
        
        ## Initialize apple agent
        self.apple_agent = apple_agent
        
        ## Initialize DSPy definition service
        self.definition_service = HydeRAG() #Defined in HyDE and Seek article
        self.definition_service.load("../compiled.json")
    
    @step
    async def route(self, ctx: Context, ev: StartEvent) -> AppleEvent | InvestopediaEvent:
        ## This is the routing step!
        selector_result = await self.router.aselect(self.choices, query = ev.query)
        await ctx.set("routes", 0)
        for result in selector_result.selections:
            if result.index == 0:
                ctx.send_event(AppleEvent(query=ev.query))
            else:
                ctx.send_event(InvestopediaEvent(query=ev.query))
            routes = await ctx.get("routes")
            routes += 1
            await ctx.set("routes", routes)
        
    @step
    async def apple_event(self, ev: AppleEvent) -> CompileEvent:
        ## This is the step that we invoke the Apple agent
        response = await self.apple_agent.achat(ev.query, history=ev.history)
        return CompileEvent(query=ev.query, response = str(response), source = "apple_agent")

    @step
    async def investopedia_event(self, ev: InvestopediaEvent) -> CompileEvent:
        ## This is the step that we invoke the Investopedia definitions agent
        response = self.definition_service(ev.query)
        return CompileEvent(query=ev.query, response = str(response.answer), source = "investopedia_agent")
    
    @step
    async def compile(self, ctx: Context, ev: CompileEvent) -> StopEvent | AppleEvent | InvestopediaEvent:
        ## This step compiles the answers
        routes = await ctx.get("routes")
        ready = ctx.collect_events(ev, [CompileEvent] * routes)
        for i in range(len(ready)):
            reroute = await self.llm.astructured_predict(
                Reroute, self.reroute_prompt_template, query=ev.query, response = ev.response
            )
            if reroute.reroute is True:
                if ready[i].source == "apple_agent":
                    return AppleEvent(query = f"""Here's some feedback to better address the query. 
                                      Feedback: {reroute.improvements},
                                      Query: {ev.query}""")
                else:
                    return InvestopediaEvent(query = f"""Here's some feedback to better address the query. 
                                            Feedback: {reroute.improvements},
                                            Query: {ev.query}""")
        
        if routes == 2:
            response = await self.manager_llm.achat(
                f"""
                 A user has provided a query and 2 different strategies have been used
                to answer the query. The query was: {ev.query}

                Response 1 ({ready[0].source}): {ready[0].response}
                Response 2 ({ready[1].source}): {ready[1].response}

                Please compile the responses into a single coherent argument.
                """
            )
        else:
            response = ready[0].response
        return StopEvent(result=str(response))
```

In this workflow:

-   Each event-driven action is managed by an `@step`\-decorated asynchronous method, improving readability and maintaining a clear flow of events.
-   Feedback-based rerouting dynamically triggers agents as needed.
-   The `compile` step ensures that responses are coherently combined when both agents are engaged.
-   Notice that we use two different LLMs in this workflow — Gemini 1.5-flash and GPT-4o-mini. This flexibility allows us to tailor the model selection to balance speed-accuracy tradeoffs and address data privacy concerns by incorporating local LLMs when necessary

Here are a few key details to highlight:

-   **Workflow basics**: A `Workflow` in LlamaIndex is an asynchronous, type-checked class. Be sure to mark each `@step` method as `async` and include type hints for input and output variables.
-   **The** `**Context**` **variable**: Think of `Context` as a session-specific storage area, similar to class variables. You can store and retrieve values throughout the workflow without using direct class attributes, allowing for seamless data passing between steps, event transmission, and response gathering within the workflow.
-   **Workflow initiation and termination**: The workflow begins with a `StartEvent` and ends when a `StopEvent` is returned. Notably, any step—not just one specific step—can return a `StopEvent`, offering flexible entry and exit points.
-   **Steps and events**: Each step is a function that takes an event and returns another event. This design allows you to define each function according to your requirements, whether to invoke an LLM service or handle non-LLM-related steps. Steps can also trigger looping events, enhancing workflow adaptability.

Here’s what our workflow looks like:

Wait…when did we build a digraph? We didn’t! LlamaIndex built it for us. LlamaIndex’s event-driven workflow paradigm is based on declarative programming, so all we have to do is declare our events and steps consuming these events — LlamaIndex handles the rest. This immediately reduces the learning curve compared to lower-level frameworks like LangGraph, and increases the reliability of results by giving us more control than high-level frameworks like Autogen.

Let’s say you’re working on a project, and your colleagues have already deployed LangGraph and Autogen services. You’ve done your initial multi-agent system using LlamaIndex Workflows — **did we just waste our effort?** Not at all!

To illustrate the flexibility of workflows, let’s build a larger parent workflow that encapsulates our StockSME workflow, along with the LangGraph workflow and Autogen multi-agent system defined in previous articles.

### “Avengers Assemble!”

In this new workflow, we’ll walk through the parent flow step by step, explaining each component’s function.

**Defining Events:** The parent workflow begins by defining key events that facilitate query handling and response generation across different agents:

```python
class GuardEvent(Event):
    answer: str

class AppleInvestopediaEvent(Event):
    query: str

class AnalysisEvent(Event):
    query: str

class PlanningEvent(Event):
    query: str

class BadQueryEvent(Event):
    query: str

class SearchEvent(Event):
    query: str
    
class ResponseEvent(Event):
    query: str
    response: str
    source: str
```

**Defining the Parent Workflow:** Next, we define the `StockAssistant` workflow class, initializing the LLMs needed for managing different aspects of the workflow:

```python
from llama_index.llms.ollama import Ollama

guard_llm = Ollama("llama-guard3:latest")

class StockAssistant(Workflow):
    def __init__(
        self,
        manager_llm = llm,
        guard_llm = guard_llm,
        config_list = config_list,
        *args,
        **kwargs
    ):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.guard_llm = guard_llm
        self.manager_llm = manager_llm
        self.choices = [
            ToolMetadata(
                name = "Apple_and_Investopedia_Agent",
                description = """Choose this option to answer any questions related to Apple's financial performance in 2021
                including risks, opportunities, and financial statements; or questions relating to investment terminology definitions."""
            ),
            ToolMetadata(
                name = "Analysis_Agent",
                description = "Choose this option to write blogposts about the financial performance of any stock ticker."
            ),
            ToolMetadata(
                name="Search_Agent",
                description = "Choose this option to search the Internet."
            )
        ] 
        self.router = LLMSingleSelector.from_defaults(llm=self.manager_llm)
        self.reroute_prompt_template = PromptTemplate(
            """Given the query: {query} and the interim answer: {response}, determine if the interim answer satisfies the question.
            This does not need to be very strict. As long as the interim answer is able to address the question partially, return True."""
        )
        
        ## Langgraph setup - we take the deployed graph in our LangGraph article
        self.remote_graph = RemoteGraph(
            graph_name, 
            url=url, 
            client=client, 
            sync_client=sync_client
        )
        self.thread = sync_client.threads.create()
        self.config = {
            "configurable": {"thread_id": thread["thread_id"]}
        }
```

The `StockAssistant` workflow uses several LLMs—here, we demonstrate using **Gemini 1.5-flash** and **GPT-4o-mini**—to allow trade-offs between speed and accuracy while managing data privacy concerns by integrating **Llama Guard**, a local LLM on Ollama. Within the workflow, we also define a `router` and set up a `RemoteGraph` using LangGraph.

### Key Steps in the Workflow:

1.  **Gatekeeping Step:** This initial check prevents LLM agents from handling inappropriate queries.

```python
@step
async def gatekeep(self, ev: StartEvent) -> PlanningEvent | StopEvent:
    response = await self.guard_llm.acomplete(ev.query)
    if "unsafe" in str(response):
        return StopEvent("Your query is inappropriate and cannot be answered.")
    return PlanningEvent(query=ev.query)
```

2\. **Planning and Routing Step:** This step determines the best agent(s) to handle the query, based on relevance and query quality.

```python
    @step
    async def plan_and_route(
        self, ctx: Context, ev: PlanningEvent
     ) -> StopEvent | AppleInvestopediaEvent | AnalysisEvent | SearchEvent:
        evaluation = await self.manager_llm.acomplete(
            f"""
            Given a user query, determine if this is likely to yield good results.
            
            If it's good, return 'good', if it's bad, return 'bad'.
            Good queries use a lot of relevant keywords and are detailed. Bad queries are vague or ambiguous.

            Here is the query: {ev.query}
            """
        )
        
        if evaluation == "bad":
            final_response = await self.manager_llm.acomplete(
                f"""The user has asked a bad query. Seek for the user's clarification."""
            )
            return StopEvent(str(final_response))
        
        selector_result = await self.router.aselect(self.choices, query = ev.query)
        # print(selector_result)
        routes = 0
        await ctx.set("query", ev.query)
        for result in selector_result.selections:
            if result.index == 0:
                ctx.send_event(AppleInvestopediaEvent(query=ev.query))
            elif result.index == 1:
                ctx.send_event(AnalysisEvent(query=ev.query))
            else:
                ctx.send_event(SearchEvent(query=ev.query))
            routes += 1
        await ctx.set("routes", routes)
```

**3\. Handling Different Events:** Each event routes to a specific agent (e.g., `StockSME`, `LangGraph`, or `Autogen`).

```python
    @step
    async def apple_investopedia_event(
        self,
        ev: AppleInvestopediaEvent,
        apple_investopedia_workflow: StockSME
    ) -> ResponseEvent:
        ## This runs our LlamaIndex StockSME Workflow
        response = await apple_investopedia_workflow.run(query=ev.query)
        return ResponseEvent(query=ev.query, response=response, source = "apple_investopedia_agent")
    
    @step
    async def search_event(
        self,
        ev: SearchEvent
    ) -> ResponseEvent:
        ## This is our Langgraph step!
        result = await self.remote_graph.ainvoke(
            {
                "messages": [HumanMessage(content=ev.query)]
            },
            config = self.config
        )
        return ResponseEvent(
            query = ev.query,
            response = result['messages'][1]['content'],
            source = "search_agent"
        )
    
    @step 
    async def analysis_event(
        self,
        ev: AnalysisEvent,
    ) -> ResponseEvent:
        ## This is our Autogen step!
        with Cache.disk() as cache:
            chat_history = await user_proxy.a_initiate_chat(
                assistant,
                message=ev.query,
                cache=cache,
            )
        return ResponseEvent(
            query = ev.query,
            response = chat_history.chat_history[-1]['content'],
            source = "analysis_agent"
        )
```

**4\. Compile Responses:** This step combines responses from multiple agents if multiple routes were triggered.

```python
    @step
    async def compile(
        self,
        ctx: Context,
        ev: ResponseEvent
    ) -> GuardEvent:
        routes = await ctx.get("routes")
        ready = ctx.collect_events(ev, [ResponseEvent] * routes)
        for i in range(len(ready)):
            reroute = await self.manager_llm.astructured_predict(
                Reroute, self.reroute_prompt_template, query=ev.query, response = ev.response
            )
            if reroute.reroute is True:
                if ready[i].source == "apple_investopedia_agent":
                    return AppleInvestopediaEvent(query = f"""Here's some feedback to better address the query. 
                                      Feedback: {reroute.improvements},
                                      Query: {ev.query}""")
                elif ready[i].source == "analysis_agent":
                    return AnalysisEvent(query = f"""Here's some feedback to better address the query. 
                                            Feedback: {reroute.improvements},
                                            Query: {ev.query}""")
                else:
                    return SearchEvent(query = f"""Here's some feedback to better address the query. 
                                       Feedback: {reroute.improvements},
                                       Query: {ev.query}""")
        
        if routes == 2:
            response = await self.manager_llm.acomplete(
                f"""
                 A user has provided a query and 2 different strategies have been used
                to answer the query. The query was: {ev.query}

                Response 1 ({ready[0].source}): {ready[0].response}
                Response 2 ({ready[1].source}): {ready[1].response}

                Please compile the responses into a single coherent argument.
                """
            )
        elif routes == 3:
            response = await self.manager_llm.acomplete(
                f"""
                 A user has provided a query and 3 different strategies have been used
                to answer the query. The query was: {ev.query}

                Response 1 ({ready[0].source}): {ready[0].response}
                Response 2 ({ready[1].source}): {ready[1].response}
                Response 3 ({ready[2].source}): {ready[2].response}

                Please compile the responses into a single coherent argument.
                """
            )
        else:
            response = ready[0].response
        return GuardEvent(answer = str(response))
```

**5\. Final Safety Check:** Ensures that the compiled response is appropriate.

```python
   @step
    async def check_answer(self, ev: GuardEvent) -> StopEvent:
        response = await self.guard_llm.acomplete(ev.answer)
        if "unsafe" in response:
            return StopEvent("""The LLM has given an answer that is unsafe. 
                             We have logged this and reported this to the administrator. 
                             We apologize. Please ask another question.""")
        return StopEvent(str(ev.answer))
```

Here’s what our final workflow looks like:

As a side note, notice that LlamaIndex’s Workflow drawing utility only renders the top-level workflow; our nested `StockSME` workflow, triggered by the `AppleInvestopediaEvent`, is visualized as a single node. This prevents the image from becoming cluttered when multiple nested workflows are involved.

**Running the Workflow:**

```python
stock_assistant = StockAssistant(timeout=3600, verbose = True)
stock_assistant.add_workflows(apple_investopedia_workflow= StockSME(timeout=600))
result = await stock_assistant.run(query="What is the boiling point of water?")
```

```python-repl
The boiling point of water is typically 100 degrees Celsius (212 degrees 
Fahrenheit) at standard atmospheric pressure (1 atmosphere or 101.3 kPa). 
However, the boiling point can vary with changes in atmospheric pressure; for
example, at higher altitudes, where the pressure is lower, water boils at a 
lower temperature.
```

It works! The manager LLM successfully routed this question to our deployed LangGraph multi-agent system, which provided the answer. **The multi-agent system of multi-agent systems operates smoothly, even with LLM services constructed using different frameworks.**

### The end? Not quite

You might notice that this article is titled _“Part 3a”_, and there’s a reason for that!

To be fair, both LangGraph workflows and Autogen GroupChats can invoke LLM services from any framework, including LlamaIndex. However, the experience of doing this differs significantly.

LangGraph is a very low-level library, requiring developers to build entire workflows as digraphs in code. This design enhances reliability but comes with a steep learning curve, more code, and consequently, an increased chance of bugs — all of which can slow down development.

On the other end of the spectrum, Autogen employs a “society of agents” approach like CrewAI’s `Crew`, where agents autonomously interact and collaborate, guided by human input. While this setup allows for complex multi-agent interactions, it sacrifices some reliability due to the challenges of replicating GroupChat interaction patterns consistently. This limitation may explain why Autogen is now evolving toward an event-driven workflow approach and why CrewAI created its `Flow`abstraction to orchestrate between agents/crews like LlamaIndex. Through declarative programming, LlamaIndex achieves both the reliability of results and a lower barrier to entry for developers.

If you’ve followed my series of articles, you’ll notice that two elements are missing in this one:

-   **Human-in-the-loop**
-   **Deployment**

I’ve chosen to omit them here to avoid making the article too lengthy and to keep the focus on LlamaIndex’s developer experience, particularly its declarative programming and event-driven paradigm. Incorporating human-in-the-loop capabilities in Workflows is a lot of fun— _as is deployment!_

We continue the story in the next article!

body:
* * *

This article is the second instalment in our series on the LLM multi-agent multiverse. After exploring Langgraph and its impressive capabilities in the [previous article](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multi-agents-multiverse-part-1-langgraph-2ac56f1b5b3c), we now continue our journey with [Autogen](https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/0.2/docs/Getting-Started), a multi-agent orchestration library developed by Microsoft. Autogen stands out as a key player in a diverse and competitive ecosystem, which includes at least five major alternatives: Langgraph (which we’ve covered), LlamaIndex, CrewAI, Camel, and most recently, OpenAI’s Swarm. For developers entering the generative AI space, it’s an exciting time, with innovation rapidly expanding what’s possible with multi-agent frameworks. This series will cover four of these frameworks — Langgraph, Autogen (this article), LlamaIndex, and CrewAI — which I use frequently. We’ll see if I can teach myself the other 2 frameworks to cover them, too!

As before, all my codes are available in my [GitHub repo](https://github.com/tituslhy/literate-octo-tribble/tree/main).

### Introducing Autogen

The Autogen library was released in late 2023, a few months before Langgraph, making it one of the pioneering frameworks in multi-agent LLM systems. Autogen takes a markedly different approach from Langgraph. With an impressive 32k stars on GitHub — significantly more than Langgraph’s 6k stars — Autogen seems to have captured the community’s attention and preference with its higher-level design over Langgraph’s low-level approach. But is this popularity justified? We’ll revisit the strengths and trade-offs of these frameworks in this article’s conclusion.

As before, I will introduce this framework through a mini proof-of-concept project — a stock analyst!

### Building our stock analyst

We’re going to do this using 2 different approaches on Autogen to showcase Autogen’s amazing capability. Let’s get it to generate a stock performance report for Illumina — the company I work for.

### 1\. The Group Chat Way

One of the main features that attracted me to Autogen was its `GroupChat` abstraction because it reminded me of group chats on communication channels like Slack, Teams, WhatsApp, etc. The user experience of group chats in Autogen is the same, except here we are “collaborating” with LLM agents.

```python
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv, find_dotenv
import warnings
import agentops

from autogen import (
    AssistantAgent,
    GroupChat,
    GroupChatManager,
    UserProxyAgent,
)
from autogen.cache import Cache
from autogen.coding import LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor

from datetime import datetime

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
_ = load_dotenv(find_dotenv())
agentops.init(api_key=os.environ["AGENTOPS_API_KEY"])

## Initializing our LLM configuration and our task
config_list=[
    {"model": "gpt-4o-mini", "api_key": os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"]}
]
task = (
    f"""Today is {datetime.now().date()}. Write a blogpost about the 
    stock price performance of Illumina in the past month."""
)
```

In this block of code, we import libraries, set up traceability using AgentOps, and initialize our LLM configuration and task. Autogen prefers specifying LLMs as a configuration list that holds key-value pairs of different LLM models and API keys. This allows Autogen to seamlessly move to the next LLM in the list if we run into any issues such as rate limit errors. Let’s define our agents and the `GroupChat` .

_Sidebar: There is also a ‘multiverse’ of LLM traceability tools and frameworks. LangChain, for example, integrates best with LangSmith. Since Microsoft didn’t develop a traceability tool, we’ll use AgentOps, another robust framework that captures session replays and latency data for individual agents. Its free tier supports up to 1,000 traces, making it a great option for this project._

```python
# Define agents in the group chat
## This is us!
user_proxy = UserProxyAgent(
    name="Admin",
    system_message="A human admin. Give the task and send instructions to writer to refine the blog",
    code_execution_config=False
)

## The agents
planner = AssistantAgent(
    name="Planner",
    system_message="""You are a planner. Given a task, please determine what information is needed
    to complete the task. Do note that all the information will be retrieved using Python code, so 
    only give suggestions that can be retrieved by Python code.""",
    llm_config={"config_list": config_list, "cache_seed": None},
)

engineer = AssistantAgent(
    name="Engineer",
    llm_config={"config_list": config_list, "cache_seed": None},
    system_message="""You are a software engineer. You write python/bash to retrieve relevant 
    information. Wrap the code in a code block that specifies the script type. The user cannot
    modify your code so do not suggest incomplete code. Do not use a code block if it's not intended
    to be executed. Don't include multiple code blocks in one response. Do not ask others to copy
    and paste the result. Check the execution result returned by the executor. If the result
    indicates that there is an error, fix the error and output the code again. Suggest the full code
    instead of partial code or code changes. If the error can't be fixed or if the task is not 
    solved even after the code is successfully executed, analyze the problem, revisit your assumptions,
    collec additional info you need, and think of a different approach to try."""
)

writer = AssistantAgent(
    name="Writer",
    llm_config={"config_list": config_list, "cache_seed": None},
    system_message="""You are a writer. Please write blogs in markdown format (with relevant titles)
    and put them in pseudo ```md``` code blocks. You will write it for a task based on previous chat
    history. Don't write any code.""",
)

code_executor = UserProxyAgent(
    name="Executor",
    system_message="You are a code executor. Execute the code written by the engineer and report the result.",
    description="Executor should always be called after the engineer has written code to be executed.",
    human_input_mode="ALWAYS",
    code_execution_config={
        "last_n_messages": 3,
        "executor": LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor(work_dir="blogs")
    }
)

# Define group chat
groupchat = GroupChat(
    agents = [user_proxy, engineer, code_executor, writer, planner],
    messages=[],
    max_round=20,
    speaker_selection_method="auto"
)

# Define group chat manager
manager = GroupChatManager(
    groupchat=groupchat,
    llm_config={"config_list": config_list, "cache_seed": None}
)

# Ensure that the 'blogs' directory exists
if not os.path.exists("blogs"):
    os.makedirs("blogs")
```

Wait a minute, where are all the _nodes, edges, graph state, breakpoints, and checkpoint_ abstractions we saw in Langgraph? **They’re simply not needed here!**

An important concept of Autogen is the use of a **UserProxyAgent** — this is simply an agent that acts as the “customer” that the other agents are trying to serve. Notice that there are two `UserProxyAgent` classes in our group chat. The first serves as the "admin" to provide our instructions, while the second serves as a **code\_executor** with the **human\_input\_mode** set to "ALWAYS," meaning that the group chat will always request our feedback before proceeding.

Autogen allows us to enable `human_input_mode` for any agents—just be prepared to provide ongoing feedback. The `code_executor` agent also includes a `code_execution_config` parameter, where we can specify that it should use the last three messages as context. Additionally, it leverages Autogen's `**LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor**` abstraction to execute code and save the output in a folder called _blogs_.

For enhanced security, Autogen also offers the `**DockerCommandLineCodeExecutor**`, which runs code in a sandboxed Docker environment. Just ensure that the Docker engine is running in the background! Both of these command-line code executors offer far more reliability than LangChain’s `**PythonREPL**` tool that we saw in our previous article (which tends to be buggy).

Now that we’ve established the agents in our `GroupChat`, let’s break down their roles and the configuration settings we’ve chosen:

**Our group chat includes:**

-   **User Proxy**: Transmits our messages to the group.
-   **Planner**: Plans the execution strategy to address our requests.
-   **Engineer**: Writes Python/Bash scripts but does not execute them.
-   **Code Executor**: Executes the engineer’s scripts while incorporating our feedback.
-   **Writer**: Takes the results of the code execution and crafts a blog message.
-   **Group Manager**: Selects the next speaker (or agent) to follow up on the next task, including the user proxy (i.e., us).

To define our Autogen `GroupChat`, we only need to specify the agents in a list and set a few important arguments:

-   **max\_round**: This parameter ensures that the `GroupChat` automatically terminates once we've reached a specified limit, preventing excessive rounds that could be costly in terms of LLM usage.
-   **speaker\_selection\_method**: This crucial argument allows the `GroupChatManager` to determine who speaks next. If the agent `description` fields are well-written, setting this to "auto" gives the manager full control.

_Other speaker selection options include:_

_a)_ **_“random” (_**_Selects the next speaker at random)_

_b)_ **_“round\_robin” (_**_iterates through the agents in order, ensuring everyone has a turn to speak)._

_c)_ **_“manual”_**_: Requires user input to select the next speaker._

_d) Accepts a_ [_custom function_](https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/0.2/docs/topics/groupchat/customized_speaker_selection/) _for more tailored control over speaker selection._

-   **allowed\_or\_disallowed\_speaker\_transitions**: We didn’t set this parameter, but it allows for specifying which transitions are allowed or disallowed as a dictionary. This allows us to have a firmer control over conversation dynamics, ensuring that an agent will always/never consult another specific agent depending on our use case.

We selected “auto” for the `speaker_selection_method`, giving the `GroupChatManager` full control over the conversation's flow and termination. If your preference is for dynamic conversations then this setting is great, but if you prefer lower-level control, do consider using `manual` or a custom function.

To execute the group chat:

```python
## Cache LLM response
with Cache.disk(cache_seed=41) as cache:
    chat_history = user_proxy.initiate_chat(
        manager,
        message=task,
        cache=cache
    )
```

The output (truncated) of the execution is jaw-dropping — just look at the agents chatting with each other! Do take note that any `Admin` or `Executor` agent lines are from us — we contributed to the discussion in the group chat.

#### Breakdown of the Interaction

Once the group chat commences, the **Admin agent** approaches the `GroupChatManager` with the task. The `GroupChatManager` then consults the **Planner agent** to develop a plan to answer the user's question.

-   **Planner Output**: Returned to the `GroupChatManager`, which then routes it to the **Engineer agent** to write the necessary Python scripts.
-   **Engineer Action**: The Engineer crafts a script and hands it to the `GroupChatManager`, which routes it to the **Code Executor**. Because `human_input_mode` is set to "ALWAYS," the Code Executor seeks our feedback.
-   **User Input**: Initially requesting data for the past month, I corrected myself, asking for the past 12 months instead. This input was routed to the `GroupChatManager`, which decided to approach the **Engineer** again, recognizing that the previous plan was still valid.
-   **Engineer Revision**: The Engineer updates the script and submits it to the Code Executor. When I provided no input, I pressed “Enter,” triggering Autogen’s “AUTO REPLY,” allowing the Code Executor to execute the code written by the Engineer.
-   **Execution Result**: The results were passed to the `GroupChatManager`, which then selects the **Writer agent** to compile a report.
-   **Feedback Loop**: The Writer’s report is sent to the `GroupChatManager`, which routes it to me for feedback. I requested "Buy/sell/hold" recommendations, which were routed back to the `Writer` agent instead of going to the Planner, as the current information sufficed.
-   **Final Report**: The Writer revises the report to include the recommendations, presenting it for my approval. With no further feedback, I typed “exit,” concluding the conversation.

**_Note_**_: Typing ‘exit’ is the only way to terminate an Autogen conversation, aside from reaching the maximum rounds._

We finished a complex task in not many lines of code! And we spent less than USD 0.01 on this entire interaction according to AgentOps. Nice!

### 2\. The tool calling agent way

When the task is specific and doesn’t require complex multi-agent coordination, we can simplify the setup with a 2-agent tool-calling approach. We start by defining the agents:

```python
user_proxy = UserProxyAgent(
    name="Admin",
    system_message="A human admin. Give the task and send instructions to writer to refine the blog",
    is_termination_msg=lambda x: x.get("content", "") and x.get("content", "").rstrip().endswith("TERMINATE"),
    human_input_mode="NEVER",
    max_consecutive_auto_reply=10,
    code_execution_config=False
)

assistant = AssistantAgent(
    name="Assistant",
    system_message="""You are a helpful assistant. Only use the functions you are provided with. 
    Reply TERMINATE when the task is done""",
    llm_config={"config_list": config_list, "cache_seed": None}
)
```

Then we define the tool/s. Tools can be registered with agents in three main ways, shown below. For each tool, you’ll register it at least once with the agent responsible for suggesting calls and the agent executing them.

**The first way: double decorate tools**

```python
from typing import Annotated, Optional, Dict, Any
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
import yfinance as yf

@user_proxy.register_for_execution()
@assistant.register_for_llm(description="Gets stock data for ticker of interest")
async def get_stock_data(
    ticker: Annotated[str, "Ticker of interest"],
    end_date: Optional[str] = datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d"),
    start_date: Optional[str] = None
) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    end_date = datetime.strptime(end_date, "%Y-%m-%d")
    if start_date is None:
        start_date = end_date - timedelta(days=365)
    data = yf.download(ticker, start=start_date, end=end_date)
    # Calculate percentage change over the 12 months
    data['Percentage Change'] = ((data['Close'] - data['Close'].iloc[0]) / data['Close'].iloc[0]) * 100

    # Identify the highest and lowest stock prices during this period
    highest_price = data['Close'].max()
    lowest_price = data['Close'].min()

    # Calculate average trading volume
    average_volume = data['Volume'].mean()

    # Prepare results
    result = {
        'start_price': data['Close'].iloc[0],
        'end_price': data['Close'].iloc[-1],
        'percentage_change': data['Percentage Change'].iloc[-1],
        'highest_price': highest_price,
        'lowest_price': lowest_price,
        'average_volume': average_volume
    }
    return result
```

The second way: use the`register_for_llm` method to register this for the `Assistant` and `register_for_execution` to register this for the `UserProxy` .

```python
# Register the tool signature with the assistant agent.
assistant.register_for_llm(name="get_stock_data", description="...")(get_stock_data)

# Register the tool function with the user proxy agent.
user_proxy.register_for_execution(name="get_stock_data")(get_stock_data)
```

The third way: use the `register_function` function and define the caller and executor arguments.

```python
from autogen import register_function

# Register the stock analysis function to the two agents.
register_function(
    get_stock_data,
    caller=assistant,  # The assistant agent can suggest calls to the tool.
    executor=user_proxy,  # The user proxy agent can execute the tool.
    name="get_stock_data",  # By default, the function name is used as the tool name.
    description="...",  # A description of the tool.
)
```

I believe there’s room for optimization in the registration process, especially when managing multiple tools — double registration for each tool. Just imagine if we had many different tools! We’d be adding so many lines of code just to register them.

Once ready, we can initiate a conversation with the `Assistant`! We’ll get similar results to the `GroupChat` approach and save more on our execution costs — because we only have 2 agents.

```python
from autogen import Cache

with Cache.disk() as cache:
    chat_history = await user_proxy.a_initiate_chat(
        assistant,
        message="Write a blogpost about the stock price performance of Illumina for the past year.",
        cache=cache,
    )
```

### There is a 3rd way — Autogen Studio

While Langgraph Studio provides a UI, Autogen Studio goes a step further by enabling you to build multi-agent systems directly through the UI — requiring little to no code — and is compatible with all operating systems. Just type the following into your terminal to launch the Autogen Studio UI.

```bash
pip install autogenstudio
autogenstudio ui
```

The first thing we should do here is to create a new “model” — our GPT-4o-mini model with our API key.

Once the model is defined, we can specify for our agents to use it.

Notice here that Autogen Studio **does not support human-in-the-loop**. This automatically limits the complexity of the agents we can create with the Autogen Studio, so the second approach (tool-calling two-agent system) is preferred.

Let’s proceed to create our tool (as a Python function) under the “Skills” tab. The tool we created is the same as our previous `get_stock_data` function above.

In Autogen Studio, registering tools to an agent is simplified to a few clicks.

Once we’re done, Autogen Studio requires us to create a Workflow specifying the receiver (this is the agent “receiving” our query, i.e. the stock\_analyst) and initiator (the agent sending our query on our behalf, i.e. the user\_proxy) agents.

Autogen Studio also lets us test the workflow setup in its **Playground** sandbox area, which is useful for troubleshooting any issues.

Everything in the Playground session can be downloaded for later review. But an even better option is **exporting the workflow**.

Exporting creates a `workflow.json` file, which can be invoked or deployed directly as a RESTful API by using the command:

```bash
autogenstudio serve --workflow=workflow.json --port=5000
```

**Do note that deployment is only available on Autogen Studio and not the Python SDK.**

### Concluding Thoughts

One of the most enjoyable aspects of using Autogen was watching agents interact in a `**GroupChat**`. Not only did we observe how the LLM agents influenced each other, but we also had the ability to guide the conversation, as we demonstrated in our example. However, once a GroupChat is served as a RESTful API, the multi-agent dynamics are hidden, and it feels more like interacting with a single agent.

For use cases where you want to preserve that interactive, multi-agent experience, running the GroupChat alongside a frontend framework like **Streamlit** or **Chainlit** might be more suitable than turning it into a microservice. This approach keeps the multi-agent conversation alive and visible to the user.

As a practical example, I developed a more in-depth investment analysis system called **“The Margin Call,”** which enables agents to discuss financial metrics and provide real-time insights to users. **PS**: Autogen even allows **LlamaIndex** agents to be deployed directly in a GroupChat, which is exactly what I did here.

All things considered however, the Autogen framework is incomplete, unlike the LangChain-LangGraph-LangSmith-LangServe ecosystem. In production, it can also be risky to give the `manager_llm` of a group chat so much control, because you could get a huge variety of results. For example, after we gave it our feedback to include a buy/sell/hold recommendation in its report, the `manager_llm`could have simply routed it to the `Planner`agent again to re-plan the entire flow, or it could have directed it to the `Engineer`to write new code. This is where Langgraph excels — offering low-level control through the definition of edges, conditional edges and breakpoints to ensure more reliable outputs.

However, the story isn’t finished yet! Autogen is currently undergoing a [major rewrite](https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/0.2/docs/Migration-Guide/) towards an event-driven, workflow-oriented, multi-agent system abstraction. Coincidentally, this approach has already been adopted by **LlamaIndex** and **CrewAI**. **LlamaIndex** first pioneered this method to improve the developer experience in **LangGraph** (seriously, using **LlamaIndex** will not result in any hair loss, unlike **LangGraph**), while maintaining reliable results. Recently, **CrewAI** developed a similar **Flow** abstraction, and now it seems Autogen is following suit.

They say imitation is the sincerest form of flattery — though the question remains: did **LlamaIndex** perfect the approach, or did **CrewAI** take it to the next level? Stay tuned for more insights in the next article!

body:
* * *

#### A gentle introduction to the LLM Multi-Agents Multiverse

Just when it seemed the ‘Multiverse’ saga for LLM orchestration libraries ([LangChain](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multiverse-part-1-langchain-023a899d294e), [Haystack](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multiverse-part-2-haystack-c6af2548df04), [LlamaIndex](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multiverse-part-3-llamaindex-798344050c49)) had concluded, we take a deeper dive down the rabbit hole! With recent advancements in the LLM ecosystem, 2023 marked the year of RAG, while 2024 is shaping up to be the year of agents — not just single agents, but entire agent orchestras. Our previous series focused on the three core orchestration libraries that led the LLM orchestration field, exploring how to use these libraries to orchestrate single LLM and single-agent operations.

Now, the world of multi-agent LLM systems is an entirely different league, with at least six prominent multi-agent libraries. They are Langgraph, LlamaIndex, Autogen, CrewAI, Camel and most recently Swarm by OpenAI. Instead of the ‘simpler plot’ of three Spider-Men in _Spider-Man: No Way Home_, this time it’s more like the ‘incursion’ event in _Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness,_ with Avengers from different realms colliding. It is the golden age of generative AI. In this series, we’ll dive into at least four of the most popular frameworks starting with Langgraph, along with the main players of the ecosystem, namely crewAI, LlamaIndex, and Autogen (I’ve used all 4 frameworks for app developments — we’ll see if I can teach myself the last two!).

As before, all codes can be found in my [GitHub repo](https://github.com/tituslhy/literate-octo-tribble/).

### Introducing Langgraph

Langgraph was released in January 2024 (“this year” at the time of writing) by the creators of LangChain, aiming to empower developers to [build stateful, reliable multi-agent applications](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/) extending the capabilities of the LangChain framework. To my knowledge, Langgraph’s developers were the first to conceptualize multi-agent systems as workflows, envisioning that these workflows are best structured as directed graphs (“digraphs”). This approach represented a paradigm shift, much like how LangChain initially redefined LLM orchestration with chains. Just as the ecosystem of LLM orchestration libraries often takes LangChain as a reference point, the multi-agent systems landscape frequently looks to Langgraph, building their frameworks on similar core principles.

Langgraph is an even lower-level framework than LangChain, offering developers even more control. It’s also worth noting that Langgraph’s first-mover advantage doesn’t necessarily translate to popularity. The Langgraph GitHub repository currently boasts 6.4k stars, which is a considerable difference compared to LangChain’s impressive 93k stars. Don’t let Langgraph’s “low” number of GitHub stars fool you though, it is one of the most in-demand libraries with many job applications seeking data scientists with Langgraph expertise. It is my opinion that this is the consequence of the LangChain framework’s prevalence in the industry — since Langgraph is an extension of LangChain, it automatically is high in demand.

Does this mean that Langgraph is the best in the multi-agent ecosystem? I’ll tackle that question once we’ve reviewed all its competitors.

### Building a personal assistant

I believe in introducing frameworks with proof-of-concept projects so let’s do something really cool with Langgraph and build a personal assistant. Our multi-agent system will comprise a manager LLM, a web search agent and a coder agent — yep this app will search the web for us and even write code, seriously what more can we ask for?

_Full disclosure: This example is a simplified adaptation of_ [_Langgraph’s original cookbook recipe_](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/tutorials/multi_agent/agent_supervisor/) _— chosen deliberately to introduce the core principles of Langgraph — to include human-in-the-loop and memory. In practice, I’ve also used Langgraph for more complex applications, like_ [_stock analysis_](https://github.com/tituslhy/TheMarginCall/blob/main/experiments/langgraph.ipynb)_._

```python
!pip install -U langchain langchain-community langchain-experimental tavily-python

import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv, find_dotenv
_ = load_dotenv(find_dotenv())

from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langchain_community.tools.tavily_search import TavilySearchResults
from langchain_experimental.tools import PythonREPLTool
from typing import Annotated, Literal

## Set tracing on LangSmith (entirely optional)
os.environ["LANGCHAIN_TRACING_V2"]="true"
os.environ["LANGCHAIN_ENDPOINT"]="https://api.smith.langchain.com"
os.environ["LANGCHAIN_API_KEY"]=os.environ["LANGSMITH_API_KEY"]
os.environ["LANGCHAIN_PROJECT"]="pr-virtual-piglet-90"

llm = ChatOpenAI(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    temperature=0
)

## The tools, a search tool and a code tool
tavily_tool = TavilySearchResults(max_results=5)
python_repl_tool = PythonREPLTool()
```

We start by importing all the necessary libraries and instantiating our LLM and tools. Multi-agent systems tend to be more costly and are more likely to hit the rate limits of free-tier LLM service providers compared to single-agent systems. For this project, I’m using OpenAI’s affordable ‘gpt-4o-mini’ model as my LLM — it’s sufficient for our current use case. We set Langchain tracing to be “true” so that we can view our traces on [LangSmith](https://docs.smith.langchain.com/observability/how_to_guides/tracing/trace_with_langchain), LangChain’s proprietary LLM tracing software.

The paradigm shift promised by Langgraph revolves around digraphs, which consist of nodes and edges. Each agent represents a node that we must define. Let’s get started!

```python
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage

def agent_node(state, agent, name):
    result = agent.invoke(state)
    return {
        "messages": [HumanMessage(content=result["messages"][-1].content, name=name)]
    }
```

In Langgraph, nodes are defined as functions, so our agent node is essentially a Python function that takes in a state, an agent, and the name of the agent. This flexible approach allows us to define as many agent nodes as we want — just remember to pass in different parameter values! Additionally, this means we can invoke another Langgraph app through this function, perform non-Langgraph operations like invoking a LlamaIndex RAG tool, or execute non-LLM operations such as querying a database.

Defining an agent node is sufficient for some use cases, but our multi-agent system requires a supervisor. The supervisor’s main job is to route to the next agent or finish and return the final answer. Therefore, we’ll need to define the supervisor node differently.

```python
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate, MessagesPlaceholder
from pydantic import BaseModel

members = ["Researcher", "Coder"]
system_prompt = (
    "You are a supervisor tasked with managing a conversation between the"
    " following workers:  {members}. Given the following user request,"
    " respond with the worker to act next. Each worker will perform a"
    " task and respond with their results and status. When finished,"
    " respond with FINISH. Only route coding requests to the Coder."
    " All non-coding requests are to be routed to the Researcher."
)
options = ["FINISH"] + members

class routeResponse(BaseModel):
    next: Literal[*options]

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages(
    [
        ("system", system_prompt),
        MessagesPlaceholder(variable_name="messages"),
        (
            "system",
            "Given the conversation above, who should act next?"
            " Or should we FINISH? Select one of: {options}",
        ),
    ]
).partial(options=str(options), members=", ".join(members))

def supervisor_agent(state):
    """This is the supervisor node
    
    It just picks the next agent to process and decides when the work is completed"""
    supervisor_chain = prompt | llm.with_structured_output(routeResponse)
    return supervisor_chain.invoke(state)
```

You might recognize the use of Pydantic’s BaseModel here — we covered the use of Pydantic for routing in the [LangChain article.](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multiverse-part-1-langchain-023a899d294e) But there are many new things we need to talk about.

1.  First, this is the first time that we’ve outrightly named our agents (under the `members` list). We need to be careful to stick strictly to the names in this list or your graph will throw an error.
2.  I’ve edited the `system_prompt` from the Langgraph cookbook, which is a generic system prompt. I’ll explain why later.
3.  The use of `.partial` is pure genius — Langgraph wrote their own definition of the `.partial` implementation of the `functools` library. This allows us to partially fill the placeholders (or fill all of them) of the `ChatPromptTemplate` object.
4.  The supervisor agent is a LangChain `chain` object! How cool is that! The reason it only takes in `state` as an argument is because it is a chain (therefore not an agent), and it does the routing (so it technically does not need a name).

#### By the way, what is ‘state’?

In Langgraph, `state` refers to the workflow or graph's overall state. Think of it as a global variable within the graph, used to determine the next course of action and to store intermediate results and chat history. It’s typically structured as a key-value pair, and here’s how it’s defined in Langgraph:

```python
import functools
import operator
from typing import Sequence
from typing_extensions import TypedDict

from langchain_core.messages import BaseMessage

class AgentState(TypedDict):
    messages: Annotated[Sequence[BaseMessage], operator.add]
    next: str
```

The `AgentState` class serves as our global state, inheriting from `TypedDict`, which lets us define as many key-value pairs as we need for storing intermediate results. In this example, we only need two keys: `messages`, which stores the conversation history (including intermediate outputs), and `next`, which helps the graph decide the next action—either to route to another agent or finish.

In the `AgentState` class, the line `messages:Annotated[Sequence[BaseMessage], operator.add]` is used to set up a key that will hold a growing list of messages. But let’s break it down into simpler terms:

1.  `**Sequence[BaseMessage]**` means that `messages` will store a list of message objects, specifically LangChain’s `BaseMessage` type.
2.  `**Annotated[ ... , operator.add]**` adds a bit more instruction: it tells Langgraph to treat the list of messages like a “growing list.” The `operator.add` part means “keep adding each new message to the end of the list,” ensuring that the list keeps a history of all the messages as the workflow continues.

In short, this setup tells Langgraph: “Keep a growing list of messages here, and keep adding each new message as it comes in.” This approach is commonly used in Langgraph workflows to keep track of ongoing conversations. Since this is only used on `messages` and not `next` , the value of `next` will always be overwritten.

Phew! That’s a lot to take in, but it’s essential for understanding how Langgraph handles state.

#### Let’s start constructing the graph

As hard as it is to believe, we’ve actually not started on our Workflow yet!

```python
# Create agents
from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent

## Researcher agent
research_agent = create_react_agent(llm, tools=[tavily_tool])
research_node = functools.partial(
    agent_node,
    agent=research_agent,
    name="Researcher" #must match the name in the 'members' list above
)
## Coder agent
code_agent = create_react_agent(llm, tools=[python_repl_tool])
code_node = functools.partial(agent_node, agent=code_agent, name="Coder")
```

```python
from langgraph.graph import END, StateGraph, START
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver

workflow = StateGraph(AgentState)

## Add nodes
workflow.add_node("Researcher", research_node)
workflow.add_node("Coder", code_node)
workflow.add_node("supervisor", supervisor_agent)

## Add edges
### We want our workers to always report back to our supervisor when done
for member in members:
    workflow.add_edge(member, "supervisor")

### The supervisor then fills in the 'next' field in the graph state for routing
conditional_map = {k:k for k in members}
conditional_map['FINISH'] = END
workflow.add_conditional_edges(
    "supervisor", lambda x: x['next'],
    conditional_map
)

### Connect entrypoint to supervisor
workflow.add_edge(START, "supervisor")

## Add memory - this creates chat history of the graph in an in-memory SQLite database
memory = MemorySaver()

## Compile
### We interrupt before the code execution just to ensure that we're not doing anything cray
graph = workflow.compile(
    interrupt_before=["Coder"], 
    checkpointer=memory
)
```

We first start by creating our agent nodes (recall that we’ve already created our supervisor node), adding these nodes to the graph using the `.add_node()` method, and then linking nodes by adding edges to the graph.

There are two types of edges here:

**Firm Edges** — These edges connect nodes regardless of state. We use firm edges for:

-   The start node to the supervisor node (the entry point of the workflow)
-   Every agent node to the supervisor node so that each agent’s results are sent to the supervisor to determine the next best course of action by updating the `next` field in the `state`.

**Conditional Edges** — These edges are used only when certain conditions are met. For our setup, the supervisor has conditional edges:

-   To route back to either the researcher or coder agent nodes, based on what’s in the `next` field.
-   To route to the “finish” node if the results are deemed sufficient to conclude execution.
-   You can either use a python function, or a lambda function like we do in this case.

Next, we incorporate shared memory across the entire graph using an in-memory SQLite database. This allows us to store conversation history for easy access throughout the workflow.

After defining our graph setup, we compile it and introduce “human-in-the-loop” functionality by adding breakpoints. The `interrupt_before=["Coder"]` line, for example, pauses the graph before executing the coder agent. This lets us double-check the workflow or prompt for feedback, such as “Are you sure?” or “Can you review the current plan?” before proceeding.

**We’re done constructing the multi-agent system!** It was quite a journey, and as you might have realized, it’s easy to make mistakes as your multi-agent system grows in complexity. For instance, if one of your nodes invokes another Langgraph object, you’ll need to define a second state for the nested Langgraph and create a mapping function to sync the main graph’s state with the subgraph’s state. You might also notice that the code can become extensive and isn’t always intuitive. But, as with most things, practice makes perfect! LangChain has a supportive community that is incredibly helpful, which is why both LangChain and Langgraph maintain a relatively low number of open GitHub issues despite their steep learning curve. Here’s what our final graph looks like

### Invoking the graph

Now, how do we actually make the graph ‘do’ something? Unlike LangChain which only uses the `.invoke()` method, in Langgraph the common way to do this is using a for-loop. Since our graph has the memory feature, we’ll need to pass in a dictionary with a `thread_id`to our invocation.

#### Let’s do some research into the value of generative AI

```python
for event in graph.stream(
    {
        "messages": [
            HumanMessage(content="Is generative AI just a gimmick? Does it have any quantifiable business value?")
        ]
    },
    {"configurable": {"thread_id": "1"}, 
      "recursion_limit": 5
    },
    stream_mode = "values"
):
    event['messages'][-1].pretty_print()
```

```python
================================ Human Message =================================

Is generative AI just a gimmick? Does it have any quantifiable business value?
================================ Human Message =================================
Name: Researcher

Generative AI is not merely a gimmick; it has demonstrable business value across various sectors. Here are some key insights:

1. **Business Value**: According to Gartner, organizations that are early adopters of generative AI are leveraging it to enhance their competitive edge. They are focusing on use cases that improve existing processes, differentiate their offerings, and even transform their business models. Generative AI is seen as a tool to increase revenue, reduce costs, improve productivity, and manage risks effectively. For instance, it can automate tasks, generate content, and provide insights that were previously time-consuming to obtain.

2. **Applications Across Industries**: Generative AI has applications in numerous fields, including customer support, marketing, finance, healthcare, and product design. It can create original content, such as text, images, and even software code, which can streamline operations and enhance customer experiences. For example, it can be used to generate medical images, synthesize data to mitigate bias, and improve chatbot performance.

3. **Quantifiable Impact**: Research from McKinsey indicates that generative AI could significantly impact various business functions, particularly those with high operational costs. The technology is expected to drive productivity improvements and cost savings, making it a valuable investment for businesses.

4. **Concerns and Challenges**: Despite its potential, there are concerns regarding privacy and the ethical use of data, which may hinder some organizations from fully embracing generative AI. Additionally, the technology's ability to produce errors or "hallucinations" can pose risks if not managed properly.

5. **Future Potential**: The economic potential of generative AI is substantial, with estimates suggesting it could contribute between $10 and $15 trillion to the global economy by 2030. This highlights its transformative potential across various sectors.

In summary, generative AI is far from being just a gimmick; it offers quantifiable business value and has the potential to reshape industries by enhancing efficiency, creativity, and decision-making processes.
```

In this example, the `thread_id` is `"1"`, allowing us to track the session if we want to review it later. Additionally, setting a `recursion_limit` of 5 prevents the graph from looping indefinitely—an important cost-saving measure! Bear in mind that if we invoke the graph with a different thread\_id value in the future, the messages will not be stored within the same memory!

#### Let’s make our assistant write code!

```python
for event in graph.stream(
    {
        "messages": [
            HumanMessage(
                content= "Write python code to calculate the remainder of 15/2"
            )
        ]
    },
    {"configurable": {"thread_id": "1"}, 
      "recursion_limit": 5
    },
    stream_mode='values'
):
    event['messages'][-1].pretty_print()
```

```python-repl
================================ Human Message =================================

Write python code to calculate the remainder of 15/2
```

But wait — the graph just terminated its execution right before the “Coder” node, as expected, thanks to the breakpoint we set. So, now what? This is where our `thread_id` comes in handy.

Using the thread ID, we can retrieve the current graph state:

```python
thread = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "1"}, "recursion_limit": 5}
state = graph.get_state(thread)
state.values['messages'][-1] #show last message
```

```python-repl
HumanMessage(content='Write python code to calculate the remainder of 15/2', additional_kwargs={}, response_metadata={})
```

Now, let’s edit this message to give the assistant new instructions and check that the state has been updated:

```python
graph.update_state(
    thread,
    {
        "messages": [HumanMessage(
            content="No, actually write python code to print 'hello world!'"
        )]
    }
)
```

To continue execution from where the graph left off, we pass in `None` as input:

```python
for s in graph.stream(None, thread):
    if "__end__" not in s:
        print(s)
        print("----")
```

```python-repl
{'Coder': {'messages': [HumanMessage(content='The output of the code is: `hello world!`', additional_kwargs={}, response_metadata={}, name='Coder')]}}
----
{'supervisor': {'next': 'FINISH'}}
----
```

With our revised message, the Coder node has successfully completed the task.

_Note: LangChain’s Python REPL library is experimental and very buggy. I was unable to get it to write a function to calculate the volume of a sphere or even compute the remainder of 13/3. Had to pick the easiest example to make it work._

You might be wondering — prototyping and debugging Langgraph objects can sometimes be tricky. Earlier, I modified the `system_prompt` from Langgraph’s cookbook recipe. Before this edit, I noticed that my supervisor node often routed research queries to the researcher node and then to the coder, rather than simply finishing. Since it routed unnecessarily to the coder, the entire thread was interrupted, which was baffling.

Thankfully, LangChain offers a tool to simplify this debugging process, sparing us from manually managing for-loops each time. Langgraph Studio, currently in beta is available only for Mac users. Follow the setup instructions [here](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph-studio).

Once loaded, you can use the user interface to simulate how your Langgraph object responds to prompts, adjust interrupt points, and modify any aspect of your Langgraph object — all through an intuitive user interface, without writing additional code.

### Deployment

_Full disclosure: This section was completely re-written. LangChain released the Langgraph Platform (previously known as Langgraph Cloud) with a free, self-hosted option on the same day this article was published. I’ve since tested it, and I’ll now share the results._

LangChain’s recommended deployment method is now the Langgraph Platform, which includes a free tier! However, note that the free-tier deployments are all self-hosted (i.e., run on your machine rather than in the Cloud) and support up to one million node executions. Here’s how to set it up:

1.  **Install Langgraph CLI**: First, activate your `venv` or `conda` environment, then run: `pip install langgraph-cli` . Also make sure your Docker is up and running
2.  **Build the Docker Image**: Navigate to the same folder from which you launched Langgraph Studio, then run:

```bash
langgraph build -t personal-assistant #this is the name of the image
```

This command uses Docker in the backend to build an image of your application, giving it the specified name.

3\. **Set Environment Variables & Start Deployment**: Export your environment variables and use Docker to start the deployment:

```bash
export LANGSMITH_API_KEY=... #Add your API key here
export IMAGE_NAME=personal-assistant
docker compose up
```

LangChain provides a helpful `docker-compose.yml` template to get you started, complete with a PostgreSQL database and Redis message queuing. This setup enables real-time streaming outputs for background runs, making deployments smooth and efficient.

#### Let’s invoke our deployment!

```python
from langgraph.pregel.remote import RemoteGraph
from langgraph_sdk import get_client, get_sync_client

url = "http://0.0.0.0:8123"
graph_name="agents"
client=get_client(url=url)
sync_client = get_sync_client(url=url)
remote_graph = RemoteGraph(
    graph_name, 
    url=url, 
    client=client, 
    sync_client=sync_client
)

thread = sync_client.threads.create()
config = {
    "configurable": {"thread_id": thread["thread_id"]}
}

async for chunk in remote_graph.astream(
    {
        "messages": [
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": "What is the boiling point of water?"
            }
        ]
    },
    config = config
):
    print(chunk)
```

```python-repl
...
StreamPart(
     event='values', 
     data={'messages': [{'role': 'user', 'content': 'What is the boiling point of water?'}, 
      {'content': 'The boiling point of water is 100 degrees Celsius 
                  (212 degrees Fahrenheit) at standard atmospheric pressure 
                  (1 atmosphere or 101.3 kPa). However, the boiling point can 
                   vary with changes in atmospheric pressure; at higher 
                    altitudes, for example, the boiling point decreases.', 
        'additional_kwargs': {}, 
        'response_metadata': {}, 
        'type': 'human', 
        'name': 'Researcher', 
        'id': None, 'example': False}], 
    'next': 'FINISH'})
```

To invoke our deployment, we first set up the `RemoteGraph` by providing the URL of our deployment and the corresponding `client` and `sync_client` objects. Then, we create a thread and run it as we did previously, without any additional changes. How cool is that?

### Concluding Thoughts

Langgraph is a low-level, flexible abstraction suited for building everything from complex RAG applications to sophisticated multi-agent systems. Its design offers developers more control than the LangChain framework, while also extending LangChain’s capabilities. However, Langgraph’s steep learning curve means developers should be prepared to write more code and spend additional time debugging Langgraph objects, especially with intricate multi-agent systems. Hopefully, once Langgraph Studio becomes widely accessible, this process will become much smoother.

I must commend the LangChain team for their efforts in creating an [in-depth course](https://academy.langchain.com/courses/intro-to-langgraph) on Langgraph that covers the basics and more — far beyond the scope of this gentle introduction. I highly recommend this course to anyone interested in multi-agent LLM systems, even if you’re not planning to use Langgraph in production. It provides a solid foundation on the core principles and considerations of multi-agent architectures.

Furthermore, LangChain is known for its rapid development velocity, with new features added regularly. The recent launch of the Langgraph Platform (on the same day this article was written!) exemplifies this trend, allowing for robust and easy deployment of Langgraph objects. Invoking these features is straightforward as well!

LangChain continues to lead in the LLM ecosystem, offering concrete and comprehensive solutions — albeit with a steeper learning curve. I look forward to exploring more about their innovations in future writings!
