body:
* * *

#### With just 5 lines to build a fully functioning RAG

The rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) has introduced a new challenge: efficiently orchestrating complex interactions while ensuring scalability. This is where LLM orchestration libraries come into play. In this article, we conclude our trilogy on these essential tools by introducing LlamaIndex — a strong contender to the LangChain and Haystack orchestration libraries.

In the previous articles, we explored the capabilities of [LangChain (Part 1)](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multiverse-part-1-langchain-023a899d294e) and [Haystack (Part 2)](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multiverse-part-2-haystack-c6af2548df04), highlighting how both can be used to build impressive applications. Now, we’ll dive into LlamaIndex, uncovering its unique strengths and showing how it excels at similar tasks. We conclude by comparing all three libraries, and I’ll share my opinion on which library stands out as “the best.”

This article will focus on using LlamaIndex on LLMs from chatting up to the single-agent abstraction. Multi-agent systems, a fascinating topic in its own right, will be covered in separate articles. As before, all codes can be found in my [GitHub repo](https://github.com/tituslhy/literate-octo-tribble/).

### Introducing LlamaIndex

LlamaIndex is the youngest of the LLM orchestration libraries when compared to Haystack and LangChain. To date, LlamaIndex’s GitHub repository has 36k stars which far exceeds Haystack but still trails very far behind LangChain.

Initially named “GPT Index,” its primary strength lies in improving data indexing and retrieval. LlamaIndex gained attention when retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) became a hot topic in LLM applications. Chatting with your knowledge base was certainly more exciting than manually reading every document!

[An experiment by tonicAI](https://www.tonic.ai/blog/rag-evaluation-series-validating-rag-performance-openai-vs-llamaindex) revealed that a basic RAG application using LlamaIndex significantly outperformed a RAG application using the OpenAI Assistant, even though both were working with the same data sources. The key difference between a good and bad RAG application often lies in the quality of data indexing and retrieval — after all, incorrect retrieval results in an incorrect response from the LLM.

It is my opinion that LlamaIndex was not initially intended to be a competitor to LangChain, but appeared to be positioning itself as an alternative to some of the libraries that LangChain orchestrated. As a result, LlamaIndex has always integrated well with the LangChain ecosystem, allowing seamless conversion between LangChain abstractions and LlamaIndex components. As an example, LlamaIndex has a `LangChainLLM` [component](https://docs.llamaindex.ai/en/stable/examples/llm/langchain/) that allows for any LangChainLLM to be used in LlamaIndex, and any data loader or query engine [can be used as a LangChain tool](https://docs.llamaindex.ai/en/v0.10.17/community/integrations/using_with_langchain.html).

The name change from [GPT Index to LlamaIndex](https://x.com/jerryjliu0/status/1650673187896844288) was primarily to avoid confusion with OpenAI’s GPT models. Later, LlamaIndex expanded its abstractions to orchestrate LLM ecosystem components — perhaps because of a difference in programming philosophy with LangChain or possibly because its team believes they can do it better. Is that the case? Let’s find out together by exploring how LlamaIndex enables exciting possibilities with LLMs!

### 1\. Importing an LLM and running it

Like LangChain and Haystack, LlamaIndex has LLM integrations with almost any LLM service provider you can think of — just `pip install`the integration package. However, unlike LangChain and Haystack, there are many ways to run an LLM in LlamaIndex — the most common are `chat` and `complete` . Here, we’re using the Mistral Large LLM and GeminiEmbedding models, both free of charge.

```python
!pip install -U llama-index llama-index-llms-mistralai llama-index-embeddings-gemini

import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv, find_dotenv
import nest_asyncio
import warnings
from IPython.display import display, Markdown
from llama_index.llms.mistralai import MistralAI
from llama_index.embeddings.gemini import GeminiEmbedding

_ = load_dotenv(find_dotenv())
nest_asyncio.apply()
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

llm = MistralAI(model="mistral-large-latest")
embed_model = GeminiEmbedding()

response = llm.complete("Why is the sky blue?")
display(Markdown(str(response)))
```

```python-repl
The sky appears blue due to a process called Rayleigh scattering. Here's a simple explanation:

Light from the Sun: The Sun emits light at all the visible wavelengths, which is why we see it as white. When this light reaches Earth's atmosphere, it interacts with the gas molecules and tiny particles in the air.

Rayleigh Scattering: Shorter wavelengths of light (like blue and violet) are scattered more by these molecules and particles because they travel in shorter, smaller waves. This is why we see a blue sky most of the time.

Why not violet?: Although violet light is scattered even more than blue light, the sky appears blue, not violet. This is because:

The Sun emits less violet light compared to blue light.
Human eyes are more sensitive to blue light than violet light.
Some violet light gets absorbed by the atmosphere, further tilting the balance towards blue.
So, the combination of these factors makes the sky appear blue to us on a clear day. During sunrise or sunset, the light has to pass through more of Earth's atmosphere, which scatters more of the blue and green light away, and we're left with the warmer colors of sunrise and sunset, like red, orange, and yellow.
```

The `complete` function is used when you want to pass in a string. To pass a list of chat messages, we use the `chat` function instead

```python
from llama_index.core.llms import ChatMessage

messages = [
    ChatMessage(role="system", content="You are a helpful assistant"),
    ChatMessage(role="user", content="Why is the sky blue?")
]

response = llm.chat(messages)
display(Markdown(str(response)))
```

LlamaIndex also has a `stream_complete` function which creates a Python [generator](https://wiki.python.org/moin/Generators). So you can use a `for` loop to display the response incrementally.

```python
response = llm.stream_complete(
    "Why is the sky blue?"
)
for r in response:
    print(r.delta, end="")
```

#### Chat History!

Unlike LangChain and Haystack, it takes just one line to include Chat History — no need to create a list of messages and pass the whole thing in again (though you can still do this)! Simply wrap the LLM under a `SimpleChatEngine` object.

```python
from llama_index.core.chat_engine import SimpleChatEngine

chat_engine = SimpleChatEngine.from_defaults(llm=llm)
```

### 2\. Structured Prediction

LLMs don’t always have to reply in plain text, they can also return structured responses. For example, let’s ask the LLM to generate a workout plan, similar to what we did in our Haystack and LangChain articles.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from llama_index.core.prompts import PromptTemplate
from typing import List

class Exercise(BaseModel):
    """Generates a workout plan given a focus area"""
    exercise: str
    number_of_reps: int
    number_of_sets: int

class WorkoutPlan(BaseModel):
    exercises: List[Exercise]

prompt_tmpl = PromptTemplate(
    """Generate a workout plan given that the user wants to focus on {focus_area}"""
)
```

There are 2 ways to achieve this! The first way is to chain commands on the LLM

```python
workout_plan = (
    llm.as_structured_llm(WorkoutPlan)
    .complete(prompt_tmpl.format(focus_area="biceps"))
    .raw
)
```

The second way is simpler and only requires one line using `structured_predict`!

```python
tricep_plan = llm.structured_predict(WorkoutPlan, prompt_tmpl, focus_area="triceps")
tricep_plan
```

```less
WorkoutPlan(
  exercises=[
      Exercise(exercise='Tricep Dips', number_of_reps=10, number_of_sets=3), 
      Exercise(exercise='Tricep Pushdowns', number_of_reps=12, number_of_sets=3),
      Exercise(exercise='Overhead Dumbbell Extension', number_of_reps=12, number_of_sets=3)
  ]
)
```

#### Why two approaches?

These two methods offer different levels of control. If you need more customization, the first method gives you the flexibility to chain commands. However, for simplicity and quick results, the second method works just as well with fewer lines of code.

This is a recurring theme in LlamaIndex: it’s designed with developer experience in mind, offering high-, mid-, and low-level abstractions to suit different levels of control. The barriers to entry with LlamaIndex are much lower compared to LangChain and Haystack. You can get the same results with LlamaIndex using one-liner commands like `structured_predict` or `SimpleChatEngine`, while other libraries may require far more code!

### 3\. Zero-Shot Classification (also known as routing in LLM land)

Gone are the days when you had to train NLP models from scratch or fine-tune BERT on training data that was painstakingly curated. Just throw everything to the LLM and it will categorize the data without needing specific period examples. There are two main ways to do this!

#### **3a. The Pydantic Way (Again):**

```python
from typing import Literal

class DocumentFolder(BaseModel):
    """Returns only one output folder name given a document name"""
    
    folder_name: Literal[
        "finance",
        "presentations",
        "sketchbook",
        "code"
    ]

prompt_tmpl2 = PromptTemplate(
    """Help the user sort their documents into folders. This is the document to be sorted: {document_name}"""
)

folder = llm.structured_predict(DocumentFolder, prompt_tmpl2, document_name="llama_sketch.pix")
```

This approach is similar to LangChain’s implementation. I recommend using this method if your class labels are clear and distinctive. However, be cautious in cases where folders have ambiguous names. For instance, distinguishing between “Llama Projects” and “Llama Experiments” might confuse the model, as the labels aren’t as easily differentiable. In such scenarios, manual review or more precise prompting might be needed to improve accuracy — or just use the second way.

#### **3b. Selections as Tools**

```python
from llama_index.core.tools import ToolMetadata
from llama_index.core.selectors import LLMSingleSelector

choices = [
    ToolMetadata(
        name = "presentations",
        description = "choose this option if the input document has a .pptx or .ppt extension"
    ),
    ToolMetadata(
        name = "python_code",
        description = "choose this option if the input document has a .py or .ipynb extension"
    )
] 

selector = LLMSingleSelector.from_defaults(llm=llm)
selector_result = selector.select(
    choices, query = "Where should I keep this folder: abc.py"
)
print(selector_result)
```

LLMs often use routing (i.e. zero-shot classification) for tool selection, so we can treat our class labels as tools by assigning them a name and description and wrapping them in a list. LlamaIndex offers a convenient `LLMSingleSelector` abstraction, which not only makes a selection but also provides a reason for its choice. **How cool is that!**

```python-repl
MultiSelection(
  selections=[
    SingleSelection(
        index=1, 
        reason='The input document has a .py extension.'
     )
  ]
)
```

Notice that the final output type is a `MultiSelection` class, so this abstraction also supports multi-classification out of the box.

### 4\. Tool Calling

Tired of LLM hallucinations? Write tools for your LLM to use! There are 2 ways of doing this in LlamaIndex. The first is by wrapping any function into a `FunctionTool` abstraction.

```python
from llama_index.core.tools import FunctionTool

def multiply(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Multiplies two integers and returns the resulting integer"""
    return a*b

def mystery(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Mystery function on two integers"""
    return a * b + a + b

# Wrap each function into a LlamaIndex FunctionTool
mystery_tool = FunctionTool.from_defaults(fn=mystery)
multiply_tool = FunctionTool.from_defaults(fn=multiply)
tools = [mystery_tool, multiply_tool]
```

The second way is to write a tool as a class object by inheriting from LlamaIndex’s `BaseToolSpec` abstraction.

```python
from llama_index.core.tools.tool_spec.base import BaseToolSpec

class ArithmeticTools(BaseToolSpec):
    spec_functions = [
        "add",
        "divide",
        "minus"
    ]
    
    def __init__(self):
        """Initialize the tool. You don't actually have to define anything 
        under the class constructor method!"""
    
    def add(self, a: int, b: int) -> int:
        """Use this tool to add two integers together"""
        return a + b
    
    def minus(self, a: int, b: int) -> int:
        """Use this tool to return the difference between two integers"""
        return a - b
    
    def divide(self, a: int, b: int) -> int:
        """Use this tool to perform integer division between two integers"""
        return a //b

    def mystery(a: int, b: int) -> int:
      """Mystery function on two integers"""
      return a * b + a + b

ar_tools = ArithmeticTools()
tools = ar_tools.to_tool_list()
```

Wait, aren’t they the same? Not quite! Classes allow you to define tools more “pythonically” by letting tools share common utility functions, class attributes, and methods. This provides greater flexibility in developing your tools, making them more complex and reusable. However, you do need to list the class methods you want to turn into tools as strings in the `spec_functions` list. Instead of wrapping each method individually as a `FunctionTool`, simply instantiate the class and use the `to_tool_list()` method to get all your tools in a single list.

To call your tools, just use the `predict_and_call` method on the LLM.

```makefile
response = llm.predict_and_call(
    tools = tools,
    user_msg="What happens when I run the mystery function on 5 and 7"
)

display(Markdown(str(response)))
```

```python-repl
47
```

### 5\. RAG

We finally got here. This is where LlamaIndex blows its competitors out of the water — it takes just 5 lines to build a fully functioning, high-performance, basic RAG application. Ready? Here we go:

```python
## Get data
!mkdir -p '../../data/paul_graham/'
!wget 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/run-llama/llama_index/main/docs/docs/examples/data/paul_graham/paul_graham_essay.txt' -O '../../data/paul_graham/paul_graham_essay.txt'

## Import libraries
from llama_index.core import (
    SimpleDirectoryReader,
    StorageContext,
    load_index_from_storage,
    VectorStoreIndex
)

## The RAG application - in 5 lines
### a. Read document source
documents = SimpleDirectoryReader(input_dir = "../data/paul_graham").load_data()
### b. Create embeddings and stuff them into a vector index
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(documents)
### c. Create query engine
query_engine = index.as_query_engine(llm=llm)
### d. Ask a question!
response = query_engine.query("Hi! My name is Titus. What happened at Interleaf and Viaweb?")
display(str(response))
```

```python-repl
"Hello Titus! Interleaf was a company that, despite having smart people and 
impressive technology, was eventually overtaken by the rapid advancements 
in commodity processors, as described by Moore's Law. On the other hand, 
Viaweb, which was an online store builder, faced challenges in its early 
stages due to the lack of users, which was evident because they were hosting 
the stores. To address this, they had to recruit an initial set of users and 
ensure their stores looked decent before they could launch publicly."
```

How cool is that!

**But is there a tradeoff?** Not really — this is how you would build a **basic** RAG application. LlamaIndex also offers many has [many advanced RAG abstractions](https://www.llamaindex.ai/blog/a-cheat-sheet-and-some-recipes-for-building-advanced-rag-803a9d94c41b) that can be easily orchestrated. To answer how it can be _this_ easy, it’s because LlamaIndex provides a mix of low, medium, and high-level abstractions. Customize the app if you need to; otherwise, ship it — reliable apps with just a few lines of code.

**But wait…** what vector database did we use? What LLM? What embedding model? By default, LlamaIndex uses OpenAI’s `gpt-4o-mini` and the `ada` embeddings model. So, if you don’t have an OpenAI key in a `.env` file, this code will error. LlamaIndex even includes its own `SimpleVectorStore` abstraction, which is the default vector database if none is specified. It's amazing how much care they’ve put into optimizing the developer's user experience.

To add chat history, just define your index as a chat engine:

```python
chat_engine = index.as_chat_engine()
response = chat_engine.chat("your query here")
```

To convert your query engine into a tool for an LLM agent, use LlamaIndex’s `QueryEngineTool` :

```python
from llama_index.core.tools import QueryEngineTool

query_engine_tool = QueryEngineTool(
    query_engine = query_engine,
    metadata = ToolMetadata(
        description="Use this tool to answer questions related to Paul Graham",
        name="Paul_Graham_Tool" #remember to use underscores here instead of spaces
    )
)

tools.append(query_engine_tool)
```

Now our LLM can answer arithmetic questions and questions on Paul Graham. How simple was that?

### 6\. Finally here’s how you build an agent

As you can imagine, it’s once again very easy to do this in LlamaIndex:

```python
from llama_index.core.agent.react import ReActAgent

agent = ReActAgent.from_tools(
    tools = tools,
    llm = llm,
    verbose = True #To print steps
)

response = agent.chat("What is the mystery function's output on 57 and 26")
display(Markdown(str(response)))
```

```python-repl
The mystery function's output on 57 and 26 is 1565.
```

Each agent comes built with a chat history so there’s no need to do any further customization — just use it out of the box with just a few lines.

### 7\. Comparing LlamaIndex, Haystack and LangChain

We’ve used LlamaIndex, Haystack and LangChain to do pretty cool things — the same tasks. These libraries are perfect competitors of each other, each having rich integrations. The differences between these libraries however go beyond “stylistic differences”.

#### Where Haystack stands out

Jinja2 prompting. No other LLM orchestration library supports this. The ability to offload pre-processing steps into the prompts is an amazing feature because it allows us to build more expressive prompts, reducing code bugs that might arise from writing lengthier code.

#### Where LangChain stands out

Expressive chaining. How cool is it to orchestrate LLM applications using `|`? Low-level components can quickly be chained together using the pipe operator to form sophisticated, reliable LLM applications.

#### Where LlamaIndex stands out

In my opinion, however, none of the above are essential to an LLM library. The most important components are I) the user experience of a developer and II) code mileage, which I think LlamaIndex does exceedingly well.

#### I) The Developer’s User Experience

If you recall from my prior articles, Haystack requires LLM applications to be orchestrated using a pipeline, and LangChain’s LLM applications are to be orchestrated using a runnable. In my experience, both can be buggy due to the complexity of defining many low-level components. It is easy to connect these components but that’s just syntax — you’ll often face many errors when running them especially if you’re still picking up the library. Sometimes the error message doesn’t make sense, and in one of my experiences with LangChain I never knew that the bug plaguing my sophisticated chain was a missing component — I simply never thought of including it. I only came back to it after learning LlamaIndex — which helped me to figure out what was missing.

LlamaIndex’s high-level abstractions means that it’s easy for anyone to pick up LlamaIndex quickly. Need chat history? Use the`chat_engine` abstraction. Want your RAG application to handle sub-questions and incorporate hypothetical document embeddings (HyDE)? Wrap your query engine into the HyDE and SubQuestionQueryEngine abstractions:

```python
from llama_index.core.indices.query.query_transform import HyDEQueryTransform
from llama_index.core.query_engine import (
  TransformQueryEngine, 
  SubQuestionQueryEngine
)
from llama_index.core.tools import QueryEngineTool, ToolMetadata

hyde = HyDEQueryTransform(include_original=True)
hyde_query_engine = TransformQueryEngine(query_engine, hyde)
query_engine_tools = [
    QueryEngineTool(
        query_engine=hyde_query_engine,
        metadata=ToolMetadata(
            name="pg_essay",
            description="Paul Graham essay on What I Worked On",
        ),
    ),
]

query_engine = SubQuestionQueryEngine.from_defaults(
    query_engine_tools=query_engine_tools,
    use_async=True,
)
```

Now, you have a query engine that creates 4 different sub-questions (the default — can be edited) given a single user question and answers all 4 sub-questions using the HyDE approach. Your RAG application has instantly become far more complex with fewer lines of code. LlamaIndex makes any developer look really smart by allowing developers to build and ship high-quality apps at such high velocity.

But LlamaIndex doesn’t stop at high-level abstractions; it also provides medium-level (FusionRetrieval, for example) and low-level abstractions (Workflows—these are equivalent to the Langgraph library, which we will cover in the future). So, it is a flexible tool that is easy for a developer of any skill level to use.

#### II) Code Mileage

Code mileage refers to the need to heavily edit your code once new versions of LlamaIndex come out or if you want to customize your code further. In both cases, you can use high-level abstractions if the defaults are good enough and choose to use lower-level abstractions for components that need more love and care. And everything will still work well — even if LlamaIndex pushes a new update (just upgrade the package). The same cannot be said of LangChain (LCEL vs Chain for example) and Haystack (Haystack v2.0 vs Haystack v1.0 for example) in my experience. It doesn’t mean that both libraries are bad at all, I just prefer LlamaIndex for its code mileage because you never have to worry when versions change even for major changes.

#### Of course, you don’t have to take my word for it.

You’ll have to try it yourself!

With that, I conclude my trilogy of articles gently introducing everyone to the land of LLM orchestration libraries. But we are not done. Up next I’ll introduce everyone to the land of multi-agent systems — this time it’ll be like an ‘incursion’ event, where the Avengers from different realms collide — think Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, rather than the simpler team-up of the 3 Spider-Men in Spider-Man: No Way Home.

body:
* * *

#### Introducing Haystack Pipelines

If you’ve seen _Spider-Man: No Way Home_, you’ll remember the moment that three versions of Spider-Man — each from a different universe — appear on screen. They all have similar abilities (even the same costume), but each brings their unique style and approach to saving the day. The same goes for orchestration libraries in the LLM space. Just like our three Spider-Men, there are three standout orchestration libraries in the LLM space: LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Haystack.

In [_Part 1_](https://medium.com/mitb-for-all/a-gentle-introduction-to-the-llm-multiverse-part-1-langchain-023a899d294e), we introduced LangChain, the most popular LLM orchestration library and showed how it can be used to do some cool things. This article introduces [Haystack](https://haystack.deepset.ai/), its perfect competitor. Both libraries have similar “powers”, but offer different approaches to organizing and orchestrating LLM tools for tasks.

When comparing between libraries that are perfect competitors we know that they can accomplish the same tasks. What differs is how they get the tasks done. So if you have read the first article don’t be so quick to leave yet — Haystack’s capabilities might surprise you. And if you haven’t read the first article, I hope that this article will be useful in showing the amazing capabilities of LLMs, and encourage you to read the previous article on LangChain. As before, all codes can be found in my GitHub repository (All codes can be found in my [GitHub repo](https://github.com/tituslhy/literate-octo-tribble/).

### Introducing Haystack

The Haystack framework precedes the LangChain framework — if you checked the publication history of [Haystack v1.0](https://pypi.org/project/farm-haystack/#history) against [LangChain’s](https://pypi.org/project/langchain/#history), you’ll notice that Haystack was published almost 3 years earlier! Haystack is a widely used orchestration library, and its [GitHub repository](https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack) has 17k stars — and yet you might not have heard of it if you’re just starting to dabble in LLM applications.

Why isn’t Haystack as popular as LangChain? I have a theory. When Haystack was released in 2019, the generative AI space was quite different. OpenAI’s LLMs (GPT-2 and below) were open-sourced. Users would therefore orchestrate LLMs using HuggingFace and PyTorch (and this way is still good today). When ChatGPT was released later in 2022, the generative AI space went into hypergrowth. LangChain, debuting in late 2022, was the first to **frame** LLM orchestration as “chains” and extended its integrations beyond the LLMs to include vector databases and other components of the LLM ecosystem. Since then, Haystack has evolved its capabilities to orchestrate the LLM technology stack similarly, albeit with a different approach.

Let’s check out the Haystack library and learn how to use it to do cool things with LLMs!

### 1\. Importing an LLM and running it

Haystack has integrations with almost any LLM you can think of. Just `pip-install` the respective integration package and you’re good to go! As in the LangChain article, I will use Mistral Large as my LLM and GeminiEmbedding as my embedding model. Both models are **free of charge**!

```python
# !pip install -U haystack-ai
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv, find_dotenv
import warnings
from IPython.display import display, Markdown
from haystack.dataclasses import ChatMessage
from haystack_integrations.components.generators.mistral import MistralChatGenerator

_ = load_dotenv(find_dotenv())
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')
model = "mistral-large-latest"
client = MistralChatGenerator(model=model)

response = client.run(
    messages=[ChatMessage.from_user("What is the capital of France?")]
)

print(response)
```

```python-repl
{'replies': [ChatMessage(content="The capital of France is Paris. Known for its art, culture, cuisine, and fashion, Paris is also the most populous city in France. It is home to iconic landmarks such as the Eiffel Tower, the Louvre Museum, and Notre-Dame Cathedral. Paris has been the capital since 508 AD, and it is the seat of the French government and the country's political, economic, and cultural center.", role=<ChatRole.ASSISTANT: 'assistant'>, name=None, meta={'model': 'mistral-large-latest', 'index': 0, 'finish_reason': 'stop', 'usage': {'completion_tokens': 96, 'prompt_tokens': 10, 'total_tokens': 106, 'completion_tokens_details': None}})]}
```

Like LangChain, there is only one function you need to remember when interacting with any Haystack component, and that function is `run` . Depending on the Haystack object, the `run` method takes in different input types. The `ChatGenerator` object takes in a list of messages (i.e. the conversation history), where each message must be wrapped in a `ChatMessage` class with the messenger roles clearly defined as either from user or assistant. The response object is a dictionary including the ChatMessage reply and some metadata.

Haystack also allows for streaming replies. Just add a callback function as an argument to `run` .

```python
from haystack.components.generators.utils import print_streaming_chunk

streaming_client = MistralChatGenerator(
    model=model,
    streaming_callback=print_streaming_chunk
)
response = streaming_client.run(
    messages=[ChatMessage.from_user("What is the capital of France?")]
)
```

The output type is **the same**. The only difference is that the streaming client prints out the response word by word as it is generated by the model.

**2\. Structured Prediction**

LLMs can also reply to questions in a specific “format”. We’ll be using the same example from our LangChain article (and later in our LlamaIndex article) to have an LLM to design a workout plan. Pydantic is our best friend for this task.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import List

class Exercise(BaseModel):
    """Generates a workout plan given a focus area"""
    exercise: str
    number_of_reps: int
    number_of_sets: int

class WorkoutPlan(BaseModel):
    exercises: List[Exercise]
```

Once we have our schemas defined, we have to convert this into a JSON string like so:

```python
json_schema = WorkoutPlan.schema_json(indent=2)
display(Markdown(json_schema))
```

```python-repl
{ "$defs": { "Exercise": { "description": "Generates a workout plan given a focus area", "properties": { "exercise": { "title": "Exercise", "type": "string" }, "number_of_reps": { "title": "Number Of Reps", "type": "integer" }, "number_of_sets": { "title": "Number Of Sets", "type": "integer" } }, "required": [ "exercise", "number_of_reps", "number_of_sets" ], "title": "Exercise", "type": "object" } }, "properties": { "exercises": { "items": { "$ref": "#/$defs/Exercise" }, "title": "Exercises", "type": "array" } }, "required": [ "exercises" ], "title": "WorkoutPlan", "type": "object" }
```

#### Introducing Haystack Pipelines

Haystack’s core philosophy revolves around the `pipeline` abstraction. So we will have to write the structured prediction task in a Haystack `pipeline` . Think of a pipeline as a graph with nodes and edges. `components` are the nodes which can be predefined Haystack components or classes that we can define. Let’s define a validator object that can check the typing of the structured output result from the LLM, and if the typing fails, we’ll send it back to the LLM for regeneration. Haystack makes this type of orchestration easy! We’ll be lifting their code for the output validator component entirely from one of their [cookbooks](https://haystack.deepset.ai/tutorials/28_structured_output_with_loop).

```python
import json
from pydantic import ValidationError
from typing import Optional, List
from haystack import component

@component
class OutputValidator:
    def __init__(self, pydantic_model: BaseModel):
        self.pydantic_model = pydantic_model
        self.iteration_counter = 0
    
    ## Define component output
    @component.output_types(
        valid_replies = List[str], 
        invalid_replies = Optional[List[str]],
        error_message = Optional[str],
    )
    def run(self, replies: List[str]):
        """Method to run the class component"""
        
        self.iteration_counter += 1
        
        ## Parse LLM reply
        try: #If the output is valid
            output_dict = json.loads(replies[0])
            self.pydantic_model.model_validate(output_dict)
            return {"valid_replies": replies}
        
        except (ValueError, ValidationError) as e: #if the output is invalid
            return {"invalid_replies": replies, "error_message": str(e)

output_validator = OutputValidator(pydantic_model=WorkoutPlan)
```

To define a custom pipeline component, decorate your class with a `@component` and include an implementation of a `run` method decorated with `@component.output_types` . In this example, our validation component returns `valid_replies` and `invalid_replies` as a list of strings, and an `error_message` string when a reply is deemed to be invalid.

The ability to define your pipeline components as a class means that we can potentially add more complex logic to each component. This confers a lot of flexibility for us to design our pipelines to our imagination.

#### Introducing Haystack Prompts

Haystack pipelines typically start with a `prompt_builder` object which wraps a system prompt. In my opinion, Haystack’s approach to prompts is extraordinary. Let me show you what I mean before elaborating more:

```python
from haystack.components.builders import PromptBuilder

prompt_template = """
Create a workout plan from the user's question: {{question}}.
Follow this JSON schema, but only return the actual instances without any 
additional schema definition:
{{schema}}
Make sure your response is a dict and not a list.
{% if invalid_replies and error_message %}
  You already created the following output in a previous attempt: 
  {{invalid_replies}} However, this doesn't comply with the format requirements 
  from above and triggered this Python exception: {{error_message}}
  Correct the output and try again. Just return the corrected output without 
  any extra explanations.
{% endif %}
"""
prompt_builder = PromptBuilder(template=prompt_template)
```

There are 4 placeholders in this prompt — 2 compulsory placeholders “question”, “schema” which is the user’s question and the Pydantic object schema in JSON form. But here’s where it gets interesting — there’s an `if` statement in the prompt and 2 additional placeholders that become required if the `if` condition is met. This is Jinja2 syntax — if you’ve done any full stack development using Python’s Flask library (and FastAPI library) you’ll recognize this immediately. This means that Haystack prompts can include if-else, for loops and a combination of both.

**How cool is that!** To my knowledge, this capability is currently not available in LangChain or LlamaIndex — you would typically try to handle these logic blocks in your Python code upstream before passing the prompt to LangChain or LlamaIndex. Haystack has a much tighter integration with Jinja2, so you can pass the “upstream processing” directly into the prompt!

#### Back to our structured prediction task

Ok, so we’ve built our Pydantic validator component and our prompt builder component. Now, we just need to connect everything in the pipeline!

However, here’s where we hit a bit of a roadblock. Not every LLM can be used in a Haystack pipeline. For example, the `ChatGenerator` classes are not supported—only `Generator` LLM classes can be used, and unfortunately, Mistral does not have a `MistralGenerator` class in Haystack. This means we can’t use it in our pipeline.

**So, while Haystack offers great flexibility, the current extent of LLM integrations can be somewhat inconsistent.** To ensure our example runs smoothly, we’ll use an OpenAI LLM.

```python
from haystack.components.generators import OpenAIGenerator
from haystack import Pipeline

generator = OpenAIGenerator(model="gpt-4o-mini")

## Create pipeline
pipeline = Pipeline(max_runs_per_component=5) #don't let the llm go crazy

## Create nodes
# Add components to your pipeline. These are the nodes in the graph.
pipeline.add_component(instance=prompt_builder, name="prompt_builder")
pipeline.add_component(instance=generator, name="llm")
pipeline.add_component(instance=output_validator, name="output_validator")

## Create edges
# Now, connect the components to each other. These are the edges in the graph.
pipeline.connect("prompt_builder", "llm")
pipeline.connect("llm", "output_validator")

# If a component has more than one output or input, we need to explicitly 
# specify the connections (pay attention to the mapping)!
pipeline.connect("output_validator.invalid_replies", 
                  "prompt_builder.invalid_replies")
pipeline.connect("output_validator.error_message", 
                "prompt_builder.error_message")
```

Notice how we’re connecting the `output_validator` in the pipeline. We have to connect every possible output to something. In this case, for Haystack to update the prompt with our Jinja2 logic, we need to connect the validator back to the `prompt_builder` component, mapping the component’s output type to the exact placeholders in the `prompt_builder` .

Haystack has a neat utility function to visualize your pipeline.

```python
pipeline.show()
```

Let’s test it!

```python
question="Generate a workout plan for biceps"
result = pipeline.run(
    {"prompt_builder": {
        "question": question, 
        "schema": json_schema}
    }
)
```

The pipeline’s `run` function takes in a dictionary, which populates the required placeholders in the `prompt_builder` component. `result` is not a string but an `output_validator` class minimally containing `valid_replies` . In the event of an execution failure, it also includes `invalid_replies` and an `error_message` .

```python
valid_reply = result["output_validator"]["valid_replies"][0]
valid_json = json.loads(valid_reply)
print(valid_json)
```

```python-repl
{'exercises': 
      [{'exercise': 'Bicep Curls', 'number_of_reps': 12, 'number_of_sets': 3},
       {'exercise': 'Hammer Curls', 'number_of_reps': 10, 'number_of_sets': 3}, 
       {'exercise': 'Concentration Curls', 'number_of_reps': 12, 'number_of_sets': 3}, 
       {'exercise': 'Barbell Curls', 'number_of_reps': 10, 'number_of_sets': 3}, 
       {'exercise': 'Preacher Curls', 'number_of_reps': 8, 'number_of_sets': 3}
]}
```

Quite a crazy workout plan (say goodbye to all bicep muscle coordination if you do this) but ok it’s correct!

#### Zero-shot classification (also known as routing)

An extension of structured prediction is zero-shot classification. Gone are the days when you had to train NLP models from scratch or fine-tune BERT on training data that was painstakingly curated. Instead, get an LLM to return an appropriate folder name (from either “presentation” or “coding”) to store a file given the file’s name. Haystack has a useful built-in pipeline component for this task — conditional routers!

```python
from haystack.components.routers import ConditionalRouter

## Instantiating the choices as a list of dictionaries
# Notice the Jinja2 syntax
routes = [
    {
        "condition": "{{'presentation' in replies[0]|lower}}",
        "output": "{{query}}",
        "output_name": "presentation",
        "output_type": str,
    },
    {
        "condition": "{{'coding' in replies[0]|lower}}",
        "output": "{{replies[0]}}",
        "output_name": "coding",
        "output_type": str,
    },
]

## Instantiating conditional router as a component
router = ConditionalRouter(routes=routes)

## Instantiate prompt
prompt_for_routing = """
Answer the following query with either 'presentation' or 'coding'.
The user is only seeking for your opinion on the folder to save their
file of interest in the query.

Query: {{query}}
"""

prompt_builder_for_routing = PromptBuilder(prompt_for_routing)

## Build new pipeline
router_pipe = Pipeline()
router_pipe.add_component(
    "prompt_builder", prompt_builder_for_routing
)
router_pipe.add_component(
    "llm", OpenAIGenerator(model="gpt-4o-mini")
)
router_pipe.add_component(
    "router", router
)

router_pipe.connect("prompt_builder", "llm")
router_pipe.connect("llm", "router")

query = "Where should I keep this file: abc.py?"
router_pipe.run(
    {"prompt_builder": {"query": query},
     "router": {"query": query}
    }
)
```

```python-repl
{'llm': {'meta': [{'model': 'gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18',
    'index': 0,
    'finish_reason': 'stop',
    'usage': {'completion_tokens': 1,
     'prompt_tokens': 55,
     'total_tokens': 56,
     'completion_tokens_details': CompletionTokensDetails(reasoning_tokens=0),
     'prompt_tokens_details': {'cached_tokens': 0}}}]},
 'router': {'coding': 'coding'}}
```

Notice the last key `"router”`shows that the folder to be stored is `coding` which is the correct answer.

### 3\. Tool Calling

LLM capabilities can be extended with tool calling, which can be imported or coded from scratch.

**I have to be upfront: I am not a fan of the way Haystack implements tool calling.**

Unlike Haystack pipelines, tool calling is done using`ChatGenerator`models instead of `Generator`models (which was confusing to me).

The main way is to represent the function manually in JSON format. This is similar to how you would invoke a function in OpenAI, and other LLM providers. Frankly, this feels counterproductive. One of the key goals of an orchestration library is to simplify interactions across LLMs, and this approach doesn’t quite achieve that, in my opinion. Here’s an example from the [documentation](https://docs.haystack.deepset.ai/docs/function-calling):

```python
 ## You have to write this yourself!!
tools = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "get_current_weather",
            "description": "Get the current weather",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "location": {
                        "type": "string",
                        "description": "The city and state, e.g. San Francisco, CA",
                    },
                    "format": {
                        "type": "string",
                        "enum": ["celsius", "fahrenheit"],
                        "description": "The temperature unit to use. Infer this from the users location.",
                    },
                },
                "required": ["location", "format"],
            },
        }
    }
]
```

Running an LLM in Haystack with `tools` as defined, we get:

```python
messages = [ChatMessage.from_user("What's the weather like in Berlin?")]
response = client.run(messages=messages, generation_kwargs= {"tools": tools})
response_msg = response["replies"][0]
print(response_msg)
```

```python-repl
ChatMessage(content='[{"id": "VhPmtlGoL", "function": {"arguments": "{\\"location\\": \\"Berlin, Germany\\", \\"format\\": \\"celsius\\"}", "name": "get_current_weather"}, "type": "function"}]', role=<ChatRole.ASSISTANT: 'assistant'>, name=None, meta={'model': 'mistral-large-latest', 'index': 0, 'finish_reason': 'tool_calls', 'usage': {'completion_tokens': 35, 'prompt_tokens': 135, 'total_tokens': 170, 'completion_tokens_details': None}})
```

Notice that Haystack only tells you which tool was selected (which in this case is the `get_current_weather`tool). You would have to invoke the function selected by the LLM separately and pass the tool’s results back to the LLM to construct a final reply.

### 4\. RAG

This is one of Haystack’s most popular use case applications. RAG applications are defined to be Haystack pipelines so we can only use `Generator` abstractions and not `ChatGenerator` abstractions.

A typical RAG workflow involves loading a file, chunking the file, generating embeddings from each chunk, and ingesting the chunk into a vector database which we will use for retrieval depending on the question asked by the user. Haystack requires the ingestion and RAG pipelines to be done separately. Let’s start by defining the ingestion pipeline:

```python
from haystack.components.embedders import OpenAIDocumentEmbedder
from haystack.components.converters.txt import TextFileToDocument
from haystack.components.preprocessors.document_splitter import DocumentSplitter
from haystack.components.writers import DocumentWriter
from haystack.document_stores.in_memory import InMemoryDocumentStore

document_store = InMemoryDocumentStore()
text_file_converter = TextFileToDocument()
document_splitter = DocumentSplitter()
document_writer = DocumentWriter(document_store=document_store)
embedder_model = OpenAIDocumentEmbedder(model="text-embedding-3-small")

ingestion = Pipeline()
ingestion.add_component("converter", text_file_converter)
ingestion.add_component("splitter", document_splitter)
ingestion.add_component("embedder", embedder_model)
ingestion.add_component("writer", document_writer)

ingestion.connect("converter", "splitter")
ingestion.connect("splitter", "embedder")
ingestion.connect("embedder", "writer")
```

Files are split into chunks, embedded by an embedded document, and written in an in-memory document store. Let’s embed our Paul Graham Essay:

```python
!mkdir -p '../../data/paul_graham/'
!wget 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/run-llama/llama_index/main/docs/docs/examples/data/paul_graham/paul_graham_essay.txt' -O '../../data/paul_graham/paul_graham_essay.txt'

ingestion.run(
  {"converter": 
    {"sources": ['../../data/paul_graham/paul_graham_essay.txt']}
  }
)
```

Now let’s build our RAG pipeline

```python
from haystack.components.embedders import OpenAITextEmbedder 
from haystack.components.retrievers.in_memory import InMemoryEmbeddingRetriever

rag_prompt = """
Answer the question based on the provided context.
Context:
{% for doc in documents %}
   {{ doc.content }} 
{% endfor %}
Question: {{ query }}
"""
rag_prompt_builder = PromptBuilder(template=rag_prompt)

query_embedder_model = OpenAITextEmbedder()
document_retriever = InMemoryEmbeddingRetriever(document_store=document_store)
answer_generator = OpenAIGenerator()

rag = Pipeline()
rag.add_component("query_embedder", query_embedder_model)
rag.add_component("retriever", document_retriever)
rag.add_component("prompt", rag_prompt_builder)
rag.add_component("generator", answer_generator)

rag.connect("query_embedder.embedding", "retriever.query_embedding")
```

For our RAG pipeline, we have to import a `TextEmbedder` which does the same function as`DocumentEmbedder` , just that it is applied to the user’s query. I’m not sure why there needs to be a separate abstraction for this.

We then have to instantiate an embedding retriever wrapped around our `document_store` , then connect these components. Running the RAG pipeline does bring an unpleasant surprise.

```python
question = "Did Paul Graham write code??"

result = rag.run(
    {
        "query_embedder": {"text": question},
        "retriever": {"top_k": 1},
        "prompt": {"query": question},
    }
)

print(result["generator"]["replies"][0])
```

```python-repl
The provided context does not explicitly mention whether Paul Graham wrote code. It focuses on the development of the Y Combinator batch model and their approach to funding startups. Therefore, based on the information given, we cannot determine if Paul Graham wrote code.
```

We know that this answer is wrong. Because the basic LangChain RAG application and LlamaIndex RAG application (spoiler alert) answered this correctly. This does suggest that the retrieval was a problem. But we won’t go further into that for now.

Haystack does allow for pipelines to be saved by serialization to YAML files!

```python
with open("rag.yml", "w") as file:
    rag.dump(file)
```

To load a saved pipeline isn’t so straightforward, and the Haystack [documentation](https://docs.haystack.deepset.ai/docs/serialization) could be more helpful in this regard — it assumes you’ve read the entire YAML file as a single text string, without providing a clear example. So here’s my implementation

```python
import yaml
from haystack import Pipeline
from haystack.core.serialization import DeserializationCallbacks
from typing import Type, Dict, Any

# Load the YAML file and convert it to a string
def load_yaml_as_string(file_path):
    with open(file_path, 'r') as file:
        # Load YAML content as a Python dictionary
        yaml_content = yaml.safe_load(file)
        
        # Convert the loaded YAML data to a YAML formatted string
        yaml_string = yaml.dump(yaml_content, default_flow_style=False)
        
    return yaml_string

def component_pre_init_callback(
    component_name: str, 
    component_cls: Type, 
    init_params: Dict[str, Any]
):
   # This function gets called every time a component is deserialized.
   if component_name == "rag":
      assert "rag" in component_cls.__name__
      # Modify the init parameters. The modified parameters are passed to
      # the init method of the component during deserialization.
      init_params["remove_empty_lines"] = False
      print("Modified 'remove_empty_lines' to False in 'cleaner' component")
   else:
      print(f"Not modifying component {component_name} of class {component_cls}")

pipeline_yaml = load_yaml_as_string("rag.yml")
pipe = Pipeline.loads(pipeline_yaml, callbacks=DeserializationCallbacks(component_pre_init_callback))
```

### 5\. Agents

As of now, Haystack 2.0 **_does not have agent abstractions_**! Haystack 1.0 did, but I think they are still in the process of migrating this function over. According to the [migration notes](https://docs.haystack.deepset.ai/v2.0/docs/migration#agents), Haystack 2.0 is a comprehensive overhaul of Haystack 1.0 so give them time on this.

### Concluding Thoughts

**To be candid, I challenged myself to learn Haystack in a day — and I did!** But this was mostly thanks to my prior experience with its direct competitors, LangChain and LlamaIndex - I’ve already used these tools to build applications.

Haystack stands out with its stellar integration of Jinja2 for prompting, but in my opinion has areas that feel incomplete, such as the lack of well-developed abstractions for LLM vendors beyond OpenAI, tool calling and abstractions for LLM agents. **The pipeline approach in Haystack appears to be more flexible than LangChain’s “chain” method**, but that’s because LangChain has an even lower-level, graph-centric approach (Langgraph, which we will cover in a future article) that adds to its versatility. It is also noteworthy that the chain approach already works without the need for a lower-level pipelining approach.

**Be prepared to write more code in Haystack compared to LangChain**, mainly because almost every task requires a `pipeline`. We had to code out 2 pipelines for basic RAG.

Orchestration frameworks like Haystack, LangChain, and LlamaIndex provide developers with powerful tools to create LLM applications. Naturally, the question arises — **which framework is the best?** It’s tempting to dive into a comparison and pick a winner right now, but we won’t do that just yet. There’s still one more library to introduce — **LlamaIndex** — and it brings its unique perspective to orchestrating LLM components. Each framework has its strengths and trade-offs, and only after fully exploring all three can we make a fair comparison. Stay tuned for the next article, where we’ll dive into LlamaIndex and continue our journey through the LLM multiverse!

body:
* * *

#### A gentle introduction to the LLM Multiverse

If you’re just starting on your LLM journey, you will find yourself overwhelmed by the many different (and endless) technology stacks and tools. Worst still, they all seem to do the same thing! There are many vector database vendors, graph database vendors, reranker models, embedding models, LLMs, etc. Confused, you google if there is any code library that you can use to orchestrate each of these components and you find that there are even multiple orchestration libraries that exist! Which should you choose?

When thinking of the LLM space I’m often reminded of the Spider-Man No Way Home movie where the 3 Spider-Men from parallel universes met. I’ve therefore decided to start an article series known as “A Gentle Introduction to the LLM Multiverse” to explore these technologies in greater detail.

We start with the orchestration libraries, namely Langchain, LlamaIndex and Haystack. We’ll cover each of these libraries in their respective articles showing some common recipes from invoking an LLM up to building single agents. After these future articles, we will then cover multi-agent orchestration libraries such as crewAI, Langgraph, LlamaIndex (again) and Autogen. As much as possible, I try to use the same LLMs, embedding models, and tasks. The aim is to help everyone understand how to use these respective libraries and of course, decide which library you prefer for yourself. Naturally, I have a personal preference. More on that later. All codes can be found in the GitHub repo: [https://github.com/tituslhy/literate-octo-tribble/tree/main](https://github.com/tituslhy/literate-octo-tribble/tree/main)

### Introducing Langchain

Langchain came to be as a result of the burgeoning LLM technology space — everyone was looking for a common library to orchestrate everything in their LLM application. It was therefore no surprise when Langchain launched that the uptake in users was immediate. What was surprising was that Langchain was not the first orchestration library to exist — Haystack was founded earlier and we will cover this in a subsequent article. But that doesn’t mean that Langchain users had no complaints. Nonetheless, Langchain remains a central Python library in LLM-land (>93k stars and counting!), and almost every LLM-related job you see will ask for demonstrable Langchain experience. Without further ado, let’s talk about how we can use Langchain to do some cool things!

### 1\. Importing an LLM and invoking it

Langchain has integrations with almost any LLM you can think of! Just `pip-install` the respective integration package and you’re good to go! I will be using Mistral Large as my LLM and GeminiEmbedding as my embedding model throughout this article. Both models are **free of charge**!

```python
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv, find_dotenv
import warnings
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

_ = load_dotenv(find_dotenv())
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

from langchain_mistralai import ChatMistralAI

llm = ChatMistralAI(
    model="mistral-large-latest",
    temperature=0,
    max_retries=2,
)
```

Every interaction in Langchain is espoused by the `invoke` function. This makes it easy to remember how to interact with anything Langchain-related. The `invoke` function is also very flexible and can take in string inputs, list inputs, key-value pair inputs, etc.

```python
response = llm.invoke("Hi!")
```

```python-repl
Hello! How can I assist you today? Let's chat about anything you'd like. 😊
```

```python
# Invoke on a list of messages
messages = [
    (
        "system",
        "You are a helpful assistant."
    ),
    ("human", "Why is the sky blue?")
]
response = llm.invoke(messages)
display(Markdown(response.content))
```

```python-repl
The sky appears blue due to a process called Rayleigh scattering. As light from the sun reaches Earth's atmosphere, it is made up of different colors, which are essentially different wavelengths of light. Shorter wavelengths (like blue and violet) are scattered more by the tiny molecules and particles in the atmosphere because they travel in shorter, smaller waves. This is why we perceive the sky as blue most of the time.

However, you might wonder why the sky doesn't appear violet, since violet light has an even shorter wavelength than blue light. The sky appears blue, not violet, because the sun emits more blue light than violet light, and also because our eyes are more sensitive to blue light. Additionally, some of the violet light gets absorbed by the atmosphere, further tipping the balance toward blue.

During sunrise or sunset, the light has to pass through more of Earth's atmosphere, which scatters more of the blue and green light away, and we're left with the warmer colors of sunrise and sunset, like red, orange, and yellow.
```

The more fun way (and Langchain’s claim to fame) is to use chains! Chains can be defined using the LangChain Expression Language (LCEL) by adding the pipe `|` operator to connect components into a chain. Chains are also known as “Runnables”.

```python
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser

parser = StrOutputParser()

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages(
    # Now we instantiate our list of messages
    [
        (
            "system",
            "You are a helpful assistant."
        ),
        ("human", "{input}") #input is a placeholder
    ]
)
chain = prompt | llm | parser

response = chain.invoke(
    {"input": "Why is the sky blue?"} 
#Notice that we have to pass in an 'input' key here
)
```

When invoking a chain, be careful to ensure that any placeholder variable names defined upstream are passed in the input invocation — or the chain will error. To add message history:

```python
from langchain_core.chat_history import (
    BaseChatMessageHistory,
    InMemoryChatMessageHistory,
)
from langchain_core.runnables.history import RunnableWithMessageHistory
from langchain_core.prompts import MessagesPlaceholder
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage

store = {} #we're just using a dictionary as our document store for now

def get_session_history(session_id: str) -> BaseChatMessageHistory:
    if session_id not in store:
        store[session_id] = InMemoryChatMessageHistory()
    return store[session_id]

# Define our base runnable again
prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages(
    [
        (
            "system",
            """You are a helpful assistant. Answer all questions to the 
            best of your ability in {language}."""
        ),
        MessagesPlaceholder(variable_name="messages") #placeholder
    ]
)
chain = prompt | llm | parser

# Wrraping the runnable on top of another runnable
with_message_history = RunnableWithMessageHistory(
    chain,
    get_session_history,
    input_messages_key="messages" #Must be the same as the placeholder
)

# Set a session_id within the config - the session_id is what you'll use for 
# tracing
config = {"configurable": {"session_id": "abc123"}} 

response = with_message_history.invoke(
    {
        "messages": [
            HumanMessage(
              content = "Hi my name is Titus! Why is the sky blue?"
            )
         ],
        "language": "Chinese"
    },
    config = config
)
```

```python-repl
你好，Titus！天空之所以是蓝色的，主要是由于大气层中的光散射现象。当太阳光进入地球大气层时，光线会与空气分子和微小颗粒发生碰撞，导致光线发生散射。蓝色光的波长较短，散射的程度比其他颜色的光更强烈，因此我们看到的天空是蓝色的。这种现象被称为瑞利散射。
```

```python
response = with_message_history.invoke(
    {
        "messages": [HumanMessage(content = "What's my name again?")],
        "language": "French"
    },
    config = config
)
```

```python-repl
Bien sûr, je suis là pour t'aider. Ton nom est Titus.
```

Cool right!

### 2\. Structured Prediction

LLMs don’t always have to reply in text form. You can also have an LLM reply to your questions in a specific “format”. Let’s say I want the LLM to design a workout plan for me but I just want the essentials without all the other words. (We’ll be using this example for our Haystack and LlamaIndex articles too btw)

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import List

class Exercise(BaseModel):
    """Generates a workout plan given a focus area"""
    exercise: str
    number_of_reps: int
    number_of_sets: int

class WorkoutPlan(BaseModel):
    exercises: List[Exercise]

structured_llm = llm.with_structured_output(WorkoutPlan)
response = structured_llm.invoke("Suggest a workout plan for biceps")
```

In any structured prediction use cases, Pydantic is your best friend. Specify the output and class you want, and the LLM will always comply with it. In this case, I want a `WorkoutPlan` with some `Exercise` that includes the number of reps and the number of sets.

```python-repl
WorkoutPlan(exercises=[Exercise(exercise='Barbell Curl', number_of_reps=10, number_of_sets=3), Exercise(exercise='Hammer Curl', number_of_reps=10, number_of_sets=3), Exercise(exercise='Concentration Curl', number_of_reps=10, number_of_sets=3)])
```

#### 2a. Zero-Shot Classification (Also known as routing in LLM land)

An extension of structured prediction is zero-shot classification. Gone are the days when you had to train NLP models from scratch or fine-tune BERT on training data that was painstakingly curated. Just throw everything to the LLM. There are 2 ways to do this!

#### 2b. The Pydantic Way again

Let’s say we want the LLM to suggest where to keep a specific file in our computer — PS you can use this as a way to automate file sorting and storage!

```python
from typing import Literal

class DocumentFolder(BaseModel):
    """Returns only one output folder name given a document name"""
    
    folder_name: Literal[
        "finance",
        "presentations",
        "sketchbook",
        "code"
    ]

folder_sorter = llm.with_structured_output(DocumentFolder)
response = folder_sorter.invoke(
    "Where should I store the file 'llama_sketch.png'?"
)
```

```python-repl
DocumentFolder(folder_name='sketchbook')
```

But this way might fail if your class names are too challenging (for example langchain\_project, llamaindex\_project). In these cases, you will need to provide some metadata.

#### 2c. The metadata way — semantic similarity

```python
from langchain_google_genai import GoogleGenerativeAIEmbeddings
from langchain_community.utils.math import cosine_similarity
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnablePassthrough, RunnableLambda

## The class labels and their descriptions. Notice the placeholder
presentation = """choose this option if the input document from the user's 
                query has a .pptx or .ppt extension. 
                Here is the user's query: {query}"""
python_code = """choose this option if the input document from the user's 
              query has a .py or .ipynb extension. Here is the user's 
              query: {query}"""

## The embedding model
embeddings = GoogleGenerativeAIEmbeddings(model="models/embedding-001")

## Wrapping the class labels into a list of prompt templates and embedding them
prompt_templates = [presentation, python_code]
prompt_embeddings = embeddings.embed_documents(prompt_templates)

def prompt_router(input):
    """This is the function that determines which class gets chosen.
    Under the hood we are implementing cosine similarity search.

    Source: https://python.langchain.com/v0.1/docs/modules/model_io/prompts/example_selectors/similarity/
    """
    
    ## Embed the user's query
    query_embedding = embeddings.embed_query(input["query"])
    
    ## Compute the similarity of the user query vector to the vector embeddings
    ## of the choices
    similarity = cosine_similarity([query_embedding], prompt_embeddings)[0]
    most_similar = prompt_templates[similarity.argmax()]
    
    if most_similar == presentation:
        return "presentation"
    return "python_code"

from langchain_core.runnables import RunnablePassthrough, RunnableLambda

route_chain = (
    {"query": RunnablePassthrough()}
    | RunnableLambda(prompt_router)
)

result = route_chain.invoke("Where should I keep this file: abc.py?")
print(result)
```

```python-repl
'python_code'
```

By now you’ll notice that the ‘chain’ way is cool but not so straightforward. What’s a `RunnablePassthrough` and a `RunnableLambda` ? A `RunnablePassthrough` is a placeholder. It allows for the placeholder to “pass-through” the runnable and not throw an error when you’re instantiating the runnable — because the prompt\_router is expecting an input with the key “query”. A `RunnableLambda` is like Python’s `lambda` expression function, but instead of executing a lambda expression, executes a function that exists within a Langchain Runnable.

Whoa!

### 3\. Tool Calling

The plot thickens! LLMs can call tools that we define (or import) to reduce hallucination risks! Langchain allows for any function to be registered as a tool. Just decorate any function with the `@tool` decorator! Here are some simple example tools we’ll be using for our demo

```python
from langchain_core.tools import tool

@tool
def multiply(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Multiplies two integers and returns the resulting integer"""
    return a*b

@tool
def mystery(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Mystery function on two integers"""
    return a * b + a + b

@tool
def add( a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Use this tool to add two integers together"""
    return a + b

@tool
def minus(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Use this tool to return the difference between two integers"""
    return a - b

@tool
def divide(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Use this tool to perform integer division between two integers"""
    return a //b

tools = [add, multiply, mystery, minus, divide]
```

Once defined, all tools must be wrapped in a list. We can then bind these tools to an LLM like so:

```python
query = "What is 3 * 12? Also, what is 11 + 49?"

llm_with_tools = llm.bind_tools(tools)
response = llm_with_tools.invoke(query)
print(response)
```

```python
AIMessage(content='', additional_kwargs={'tool_calls': [{'id': '0AXkLCfCQ', 'type': 'function', 'function': {'name': 'multiply', 'arguments': '{"a": 3, "b": 12}'}}, {'id': 'NpiIIdDDt', 'type': 'function', 'function': {'name': 'add', 'arguments': '{"a": 11, "b": 49}'}}]}, response_metadata={'token_usage': {'prompt_tokens': 390, 'total_tokens': 439, 'completion_tokens': 49}, 'model': 'mistral-large-latest', 'finish_reason': 'tool_calls'}, id='run-83123bb6-41a3-4103-a456-2cdb3d63389f-0', tool_calls=[{'name': 'multiply', 'args': {'a': 3, 'b': 12}, 'id': '0AXkLCfCQ', 'type': 'tool_call'}, {'name': 'add', 'args': {'a': 11, 'b': 49}, 'id': 'NpiIIdDDt', 'type': 'tool_call'}], usage_metadata={'input_tokens': 390, 'output_tokens': 49, 'total_tokens': 439})
```

Hang on, if you look at the `content` attribute of the response, you’ll see that it’s a blank string! Where’s the output? Well. Langchain’s abstraction means the llm only ‘chose’ the tool it was going to use without actually executing it yet.

Now let’s execute the tool outputs and pass the outputs back to the llm. We’ll start by doing the exact same thing earlier, except that we instantiate a message list over the user’s query wrapped in a \`HumanMessage\` class.

We then invoke the llm with tools over the list and append the llm’s tool selection to the messages list.

```python
from langchain_core.messages import ToolMessage

## Do the same as before, just that we wrap everything in a list of messages
messages = [HumanMessage(query)]
response = llm_with_tools.invoke(messages)
messages.append(response)

## Now we invoke the tool and store the output of the tool
for tool_call in response.tool_calls:
    selected_tool = {
        "add": add,
        "mystery": mystery,
        "multiply": multiply,
        "divide": divide,
        "minus": minus,
    }[tool_call['name'].lower()]
    print(selected_tool)
    tool_output = selected_tool.invoke(tool_call["args"])
    messages.append(ToolMessage(tool_output, tool_call_id=tool_call["id"]))

## And now we invoke the llm with everything again
final_reply = llm_with_tools.invoke(messages)
print(final_reply)
```

```python-repl
AIMessage(content='The result of 3 * 12 is 36.\n\nThe result of 11 + 49 is 60.', additional_kwargs={}, response_metadata={'token_usage': {'prompt_tokens': 495, 'total_tokens': 526, 'completion_tokens': 31}, 'model': 'mistral-large-latest', 'finish_reason': 'stop'}, id='run-55f80c86-9ee3-4bbf-9092-d1607e005af5-0', usage_metadata={'input_tokens': 495, 'output_tokens': 31, 'total_tokens': 526})
```

Ah, now there’s actual content in the result!

A quick observation is that Langchain does require the user to define quite a lot of “things” to get anything done. But there is an advantage to this super low-level approach and that’s greater controllability and functionality — it’s easy to customize anything.

As an example, we can do few-shot prompting by adding examples to the messages list! Few shot-prompting can be quite useful for an LLM in learning how to use very complex tools (_The examples are copied from_ [_https://python.langchain.com/v0.1/docs/modules/model\_io/chat/function\_calling/#response-reading-tool-calls-from-model-output_](https://python.langchain.com/v0.1/docs/modules/model_io/chat/function_calling/#response-reading-tool-calls-from-model-output)_)_

```python
from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage

## Define few shot examples
examples = [
    HumanMessage(
        "What's the product of 317253 and 128472 plus four", name="example_user"
    ),
    AIMessage(
        "",
        name="example_assistant",
        tool_calls=[
            {"name": "multiply", "args": {"x": 317253, "y": 128472}, "id": "1"}
        ],
    ),
    ToolMessage("16505054784", tool_call_id="1"),
    AIMessage(
        "",
        name="example_assistant",
        tool_calls=[{"name": "add", "args": {"x": 16505054784, "y": 4}, "id": "2"}],
    ),
    ToolMessage("16505054788", tool_call_id="2"),
    AIMessage(
        "The product of 317253 and 128472 plus four is 16505054788",
        name="example_assistant",
    ),
]

system = """You are bad at math but are an expert at using a calculator."""

few_shot_prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages(
    [
        ("system", system),
        *examples,
        ("human", "{query}"),
    ]
)

## Define chain
chain = {"query": RunnablePassthrough()} | few_shot_prompt | llm_with_tools
```

### 4\. Building a basic RAG application

Well… It’s never simple when you’re using Langchain because you need to write and build a lot of components yourself. Let’s build a single RAG application over Paul Graham’s essay

```bash
mkdir -p '../../data/paul_graham/'
wget 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/run-llama/llama_index/main/docs/docs/examples/data/paul_graham/paul_graham_essay.txt' -O '../../data/paul_graham/paul_graham_essay.txt'
```

```python
from langchain_community.document_loaders import TextLoader

loader = TextLoader("../../data/paul_graham/paul_graham_essay.txt")
docs = loader.load()
print(len(docs))
```

We first pull the essay file and load the file using one of Langchain’s document loaders. Executing the statement above brings another nasty surprise — there’s only 1 document! Langchain’s text loader essentially just reads all the text there is — kind of like using Python’s `open()` function on a text file. We can’t give the entire document to the LLM though because it might exceed the LLM’s context window. So let’s break it up into chunks.

```python
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter
from langchain_chroma import Chroma
from langchain import hub

## Split documents into chunks
text_splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1024, chunk_overlap=20)
splits = text_splitter.split_documents(docs)

## Convert chunks into embeddings and ingest them into ChromaDB
vector_store = Chroma.from_documents(
    documents = splits,
    embedding = embeddings,
)
## Instantiating the vector store as a retriever object
retriever = vector_store.as_retriever()

# Pull prompt (or you can define your own system prompt)
prompt = hub.pull("rlm/rag-prompt")

def format_docs(docs):
    return "\n\n".join(doc.page_content for doc in docs)
```

A typical RAG workflow involves loading a file, chunking the file, generating embeddings from each chunk, and ingesting the chunk into a vector database which we will use for retrieval depending on the question asked by the user. Langchain also has some commonly used system prompts that we can pull from Langchain’s hub. We’ll pull the one for RAG here and define a utility function to string-join retrieved documents so that we can feed this into an LLM. Defining our RAG chain:

```python
rag_chain = (
    {"context": retriever | format_docs, "question": RunnablePassthrough()}
    | prompt
    | llm
    | StrOutputParser()
)
response = rag_chain.invoke("Did Paul Graham write code?")
display(Markdown(response))
```

```python-repl
Yes, Paul Graham wrote code. He mentioned working extensively on a project called Bel and developing a new dialect of Lisp called Arc. He also wrote all of Y Combinator's internal software in Arc.
```

Notice that the rag\_chain comprised a smaller chain `retriever | format_docs` , and the start of a chain comprised of a dictionary object that is then piped into the prompt. Writing LCEL statements like this takes practice (basically by banging into walls from too many errors). I’m sorry but there is no other way (aside from copying what is written by others) to write such LCEL statements without practice. For more advanced RAG applications that require reranking, parallel retrieval, etc., you will build longer chains. But this is all that’s needed for our basic RAG application.

### 5\. Finally, here’s how you build an agent

This is the only part of Langchain that can be done easily in one line! Langchain provides high-level abstractions for agents. There are many different agent types to choose from. Let’s just call the simplest agent!

```python
from langchain.agents import create_tool_calling_agent, AgentExecutor

prompt = hub.pull("hwchase17/openai-functions-agent")
agent = create_tool_calling_agent(llm, tools, prompt)
agent_executor = AgentExecutor(agent=agent, tools=tools, verbose=True)
response = agent_executor.invoke(
    {"input": "What is the mystery function's output on 57 and 26?"}
)
```

```python-repl

> Entering new AgentExecutor chain...

Invoking: `mystery` with `{'a': 57, 'b': 26}`

1565The mystery function's output on 57 and 26 is 1565.

> Finished chain.
```

Where’s the `|` operator? It’s not needed! What is strange is that you have to wrap the agent’s tools again into an agent\_executor.

Also, be mindful that the output of the agent executor is a dictionary!

```python-repl
{'input': "What is the mystery function's output on 57 and 26?",
 'output': "The mystery function's output on 57 and 26 is 1565."}
```

### Summing Up

Wow, we’ve covered so much! LangChain is an amazing library and its affection by the community is not surprising — you can build so many things with it. Langchain is however a low-level abstraction-centric Python library so the learning curve can be very steep. When I first started, I was often scratching my head at runnable errors — and sometimes it’s because I didn’t know that I had to define a component to handle something.

LangChain does however have many cookbook recipes and a very active community. So it shouldn’t be too difficult to get help.

I confess however that I only got much better in LangChain **after** I learnt LlamaIndex — another orchestration library. And that’s because all orchestration libraries try to do similar things and LlamaIndex has a much gentler learning curve due to its abundance of high, medium and low-level abstractions to cater to different use cases. More on this later.

We also didn’t cover multimodal applications. But the article is already of considerable length so we’ll leave this to the future.

I hope you found this article useful. LangChain’s capabilities are extended by other LangChain products such as [LangServe](https://python.langchain.com/docs/langserve/) (serving runnables as RESTful APIs), [LangSmith](https://www.langchain.com/langsmith) (LLM tracing) and LangGraph (which we will cover in a future article). I’ve used LangChain for some projects and even used LangServe to quickly spin up a playground for quick experimentation of runnables.
